This morning I thought I'd talk a bit about the science behind our materials. And how we study them.

The core of this is the interplay of chemistry and structure on various properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
For eg, our metal alloy films (40-ish nm layer) we use X-ray Diffraction (XRD) and X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) to look at the atom arrangement and orbital interaction.

This dictates a lot of the mechanical, optical and electrical properties.

https://t.co/fmXaRSM2p7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Similarly we use these to look at how structure and chemistry define properties of conducting polymers.

https://t.co/J4k995dZf4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Understanding how molecules and atoms arrange and interact on the nm scale is key to designing materials. 

From that different properties can be achieved.

We then use that to make new devices with industry. 

Linking them together is an exciting space.

https://t.co/HRMRptNqe4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In another study we used techniques to get details on the electrical properties of our materials.

Such as studying the density of states and charges in a polymer.

From this we uncovered semimetallic polymers.

https://t.co/vUW3bBNNmg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
More recently this has led us into looking at how different anions influence the properties of the polymers.

Not totally sure yet what's happening, but appears to be specific ion effects.

https://t.co/zb5HYBuYFL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This opens the door to exploring sensing. As we have done with nitrate using a polymer called PEDOT.

https://t.co/VlLtKF4eaH

tweets.text:
One big aspect of making our materials is understanding how they form.

A technique we use is Vapour Phase Polymerisation (VPP).

http://dx.doi.org10.1016/j.pmatsci.2017.01.004

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There's more to it than simply polymerising a monomer.

On the molecular scale we have controlled reactions at the liquid-vapour interface. The interface is structured using non-ionic copolymers.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This is a trick borrowed from colloid chemistry. In one form used to make mesoporous metal oxides.

We use the structure to direct how the conducting polymer grows directly on the substrate. 

By changing the structure we can drastically change the polymer properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The nice thing about this process is we can (somewhat) control;

- how the polymer forms on the nanoscale

- over large areas (up to m2)

This works for oxidative polymerisation of any volatile monomer.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Understanding processes like this helps us bridge the fundamental science with commercial manufacture.

We do a similar level of work on magnetron sputtering and chemical vapour deposition.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
For example, understand how processing of dielectric films can enhance their properties for certain applications. 

https://t.co/EF2vObMRZa

We name our coating equipment after objects in our solar system.

We do sputtering in Saturn, Mars and Jupiter. Yes, Jupiter is the big machine.

We do conducting polymer coatings in Callisto, Io and Europa.

Our thermal evaporator is called Mercury. https://t.co/TtuzSn0OtF

It's Friday. I figured I'd raise a challenge facing many researchers - work with industry or do fundamental research?

More specifically, can you do one only? Or both?

What does it mean for your career, and meeting the 'metrics' for promotion?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Many industry engaged projects have a long lead time to publish, if at all. 

Considering intellectual property, confidentiality, trade secrets, and so on.

This poses a challenge when an academic researcher needs publications.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This is particularly relevant for Early Career Researchers. They are less likely to have other avenues to publish.

But also less likely to have employment length to see an industry project through.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So what to do?

One thing to note is research is done in teams. Get a good group of people around you. Together you'll figure out how to do it.

Also, make an end-user is part of that group. Someone who can help you shape your research to be relevant to industry.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This still doesn't answer whether you can do both.

I found that early in my career it is very hard to do. But not impossible. 

It takes a lot of time to plan strategically how it all goes together. 

What is core fundamental and what is applied research?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Then comes the next step - who pays?

Neither funding agencies or business have endless money to fund research. 

So make an assessment of which to focus on first. You can't do everything from day one.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
A key thing I have learnt is that the path from idea to products is not linear.

Some of my best (IMO) fundamental research came from questions in an industry project.

So maybe think backwards about products and ideas. Working with industry may spawn your basic research.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Time...... 

How do you balance it?

How do you allocate it?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
As I try to get out with my kids to do the grocery shopping; I've spent several hours of Saturday morning working.

After a week predominantly spent doing admin, and helping others at work....I find the time to do 'my stuff' gets pushed out of hours when I want to be not working.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Many academic roles have scope creep.

The slow expansion of your tasks, including increased contribution to the greater sector. Boards, committees, panels, etc.

All worthy things. But does it impact your day job? Time for teaching or research?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Or even more importantly, is it forcing you into decisions about out of work hours choices?

Everyone is different. Everyone balances things differently.

How to manage the expectation to 'do it all'?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I've been lucky these past years that out of hours work is infrequent. Others are not so lucky.

This is a challenge I see for the sector.

A research career should not have to contain sacrifices (unless you want to).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Is this something people in your local area discuss?

Keen to hear how others manage this in their situation.

My plan for today: introducing myself and the Tandem lab where I’m working.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hi again 👋 let me start by telling you a bit about myself and how I got here. As I said I'm now tweeting from Sweden but I'm originally from northern Germany. For my physics studies I first moved south (@UniOldenburg then @UniHeidelberg) before heading north for my PhD.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Since around 3.5 years I've been living in Sweden and doing a PhD in the Ion physics research group @uppsalauni (yes, I'm in my last year, no questions about my defence date please 😬).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I’m working very on brand in a building called Ångström laboratory. Our local café has the conversion to more common length scales handy: 1 Ångström = 0.0000001 mm or for this account 10 Å = 1 nanometer! https://t.co/GV5l5EO1Sq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This unit is btw named after Anders Jonas Ångström who both studied and worked @uppsalauni. There’s a small exhibition about him in the building (in Swedish though). https://t.co/UsnvwOAeAj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @uppsalauni But back to me and my reserach. So, how come that I'm curating an account for materials science (except the building name)? To be honest past me probably would have been surprised. As a student I found it really hard to choose a specialisation and...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ...I've done student research projects in theoretical physics, medical physics and high-energy physics. I realised after a while though that I really enjoyed working hands-on in a lab and I've definitely became fascinated by accelerators + the diverse research you can do w/ them.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm now doing a PhD in a field where we use ion beams from accelerators for materials analysis (and also modification). But to be able to do this, we first need to understand the interactions between ions and matter.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My PhD project focusses on the interactions of very slow ions with materials (actually mostly the electrons in the material) but we get to that later this week.

tweets.label: Takeover

https://t.co/TwKlyXeVps

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Btw, there is a big conference on ion beam analysis going on this week. I'm not there personally but several of my colleagues are. I couldn't convince any of them yet to be active on twitter but other people are and apparently using the #IBA2019 hashtag! https://t.co/baa6dO45DT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Introducing the Tandem lab!
This is where I do my experiments. The Tandem lab is named after our biggest machine - our tandem accelerator. The photo shows me in front of it! https://t.co/eGfpqwPZzv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here’s a short video following the beam line from the accelerator to the end stations. You can see in the end how the initial beam line splits up into 6 different ones. We have a range of different set-ups for different analysis methods and the Tandem provides ions for them all. https://t.co/4G50n3VJuV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, why do we need so many different set-ups? First, I should explain that the Tandem lab’s a Swedish National research infrastructure. That means that not only people from my group do experiments here but that researchers from all over Sweden (and abroad) can apply for beam time

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That means that research questions and samples vary quite a bit - from coating materials to steel used in fusion research to DNA samples to backing materials for solar cells.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Additionally, all analysis methods have their strengths and weaknesses so often a combination of several is needed for complete characterisation of a sample.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
When I say characterisation what do I actually mean? 
Here are some examples of what you can do with ion beams based methods:
- find out which chemical elements are contained in a sample
- and in which concentration

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
- atomic structure (is the sample crystalline?)
For thin films (that means nanometre up to about 1 micrometre for us):
- thickness, position or concentration gradient of layers

tweets.text: I will explain the principle of some basic methods tomorrow! Feel free to ask questions any time though! https://t.co/fRiEME1p1W

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.text: I had my own challenges with teaching this course. Since it’s on bachelor level, teaching language is Swedish! I started teaching when I’d only been learning Swedish for 1.5 years. It  was definitely hard but it also made me learn so much more Swedish so much faster!

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Yesterday I gave you a short glimpse of our lab. https://t.co/Lp2SlH7z43

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I also briefly talked about which kind of research questions can be addressed with ion beam: https://t.co/elDgAp8omZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now I want to tell you bit more about some basic methods and how they work in principle. We start with maybe the most basic ion beam analysis method - Rutherford Backscattering Spectrometry!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Quick note on the side: Researchers love acronyms! So, we would just say RBS instead of Rutherford Backscattering Spectrometry for obvious reasons. However, please stop me if I should start throwing around acronyms and you don't get their meaning!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The principle of backscattering spectrometry can be understood as some kind of atomic billiards. We have a material that consists like all matter of atoms and we shoot an ion onto it. https://t.co/E6KD4KmZT7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If the ion and an atomic nucleus of the target material come close enough to each other, the positive charges repell each other and the ion gets scattered. https://t.co/k2INw5LX6Q

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Like in billiards, the direction in which the ion gets scattered depends on the incident angle. In backscattering spectrometry we look as the name says only at particles scattered in a backwards direction.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Unlike in the game in our experiments the masses of our two atoms don't have to be the same. The masses of the atoms, the energy of our incoming ion (determined by the accelerator) and the geometry of the experiment all determine the energy of the ion after the collision. https://t.co/pDYC92mXRt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And this energy is what we measure! Since we know the beam we send in (energy and mass) and the geometry of our set-up, we can then calculate the mass of the atomic nucleus from which the ion scattered. And thereby we identify chemical elements in a sample!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @vynisle Thanks ☺️

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This afternoon I had a meeting with the doctoral board of @uppsalauni. I’m one of the vice-chairs of the board for this year and I’d like to talk a bit about being active in student representation and why I think it’s important.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To start this conversation one has to have a look at the Swedish law on higher education. This laws guarantees students a vote in all decision making organs of a Swedish university. This means students have representatives on all level from department to the university board.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: PhD students are full students from a legal point of view in Sweden (we’re also employees so we get the best from both worlds like a salary and student discounts 🙃) so we also have representatives and get a say in university matters.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I think this is super important. A university is so much more than just tenured professors and management! And all the voices need to be heard to create a learning + researching environment where everyone can thrive.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @uppsalauni PhD students are organised in PhD boards both at faculty and at university wide level to speak as the voice for the respective group of PhD students. These boards also  appoint the representatives to university boards I was talking about earlier.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: They also organise and support different kind of events from seminars to afterwork to help PhD students to connect to others.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A PhD can look very differently depending on the field. The doctoral board is there to have a voice for all PhD students at the university no matter their specific situation. We therefore consist of representatives from all faculties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To wrap this up: The situation of PhD students in Sweden is probably a lot better than in other countries (in terms of rights and employment benefits). However, I think it's important not to take these rights too much for granted.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: An example: Allowing scholarships instead of employment is a current (and reoccurring) discussion topic, which would not really be in our interest.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Additionally, it's not always straightforward to know and claim your rights especially when you're maybe in a stressful situation. The PhD boards (and ombudsman) are also there to give support and information.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Getting engaged in student representation has also been a lot of fun for me. I've been working together with a diverse group of nice people plus I learned tons about how a big organisation such as a university is working. I really recommend it!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Good morning! If you folllowed along yesterday you might have noticed that I did a lot of things other than research. Yes, doing a PhD often entails more things than just standing in the lab! I honestly find it hard sometimes to balance out all my activities. Any tipps?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I should add though that I'm actually only teaching one course running for around 2.5 months every year so the rest of the time it's one thing less and more time for research

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today I'm going to focus more on physics though! https://t.co/xUcDzje7aL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Yesterday I explained how we can use scattering to identify the elements contained in a sample: https://t.co/amOr0XGFQs

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You might have noticed that in my explanation I only talked about one part of the sample atoms - the atomic nuclei. The thing is that these are actually very small even compared to the size of the whole atom. So atoms are mostly "empty"!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That also means that it's actually quite rare that an ion is backscattered from the first layer (or any layer) like shown in my illustration. More likely it travels further into the material.  In this case we will need to look at the other parts of the sample atoms - electrons!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The ion also collides with the electrons. But cause electrons are much lighter than the ion (even hydrogen is 1836 times heavier), it doesn't change direction much and only loses a tiny bit of energy in every collision. https://t.co/QU4uXAg9Lg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But since they're many electrons and many collisions, this process noticably slows down the ion. Eventually the ion will stop inside the material if it is thick enough (how thick is thick enough depends on the ion energy and mass and the sample material)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Alternatively, the ion meets an atomic nucleus before it has lost too much energy and is scattered in the same way as from the surface. It can then travel back through the sample and we can detect it! https://t.co/88tsXcVAII

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: With enough understanding of the ion-electron interaction we can translate the energy lost to the electrons to information about depth. For example: we can determine the thickness of a layer or calculate the depth in which the ion will stop.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We call the average energy loss by the ion per distance travelled the stopping power. Since it's such an important quantity, all measurements of it are collected in a big data base: https://t.co/YIIntSxqOL

tweets.text: So I talked quite a bit of theoretical background and measurement principles yesterday and this morning. But I guess you’re all excited to see more of my lab, right? https://t.co/VVv5rk8M9H

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Scattering experiments can be done in quite different energy regimes and we have several set-ups based on this principle. But let’s start with high energies and continue where this video stopped. https://t.co/fDTn4YD8S9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After the switching magnet (in blue in the final shot of the last video) we now follow one of the beam lines to our RBS chamber https://t.co/gA3JvSy5Sx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let’s talk a bit about what we see in these videos. First, all the beam lines (the metal pipes) and chambers you see are in vacuum. That means all experiments we do are happening in vacuum!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Remember when I said that ions are scattered and slowed downs by nuclei and electrons in matter? Well, that’s not only true for solids but also for gases means also air!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Since we want the ions to reach our sample as a focussed beam with the full energy we’d chosen,  we work in vacuum! This way we also make sure we really measure the interaction with the sample material and not with air.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The experimental chamber was already under vacuum when I filmed the video but I have some photos from a while ago to show you how it looks inside. https://t.co/DkF3hhWeaX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I first talked a bit about how ions interact with electrons. https://t.co/WIf32PcgPO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In this context I introduced the stopping power. The thing is that the strength of this quantity (you can think of it as a force that slows down the ion) depends strongly on ion energy. Here is an example: https://t.co/99ON1O72fM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For various reasons (physics,technical, historical...) we understand much more about the high energy region of this graph. This is why my PhD project focusses on slow ions and how they interact with electrons.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Side note: this is also why I measured my samples at the high-energy set-up the other day. I characterise my samples (mainly their thickness and composition) first with a well-established method before I use them to learn about interactions at low energies.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These are super good questions because they very much lead to why interactions of slow ions are more complicated. I try to answer as good as I can. Please continue asking if something stays unclear. https://t.co/JXwTHgbuiM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 1. The easiest case to consider is this: The ion is much faster than the electron in the atom and they get relatively close to each other. Then the Coulomb force between them is acting and momentum is transferred to the electron.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If it would be a free electron, the interaction would be like in the scattering case more or less billiard like. However, the electrons usually are bound and they have discrete binding energies in the atom.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, if the energy transferred is not enough for the electron to leave the atom, it might still be transferred to a different energy shell --> the atom gets excited.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So far so easy. But there is more that can happen: If the ion is slow and/or heavy (i.e. has a high nuclear charge) it has a rather high chance to capture an electron. That means the electron becomes part of the travelling ion/atom (it might become neutral).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I try to explain this process in this tweet here: https://t.co/EnZRzkEnX9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Note that the reverse process is also possible, i.e. that the ion transfers an electron to the solid and becomes (higher) charged. This process depends strongly on how close the ion gets to the target atoms though cause the two electron levels needs to be resonant with each other

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Then there is a process called "molecular orbital formation". Which means that the ion is so slow that for a time it seems like it's forming a molecule with a target atom. That has again an influence on the electron energy levels and thereby on the energy loss.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Considering this question: "Could we even discriminate between these possibilities, even theoretically?"
Theoretically we can look at single events. Experimentally, we always look at the average of many collisions. There are some tricks though...

Hi, I'm Steve, you can call me Steve.
<squints at picture>
Wait, that isn't me yet.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Anyway, a little something about me.

I'm a chemist and science communicator from Canada.  I did a Masters in photonanochemistry at the University of Ottawa   (@uOttawaScience).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Small confession: I finished in 2006 and haven't done a whole lot of nanostuff since then.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In addition to my https://t.co/4ASfUWWicg. research, I'll also be talking about how to survive grad school, what happens when things don't go entirely as planned, and how to communicate your nanoscience.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is just a brief introduction.  I'll be back a little later when the west coast of North America starts waking up (sorry, Rest Of The World and other inconvenient timezones.)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Before I start in on the research, I should tell you how I became a scientist.

I knew I wanted to go into science at age 12 because of Star Trek.  I watched TNG as an impressionable lad, and I was captivated by all the sciencey solutions to the problems of the week.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I say "sciencey" because once I started studying science for real, I discovered that all the Treknobabble was quite literally babble.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The character I identified with most was Wesley.  I've met Wil Wheaton at a couple of cons and told him that, and he was absolutely thrilled.

(I didn't tell him that the reason I identified with Wes was that I was the obnoxious kid that nobody liked.)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Poor guy's had to deal with a lot of undeserved grief over the years because of how terribly his character was written.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I didn't zero in on chemistry until grade 11.  I had a great teacher, and something about balancing reactions and finding out what things are made of at the atomic level appealed to me.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I knew before I finished high school that I was going to take chemistry at university.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I did a Bachelor's degree in Kelowna, British Columbia, Canada at Okanagan University College, now called UBC Okanagan.  I got interested in zeolites, which are essentially rocks with tiny channels in them where interesting chemistry happens.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I went to grad school at the University of Ottawa, because there was a prof there working with zeolites.  I got accepted into his lab, and turned up on my first day to be given a project involving...not zeolites.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Instead, it was a project investigating oxidative stress in...something or other.  I can't remember, because I was only on the project two days before discovered a paper describing exactly that project.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I couldn't do something that was already published, so my boss switched me to a different oxidative stress project...with the same result.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The third time turned out to be the charm.  My boss found a paper describing making silver nanoparticles using light.  He was a photochemist, and had done work on a photochemical system that would be much better at making nanoparticles.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm going to leave it there for today, because it's a little weird tweeting under someone else's name and picture.  Tomorrow I'll describe my nanoresearch, and the trials and tribulations along the way.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #NewProfilePic

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: RT @sciencenotscary: I tried to throw a neutrino pumpkin through the detector, but it just smashed on the outside of the support structure…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: OK, nano-time.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I started my Masters in December of 2003.  Was that really 16 years ago?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I took an overnight flight to Ottawa from the other side of the country, and got no sleep.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
When I got to campus, I went looking for the lab and was confronted by a sign that said "authorised personnel only."

I stopped for a second, then thought "wait a minute, I'm authorised personnel."

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As I mentioned yesterday, the first two projects I was assigned quickly proved to be already published.  I can't remember exactly what they were, but they weren't nano, so they aren't important.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The third project was the charm.  My supervisor was Tito Scaiano, who at that point had not had any interest in nano-anything.  He was a photochemist, and had spent a lot of his career finding rate constants for various photochemical reactions.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
He read a paper describing the production of silver nanoparticles in thin polymer films using light.

The process took two hours, and resulted in an unpleasant brown colour.

Tito figured he could do better.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Incidentally, explaining why the state of the art is terrible and you're so amazing is pretty standard in writing grant proposals.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Anyway, this paper described how their polymer film had molecules dissolved in it that would produce ketyl radicals in it that would convert silver salts into silver nanoparticles when hit by light.

Cool.  What does all that mean?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let's start with radicals.  Most organic molecules are held together by bonds between adjoining atoms.  Each atom contributes an electron, and those two electrons are shared between the two atoms and form the bond.  This is covalent, a term that might be familiar from highschool.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Generally, all of the electrons in the molecule will be paired up, either in a bond or just hanging out on one atom.

Radicals are what happens when one of those pairs is sundered.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
A radical is an unhappy molecule, generally, and it spreads that unhappiness around with a shovel.

It wants its electrons to be paired, so it starts stealing electrons from other molecules.

Which then makes more radicals.  The circle of life.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The particular type of radical in this study is derived from ketones, hence the name ketyl (ket + -yl suffix).

Great, what's a ketone?

Hang on, let me find a picture.

(Public domain image from Wikipedia user Benjah-bmm27) https://t.co/rGCDXzshIK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The big R groups simply represent chunks of molecule we aren't bothering to specify.  The important part is the C=O, which represents a double bond between carbon and oxygen.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's a carbonyl.  This time the suffix is -onyl, and represents a double bond to oxygen.  It's also pronounced differently.  Here the y sounds like a long e (neel), and in ketyl it sounds like a short i (till).  There's no rhyme or reason to this.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Anyway, when you have a double covalent bond, the electrons in the second bond are a lot more playful than those in the first.  In addition, the oxygen has two more pairs of non-bonded electrons, so there are lots of options to steal one to make a radical.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Alternately, the plain ketone can steal an electron from another molecule and make itself a radical.  This is where photochemistry comes in.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Electrons live in orbitals, which are mathematical descriptions of where electrons can be found 95% of the time.  There's a lot of uncertainty about where an electron is at any given time, hence the elaborate math and stats involved.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Each orbital can hold two electrons...which is also the number in a covalent bond.  This isn't coincidental.

For the purposes of this discussion, the covalent bonds between atoms can be considered molecular orbitals.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Everybody keeping up?  Do I need to go back and explain something in more detail?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: OK, all of these orbitals exist at different energy levels, usually expressed relative to some arbitrary zero points.  It's nearly impossible to measure absolute energies, so we just pick some point we can measure and call it zero.  Everything else is relative to that.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All of these orbitals contain 2 electrons...but there are a bunch of empty ones as well.  Whether or not they actually exist if they're empty is a question for the philosophers, but they're real enough that an electron can jump into one.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's jump between orbitals is a quantum leap, if you're wondering where that term came from.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
A quantum leap can only happen if an electron suddenly receives exactly enough energy to make that jump.  Too much or too little, and it's not happening.

In organic molecules with C=O double bonds, that energy can be delivered by UV light.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's the basis of photochemistry right there: light carries energy, and molecules can absorb that energy if it matches the difference between one of its full and one of its empty orbitals.  After that, chemistry happens.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So where does the nano come in?  Patience, I'm getting there.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (This story is quickly becoming How I Met Your Nanoparticle.)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If that ketone absorbs a photon of light, one of the playful electrons in the C=O double bond gets booted up to a higher orbital.  Once it's there, it can grab a hydrogen atom from a C-H bond of another molecule, and drag along one of the electrons from that bond.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now that C=O is a C-OH, and that other poor molecule is now a radical, with the remaining electron from that C-H bond sitting sadly on the C.

But what about the other electron left behind when the photon kicked the other one upstairs to start this process?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It's still there, also unpaired, sitted forlornly on the C of the C-OH.  That's the ketyl: a radical derived from a ketone.

Took a while, but we got there eventually.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
After all that, why did we care about these ketyl radicals?

It turns out that unhappy radicals can also make themselves happy by giving away that unpaired electron, if it results in something stable.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
If our ketyl gives away its unpaired electron, now there's a big empty hole on that carbon atom.  That hole can be filled by remaking that C=O bond.  Currently it looks like this:
+C-OH, where the + is the positive charge caused by the loss of the radical electron.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There are two electrons in the O-H bond.  If the H takes off and leaves behind its share of the bonding electrons, those two can then pivot around and slam down into the hole on the carbon.
C=O    H+

There's a + on the H because now it's got a positive charge.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Clear as mud?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Half the reason the ketyl can give away its electron is because this stable, happy non-radical molecule is the product.  Reactions generally want to end up stable and happy.

However, the other half depends on finding something stable and happy to give the electron to.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Enter silver.  Silver is a metal, and metal chemistry is quite unlike non-metal chemistry.  For starters, metals tend not to* form covalent bonds.

* - OK, some do under very particular circumstances, but not in the system we're considering.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Metals generally form ions by losing electrons.  If you've seen corroded steel or copper, that's what's happened.  The metal atoms in the solid metal chunk lost their electrons and were dissolved into any nearby moisture as freefloating ions.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Because the universe is electrically neutral, those positive ions need negative partners, which are usually formed during the corrosion process.  Compounds made of these positive-negative ion pairs are called salts.

tweets.text:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you take a covalent organic molecule and slice a bond such that each fragment gets one of the electrons in that bond, you end up with radicals: molecules with an unpaired electron.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Things with unpaired electrons tend not to be happy, and they spread that unhappiness around with a shovel.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Normally this unhappiness is manifested by the radical shredding another molecule in search of electrons to pair with.  This just results in the formation of another radical from the wreckage.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Sometimes two radicals will find each other and peacefully combine their unpaired electrons to form a new bond.  This stops the make-a-new-radical chain reaction and is called the termination step.  These two things are common in reactions that grow long-chain polymers.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Finally, and most relevant to the discussion at hand, a radical can sometimes give away its unpaired electron to something else, if both resulting molecules end up happy and stable.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A radical can give away its electron if it can rearrange itself afterwards to fill the hole left behind.  This usually requires the formation of double bonds, and requires a source of mobile electrons within the structure of the molecule.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A simple chemical way is to throw something at it that will do that reaction spontaneously.  You have to do it in a controlled manner, otherwise you'll end up with a mirror on the inside of your beaker.

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Silver in salt form has a charge of +1, and in the metallic form it's 0.  These also correspond to the oxidation state.  When it gains the electron, the state is reduced from 1 to 0, hence reduction.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: "Oxidation" is a holdover term from the early days of chemistry, when the compounds they were studying got more oxygen atoms glommed onto them.  The term it more broadly applied now to any reaction where the oxidation state increases.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Anyway, making nanoparticles from salts is a reductive process, and requires a reducing agent, some other chemical that serves as a source of electrons.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Making silver mirrors is as simple as throwing them together.  Making nanoparticles requires some way of persuading them to grow to nano-size and then stop.  We usually add yet more chemicals called capping agents, because they cap the growth.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Something like sodium citrate acts as both reducing and capping agent, and is readily available and fairly inexpensive, so it's a popular choice.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The citrate molecule physically binds to the surface of the growning nanoparticle, stopping its growth and preventing it from agglomerating with any other nanoparticles.  You get a nice golden-yellow solution rather than brown crud.

tweets.text: So far this week, I've described using light to create a radical that can donate an electron to a silver salt and reduce it to silver metal.  These metallic silver atoms can then grow into nanoparticles, provided something stops them glomming together or turning into a mirror.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The process of growing nanoparticles is more complicated that simple throwing stuff together.  There are two main phases, and the being able to influence them allows greater control over the final product.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The first phase is nucleation.  This is where silver atoms are formed from the salt and first come together in clusters.  These are the nuclei that the particles grow around.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The same principle happens to snowflakes: water crystallises around something (usually dust particle or some other tiny piece of schmutz) and grows in a regular hexagonal pattern.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Controlling the speed and duration of nucleation allows you control over what the final product looks like.  A fast burst of nucleation means you have fewer nucleation sites, which means you end up with fewer nanoparticles, but they tend to be larger.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
A longer nucleation phase has the opposite effect: you have oodles of sites competing for a limited amount of growth material (in this case, silver), so they don't get as big.

Controlling this during chemical synthesis is very difficult.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It's much easier to control if you can just turn a lamp on and off.  Because reduction of silver only happens while the light is shining, you can start and stop nucleation with a flick of a switch.  I usually gave it 15-30 seconds.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Photochemistry is just better than regular chemistry*.

* - in this particular set of circumstances, under these conditions, offer not valid during months with an R in the name

tweets.text:
After nucleation comes growth.  This can start happening before the end of nucleation  In systems where all the growth material already exists, it can keep happening after the end of nucleation.
For example, snowflakes will keep growing as long as there's moisture.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There's a minimum size that nanoparticles need to achieve in order to be stable and happy.  If they're smaller than this, they simply fall apart, and the material is incorporated into larger particles in a process called Ostwald ripening.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Put another way, the big ones eat the small ones.  In the nanorealm, it's survival of the fattest.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is how you can get growth in silver nanoparticles even after the light has shut off.  As long as there's a capping agent present, they'll stop growing before they pass out of the nanoscale and stay suspended in solution.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You can see by the regular rows of atoms that the particles are crystalline.  That's the definition of crystal: having a regular repeating pattern to its atoms.  "Crystal" isn't a substance, it's a property of substances.

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.text: So where do the magnets come it?  When I made my nanoparticles, it only took 30 seconds.  If I did it with the vial sitting next to a magnet, it took 15.  Taking 15 seconds off the synthesis time may not seem like much, but it made it go twice as fast.  That's not trivial.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Why did the magnet make it go faster?

We need to go back to radicals and their unpaired electrons.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
An electron has a property called spin.  This spin can point up or down.

I didn't fully understand what that meant during my Masters, and I'm not sure I understand it now.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I once heard a particle physicist describe spin as "a property particles have."  I'm not sure they fully understand it either, or what it represents.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It's usually shown graphically as an arrow stuck through a ball.  The ball is the electron, and the arrow is the axis that the electron spins around.  If the electron was a globe, the arrow would be sticking out of the North Pole.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This explanation is just simple enough to be a useful metaphor while simultaneously being completely wrong.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
When two electrons form a bond or occupy the same orbital, the spins need to point in opposite directions.

Why?
Because.  That's why.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This paired-up state is called a singlet.  The name comes from the way electronic systems like this were studied.  When something with no unpaired spins emits a photon, the resulting spectrum has a single line.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
When something with a single unpaired electron emits a photon, the spectrum has a doubled line, or doublet.

If we can get two unpaired spins, we get a triplet.

The pattern is # of unpaired spins + 1.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Why?

<embarrassed pause>

Like I said, I didn't fully grok it then, and I've never had cause to come back and learn it properly.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Anyway, the important thing here is the triplet.  I described how ketyl radicals form when an excited ketone rips a hydrogen and electron off another molecule, resulting in two radicals.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Those two radicals form a radical pair, especially if they're caged in micelles and can't get away from each other.  The cage is important.

The two spins can either point in opposite directions and form a singlet, or the same direction and form a triplet.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If they're a singlet, they can easily recombine and go back to the starting materials.  Remember, two electrons can only occupy the same orbital if the spins point in opposite directions.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If they're a triplet, the spins point the same way, and they can't do this.  This means the ketyl lives long enough to wander around, find its way out of the cage and meet up with a silver atom outside.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The more triplets there are, the more often this happens.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Thing is, the spin direction is not set in stone.  The triplet can flip back to the singlet, which then results in recombination.  However, it can only do this is the triplet and singlet states are reasonably close in energy.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This is where the magnet comes in.

It turns out there are three different triplet substates, based on how the spins line up.

If you can't picture that based on the arrow-in-a-ball picture, this is why I said it was completely wrong.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I can't actually describe how this works, so you'll just have to go with me on this one.

I am deeply sorry.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Anyway, when you put this triplet radical pair in a magnetic field, one of the substates is raised in energy, one is lowered, and one stays the same.  The corresponding singlet is unaffected.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What this does is move two thirds of the triplet substates far enough away from the singlet that they can't flip over and recombine.  You've basically made two thirds of the triplet molecules immortal.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This means they have all the time in the world to float out of the cage and go play with the silver outside.

More triplets getting out means the reduction reaction happens faster, which is why it only takes half as long to get nice nanoparticles.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But if 2/3 of the triplets are immortal, why is it twice as fast?  Shouldn't those numbers match up better?

Don't try to read too much into it.  My irradiation times were fairly arbitrary, and I didn't try to accurately measure reaction rates.

tweets.text: If anyone wants to revisit this, go right ahead.  Just remember to cite me.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This magnetic effect on the triplet state requires the two radicals to be caged together, hence the blob of soap molecules.

tweets.text: Let me describe my #SciComm credentials.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I am the 2013 winner of the Flame Challenge, awarded by the @AldaCenter for Communicating Science.  The center was founded by and named after Alan Alda from M*A*S*H and The West Wing.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The premise of the first Flame Challenge was for actual scientists to explain to actual 11-year-olds what a flame is, because of Alan's dissatisfaction with the answer he got when he asked the question of his teacher when he was 11.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The entries were judged by Grade 5 and 6 classrooms.  That was in 2012.  After the first year, the kids themselves started picking the questions for the following contests.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:

Of course, the previous year was a chemistry question and a physicist won.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Anyway, I pressed on regardless and made a little video.  It had terrible production values, and it won.

This be it:
https://t.co/ACzl5kT6Ni

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It's just me in front of a horrible orange wall for four minutes.  The other two finalists had fancy animations and cartoon dinosaurs, but mine was the only one where the audience could see the person talking to them.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Lesson 1: don't get caught up in bells and whistles if you don't have a clear message.  You can do a lot more with simple clarity and charisma than you can with 10 hours in an editing suite.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I spoke in a conversational style, rather that using a stiff, formal lecturing mode of speech.  I also aimed it at an 11-year-old audience.  It's very easy to get that last bit wrong.  Do not aim too low, because that will come off as condescending.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I remember being 11 (dimly), and I always hated it when grownups talked down to me.  These kids are on the cusp of their teenage years.  You don't need to talk to them like they're toddlers.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I tend to use humour in my videos, because it's impossible for me to not try to be funny.
That said, humour isn't mandatory.  Being funny isn't as easy as it looks.  If you aren't a natural joker, best leave it to the professionals and talented amateurs.

tweets.text:
So how do you explain your nanoscience to the uninitiated?

The standard comparison is expressing a nanometre in some unfathomable fraction of the width of a human hair.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Thing is, the human mind has a hard time comprehending how big a nanometre is, and saying it's one millionth of a millimetre isn't really all that helpful.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You could say it's bigger than an atom but smaller than a virus, assuming your audience has any sort of conception of the relative sizes of those two things.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When you're not talking to a technical audience, mathematical precision doesn't really matter.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What really matters, and this is true of any scicomm, is to lead with why your audience should care about your work.  Why is it important, why is it exciting, how does it matter to them?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Take them through the story of what you did.  Even when you're writing for an audience in your field, your article should have a narrative describing the process of your work.  The same idea applies outside your field as well.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you've giving an outreach talk, formal or otherwise, remember to wrap up by recapping the important points you want them to remember.

tweets.text: I never spell a word wrong, I just spell the wrong word right.

Hi everyone, I'm back. 
And today I plan to talk about thin film deposition. 
And if I say thin films, what do I mean? Well a thin film is a continuous layer of material that is, for my research, anywhere between a single atomic layer and a few micrometers in thickness.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
generally, for me I grow a film to be between 50 nanometers (5*10-6mm) and 2 micrometres (0.002mm), depending on the application. 
When you consider that a human hair is around to be around 0.05 millimetres thick, I think we can say it is fairly thin. (for me, 0.05mm is huge!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are a lot of ways to make a thin film. Most of the techniques I use fall under physical vapour deposition (PVD). These techniques create a vapour of material that coalesces on a substrate material (the material we are growing the film on).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Mostly, PVD techniques grow films under vacuum. I tend to use high vacuum, with a ballpark figure of around 6*10-3 mbar, or 0.6 Pascals (Pa) in SI units. The atmosphere is around 100 kPa and space can be taken as around 1*10−11 Pa.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My vacuum chambers (the box inside which I grow my films) will pump overnight to the range of between 1*10-6 and 1*10-8mbar, depending on the system and vacuum pumps. This is important as is removes air, water and other materials that may contaminate our process from the system.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We need to start at low vacuum as our vapour material can easily react with a residual gasses in the vacuum. For example, if we have an aluminium vapour, it reacts very readily with oxygen to form aluminium oxide. If we want aluminium, then this is not good!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another benefit of vacuum is that if we have a higher pressure, our vapour will collide with atoms, molecules, etc in our chamber and change direction. When we deposit, we generally want the vapour created to travel to our substrate directly. Collisions may cause it to 'miss'

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If playing snooker we want the ball we hit to travel in a specific direction. When it hits another ball, the direction is changed. If this is unintended, our ball misses where we meant to place it such as eg, in a pocket in the snooker table.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The same is true for our vapour which is, basically, atoms, ions and molecules acting as 'balls' and the substrate is the pocket. How we 'strike the ball' and control the angle depends on the technique, and I'll discuss more details in my next batch of tweets!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However I mentioned earlier that for example, aluminium would react with oxygen if it was in our chamber. It may be that we want aluminium oxide (AlOx) so we would introduce (pure) oxygen to the chamber and create an AlOx vapour.

Morning all. 
I had hoped to follow up my chat about magnetron sputtering but didn't have the images I wanted to share.

So I will continue this now, with a little more in-depth look at sputtering.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Sputtering has various properties that we can control. 
The pressure, partial pressure of the gas, power to the target, the magnetic fields behind the target, the distance between the substrate and target and more. I'm not sure there is any such thing as a 'controlled experiment'

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But we control and fix what we can in order to have usable data. 
With power, we can actually supply the voltage to the target in different ways. 
Most common in research is probably DC power, a fixed power to the target. In industry, it can be common to supply the ower as AC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
DC is great, it is fairly easy to fix and we can manipulate the makeup of the power, i.e. the voltage and current. 
However, if a material is not conducive, we run into problems. And sputtering from ceramics is not uncommon (such as using a lithium oxide composite target)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Thus, using an RF power supply is a good way to get around this. You can set an RF offset to the power, or have a net-zero power level. In this way we can sputter materials that otherwise would act as an insulator and prevent us from striking a plasma.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: During my PhD and post-doc positions, I made use of an emerging type of power generation, HiPIMS (high power impulse magnetron sputtering). In the technique, we pulse the DC power, having an on-time of 100-200 microseconds, and long off time, in frequencies of 50 - 100 Hz https://t.co/BlWNbKKEmf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This is compared to the frequencies of RF, which is commonly 13.56 kHz and an RMS voltage of zero, or 50 V). 
As a result, we get duty cycles of around 1%. Which may seem pretty low, but the trade off is that we can generate very high voltages and current during this time. https://t.co/34VnnzXgTS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Note, in the above image the on time is the sharp spike voltage. (The system had grounding issues initially, this the odd offset during the off-time. This was when I started working with HiPIMS, in 2007!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Having currents of the magnitude of 100 A is not uncommon with associated voltages of 1000 V. Below is a real IV curve that I used frequently during my PhD. 
Compared to common DC systems, where we use maybe 2 A and 400 V. https://t.co/69nQwG72oW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: During my post-docs, I had access to a power supply that could shape these pulses even further. I spent a lot of time 'chopping' the on-pulse of HiPIMS into smaller 'micro-pulses'. I called this c-HiPIMS, chopped HiPIMS, but we still had low duty cycles with long off-times. https://t.co/SjAUQ1K17C

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: With HiPIMS, we experience a phenomenon called gas rarefaction. The high on-pulses ionise all the gas close to the target, and cause lower partial pressure at the target. Because we use this working gas to cause collisions, we quickly 'run out' of gas and our current drops. https://t.co/YA1fTsHEBO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, I saw indications that if the time between micro-pulses was long enough, gas was able to refill this area. My indication of this was the peak current of each micro-pulse, where the peak current was much lower for later pulses when  the time between them was small https://t.co/XWRtRHsZZd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Of course, this is a balancing act. Once the micro-pulses become too spread out, we can lose the long-off time between the pulse-trains. Once this happens, we lose some benefits for our growing film with these long off-times.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And I'll talk a more about these benefits in my next 'pulse-train' of tweets, finally showing a little of why I spend so much time playing with these conditions 🙂

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So, why do we want to play around with the run conditions during sputtering? 
Well, the vapour, or flux as we tend to call it, of the target material travels to the substrate and grows our think film. However, not all arriving flux is equal!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Depending upon the energy it arrives, and the rate at which it arrives, means that the way the film grows can end up looking very different. 
In the picture below we have a film grown using DC magnetron sputtering. This is a titanium film, grown to 2 micrometres thickness https://t.co/jfUuKiBi3T

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Compared to a film grown using HiPIMS. We have the same pressure, average power and target material, but the additional energy as the flux arrives means that it grows more densely, with fewer spaces between grains.
These differences can change the properties of the film we grow. https://t.co/GH9ZBoM4wc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
eg in titania films we can change the crystal structure and phases, which in turn can affect the photocatalytic properties of the film. 
These properties can be used when we create solar cells or self-cleaning glass, so optimising these properties is key https://t.co/LBefvO9Egy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the paper above, we also highlight the effective heat load at the substrate. Whilst HiPIMS has very high powers, the long off-time means that there is lower average heating of the substrate than with DC, allowing us to deposit on thermally sensitive substrates such as plastics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, one downside of using HiPIMS compared to DC is that the growth rate, or deposition rate measured as growth in Angstrom/second, A/s, can be significantly lower which can be an issue if you are trying to produce these coatings on an industrial scale https://t.co/17lDqejC87

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When using our modified c-HiPIMS, we showed an increase in the deposition rate for the right conditions (different c-HiPIMS conditions are shown in the green line). https://t.co/GEMHGO8gB3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Yet we still had the dense films for these experiments https://t.co/5Mpi6R3A4c. 
As gas is used to cause cascades, releasing the flux from our target, it makes sense that if we lose gas through rarefaction, as discussed previously, our growth rate drops. c-HiPIMS mitigates this. https://t.co/LnxEvssNWs

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As for why we have higher energy, well this can be partially explained by the ratio of ions to atoms of the target material that we release. This starts to get complicated, other people can explain this better. However, more ions at the substrate means higher energy for growth

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So whilst DC grows faster, HiPIMS and c-HiPIMS have higher ion to atom ratios, as in the example below for Ti. 
& remember yesterday I said we can measure the wavelengths in a plasma glow, well we can even differentiate ions and atoms of the same material https://t.co/j57JX3ItaD https://t.co/x86wWCrkLL

As of 2018, Nobel Prizes have been awarded to 853 men, 51 women (Marie Curie won it twice)
twelve have won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
five have won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry
three have won the Nobel Prize in Physics
Why fewer women?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I have seen newspaper headlines just this year suggesting that women don't like STEM subjects, that woman are less good at physics than men. Men seem to have made a lot of the discoveries throughout history - is there something in it? 
Quite frankly, no.

tweets.label: Takeover

It is not that long since women have been 'officially allowed' to study science. A quote on the wki for Dorothy Hodgkin says:
"where she was one of two girls allowed to study chemistry." https://t.co/GLCBDJO9xu

tweets.label: Takeover

Cambridge University did not allow women to take degrees until 1947! (It was 1920 in Oxford). 
If you are not allowed to study, how on earth are we able to make those big discoveries?

Also, if we look to other diversities, BME men are less likely to work in STEM than white men.

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A big part of this is having role models. I met 2 LGB scientists in 13 years, no trans ones. I assumed there were no trans scientists because we were unwelcome. Sure, I have faced discrimination but generally I feel very welcome. The idea is we can only be what we see.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Science is not for the few. Yes, you have to be smart, hard-working and somewhat apt at science. However, that does not mean you should be excluded because of who you are. It is a right to feel accepted at work.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You don't need to be friends with everyone, but you should not have people who hate you because of who you are, who go out of their way to exclude you.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It is actually good for your groups' output to be diverse too. When everyone can be themselves, they can be creative, work their hardest and will be able to come up with new ideas thanks to a different perspective. Recent reports show there is a benefit to the output of the group

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So what is graphene? You may have heard about it in the news... https://t.co/NbgUZU9FSK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Graphene is one of the many forms ("allotropes" if you want a fancy chemistry word) pure carbon can take. In fact, this image shows 8 allotropes of carbon. https://t.co/bK5SCrQ0Es

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The top left and top center show the forms we're most familiar with in our normal macroscopic lives - the top left is how carbon is arranged in diamond, and the top center is graphite.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
And if you look closely at graphite, you can see that it is made up of pretty distinct layers of atoms. The carbons are all covalently bonded (the kind where atoms share electrons) to other atoms in the same layer. 

These individual layers are graphene! https://t.co/M4GqpYLrhb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At first, this was just theoretical. Physicists were referring to the graphene layers within graphite since around the 1950s, as a useful concept and shorthand.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But in 2004, researchers not only showed that they could  isolate a single layer of graphene in real life, they were able to characterize its properties. And that was so impressive they won the Nobel prize just a few years later in 2010.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I have to take a break for a meeting, but more graphene fun facts will be coming later today! https://t.co/j7MDNA1NvY

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And new ones still have surprising properties. "U-carbon" was just announced and may be ferromagnetic at room temperature, which has never been seen in other carbon allotropes. https://t.co/3GyOGELnIa

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As I mentioned, "graphene" is what we call an individual layer of carbon atoms in graphite, and the image below shows the crystal structure of 3 layers in graphite. https://t.co/1VrHJN9crD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So how do we get an individual layer (or in technical terms, a monolayer)? I mentioned that a group managed to isolate monolayer graphene in 2004, and characterize it well enough to discover its properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This actually surprised some people, b/c while physicists had theoretically discussed graphene for decades, several thought it was impossible for a free-standing, single atom thick material to be stable on practical time scales.

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov actually used Scotch tape in their Nobel-winning work. They donated their tape dispenser, some graphite, and a graphene transistor to the Nobel museum! https://t.co/aL73UDUBgr

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here you can show the "Scotch tape method" being demonstrated by researchers in their lab: https://t.co/tiKnJEffJa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Also, don't Google "Scotch tape method" without mentioning graphite or graphene, otherwise you might end up finding really gross things about tapeworms you weren't expecting to learn. Or at least that happened to me a few years when I was working on my lit review.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
You can also see in the graphene Scotch tape video that you can't really make a lot at a time. It's great for research - it makes high-quality material to test out new devices.

tweets.text: Also, you might be wondering why we even want graphene. That's a good question! It turns out to be a really impressive material and illustrates some neat concepts in nano and materials science when you compare it to graphite. https://t.co/YbR3CqFKTY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For instance, graphene is the strongest material humans have discovered (~100x stronger than steel). And you might think that's wild because we use graphite to write because it's so easy to break off pieces. But the difference is what's under stress.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The bonds between carbon atoms in the graphene plane are incredibly strong (stronger than diamond!). 

When we're breaking up graphite, you're breaking it up between layers, and those bonds are very weak.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Graphene's also really conductive, but even more impressive is its "mobility" - how fast the electrons carrying charge move - which is 100 times faster than that of electrons or holes in silicon (e.g. our current computer chips).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: While graphite is reasonably conductive, it's not as impressive because it turns out even the weak bonds between graphene layers disrupt this electron motion.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So with those superlative properties, we want to use graphene for a lot of things: https://t.co/A4OwlEoj0b

Sometimes we want to use graphene straight-up, but we can also add graphene to other materials to improve their properties! https://t.co/uSSFkLam0d

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For instance, adding less than 0.1 percent (by weight) of graphene to the plastic PET (which you may know as Dacron or Terylene) increased its strength by 40% Source: https://t.co/wNGLRMIgsu https://t.co/kCgSTrKMo9

tweets.text: That's a good question! The Fermi velocity of electrons in graphene is about 0.3% the speed of light, so the Lorentz factor is still really small and you don't see much change in relativistic mass. https://t.co/ds69GGWo7x

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But, it turns out the honeycomb lattice of identical atoms leads to an interesting property. The dispersion relation between electron energy and momentum is linear, so the conduction electrons actually behave like they have zero mass in graphene!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
When people say electrons behave like light in graphene, that's the linear dispersion relationship  

More formally, they're described by the Dirac equation as massless particles (but the speed of light needs to be replaced by their Fermi velocity).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It turns out this works in other lattices with identical molecules. For instance, a lab at Stanford made "molecular graphene" by making a honeycomb of carbon monoxide molecules on a surface, and the electrons behaved similarly 
https://t.co/DExCHqPzkO https://t.co/3gpyEs7W51

tweets.text: Continuing last night's discussion, what’s cool about graphene is that you can make it both starting from graphite (a “top-down” method), like with Scotch tape, or in a “bottom-up” process where you bring together carbon atoms. Image source: https://t.co/XXal860uvQ https://t.co/q1rtjmOUv6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Check out this thread from last night on why scientists and engineers really want to use graphene! https://t.co/mMxkXWz0Pu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The application you want graphene for is often a good guideline for how you should make it. 
Do you want it for electronic devices? Then you need consistent sizes and very few imperfections. Bottom-up processes enable more control over the quality. https://t.co/eTsMGvUy9p

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Do you want a lot of graphene, like to use as a filler in composites? Then you need to mass produce it, and only the top-down processes scale up. You lose some quality control, but a well-characterized distribution of sizes can be useful in these apps.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: While the Scotch tape method is a top-down technique, the techniques that will probably be used to manufacture graphene on large scales use liquids to break down graphite. The two popular ones are (1) sonication and (2) shear exfoliation.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Sonication uses sound to make a micro-bubble bath. If you’ve seen a cleaning bath for glasses or jewelry, they’re a kind of sonicator. https://t.co/pbAq1HrE18

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Sonicators use sound waves to create small bubbles in the liquid, and when these collapse, they generate intense pressure and shock waves that break apart the graphite. Image source: https://t.co/VfQM1eh0vT https://t.co/c9wXGIG541

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It’s a bit harder to scale up sonication than first glance might suggest. Most of the sound energy gets absorbed close to the moving surface/tip, so adding more liquid doesn’t really change the working volume. Scaling up the volume requires adding power.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And those collapsing bubbles are really violent. They heat the surrounding area to a few thousand degrees C at rates of billions of degrees per second! The shock wave also creates pressures >1000 atmospheres! This turns out to make new defects in the graphene.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So instead of blowing apart graphite to make graphene, why don’t we take a clue from our pencils, and peel layers off? https://t.co/WtLp3co0IX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is where the "graphene smoothie" comes in. In 2014, a group made graphene in a blender. First, they did try it in an industrial blender, but then they found they could make graphene even in a kitchen blender! https://t.co/j46GEXOwmu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the blender, the motion of the liquid peels layers of graphene off each other. https://t.co/KRYHQMtKgl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The peeling is driven by the shear forces in the liquid. The slightly different speeds of adjacent flow can slide the graphene layers relative to each other. https://t.co/EMgXwd9ZTF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The #graphene in a blender paper was HUGE for the community, because it showed several improvements over sonication.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (1) It takes less energy to slide graphene layers off each other instead of pulling/blasting them apart from the bubble shock waves.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (2) This less violent sliding process doesn't create new defects while you're peeling off the graphene.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (3) Blending scales up better than sonication. Production in sonication is almost directly proportional to power. In the blender, it scales up with the liquid "smoothie" volume without requiring the same increase in power.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And sometimes at the end of blending graphene, you can see some flakes that were still in the middle of sliding off each other. Image source: https://t.co/wNGLRMIgsu https://t.co/8QRftHQotO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So then work started to move on from surface energy to solubility parameters. In chemistry class, you learn that "like dissolves like". Solubility parameters are a way to quantify that to help make more rigorous predictions.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In graphene work, it's popular to look at Hansen solublity parameters - one parameter for each of 3 important aspects in chemical bonding.
(1) London dispersion (when random electron motions cause attraction)
(2) the force caused by permanent dipole moments
(3) hydrogen bonding

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.text: Last night I mentioned that even the more detailed Hansen parameter framework doesn't explain all the variations seen made by blending graphite into graphene in various liquids. So what other physical properties could matter?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you look at the way the liquid moves, the sliding is driven by the shear force between the layers of fluid. The force is the product of the shear rate, that gradient du/dy in velocity between layers, and the viscosity η. https://t.co/NQgq2D0Ir6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Viscosity is the technical term for what we often call the “thickness” of a liquid. A “thick” liquid like honey is more viscous than a “thin” liquid like water.  

Or I suppose blood is metaphorically more viscous than water.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
If you increase the viscosity at the same shear rate, you increase the force. My big hypothesis for my dissertation was that a more viscous liquid could help you exfoliate more graphene.

And, yes exfoliate in the sense of a skin care routine, b/c both are peeling off layers. https://t.co/RkxCFIuwAu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So I tried blending graphene in 3 solvents with different viscosities.
1) NMP, the common solvent used for graphene, with a viscosity like water
2) Benzyl benzoate, about 5x more viscous
3) Propylene glycol, about 25x more viscous

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, I didn’t use a kitchen blender to test this. I used a “rheometer”, an instrument that let me precisely control the flow of graphite-liquid mixture at multiple shear rates, so the flow was identical for all three solvents.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After centrifuging out the graphite that didn’t break up, I measured the absorbance of these dispersions of graphene in liquid, which is roughly proportional to the amount of material at low concentrations. (Thanks Beer-Lambert Law!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You can see that at every shear rate, the most viscous PG is more absorbent than the least viscous NMP, which is a sign of more graphene being made and which confirmed my hypothesis! https://t.co/RIyQCjBgsJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You might be curious about the BB/Benzyl Benzoate, which has an intermediate viscosity but does the worst. It has a very different dielectric value from the others, which we think increases the van der Waals forces between graphene flakes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Based on the fact that BB doesn’t even seem to consistently follow a trend within itself of greater absorbance at higher shear rates, we think the flakes are clumping back together into graphite so fast it was unstable by the time I tried measuring it.
