The original inspiration for my dissertation was to add the graphene into polymers, which tied into my graduate lab’s study of “soft matter”. 

What is soft matter? Literally stuff that is soft, for the most part. Or as we say in my department, the stuff that is “squishy”.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: RT @realscientists: When talking about squishy materials, I often ask people if they like to cook. Because I think understanding cooking ca…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I talked a lot about squishy materials when I got to curate partner account @RealScientists earlier this year, so let me share some highlights from there. https://t.co/YpcytLy2RY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Most foods, except hard candy, are soft matter: https://t.co/niBrl4eW9z

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Soft matter is everywhere! Other things you may have interacted with today that are engineered soft materials: lotions, make-up, ink. You might just think these are liquids, but they’re behavior is more complicated than something just like water or even a simple solution.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Also, for another name that describes exactly what these are, we call these systems "complex fluids". Or you can also call them #colloids, which you might remember from a #chemistry class.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What's a #colloid? That's a great question! It's a mixture where microscopic particles of one (or more) chemical are uniformly mixed (dispersed) in another chemical (the dispersing phase), but these chemicals still exist as distinct phases.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So sugar water is a solution - the sugar is broken up into its molecules, which each get surrounded by water molecules. (The sugar is "solvated"). 

But milk is an emulsion - a colloid of two insoluble liquids, in this case the milk fats and water.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Or maybe I should just say modern milk is an emulsion. Cream would rise to the top of milk before homogenization because it wasn't a stable mixture. Homogenizing breaks up the fat into much smaller particles that are more stably mixed into the water. https://t.co/w31LEA9b9w

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This lovely table from Wikipedia classifies all the various colloid phases you get by mixing solids, liquids, and gases. https://t.co/q13CK5y9P0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This may also answer your childhood questions of "is dough/Jello a solid or a liquid?". It turns out they're both. Jell-o is a gel, liquid dispersed in a solid. Raw dough is also a gel, but bread is a foam. https://t.co/B5XGhOOaSS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You also may have noticed I spent most of this week using the term "dispersion" or mixture to describe my #graphene-in-liquid system. That's because it is a colloid - the liquids aren't breaking up the graphene into its constituent carbon atoms like in a solution.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is also why the electric properties of the liquids matter. Since the van der Waals force is a major force for colloidal particles, we can tune that through the difference in dielectric between the particles and the liquid.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Also, following up on this, a new favorite paper I've seen actually tries to add #graphene into polymers by adopting the pressing and folding method from making croissants! https://t.co/lWIrMyusRT https://t.co/niBrl4eW9z https://t.co/fAR3Oe56si

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.text: This is essentially two slightly differently sized concentric cylinders, and the inner one rotates at speeds to apply the shear force or shear rate I want. This geometry is really nice because it prevents turbulence, which simplifies the experiment https://t.co/bjazX29FRq

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When you're studying soft/squishy materials, you learn that many don't have a single viscosity and that they're "non-Newtonian fluids". This means they're viscosity depends on the stress being applied and/or the history of that stress over time.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Many polymer mixtures are shear thinning - they get less viscous as more stress in applied. This is because the chains will first start to untangle from each other, and then they start to line up with each other, making it easier to move. https://t.co/l4piPynTks

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ketchup is (in)famously "thixotropic". When you agitate a thixotropic material, you disrupt the bonds between molecules and becomes weaker, but it will start to recover over time. This is why you often need to tap a ketchup bottle to start pouring it out.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And "oobleck", that fun mixture of cornstarch and water, is shear-thickening - it actually becomes more viscous under stress. https://t.co/gGVOYlGPsu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Why is oobleck shear-thickening? Good question! We're still not completely sure. A study published just last month seems to have come very close, suggesting that higher shear rates cause the particles to lose the lubrication between them. https://t.co/6IhxEf7xm5

tweets.text:
Hi Everyone!
Let me start by introducing myself!  I’m Rachel Oliver (@ProfRachelGaN) Professor of Materials Science at Cambridge University and Director of the Cambridge Centre for Gallium Nitride.  I’m going to be talking nitrides and nano this week!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Why nitrides?  Well, the nitride materials I work on are used in light emitting diodes or LEDs, the technology at the heart of energy efficient LED light bulbs.  Any RealSciNano followers got LED bulbs installed at home? https://t.co/Nz3JDYqlqC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you have, I bet it’s because of how energy efficient these bulbs are!  As much as 6 times more efficient than a traditional incandescent bulb and also better than a compact florescent.  Also, they have really long lifespans, up to 50,000 hours.  Good, huh?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Inside a typical LED bulb, is a yellow hemisphere of a phosphor material, which converts some of the blue light which comes from the LED into other colours, to make white light.  The LEDs themselves are pretty tiny – a few mm across or less. https://t.co/9TNjqBU6eK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That’s not exactly nano though!  Later today, I’ll delve into the insides of an LED bulb and show you the much smaller structures from which the light is actually emitted!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: OK!  Just grabbing a quick coffee, so I’ve got a couple of minutes to take you inside an LED.  Here’s an optical microscope picture of a single LED chip: https://t.co/s1ZUeS1PGd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All we can really see here is the metal electrodes which are used to connect the LED to a power source, so let’s dig down under the surface a bit and have a closer look using a scanning electron microscope: https://t.co/QwMUqZiDDO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There's material labelled “n” and “p”.  In the family of materials we call “semiconductors” which includes gallium nitride, electrical current can flow via the movement of either negative or positive charge carriers.  We call the two sorts of material “n-type” and “p-type”.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When we apply a voltage across the LED, it forces negative and positive charge carriers towards one another.  When they meet and combine, light is given out.  That’s how we make light in an LED!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (This is very different to how we get light out of an incandescent bulb. There we use a metal wire.  Current flowing makes it hot, so it glows to get rid of some heat.  We have to create a lot of heat energy & that makes incandescents inefficient. LEDs don’t have to get hot).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we only use the n-type and the p-type semiconductor, we find that the negative and positive charges don’t often meet one another and combine to give out light.  We need to find a way to trap them together in a really small space to make them more likely to meet.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We create a trap for the charges using something called a “quantum well” – and this is where we hit the nanoscale!  Quantum wells are layers of one semiconductor material sandwiched between layers of another. The quantum well layers may only be 2 nm thick!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For nitride LEDs, the quantum wells are made of indium gallium nitride – gallium nitride with some of the gallium replaced by indium.  We can’t see the quantum wells with an optical microscope, or even an SEM.  We need to use a transmission electron microscope: https://t.co/BRgNzS0Mhm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I’ll explain the importance of these InGaN quantum wells a little more!  We need to get the positive and negative charges to meet.  Imagine that I want to meet a friend in Cambridge… how can I increase the probability of that happening?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If I say to my friend: “Let’s meet in Cambridge” we’re pretty unlikely to find eachother.  However, if I say “Let’s meet in front of the Chronophage clock” that get’s the two of us into a much smaller volume and we’re much more likely to find one another. https://t.co/pIKUCtvDA9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It’s the same with the charge carriers:  by squeezing them into a tiny space in the few nanometre quantum well, we make it much more likely they will meet, and when we increase that probability, we make the device more efficient.  Hooray for nano!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'll talk more tomorrow about the importance of nanostructures in nitride LEDs.  Later today, I'll also post some more resources about these devices, in case you want to dig into the topic a bit more deeply!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Morning all! Yesterday I talked about light emitting diodes, LEDs, and I promised I’d delve more deeply into their nanoscale structure today!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
LEDs have actually been around for ages (since the 1960s), but in 2014 the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for the development of blue nitride LEDs.  One of the reasons that making good blue LEDs was so hard is all down to their nanoscale structure.
https://t.co/gwn97Fxj8Q

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Conventional semiconductors (like Silicon) are grown as single crystals: all the atoms lie in perfect organised rows, like soldiers stood on the parade ground.  Those single crystals can be taller than a person, and contains hardly any mistakes in the rows and rows of atoms. https://t.co/0d3XaDkMUA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It’s really, really difficult to grow big crystals like that of gallium nitride (GaN).  Big GaN crystals need really high pressures & temperatures to grow, & even now – about 25 years after the development of the first LEDs – we’re a long way from the scale of Silicon crystals!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So instead, we grow GaN as layers on top of another material, most commonly sapphire.  And because the spacings between the rows of atoms in sapphire doesn’t match the spacings in GaN, the GaN crystals tend to be full of tiny mistakes in how the atoms line up.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The most important mistake (or defect) in GaN is a dislocation. It’s not really a single mistake, more a line of mistakes that runs right through the crystal. You can learn more about dislocations on DoITPoMs, a great teaching resource hosted by @cu_mat:
https://t.co/UJjezczpCq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In GaN there are really a lot of these mistakes.  If you looked at 1 cm x 1 cm area of the surface of a GaN crystal, you could find the terminations of about 1 billion dislocations.  (For comparison, in Silicon, a 1 cm x 1 cm area hardly ever has even one of these defects).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For LEDs, the key thing you need to know about dislocations, is they can really mess up the performance of the device.  For an LED emitting in the infra-red based on GaAs, if you have more than about 1000 dislocations in a 1 cm x 1 cm area it will very rapidly fail.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That’s because when negative and positive charges meet at a dislocation, they combine and give out heat rather than light.  The device gets hotter and hotter, and the heat eventually causes it to fail.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Because GaN is full of dislocations, most scientists thought it was a dead loss for light emitting devices.  However, it turns out that GaN devices are incredibly robust to the presence of defects.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Understanding the reasons for that robustness was a really challenging puzzle to solve, and caused huge controversy in my field.  I’ll come back later and tell you a bit more about that!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Right!  I’m back and ready to talk about major nitride controversies!  Earlier I said that there are loads of defects in GaN LEDs and the devices survive amazingly well.  How could that be? Well there are basically two options:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Option 1:  Perhaps dislocations in GaN just aren’t a problem like they are in other materials? https://t.co/hjCPqKasGC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Sadly option 1 doesn’t hold up.  We can take pictures of the light emission from GaN and when we do that we can see that dislocations and the areas around them emit a lot less light than material without defects. Dislocations do mess up the light emission in GaN.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Option 2:  If the dislocations are a problem, something must stop the charge carriers from reaching them, and hence limit the damage they can do.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Option 2 has legs – there’s lots of experimental evidence suggesting that charge carriers in the InGaN quantum wells (which make up the light emitting bit of a nitride LED) can’t move around freely.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The next big question was this: What is it about the structure of those InGaN quantum wells that prevents the charge carriers moving around?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is where the big controversy arose.  Because there were some really interesting early electron microscopy images which suggested that the indium wasn’t spread out evenly through the InGaN quantum well layer.  Instead, the indium atoms seemed to be in little clusters.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Those indium rich clusters would act to trap the charge carriers really effectively, and stop them moving to the defect sites.  It sounded like a solution – but it wasn’t.  Because later images, taken with other techniques showed no clusters at all.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Tomorrow, I’ll talk a bit about the different techniques that were used.  The microscopy is really cool!  For now, I’m going to admit that it all got a bit shouty.  We scientists can be pretty passionate about our ideas.  Not as calm and collected as you might expect! https://t.co/1OMCceyXh8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the end, most people agreed that the indium atoms were pretty evenly mixed through the InGaN quantum wells.  Which meant no more fighting, but we were back where we started… not knowing what it was about the quantum wells that made the LEDs robust to defects!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here, it all gets a bit complicated.  But basically, it turns out that you don’t need a lot of indium in a cluster to trap the carriers and keep them from moving to the defects.  You just need a couple of indiums almost next to each other with a nitrogen between them.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And that happens pretty often, even when the indiums and galliums are randomly mixed up through the crystal.  It’s like if you’re throwing a dice.  Throwing two sixes in a row happens quite a lot if you throw the dice a million times. https://t.co/FiLs1SDmcT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It is in the very nature of the indium gallium nitride alloy that it can trap carriers.  The natural disorder in the material is all it takes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That natural disorder is then vital to making LEDs work despite the prescence of loads of crystal defects.  It’s a lucky throw of the dice, on which the multi-billion dollar LED industry relies.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Interestingly, the same natural disorder – and its impact on charge carriers – has also been blamed for the fact that green nitride LEDs are much less efficient than blue ones.  But that’s another story!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
If you’ve made it to the end of this story, you might want to know that I talk about all this stuff in the extended version of the @RealSci_Nano podcast.  Also, I’ll be giving a seminar on this and other LED topics in Bristol on Monday:
https://t.co/EP1p8Hlb7N

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Tomorrow, I’ll tell you more about the microscopes we used to understand the nanoscale structure of LEDs.  In the meantime, do feel free to ask me about LED technology.  Other cool nitride folks on twitter who you might want to engage with are…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: From Tyndall in Cork, Ireland:  @SarojPatrares who has done fantastic work on modelling the impact of nitride nanostructures on how carriers can move and combine in quantum wells.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: From Strathclyde in Scotland:  @RobMartin100 – who uses scanning electron microscopy techniques to understand the effect of small scale structure of ntirides on light emission.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Also in Strathclyde these days:  @FabienMassabuau who is a master of transmission electron microscopy on GaN – although he’s moving towards new wonder material gallium oxide these days!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: From Bristol: @CDTR_Bristol - The Center for Device Thermography and Reliability – who may not sound like a nitride group, but actually do excellent work on nitride electronics.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Just looked back at my list of people to check out and realised that they’re all men.  I’m sad but not surprised – gallium nitride is a very male dominated field.  I’ll recommend fantastic female microscopers tomorrow!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you enjoyed hearing about the controversial nature of the nanostructure in nitride quantum wells, have a listen to the extended podcast, where I talk about this story, in a lot more detail! https://t.co/zEWC02VTOl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Good morning followers of all things nano!  Today, I’m going to talk about how we characterise the nanoscale structure of nitride materials.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Yesterday – I made a really long thread about a major controversy in the nitride field about the nanoscale structure of InGaN quantum wells.  You can read it here if you like:
https://t.co/eWrPQF0gjv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That controversy involved data from two amazing nanoscale microscopy techniques:  transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT).  I’m going to tell you a bit about each of them!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let’s start with TEM!  TEM got a bit of a raw deal yesterday, because it resulted in some controversial observations which caused some heated debate in the field.  Data from microscopes can be hard to interpret, but TEM is really an amazing technique!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Many people will have used an optical microscope to magnify the features of a sample.  Optical microscopes are great as long as the thing you want to look at is at the micrometer scale or bigger – so bigger than 1 millionth of a metre (or a thousandth of a mm). https://t.co/0X3Mvbxths

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But a standard optical microscope isn’t much use for looking at nanostructures.  Light is a wave, and when the structures are smaller than its wavelength it becomes impossible to image them using a basic optical microscope.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, we need a wave with a shorter wavelength!  And electrons (and other fundamental particles) behave as waves.  If we accelerate the electrons to high speeds, they have a high energy and a very short wavelength.  So we can use them to take really high resolution images. https://t.co/qrMRz8uGA0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In a TEM, we fire the electrons through a very thin sample.  This is like transmission light microscopy, where you shine a light through from below a transparent sample, and view it from above.  Except in TEM we usually shine the electrons from the top and view from below.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Just like in an optical microscope, we need lenses.  But we can’t use beautifully shaped pieces of glass.  Instead we might use whopping great electromagnets to shape and direct the electron beam. We call them “electron lenses”. https://t.co/SMCHrPekvF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now steering electron beams isn’t easy, and the lenses don’t work perfectly.  We call the imperfections due to the enses the lenses "aberrations", and the best TEMs have additional components called aberration correctors to deal with the problems they produce.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Once you get the electron optics right, the images can be truly astounding.  This one was taken by @fabienmassabuau and you can see it on his twitter profile.  It’s a picture of a GaN crystal, and every one of those white dots is a column of atoms viewed end on! https://t.co/B1MzQIiodN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In that image, there is one mistake in the crystal – it’s a dislocation (the sort of defect I discussed yesterday) and you can see how it mucks up the regular repeating pattern of atoms.  That mistake goes on, down a line, into the plane of the image.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That raises a very important thing about TEM.  We’re firing the electrons through the sample.  That means that we are viewing everything in projection.  And that can sometimes cause problems. https://t.co/V5JvCh7lrp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are techniques, like electron tomography, in which you rotate the sample and image it from multiple different angles, which seek to overcome this and get three-dimensional images.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Instead of getting into electron tomography, later on I’m going to talk about a completely different technique for nanoscale imaging in 3D: atom probe tomography. https://t.co/uumjmtoHtb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The next nanoscale characterisation technique I want to talk about is atom probe tomography (APT), which is an amazing way of getting three dimensional compositional maps of materials.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Unlike TEM, APT bears essentially no resemblance to the traditional light microscope.  For APT, we have to start with a very sharp needle of material, whose end is only about 100 nm across.  These can be tricky to make, but it can be done! https://t.co/BmzvSzu2CG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When a very sharp conductive object is raised to a high voltage, the electric field around the sharp end is huge, big enough to pull ions off the end of the spike. The process of pulling a material apart with an electric field is called “field evaporation.”

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In APT, we hold the very sharp specimen at a voltage just below the value needed to achieve field evaporation, and then add a pulse of extra energy to kick it up above that threshold very briefly.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The extra energy can come from a pulse of additonal voltage, or a pulse of laser light focussed on the tip of the sample. For semiconductor materials, we tend to use the laser approach.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we’re lucky, the pulse of extra energy will evaporate one single ion.  It will fly out from the end of the tip along a trajectory defined by the electric field and land on a detector.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The position where the ion lands on the detector can be traced back to tell us where it must have come from on the specimen.  That basically gives us its x and y coordinate.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Because you have to evaporate the ions at the end of the needle before you evaporate ions from lower down, the order in which the ions evaporate gives you information about the depth into the sample from which they arise: the z-coordinate.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now, to get a compositional map, we just need to know what the ion is.  We can figure that out from its mass, and we can figure out its mass from how long it took to fly to the detector.  Heavier ions go slower.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: With a certain amount of mathematical jiggery pokery, we can identify where the ion came from in 3D space and what it’s mass and hence chemical identity are.  So, we can build a 3D compositional map.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Like this data on InGaN quantum wells from the first ever atom probe tomography experiment on nitride semiconductors.  A classic!  Turquoise dots are Ga atoms, orange dots are indium. Green is gold from where we messed up the sample prep! https://t.co/h0fUk89uVT

(More about GaN-based chargers here: https://t.co/LE3qS3ZAkm)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Other applications of GaN transistors include being used in amplifiers in mobile phone base stations and in power conversion in electric vehicles.
(More about GaN in the automotive industry here: https://t.co/lE0B6x9hT8)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: GaN-based laser diodes are at the heart of “BluRay” technology and are also used in displays and even in industrial applications like welding.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ultra-violet LEDs based on GaN are being developed, and can kill or damage many of the bugs which can infect drinking water, particularly in the developing world, causing sickness and death, so GaN may in future be widely used for water purification. (https://t.co/B3uFtRIoR0)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My group is even developing GaN LEDs which emit precisely one photon (the fundamental quantum light particle) on demand, and these single photon emitters could be used in future secure communications technologies!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So increasingly, GaN is all around us:  saving energy, cleaning water, transmitting data, and lighting up our world! And all of these applications require us to understand and engineer the nanoscale structure of this amazing material!

tweets.text: When @RealSci_Nano asked me what my three wishes were to improve the world of science I said "Equality. Diversity. Inclusion."  If they'd offered me a fourth wish, I would have said "Accessibility".

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I could have spent all week talking about my passion for #equality, #diversity, #inclusion & #accessibility in STEMM! However, I also wanted to talk science! If you'd like to know more about my work & passion in this area, head over to @TIGERinSTEMM or to: https://t.co/0YOqFxjoF6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: TIGERS - The Inclusion Group for Equity in Research in STEMM - is a grass roots collective which campaigns for a more inclusive future for science.  We've just published a document - led by @DrJessBoland - about accessibility in STEMM, with particular focus on funding processes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Please do read the document, and if you have a disability, let us know what we've missed by joining the discussion on @tigerinstemm:  https://t.co/6AhE2TnFsz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Before I got involved in @tigerinstemm, I hadn't really thought about the barriers disabled people face in scientific research.  The more I learn about this, the more shocked I am at how poorly we accommodate talented scientists who happen to have a disability.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: TIGERS are focused on funding processes currently, so here are just a few of the things I have learnt about accessibility issues around UK funding processes:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 1.  Blind and visually impaired researchers use screen readers to access web-pages and documents.  However, the main UK funder, @UKRI_News, uses a web-portal for grant submission which is incompatible with screen readers.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
2.  Similarly, when @UKRI_News publishes grant guidance, they use a pdf format which is also incompatible with screen readers.
3. Sometimes grant info comes on a video instead... but those videos are not subtitled, so deaf researchers can't access them.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4.  Some grant processes require interviews.  If your disability makes it difficult for you to travel to an interview, you can dial in remotely.  But if the technology doesn't work within 5 minutes of the interview start time, your interview will be cancelled.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (How often do any of us get a Skype conference working within 5 minutes?  It usually takes me at least 10 minutes of swearing).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5.  If you need extra funding for accommodations for a disability, you can request that - but you have to put it in your main proposals documents.  Which is a bit like writing "HEY, I HAVE A DISABILITY, DISCRIMINATE AGAINST ME!" across your Justification of Resources document.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I could go on, but if you want to know about this stuff you'd be far better reading the TIGERS report which was written and reviewed by actual disabled people:  https://t.co/6AhE2TnFsz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So I'll stop here, but say this:  whilst there are a lot of other issues facing disabled scientists, the system problems above are all really fixable.  So why aren't we fixing them??  Answers on a postcard to @tigerinstemm please!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Well folks, I hope you've enjoyed hearing a little bit about what I've been learning about the (lack of) accessibility of STEM today!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today we're looking at applications of superconductivity. Specifically, how do nano-engineered superconducting materials enable some of the biggest science projects on the planet?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Application of superconductivity #1: Particle physics

It turns out that if you want to know what something is made of, smash it! Physicists have utilized this highly scientific idea for decades to explore the structure of the atoms that make up our Universe.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
And the biggest atom-smasher we've built so far is the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at @CERN. 

Here's a nice write-up on the LHC and what it does: 

https://t.co/NCjSqx9dHB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @CERN There's a basic challenge with this design of particle collider...you need to move the particles, in a circle, at something approaching the speed of light. To do this without blowing a hole in the side of your very expensive device, you need to BEND and FOCUS the particle beam.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @CERN Enter superconductivity. Superconducting NbTi wire is used to create dipole magnets that each generate around 7 Tesla (T) of magnetic field. A 1 T magnet is strong enough to lift a small car, so these things put your refrigerator magnets to shame.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
@CERN There are over 1300 of these dipole magnets in the LHC ring, and each one weighs 35 tons and is 15 meters long! Here's a short video of CERN engineers manipulating one of the dipole magnets during LHC construction.

https://t.co/UlPkUyG67q

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @CERN Without superconductors, the LHC ring would have to be much larger in size (and thus much more expensive), and the energy cost to run the magnets would be prohibitive.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
@CERN So superconductivity is one important "enabling" technology for particle physics. In the 10 years it has been running, the LHC has realized a number of important discoveries, most significantly the discovery of the Higgs boson.

https://t.co/NGRKBVryl5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Application of superconductivity #2: Fusion energy!

The old joke is that fusion is 30 years away....and always will be. But in fact there are a number of feasible fusion projects in construction right now, and superconductivity is a big piece of making them possible.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The big big big fusion project is ITER (@iterorg) in southern France. This machine is attempting to generate net-positive fusion energy and (just as important), sustain the fusion reaction for 500 seconds. 

https://t.co/zQ8LXimzk0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
@iterorg I did a postdoc at ITER and worked on their magnet system. Enormous cables of NbTi and Nb3Sn superconducting wires are used to levitate and stir the plasma. 

https://t.co/VEwEK9vHvm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @iterorg The 500 tons of Nb3Sn needed for ITER were the largest procurement of that material in history...by far! Manufacturing all that complex, composite wire involved eight manufacturers in six countries. We spent a lot of time in airplanes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @iterorg The key point to understand is that if you tried to generate the ITER magnetic fields with conventional (e.g. copper) magnets, you would need *many* gigawatts of electric power, and you would never achieve break-even fusion.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @iterorg This is a theme for superconductivity: these big science projects (like the LHC or ITER) are already massive in scale. But without superconductors, their size and cost would be absurdly enormous, or (in the case of ITER), they simply could never achieve their design goal.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Hey look at that...those big LHC superconducting magnets we were talking about earlier today? They're getting an updgrade:

https://t.co/SuWWeoxJnn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Application of superconductivity #3 - medicine! https://t.co/SN6yMVmMmz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
You've maybe spent some time inside a superconducting magnet and didn't even realize it. 

The largest commercial application of superconductors, by far, is in MRI machines in hospitals.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The big doughnut of the MRI machine is a helium-cooled, NbTi superconducting magnet. 

https://t.co/pvqsOAN7wq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: MRI machines require a highly *stable* magnetic field. With a conventional electromagnet, the magnetic field can vary slightly due to variations ("ripple") in the voltage powering the magnet.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But with a superconductor, you can charge the magnet, and then actually *remove* the electrical leads, and the current will continue flowing in the magnet. https://t.co/08s2mNC5t2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This "persistence" of the superconducting current flow is a crazy physics trick, but it is also technologically critical for MRIs. Producing an accurate MRI image requires knowing the magnetic field value in the magnet bore to something like 1 part per million.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So it's superconductors to the rescue...generating a high, stable, and uniform magnetic field that allows doctors to take that peek inside your body without having to, you know, actually take a peek. https://t.co/luOMkzF5My

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Superconductors are also being used to make proton therapy - a more precise and farr less invasive form of radiation therapy for cancer patients - more accessible. 

https://t.co/baU5CWa6uf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Proton therapy requires manipulating a beam of protons so they can be deposited exactly at the tumor location in a human body. But bending and focusing proton beams takes...wait for it...big magnets.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As a result, there are just a few dozen proton therapy clinics in the U.S. The treatment is massively expensive. Compact superconducting magnets will help make proton therapy more widely available by reducing the size of the machine and lowering the cost.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So there's lots going on in the world of superconductivity...in physics, in fusion, and in medicine. How does this all relate to nanotechnology? Well it turns out we design these superconductors at the nanoscale to get the properties we need to enable all these advances.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Stay tuned for more on how we do that! https://t.co/TCyyo9MPk1

tweets.text: @ClaraMBarker @StemCorps https://t.co/UsZvJWizMe

tweets.text:

Check it out: https://t.co/A8f4zCiJxk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Superconductors are used to build some of the largest science projects on the planet. But they are also exquisitely engineered at the nanoscale. Today we'll see how!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
To help me, I'll be utilizing images from the incomparable Peter Lee at Florida State University. Check out his full gallery of superconductor microstructures here:

https://t.co/vpYVFkqZId

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Let's start with the workhorse: NbTi.

A high-current NbTi wire is comprised of thousands of individual Nb-47 wt.% Ti filaments in a Cu matrix. But there's a lot going on in every single one of those little strands.... https://t.co/xoj0DpRCEX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Magnetic flux in superconductors is quantitzed, and those quanta of flux need to be "pinned", or held in place, to prevent heat generation when current flows in the superconductor. In NbTi, this is done by engineering in ribbons of alpha-Ti in the NbTi matrix. https://t.co/fa8fHJ7NGZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is a great triumph of metallurgy...the alpha-Ti precipitates are strain-induced, meaning they develop as the wire is drawn. So the original billet and the desired final wire size have to be engineered to cause just the right amount of Ti precipitation.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Too little Ti and the precipitate spacing won't match nicely the quantitized flux line lattice spacing. Too much Ti and the superconductivity starts to degrade. The LHC was able to be designed and built in the 1990s because NbTi was metallurgically optimized in the 1980s.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Next up is my personal favorite, Nb3Sn. Nb3Sn powers the toroidal field and central solenoid magnet systems of the ITER fusion reactor, under construction in southern France. 

Like NbTi, Nb3Sn is used by the ton in cables that carry thousands of amps of current... https://t.co/XgewnbsPsr

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
...and like NbTi, Nb3Sn is able to do it's job because it's been engineered at the nanoscale.

In Nb3Sn, there are two competing forces. First, the phase itself has some significant solid solubility. In other words, it doesn't exist only at 25 at.% Sn.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The phase can be tin deficient, down to about 18 at.% Sn. This is a problem, because the superconductivity degrades as the tin content drops off. So metallurgically we want to keep the tin content in the Nb3Sn filaments as high and as uniform as possible.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, metallurgy students, how do you get and maintain a high, uniform Sn content? Consult a phase diagram and a kinetics textbook, and you'll agree that what we want is a LONG and HOT heat treatment, which for Nb3Sn might be something like 700C.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So what's the problem? Well the problem are the individual Nb3Sn grains. Here they are shown in grey, in a false-colored (red) Cu matrix. Just like in NbTi, we need to pin the quantitized flux somehow. In Nb3Sn that's done mostly via the grain boundaries. https://t.co/uarWPIxhkL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So for maximum flux pinning, we'd like a very fine grain structure, i.e. the formation heat treatment should be as SHORT and as LOW TEMP as possible!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's the basic challenge with Nb3Sn. We need temperature and time to form the phase via a diffusional heat treatment with high Sn content, but all that diffusion goodness also grows the grain size. What are we to do?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Well we put our engineer hats on, that's what. We've found a few ways to outsmart the material. For example, we can:

1. Keep the filaments small (a few microns in diameter). This reduces the diffusion distances, allowing phase formation to happen without excessive grain growth.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2. We can introduced precipitates (artificial pinning centers, or APCs) that both help to pin the quantitized magnetic flux, and also help supress grain growth.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3. Last, we go for lower temps and longer times in our heat treatments, since diffusion is exponential with temperature but parabolic (square root dependence) with time.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Not every Nb3Sn conductor employs all these strategies (for example the ITER material does not utilize APCs), but together they represent a toolbox that allows us to design a micro- and nano-structure that maximizes the current we can push through the wire.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For example, the ITER Nb3Sn wire can carry about 1,000 A/mm^2 at 12 Tesla and 4.2 K, and Nb3Sn wires designed for high energy physics applications (such as the upcoming luminosity upgrade for the LHC) can carry around 3,000 A/mm^2.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's some serious current density! https://t.co/cRiKvcegdq

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So if we're going to talk about magnets, we need to know about magnetism. I can't really do better by way of simple explanation that National Geographic, so I'm not going to try: https://t.co/kJWmWoqj1O

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In sum - electrons have a property called "spin," and you can think of this like spinning a basketball on your finger (SHOOSH PHYSICISTS I KNOW!). If you have one ball spinning clockwise and the other spinning counterclockwise at the same speed, the sum of the spins is 0.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The same is true with electrons - if electrons are paired up they have opposite spins (+/- or ↑/↓ or ɑ/β) and the net spin of the system is 0. 

If electrons are unpaired, the net spin of the system is not zero. Non-zero spin = magnetism.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
That's the gist, anyway. Things can be more complicated than that, but for our purposes at the molecular level that's what we care about. 

Okay, great. Well... there's more than one kind of magnetism and that's where things start to get funky.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I'm going to link you to the Wikipedia page on magnetism, but only because the references are okay. It's really jargony and I'm new to working a lot on magnetic systems myself.

https://t.co/6lwLryKq9E

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Broke the thread because I am a foolish fool. 

https://t.co/eQQRwmIGYk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, there are several kinds of magnetism and we should talk about a few of them so we can start talking more about the magnetic properties of nanoparticles tomorrow.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Diamagnetism - we usually think of it as all the spins being paired up so the system doesn't magnetize in response to a magnet. Think of a block of wood, or a gold watch band.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Paramagnetism - there are unpaired electrons. What's that mean? Non-zero spin and therefore magnetism. They'll magnetize when exposed to a magnet, but when the magnet goes away don't remain magnetic.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ferromagnetism - This basically means "magnetic like iron." There are unpaired spins in ferromagnetic systems just like in paramagnets, but ferromagnetic materials can be made into permanent magnets below a certain temperature.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In ferromagnets spins near each other align parallel* to each other.

↑↑↑↑↑↑↑↑↑↑↑↑↑

Because the spins all point in the same direction, they add together.

*technically the moments of neighboring magnetic domains, but that starts to get REAL complicated.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There's also ANTIferromagnetism. Those are systems where there are unpaired electrons but the overall spin is zero because the spins of individual unpaired electrons align anti-parallel:

 ↑↑↓↓↑↑↓↓↑↑

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Lastly there's ferrimagnetism. This one is the weirdest because it has properties of both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic systems depending on temperature.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ferrimagnets, like ferromagnets, will remain magnetic after they've been exposed to a magnetic field if they are cold enough. HOWEVER like antiferromagnets, their spins tend to align anti-parallel if left to their own devices.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This can happen because of the structure of ferrimagnetic materials - in a sense there are more spins aligned one direction than in the opposite.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ferrimagnetism and another property called SUPERPARAMAGNETISM will be important when I talk about the nanoparticles I'm working on tomorrow.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Good morning everyone! Light I left off with a brief intro to magnetic materials written from the perspective of a chemist who is pretty new to working on magnets. https://t.co/eImttztZuA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today I want to get into why anybody would care about nanoscale magnets and what some of the goals of my present research are. As always, any opinions expressed are mine alone and do not reflect any position of the DoE, Sandia Lab, or NTESS.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I mentioned superparamagnetism yesterday, and I want to take a second to explain what that means. So there's a super jargony Wiki page, like one might expect - https://t.co/KNveIZ4X5Q

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In terms that make sense to me, a person without a degree in physics and who hasn't done math more complicated than calculus in years, it's like all the spins in nanoparticles are acting like one GIANT spin.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you have a nanoparticle made of a ferromagnetic or ferrimagnetic material - like magnetite, say - the spins will all couple up so the particle will have what we call a single magnetic domain.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: More or less that means that when you put them into a magnetic field they behave a lot like paramagnets but they respond more. Their susceptibility to external magnetic influence is higher.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Unsurprisingly, we call how much a sample responds to an external magnetic field its "magnetic susceptibility." Higher susceptibility can be important for a lot of things - data storage, medical imaging, electronics.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Susceptibility is also related to another property that can be important for how your magnets perform called hysteresis. Again, I'll give you a link to the wiki for the references: https://t.co/niE0tCRZid

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So we've talked about how magnetic materials will respond to other magnets, well, if you put them in a strong enough magnetic field the magnetic moment of your sample will align with the direction of the external field.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It's not unlike how a magnetic compass works, but you're using a field you generated rather than the earth's magnetic field. And if you have ever used a compass, you've probably noticed that there is a delay between when you turn and the needle moving to a new position.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you take magnetic particles, put them in a big magnetic field, and then change the orientation of that magnetic field while observing your sample's magnetic orientation you'll see a delay as well. Your sample won't instantly realign with the field, it'll take some time.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We measure how magnetized the sample remains as we change the field strength and orientation, and that tells us about the magnetic behavior of our particles. Sometimes you want a lot of hysteresis - like with a hard drive - in our case, we want none.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Why would particles that respond nearly instantly to the orientation of a magnetic field be useful? That's going to have to wait until I've gotten some science going in the lab.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All right, I have my experiment going and it's going to have to run for most of the rest of the day, so let's talk about why having particles with no hysteresis can be useful. https://t.co/HLA2yW4rEq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Transformers are a part of the electrical grid, I'm sure everyone knows this. Some hang on power poles in your neighborhood, some are huge and centralized somewhere in the grid.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Transformers change the voltage between the input and the output - for instance taking the high voltage transmission power from the lines outside down to something usable in your house. In the US residential voltage is 120/240 V.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What does that have to do with magnetic nanoparticles? Well, a key part of a transformer is an inductor, which is basically a magnet with some wire wrapped around it. These are often called cores. Inductors store energy when current is passed through them.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Inductors also appear on circuit boards, in radios, etc, for a variety of different applications. I'm not an electrical engineer, so my knowledge of this stuff is a bit sparse, but the point is that inductors are important and that inductors are made of magnets.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Well, because electric current and magnetism are really the same thing - the electromagnetic force (one of only four fundamental forces in the universe no matter what some cranks in Austria say), the magnetic field of an inductor responds to the field generated by current.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As the current changes so does the field it generates, and the inductor's magnetic moment will follow it - like the compass responding to the Earth's magnetic field.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
And as we may remember from earlier, there's a bit of a delay in the response. Over time, this adds up and the inductor's magnet gets less and less synchronized with the current's field. That leads to a loss of stored energy.

https://t.co/uBGFMmJ8KE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As time passes you get a build up of magnetization in the inductor, leading to hysteresis like we talked about early. The higher the hysteresis the greater the loss of energy in your inductor, leading to worse efficiency.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To bring this back around to nanoparticles - superparamagnetic nanoparticles have almost no hysteresis (ideally none) at ambient temperatures. So if we could make inductors out of superparamagnetic particles we could massively improve efficiency across all kinds of applications.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The big one is large transformers in the power grid, which are something like 80% efficient if I remember correctly. The transformers in your neighborhood are about 96% efficient, but because there are so many small gains represent major energy savings.

tweets.text: Today I while I have some time during the day I want to talk a bit about what I actually do. By training, I am a synthetic chemist. That means that I take molecules we don't like, and use chemistry to turn them into molecules or materials we want.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
My synthetic experience is pretty broad - I've done everything from small molecule chemistry to inorganic nanoparticle synthesis. I joke that I'm one of the only people I know who's comfortable working in a glove box or running PAGE.*

*polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But, the reason I've spent so much time earlier in the week talking about magnets is that at the moment I'm working on magnetic iron oxide particles.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We're interested in magnetic nanoparticles because magnets are super important to the modern world, like I mentioned yesterday.

https://t.co/BPvwiuUYZH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One problem in magnetic nanoparticle synthesis is reproducibility. Another is size control - both in terms of getting the desired size and in having a narrow size distribution.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These two problems exist across a lot of nanoscience, but can be particularly troublesome for iron-based particles. Why? Well, FeNP synthesis is usually done at really high temperatures, like 350 °C high. At that kind of temp, all kinds of things happen, it's a mess.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You also run into issues of thermal transport - it is really hard to keep your reaction vessel a consistent temperature when it's that high.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So how do we overcome the temperature challenge? By using a molten metal bath! Our awesome tech (BIG UPS TO TECHNOLOGISTS & TECHNICIANS!) converts soldier pots for use with some custom software he wrote & high performance thermocouples.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
As a result, the group developed a pretty cool and very reliable synthesis of magnetite nanoparticles a few years back.

https://t.co/DE3KPBjW18

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Not everyone will have access to that paper (I am happy to send a pdf if you don't, just let me know), but there are some pretty cool images I think are worth seeing. All the scale bars are 20 nm. https://t.co/iee7Qu6wfv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These images are from a transmission electron microscope (TEM), that we use to see stuff too small for optical microscopy. As you can see the drip-feed synthesis the group developed makes very regular particles with size predictable by reaction time.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And also in that third image look at how nice and hexagonally close packed those spheres are! Symmetry is fun.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
If you want to know more about electronmicroscopy, I can't say enough good things about Grant Jensen's lectures. He's a professor at Cat Tech, and what he's put up on YouTube is a really great way to get started (it's how I learned the basics).

https://t.co/VxWTTbQIfo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, the group developed this extended FeNP synthesis a few years back, so what am I working on? Well, it's an update to that procedure that is easier to do. I'm also working on making particles that don't just contain iron, materials called ferrites.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Because of my interests and experience I'm trying to control particle size in our new synthesis, figure out the best way to incorporate other transition metals, and the best ways to stick different stuff to the surfaces to make the particles better for inductor applications.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I can't show you any of the results from those experiments for a few reasons - mostly they're not published or in a publishable state yet. But, because I work at Sandia, any photo I release has to go through an approval process that can take some time.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ETEM is "environmental TEM" it allows us to do things like flow gas into the microscope and look at reactions in progress. 4D STEM is a technique that collects just A TON of data and lets you understand really fine details about your samples. https://t.co/L7z0wXBcBX

tweets.text:
Hello all, good morning, I haven't had as much time to tweet this week as I had hoped, but that's good for my life here at the science factory!

As always opinions of mine do not represent SNL, DoE or NTESS.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Yesterday one of the microscopists here got some really nice images showing that I'd made particles without any surface oxidation. 

They're an intermediate of our synthesis of magnetite, which is why we're interested in them. Understanding how these convert to magnetite is good.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So the result from yesterday means today we're doing Environmental TEM on the samples. We'll be exposing these nanoparticles to gas while they're in the TEM and observing what happens. Some serious #RealTimeChem to help us understand more about our particle synthesis.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm pretty excited because it took a few tries to get the particle quality we needed. I synthesized them in a molten metal bath under nitrogen, capped them, pumped them down on my hi-vacuum line, and immediately put them in our inert glove box.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I had to build a custom nitrogen tent around the metal bath, and figure out how to get the mechanical stirrer setup so not to interfere with it and also not melt the plastic on the 350 °C metal. I wish I could post the pictures, but I'd get in a serious amount of hot water.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The nitrogen tent was needed because you do part of the reaction with your flask open under nitrogen flow to cook off some of the stuff from the precursors, so I needed a way to have an inert atmosphere around the reaction vessel while I did that.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After the reaction was done and I had them in the glovebox, I had to figure out how to purify them. Normally we use a centrifuge, so I had to track down a very tiny centrifuge that I pumped into the box.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Once I had the tiny centrifuge and some tiny centrifuge tubes in the box, it was a matter of repeatedly precipitating, centrifuging, and resuspending the particles. Over the course of 10 washes I got essentially all of the stuff we didn't want off of them.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Next our microscopist pumped a special kind of holder into the glovebox, it keeps samples inert and he used that to load our sample into the ETEM. Once it was in the instrument, it could just sit there because it's under a pretty hard vacuum.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today we're flowing gas to look at some surface reactions. We'll probably get some video, but it's 2 GB per second so we won't get long videos. We'll definitely get some high quality images every few minutes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The computer setup running this microscope (the instrument is from FEI) has a half a terabyte of RAM and a 40 TB storage setup. It can't be connected to a network for security reasons, so with huge file sizes it needs a lot of local storage.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And now I'm off for lab cleanup day! Sandia does an official shutdown from 25 Dec to 2 Jan, so my last day of work for the year is Tuesday next week. As such, we're cleaning the labs today and tomorrow so everything is in a nice state when we get back, and safe for the break.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Crystals are a pretty fascinating topic for a lot of people, but for a lot of different reasons. People recognise some things as being crystals (i.e. the image above) but not a lot of other common materials - iron / steel, rocks, many sands, etc.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Even a lot of plants have some degree of crystallinity in their cellulose fibres! But of course, this gets to what it means to be a crystal as far as scientists think: being a crystal is about being ordered and regular at the atomic and molecular scale.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Lets take a pretty common example: table salt! 

A lot of people might remember that table salt has the chemical name sodium chloride, which means it is made up of equal parts from the elements sodium and chlorine. https://t.co/KgSNgPZrfI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Salt has another name: Halite! 

Theres not a huge difference between what we call salt or halite (im sure the geologists will have something to teach me on this, but im talking broad brushstrokes). https://t.co/1Nn4N7B57I

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In both cases, when you zoom in to the atomic scale, they look like this (but obviously without colour!) https://t.co/BpWGel2qhK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The regular structure of crystals is extremely helpful for physicists like me, because it means we can mostly get away with understanding what happens in one little bit of the crystal - by the principle of symmetry it is enforced to be the same everywhere except the surface https://t.co/BlPAysaMu1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: not all materials are so simple, however. Most high temperature superconductors have a very complicated crystal structure! https://t.co/BMbIqDs1zD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @tonyver45 There really is! The mathematics of group theory was developed mostly in the early 20th century. It has very deep applications in quantum physics but also in the study of crystal structure.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
@tonyver45 You can use group theory to show, for instance, that there are only 230 possible three dimensional crystal structures! 

And by relating the symmetry of properties like magnetism and the symmetry of crystals, you can tell if a given crystal can display a particular property

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @tonyver45 This has been especially useful in studying multiferroic materials, which display magnetism AND a property called ferro electricity. There are only a handful of crystal structures which can support both

tweets.text: Okay, theres been a bit of a break because I had to change countries and the lack of sleep has left me a bit frazzled, but I am here to do my best to explain the phenomenon of magnetism! https://t.co/Fomslgeq6l

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
To start, I will take the humble bar magnet. 

And then I will do terrible things to it https://t.co/ifP0fowlAZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
What would happen if we cut our bar magnet in half? 

The universe does not permit the separate existence of a north and a south magnetic pole, so you must end up with two separate bar magnets! https://t.co/2zfL4ktJ57

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: BUT WHAT IF WE KEEP CUTTING!?! https://t.co/hHPN5N3bg6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It turns out that the very atoms in a bar magnet behave themselves like bar magnets!

If you really wanted you could keep going beyond the level of atoms, down to electrons and subatomic particles, but this is detail that isnt necessary for us. https://t.co/SZoEl3ybRd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is due to a quantum mechanical feature of particles could Spin: electrons have it, and because electrons can be either paired (with an electron that has opposite spin) or unpaired, atoms with unpaired electrons will tend to have a spin and can thus show magnetism. https://t.co/vaTWfFG8Rf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: atoms having a magnetic moment like this is fairly common, so we might wonder why more materials arent magnetic. But when we look at two atoms next to each other, theres a lot of different ways they could be aligned right? Why one and not others? https://t.co/A5bV1Vsb1K

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The detailed answer requires a pretty astonishing amount of quantum mechanical calculation, but it actually turns out you can often reduce this problem to an interaction that says: the atomic magnets want to be either parallel, or antiparallel, and antiparallel usually wins!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But this is based on a fairly simple idea where each atom only cares what the atoms right next to it are doing. What if you care about what atoms further away are doing? 

Well, then it gets very complex! But my favourite result is the spin spiral: https://t.co/cyqMnJl3le

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Spin spirals can happen for lots of reasons, but the simplest one is that you want to be antiparallel to your neighbour, and to your neighbours-neighbour (the next-nearest neighbour).

Spin spirals happen in a lot of materials, especially one with rare-earth elements.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Its also easy if you have simple geometries: you can be antiparallel to all of your neighbours in a chain, or on a square (or cube) but what about in a triangle? https://t.co/OM8Zped11j

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The triangle has two possibilities, depending on whether the little atomic magnets are free to rotate or not - we call this magnetic anisotropy, and it basically is just about whether there is a cost to change your direction and how large is that cost.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When that cost is low, we get this, and everyone is happy. https://t.co/SC9Qo1aurk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When the cost is high - when the atomic magnets can only point in a single direction and be either up or down, there is actually no nice solution at all! We call this kind of system geometrically frustrated. https://t.co/R0ZiQG6NPQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Although the atomic magnetic moments, and the interactions between them, i have talked about so far are of course a consequence of  quantum mechanics, all of the above you can understand by treating the magnetic moments as being classical objects.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When we get into quantum magnetism a bit later today, things will get much weirder https://t.co/eXDJjoAtXi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Unfortunately, we have to get a *bit* mathy here, but I will try to do this as nicely as possible. 

In the classical world, we had two atoms which had a bar magnet each, and that bar magnet could point essentially anywhere. In the language of math, these are vectors. https://t.co/9dQL4C0xpX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The equation that determines how these will behave is the Hamiltonian, which is an equation that tells you the energy of a system. The lowest energy state is what we call the ground state, and is where we would find the system at zero temperature. https://t.co/L6DRSnBK6L

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The simplest classical Hamiltonian that describes what our atomic magnets will do is this one: 

It just considers a pair of atoms, treats them like a vector, and wants to know what their dot product is (if you need a quick refresher on what that is, now is the time!) https://t.co/vpNKkavyZ0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Based on whether J is positive or negative, the lowest energy will be when the atomic magnets are either aligned or antialigned, which are the two simple cases from before. 

J is usually something we would measure, because its very hard to calculate just from quantum mechanics. https://t.co/VLZ826F8Kd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What really defines quantum mechanics is that things are quantised. Crazy, right? In the case of our atomic magnets, this means (and ill call them spins now) that they cant point in any direction, they can only point in certain directions separated by a small jump. https://t.co/diT1ShF7Mi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We are going to consider the simplest, and most quantum case, where "spin" has a maximum value of 1/2, must also have a minimum value of -1/2, and since it can only change by 1 each time, it has no other values. 

Conveniently this means i can say its pointing up or down ;) https://t.co/H0t3r2pZiR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Another consequence of us being in the quantum world is that the equation we were using before is busted. You cant use an equation based on vectors any more!

Vectors have to be replaced by these things called operators, but thankfully i can just show you what they do: https://t.co/5jPrrIes1r

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: each of the operators, when it acts on a spin, gives you something back. the Z operator gives you the spin back, but + and - flip the spin. If the + operator tries to flip an up spin up, nothing happens. if the + operator tries to flip a down spin up, you get an up spin. https://t.co/GT8qmDpbvn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another small caveat is that these operators care about who they are operating on! So where the equation above reads i and i+1, this refers so the atom on the left or the right in our picture with just two atoms. https://t.co/p9OF4v7iCy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So, now we have to consider two cases: J is positive, and J is negative. 

For J > 0 we try our regular solution before, and it gives us our trial back times its energy. https://t.co/AbDbBO6ZR4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Thats great! Thats exactly what quantum mechanics requires. https://t.co/ZOZtg3zJjL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For the solution where the spins are antialigned though, something funny happens. https://t.co/mO1vpZ992g

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It just flips our spins! This means that what is a solution in the classical case, is NOT a solution in the quantum case. 

Because the quantum world is radical, we can try other things as solutions and see if they work. The most radical solution of all is this: https://t.co/md5vs5NbcT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What we have done, is taken the quantum superposition of two different, but equally valid classical solutions, and somehow this turns out to be the right answer! But, is it still even a magnet? https://t.co/ScWnmrvhNz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The answer is tricky, but basically: not really. This superposition takes a magnet pointing in one direction, and entangles it with a magnet pointing in the opposite direction. The superposition has to average everything out to zero, so quantum mechanics has turned off magnetism!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This is just for two atoms though. What if we had a more realistic situation, like a chain, here we see a problem... 

How did we choose which atoms to pair?? https://t.co/grXbYjsFGs

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
You know theres only one way we can possibly resolve this ambiguity fairly. 

SUPERIMPOSE THEM BOTH! [evil laugh, lightning] https://t.co/Ugbf4QWKqX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This madness continues, of course, if you have atoms arranged on a lattice (like a crystal) instead of a slightly artificial chain https://t.co/b9N2S92f8w

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the end the description is very hard, because the object we call the groundstate is the superposition of VERY many different states which are themselves made up of a lot of superpositions. https://t.co/FNiMPFsRLB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But what actually is this crazy thing that ive spent a hundred tweets building towards? https://t.co/s4h4aE5qal

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We call this a Spin Liquid. It is, really, a giant quantum soup of spins which is very chaotic even at low temperatures (near absolute zero). It is a challenge to describe, but its also a big challenge to measure! 

Trying to measure and understand these is an ongoing problem. https://t.co/5pv6NMsBoh

tweets.text: I do, sometimes, a LOT of travel for my work. In a really busy year I might make as many as 10 overseas trips and several ones within the UK. This can take a toll. https://t.co/mid4NUnhDF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is especially a problem for someone like me who is very disorganised. In the last 5 years I have missed two flights due to being late (booked the wrong airport coach and was simply caught in traffic), forgotten my passport, and booked flights on the wrong day several times. https://t.co/aYpBHKIj3q

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In some cases I am *very* lucky and work pays for these mistakes. In other cases, I am severely out of pocket (usually because I'm on holiday and trying to get back for a work event like an experiment or conference, a happened this week)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is separate to social and emotional costs, like how often I go on holiday with my friends and partner but have to leave early because I have an experiment scheduled https://t.co/EZJR2BEMaX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In scattering physics, your experiments are a big deal - you have to go to a major facility and you get a certain number of days between 1 and ~10 to do your experiment. You applied to do this work competitively, and you have probably waited 6 months for this to happen... https://t.co/2DoSRRlU5U

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
And when I say days, I mean that literally. Your 6 day experiment is them giving you part of the instrument for 144 hours and if you dont have a big team, say goodbye to your sleep patterns! 

You also dont get much say in when these experiments are scheduled. https://t.co/yjxkVCy0jt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So I often find myself sneaking off during term time, carrying a big stack of marking, ready to teach the day that I crawl home however shattered I might be. https://t.co/tsIeeWrFlc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This, combined with international flights, means i cannot recommend Melatonin tablets highly enough. It is MAGICAL for adjusting your circadian rhythm and helping to mitigate jetlag or coping with night shifts. https://t.co/NgHaE1gSiH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, I should finish by saying conferences are great fun, and experimental are the lifeblood of science, but they can extract a heavy toll! Especially if you require childcare, or you cant/dont want to leave your partner or a family member for too long.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you were interested in what I had to say about magnetism yesterday, here is a fairly accessible essay about an extremely powerful technique in physics (called Renormalisation) which unites the study of liquids, alloys, and magnets into a single framework. Powerful *and* cool! https://t.co/ve1aYvPRmQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Sure Majorana Fermions are interesting, but so is Majorana himself - he vanished without a trace at age 32! https://t.co/srCPgK11Wb https://t.co/STNmrZtOeQ

tweets.text: If you were *really* interested by all this and you have a basic knowledge of @MATLAB, I can give you a copy of some Matlab routines that will calculate the properties (energy, susceptibility, correlation length, heat capacity) of the 2D Ising model as a function of temperature.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It also contains a much more exciting routine to so the same calculations for the 2D XY (or magnetic compass) model, the study of which led to the 2016 @NobelPrize in physics!

https://t.co/zSI1CFpAuj
