tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Made it! I missed Professor Seamus Davis' plenary on measuring magnetic monopoly noise in spin ice, but it was a tactical choice so I could catch up on the sleep i missed travelling yesterday, and I've had the opportunity to see Seamus give this talk recently

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So first up I get to see a talk on getting magnetism out of nonmagnetic materials! https://t.co/B6S4nmLRD9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It's quite exciting because they are doing the world using metal organic frameworks, which is something I work on in collaboration with @goodwingroupox https://t.co/I8B0rXSqU3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Theres a lot going on, because for starters they are trying to look at something similar to skyrmions, which are a peculiar magnetic phase people are looking at for magnetic memory https://t.co/CxvXgKbzdb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But to make it more exciting/ complex, they are doing it with orbital quadrupoles instead of magnetic dipoles https://t.co/46kpTRhuUa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
They have managed to show that these phases can exist theoretically, but are yet to find any systems which realise this experimentally. 

Its early days yet though! This talk was by Emma Wolpert from @UniofOxford

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Next up is the man who had my current position before I did, Dr Paul McClarty of @tudresden_de https://t.co/13FDiqh0Uv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Paul is an incredibly clever theorist, and I definitely cannot so justice to such a complex topic in tweet form, so I'll just tell you what a magnon is!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Remember yesterday we had ferromagnets? https://t.co/RoomAgPtxL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Well we said this is the ground state, which means there are some states which are "excited" states. 

If we consider our magnet to be fairly classical, these excitations are just wiggles of our atoms, a lot like vibrations

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Because what one atomic spin is doing affects what its neighboura are doing, these wiggles move along the crystal, like any other kind of wave in water, air, or a crystal vibration (which is called a phonon btw!) https://t.co/7Fmfzjig7m

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
These magnets have an energy cost, and a wavelength, and these have a complicated relationship. 

Ones with a very long wavelength have very low cost because nobody is moving very much. 

Ones with a short wavelength have a higher cost because the spins are further from home.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This gives you what we in physics call a dispersion, in this case a magnon dispersion! 

They give you very pretty pictures to show at conferences (cheating because this is data from a much more complex system, but it's one we saw yesterday!) https://t.co/jHzcMu3Mzm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The following talk is also about magnons https://t.co/LzGdPK6jgY https://t.co/QV4o1g2nm9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The kind of magnons I showed you before are what we call transverse magnons. This means that the direction the magnetic moments wobble in is perpendicular to the direction they point in.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The current case being talked about by Harry Keen from @uniofedinburgh is that of longitudinal fluctuations: this means that instead of wobbling around their axis, the spins fluctuate in size in a way that is correlated with their neighbours.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We normally ignore this, because in a lot of materials this costs far more energy than the system has access to (generally that is set by the temperature). 

But there is a case where it's very important: magnetic metals!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Side note, it was awesome to see someone cite a classic book in their talk. Importantly one that I own! https://t.co/1FeE3QhiJ5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Understanding magnetism in metals is actually very hard. The framework we used yesterday doesnt work well - you might get something that behaves similarly, but all the numbers are wrong and you can see some behaviour (like longtitudinal magnons) that you wont see in insulators.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now it's time for a talk from an old labmate of mine, Dr Matt Watson who has recently moved to @DiamondLightSou https://t.co/dTvfMZoZFK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Matt's work focuses on very thin magnets, sometimes even only a few atoms thick! 

Thats quite thin https://t.co/1Q9fJpSIVe

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: He is working on CrGeTe3, a material which has a honeycomb of Chromium atoms in its crystal structure that give rise to its magnetic properties https://t.co/J6xXeMRl48

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Matt does a technique called Angular Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy or ARPES, which basically uses the photoelectric effect to kick electrons out of a material and studies the energy and momentum of these electrons https://t.co/Apjxn29Qrx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @MySci_PK @GrapheneCA @GrapheneLabs @2DResearch @MyGraphene I thought you could use sticky tape? ;p

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here they see some really interesting results: while normally you expect the behaviour of electrons to be fairly unaffected by the magnetism (it's an insulator, these energy scales are fairly different), but instead they find the chromium electrons to change dramatically!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The energy levels and the lifetimes of the chromium electrons are completely changed when the material becomes magnetic. 

Magnetism is a very low energy phenomenon (most things become magnetic below room temperature) but metallicity is a very high energy behaviour.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It's a bit like you walking into an office block changing the very shape of the whole building!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now theres a talk from my colleague Dr Pascal Manuel at @isisneutronmuon 

Ans he is talking about spin liquids! https://t.co/LJFP0Sk5UI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Most spin liquids, he reminds us, exist in systems that have triangular arrangements of atoms. 

This is because spin liquids are very delicate, and the triangular lattice is very good at preventing a normal magnetic order from occurring https://t.co/aQ74YBnO2Q

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Something which is very important about the material he is studying: NaYbO2, is that the crystals are very perfect. 

Even 0.1% of chemical impurity or disorder can wash out or even kill your spin liquid, and in some materials this just isnt possible to avoid https://t.co/bPcaxPMJYa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This work had used a lot of different techniques because spin liquids are really tricky to understand: neutron and xray diffraction, neutron spectroscopy, heat capacity, and muon spin rotation.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And heres the money shot, they observe only diffuse excitations showing conclusively that theres no proper magnetic order, the excitations have no gap - I.e. there are excitations which cost no energy, and this is a really nice result! https://t.co/ENR2k1akyP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is kind of how you look at spin liquids though. You measure EVERYTHING, and spin liquids are a weird amorphous blob that exists only in the absence of anything else.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We now have Johnathan Bulled, also from @UniofOxford 

He is talking about Frustrated metal-organic magnets https://t.co/liaS3W7Yhm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The magnet Johnathan is looking at doesnt become magnetic till a VERY low temperature: 0.2 degrees Kelvin!   That's -272.95 degrees C or -459.3 F for people using freedom units :p https://t.co/X8UyDWW0Cs

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
What makes this material really cool (hah) is that because of the the magnetism is very frustrated there is a lot of entropy associated with  it. 

This means that if you play with a magnetic field, you can use it like a magnetic refrigerator - the magnetocalorcic effect!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And now we break for lunch!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: First up after lunch is Dr Neil Wilson from @warwickuni walking about layers of 2D materials and their electronic properties. https://t.co/XhoVZmr4mD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It's quite interesting that even though the layers are 2D and dont really fork chemical bonds, stacking layers of graphene on top of each other fundamentally changed their properties, even within the layer. https://t.co/ilEFyRPcHR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Some of the interesting changes of the properties when you stack layers on top of each other are due to complicated processes that essentially amount to quantum tunneling of electrons from one layer to another. https://t.co/vjBNkRRtXs

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Neil is also using ARPES to measure the electronic properties of these materials (mainly WSe2) 

It's a great technique for looking at what the electrons are doing, but it requires ultra high purity samples, in an ultra high vacuum, prepared meticulously to get good results.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: They have obtained a lot of really exciting results from examining what happens if you change the number of layers that are stacked on top of each other. Remember, each layer is only about one atom thick!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The experimental are also supported by quantum mechanical calculations performed on supercomputers https://t.co/tIUP2bsPf4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The main thing they have found is that the effects strongly depend on how the layers are aligned relative to each other, which thankfully they are able to control to better than 0.5 degrees. 

In graphene this has resulted in an explosion of exciting results btw!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You can probably guess why if you look at the Moire pattern formed by stacking two sheets of graphene on top of each other with a slightly different alignment: https://t.co/WRDDTFPTpv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Even though graphene is (to me, anyway) quite boring, the twisted bilayers have shown magnetism, superconductivity, insulating and metallic behaviour. It's really crazy.

tweets.text: We have another talk on layers of graphene now, from Glenn Wagner of @UniofOxford who is a theorist. https://t.co/UANelq0edL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
He is looking at what mechanism give rise to the scattering of electrons in this material. This is based on comparing his simulations to data, and his equations are a quantum version of the Boltzmann Equation 

https://t.co/Z9xsqt1ThD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
They are able to show using a very clever analysis that the sub-dominant contribution to the scattering is due to phonons (vibrations in a crystal) ruling out other options. 

They then are able to model the electrical properties as the motion of two fluids: one made of electrons https://t.co/A8vkvNBEmb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And one made of holes! Holes are a concept we have in physics that describes the absence of an electron. It nevertheless behaves a lot like an electron with positive charge.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So this means that the dominant scattering is electrostatic and basically is down to the scattering of an electron fluid and a hole fluid.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Next up we have Dr Marcin Mucha-Kruczynski from @UniofBath   talking about those amazing patterns you get from stacking two layers of graphene! https://t.co/YZiju4SUzW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Moiré patterns are really fascinating generally! 

https://t.co/sMZ6mOjqjH https://t.co/jICHQ66vhm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In this case the effect is to trick the electrons into thinking they are in a different crystal than the kind they really are. https://t.co/a5jy0P1EB3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Because the crystal symmetry has a strong effect on the properties of the electrons and the way they move, this is why the formation of these patterns has a spectacular effect on the way the electrons behave! 

https://t.co/vH7b2lw2Ua

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The late afternoon session begins with a topic which is very big here in @BristolUni - high temperature superconductors! 

This talk will be by Professor Ted Forgan, head of condensed matter here https://t.co/cNMZnbDcGJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Superconductors are pretty amazing things- conducting electricity without resistance, expelling magnetic fields, and my favourite related effect: magnetic levitation https://t.co/AHujZgrOGa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Superconductivity is pretty amazing, because before we understood really how it works, we still understood that it was caused by two electrons forming a pair that then conducts electricity without resistance.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now, given that electrons are negatively charged they should repel each other, so how could they become paired together?

The surprising answer that won the 1972 nobel prize is that they are glued together by crystal vibrations! https://t.co/cdJEtNFE1H

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The way this works is a bit funny - a negatively charged electron moves along, and disturbs the positively charged atoms of the crystal. These disturbed atoms then attract a nearby electron, and it results in an effective attraction between the electrons. https://t.co/LuX1Cf0XGd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This only works up to a point though. The normal superconductors only really work up to about 45 degrees above absolute zero, or -230 Celsius. Not very practical! https://t.co/D6tuonuSD8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Thankfully we then discovered high temperature superconductors, which are complex and usually based on copper or iron. These can superconduct up to much more useful temperatures and form the basis for hospital MRIs https://t.co/hWiA9KAmQh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The reason they work at a much higher temperature is because the glue between the electrons is not provided by crystal vibrations but instead by magnetism - the magnons which I spoke about earlier 

https://t.co/yLyVkhbrwc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We have, however, recently made some new superconductors using ultra-high-pressure methods (and they only exist at high pressures!) based on hydrogen. 

https://t.co/HEPzlgOR0w

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These are again based on vibrations to provide the pairing of electrons, but because the energy of the hydrogen vibrations is so high, they work almost at room temperature (just, not at room pressure 😭)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Next up is Dr Alexander Petsch who is also from @UniBrisPhysics talking about the importance of charge density waves in high temperature superconductors https://t.co/d3HvqpdFTf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @NotHF It was a very pedagogical talk, but unfortunately quite brief so it would have been hard to follow for the uninitiated! https://t.co/6jwZsYdRKh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Charge density waves are an unusual feature exhibited by some insulating materials, where the density of electrons varies in some direction of the crystal. https://t.co/7k25DoLT7M

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
A simple example of this might be an element like Cr which can be 2+ or 3+, but in Cr3O4 the average number of electrons per chromium is 2.666. 

There are many ways this could work out in practice, because each chromium in an insulator needs an integer number of electrons

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The charge density wave solution might have a pattern where the chromium atoms went 

3 - 3 - 2 - 3 - 3 -2 - 3 - 3 - 2

The crystal symmetry would be different here than if the arangement was simply random, because the symmetry cares about what each chromium is doing!

You can exploit this to generate a current. https://t.co/PmkBo25cSN

tweets.label: Takeover

Specifically stars within the Arches cluster in the milky way galaxy

https://t.co/ZQhpwRL4Af https://t.co/H0q6I8UcH5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This is of interest because it contains a high density of massive stars, and in particular binary massive stars. 

We want to understand these because they will eventually lead to the binary black hole mergers we have recently observed using gravitational waves.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Nearly a third of all the observed targets in the survey met criteria that suggests they are binary stars. Thats a lot! https://t.co/7ZW6txQ7hL

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: First up to talk at the #LGBTSTEMinar20 after the morning break is @Sunkensie to tell us about simulating the impact of plant levels on waterways https://t.co/aWRQMltdvU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is important because river vegetation has a profound impact on flooding, which has increased in frequency and intensity in the UK in recent years https://t.co/sUum938f7f

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: "Here is what a plant looks like in case you didnt know" https://t.co/CiOhERkvH2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
@Sunkensie's research, which uses a sophisticated 3D model of the effect of vegetation on water flow indicates that the plant coverage has a huge impact on the water flows. 

This has big implications for flooding in the future https://t.co/WXZf7zhVLu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Climate change is expected to cause the amount of water plants to peak later in the year, to coincide with autumn storms, which will create a feedback loop of worsening flooding 

(Aligators not included) https://t.co/lQoQH7O04A

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Unfortunately the answer is not just more or less plants. Fewer plants near settlements will decrease flood risk locally, but that just means worse flooding downstream.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now we have @Tuffers_c who is both gay and northern 😅

They will be talking to us about the origins of misalignment between stars and planets. https://t.co/FA4HQJM98n

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The way solar systems form normally, is why all if the planets are in the same plane, and that's the plane that the sun rotates in also. https://t.co/Ype5aocpnX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But thanks to deep space imaging like Kepler, we now know that not all solar systems are like this. Some of them are... a bit wonky. https://t.co/hnkDLZtXaW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There are a few ways this is thought to happen: the star shits alignment after the disk that will eventually become planets has formed. 

Something happens to a planet that changes its axis.

Or the disk forms in a completely unusual way.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The data for the alignment between stars and its planetary orbits is quite sparse, because it is hard to measure and may take decades of observation. There are only 15 extrasolar systems characterised properly.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Statistical analysis indicates that the number of misaligned systems may not be unusual, but their degree of misalignment is very difficult to understand.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: First up after lunch at the #LGBTSTEMinar20 is an address from Professor Tim Softley FRS, the PVC of research @unibirmingham affirming that the new british government will commit us to a strong investment in scientific endeavour, to uproarious laughter and applause.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now we have a talk on autophagy and motor neurone disease, which I am glad we have after lunch, given by @mattjaywhy #LGBTSTEMinar20 https://t.co/ZwP7JN92qw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
MND or ALS is a terrible disease. Famously Professor Stephen Hawking suffered from it, but he was very lucky - he lived 55 years after his diagnosis which is far longer than most. 

https://t.co/Y7kC8zmlwJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @JostMigenda We needed the laugh 😅

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Neurons are also wild. And somehow, huge! 

The nerve fibres called Axons may stretch the whole length of the body https://t.co/djms6dRTKC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Neurons are very large and long-lived cells. Autophagy is the process whereby cells eat some of the broken parts or bits which arent necessary anymore. Neurons therefore have an important balance between growing new parts and eating old or broken parts https://t.co/W32SJtCjcn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When the balance is broken, and autophagy happens too much or in the wrong way, this can lead to diseases that affect the brain, especially ones like Motor Neurone Disease

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It's also a problem when you turn off autophagy! This can lead to neurons growing too long, which leads to other disorders.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now the #LGBTSTEMinar20 gets some supersymmetey from @GeeknProud42 https://t.co/WkNgseuJzA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @MarinaLogares @PRISMAciencia Sorry! This is what I thought might be the case but I was in a rush 😅

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Important note: this talk is making use of text-to-speech technology, and we had a brief technical glitch setting it up but now it's working great. 

A question for conference organisers: would your conference be able to support this?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The standard model has 3 generations of fermionic particles, force carrying bosons, and the higgs. https://t.co/sx8awZDijW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Gluons are some of the most important, because they bind quarks together into protons and neutrons and hence atoms. And are not to be confused with some warlike races from the star trek universe https://t.co/fCHNvrhe5Z

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But the standard model has to be incomplete, because it seems to account for only 5% of the universe, there is seemingly a lot of missing energy and matter. It also cannot explain why we are all made of regular matter and there isnt really any antimatter floating around. https://t.co/tgctWnWtJB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Supersymmetry is a model which might solve some of these problems. It posits the existence of a super-partner particle for every known particle, which is almost the same as every particle but much heavier. https://t.co/svExbIU1BS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: They also have TERRIBLE names. For every particle there is a supersymmetric sparticle. For the quarks, their super-partners are the squarks, and for the top quark, there  is the stop quark. https://t.co/QsssmqUS0B

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Many people hope that this would provide a complete picture of the universe, because if it isnt, we should all give up and go to the pub 😅 https://t.co/YopamuPU5T

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The final talk of this post lunch session at #LGBTSTEMinar20 is from Jon Davies talking about the variation of gene regulation in brain development and autism spectrum disorder https://t.co/1TbkluR2f4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This talk is mainly about the phenomenon of epigenetics. If genetics is the blueprint, epigenetics is the person reading the blueprint to build an ikea table but maybe sometimes making it into a bookshelf. https://t.co/IwTnaEVAQz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
All of your cells have the same genes, but epigenetics is what determines whether a stem cell becomes a muscle cell, or a skin cell, or a brain cell, etc. 

This is important because twins have the same genes, but in 70% with autism spectrum disorder of twins only one has it

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This means there must be an epigenetic component. If it was just down to your genes, then it would always be both or neither. 

This is actually true of many diseases and conditions which are known to have a genetic component.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Terrifying takeaway from this talk: by examining your genes people can tell if you have smoked, drunk alcohol, or taken drugs. They leave a permanent mark on your body which is part of your epigenetics!

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.text: Now we break the #LGBTSTEMinar20 into two parallel sessions. I will be in the session "creating and running LGBTQ+ STEMM Networks" cohosted by @PRISMexeter and @Birminghamostem

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After the breakout panel we have @GayRollerCEng giving us the lowdown on the nuclear robots she builds today at the #LGBTSTEMinar20 https://t.co/K7HqXzbmEi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These robots are meant to assist in fusion power plants, like the tokamak under construction at ITER https://t.co/Bd9oXeoS1H

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The heat involved in fusion power is immense, the plasma is about 15 million degrees. This is wrapped in coils of superconducting magnets at -270 degrees. That's quite a huge difference! https://t.co/TjLXEC7W53

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It's difficult enough containing that heat, but fusion also produces a lot of neutrons.

When neutrons smash into materials, they dont just make them radioactive, they leave behind damage at the atomic level which makes the material brittle https://t.co/gXUwz384hi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Theres also a lot of radiation flying around. Radiation is usually pretty bad 😅 https://t.co/RGzQue0UKe

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As a result of all this radiation, we would like to use robots to do work inside the fusion reactors! https://t.co/I75daZClXj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These robots need to be able lift 80 tonnes, be incredibly precise, and all their parts need to be easily replaceable.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Basically: It's really hard! https://t.co/OAn101qt2X

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But its worth it. For the amount of lithium in your phone battery, and a bathtub full of seawater, you could have power for 40 years. 

It's also quite safe! Fusion power plants basically just stop working when they go wrong. They safely turn off. https://t.co/l1VOB53TUH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Why do we not have fusion yet? Mostly money. ITER will cost about 20 billion, and if we spent more we could have it faster. 

For reference the soccer world cup in Quatar will cost 150 billion. https://t.co/11ULb8k6Ql

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Also @GayRollerCEng is REALLY funny. https://t.co/0xfA2sm5o4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The final talk of the day for the #LGBTSTEMinar20 is by @Dr_KTaylor talking about the relationship between HIV and a heart disease https://t.co/07DyEBwJBk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It is quite difficult for people of my generation and later to really understand what it was like living through the epidemic of the early 80s. 

It's also impossible to overstate the importance of activism in forcing action on the epidemic from the establishment https://t.co/OZH1vjnPo8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It's also amazing to note that almost half of all people diagnosed with HIV are women, despite the association with gay men. Although this ignorance around infections in women led to the phrase "women dont get aids, they just die from it"

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The world has moved on greatly from this. We now have PrEP, PEP, and antiretrovirals that enable people to avoid infection or live a normal lifespan once infected. 

However, antiretrovirals are associated with an increased risk of heart failure.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In order to avoid complicating lifestyle factors, @Dr_KTaylor studies blood of people who do not have HIV and how antiretroviral drugs affect blood clotting.

Knowing these effects would enable therapies to be tailored to avoid damaging heard health.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Additionally thanks to these medications (undetectable = untransmissible, and PrEP preventing infections) we are on the verge of ending the HIV epidemic

tweets.text: Let me share a bit about myself before we indulge into the field of nanophotonics. I am a Ph.D. student at Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Trivandrum, India. I work in the area of microwave photonics. I am not exactly a nanotech person so why am I here?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Microwave Photonics as a field is a convulsion of Photonics and microwave engineering. While I don't tinker with anything at the nanoscale level, the work that I do has applications in nanotechnology.
#nanophotonics #microwave #photonics #scicomm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I work of creating proof of concept experiments in the field of Photonics. One primary example is the creation of notch filter for use in satellite communication and RADAR. But I do these experiments with the help of kilometers of optical fibers. https://t.co/9j1WOEOUdv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But if these concepts have to be employed for creating a device for employment in field, then optical fibers cannot be used for they become bulky. Thus there is a need to miniaturize them and thus we go to the nano regime. #nanophotonics #photonics #scicomm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
That's a bit about me and I will tell more about myself in the coming days. Now that I have introduced myself, let us see what I have in store for you all today. 

Well, we will be looking at how the world of nanophotonics emerged and why it is so important? #nanophotonics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In 2k15, we celebrated the international year of light. It marked the anniversary of many great achievements in the field of optics. It was 150 years since Maxwell came up with electromagnetism and 100 years since Einstein's General relativity. #optics #light

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We are quite familiar with the way optics work. We use glasses and mirrors on a day to day basis. Phenomena such as reflection and refraction can be seen with naked eye. #optics #light

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As time passed, the race to make a strong light source began. The light beam should be of single colour and coherent (analogous to two people walking in phase). Thus the race to make lasers began! #optics #lasers #photonics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But that was not it. There was a necessity to carry data over long distances and hence a new form of cable was invented - fiber optic cable. It then became faster and more efficient to transmit signals over fiber optic cables than copper wire. #fiberoptics #light #data

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The field of fiber optics thus emerged - a way to guide light using fibers! Fiber optics finds application in a variety of fields such as sensing, medical diagnosis, apart from optical communication. #fiberoptics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: With the dawn of #fiberoptics emerged yet another interesting field called #photonics. Photonics is about the generation, detection, and manipulation of #photons.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Optical fibers are capable of transmitting data over long distances and is the backbone of today's internet. Every smartphone manufacturing has something to do with Photonics. Lithography uses laser to etch out micro patterns, optics are used in display, etc.. #fiberoptics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So what is #nanophotonics? While so far, #photonics has been used in technology to create devices, the next leap is to see what will happen if light is allowed to interact with matter at the nanoscale level.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 21st century saw the convulsion of of nanotechnology and photonics. Nanophotonics emerged and revolutionized the way we look at light. #nanophotonics #light

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So what is a nanometer? You take a meter scale and split it a billion times and then look at just one unit. That's nanoscale! #nanophotonics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At this scale, light does not behave as it behaves at higher scales. The physical structure of the matter with which it starts interacting comes into picture. #nanophotonics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So how do we induce interactions between light and matter at nanoscale level. There are two ways to do it. One, confine light to dimensions that are smaller than the wavelength of light and two, confine matter to nano dimensions. #nanophotonics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Some prominent areas where nanophotonics has tremendous applications are spectroscopy, optical communication, solar cells, etc. We will look at them in more detail from tomorrow.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's a brief story of how nanophotonics emerged. Do you have any question? #nanophotonics https://t.co/cM3zv2R5Ce

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I will meet you all tomorrow with more nanostuff. Stay tuned! https://t.co/Lhu55suYbx

tweets.text: Hey all! Good evening! Today, let us talk about nanophotonics that is bioinspired. We will talk about photonic crystals, chemical linking, and biomaterials. #nanophotonics #bioinspired https://t.co/cG2ZHJqzMJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Nanophotonic structures can be found everywhere in nature. Some examples include the wings of Morpho butterfly, moth eye, and beetle's cuticle. #nanophotonics #bioinspired

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What is the reason for such nanophotonic structures to occur in nature? #nanophotonics #bioinspired https://t.co/tV2ofHayYz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In nature, we have both preys and predators. Some moths have evolutionarily developed an anti-reflective ability on the eyes, thanks to the presence of nanophotonic structures. This prevents visible light from being reflected off moths' eyes and thus helps moths to escape.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So what is there to be inspired from the moth eyes? #nanophotonics #biomimicry https://t.co/QsYHzUAVQl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Scientists are now designing novel procedures to construct a nano sphere monolayer using several deposition and plasma techniques. The biomimicked structure can now be applied to solar cells, monitors, and LEDs. #nanophotonics #biomimicry

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let me give some more examples. For improving light extraction from LEDs, directionally controlled fluorescence emission in butterflies has been an inspiration. #nanophotonics #biomimicry #butterflies https://t.co/F1DarR9iXA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another example is that of a chameleon's skin which has a dynamically toned periodic two dimensional structure. #nanophotonics #biomimicry https://t.co/jX0UW7oIDV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Biomimicking certain natural nanophotonic structures has avoided overheating in hot climates. For example, desert ants have surfaces covered with nanostructures which reflect off light and hence they can search for food without feeling the heat. #nanophotonics #biomimicry https://t.co/QigizY0dXJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But is it easy to develop these nanostructures in lab? #nanophotonics #biomimicry Not really and thus we again look into nature itself for solution.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The answer to the question is a process called biotemplating. With this technique, researchers exploit natural biological materials for creating replica of their highly ordered morphologies. #nanophotonics #biomimicry

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Nature has also inspired the development of photonic components such as lasers and mirrors. The question we need to ask is why we need biocompatible and nanoscale photonic components? #nanophotonics #biomimicry

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Optical technology is essential for rapid and efficient delivery of healthcare to patients. Hence there is a need to miniaturize devices that can be implanted in patients for continuous monitoring. #nanophotonics #healthcare #bioinspired

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Optical components such as diffraction gratings, photonic crystals, plasmonic devices, and photodetectors have been designed based on the natural world. #nanophotonics #nature #opticalcomponents

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #silk has been used to create a micro prism reflector array that acts as a diffraction grating. The grating had been used for imaging and sensing. #nanophotonics #bioinspired

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Three dimensional photonic crystals have been fabricated with the help of silk. These shows iridescence when used inside biological tissue which can be used for refractive index measurement and for laser induced heating. #nanophotonics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A lot of biomaterials fluoresce and a few of them have quantum yield which makes them suitable for use as optical gain media which is of prime importance in creating lasers. #nanophotonics #nature #lasers

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Biopolymers in thin film form can be used as cavity mirrors which are again important for creating nanoscale lasers that are biologically compatible. #nanophotonics #lasers

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: With the combination of such nanoscale gain media and cavity mirrors, one can efficiently create nanoscale lasers that can be implanted in patients for sensing and diagnostic purposes. #nanophotonics #lasers

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: With this we come to the end of today's session. Any doubts? Is there anything else you would like to know regarding bioinspiration in Photonics? Do ask. See you tomorrow! #nanophotonics #bioinspired https://t.co/HNmv8aZJfI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Good evening people! I hope you all are having a great day :) It is time to begin today's session. Today, we will talk about nanoscale quantum optics! #nanophotonics #quantumoptics #light https://t.co/A4cK2WWSUy

tweets.label: Takeover
Takeover
tweets.text: On monday, we talked about how photonic technologies are important for us. To better develop these systems at the nanoscale level, we need to understand the fundamental laws of quantum physics. Nanoscale quantum optics is all about that. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics #light

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These sophisticated technologies are of use for our well being such as health care, security, and economic growth. Photonic devices have gained prominent importance over other technologies, thanks to the advantages they offer at the quantum level. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Light based processes such as absorption, propagation, and even light storage can be exploited at the quantum level. But the interaction of single photons with matter at nanoscale level is very weak. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics #light

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This dearth is obstacle for creating a rapport between quantum physics and photonic devices. Nanophotonics, as as field, addresses these issues by funneling down light to nanoscale dimensions. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: On overcoming the challenges, we can see significant breakthroughs in the field of sensing, metrology, information processing at the quantum and classical level, etc. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics #light

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let us look at what the current scenario is like in this area of research. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics #lightmatter

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The first focus has been on the creation of novel materials like graphene, silicon, and meta materials that can be used for probing light matter interaction at the nanoscale level. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The next focus is on devices that will be used for facilitating and controlling strong light matter interaction. Some examples of this include photonic integrated circuits, nanofibers, plasmonic structures, and superconductors. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now that we know the possible materials and devices, the next aspect is to look into quantum degrees of freedom. For this, color centers in solids, ions, and neutral atoms have been used. For single photon sources, organic molecules, 2D materials are used.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This is an example of a fully integrated quantum circuit. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics
Cred: Agio M. https://t.co/lwaMFdS9Vw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To funnel light to nanoscale dimensions, one uses metamaterial which unlike conventional material such as glass does not possess a positive index of refraction. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The origin of such a behaviour for metamaterials is due to rationally designed geometry, composition, and arrangement of nanostructured building blocks. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: By using single photons for switching and routing through the exploitation of quantum mechanical phenomena, one can have efficient computing in the future. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When combined with tiny optical emitters, metamaterials could make possible a hybrid technology that uses quantum light in future computers. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Computers that operate on quantum optics would exploit qubits which exist in both the on and off state simultaneously. #nanophotonics #quantumoptics https://t.co/3g1AY7GzLF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The prowess of employing qubits is that it enhances the computer's power and memory, thereby increasing it's working capacity. #nanophotonics #QuantumComputing https://t.co/nGBNIyUCtY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That is just a brief introduction to quantum optics at the nanoscale level. If you would like to know more, do let me know! Until then, bye people! #nanophotonics #quantumoptics https://t.co/dfon8NjvTi

tweets.text: Hey tweeps! How is the day treating you so far? I had a long day and I will be winding it up with this Twitter session. Here is what we are going to look at. Are we facing a telecommunication crunch? #nanophotonics #optics #telecommunication #data

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you are reading tweet on your phone or your laptop, thank optical physicists. The world of internet is revolutionized by optical principles. #telecommunication #optics #data #internet

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: While browsing, your computer converts the human language into electrical signals. These electrical signals are then converted into optical signal through a certain optical process. The optical signal reaches the server to collect information and returns back to the computer.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The optical signals are light pulses generated using lasers and the medium which carry these signals back and forth are called fiber optic cables. #telecommunication #optics #data #internet #nanophotonics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The cables carry light through total internal reflection which is a process by which light gets guided inside the fiber. The fibers are referred to as single mode fiber since they have the capacity to support just one mode of the light. #fiberoptics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Though the information travels at the speed of light, encoding data onto light and processing them affects data speeds. #telecommunication #data #internet

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Apart from that, we do not have the capacity to meet the growing demands for faster internet and more channels. We are already at the verge of using the visible light bandwidth. #telecommunication #fiberoptics #data #internet

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, there are two missing links to achieve ultrafast, broadband transmission. 1. To enhance the amount of data transferred and 2. To enhance the processing of signals at launch and output. #nanophotonics #telecommunication #internet

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let us look at the issues one by one. To enhance the amount of data that can be transferred, the way is to let the optical fibers carry more modes. So instead of encoding data just on light's spectrum, it is essential to look at other properties that can be exploited.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The oscillation or shape of light are other parameters that can be used to encode data. This way, we can make use of the several modes at the same time without any interference. #telecommunication #nanophotonics #data

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The idea is to twist the light beam into a spiral to increase its capacity. This is referred to as light in a state of orbital angular momentum. #telecommunication #data

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But how to improve the encoding process. For that, a nanophotonic chip designed by RMIT's laboratory comes into picture. #nanophotonics #data #internet

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The miniature chip is designed to separate different orbital angular momentum states of light in a continuous order and to decode the information carried by twisted light. #nanophotonics #telecommunication #internet

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Previously, this would call for instruments the size of a table which we know is not practical for telecommunication. So the researchers use topological nano sheets a fraction of a millimeter and they fit well on the end of an optical fiber. #nanophotonics #telecommunication

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another main advantage is that the material used in the device is compatible with silicon based materials used in the telecommunication industry. #telecommunication #nanophotonics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The technology is of high performance, low cost and tiny size and makes it a viable application for the next generation of broadband optical communications.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It is demonstrated that the processing speed has been increased by about 100 times which is quite exciting for the telecommunication sector. #telecommunication #nanophotonics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So yay! It is going to be all the more better soon! With this, I sign off for today. https://t.co/GoBOH3slzf

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5. Nanoscale imaging involving probes, optical antennas or super-lens techniques to image beyond the diffraction limit. #nanophotonics #imaging

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 6. Molecular scale sensors using nanophotonic technology to offer single-molecule detection and identification. #nanophotonics #sensing

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
7. Nanotagging, in which metamaterials and nanostructured barcodes can be used to combat counterfeiting.
#nanophotonics #barcodes

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 8. LEDs and solar cells, where nano structuring can be used to optimize the emission and absorption of light. #nanophotonics #efficiency

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover

#visuallyimpaired

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another common challenge is to convince the importance of #scicomm. Most of the time, the efforts of science communicators go unnoticed. In a university or college, professors don't appreciate the idea of their students taking part in science communication activities.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Oftentimes, I have felt confident about concepts that I have explained school students before writing a paper. This raises another important question. How well do we write our scientific and technical papers?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My personal opinion is that a scientific paper should read like a story instead of an agglomeration of random facts that are results of an experiment. Just ripping off content and putting them under titles such as 'introduction', 'results' doesn't make a paper appealing. #scicomm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is something which is usually ignored as a result of which the difficulty arises to read a lit of scientific papers. #scicomm

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover

Hey Twitter! Sorry I’m late to start this Monday party! 

I, @itskameronyall, will be curating @RealSci_Nano this week, so it’s only fair I introduce myself and tell you what I do. 

(A thread)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I grew up in the heart of Cajun country, in south Louisiana. 

I went to my local state flagship university, @LSU (#GEAUXTIGERS). 

Which, by the way, let me say—public schools are important. Call your state legislators and tell them how important your public unis are!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
While I was at LSU, we faced several incredibly painful budget cuts that caused tuition to go up (RAPIDLY) and cut services on campus. 

I majored in biological engineering. Three major memories stick out to me, and some minor ones.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 1, I was very active in my schools LGBTQ group, @SpectrumLSU. This was a major part of our social lives in the capital of a very conservative state. Do you part to create a supportive community for those around you!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
2. It is hard to understate how jealous I was of schools with more resources (and we had decent resources!). I really wanted to major in biomedical engineering, but the major wasn’t offered. Luckily...

3. I was able to do undergrad research in a tissue engineering lab...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ...where we studied nanocomposite materials and how they interacted with cells. I learned analytical techniques like scanning electron microscopy, which lets us look at extremely small things.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I also had the opportunity to do some cool undergraduate research in the chemistry department, where we studied how flame retardant particles were distributed in plastic, and how these particles moved and dissolved under heating.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: THE TECHNIQUE TO DO THIS WAS NUTS!!! My prof built a μ-CT using the X Ray emissions of a synchrotron at the Louisiana Center for Advanced Microstructures and Devices. This is basically a giant ring in which electrons in a vacuum tube are accelerated to a significant fraction...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ...of the speed of light. Giant electromagnets bend the electrons back into the ring. Every time the electrons get bent, they let out a stream of high energy photons called bremsstrahlung. We used these photons to take projection Xrays of our sample, then turn it a bit & repeat

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This gave us projections which were then reconstructed into micron scale 3D reconstructions. This was my introduction to computational image analysis, a set of techniques I turn to time and time again.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Eventually, I applied to graduate schools all over the country. I knew I was interested in nano, biomedical engineering, tissue engineering, and drug delivery. I wanted to make an impact on human health.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: With some fantastic mentorship from a prof in my dept, I wrote a successful @NSFGRFP application. Before getting the fellowship, I wasn’t sure I wanted to go to grad school.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In fact, this is a lesson I’d like to share with you: let life make some important decisions for you, and don’t fight it. If a pretty door opens, walk through it. (But think about what kind of doors you’re looking for, and keep an eye out)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So I visit some grad schools and after a couple visits I’m told I won this fellowship. Lucky for me, I had REALLY enjoyed my visit to @VandyBME and decided to join @Duvall_Lab_VU where I got to study nanoscale drug delivery. A dream come true!

tweets.text: Not only did I get to spend those years learning about self assembling polymers that form nanoscale drug delivery vehicles, but I got the opportunity to build a broad base of knowledge in several different areas.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I think that’s about enough ancient history, let’s talk about more recent stuff. 

My PhD research resulted in 3 research stories, and I’ll give you the short summary.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But first: some scientific background.  

A variety of molecules could be great medicines, but they’re not very effective because of specific cellular barriers that evolution has created. The one I have spent the most time thinking about is the endosomal membrane.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You can think of the endosome as a little cell stomach. It’s the digestive system for a cell. Our craziest drugs made of nucleic acid’s and proteins get destroyed here. The focus of my PhD lab was to get those drugs out of the endosome and into the cell where they can be active

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A previous grad student had developed a nanoscale drug delivery system for peptides that worked really well. It was my job to figure out how it worked so well, and we did! We used pharmacologic techniques as well as SEM and TEM to figure out how our nanoparticles worked

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Along the way, I was really frustrated by how hard this research was. We discovered a paper another lab had published showing a protein called Gal8 works to find damaged endosomes. When we watched fluorescent Gal8, it went straight to disrupted endosomes!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We still weren’t really satisfied with this system, so we thought about how to improve it. We then created a split Luciferase system wherein a luciferase enzyme becomes bioactive upon endosomal disruption. We can now measure endosomal disruption in even higher throughput!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We recently submitted this manuscript as a pre-print, the first ever from that group! You can read all about it over at @biorxivpreprint !

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As I finished up my PhD (defended July 28! Woohoo!), I applied for industry jobs all over the country and eventually settled on an industry postdoc doing cutting edge research with protein therapeutics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: with @JanssenUS here in La Jolla where I have the coooooolest project, exploring new applications of our tech. Hopefully I’ll be able to share this work when we have a paper in the next couple years!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Biology is made of large molecules. DNA is used to make mRNA and mRNA is used to make proteins. Proteins fold up and do useful stuff. Cells use proteins to talk to each other. 

Sometimes, proteins misbehave, due to improper instructions from the DNA or the RNA.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We've come a long way in terms of understanding what genes can cause disease, but what if there were a way to turn off diseases by turning off the bad gene?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
That's exactly what some types of intracellular-acting medicines do! 

Therapies like antisense oligonucleotides, small interfering RNAs, and even gene editing platforms like CRISPR, TALENS, and ZFNs can be used to reprogram cells from the inside out.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Unfortunately, those things are stuck on the outside of cells. And if they do enter cells, they're probably stuck in an endosome. My PhD research looked at the molecular mechanisms of these processes, to understand how we could engineer smarter nanoparticles...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
to break down endosomal membranes to deliver drugs to the inside of cells.

https://t.co/FrQaddOTSQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Personally, I think viruses are definitely nanoparticles, and they're more efficient at getting foreign DNA into our cells that anything humans have invented! 

Viruses are the ultimate "smart" nanoparticle.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Viruses are used to reprogram cells for therapies, like CAR-T cells, which use synthetic lentivirus to reprogram T-cells to turn them into cancer killing machines. There are two CAR-T cell therapies on the market today! Amazing stuff!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There are also viruses being used to give patients a shot at a normal life, by giving them a gene they were born without. Truly, truly, crazy! 

There are two FDA approved viruses. One delivers RPE65 gene to the retinal pigmented epithelium, which literally cures blindness!!!!!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The other gives patients back SMN1 gene. Babes born with broken SMN1 will never sit up on their own. Most don't survive to their second birthday. In the clinical trial, 10 of the 21 patients could sit on their own for >30 seconds. 

AMAZING.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, in my opinion, viruses are some of the oldest nanoparticles on earth!

tweets.text: I've been thinking about this a lot lately, but I think that when peer reviewers request additional experiments "to improve impact" (rather than to support unsupported claims), authors should withdraw the manuscript and resubmit to higher impact journals.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The editor screens for interest and impact. 
The peer reviewers screen for solid science, sound methods, and well-supported claims. 

If my paper clearly says "XYZ in mice" and reviewers ask me for data in human cells/tissue, the scope of the paper has now changed.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Peer review is broken. Rather than focusing on whether claims are well-supported, reviewers often ask for new experiments to expand the impact/scope of the paper. 

Suggestions are welcome, but almost any critique of the manuscript should be addressable by either:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
1. Doing a "killer" experiment that was not performed, i.e., was the central hypothesis directly tested or not?

2. Removing / weakening the claim. If the claim is central to the paper, see 1. 

All too often, authors say "We show ABC" and reviewers ask "but can you show DEF?"

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This back and forth dance slows down science and cloisters results. 

My last published paper took ~13 months from first submission to the first journal to final acceptance in a second.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We had 7 peer reviewers at the second journal. Their comments certainly polished the manuscript and broadened its impact. But I don't believe the additional experiments substantially strengthened the central claim.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So, 13 months from 1st submission to acceptance. 

My most recent manuscript? It was about 13 months **from conception** to pre-print. Those results are there for the world to see and can stand on their own merits.

tweets.text: Today I’m going to attempt to answer the question “what is soft matter”? The term covers a huge variety of systems and I’m only going to touch on a few of my favourite ones. I guess the flippant answer is soft matter is condensed matter that is soft

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What do I mean by soft? It’s not very obvious. E.g., if you have a plastic bottle of liquid soap, both the packaging and the soap fall under soft matter despite seeming to have very different material properties. So what do these 2 materials have in common to both be soft matter? https://t.co/bYwlPY5TBy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we consider the two at the mesoscopic level, somewhere between the nanoscale (i.e. size of an atom) and micron size (i.e. visible under a microscope), they share a number of similarities. Both have physical structures on this level that determine the overall properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In both cases the mesostructure can be deformed with relatively little energy, on the scale with thermal energy at room temperature. This is why the soap is “liquid”, and the bottle can be produced at easily accessible temperatures.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These mesostructures can make it difficult to predict the physical properties from molecular composition alone – and (to me) this is what makes soft matter so interesting! The term “soft matter” can cover a huge range of materials, across all areas of our daily lives.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: From make-up to tires, even mobile phone screens, all wouldn’t be possible without soft matter somewhere. With so much variation, this is a huge and vibrant field of research. Personally, I’ve been involved with work on liquid crystals, surfactants (like in the soap) and polymers https://t.co/g3C48u4dqy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Happy Tuesday everyone! In my opinion the worst day of the week. So to brighten it up today I’m going to talk a bit about the type of simulations I use to investigate soft matter. Simulations are basically virtual experiments that run “in silico”, i.e. on a computer. 1/13

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As with “wet” science, there is a vast range of possible approaches, so I’m just going to talk about my little corner of them. I use virtual beads to represent atoms (or groups of atoms). Deciding how to model different interactions depends on what you are interested in. 2/13

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Each bead you model costs computer processing power and it is currently not possible to model huge systems at an atomic level (i.e. one bead per atom). So you have to choose your model based on the length and time scale you are interested in. 3/13 https://t.co/qQFIDARdVg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you want to look at the interaction between a few molecules, it is easy to represent each atom separately. That’s what I did in this paper looking at polymer actuation. https://t.co/kcTxClez2T 4/13

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you want to look at a much larger system, you might not care what all the individual atoms are doing and you might represent a group of atoms as a single bead. This means that instead of the atomic scale, you can look on a mesoscale. https://t.co/jm7XK2rFsy 5/13

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: On an even larger scale you might not be interested in what the single molecules are doing and you model a group of molecules as a single bead. This is what I did for my PhD, we looked at micron-sized liquid crystal bubbles.  https://t.co/lODKIYZwek 6/13

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Deciding the model is a very important part, you put rubbish in you get rubbish out. There are a huge number of papers purely on model (also called force field) development. 7/13 https://t.co/Gin5dryFae

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of the trickiest things to model is water! Given the ubiquitous nature of water, a wide number of models exist (and are still being developed). No one model captures it perfectly and you have to carefully chose given what physical property you are interested in. 8/13

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: With all this difficulty in selecting a model, why bother doing it at all? In the lab, we know what water is and the melting temperature of ice. There are loads of really good reasons! 1. I’d be out of a job if we did that! 9/13

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2. It is very difficult to know what is going on at the mesoscale experimentally. In the lab there may be impurities, the conditions at a specific point might not be known exactly. It’s possible to control all these things precisely in simulations. 10/13

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3. We can see how changing one specific attribute can affect the system -e.g. changing a methyl group to a t-butyl group. This is much easier to do in simulations than having to do a whole new synthesis. 11/13

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4. It gives information that might be very difficult (or even impossible) to know experimentally, such as how much energy it takes to break a micelle or how the molecules align in a liquid crystal phase. 12/13

tweets.text: Hi everyone! Today I’m going to talk about liquid crystals, seemingly an oxymoron. How can crystals be liquid? Well, liquid crystal is actually a term for any state of matter that flows like a liquid but has some form of long range order. 1/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The term liquid crystal (LC) actually covers lots of different phases. Broadly LC’s fall into two types, lyotropic and thermotropic. Today I’m going to focus on thermotropic – these are materials whose phase depends on the temperature (and pressure).  2/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One thing all LC molecules have in common is some form of anisotropy, shape being a common one. For example, rod-like or disc-like molecules often form LC phases. This phenomenon isn’t unique to the molecular scale, anisotropic colloids can form LC phases. 3/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You can even see LC ordering on a much bigger scale, a pile of coins or tree trunks floating down the river. 4/15 https://t.co/NgjBEZd7ey

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The most disordered phase is called the nematic phase where all the molecules (say) point in average in one direction but have no positional order. This long range order but low viscosity means that the nematic phase has a number of unique and interesting properties. 5/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For example, it is birefringent meaning it a different refractive index depending on the orientation of the molecule. This can lead to beautiful images under cross polarisers 6/15. (check out https://t.co/4CohduyQcx for some cool photos).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The direction that the molecules tend to point in can be influenced by a number of things, including surface treatment and applying a voltage. When doped with a small amount of chiral material, it causes a helical twist; like stacking tables that start to twist as they stack. https://t.co/z6dQB9xR5C

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now this is where things start to get even. This twist can actually guide light! And this is the basis for a lot of LCD displays. I found this awesome gif but couldn’t find who made it – if you know please tell me! 8/15 https://t.co/kqnYBBhDCL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here the LC is sandwiched between cross polarisers. Without a voltage there is a twist in the molecules and the light can pass through. When a voltage is applied, this causes the twist to disappear and the light can no longer pass through the second polariser, appearing dark.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: During my PhD I investigated what would happen when you confine the nematic (and chiral nematic) phase in bubbles of various geometries, including shells and toroids (donut-shaped). By confining the LC, you can induce (and hopefully control) defects in the fluid. 10/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: With planar anchoring the molecules lay flat at the surface and it’s physically impossible to cover a sphere with rods, similarly to this spherical dog. These ‘partings’ or defects are regions of disorder that have different properties to the surrounding nematic phase. 11/15 https://t.co/JlFfSo0moK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For example, they show up as black under cross polarisers. But remember, they are not “physical” objects and are free to move. We found that you can control the position, type and number of defects by varying in the shell thickness and the chiral pitch length. 12/15 https://t.co/RnY7fvSPR6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of the nicest findings from my PhD work was that I predicted a transition from 4 to 2 defects as the chiral pitch length decreased which was later confirmed from experiments. Predictions like this is one of the ultimate goals of doing simulations! 13/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I’ve written a short intro into this paper here: https://t.co/mEPUoNyUnB that explains the findings and importance in plain English. 14/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And I’m going to leave it there today. There is so much I haven’t touched on, I’ve only really talked about a small bit of the most disordered phase. I didn’t even get to put in my gif of a mood ring! (Also based on LCs!). 15/15 https://t.co/WGNwoR8x6R

tweets.text: Happy Friday everyone! We’ve finally made it to the end of the week. Today I want to talk today a bit about something I’m currently working on – surfactants. They are super useful in everyday life and are found in a lot of household products. 1/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All surfactants have the same basic molecular structure with a long water-hating (hydrophobic) tail joined to a water-loving (hydrophilic) head group. 2/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This duality of behaviour causes surfactants to self-assemble in water. These phases can have long range order, or no order. In fact, phases with long range order are an example of the (other type) of liquid crystal phases. 3/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These systems are called lyotropic liquid crystals, and again covers a range of different phases but I don’t want to go into that today. If you want to learn more about them, there’s a good video here: https://t.co/3QGOgEvuJ2 4/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My current work looks at isotropic surfactant systems, that’s systems with no long range order. I work as part of @cafe4dm. The systems I’m specifically interested in are shampoo! 5/15 https://t.co/NXCAA2E47i

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of the most common ingredients in shampoo is SLES (aka sodium laurylethoxysulfate) is one of the most important ingredients in shampoo and shower gel - pick up a bottle and it is very likely to be the second ingredient listed after water! 6/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: SLES has a charged head group, which means that the salt concentration of the liquid affects the self-assembly. We use computer simulations to investigate what the phases look like. In particular we are interested in how these affect the thickness (viscosity) of the fluid. 7/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We recently published the phase diagram of SLES, you can read a “plain English” summary here https://t.co/ZTqJzVXOFu. Most of this work that I’m going to talk about was actually done by Maria Panoukidou, a PhD student in the group. 8/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At low salt concentration, the surfactants assemble into spherical aggregates known as micelles, protecting the water-hating tails from the water whilst exposing the water-loving head groups to it. This complex fluid is a similar thickness to water. 9/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As the salt concentration increases the interactions between the charged head groups decreases and they can pack closer together and the micelle starts to grow into rod-like micelles. 10/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As the salt concentration continues to rise, the micelles continue to grow and form long, wormlike micelles. 11/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These micelles can be up to microns in length and they can become entangled, increasing the thickness of the fluid. A good analogy of this is a plate of spaghetti, when you try to pull one strand out more come with it. 12/15 https://t.co/cFw5Sl99VS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In shampoo the surfactants form this type of wormlike micelles. The mean micelle length and breakage time are really important, but very difficult to measure experimentally. This is where computer simulations come in handy. 13/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As you keep adding salt to the wormlike micelles, there comes a point where branches start to form. These branches allow the stress to be relaxed in more ways and the thickness of the fluid actually decreases again. 14/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Again these branches are difficult to quantify experimentally which is why we use computer simulations. If you are interested in reading the full paper, you can find it here. https://t.co/jm7XK2rFsy 15/15

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today is my last day curating here and I have to say I’ve really enjoyed it and had a great time. I didn’t really have anything planned for today, but looking over my threads this week I realised I haven’t actually talked about how to do simulations yet. 1/10

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Performing a simulation itself isn’t very difficult, there is loads of user-friendly free software available to do it. The difficult thing is picking the appropriate approach. Rubbish in = rubbish out 2/10

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I perform particle-based simulations which means I use virtual beads to represent atoms (or groups of atoms). From these we tend to be interested in averages over a large number of snapshots, or configurations. 3/10

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are two main categories to generate these snapshots – molecular dynamics type or Monte Carlo type methods. Both have pros and cons and I’ll go through them quickly here. There are also more advanced methods that use a combination of the two but I won’t go into those. 4/10

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Molecular Dynamics a.k.a. MD. It essentially solves Newton’s equations of motion to advance the system. You* split the simulation into small time steps and calculate the change in forces, velocities and position acting on each bead. (* the computer) 5/10

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Pros of MD: 
+ You can get dynamical information out, such as diffusion, viscosity
+ It is conceptually easier than Monte Carlo (MC) 6/10 https://t.co/uYXb7Noo6F

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Cons of MD:
-  You have to calculate the forces and store them. It may be non-trivial for non-spherical particles. 
- It is easy to get stuck in a meta-stable state which we are not interested in 7/10 https://t.co/KSnHbeZrZQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Monte Carlo a.k.a. MC. It takes a completely different approach. You make a move at random – it could be a particle translation/rotation and accepts it based on an underlying probability distribution based on the conditions of interest (temperature, pressure etc). 8/10

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Pros of MC:
+ Quicker than MD, you don’t need to calculate forces for the particles and so you store less information
+ You can perform “unphysical moves” (e.g. particle insertion) so you are less likely to get stuck in a high energy state and you need shorter simulations 9/10 https://t.co/aAyHzUndcp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Cons of MC:
- No kinetic/dynamic information (there is no concept of time in MC!)
- Not as many programs readily available to use as for MD 10/10 https://t.co/V5JgIZPhuD

tweets.text: First thing’s first [long thread] – How do we see the building blocks of life? It’s (relatively) easy. #superresolution microscopy. It’s a family of fluorescence microscopy techniques which allow us to see structures in the scale of ~ 1-200 nanometres. (1/n)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
“WHY”, you may ask. What we know is, this is the scale in which the tiniest processes of life are carried out. These range from single biomolecules (e.g. DNA, proteins) doing their own things, to tiny machines and compartments inside cells. (2/n)

[GIF: Liam Neeson saying “Why”] https://t.co/njF7zXkkvv

[GIF: conductor] https://t.co/keeeh61XyH

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover

🧬🎨: We separate the fluorescent tag from the 🎯. The tag is now linked to a short diffusible single-strand 🧬. The matching 🧬-strand marks the 🎯. It is lit by a thin sheet of light. You see the tag *only* when the tag has ‘docked’ with the target (12/n)

You see them as lots of blinks because these dockings of the 🧬+tag are short-lived (~ 1 s). They actually looks like lots of blinks. They are not blinks #fakeblinks.

But for us microscopists, these ‘blinks’ can be used the same way as blinks (13/n)

[GIF: lots of eyes blinking] https://t.co/qvetG4BUwA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: AFM is a type of scanning probe microscopy - a technique which won Gerd Binning and Heinrich Rohrer the 1986 Nobel Prize for Physics. In its simplest form, a physical probe is scanned across a surface and a laser is used to measure deflections of the probe. (2/6) https://t.co/1Krk18WcBd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As AFM involves 'feeling' the surface to produce an image or information, we aren't limited by the optical diffraction limit and can measure down to the picoscale (depending on your experimental set-up, of course!). (3/6)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Additionally, the only sample preparation required is that your sample is adhered to some degree to a substrate - no loose particles or floaties allowed!  (4/6) https://t.co/zEHdlH0jC1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Finally, as this is a physical measurement, we aren't shackled by the need to dry, fix, stain, or resin mount samples. And we can perform these measurements in situ, in ambient or controlled environments. Which leads us to... (5/6)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The ideal technique to study single living cells!

☑️ Adherent cells grow happily on a substrate
☑️ In situ measurements- living cells in media and heated to the perfect 37C
☑️ No fixing or staining required to probe the cells
