tweets.text: This was a commercially pure titanium particle (5-25 micrometers in diameter) hitting a 300 series stainless steel substrate at a velocity above 600 m/s. There was no heat involved. /2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This as my first ever experiment to make a commercially pure titanium coating. In a cold spray setup we have a powder feeder and a high pressure gas (in my case helium). We push the helium through a convergent divergent nozzle, also called a de-label nozzle like a rocket nozzle/3 https://t.co/MWMl0wKbA1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Helium going through the nozzle accelerates the powder particles to supersonic velocities. The powder we use are small. My hair is around 100 micrometer. The powder we use are in the range of 5-20 micrometer. /4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When the cold titanium hits the steel it deforms very quickly (strain rate of 10^9 per second of you really need to know). At that sort of conditions metal start behaving very differently. There is something called thermal softening. /5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This very soft metal start flowing and forms a jet. This jet (see the edge of the particle) removes any oxide from the metal surface and two metals come together and weld—it’s like magic. Cold welding. This bonding is super strong, more than 100 MPa. /6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: How much is 100 MPa? You can hang my weight from a small disc and it won’t fail. This was my intro to surface engineering—a cold spray process. Those materials scientists out there would enjoy this seminal paper by Prof Assadi at Brunel https://t.co/U1l0uhFyDH /7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 👆🏼was my first journal paper that I read on cold spray in 2006. It was tough but I fell in love with materials after reading that. What is happening here is similar to hitting a wall with a flour dough and the dough sticking to the wall for a couple of sec. /8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now imagine being able to engineer the dough so it will not fall off. It will stick to the wall for ever! That is what I started my career on in 2006. /9

tweets.text: I am continuing the theme of cold gas spraying. 10+ years ago there was a big controversy. We all thought the bond strength of the coatings only come from metallurgical bond. My first ever journal paper introduced a concept called mechanical bonding. https://t.co/2dmF28XTl2 /1 https://t.co/q9xF4l5ujM https://t.co/6zq5b3wx9d

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We figured out the entire strength of the coatings cannot simply come from metal-metal bonds. There was someone else in play. When a particle (copper here) hits a substrate (aluminium), the substrate also deforms and it gets squeezed between particles. /2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When the bond fails, copper-aluminium contact fails as well as the squeezed bit of aluminium, which gives the additional strength. /3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I was hooked. I could not have asked for more supportive supervisors. One was Cambridge trained tribologists and other was Oxford trained metallurgist—a great combo to deal with surface engineering problems. /2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I have a UG degree in Mechanical Engineering and a PG degree from @Uniofnottingham in Manufacturing Engineering. I stayed on and decided to do a PhD in Materials Eng. My masters thesis was on understanding bonding in cold sprayed copper & aluminum with a simple heat treatment. /2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The idea was if you can apply a low temperature heat treatment it will form intermetallics where there is atom-atom contact. I loved the idea so much I stayed on to do a PhD in cold spraying of titanium, funded by TWI. /3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Following PhD (& 5 decent quality journal papers) I went to @CranfieldUni for a Research Fellow in Energy Materials where I was exposed to power plant & gas turbine coatings. I was developing over 24+ plasma and high velocity oxy-fuel (HVOF) (more about those later) coatings./4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I was introduced to high temperature materials, biomass combustion and how to develop coatings for the next generation of power plants which are going to burn biomass. There was also this idea of USC (ultra supercritical power plants) to make carbon capture and storage viable. /5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I worked in a range of EU FP7 and TSB (Technology Strategy Board) projects to look into coatings to make USC boilers viable. Power plant heat exchangers cannot cope with nasty species like sulphur and chlorine at high 700 C+ temp from the biomass or other fuels. /6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I was developing these metallic and ceramic coatings to protect these tubes. In 2013, I headed back to Nottingham to take a fixed term fellowship in surface engineering to get back to developing coatings rather than destroying. I left a permanent  job & a lecturing job for it! /7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I came over to build the UK's first suspension and solution precursor thermal spray facility, which means instead of using 5-45 um powder we can use 10 nm to 5 um particles. In 2015, I was appointed as an Assistant Professor in Materials Engineering & in 2018 as Associate Prof./8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I was working with commercially pure titanium powder in my PhD. I was making titanium coatings for biomedical implants (the hip replacement part) and aerospace components (aero engines). Titanium is biocompatible since it has a protective titanium dioxide and it has low density/1 https://t.co/E2Bp34VpHe

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Low density means, aerospace sector loves it. It is lighter to fly. It is hard to spray titanium using other techniques as it reacts with air (oxygen) and loses it wonderful properties. I was using a cold spray (like firing bullets to a surface) which had no heat, no melting. /2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The problem in those days used to be porosity or holes in the coating. The deformation of the bullets (titanium) was not complete so we ended up with holes. I was using a laser to melt the top surface to seal it, which dramatically improved the properties. /3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Also, titanium is excellent for salt water corrosion so the coating is needed in many process plants and desalination plants. Want to read more here is a paper https://t.co/8zKOkF2TWd /4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Time to talk about various spray technologies. Let’s start with Arc spray. Here a pair of electrically conductive wires are melted by means of an electric arc. The molten material is atomised by compressed air and propelled towards the substrate surface https://t.co/gKPwOfT51j /1 https://t.co/yM5a1KVpbF https://t.co/1l2o6uOHGk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Arc spray particles are travelling relatively slower and cooler but the coatings are usually denser than the wire flame sprayed coating and higher deposition efficiencies. Examples include mostly corrosion and wear coatings for large components. https://t.co/crVdVvkZwN /2 https://t.co/y9jyWdoNcz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Aerospace companies in the U.K. uses a version of wire arc spray for metallizing polymer composites, for plane wings. These are deicing coatings based on joule heating—pass a small current and it will melt the ice. /3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Flame spray, a low cost option, with similar particle velocities to arc spray but much higher particle temperature. Typically we use oxyacetylene flame or hydrogen flame (3000 C). Fig courtesy of Gordon England. Also known as a low velocity oxy fuel spray. /1 https://t.co/yM5a1KVpbF https://t.co/C0EvYMro1f

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We have an @OerlikonGroup combustion flame spray https://t.co/cMc7OFoROz . Instead of coating my colleague @Dr_Ifty_Ahmed uses it to make porous powder. /2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I am back talking about HVOF (High Velocity Oxy Fuel) thermal spray—the industry standard process for cermet (ceramic+metallic) coatings. The particles are travelling much faster here but temperature cooler than plasma spray. It’s essentially a rocket engine burning O2+Fuel. /1 https://t.co/XNS7rk1p0O

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The combustion here is supersonic so one can see the shock diamond in the flame. JP5000 is an industry standard HVOF torch. There two types of HVOF spray, gas fuelled and liquid fuelled. Gas fuelled torches can spray ceramic powder and the particles are injected into burner./2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Liquid fuel or kerosene fuelled guns are much more powerful (250 kW) but the particles are much cooler as we inject the powder in after the nozzle (cooler part). Tungsten carbide cobalt and chromium carbide nickel chrome are two popular coatings for HVOF /3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: WC-Co is used for <500 C and CrC-NiCr is used >900 C in your plane engine to protect from wear. We need a finer cut powder 5-38 micron here where the carbides could be Nano sized <100 mm. /4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Where is this nano in surface engineering? Thermal spray is mostly micron scale business but nano came in 1990s and it opened a whole new world for us. We call it suspension thermal spray (STS). Instead of using powder we can use a suspension with nano particles./1 https://t.co/CRaNTM0ve3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The benefits: finer particles result in uniform properties in all directions and the hardness can be increased significantly which is good for wear. You can see  suspension thermal sprayed alumina coating here. /2 https://t.co/tyY3J2PZtu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You can improve the wear performance of alumina by an order of magnitude by using suspension (nano) over micron sized powders you can see an AFM image showing how hard these particles can be./3 https://t.co/0agDWxvGV5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Link to our first suspension thermal spray work https://t.co/m1Z0vS0m88

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A suspension high velocity oxy fuel thermal spray setup to spray sub-micron to nano range particles. We are spraying cerium oxide here to make surfaces super hydrophobic. /1 https://t.co/NzGCTGrPDv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Benefits: water would roll off easily. The surface can be self cleaning. Also bugs wouldn’t grow if the water doesn’t stay there for long. For icy conditions, if water doesn’t stick there won’t be any ice—a great idea. More details here https://t.co/BVws2uFAAM /2 https://t.co/dzKzfcDCdK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Continuing the theme of suspension spraying, one can mix nanoparticles like  graphene nanoplatelets with sub-micron alumina to make beautiful nanocomposite coatings. Cross section images below. /1 https://t.co/kYP5MA1d0h

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Using a spectroscopy like Raman spectroscopy one can measure the vibrational modes of the molecule which can tell us how many layers are there in the graphene nanoplatelets after the spray. Carbon has D, G & 2D peaks. More about Raman https://t.co/WDWUE7vbh4 /2 https://t.co/dF6hJox3W7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There is a barely a scratch on the sample which was sprayed with graphene nanoplatelets, compared to the sample which was pure alumina after a wear test. Details here https://t.co/cx3ufc4aLs https://t.co/X97zwy0lKZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Breakup of a suspension in a plasma is a beautiful process. Look here. When fine particles are injected in a plasma they behave very differently. They follow the gas trajectories. /1 https://t.co/piNLqaXpk5 https://t.co/z0vxqvJ8qa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: SPS (Suspension Plasma Spray) setup. These fine particles hit the asperities of the substrate and form beautiful columnar structure. These columnar structures are highly desirable for thermal barrier coatings for aero engines. They can expand and contract better in service/2 https://t.co/ui6JXWkFdm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These columnar structure could only be formed using a very expensive process called EB-PVD (electron beam physical vapour deposition). We can now form these using a much cheaper SPS process—thanks to nano particles. https://t.co/Pn5vaJ2lLx /3 https://t.co/YSlhdeXwiH

tweets.text: Polymers are long chain molecules, with many repeat units. Scientists are usually very good at determining 'what' a chemical is but they are not quite at adept at determining how big something could be https://t.co/3VxUpcoSFe

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In its simplest form 'Mass Spec' works by flinging the molecules down a tube and seeing how far / fast they fly. For small molecules it is an incredibly sensitive method of detection - hence the use in mass spectrometers https://t.co/nUX17apSvg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A high end mass spectrometer can spot the extra mass of one single neutron in a molecule. This means it can be used for radiocarbon dating of fossils - determining how much C14 in the molecule remains can tell you if a dinosaur if 65 or 165 million years old https://t.co/MtLtkSCBgV

tweets.text: So - if we want to work out a molecule's size - we can watch how fast it moves. You may have heard of Brownian motion - the idea that all particles are vibrating and moving - this holds just as true for polymers https://t.co/aSOCgeeFP6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Polymers move just like any other molecule, however they are a little slower because of their size. This means using NMR to study their diffusion (speed) in solution is particularly appealing https://t.co/lCqNd4nhVx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So how does DOSY work? Well we put a magnetic pulse into the field (pointing in different direction across the tube) and then we fire a reverse pulse to bring the molecules all the way back to way they started. https://t.co/bB8eP921Io

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It sounds simple but because the molecules wont keep still they won't end up pointing in a uniform direction. It is this 'abnormality' we can measure - we can catch how fast our particles are moving by how out of line they are when we've fired our second pulse https://t.co/U1iHY7iLio

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
@NPL My research is in materials science. I look at how microstructure ('micro-scale structure') of materials change as they break or deform. 

Understanding how materials break helps us to make the most of the material when making things. [2/]

tweets.label: Takeover

Fundamentally, EBSD measures the crystal structure of the material you're looking at.

What's 'crystal structure'?

Crystal structure describes how atoms in many materials stack together symmetrically, like the fruits here:

https://t.co/dvAIgtimzr

tweets.label: Takeover
Takeover
tweets.text:
Why do we care about crystal structure?

One reason is: material properties change with crystal orientation.

For the hexagonal crystal structure here - the material's strength differs depending on which direction (red/blue arrows) I push. https://t.co/jDhg21QreX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Q: Why do we care about crystal structure?

A2: The size of the crystals in a material (grain size) affects its strength. Usually, small grains -> strong material. 

Sometimes, interfaces weaken the material! That's why turbine blades in jet engines are made of single crystals.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'd like to talk about initiating/maintaining research while dealing with big challenges like covid. In a way I was almost prepared for covid. The Christchurch earthquakes/ terroist attack, multiple management changes, poor funding/resources ... A decade of disruption in my life!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Worrying about covid feels very much like living through the Christchurch earthquakes; poor sleep, distracted thoughts, difficulty focusing, fuzzy brain. At the time of the quakes we called it "quake brain"

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So for a few weeks leading up to and since stay at home was ordered in NZ I've expected nothing of myself or my team. We all need to deal with things in our own way; mine was making hand sanitizer and setting up a home office. Basically tidy a few things and do a little often.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What ever the new normal is (or return to the old normal) will need to be established before we can set ourselves concert targets (not aways the attitude of management sadly). Till them I remind myself of 3 good bits of advice I've had over the years from mentors..

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 1) don't worry if you can't do what you wanted to, just do something. 2) do something that you find exciting. 3) do a little often. Keep in contact with friends and if you find yourself at a road block ask around, someone will appreciate any offer of or request for assistance...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There's always someone who needs a manuscript edited (or someone who can help you with yours). Volunteer for a committee. Start scoping a review you may never submit. Or just do nothing, sometimes this has been the hardest but most effective thing I've ever done.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Speaking of maintaining/initiating research, ugggh funding! In NZ 10% success is a well funded scheme, so typically less that 1 in 10 applications successful. I can handle reject as well as the next person, but in NZ there's no feedback!

"Reading the Fine Print – How Material Science Informs Both Art and Manufacture"

Please welcome Damien Leech (@dr_djleech )

https://t.co/f5teLu5UCP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hey everyone! Damien @dr_djleech here, will start as I mean to go on - with an overuse of the gif function. https://t.co/XxiDHHy3WT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A bit of background - I did my PhD on models of the interactions between stacked layers of 2D materials. With a focus on the electronic structure of graphene, particularly in a bilayer form, and moire pattern formation. https://t.co/DFOMR2UZqc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you've ever been remotely adjacent to work on graphene, you'll have probably seen the figure of a van der waals heterostructure represented as lego bricks. This stack of 2D materials is built layer-by-layer and has properties that depend on the stacking https://t.co/0Z4f13Gk46

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But this simple picture misses out two of most interesting parts of the problem - how adjacent layers affect one another and what happens when the periodicity of the lego bricks don't match up. https://t.co/KDCe4jrCoj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Both graphene and hexagonal boron nitride have, yep, hexagonal structure.And this structure is very similar. So much so that hBN is the perfect substrate to place graphene onto to study the behavior of it - it's insulating so it doesn't interfere, flat, relatively easy to make... https://t.co/RHJ9JqfL9T

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But there's a lattice constant mismatch of 1.8% and, over many hexagons, this makes all the difference. A moire pattern forms and a new periodicity arises, much larger than before - this has a subtle but very real effect on the electronic structure.
https://t.co/wEKQ2fbEhB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This interaction changes depending on the materials used and orientation between them, giving us many avenues of manipulation. And vertically, we can just keep stacking - some groups are making mind-bogglingly complex stuff! https://t.co/j6zTm9hkgU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: How does bilayer graphene come into all this? Well, when your stack is built, you are mostly locked in, in terms of properties. The materials, stacking and orientation won't change. But bilayer graphene has some symmetry breaking properties that make it distinct from monolayer...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Place bilayer graphene in a perpendicular electric field and the symmetry breaks, one layer has a differing on-site energy to the other. This causes a band gap to open, with a magnitude proportional the strength of the electric field.
https://t.co/FdEGSZVGzX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now you have an avenue for tuning the properties of a stack externally! It can produce all sorts of strange electronic behavior, including extremely flat energy bands...
https://t.co/rHODUNseyU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
One thing I always loved about 2D materials research was the ever-increasingly-obscure materials being suggested/isolated - from silicene to graphyne(?) to bismuthene(!?). It's really fascinating to keep up with!

2019 saw isolated plumbene!
https://t.co/Mzpi7m9mce

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So what's the 'I knew about them before they were cool' monolayers I should be keeping an eye out for next? 

Because I only really enjoyed stanene's first album.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After PhD, I moved 10 mins down the road to Bristol to work @CFPRresearch @UWEBristol on print technologies, alongside scientists, engineers, and even artists and craftspeople. It's a fascinating place! https://t.co/GYLZ079icK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The research in the centre encompasses print in all forms - going from additive manufacture and inkjet all the way to more traditional approaches like screen printing and letterpress. All for industry, academic research and even artistic use...
https://t.co/FtJzhXeVea

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This includes 3D printed ceramics, custom glassware, laser-dyed textiles, artist's books, colour perception, robotics driven design, texture mapping, jewelry production, stop-motion animation, maintaining/resurrecting dying crafts and manufacture processes... All sorts!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So how does a materials scientist even be useful when it comes to print technology? 

Printers, in all sorts of forms, are complex kit that often work on the premise that the ink you put in is well defined and consistent. Lest you go all Office Space on your printer... https://t.co/YbMsoAmGMb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Therefore ink characterisation is incredibly important and properties such as the rheology, surface tension and even colour all arise from effects on the micro/nano scale. First principles models can be really useful in determining what is going wrong! https://t.co/xTl4lETYiZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There's this term 'printability' that contains all the vague concepts that make an ink printable. It's not usually strictly defined - notable exception is inkjet, where it's driven by the Ohnesorge number, which gives a thin window of opportunity! https://t.co/UOjCi0048c

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: By the way, 'ink' is another vague term used to describe whatever 'input material' you give the printer! It can be liquid ink, 3D printer filament, powders, chocolate...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But what do I do? 

Printing has a lot of history to it - there's been plenty of methods that have come and gone and a lot of lost knowledge there. I look at forgotten 19th century print methods with unique advantages and how we can revive and modernise them (Daguerreotype, 1837) https://t.co/g4mxrMk2gn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This time was particularly exciting as print was some sort of weird collision between print, photography, chemistry and physics. So the methods use elements of all of them. One focus is the Woodburytype - it's a relief print method that uses a gelatin and carbon black ink (1880) https://t.co/HEZVG4qq9b

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The darkest regions of the print stick out from the page further than the lighter parts, trapping more pigment - it's very intuitive in terms of optics, but not very common in print. You can read more about the process here:
https://t.co/hBacHunedd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @MaterialsDan Love this! Really fascinating read

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: RT @MaterialsDan: @RealSci_Nano This New Yorker article about printer science is a great read https://t.co/u7BmsEDsCZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One aspect of updating old print processes is moving monochromatic processes to polychromatic. Colour perception is a whole field of its own that encompasses pigment chemistry, ambient optical conditions and even how the brain/eye combo reads and interprets these signals. https://t.co/3WTsdhLKQJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This plot represents the response of the three types of cones in the human eye. They're not uniform at all and therefore neither is our interpretation. (Side note: some people have 4 cone types! As do plenty of animal species, in this case it is usually located toward the UV end) https://t.co/QgXKwdrR21

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Using this knowledge, we can begin to map our colour perception. This horseshoe represents it, white is in the middle and colours become more purely monochromatic as you move towards the outside edges. There's a secret 3rd dimension to it, lightness, giving lighter/darker tones. https://t.co/NsFgtQlYWx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Tracking the outermost regions of the plot that we can reach defines a colour gamut, within which contains all the possible colours from that technique. sRGB is shown here, the standard digital colour space, reproducible by 99% of all digital monitors. https://t.co/2hiHzZvGbU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The Woodburytype has no photoactive element in the print and so very little fading occurs, giving surprisingly high-quality windows into 19th century life. Street Life of London (1876) gave 'direct communication with the people' in 'unvarnished language'
https://t.co/GvmCGTM2ag

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3D Printing? That's kind of a big thing, huh?

More generally known as additive manufacture, you're probably familiar with fused deposition modelling process whereby plastic is selectively extruded from a heated print-head. https://t.co/E7wHpyQHBT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This works really well for a whole range of shapes and high-end printers are regularly getting beneath a 100 micron layer thicknesses for a handful of materials. The print is self-supporting so sometimes excess supports are added and removed after printing. https://t.co/JNOvYtPLXU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But theres other options - stereolithography uses laser to selectively cure photopolymers and can breach sub-50 micron layer thicknesses.Still requires supports and materials must contain a photopolymerizable component. Optical methods tend to be sharper!

https://t.co/VIgcKwwFUI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Selective laser sintering spreads a 'powder' layer, uses a laser to sinter regions of it, and repeats for the next vertical layer. This means no supports! But requires an excess of the feed material and the object has to be 'excavated' from the powder. 
https://t.co/WWTk6jd15H

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There's all sorts of others, but some of the most interesting are hybrid manufacture. This uses additive techniques to build the main bulk and then switches to subtractive in order to give a smooth finish and smaller feature sizes. 

https://t.co/uC6hpXiZd4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Additive manufacture loves three-lettered acronyms (FDM, SLA, SLS, FFF, EBM, STL...?) but usually you pick your technique based on the materials you want to print... So we'll talk about that in a bit!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And it probably goes without saying... But if you do have access to 3D printers at the moment, please look into local groups printing PPE! There's many amazing initiatives going on at the moment!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3D printing (FDM) typically utilises plastics like PLA and ABS - they're a standard. But some of the most fascinating research, for me, is when people use these printing platforms to print material that is 'unprintable'.

Want a new coffee mug? Print one! https://t.co/QtOIsJ6mHD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Ceramic 3D printing tends to come in two flavors - an extrudable clay is formed or a powder base is selectively bound together via light/chemical reaction. It makes structures not traditionally possible and is used in both tableware and biomedical apps

https://t.co/UqEkytMl7b

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But what's really awesome here is the enthusiast community that exists for clay/ceramic printing. This wikifactory contains so much useful information, all on how you can modify your own setups and produce suitable clay inks.
https://t.co/SXi6MyZB1j

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: RT @UniofBath: For the first time, labs around the world can 3D print their own precision microscopes to analyse samples and detect disease…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Ceramics not your thing? OK, how about bioprinting? 

This is loosely defined as the printing of biomaterials, ranging from directly (and carefully!) printing materials loaded with cells to constructing complex scaffolds that can later be seeded with cells. https://t.co/Z274rKf6vQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This is an incredibly complex field, that requires expertise from a whole range of backgrounds. But the ultimate goal is the realisation of complex and biocompatible printed tissues. This paper sums it up far more eloquently than I can!
https://t.co/jwAIH3i0Ur

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But surprisingly, I have to refer to the literature for this field a lot. No one understands the rheological and optical properties of gels and soft materials (and particularly gelatin) better and so my work with gelatin is often propped up by these, frankly mind-blowing, papers. https://t.co/AzTJWorF6v

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This, for instance, is just exceptionally cool!
https://t.co/36UM9ERroM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
And this really encapsulates that interdisciplinary approach that is so necessary for these sorts of complex problems!
 https://t.co/RfiPTwrR9f

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Alright, how about printing chocolate instead? 

Fed up with delicious chocolate in simple shapes? Reprocess and print into all manner of shapes! This paper covers a custom setup for a chocolate extruder and explores the flow properties of chocolate inks.

https://t.co/NWoPrAik83

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This system is particularly interesting as it turns out the key here is in the temperature control, just as much as it is in the rheological control. It represents a fascinating test case into the effects of cooling and air flow on the print process... And it's delicious.... https://t.co/jOs4TxwISF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Currently working on a similar homebrew setup and making some progress (and a lot of mess). Just need more ink making supplies from @CadburyUK! https://t.co/doxBwX8eSW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
No sweet tooth? 

Try 3D printed mash instead! Also includes NMR analysis!

https://t.co/MFaQmlxfEW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Colour from pigments is one thing, but nature explores more complex setups quite commonly. The iridescent colours seen in beetles for instance arise from multi-layers reflectors of chitin/proteinous material. The thickness/structure determines colour and lets it varies with angle https://t.co/rv0bpWnx83

tweets.label: Takeover

This paper looks at how this effect changes through the lifecycle of a particular type of beetle, mostly through optical characterisation.
https://t.co/Dsn6dnPecD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Plants are a bit overlooked - but the buttercup produces a complex colour response based on a mixture of structural and pigmentary colour. This paper posits this is not only for visual signals, but also as a directed heating element!
https://t.co/q5ToTJr9eG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
If anyone knows of anymore interesting examples of structural colour please do share! Another commonly mentioned example is the goth-as-hell Queen of the Night tulips.

https://t.co/Z2gRCrWI6V

Listen hard enough while reading and you can hear Sisters of Mercy playing.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Nacre (mother of pearl) occurs on the inner layers of many mollusks. It consists of platelets bound in a matrix of biopolymers and produces the lustre seen on shells/pearls. An example below from a common flattop shell, with the upper patter scraped away. https://t.co/EJWlcfZE9w

tweets.label: Takeover

This one I've never quite got my head around, because a lot of times you'll find shells that display this effect, but only in regions where the outer layer/pattern has been scraped away by wear and tear. It's mostly hidden!

"Making Cells Dance - Acoustic Tissue Engineering"

Welcome James @jrmstrng 

Listen to the podcast #53 to learn what's coming youe way this week - https://t.co/UzpvJUbbwT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hi everyone at RealSci_Nano - my name is James Armstrong @jrmstrng, I'm a research fellow at @ImperialCollege and this week I'll be tweeting about some of my favourite science things - #cells #sound #3Dprinting and more!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So I learnt about RealSci_Nano through my former colleague Amy (aka @DrTinyTaps) who curated this account in week 39. If you missed it first time round then I recommend checking it out here - https://t.co/isbMODiynl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Shout out also to Gregor (@FuhrmannGregor), another of my former colleagues and RealSci_Nano curator just a few weeks ago - https://t.co/Q4RivDhv03

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So before I launch into the science tomorrow, let me introduce myself! I am a proud dad to two kids, a keen footballer and traveler, and reluctant jogger. I feel very lucky to be in my dream job, where I can do so many of the things I love - learning, creating and educating!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'll talk about this more on Saturday but I've recently been co-organising these #Virtual #Seminars in #Biomedical #Science with @BrianAguado. We kicked off with two fantastic postdoc talks last week and can't wait for the rest. Please share this and join us every Thurs in May! https://t.co/u3R4PGdv3t

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: OK science time! This is a thread about how I “painted” stem cells during my PhD with the @perrimangroup. I chemically modified proteins so that they would “stick” to cells to give them superpowers (sort of)...check it out here in @NatureComms  https://t.co/P3qG0lznEQ https://t.co/QVE5aahsa1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: How did we do this? Well, cell surfaces are negatively charged, so if you make your protein positively charged then it will spontaneously bind through electrostatic interactions. Simple! But how do you go about making a protein positive...?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Well, proteins are made of positive, neutral and negative amino acids – these usually cancel each other out and you end up with a “net charge” that is either slightly negative or slightly positive. But we can mess with this!!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Some groups use genetic manipulation to switch out these amino acids and make #supercharged proteins. I particularly love this paper by the Liu group: https://t.co/ejFBmRPgeg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But we did something totally different. We took proteins and used a simple chemical reaction to turn the negative amino acids into positive ones – a process called #cationization

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When we added these cationized proteins to cells, they stuck to the cell membrane! However, we could make even more protein stick by using a neat trick - attaching a surfactant to the surface of the cationized protein.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These proteins stick to the cell membrane through hydrophobic interactions - and stayed for over a week! Here is a picture of a stem cell "painted" with surfactant labelled green fluorescent protein. We estimated that there were around 6 billion proteins per cell! https://t.co/KIyfVqyILv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So why is this useful? Well, we wanted to see if this could address a big problem in tissue engineering - the starvation of cells in the middle of big tissues. We figured that we could use our method to "oxygenate" our cells with myoglobin...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So together with the Hollander group, I grew lots of chunks of cartilage using either "painted" cells or "unpainted" cells... https://t.co/hUIqQatvhA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ...and to skip over a lot of work (!) this was the final result: the left column shows tissues grown with unpainted cells (big hole in the middle) while the right column shows tissues grown with painted cells (much smaller hole). https://t.co/y5N8VGePno

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This means that we could grow big* tissue constructs simply by pre-treating the stem cells! This could be potentially used in the future to replace cartilage lost through osteoarthritis or sporting injury.

*big = 5 x 6 mm which is pretty big for cartilage!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But what else can you do with this? Well the @perrimangroup attached surfactant-modified thrombin to stem cells to grow fibrin hydrogels from the cell surface, potentially offering a new route to wound healing...check it out here in @NatureComms:  https://t.co/vh4fBmXRVI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @sciborgess @Pingosaurus and others then magnetized cells using cationized magnetoferritin. This took just 1 minute, with the cells responding to an external magnet and detectable by MRI...check it out here in @nanoscale_rsc: https://t.co/k9uEwHyokn ... more on magnets tomorrow!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I should also say that this bioconjugation method was adapted from some incredible work by @perrimangroup and @apsbrogan who used surfactants to make liquid solvent-free proteins. If you've not seen this before then definitely check it out here: https://t.co/eDQx0vSIkQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We can also adapt cell modification strategies for the modification of extracellular vesicles. These tiny membrane-bound particles have potentially interesting therapeutic opportunities, and surface modification can allow in vivo targeting or imaging:
10.1021/acsnano.6b07607

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This is (hopefully) a working link for the extracellular vesicle modification review, co-written with @maggieholme and published in @acsnano:

 https://t.co/Av9xOkw2Kf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So today's thread is on magnetizing proteins, DNA and cells - and how you can use this to build complex tissues! https://t.co/coO8OAg9EQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As I mentioned yesterday, @sciborgess and I developed a new ultra-fast method for delivering #magnetic #nanoparticles to cells. These magnetized cells could be detected by MRI - offering a potential opportunity for tracking #stem #cell #therapies!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Other people have used magnetic fields to manipulate magnetized cells - I especially like this paper in @naturecomms, which used a magnetic "microtip" to cluster and stretch stem cells - this caused them to become more like heart cells!

https://t.co/5bKhBjwvm5 https://t.co/HwQysR1AOx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, there are problems with magnetic cell manipulation. Cells are relatively big (~0.01-0.02 mm) and to move them, you need quite a lot of magnetic nanoparticles - but lots of nanoparticles can harm the cell, or change the way it functions...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So @sciborgess and I thought - can we magnetize growth factors instead 🤔? Growth factors are proteins that can make cells produce a certain type of tissue (e.g. cartilage, bone)...if we made magnetic growth factors then we could move them and maybe build complex tissues!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
An amazing PhD student (Chunching Li) made this reality! His secret was to cover the magnetic nanoparticles in a "sugar coating" which soaked up growth factors and then released them slowly over time. Just what we needed!

Red = nanoparticle
Blue = sugar
Green = growth factor https://t.co/Y2K6EDGuNH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
He used a magnet to make a gradient of bone-forming growth factors across a material full of #stem #cells. After 3 weeks:

- The end with growth factor - turned into bone
- The end without growth factor - turned into cartilage

We made an "#osteochondral" (bone-cartilage) tissue! https://t.co/PBJ8AotV65

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Why is this useful?? Well, #osteochondral tissue is often missing in damaged knees - which is incredibly painful. This is a potential way to grow replacement osteochondral tissue in the lab!

Check out Chunching's @biomaterials_ paper here:

https://t.co/S3u13cFCXX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We used a bone-forming growth factor - but if we switched this out for another growth factor then we could potentially make other #gradient #tissues! 

Any ideas, please let me know (DM @jrmstrng)!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
[admin]

"Making Cells Dance - Acoustic Tissue Engineering"

@jrmstrng talking about his science on podcast episode #54, out now 

https://t.co/UzpvJUbbwT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Today’s #RealSci_Nano thread is all about my favourite topic and the tagline for this week – how to use sound to “make cells dance.”

This is a video of cells patterned by an ultrasound wave...read on to hear more about how we can use this for #tissue #engineering! https://t.co/rpaRvMgZMx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What is going on here? Well, what we have here is a "standing wave" which means that we have made sound waves but they are not travelling. This creates static regions of pressure - some higher than usual, some lower than usual, and some unchanged.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This is a slightly unusual situation for cells to find themselves in!

Cells in areas of high and low pressure will feel an "acoustic radiation force" which pushes them into areas of unchanged pressure. This is what we see in the video - the cells accumulate in the "nodal plane."

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What is great about this is that you don't need to modify/label the cells or the culture media in any way! This works because the cells have a different density and compressibility to the surrounding liquid.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are things that can mess with this - gravity, viscosity, cells sticking to things and an effect called acoustic streaming. A lot of what I do is trying to figure out how to get around these problems!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
...but when you get the conditions right, you can start to pattern cells in gels. This is an image of cells all lined up in a collagen hydrogel.

This is exciting because this means we can start making a patterned tissue! https://t.co/c3BkviERVE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We first used this to make muscle - because muscle is naturally made of parallel bundles of long cells. Using our sound waves, we were able to make something similar!

If you are interested in this, see our Advanced Materials (@AdvSciNews) paper here:

https://t.co/PJIdJqwE2F https://t.co/JCiwpkItgv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The possibilities for this are endless! I worked with @sonic_bruce and his team to make these patterning devices - they are easy to use and compatible with normal cell culture. By tuning the ultrasound properties we can make all sorts of different cell patterns! https://t.co/YO1i0FVMi9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm now working with my brilliant student @katya_pch to use these devices to make different patterned tissues and create smart cell culture systems!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Others have also worked with acoustic cell patterning - my favourite is this work by Peer Fischer's group published in Advanced Materials (@advscinews): 

https://t.co/Uj1hjnuISo

tweets.text:
In today’s thread, I want to talk about some other fun things we do with sound!

I've been lucky to work with a brilliant team (@NeleValeria @AcoustiCarolyn) on an exciting project using sound to trigger #enzyme #catalysis and #gelation! 

Read on for more details... https://t.co/91Yer3DLLX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Our idea was based on using #liposomes - small droplets that can be filled up with different "cargo" (e.g., chemicals, drugs). Under the right conditions, you can use ultrasound to release this cargo into the surrounding liquid.

This cargo can then be used for many things!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
For example, we used ultrasound to release a cargo of calcium ions - these ions could then stick to an enzyme (#transglutaminase) and activate it so that it could catalyze a chemical reaction.

This was the first example of an ultrasound-triggered enzyme!

But there is more...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
...once the enzyme is activated, it can then turn a liquid solution into a gel (#fibrinogen)!

This was only the second example of an ultrasound-triggered hydrogelation (the other one used radicals - ours didn't).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
As usual, we should ask, why is this important?

Well, enzymes are used all across industry and bio-sciences to catalyze chemical reactions, and hydrogels are commonly used as soft biomaterials for cell culture, tissue engineering, drug delivery, soft robotics and lots more...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
...and now we have a new way to activate enzymes and make gels!

Unlike a lot of light sources, ultrasound can pass through opaque walls and through the human body, which means we can now start to trigger these processes in previously inaccessible locations!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Another useful thing about this method is that it is "modular" - which means we are not limited to this exact system (calcium, transglutaminase, fibrinogen).

We can switch out the cargo, the enzyme or the gels - something that we are exploring this now!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We also showed that you can stick the cargo-loaded liposomes onto tiny gas bubbles. Ultrasound can be used to expand, contract and burst the bubbles- which helps to release the cargo even better! https://t.co/UyDuChEwOk

tweets.text:

For more details, see our Advanced Materials @advscinews paper published earlier this year:

https://t.co/h0n8CEeg7v

tweets.text:
In my last "science" thread, I want to talk about other ways to build complex tissues - and why this is so important!

If this interests you, check out our Advanced Functional Materials review on complex tissue engineering, written with @liliangouyang:

https://t.co/Awt9ZcTzpn https://t.co/Ozcra59Lbb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Why is complex tissue engineering important? Well, tissues are naturally complicated!

They have layers, gradients, blood vessels, nerves, patterns of cells and lined-up fibres - all features that have evolved to keep the tissue healthy and play important functional roles!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The take-home message is:

If we can't replicate this structural complexity, then our lab-grown tissues will simply not work as they do in nature - and we won't be able to use them to effectively replace or study natural tissues.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Luckily we have a lot of new methods for growing complex tissues.

The review that I posted is about "bottom-up" methods. This means that we start with smaller "building blocks" - such as cells, organoids, fibres or sheets - and then assemble them into complex tissue structures.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I've already spoken in previous threads about "remote assembly" methods using sound, light, magnets.

There are also "self-assembly" methods that use a particular property of the building block (e.g., their shape or chemistry) to spontaneously and predictably assemble!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
However, you can do this in a far more controlled way by using a broad set of methods called "directed assembly".

There are lots of examples of this - in fact, many methods used for tissue engineering (weaving, knitting, braiding) are borrowed from the textile industry! https://t.co/2NymcXDDNd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Like many people, my favourite directed assembly method is 3D #bioprinting!

Here, the "ink" contain cells and/or materials, and the printer deposits the ink into custom shapes. I've worked with many smart people on some exciting printing projects. Here, I will share 2 of these!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The first of these was the development of a new type of ink with @perrimangroup @madelineburke3 and @BennyC. The problem we found was that some materials were "printable" and some materials were "cell-friendly" but rarely could materials do both jobs well!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So we decided to make a "hybrid ink" - containing a printable material (#pluronic) and a cell-friendly material (#alginate).

Pluronic is quite unusual - it turns from a liquid to a gel as it heats up! This meant we could print a cold ink that would set on a warm (37 deg) stage.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We then washed our printed structure in a cool calcium bath, which did two things:

- the calcium very quickly gelled the alginate.
- the cooling washed away all the pluronic.

This meant we could make large alginate structures (like the nose in this picture!). https://t.co/yvyKT00x7M

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We included stem cells in this ink and use it to grow cartilage and bone tissue.

For more info, check out our Advanced Healthcare Materials paper: https://t.co/Jx0bMeVEqs

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I now want to talk about some awesome work, which was done with the amazing @liliangouyang!

Here he addressed a big problem in tissue engineering: building tissues with blood vessels. Bioprinting is perfect for this as it allows you to build structures with open channels... https://t.co/7jbjdlvWgv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ...however, a problem with open channels is that you then need to put blood vessel cells in and let them stick to the channel walls. This is difficult and doesn't always work, particularly if you are trying to build small and complicated vessels...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So what Liliang did was to use two materials - one filled with blood vessel cells to print tubes, and the other to print the surrounding tissue. The latter was then strongly gelled with UV light (it was GelMA for those interested).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
...the clever bit was that the tube material was gelatin - which turns into a liquid when warmed!

As the gelatin turned to liquid, it released the blood vessel cells, which then stuck onto the walls of the channels. This worked even for thin and complex blood vessel networks!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We call this method: "in situ endothelialization."

If you are interested, check out our Advanced Functional Materials paper: https://t.co/tjH1SK5MQo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @badz_nithin @liliangouyang Hi, thanks for a great question! Yes we are definitely looking at combining ultrasound patterning and gradient casting - the application here could be for osteochondral tissue where you have aligned deep zone chondrocytes plus a collagen / gag / mineral gradient!

My last #RealSci_Nano thread! I want to talk about the important role of online seminars/conferences as free, open-access science during (and maybe after) this pandemic.

I say this, as co-organizer (with @BrianAguado) of these #Virtual #Seminars in #Biomedical #Science 👇 https://t.co/u3R4PGdv3t

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I totally love the #TissueTalk series by @GVNlab, where you get to see incredible Professors such as @burdicklab and @kaplan_lorax. But I feel that it's just as important for graduate #students and #postdocs to have a platform to disseminate their results and build their network!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This was the motivation behind the #Virtual #Seminars in #Biomedical #Science - and it is great to see so many similar initiatives focussing on early-career scientists. @gecedillo has compiled a great list of these events:

https://t.co/6gYtjp8MWB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I really strongly feel that this helps “democratize” science – free-to-access and open to anyone with the internet.

I’ve been lucky to attend some great in-person conferences over the years - but these are expensive to attend and are therefore exclusive to those with funding!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another real issue with in-person conferences that needs to be discussed is that they can exclude those with care responsibilities or those with certain medical requirements. Providing talks online could make a major difference to these individuals.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: On this note, there are steps that organizers can take to make sure that their online events are really accessible to all. You can’t pick a timezone to suit everyone – I myself have had to miss some really great talks due to parenting duties...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One option is to post talks online after the event so that they can be watched at a convenient time. With speaker permission - we are looking to do this with #virtual #seminars in #biomedical #science, and I know other organizers (such as @BEaTSResearch) have taken this approach.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In summary - while nothing beats an in-person conference, I truly think that online science conferences & seminars (#free, #accessible and #ecofriendly) – can play a big role during the pandemic and also in complementing in-person conferences in a post-COVID world! 🤞

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hello Real Scientists Nano! My name is Upulie Divisekera (@upulie) and I'll be your curator this week! I can't wait to talk to you about nanoscience and my other scientific work in cancer research and endometriosis. I'll also be talking about my science communication work

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But it's very early in the morning AND very late at night here in New Zealand, so I'll see you in a few hours!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hello! Good to be back again. It's hard to figure out which timezones are best to talk to you but I'm just here to say hi before delving back into my work. It's late morning here in Auckland New Zealand, a really beautiful sunny day and I have meetings to prep for

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I might start with talking about how I ended up in science. I'm a molecular biologist, I did my basic degree at the University of Melbourne in molecular biology/biochemistry and pharmacology. I did a Masters at the ANU and I have a doctoral thesis still to submit

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm currently at the University of Auckland. Through various twists of fate, I've spent most of my professional life as a research assistant or student(!); and so I've ended up doing research in many different fields.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My Honours year was spent playing with Trypanosome parasites, I've worked in cancer genetics and immunology, spent time making antibodies on a near-industrial scale, studied fruit flies - which are surprisingly beautiful under a microscope - spent small stints in materials

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: science and my doctoral research is in nanoscience and drug delivery. And now I'm working on bioinformatics of endometriosis.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I did not expect that I would accidentally end up working in so many areas of science. I decided I wanted to be a scientist when I was 6-7, and like most kids I was keen on palaeontology. But I was keen on any kind of science I could read about and particularly space

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I decided to be an astronomer, and was pursuing this single-mindedly until I was given a book on molecular biology. The principles of genetic engineering were so fascinating to me, and the possibility of reanimating extinct species so alluring that I switched immediately 🤣

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I tried to perform my own experiments and even had a lab book set up for it. Still, my true loves are molecular biology, materials science and theoretical cosmology. We're allowed to have more than one, right?!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Anyway, that's just for starters. It hasn't been the straight path through science I expected, and I've missed being able to establish myself in a particular field; but it's also been a true privilege to be able to learn from so many scientists in so many fields.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When I decided to become a scientist at 7, I wanted to know how everything in the universe worked, from the tiniest atom to supermassive black holes, and how all the life forms function at the most basic level. It's impossible to know everything, but I've been fortunate enough

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: to explore so many fields of science, just as I always wanted to as a kid.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Just letting you know, @elonmusk, that we have a nanoscience #rocur and I'm hosting this week

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Meeting done! Does anyone have questions and anything they'd really like me to talk about this week? I'll be talking about my cancer research, endometriosis and the nanoparticle-based drug delivery systems I was developing

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It depends on which field of science you're in. Not all fields require a lot of advanced maths and programming. But the point of the training in science is to be good at learning and problem solving - so you can *learn* to be good at programming and maths https://t.co/1VWsspYA0Z

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So how does a molecular biologist end up researching nanotech and dabbling in materials science? The scales involved are pretty similar, I would say. And some of the concepts.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Basically, it's all chemistry and crafting things from atoms. In biochemistry, it's molecules that have a biological function - tiny machines that are part of how the cell works

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In materials science and nanotech, it's the design of molecules and objects at the nanoscale that can act as tiny machines. It's basically mimicking the evolution of life through the evolution of inorganic structures. These structures, and machines - they are all

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: designed to work the way biomolecules work; in a structured and ordered way. It fascinates me that we can do this with inorganic materials. It's also kind of fun to figure out what we can make and ways to make these devices

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So what is "inorganic" vs "organic?" Organic chemistry isn't pesticide free range chemistry 🤣

sorry

basically, organic chemistry involves carbon chemistry; and inorganic chemistry covers everything else.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Most of the huge biomolecules in our bodies and in all life are carbon based - carbon is an incredibly flexible atom. Most of the materials we use in nanotech are not carbon based, but can have some carbon components. But they can be made of metals - silver, gold, titanium -

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: or made of silica - the atomic cousin of carbon - and so many other materials. Some of these devices are also made of organic molecules. What's so fascinating about it is that you can make use of the chemical properties of each of these substances to design particular devices

tweets.label: Takeover
Takeover

Are you a materials and/or nano scientist?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hellloooo everyone! Sorry for the silence at my end, I've had a bit of a cold and felt exhausted for a few days. But I want to talk to you for a bit even though it's about 2.30am where I am

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So I spoke earlier about how we can use inorganic materials to mimic organic molecules. Think of it this way - instead of a biomolecules like a protein, an enzyme  - you can try to make something that does the same thing, but it's made of a metal or silica - something inorganic

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: and as a biologist, that is just amazing to me. For example, you can actually make tiny nanoparticles that can be used as catalysts - like enzymes . Or you can make gold nanoparticles of any shape or size you like - bipyramids, stars, spikes, spheres, rods - by just using

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
chemical processes. It's *almost* like alchemy. 

So what does cancer research have to do with nanotech?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We want to take what we know about cancer and its weaknesses and create treatments that target those weaknesses - you can think of it like looking for chinks in the dragon's armour

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We know what some of these chinks are. But with nanotech, you can be creative about how you deliver an attack - or an arrow to bring the dragon down.[ all i can think of right now is The Hobbit]

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So what are some of those ways we can beat the cancer dragon?

We know that chemotherapies are really effective, but while they attack fast growing cells like cancer, they can also attack healthy tissue in the body - this is why chemo takes a lot out of patients

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So what would be ideal? We have chemotherapies - and other anti-cancer therapies - and we'd like to get them just to the cancer cells. Or even just most of it to just the cancer cells. Or we'd like to mark the cancer cells so we can find them without having to perform surgery

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We could also mark the cancer cells - and destroy them - without invasive surgery. And finally, we could try to deliver gene therapy to the cancer cells, so that we can modulate genes that can shut the cancer down.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
How would we do this? I have one word: nanotechnology.

Tune in tomorrow to find out more.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Before I talk about how we can attack the cancer dragon, does anyone have questions? Let me know if something was unclear, I will do my best to explain

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
How can nanotech slay the cancer dragon? 

With gold.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Of all the elements on earth, I never expected that the most venerated and valuable metal to be an almost magical substance with multiple properties that would make it ideal for attaching drugs, attacking cells, converting energy.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Gold is actually quite non-reactive and can be turned into a range of nanoparticle shapes. It can be coated in antibodies and nucleic acids, modified so you can attach other drugs. It's surprisingly handy. Studies about its toxicity aren't extensive though

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It turns out that the shape of a gold nanoparticle matters; and each shape has unique properties.

For starters, the colours of different particle shapes differ.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Colloidal suspensions of gold nanoparticles don't look like gold. The particle size is so small, at the nanometer level, that they interact with light in a very specific way, producing what's called a surface plasmon resonance (SPR). We can use this to identify particles, to

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: make barcodes made of gold; devices made of gold. We can use it to characterise gold particles with different coatings, and so on.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So, the colours of gold particle suspensions:

stars: green
bipyramids: brown
spheres: depending on the size, anything from brick red to maroon to purple
1-5 nm: brick red
10-25 nm: blood red
30-40 nm: dark red towards maroon
45-upwards: purple

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
capsule-shaped nanorods of gold: green.

Well, gold nanoparticles are colourful, and you can do some pretty great and specific surface modifications to them. But what's even more fascinating is that some particles can actually convert energy.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Gold nanorods can be exposed to laser light at certain wavelengths, and they'll convert that energy down to heat. But not just a little heat, a lot of heat. Heat that can burn.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of the therapies developed by my colleague was gold nanorods that used an aptamer to target the rods to a specific kind of cancer cell. A low intensity laser was shone on the sample; the energy was converted by the nanorods into heat that destroyed the cancer cells

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Isn't that nifty? It's a very simple and elegant way to destroy the cells; and the aptamer made all the difference because it was selected specifically target that cancer cell. This is just one of the ways we can use gold nanoparticles to treat cancer.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another way to treat cancer cells is to blast them with gold nanoparticles with chemotherapies, gene therapies or antibodies attached to them. These therapies are aimed at killing the cancer cell; and the gold nanoparticle is used to attach the therapy and deliver it

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is a basic principle - attaching an existing therapy to a nanoparticle - that's being developed for treating cancer and other diseases that need a little extra effort to treat. It's basically making teeny tiny nanocapsules - nanopills! - to treat disease.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And you don't have to just use gold - you can use so many kinds of materials to make these tiny nanopills - polymers, chitin, silica, squishy heat reactive polymers, and other materials that you can use to make millions of regular particles and attach therapies to.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is the basic principle of using nanotech in drug delivery - and why a molecular biologist can end up working in this field (also, it turns out that engineers are not always keen to work with cells).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Good morning everyone. I'll be hosting this week and will try my best to discuss materials, including ferroelectric and piezoelectric materials. It is a bit early, so I will try and wake up first.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The direct piezoelectric effect relates to materials that develop a charge when subjected to a mechanical stress.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Applications for the direct effect include sensors of force, pressure and acceleration. Microphones and hydrophones too.

If you have used a gas lighter that generates as spark when you press it, that's also probably piezoelectric.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I've been for a walk around Bath, which is where I live in the UK. Earlier I discussed the direct piezoelectric effect. My next posts will be on the indirect piezoelectric effect. https://t.co/vVrv4j1NQG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The indirect (or converse) piezoelectric effect relates to the piezoelectric material developing a strain under the application of an electric field.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Applications include actuators, nano-positioners, speakers, active SONAR (to send out the 'ping'), ultrasonic baths, nebulisers, & fuel injectors. If you ever received a card that played a tune when you opened it, it probably used a piezoelectric buzzer, like the one below. https://t.co/gZHIcTnVoj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @palebluedot92 It will be a ferroelectric ceramic material based on lead zirconate titanate (PZT).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, why do certain materials exhibit piezoelectric properties? Well, it is usually a lack of symmetry in ionic materials.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: An example is lead zirconate titanate (PZT). At high temperatures (left image) the crystal structure is cubic/symmetric and non-piezoelectric. But on cooling  is becomes tetragonal (right image) and you can see the black ion (Zr4+ or Ti4+) is displaced upwards, forming  a dipole. https://t.co/yS8Gn8vhrd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It is this dipole that provides the material with a direct or indirect piezoelectric response.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In a material like quartz (SiO2) it is a little different, since in the stress free state the structure is symmetrical. It is the application of stress or field in a specific direction that leads to a loss of symmetry.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For this tetragonal structure the black Zr4+ or Ti4+ ion can displace up, down, left, right and in and out of the image above. So, the dipole can be aligned in six possible directions.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There are other crystal structures, but I find the tetragonal easier to visualise and it is important for materials such as PZT and barium titanate.

For the rhombohedral phase the dipole can be along the eight possible diagonal directions.

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.text:
Hi everyone, I'm back to talk some more about #3DPrinting.  

First up take a look at the thread I made for @scottishscicomm's global science day back in March, to give you a quick whiz through what 3D Printing is and why it matters:  https://t.co/W5hO8lujgH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Then in a while I'd like to tell you about some of my favourite applications and processes, before we start getting into details about the science behind the processes and materials.

As always let me know if you have questions or things you'd like me to talk about!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So let's start talking about #3DPrinting processes.  Almost all of them work from the same principle of building parts one layer at a time.  (We're starting to see a few processes which have moved away from the layered approach, but I'll talk a little about that later.) https://t.co/TzJ7aIeamP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now for many years we couldn't all agree on how to categorise the processes.  Should we focus on the type of material they use, the method used to join the layers, the properties of the parts, or something else entirely?  After a lot of discussions (arguments?) a group of...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: process categories was defined, based on how we join our layers together.  I'm not going to go through all of these now, but you can see a list in Section 2.2 of the ISO/ASTM standard here: https://t.co/5IxiDOPX2x

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'll highlight a few example processes shortly, but what's quite interesting is the way in which processes have changed over time.  The very first commercial processes had one thing in common, which is that they all used some form of single-point 'scanning' to produce the layers.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You can think of this as being similar to colouring a picture - everywhere you want to colour, your pencil must touch the page.  While this is an *effective* way of colouring, it's also pretty inefficient, and that's one reason why the early 3D Printing processes were a bit slow! https://t.co/b0Z3qXl2jP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It became quite clear that having to scan, melt, or deposit each pixel of material in a layer individually wouldn't allow for the speed increases that were needed for many applications, and people started to look at ways to cover more area in a shorted time.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Quite a few processes sprang up where a layer was covered in a single 'pass' of a print-head, array of nozzles, or similar.  This allowed for quicker printing of each layer, but also in some cases had benefits in terms of processability and consistency. https://t.co/SNd9HHRIce

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: From there it's a relatively quick stretch of the imagination to move towards producing the whole layer in a single 'flash', saving time per layer but with perhaps some added complexity to the overall process, or working to constantly 'grow' the parts without specific layers...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'll be back in a short while to give you an idea of just some of the range of processes we've seen since 3D Printing started, many of which are great and some of which might be better categorised as 'interesting'... I'll probably leave you to decide which are which!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @John_Sevigny @KLeoPullin I agree! That's part of the fun of it for me, never knowing what will come up next!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @KLeoPullin @John_Sevigny @RealSexyCyborg I didn't, but I do now!  Thank you for the tip! :)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let's talk a little bit about #3DPrinting processes.  The first to be commercialised was Stereolithography, which works by selectively curing cross-sections of a photo-curable resin using a laser.  Laser Sintering (similar technique but using a powder rather than a resin) and...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Fused Deposition Modelling (which effectively 'draws' the layer by extruding molten material from a nozzle) came relatively soon after, with variations of each method still being used a lot today. But what about some of the other processes which have been important along the way?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of my favourites when I first got into this was Z-corporation's 3D Printer range.  They were the first people to enable full colour 3D Printing (OK, it was only surface colour but it was early days and quite exciting!).  The process works by printing a binder onto a layer...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: of powder and bonding the particles together.  The parts were quite fragile and needed some post-processing in order to get good colour vibrancy, but opened up a lot of potential especially for more realistic-looking prototypes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
You can see some example parts in this video if you're interested in the sort of things these printers were making:

https://t.co/7b4NHxiAo9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: On similar lines, the Connex systems from Objet Geometries were pretty ground-breaking, as they introduced systems than that could process more than one build material at the same time.  Multi-material printing opens up a lot more design possibilities, so this was big news!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These processes work by printing a UV-curable material, and following it with a UV lamp in order to cure it.  Add more than one print-head, and you can print more than one build material.  By 'grading' the amount of material you print across the build area, you can get a big...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
change in properties.  After quite a few years they also launched full-colour systems taking advantage of the same build process.  You can see a video of the process here, complete with enigmatic background music:

https://t.co/Zyifi15deU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of the most exciting developments in recent years was Carbon 3D's Digital Light Synthesis technology (https://t.co/vQJrROLqob).  Using UV light, a curable resin, and some clever chemistry, they 'grow' a part continuously, helping to eliminate some of the issues often found...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: at the boundaries between discrete layers.  Although there are still downsides as with any process, lot of process developments have been quite small iterations from where we were so it was quite exciting to get something  genuinely a bit different!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To finish off today I thought I'd highlight a few processes you won't hear much about, but that always grabbed my attention for one reason or another!  Early on I came across  Rapid Freeze Prototyping.  As you might guess, this involved... well... freezing stuff quickly!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In this process you'd deposit droplets of water out of a nozzle onto a sub-zero plate or environment, where they would quickly freeze.  Subsequent droplets will freeze on top of the previous layers, and you'd keep building up the part until it was complete.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The most obvious application area was for making complex ice sculptures, but with potential for some casting or moulding applications.  Of course the main disadvantage was that your part melting if you didn't use it quickly enough, but that was part of the charm for me!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And a couple of others that aren't really around any more, but that I had a soft spot for!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Araldite Digitalis (watch a video here - https://t.co/P7FDZPhLa7) used a system of micro-mechanical shutters to selective expose an entire cross-section of a photo-curable resin.  This promised to be great for increasing process speed, with one other potentially big selling point

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The system was designed by Huntsman (a chemical company), based around their in-depth knowledge of their materials.  There are a lot of potential benefits to designing processes around materials rather than the other way round, but sadly we've not seen much from this process :(

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And finally, a process I've always loved, despite it's flaws...  Solid Ground Curing, from Israeli company Cubital, Inc. had more process steps than you could shake a stick at! The process worked by first creating a mask of toner on a glass plate, and applying a layer of resin...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: onto a flat build platform.  The mask would be positioned above it, and flashed with a UV lamp to harden the un-masked areas of resin.  Any un-cured resin was vacuumed away, and molten wax spread over the build area to fill in the gaps.  Of course that layer of wax was...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: thicker than the intended layer thickness, and had to be milled back into a flat shape... Another quick cure of the resin layer, and the process started again.  Far from the most efficient process ever created, but something about it always grabbed my attention!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's about it from me for today, but if there are processes you specifically hoped I'd talk about please let me know!  I'll be back tomorrow to talk about some of the less-popular bits of the 3D Printing process chain (and why they're super important!)...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: which, almost as if I planned it that way, will lead nicely into how we go about research into materials and identifying the key things we need to consider!  Talk to you all then :)
