[admin]

"Cutting Through the Hype of 3D Printing"

Extended conversation with @CandiceMajewski is out now - https://t.co/XtQRBdQSqu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hi everyone!  As promised I'm back with more to say about #3DPrinting.  I think we all know there are bits of any subject that are the 'cool' bits and others which are important but much less exciting, and 3D Printing is no different!  Most often when we talk about these...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: processes, we focus on the manufacturing stage itself - the bit where we can watch the laser zipping around on the surface of the raw material, see the material being squeezed out of the nozzle, or various other visible aspects. https://t.co/bfjUKUlGjw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm the first to admit that those bits are fun (I'm still just as excited to watch our machines do their thing!) but in reality what happens before and after the manufacturing stage can have just as much of an impact on the quality of our parts.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My group is focused mostly on processes which use powdered polymers as feedstock, so I'll use that as an example.  (I'll talk more about the processes in detail later on, but for now it's enough to know we're talking about polymer powders).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now our powders have a lot of history before we even put them into our machines.  The powder has to be manufactured, transported and stored somewhere in our lab, and we often need to sieve the powder before we use it. https://t.co/jGtWYrUx4P

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We then pop it in the machine, deposit layers of powder onto the build platform and pre-heat the powder, all before we start the actual 3D Printing stage of the process!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Afterwards we need to allow the parts to cool, remove them from the machine, clean off any excess powder, and post-process them (often by bead-blasting).  We'll also capture any un-used powder for use later on.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At every single one of those stages we can alter (sometimes deliberately but often unintentionally!) the properties of our material.  This can also affect the final properties of our parts; that's not always a *bad* thing, but it's something we always need to be aware of.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, I thought I'd talk a bit more about a few of these aspects throughout the day, and how they tie in with some of the research we've been doing.  First of all I have some project presentations to mark though, so I'll be back in a bit to tell you that stuff!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I talked earlier about the different individual steps that make up an overall 3D Printing process chain.  What's useful is that we can use those steps as a basis for defining where we need to focus our research, and where we think we can make the biggest improvements.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we focus on the Laser Sintering process, where we selectively laser scan and melt the required cross-sections of our polymer powder, we can split the process into a couple of main stages.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: First we need to deposit a nice smooth, well-packed, layer of powder onto a build platform, and then we need to make sure the powder melts and solidifies into a dense part.  If we get either of these steps wrong, we can run into big issues!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For the powder deposition step, there are a lot of things that can help/hinder us.  The machine itself has a part to play - how does it deliver the powder to the build area and how does it ensure even spreading (for example using a roller or a blade).  We don't want potholes! https://t.co/T7KjBNfEus

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The powder manufacturing method itself has a big effect too.  Here's an image of one of the most 'standard' commercial materials, a Nylon-12, courtesy of one of our previous PhD students Alaa Almansoori. https://t.co/yZiqlR1tQg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Note that the particles are relatively smooth, with a 'potato'- like shape, and a combination of small and large particles.  Although not a guarantee of success, these things can help to allow the powder to flow and pack nicely within the powder layer.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can add small amounts of flow additives to help with this too, but we have to be careful - as with a lot of things in  the world of 3D Printing, there's a compromise to be made - beyond a certain point the flow additives can start to have a negative effect on our properties..

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But quite often, and depending on the manufacturing process for the powder itself, we may not get such nice smooth, consistent particles, as you can see in this image of some Polypropylene powder from another of our previous PhD students, Luke Fox. https://t.co/4YfrKW1cV2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When we end up with these more 'raggedy' (yes that's the technical term) powders we can still work with them but are less likely to end up with a nice dense layer of powder, putting a lot more pressure on the laser scanning part of the process to get the part quality we want.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Other things we have to watch out for are moisture uptake in our powders, which is very dependent on the specific material we're using, 'settling' of any flow additives and/or different-sized particles from the transit or storage of the powder, and any contaminants in our powder.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All of those considerations take place even before we start the build process itself, so what things do we have to look out for once we get started?  I'll be back to give you an idea of the main things in a little while!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Before I finish for the day, let's have a quick think about what happens when we start the 'making' part of the process.  At its most simple, we're 'zapping the powder with a laser to melt it into the relevant cross-section', but in reality it's a lot more complicated...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
If we look at Nylon-12, the most common Laser Sintering polymer, there are a lot of things that make it really well-suited for the process.  This chart from Mike Vasquez sums it up very nicely - x-axis is temperature, and y-axis is energy input/output.
(https://t.co/dh8EIxx6ya) https://t.co/O03hqKllPG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we look at the graph carefully, we can see a number of key aspects that really help with the process.  As we heat up the material, we come to a fairly sharp melt peak (evidenced by a relatively sudden intake of energy without an increase in temperature).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This allows us to heat our powder quite close to its melt point before scanning with the laser, which as benefits in terms of processability.  Heating further we can see a large 'Stable Sintering Region' - this is the temperature range in which we can keep heating the material...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: without causing it to degrade - if we push it further into that region we'll see a drop in mechanical properties of the resultant parts.  Where it gets *really* interesting is when we start to cool the material... The temperature at which it starts to crystallise and solidify...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: is quite a bit below its melt temperature, which is probably the most exciting thing about it!  This allows us to hold our un-sintered powder at a temperature *above* its crystallisation point, but below its melting point, meaning the areas which have been scanned and melted...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: are also held above their crystallisation temperature.  Effectively this means the scanned areas remain in a molten state throughout the whole build process, which allows for much better bonding between consecutive layers.  Pretty cool, right?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It's probably no surprise to you that most polymers don't behave anywhere near this nicely!  Many of them have much more complicated (annoying?) thermal profiles, and various other factors affect how well they can be processed.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Melt viscosity determines how long it will take to fuse two particles together nicely, as well as the accuracy of the parts themselves - too 'runny' and we'll get poorly defined geometries!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Surface tension also influences the way in which the particles will melt together, as does their physical size, and the rate (and consistency) with which we cool the parts will have a large effect on their final properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And of course some materials we're asked to try (not mentioning any collaborator names, but you probably know who you are), behave completely the opposite of every material we're used to using, which leads to a whole lot of  head-scratching while we try to figure it out! https://t.co/G8vjbE5Idq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Really this means we've got plenty to keep us busy in terms of understanding how we can process more difficult materials.  Sometimes it feels like the more we know, the more we realise we don't know, but I think that's all part of the fun of research!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All of which neatly brings me to the end of the day, and a good point to pick up on tomorrow, when I'll talk a bit about what happens once we remove our parts from the machine, and the ways in which we can characterise and understand their properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'll also go into a little more detail on a few of the projects we're currently working on, so see you all then!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It's Friday!  Well done on making it through another week, or if you work different shifts In hope you're doing OK so far 👍

As promised, I'm going to talk a bit this morning about what happens after we've built our parts, and how that affects their properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: First up, let's think about the end of the Laser Sintering process. You can picture the end of the build as a bunch of parts (still molten), encased in a tub of relatively loose, warm, powder.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Polymers have pretty low thermal conductivity, meaning it takes a while for heat to dissipate through them - if left to cool naturally, parts at the centre of the build will take longer to cool that those at the surface or closer to the metal sides of the container.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Why do we care?  Because the rate at which we let the parts cool will have an effect on how much they crystallise, which in turn has an effect on their mechanical properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we have variation in cooling rates that translates into variation in part properties, we're potentially losing some of the repeatability we're trying so hard to get!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At this stage we also have to consider the effects of processing on the un-sintered powder surrounding the parts.  We can quite easily recover most of this powder, but don't forget it's been held at a temperature close to its melt point for a long time by this point.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This leads to changes in the molecular weight of the powder, and to how well it can be processed in future builds.  It's standard to mix this 'used' powder with fresh powder to help keep things working well, but beyond a certain point we'll start to have a big effect on...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
'sinterability', part performance, and surface finish.  Check out this work from the excellent folks in Louisville, who were the first to report on this:

https://t.co/2WwXVM02kS

and in particular this image of how these changes affect surface finish! https://t.co/2mf2VoyrB9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So what can we do to check on the quality and consistency of our parts? We know that processing parameters (eg energy input, temperatures, speeds) have a big impact on part quality, and we're starting to understand a lot more about this and how we can use it to make improvements.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Within our EPSRC Future Manufacturing Hub we're doing a lot of work looking at how we can help powder-based manufacturing processes (not just 3D Printing ones) reach their full potential.  You can see more at @mapphub or https://t.co/Va04rgYI4L

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of our PDRAs, Zicheng Zhu, has been investigating the porosity of parts produced using High Speed Sintering.  This process is similar to Laser Sintering but uses a combination of a printed ink and IR light to induce melting in the relevant areas of the powder layer.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This image, taken from micro-CT data, shows what we get when we put in a lot of energy into our parts - the dark areas are solid areas of the part, and the light blue are pores within the solid structure.  (There's about 7% porosity  by volume in this part). https://t.co/OfSFfcypL2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now see what happens when we put a lot less energy into the parts - this part has about 32% porosity, and you can see how this porosity is aligned with the layers of the manufacturing process.

(Excuse the picture quality, as I don't have the originals on this computer!) https://t.co/JR5kiqUN8T

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Using this sort of analysis we can start to see which individual processing parameters have the biggest effect on the size, shape and distribution of our pores, and what effect these have on our mechanical properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: By understanding these things better, we can start to work on making improvements to the systems themselves, with a view to gaining better control of the properties and repeatability of those properties, that we can achieve.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Keep an eye out for some upcoming publications on this as well as some super cool results from some in-situ testing, where Zicheng and out colleagues in Manchester scanned some parts while tensile testing them!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I've mentioned the effect of our processing parameters, but as it's a rainy Friday (at least here in Sheffield), perhaps you'd enjoy a quick look at what happens when we don't quite get it right... https://t.co/KWkvgr3QPj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Although we can take a good guess at some parameters (often through a combination of examining the material's thermal profile and comparing with parameter sets we already use for similar materials, sometimes it comes down to luck as to whether we get it on our first attempt!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As well as understanding how things work in our processes, we're also keen to make our parts work harder!  By introducing extra functionality into them, we can start to add a lot of extra value.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I thought to end the week I'd talk you through how we go about this, using the example of some work we've done to investigate the inclusion of anti-bacterial functionality into Laser Sintered parts.  You can read our recent paper on it here: https://t.co/xgiLyemo22 if you like.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This EPSRC-funded project involved bringing together people from engineering and micro-biological backgrounds, so big thanks to @microshep, @Bobatron, Tom Paterson and James Wingham!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Our aim was to introduce anti-bacterial properties into our parts, by incorporating a silver-based additive into one of our standard polymers.  We chose nylon-12 because it's so easy to process, meaning we'd be reducing the likelihood of processing difficulties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A project like this necessarily starts by us seeing whether we can actually process the part in our machine, or whether including the additive would cause us problems.  These images might not look that exciting, but they represent getting over a key milestone! https://t.co/Wkx53isFU6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Next we want to see whether the additive has caused us any change in the mechanical properties of our parts compared with the base nylon-12 - thankfully we saw no difference between samples produced with and without the additive... https://t.co/qE4K6nTDuw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
During this time @microshep also ran some tests using human cells, in order to make sure we weren't going to hurt human cells in our attempt to get rid of bacteria!

Looking good so far, so we started seeing what would happen when we expose bacteria to our treated parts... and...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: what we found was super interesting!  Depending on the test conditions we used, our approach worked well, a bit, or not at all!  From a research perspective that's given us lots more possible avenues to explore, which we'll hopefully get back to once our labs open up again.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here's a nice (false colour) image from @bobatron, which I'm including because it's pretty awesome! https://t.co/SLhtye0r4P

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We also tried out some other interesting things along the way, including using micro-CT scanning to look at how well our anti-microbial additive was dispersed throughout the parts we produced.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Check out this lovely micro-CT image from one of my PhD students, James Wingham!  The grey areas is our base nylon-12 material, which makes up most of the part. The black areas are pores within the part, and if you look closely you'll also see some little white 'dots'. https://t.co/wEP7yZlCTQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These are where our silver-based additive is found within the part! So from this one measurement we can get an idea of how porous our sample is, where that porosity is located, how big it is, what shape it is, *and* how well our additive is distributed throughout the part.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Like all good researchers, we love when we can get plenty of information all at the same time!  Hopefully that's given you a bit of a flavour of some of the  #3DPrinting research we're doing at the moment, but please ask if you have questions or would like more info on anything.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'll finish off my week tomorrow by showing you a few of my favourite applications of 3D Printing, but for now I hope you  all enjoy the rest of your Friday!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @Bobatron Whoops, sorry!  Thanks to TOM for the image, and Bob for giving him bacteria... You're right, that does sound a *tiny* bit bad...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Edit on this Tweet - I forgot Tom is actually on Twitter @SciPaterson !

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @SciPaterson You could always have this account for a week! You get to do a podcast and everything!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Back for one last chat about #3DPrinting!  To finish the week I thought it would be fun to talk about some of my favourite applications that I've seen!  Let's start with the final frontier... https://t.co/V8PSzmybHu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Space applications of AM have been talked about for quite a while; fixing things that are broken, creative solutions to things that go wrong up there, building space habitats, or even food for astronauts.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When this was first talked about, the big question was 'can we get 3D Printing to work in low gravity situations'? One of my favourite ever images, which I can't find the reference for, is this one of a 3D Printer turned on its side as an initial test of whether it might work... https://t.co/IF8lAZXlfU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Reader, it did!  This was an extrusion-based machine, which was then tested on on the affectionately-named 'vomit comet', an aircraft following a specific profile to allow for a short time of weightlessness (see here for some more info - https://t.co/XUECyeaCGr)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Again it worked, and (to cut a long story short) we now have 3D Printing capabilities on the International Space Station!  If you're interested you can read some of my thoughts about 3DP in Space in this article I wrote a while ago here: https://t.co/XuCEmPnKyc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Something else we've seen recently is a lot more TV shows and movies using 3D Printing to create complicated and/or futuristic designs.  One of my favourites recently was Queen Ramonda's crown in Black Panther: https://t.co/Y5lh0qrYBR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
To digress slightly, fashion has shown quite a lot of interest in 3D Printing (see this *amazing* dress worn by Dita Von Teese - https://t.co/OKY1EW4I8z), and if you Google* '3D Printed high heels' you'll find a heap of cool shoe designs

*other search engines exist

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Iris van Herpen (https://t.co/UykvxQ40Tr) is definitely someone to check out if 3D Printer fashion is your thing!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Many of the big sports companies have been exploring the use of 3D Printing in their footwear, although this is yet to become really mainstream, and we can see a lot of cool jewellery and headwear designs coming through as processes have become better (and in some cases cheaper).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But back to TV/movies...  As well as just making fancy props, some companies have been really leading the way in terms of how they apply 3D Printing to movies.  Years ago I watched a presentation by someone from @LegacyEffects, and I was blown away by pretty much all of it!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I remember an advert they'd worked on for... I want to say one of the Halo games..?  as well as how they'd used 3D Printing to make alien teeth for the movie Cowboys vs. Aliens!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But what about people using 3D Printers in shows and movies themselves?  I'll be honest, this one often leaves me conflicted!  Once you know the ins and outs of how 3D Printing processes work, and what things they're suitable for, it's hard not to notice when shows get it wrong!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
If you know me, it'll be no surprise that one of my favourite movie scenes is the one in Jurassic Park 3 when they've 3D Printed a raptor's voice box... They took a few liberties with some of the detail, but this scene gets replayed a *lot* in our house!

https://t.co/DDEeHZYUXM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Small Soldiers is another favourite - who can forget watching those prototypes rise up out of a relatively realistic Stereolithography-type printer? 😃

https://t.co/JpizMvk8Ay

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are plenty of other movies featuring some 3D Printing, as well as bunch of TV shows - CSI, Batwoman, Westworld to name a few, and of course I'm always happy to argue about whether the Replicators in Star Trek count as 3D Printing!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Of course food is a big one that comes up - we've seen 3D Printed cheese, chocolate, plant-based steaks, sugar, and a (tenuous) 3D Printed pizza.  Check out this example found by one of my students a few years ago! https://t.co/bLxMs93c13

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I mentioned medical applications earlier this week, and that's likely to be a key area of continued growth for everything from surgical planning through to prosthetics and implants, and on to 3D Printed body parts.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Check out this lovely example of 3D Printing rehabilitation devices - https://t.co/8HjhwRNljy or this Ironman 3D Printed bionic hand - https://t.co/7SQm4VazT8

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.text: Hello to everyone, this is @SoftMatterHackr picking up the account for the week! I'll be talking about my colleagues' research, the ways commercial products can connect with fundamental research, and how the structure and #rheology of #softmatter affects so many things around us.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This week I'll introduce myself, go quickly through my roundabout research path, and then dive into telling you about our group and as many of my great colleagues (like Baldur here) as I can. Please add your own interests, questions, and suggestions as we go. https://t.co/2njnNvK5tx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'll end today by saying how lucky I am to get to talk to you. Events of the last year lay bare how we must do better to protect each other. In industry, our safety slogan was: "Nothing we do is worth risking someone else's safety," and we must be aware of this every day.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hi all! @SoftMatterHackr here. As promised, a bit of background on my path to research. The people in my life were critical to my experiences and I do everything I can to pay that back to those who might not get a chance to connect to science and research. https://t.co/hYlKJHWmYG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I was born in the US state of Delaware.  It’s a tiny state but has a funny divide between its north and south.  The north is urban, where the duPont chemical company and the University of Delaware were formed. https://t.co/gEDdYuNDMu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Southern Delaware is fairly rural by comparison, with chicken and corn farms everywhere. It also has great beaches that attract huge numbers of out-of-state tourists every summer. I grew up very close to the beach and was hugely influenced by my parents. https://t.co/8Bm17rAJSU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My father grew up quite poor but worked to become an accountant in the north, where he met my mom. He didn’t like working just for financial gain, so when Delaware created Community Colleges he left his corporate job to support education in the rural areas where we grew up.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Dad worked as a COBOL, FORTRAN, and RPG programmer, reporting on demographic and internal data for the college and region, and taught a number of courses over time. He taught me to code and exposed me to early modems and online games in the late 70s and early 80s.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My mom studied biology and was an amazing force, saving my life as a newborn. I had undiagnosed milk allergies that almost killed me. She was so angry at a doctor who dismissed her concerns she got more opinions and found someone who could supply infant formulas without milk. https://t.co/SXu6KzfeRd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I had a number of jobs, and even apprenticed with an industrial glassblower. This is 15yo me working on a quartz “boat” that held silicon wafers for etching into integrated circuits. The quartz melted at very high temperatures and was my first really viscous fluid system! https://t.co/Oh3tOiPFs0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I then got a summer job with the local plastics company run by a former duPont  chemist who would employ anyone local who was college-bound. He talked me into studying chemical engineering at university. I was lucky to live in Delaware, where the state uni was a top ChE school.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Once at UD, I worked as a lab assistant with Prof. Jon Sharp’s group in the Chemical Oceanography department near my home and the beach. I was there three summers, moving from simple tasks to an independent research project funded by the US NSF REU program.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The group studied nutrient distributions in the Delaware Bay and River, using phytoplankton and other indicators of the health of the waterways. I worked on carbon levels in seawater, a measure of climate change. https://t.co/7gULKq4x3C

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The REU program's purpose is getting Americans to go to grad school.  It worked! Being around the grad students, seeing research in pure and applied forms, and benefiting the health of a region and industry, won me over.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My last college summer I wanted to do engineering, luckily Prof. Art Metzner referred me to an REU program at U. Cincinnati. There I met Prof. Sotiris Pratsinis, who assigned me to study sol-gel deposition of silica nanoparticles. At the end Sotiris offered me a PhD scholarship.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My PhD was on flocculation, where small particles  aggregate in mixed fluids, enhancing settling and filtration.  This is used to treat waste and drinking water, and my project was sponsored by a company to improve recovery of valuable enzymes produced by engineered bacteria. https://t.co/6jJiDrMXnR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I was the only student in my group working on colloids, everyone else studied aerosol nanoparticle production by high-temperature combustion, sponsored by the duPont Company, connecting me to industry and combined modelling and experiment used to understand material processes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When I needed experimental equipment to quantify floc sizes and structure, my group infrastructure couldn't help with liquid studies.  My supervisor didn’t have equipment funding but had travel money. He sent me to groups in Australia and the Netherlands to use their setups. https://t.co/x9o0aYdUgU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These trips really opened my mind to other countries and cultures, and imprinted on me the importance and power of collaboration. I’ve worked from the same playbook ever since.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My time in Australia had broader long-term benefits. Returning to Cincinnati I went on a blind date with a woman who was also just back from Australia.  Our mutual amazement at the coincidence broke the ice: we married the year after. https://t.co/aGbN7rqSt0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 18 years later I moved my whole family to Sydney to take the job I’m in now, working with colleagues like Rose and Graeme who were PhD students when I first visited! https://t.co/MfQU9o4woD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After finishing my PhD, I went to work for the Procter & Gamble Company in Cincinnati.  Tomorrow I will touch on my experiences there doing a wide range of applied and fundamental research, with both industry and academic collaborators, and lots of nano!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hi, @SoftMatterHackr here again. This time a thread about my experience working in industry as an engineering researcher for the Procter & Gamble Company. P&G is a company started in Cincinnati that originally made soap and candles and is now a huge consumer products company. https://t.co/X9Vf4k3Xxl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I was hired into a group that acted as consultants for all of the product business units globally. Corporate Engineering was a scale-up consultancy, with strong knowledge about manufacturing products at a large scale (12 tons) but were developed on liter scales.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: P&G makes a lot of things, and my group focused on complex fluids, materials with non-Newtonian rheology. This simply means that their viscosity can change depending on how fast they flow, because they have properties of both solids and liquids.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Cornstarch in water is a well-known non-Newtonian fluid,  it thickens when deformed quickly. An opposite example is shampoo. If you measure the slow flow viscosity of shampoo it is nearly identical to honey. But if you make shampoo flow faster it gets thinner, or less viscous. https://t.co/SofKdQYQO9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Shear-thinning occurs as microscopic particle structures temporarily break down in the shampoo. Honey, on the other hand, stays just as thick when you move it quickly, so don’t try to wash your hair with straight honey: your hair will not last!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Complex fluids like shampoo are often water-based, but they can drastically change their flow properties when relatively small amounts of particles, surfactants, and/or polymers are added. Others: detergents, soaps, cosmetics, conditioners, shaving cream, mouthwash, toothpaste...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A key economic point is consumer products can be made, using mostly water and small amounts of additives, to feel rich, creamy, and pleasant. These aesthetics distinguish such products from fine chemicals and petrochemicals.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Petro- and fine chemicals are judged based on purity, while consumer products are judged on qualitative criteria like softness and qualitative criteria like the thickness of skin coatings. So knowledge of structures in complex fluids  is very profitable.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So a specialist organization is needed to make these materials at large scales. If the the fluid changes its properties while it is being mixed, for example, it is much more unpredictable as there is often not a reliable theory of how these products behave in processes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As a result, a lot of our work blended modeling and simulation with experimental studies of flow and structure of the products. One of my first projects with the company was studying how to make the wax crystals that are used to give shampoo a pearlescent appearance.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The optical effect occurs when lots of flat, plate-shaped crystals line up in layers in the shampoo and light scatters from their edges and centers with interference effects similar to what is seen with real pearls. https://t.co/SO99hYBMaK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After that I worked on a crystallization process forming nanoscale fibers to modify the rheology, or flow properties of beauty products. I noticed that melted droplets of these waxes could crystallize and repel their own solid phase, moving and producing "comet" particles. https://t.co/dfnZWhM4NT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Next two things happened that really affected my career direction. P&G started to get interested in nanotechnology. The US had funded the National Nanotechnology Initiative and everyone was excited by the potential of nanoparticles and other nanoscale systems. https://t.co/qOiwyiL0ba

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: P&G also realized they needed to look externally for some innovation. Big companies often can’t move fast enough to develop everything needed. Their new approach, called C&D or Connect & Develop, rather than R&D, meant partnering with others, say academics, to speed development. https://t.co/P34dYvDTNT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In my next thread I’ll tell you about my biggest nanotechnology project for P&G and, really, in my research career.  The best part of the story is that it made my employer the most money by far, but also got me in trouble for the first time there...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another post from @SoftMatterHackr here, this time about a nanoscience project we did while I worked at P&G. As with all of my projects, this was a collaboration, in this case with Dr. Matt Lynch and other colleagues at the company

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The project originally began as a conversation Matt and I had about self-assembled systems, where molecules like surfactants form larger structures on their own, without additional guidance or templating.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We were originally interested in delivering anti-inflammatory drugs across the skin, and were considering liposomes as the delivery vehicle. Liposomes are simple lipid bilayers wrapped up into spheres, and were hoped to penetrate skin well enough to deliver the drug.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But, commercially, you must avoid infringing on other patents. This was hard with liposomes. At the time there were thousands of relevant  patents we had to avoid. Despite this, the excitement about nanoscience drove us to look at soft nanoparticles like liposomes as a solution.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Fortunately, I’d just done a course on surfactant science with Prof. Stig Friberg at Clarkson U., and he’d talked about a new self-assembled particle: a cubosome. https://t.co/ZodlfZF1UE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Where liposomes form from relatively simple curved bilayers, cubosomes are dispersed particles of cubic liquid crystalline phase, where the bilayers are contorted into space-filling minimal surfaces like this: https://t.co/bDGszRdegO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When we checked, there were only four patents on cubosomes, so we felt there was a much better chance of creating something new with them. This is a nice example of patent maneuvering: we couldn’t patent cubosomes, but the key patent process could only make a few grams of them.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The existing patent mixed a lipid and water in the right proportions, forming an extremely viscous cubic phase, and then used ultrasonic treatment to blast the material into nanoparticles. This meant only small volumes could be made, as power was aimed into a small container.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Since we needed to make much larger quantities, we pursued a new approach. We treated the very viscous material as a solid, and reasoned that if we made a solution of it, then diluted it and precipitated the particles out, we could make nanoparticles with hardly any energy input.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Because our new process allowed us to make cubosomes on a large scale, we were able to patent it. https://t.co/n2YxqxOsox

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Our team grew to include new employee Kristin Hayden and Janet Burns, who studied the phase behavior of the system and made critical cryo-TEM images of the particles to verify what we were making. https://t.co/DV4SxgjEDu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The project followed a normal path for a while, and we started testing the materials for use in a skin treatment. One of the steps is to ensure that it doesn’t irritate skin. We did this with the Skin Science Institute at U. Cincinnati with Dr Marty Visscher and Dr. Steven Hoath.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As part of the normal testing, Steve noticed something unique about cubic phase. Unlike occlusive treatments like petroleum jelly, that protect against drying but block exchange with the environment by skin, cubic phase kept the skin hydrated while still allowing skin transport.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Steve hypothesized that this could be used for a  different purpose than we originally intended. At the time there was no skin treatment for premature babies to protect them against infection.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When we are born, we have a coating on our skin called a vernix, that is the remnant of the lipid template the body uses to form our stratum corneum layer. Premature babies can lack this because it hasn't finished forming and creating that skin barrier.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So when born prematurely, we often lack a barrier against infection and are very vulnerable until our skin fully develops. They proposed we adapt the cubosome product to treat premature babies. We loved the idea, but commercially it was not viable for the company.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Still, we persevered and worked with our internal tech transfer people to see about transferring the IP we’d created to Children’s Hospital in Cincinnati.This would allow them to develop a product, actually an artificial vernix, that could be applied to preemies as protection. https://t.co/AuK4T5dBND

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, the company made money by donating our patents, the University Hospital got to help the babies, and the state government used our example to announce new tech collaboration program support.  Here's the Governor of Ohio, Bob Taft, with Matt and me on the day of  announcement. https://t.co/IOvgYaedko

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: His photographer had a good sense of humor, as he carefully positioned me so that it looks like I am being immunized by a statue in the background. The statue is of Albert Sabin, developer of the live polio vaccine.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And now the trouble I got into: I gave a lot of talks after this happened, both to share our work and to increase our collaborations with academics. At one of them I mentioned that these cubosomes were nanoparticles. There was a journalist in the audience...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The journalist wrote that I said P&G products contained lots of nanoparticles. This is a big no-no for consumer product companies, as the public does not not like nano in their stuff. When I got back from the conference I got blasted by our PR people and had to help explain.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It was a good lesson about nano, that is still valid in many ways: doing nano will get you credit in science but can cause trouble in the commercial food or consumer space. (Nanomedicine people get away with it because they are trying to save lives and fight cancer!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm almost done with my curation term. For my last thread I will bring you up to date and talk about what we're doing at UNSW in research and development!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: OK, @SoftMatterHackr back again. I had a lot of fun over 15 years at P&G, but was interested in making a change, both to pursue my interests a bit more and to move my family somewhere unique. I was fortunate that a job had opened at UNSW Sydney, and moved us to Australia in 2012.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As you do, I recruited students for a while until I had built a core group of my first four PhD students: Dr. Haiqiao Wang, Dr. Jie Song, Dr. Prerna Dahiya, and Dr. Goldina Kwandou. https://t.co/GgJ12CENjP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Dr. Dahiya studied droplet coalescence, understanding how rheology can offset interfacial tension and form non-spherical droplet shapes, but also how the process of arrest can be used to build larger-scale structures. https://t.co/qMczUHg82L

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Dr. Wang looked at cubosomes and similar particles, not as nanoparticles but as microparticles and she found a number of ways to produce particles with complex, controlled shapes as well as template them using polymerization processes. https://t.co/XYGiVvHmQR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Dr. Song developed a new microrheology technique to study non-Newtonian fluids made from nanocellulose dispersions and measured complex yielding transitions of the fluids using tiny bubbles as probes of mechanical properties. https://t.co/ClHu0CkBgo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Dr. Kwandou used a number of techniques to understand how biofilms form, and respond to novel treatments like cold plasma, showing that bacteria can be opportunistic and actually be preserved from thermal treatments because of structures formed by their dead brethren. https://t.co/Cc4jg3i9aO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These days my research group focuses on the topics discussed above as well as some new areas. I discussed one of these when I spoke on the podcast: thunderstorm asthma. https://t.co/S2yIjetyGO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Thunderstorm asthma is a unique but dangerous condition that is not fully understood. It is now thought to occur when storms draw grass pollens into thunderclouds, rupture the pollen, and disperse allergenic proteins, basically biological nanoparticles, into the population.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The resulting effect on people inhaling these particles has been to cause difficulty breathing and dangerous symptoms of asthma. What’s even more remarkable about the phenomenon is that many of the people experiencing the effects had no previous history of asthma.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We are collaborating with groups at U. Sydney, QUT, and UNSW to better map the mechanisms, using microfluidic channels to expose pollen to extreme conditions, simulate the experience in a thundercloud, and directly observe rupture and subsequent release of the allergens. https://t.co/D3r5EAOBb0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Our collaborators are using these particles to quantify the level of inflammatory response the particles cause to differentiate between different starting conditions. We hope this work will lead to enhanced prediction and warning of thunderstorm asthma conditions.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I hope this week has shown a bit of what we’ve done in the area of commercial and academic soft matter. I’m grateful to @MySci_PK  for the chance to share it all and look forward to great future curators. Visit us at @SoftMatterHackr to discuss any of these topics. Bye for now! https://t.co/77kcHyp6PX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My first research project was on the topic of using optical fibres to remove wavefront aberrations induced by atmospheric turbulence to improve the performance of a stellar interferometer.- for imaging stars.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That was in 1992 and was in the early days of optical fibre technology. I like to say that at the end of this project I saw the light and decided to shift from astronomy to optical fibre research. I started by PhD in the Optical Fibre Technology Centre at the University of Sydney

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My PhD was on Nonlinear fibre optics with a specific emphasis on solitons in optical fibres. I spent 6 months at Bell Labs in 1995 where I discovered a new class of soliton -the Bragg grating soliton. I graduated in 1997 and went back to Bell Labs as a postdoc.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: From 1997 to December 2002 I was at Bell Labs, Lucent Technologies (then OFS) as a Postdoc, Member of Staff, Technical Manager and then Director. I was there during the telecom bubble & burst and then 9-11 and decided to come back to Sydney at the end of 2002.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In 2003 I started at @Sydney_Uni as a Professor in the School of Physics @sydney_physics as the founding Director of CUDOS, an ARC Centre of Excellene. Our mission was to create and develop a photonic chip - a cartoon schematic is shown here. https://t.co/0VFJpN77xS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The photonic chip is an integrated circuit that is thumbnail  sized, incorporating components for generating, manipulating and detecting photons, the building blocks of light. We use lithography to print circuits -leveraging the enormous investment that has gone into silicon https://t.co/k6pACFVH8H

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Photonic chips (photonic integrated circuits) can incorporate hundreds of components and can be used for advanced signal processing in telecommunicaitons, radar, sensing and quantum technologies. The feature sizes required to define the components is nanometre scale.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I wrote an article in the conversation on the topic of nanophotonics - https://t.co/pcZajDI65z
with a great link to a short cartoon on photonic chip: https://t.co/pcZajDI65z

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The CUDOS program finished in 2017 after 15 years and we were all ready to move on to the next exciting challenge. My research now focussed primarily on using photonics to sense the world around us - the air we breath, the electromagnetic environment, our health etc.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In 2016 Prof Justin Gooding and I established the NSW Smart Sensing Network @NSWsensing. Sensors, detect, diagnose, monitor and respond to the world around them allowing pre-emptive and predictive responses in a vast range of settings
https://t.co/CsHxCCyiU4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The @NSWsensing brings together expertise in academia, industry and government to position New South Wales as a recognised global leader in smart sensing innovation.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My group @EggletonLab focus on creating and developing photonic sensors that can be incorporated on to chip-scale circuits. https://t.co/Yf8s7DDC8F

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We use the amazing facilities and capabilities in the @SydneyNano Sydney Nanoscience Hub - to manufacture the photonic circuits using lithography https://t.co/0NoCCexDRx

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.text: So, that went well but I really felt isolated and I didn’t like how theoretical physics felt. I just could not wrap my head around a lot of the concepts and it was draining. (At the time I didn’t realize there was an entire experimental physics field where I would fit.)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Nanoscience at its core is a physics phenomena. So, as a senior physics student I took a nanotechnology course and I was introduced to microscopy and spectroscopy as fundamental techniques for exploring nanoscale phenomena.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So when it was time for me to graduate I knew I wanted to go to graduate school. I just didn’t know what to study but I knew I wanted it to be nano related. I studied earth science and GIS and my research focused on surface chemistry during my master’s.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of the first things I did during my PhD was tackle a side project working with fluorinated solvents. The reason this is especially challenging is these solvents are very volatile and they don’t really play well with others. https://t.co/gb1R3XxavL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Well lucky me. Boron nitride nano materials also don’t play well with others. Working in this system with very dense very volatile solvents trying to make boron nitride go into them you had to be prepared for failure. Lol

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The left figure shows functionalized particles, clearly suspended to some degree in a non-ideal solvent system. The right is showing non functionalized particles. The middle was just something cool I found that we played with for a little while.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Even though this started out as chasing an idea my PhD advisor had during his post doc, it turned out to be a pretty awesome way to “prove” we did something. Why? Surface modification of BN materials is very difficult but! There is no fluorine in boron nitride.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we could figure out how to detect fluorine, further learn to detect other functional groups we would be able to support the hypothesis that our technique could work.

tweets.label: Takeover

Introducing myself again: I’m Sean! I’m a postdoctoral scholar working in the Nel and Meng labs at UCLA. I research cancer immunotherapy through the use of nanoparticles as drug delivery vehicles! 

...what does that mean? I’ll get into it tomorrow!

But also like, how did I get here? What’s going on? Whose house is this?

Well to tell you all the truth, I’ve wanted to be a scientist since I was in middle school.

Ya see, in middle school my dad gave me a book called "Engines of Creation," which wikipedia helpfully reminds me is about nanotechnology.

tweets.label: Takeover

So I dropped materials science! It's okay everyone, I'm still alive!

tweets.text: So I got my masters degree @SFSU in @LauraBurrusSFSU's lab! The lab works on WNT signaling, particularly during development. In my case I was looking at a protein called wntless, and what happens in the developing chicken neural tube when you 'knock it down' with siRNA.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's a lot of words. Basically, WNT is a protein (well, a family of proteins) that gets sent out as a signal from one cell to another nearby cell. It is important in a lot of different situations! One situation is helping pattern the future parts of your spinal cord!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There is a protein that seems to be important for getting WNT properly shoved out of the first cell, so it can go signaling -- wntless (because if you get rid of it, you'll be wnt-less... Get it?)

I won't belabor the point too much, except to say that dev bio is really amazing!

Anyway, today is going to actually take a couple steps away from nanoscience to lay some groundwork on biology things!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Specifically, I'd like to talk about cancer and the immune system!

This is going to take a good amount of talking, because both cancer and the immune system are very complex *separately*, and mixing them together makes it all pretty confusing!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Okay so first of all, cancer is a pretty big term that covers things ranging from 'liquid' cancers in your blood to solid cancer in, say, your breast. Cancer can range in how aggressive their growth and metastasis is, can range in how many mutations they accumulate, etc etc!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There are cancers that are intimately related to your immune system because they arise from the same (or related) progenitors -- cancers like lymphomas and leukemias.

But most my knowledge is related to solid tumors and how the immune system interfaces with them.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The immune system is around to do a lot of work, but one of the jobs we know it best for is keeping us safe from enemies.

Those enemies aren't only 'foreign' things like bacteria and viruses, but 'domestic' enemies like misbehaving cells.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There are a lot of things that can make a cell behave weirdly (including things like bacterial infections and viruses, but other stuff too, like mutations/genetic damage).

Immune cells and neighboring cells are on the look out for cells being weird. They're on the lookout!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, for a cell to develop into cancer, there are a lot of hurdles to overcome, including avoiding this surveillance. A lot of cells get stopped in this process, so with cancer we are often seeing the 'ones that make it' or the 'ones that slip through the cracks'.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When a cell is acting weird, there are a lot of ways that other cells can tell that something is going on. Cells stick stuff on their surface to help let other cells know what their inner workings are like!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Some proteins are signals other cells *expect* to see, like an "everything is OK" signal -- if it is missing, other cells can get suspicious

Some proteins are signals that something is wrong -- so if you have that signal other cells get worried.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Our cells also have a protein called MHC I. MHC I is a protein that we stick little bits of other proteins on, almost like a 'sampler' dish of what proteins we're making inside our cell.

Most of the time we're just making normal, everyday proteins encoded in our genome!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But what about when we're infected with a VIRUS? When that happens, some (or a lot) of the proteins we're making are viral proteins because it is hijacking our machinery!

Well if the MHC system is still working, we'll end up slipping a chunk of virus protein on our surface!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This can help let your immune system know that something naughty is going down. So MHC I is something most of our cells keep updating, to show what they've been making lately!

This is important for cancer!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Cancer cells often have accumulated some mutations (how many mutations can vary pretty widely!). 

Some of those mutations change the actual amino acid sequence of proteins the cancer cells are making 

(changing that sequence sometimes changes the protein function).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Well, those parts of the changed proteins *might* be recognizable to your immune system as a 'foreign' protein if it is slapped on MHC I and put on the cancer cell surface!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
These are called *neoantigens*
Neo because they're new! The cancer just made them through mutation! 

Antigens because that is what we call chunks of stuff (often protein chunks) that your immune system can recognize and mount a response to (typically adaptive).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So cancer making these neoantigens is thought to be an important way that your body can mount an immune response against cancer -- they're little signals that your immune system can recognize that the cancer is something other than a regular cell in your body.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But if it were that easy, we wouldn't be dealing with cancer in the clinic -- our immune systems would have this handled. Now, the immune system probably takes care of a lot of stuff before it ever makes it to cancer levels, but clearly we are still dealing with cancer today.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
That is because cancer is SO TRICKY.

There are MANY ways that cancer is able to avoid the immune system.

Different cancers have a tendency to rely on different methods of immune evasion, but they can probably use more than one! Gah!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Examples! Cytotoxic T cells are a kind of immune cell that are very good at killing cancer cells when they bump into them and recognize them.

So cancer solution #1 -- don't let the T cells into the tumor.

Seriously! Some cancers set up a "T cell exclusion zone!" https://t.co/SlW4ZV5GCG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If someone is interested I can talk about some of the molecular mechanisms behind the set up of this zone (so tricky....), but for now I'm going to keep it relatively easy to digest and light on the details.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Anyway, I mentioned that cytotoxic T cells are dangerous for cancer cells. They are also important for fighting off viruses -- they kill infected cells so that the virus can't keep hijacking the cellular factory.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Cytotoxic T cells need to have an "off switch" though (all immune responses do) because you want to be able to wind things down when the infection is over!

There are several different off switches that can tell cytotoxic T cells to calm down.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
One example is the kynurenine/IDO pathway. This is a situation where cells (often other immune cells) can toss out a signal into the extracellular environment that says "okay y'all, let's calm down this immune situation!". 

T cells respond to this signal by... calming down

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
When you look inside a tumor. you typically see more than JUST cancer cells. You might see some of the 'normal' cells that were living in the neighborhood before the cancer cells started wrecking things.

But in a lot of cases you'll actually see other immune cells

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
...What the heck are those immune cells doing! Get to work killing that cancer!

But unfortunately, these immune cells have been reprogrammed in the tumor microenvironment (neighborhood) to behave a certain way.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
These are pretty recognizable names in the immune cell world! Macrophages! Neutrophils! Dendritic Cells! Often these cells do a great job with things like launching off inflammatory signals and eating up bacteria.

But in tumors, they often do the opposite!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: They often become kynurenine factories, pumping out that signal to turn off other immune cells. They can help in setting up that T cell exclusion zone I mentioned earlier! They can even put out growth signals to help egg on the cancer cells https://t.co/eIpScuhrHr

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Cancer cells can exploit another "off switch" that T cells have -- a kind of 'secret handshake' that tells the T cells that they bumped into a good cell and need to chill out.

This GIF, except not cool ⬇️⬇️⬇️ https://t.co/ALljYWJeOi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The handshake happens when certain proteins on the surface of T cells bump into and bind with proteins on the surface of other cells 

(sometimes cancer cells, but it can also be on those other pesky naughty immune cells that aren't doing their proper job!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Examples of this handshake can be:

T cell   |   Other cell

PD-1        PD-L1
CTLA-4    B7-1/2
LAG-3      MHC II
TIM-3      Galectin-9

and more!
https://t.co/aPd8WuOzfC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When a T cell gets this handshake, it'll basically back off and cool down and won't kill the cancer cell. That is a significant bummer!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Tumors can also be 'immunologically cold' in that they haven't set off enough immune alarm bells to have their neoantigens recognized as foreign.

Some cancers, by the way, hide their neoantigens by choosing to hide their MHC I! Man they are naughty.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So the thing is, even if you have a tumor where:

the cancer cells have neoantigens
AND you got to see them
AND T cells aren't excluded
AND they aren't burned out from kynurenine

some cancer cells can just shake the T cell's protein-hands and prevent them from doing their jobs! https://t.co/L87iisFlzZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
A relatively recent trend in cancer treatments has been

~Immunotherapy~

Cancer immunotherapy is about giving treatments with the goal of helping the immune system overcome all these tricky hurdles that cancer can toss up!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
An example of cancer immunotherapy success has been the use of blocking antibodies to physically keep T cells and cancer cells from "shaking hands".

So an antibody that targets PD-1, for example, binds to that PD-1 on the T cell and prevents it from hooking up with PD-L1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This has been called immune checkpoint blockade -- the handshake is an 'immune checkpoint' because it can turn off your T cells, and these cool antibodies can *block(ade)* that processs!

Nice!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now, for what is likely to be a TON of different reasons, immune checkpoint blockade works very well in some people and some cancers, and like... not at all in others.

This is truly a bummer. But that just means we need to keep working on it!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In broad strokes, one very plausible reason why immune checkpoint blockade doesn't work in everyone is that it really only deals with *one* of the immune evasion tricks cancers have up their sleeves.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
For example: 

If the tumor is super T cell-excluded, does it matter if you block a handshake that couldn't happen in the first place?

This reminds me of that thing about a tree falling in the woods with no one around.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Or another example:

If a cancer isn't mutated all that much and doesn't have many neoantigens, T cells might never care enough about them to even notice them. So what could would immune checkpoint blockade do?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are other possibilities -- antibodies are smaller than cells and viruses, but are pretty big for proteins and *definitely* big compared to "small molecule drugs" like most chemotherapeutics. Do they have any issues getting into solid tumors?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Antibodies are also pretty bioactive -- they are proteins our body produces itself and are recognized by a lot of our cells. When we use them as a treatment, do they sometimes get taken up or bound up before they get a chance to do their jobs?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It is hard to make universal statements when it comes to cancer! But it certainly is the case that immune checkpoint blockade antibodies have helped many people fight their cancers -- these treatments are getting approved for more and more types of cancer each year.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I think what is becoming clear (or at least, I'm advocating for this view) is that cancer immunotherapy is something that can work, but we probably need to combine multiple tactics so that cancer can't evade its way around our therapies!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Some of this will boil down to a more 'personalized' look at the details of a patient's cancer. Does the cancer seem like it has a lot of neoantigens? Maybe immune checkpoint blockade will work without any help!

If not, maybe we need to add something to the mix to help out...

I'll get into this more (tomorrow? I think?) but this is one place I think nanoparticles can help out -- they can help deliver more than one treatment to the same spot (i.e. the tumor)

Nano can help us make a combo punch to knock the cancer out!

The "nano" part of RealSci_Nano is coming into play today! 

Mainly, I want to go over the multiple answers to the question "why use nanoparticles for drug delivery?" https://t.co/h37h6GKoZt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Well what's the alternative, smarty-pants?!

Just kidding. Many many of the drugs that are administered to you are "small molecules" and are typically under a nanometer in size.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I have a little figure here that my friend and colleague Molly Frey made (from the Scott Lab, @NorthwesternU) at my request. These are 5 reasons I think nanoparticles are useful for drug delivery!

The little yellow shape is a small molecule drug, the green ball is a nanoparticle https://t.co/kILolY3xG6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Okay so let's do (a) first!

Some small molecules don't really like floating around in water! If you put them in water, they tend to clump together and 'precipitate out'.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Some small molecules get chemically modified to improve their water solubility, or get mixed with some stuff to try to help keep the drug from precipitating, like PEG400 (a polymer) or DMSO (an organic solvent).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But another option is to put the small molecule into nanoparticles! Nanoparticles (here I'm thinking particularly about those that are amphiphilic, like lipid or polymer nanoparticles) have areas where they like water and areas where they don't.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For example, you might make a nanoparticle out of some polymer. This polymer has two parts to it -- a 'green' part that likes water and a 'red' part that doesn't (this, by the way, would be called an amphiphilic diblock copolymer) https://t.co/T7HjsosKlk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you toss some of that polymer into water, the 'red' part that hates water will naturally try to hide from the water! This forces the polymer to 'self-assemble' with other polymer strands into little shapes where the 'red' is inside and the 'green' is outside, facing the water https://t.co/RQYcy6grDz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
That's a nanoparticle! I mean, depending on how big the polymer is (and other factors) it doesn't HAVE to be a nanoparticle -- it could be a microparticle instead.

And it doesn't HAVE to form a ball with the red sitting in the center like that -- other shapes are possible! https://t.co/Rd7V9W5sKZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But the main point here is nanoparticles can have areas inside them that are 'red', that are *hydrophobic*. Those areas can be very accommodating and welcoming for hydrophobic small molecule drugs that reeaaally don't want to be hanging out in water.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So, one big benefit of nanoparticles is you can make small molecule drug formulations with hydrophobic drugs that are otherwise really hard to make soluble!

This improvement to solubility often also improves the *stability* of the drug in water -- it won't precipitate out easily

Okay so the idea behind (c) has to do with the distribution of your small molecule -- where does it go in your body and what cells end up getting treated?

In most cases I can think of, when you take a drug it is intended to get to work on some subset of your cells

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But when you take a drug orally or by an IV injection or something, a lot of the time it ends up going to a LOT of places in your body, and can end up affecting MANY kinds of cells.

Not all of those cells were really your 'target' cells.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Sometimes that is fine, but sometimes that can cause damage and/or 'off-target' effects. Doxorubicin is a chemotherapy drug that can cause really serious heart toxicity 

(Why are you hitting the heart like that dox? Go fight the cancer!!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Well one *potential* benefit of nanoparticles is you can change where in the body the drug goes and what cells are more or less likely to take them up.

There's probably a lot of reasons why this change happens.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: First of all, small molecules are... smaller than nanoparticles. So they can squeeze out of small holes in your body than nanoparticles and end up in different spots in different amounts than a nanoparticle would!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Small molecules can also *stick* to stuff and have that seriously impact where they go. For example, there are proteins in your blood like serum albumin -- some drugs LOVE sticking to serum albumin and can get dragged into different parts of the body.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I don't, by the way, mean to say that nanoparticles themselves can't be sticky. Not only *can* nanoparticles be sticky, they almost ALWAYS are sticky.

The 'stickiness' of nanoparticles is something scientists often try to modulate to change blood circulation time

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is turning into a bit of a tangent, but in any case, the surface of your nanoparticle definitely impacts what organs it goes to and what cells gobble them up. And you can do some engineering to try to control that (some)!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Surface charge can impact where nanoparticles go! Surface hydrophobicity (and curvature, and other stuff) can impact 'protein adsorption', or basically proteins in your body glomming onto the nanoparticle. Nanoparticle SHAPE can impact cell uptake!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Yeah! Little nanostars can get taken up by different cells preferentially compared to little nanoworms, or nanodiscs, or nanofootballs, and so on!

There's a lot of thoughts as to *why* this happens... maybe we can go into that tangent sometime...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But anyway, you can also try to really specifically get your nanoparticle taken up by particular cells using *targeting stuff* attached to the surface of your nanoparticles.

These could be antibodies, DNA aptamers, sugars, or seriously a ton of other things people have tried.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I am *personally* a bit of a targeting skeptic -- I think it takes a lot of careful work and design to make a nanoparticle that *helped* by the addition of a targeting moiety more than it is *hurt*  by the added complexity.

But I love being proved wrong!

tweets.text:
So (c) is basically that you can engineer nanoparticles to change where your drug goes, compared to if it were floating around your body willy-nilly.

In the example of doxorubicin, which I mentioned earlier, a nanoparticle-delivered version of dox reduced heart toxicity!

tweets.text:
PEGylated means the liposome has some PEG polymer attached to its surface.

PEG stands for poly(ethylene glycol), so it is a polymer made up of ethylene glycol units. PEG has a reputation for helping to extend the circulation time of stuff you toss into the bloodstream

tweets.text:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Liposomes are little bubbles with water inside and outside the bubble, and a thin bilayer of lipid in between.

Some hydrophobic drugs occasionally get loaded into the lipid bilayer (this is not a trivial thing to do, you can potentially disrupt that bilayer).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
When you want to load hydrophilic stuff into a liposome, one way to do it is to simply form that lipid bubble AROUND the cargo you're trying to load!

So now the drug is floating around inside the bubble!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is not typically a very high efficiency process. Generally, a lot of the 'space' when you're forming liposomes is *outside* the bubble, so a lot of your drug never gets encapsulated in the first place! Bummer!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Small molecules can also potentially diffuse across the lipid bilayer of the liposome, meaning you can leak your drug out over time.

Also a bummer!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But that isn't to say it can't work! It is just that this kind of cargo loading has some difficulties associated with it.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Anyway, 'regular old' loading wasn't  working very well for doxorubicin. So they used a different kind of loading, one that is called 'remote loading'.

In remote loading you make your liposomes, then add your cargo drug *to the outside* of those liposomes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
"Wait Sean" you might say
"If the drug is outside of the liposome, how do you load it in?"

That's a great question, person on twitter!

You let the drug diffuse into the liposome down its concentration gradient.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now, of course, if you reach an equilibrium then you really haven't done any better than 'regular old' loading.

But with remote loading you have a cool trick -- your liposomes aren't empty, they're actually already loaded with a *trapping agent*

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The trapping agent is something that associates with your drug cargo and *traps it* inside the liposome, such that the drug cannot diffuse back out.

Your liposome becomes a drug trap! Once the drug checks in, it can't check out (for a while, anyway). https://t.co/BUSXxaWbwy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Remote loading can drive realllly high encapsulation efficiencies, like 90% -- which means out of all the drug you put into the mix with liposomes, nearly all of the drug ends up inside your little nanobubbles.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The 'trapping' part can also help reduce the leakiness, so you don't prematurely lose your drug en route to the cancer!

One downside of remote loading is that it does not work for all compounds.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Based on the trapping agents currently used, you need a compound that is a weak acid or a weak base. The compound also needs to be able to diffuse through the lipid bilayer of the liposome!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Ah also, it is nice if the compound is fairly water soluble, so you can mix a good amount of it with the liposomes. Not *too* water soluble because then it might not make it through the membrane!

Given all the rules, it is maybe impressive that any drug qualifies.

tweets.text: So what is #terahertz radiation? Terahertz radiation falls in between #microwave (think microwave ovens) and #infrared radiation (heat) in the electromagnetic spectrum. One terahertz (1 THz) is equal to one million million hertz (1^12 Hz). https://t.co/Z61D2KL9QG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The THz range encompasses light of frequencies from 100GHz up to 10THz and has wavelengths ranging from 30 microns to 3mm. It's energy range spans 0.4meV to 40meV ( heat energy from approx. -268 degrees Celsius to room temperature!) So what is exciting about this energy range?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So why is the #terahertz energy range interesting? Well..... the energy of several quasiparticles (phonons, excitons, magnons) fall in this range. If we shine terahertz radiation at a material, we can look at how these quasiparticles behave and also promote collective excitations https://t.co/W2rApYniRo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can use terahertz radiation or #terahertz #spectroscopy to look at a material's optoelectronic properties. For example, we can look at its vibrational modes, how different carriers (electrons or electrons) move and scatter within the material and its magentisation dynamics.
