tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So yesterday, we were looking at #terahertz radiation and I hope I've convinced you that THz is cool and will make a difference in your lives. Today, I want to look at another aspect of my #research -#nanomaterials! So stay tuned to find out about #semiconductor nanowires

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So why do we need #nanomaterials? You've heard about them in the news, but are they really revolutionary? Let's first think about how technology has changed during our lifetimes - the technology powering our devices has got smaller, faster and smarter, but is reaching a limit.. https://t.co/3gPjG0B8tL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This change  is known as #MooresLaw, which predicts the number of #transistors on a chip doubles roughly every 2 years. At present, we have computing power equal to a mouse brain and are close to a human brain, but this trend is slowing down! Current Si transistors are only 7nm! https://t.co/HWNWjXluSD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We are already at the #nanometre length scale. At this length scale, #quantum effects start to come into play and we need to investigate #nanomaterials to work out how we can harness them @IBM have recently demonstrated 5nm #transistors using nanosheets    https://t.co/KxvQk4mhW7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There is a lot of research into use of #nanomaterials for #device applications and there are already some examples. Below you can see some examples with  a #solar cell, a #laser, and #transistor all made out of #nanowires and #nanoparticles for drug delivery! https://t.co/w1UnB2Dy1j

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are several advantages that #nanomaterials can offer. For the past few years, I've been looking at #semiconductor #nanowires as building blocks for devices. Nanowires have diameters on the order of 100nm and lengths of up to a few microns. https://t.co/sAM5OxPSil

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are several groups working on nanowire growth and their application in devices. I've had the pleasure of working with @i_morral group @EPFL_en, who can answer any tricky questions! But one of the main advantages of nanowires is the chance to build heterostructures https://t.co/8dSpwU6RDA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can theoretically take any two materials (even if they are lattice mismatched) and grow an axial or radial heterostructure. Axial heterostructures can build p-n junctions for transistors and solar cells, whereas radial heterostructures are crucial for building nanowire lasers

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can effectively build this structures from the atom up! We can add dopants to build customised heterostructures for specific device applications, allowing us to design their optoelectronic properties from the start. https://t.co/s8eo4X6Xf1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But the best advantage of #nanowires, is that they have comparable optoelectronic performance to bulk materials! They maintain high electron mobilities (high device speeds) while reducing material composition. So expect to see nanowires in your devices soon!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So yesterday, we looked at the use of #nanomaterials as building blocks for nanodevices. But are there any other exciting materials that could influence society? I'm currently interested in some new exotic materials called topological insulators. #research #STEM https://t.co/FJqb7OJ9Vt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These materials are really weird! They are insulating in the bulk but highly conductive at the surface. So the middle of the material can't support any electrical currents but the surface hosts fast electrical currents (~100 times faster than silicon) - great for #electronics https://t.co/OCphBij1PT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These surface currents are spin polarised. There are two channels - one for electrons with spin up and one for electrons with spin down. This allows us to carry twice as much information - we can use both the charge of an electron and its spin to give us an on/off signal.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But the coolest thing about these materials, is that they are topologically protected! Surface electrons cannot be backscattered from defects or impurities (they just carry on through). They travel as if on a tramline or ice rink - in one direction with less heat and resistance. https://t.co/0crpOTjdY9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Topological materials are great candidates for #electronic #spintronic and #photonic devices and could provide  a step change in performance and energy efficiency! Recent research has also shown that they could push devices into the #terahertz range!  https://t.co/9ZchOktUMv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Good morning everyone! I hope you enjoyed seeing a small snapshot of my #research. Today is my last day of tweeting for @RealSci_Nano and I would like to share my experiences as a #deaf/hard of hearing #researcher and discuss topic close to my heart...…#accessibility in #STEM https://t.co/Y685zb3Yjy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I've been hard of hearing since birth and rely on #lipreading for everyday communication. I got #hearingaids when I was around 14 and have had a love/hate relationship with them ever since. I recently started learning #BritishSignLanguage again and am using it more and more

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Lot's of people have asked what it's like being #disabled in #STEM and it is always an interesting question for me.. First, I don't feel or identify as #disabled - it is a term I use to access support and reasonable adjustments, but I am #scientist, #engineer and Jessie foremost!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My #disability is a hidden disability, so some of my colleagues out there may not even be aware that I am #deaf (surprise!). Up until studying for my PhD, I tried to hide my deafness and fit into a #hearing world. Now, I much more proud and open about it.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Looking back, I was afraid to talk about my deafness and ask for support because I didn't want to be 'different' or a 'hassle'. I felt like a problem. I didn't want to miss out on opportunities because of #unconsciousbias or the fact that I needed subtitles, microphones, etc.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The lack of these adjustments made events (such as conferences) inaccessible for me. If we everyone to participate in #STEM equally, we need to remove these barriers and make STEM #accessible. And we need to start by asking is STEM #equal #diverse and #inclusive and #accessible? https://t.co/BxQwqIwbRt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #accessibility benefits everyone not just #disabled #researchers. For example, small changes, such as using microphones at conferences, will make a huge difference to researchers who are hard of hearing, but will also make life easier for everyone!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So I would like to start a discussion around #accessibility . Please feel free to ask any questions you may have about my experience and barriers facing #disabled #researchers.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So how can you be an #ally to #disabled researchers? First, when considering #accessibility in your events and institutions, engage us! We have a whole wealth of knowledge from lived experience to contribute. Ask us what we need and how you can support. #nothingaboutuswithoutus

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Put #accessibility first at the very start of any design process or discussion. This ensures #inclusivity  and #accessibility is embedded at all stages (It also saves time and cost later on!) Consulting with your local #disabled staff network is a great way to do this. @nadsn_uk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are also little changes that all of us can make. For example, why not make sure you use and ask others to use a microphone at conferences? If you are making a new lecture course, could you make sure all your resources use sans serif font with minimum font size 12?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #accessibility is about #raisingawareness and making small changes that will make a huge difference to others in #STEM, so I would like to ask all of you today to identify one small change you can make and to think about #accessibility in your #research #allypledge

Yes, if we use a technique called "micropatterning", where essentially we can take a surface and transform it to create small features that would reflect light like a prism does.

tweets.text: So, we know now how liquid crystals work, what happens in LCD Displays? White light passes through a polariser, gets "twisted" by a layer of liquid crystals and is then filtered through a second polariser. If we apply a voltage to the LC, there is no twisting, so we see black. https://t.co/8yVxUK6Juh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This happens because the voltage "breaks" the order of the molecules in LCs. What is a polariser? A thin patterned film that functions as a light filter. tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hello everybody! This week I will be taking over @RealSci_Nano! I will be talking about small molecules and how they are seen to form nanoclusters in water! Today, though, I will be introducing myself.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I started off my research path in my home country of Australia. I miss Australia. My undergraduate at RMIT was in Applied Science (Chemistry). I soon realised I loved Physical Chemistry - it just made sense. https://t.co/gFkZBdznsO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I then went to Greece. I worked there for a while, but I knew my heart was in exploring, discovery and manufacturing via science. I went back to uni part-time and did my 4th year degree in Chemistry at the University of Athens.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After that it was the Surface Science Research Centre, Uni of Liverpool, UK. I studied epitaxial water/ice growth on periodic metal surfaces. I love surface science! Crystallisation &/or interfaces have since been major parts of my research. #crystallisation #ice #surfacescience https://t.co/2jAodNDu1A

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That was the last time I was in a Science Department. From there on I ended up in Engineering, mainly Materials. Next stop, TU Delft, the Netherlands. Modelling and experimental research of internal precipitation in metal alloys. Look at the nanoscaled oxides! https://t.co/lPkPCdLiT8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Back to the UK! England first, Uni of Birmingham. I was involved in a few projects here but my main one was with properties of water-based surfactant-polymer thin films. I love films! Here's a video of 1 my experiments to test material properties of my film #films #surfactants https://t.co/BuAmfkxGbH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Scotland next! Glasgow doesn't have the best weather but it is, by far, my favourite city in the UK! At the Uni of Strathclyde I am, again, involved in various projects. My main one, though, has to do with nanoclusters! Stay tuned for more on that this week! Intro over & out! https://t.co/8CI3fJnjsZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today I will talk a bit about Brownian Motion (BM), as it is key to understanding how my nanoclusters are observed. BM is the random movement of particles in a fluid (liquid or gas) medium. #brownianmotion

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The fluid medium is made of many small molecules that collide with particles being observed. Collisions cause the particle to move in various directions, hence the randomness in the particles’ movements.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Think of it this way: notice how dust particles move in a ray of light. They are all over the place! They are moving within a fluid medium (air). The dust particles (bigger, observable) collide with the molecules of the air (smaller, undetected) & as such appear to move randomly. https://t.co/BBbAqWZV0N

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It was named after Scottish Botanist Robert Brown, who first studied such fluctuations (1827). He observed, under a microscope, that parts of pollen were jittering on the surface of water. At first he thought it meant the pollen was alive. https://t.co/u5gZo1CtkG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But that was not the case. Brown, like the proper scientist he was, decided to test his hypothesis. He tried the same thing with sand, which is obviously not alive. The sand produced the same movement! What was going on? His work was forgotten for a while... https://t.co/HxY3p4jADF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In 1905 some young lad was doing his PhD in diffusion of colloidal suspensions in liquids. He combining Newtonian mechanics to thermodynamics. He observed random forces and speculated they might be Brownian Motion, which was later proved to be correct. He was Albert Einstein. https://t.co/H1sjd83jIa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So why all this talk about BM and Diffusion? Because of their size, my nano bits and pieces cannot be observed using optical microscopes. Lasers are used, but not to observe the nanoclusters directly. They are used to detect the Brownian Motion of the clusters! #lasers, #nano https://t.co/BEFaGBnH6F

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Of course, there are other methods to "see" nano-sized objects, and I will refer to some throughout the week. Tomorrow, though, I will talk a bit about my current main project, my uncanny nanoclusters! See you then! https://t.co/YJhBP95kx4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So for today, a bit about the research. Recent studies have seen small molecules associate to form sub-micron clusters in some solutions. They often occur in solutions of highly soluble small molecules, e.g. concentrated protein solutions and aqueous glycine solutions. https://t.co/thW8fzCbB5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These clusters are not your ordinary clusters; they present liquid-like properties and can be fairly “large”. They are unusual, as they appear as discrete domains in the solution that contain higher solute density than the rest of the solution....

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here is the interesting bit: these domains are dispersed throughout the bulk of the solution, but are not considered a separate phase! #nano #clusters #assembly #homogeneous https://t.co/c6JcJYDW0O

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So my nanoclusters are there, but the solution is homogeneous! I mentioned before that crystallisation has featured heavily throughout my research. The crystallisation process is extremely important to understand, as it is widely used in many industries...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When phase separating a solute from a supersaturated solution to form a crystalline phase, 2 main steps are involved: 1) nucleation (formation of a stable crystal nucleus), & 2) crystal growth (material added to existing crystal lattice). https://t.co/VqNOeD2Oqr

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Many significant efforts have been made in the last 30 years to better understand the process. So why are these nanoclusters important? Their existence has rendered interest due their possibility of being metastable intermediates for crystallisation! https://t.co/puCjZstyRD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Experimental and theoretical computational results have led to alternate two-step processes of crystallization being proposed. One proposal suggests disordered metastable molecular assemblies are produced before nucleation of more ordered nascent crystals. https://t.co/qBARB5v0h7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another alternative proposal sees nanoparticles form a crystal-like lattice that ultimately transforms into a molecular crystal. Recent studies focus on identifying if there is indeed a direct link between the presence of the solute molecular clusters and a crystal formation. https://t.co/mTbgfZRv4b

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Whatever the case, the presence of these nanoclusters needs investigation!!! For example, the kinetics and thermodynamics of the formation of these liquid-like species is yet to be understood. #crystallisation #molecular #nano #kinetics #thermodynamics https://t.co/INIl9wQ8ik

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My work involves looking at various aspects of such liquid-like clusters for nanoparticle production. Collaboration with the Uni of Edinburgh (Dr. M Sweatman, Dr. C.A. Ferreiro-Rangel) using experimental and computational data aims to answer questions regarding their stability.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Collaboration with the Uni of Sheffield sees us investigating how the presence of these clusters can influence nanoparticle formation, mainly silica (with Prof. S. Patwardhan @GreenNanoRes, and @amber_keegan) and magnetite (with Dr S. Staniland & L. Norflok).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All of this is part of the @SynBIM project which works on creating transformative knowledge and toolsets for larger-scale "green" manufacture of tunable and sustainable, synbio nanomaterials. Check it out! https://t.co/pRN20TErkb  #sustainability #nanomaterials https://t.co/4QTNCOwaTA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today I will talk about one of the main techniques I use to detect the presence of my nanoclusters: Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A laser light hits the sample, whereby the light is scattered by my liquid-like clusters. A detector placed at a known angle to the incident beam picks up part of the scattered light. #laserscatter #nano https://t.co/Plt1HbZRpl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What the detector is picking up is referred to as the “speckle pattern”. This pattern fluctuates with time due to the Brownian Motion of the particles in the solution. This fluctuation is recorded by the detector, ultimately giving us the intensity (count rate) plot. https://t.co/88MSOQz3yF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @RoyDhimanSci Hello Dhiman, regarding the shape, an upcoming tweet will respond to that (short answer, it doesn't tell us much about shape!).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @RoyDhimanSci As for dimension, I will not go in depth in the tweets but yes, a lot can be determined by measuring the nanoparticles at different scatter angles (changing the detector angle). The particles' dimensions are proportionate to how quickly they diffuse (move in the sample).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @RoyDhimanSci Finally, there is no excitation wavelength measured; only the scattered laser light is detected! In fact, any excitation wavelength detected near the DLS can actually interfere with the results! Thank you for your questions Dhiman!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The time-dependent part of the speckle pattern fluctuation (intensity decaying over time) gives us the autocorrelation function. The intensity decay correlates to how fast the nanocluster is moving, i.e. diffusing in the solution. #diffusion #lightscatter https://t.co/flsOUEvKqe

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Using this Stokes-Einstein equation for diffusion, and having some known parameters, the hydrodynamic radius of the detected species can be determined. https://t.co/2pbL3LHVer

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But what happens if there are more than one scattering species with different sizes present in the solution? Well, things get a bit more complicated. For example, when 2 species of very different sizes are present, the autocorrelation function has two distinct decays. https://t.co/2UXiouLhw7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Generally, the DLS comes with special software that can give the user lots of info regarding the hydrodynamic radii of the species detected, as well as an indication of the degree of polydispersity of sizes scattering the light.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My systems are simple and as such I was able to write my own little Matlab script used to analyse the raw data away from the DLS computer. In light of the last few month, that script came in very handy! https://t.co/HLR7GF1eCw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I mentioned before that the DLS measures hydrodynamic radius. The hydrodynamic size (radius or diameter) is that of an equivalent hard sphere diffusing at the same rate as the species under observation. It does not tell us a lot about the shape, because it assumes it is spherical https://t.co/GYtiHDA5aM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @EmmRankinWilson Trade secrets - they don't want us to know! 😅

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: DLS is quick – a scan can be done anywhere between 5s  up to a few minutes! Multiple scans are necessary for  accuracy. Most often, it’s also non-intrusive. You can measure the same sample again on a later date, or you can measure it to check for changes occurring over time.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I use my 2 trusty DLS machines for more than detecting my snazzy nanoclusters.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For example, I recently used DLS to verify the presence of nanoassemblies of peptoids, which was part of the brilliant work in mediating activity and nano-assembly of antimicrobial peptoids led by Dr H.K. Aaron Lau (@LauResearch) here at Strathclyde. https://t.co/9ST2AnAIFc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Dr @ManlioTassieri of the Uni of Glasgow first combined novel theoretical models & DLS to determine the persistence length (Lp) of semiflexible polymers within solutions. We recently teamed up to get even more data for a more detailed model.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I even created a user-friendly Matlab script (based on his Labview script) that uses DLS data to give various properties of the polymers, including Lp. Hopefully this publication will also be out in 2020! https://t.co/OTks23Q1Xw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Tomorrow I will be back to talk about another laser scattering technique I have used, Brownian Microscopy. See you then!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today I am going to talk a bit about Brownian Microscopy. It shares many similarities with the DLS technique such as the fact that it too uses laser light to detect entities in the nanoscale. The sample here is placed in the sample holder, and the laser light passes through it. https://t.co/CCDkWp7kyk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The light that is scattered from the nanoentities present in the sample can actually be visualised by a 20x magnification microscope that is mounted onto a camera, an example of which is seen below #nano #microscopy https://t.co/x1HlX9Vrky

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The above shows a sample of Ludox in water. Each of the light points seen are due to a Ludox particle present in the water medium. Powerful software is used to track the movement of each light point. I am using NTA (nanoparticle tracking analysis) software. https://t.co/9X2m26XQfu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The NTA software follows the centre of the light point and determines the mean-square displacement, in the x and y axis, as a function of time. From there, it estimates the diffusion coefficient and, as we saw before with the DLS,  the hydrodynamic size of the particles is found. https://t.co/N2om21uQud

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Using NTA software allows for the determination of a size distribution profile of small particles. NTA is used for particles with a diameter of app. 10-1000 nm, whereas DLS can be used for particles as small as 1nm diameter up to even larger than a micron (in some cases). https://t.co/LF01w2kPfB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So both DLS and Brownian Microscopy rely on scattered light & Brownian Motion, but there are also differences between the two techniques.... https://t.co/6IJ2Am0gsH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A major difference is that DLS does not visualise each particle separately, but rather relies on a digital correlator to analyse the time dependent scattering intensity fluctuations. This difference is important when determining the size. #nano #nanotechnology https://t.co/YeDVAu1vhF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
DLS: size is based on the intensity of fluctuations of the scattered light. 
NTA: size is dependent on the number of scattered light points. 
Both give hydrodynamic sizes, but one is intensity weighted and the other number weighted!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That is why the same sample measured with the two techniques can give similar trends, but different size results! https://t.co/F3llvwRIS5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In general, using NTA software is preferred when you are interested in determining the concentration of nanoparticles in the sample, when you have polydisperse samples and you want better resolution of size peaks, or when you have extremely dilute solutions.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That’s it for today! Join me tomorrow when I talk about other techniques used to help with detection of my nanoclusters, such as SAXS and NMR. See you then!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are many more techniques for measuring nano-sized bits and pieces. Today I’ll be mentioning two of them, without going into too much detail - they were used as additional techniques in my research regarding my lovely nanoclusters!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: First up, NMR (nuclear magnetic resonance) It is another spectroscopic technique that can be utilised to help get data on nano-sized entities, mainly of organic molecules.  It is often used in advanced medical imaging techniques, such as in MRI (magnetic resonance imaging). https://t.co/08AbJahGgG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (Very!) simply put, NMR utilises a magnetic field to see at what energy ranges (in radio waves) specific nuclei of interest (e.g. protons, 1H) flip from being aligned to the field (low energy) from no longer being aligned (high energy), giving us info on the species examined. https://t.co/vAOPDJaVY8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For my nanoclusters,  NMR whiz Dr John Parkinson (Strathclyde) used what is known as proton NMR Diffusion-ordered spectroscopy (1H-NMR DOSY). This type of NMR is used to obtain diffusion coefficient values. And what happens once we have the diffusion coefficient?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Yep, you guessed it – we can use the Stokes-Einstein equation to determine the hydrodynamic radius! #NMR #Diffusion https://t.co/ch1u7VwFwV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Small angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS) uses a monochromatic X-ray beam in a somewhat similar manner as DLS uses a laser....

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The X-ray beam hits the sample whereby some of the X-rays are scattered by the species present in the sample. The scattered X-rays are picked up by a detector, with the scattering pattern providing info on said species. #SAXS #nano https://t.co/UA1DJErVAp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The measurements provide us with angle dependent scattered intensities I(Q), with the angular dependence being presented in terms of the scattering vector Q, as seen in the previous plots.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: By recording the scattering of X-rays at various angles, SAXS allows for the acquisition of information about the size of species within a sample. From the slope of what is known as a Guinier fit (log[I(Q)] vs Q) we can obtain the radius of gyration (Rg) of the species present. https://t.co/c1BiWpnJv3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: An (over)simplified definition for Rg is that it is the mass weighted average distance from the core of the species examined to each mass element in that species - it's not the same as the hydrodynamic radius (Rh)! Rg and Rh often have different values! https://t.co/UPM3EgmxeV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: SAXS gives info not only about size, but also about the structure of species! The Form Factor (FF) of the sample is the scattering that occurs due to the shape of species present. By fitting the data with appropriate theoretical FF we can get an estimate of the shape! https://t.co/344X8d9mYN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That’s it for today! Tomorrow will be a small recap of the week – see you then!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So here it is, the recap of the week. It will be brief, as I live in Glasgow and I want to go out for my jog before the rain begins.... https://t.co/1gmPXMfDsr

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My main current project involves research into nanoentities  formed by organic, small molecules within an aqueous medium. My nanoclusters are a bit weird. https://t.co/wvTiysTrxV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: They present liquid-like properties, and can sometimes be fairly “large”, as in much larger than the molecules present in the sample. They appear as discrete domains dispersed throughout the solution. https://t.co/qAOLD7xtlj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These domains contain higher solute density than the rest of the solution, and yet are not considered a separate phase! Can they, perhaps, be playing a vital role regarding pathways to crystallisation?! https://t.co/Q0XaL0FF9R

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I use different spectroscopic / light scattering techniques to determine the presence, size, and sometimes the shape of my nanoclusters. I also examine them for stability under varying conditions. https://t.co/Vw3zYC1Ezd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Techniques include DLS, NTA Brownian Microscopy, SAXS and NMR. I also examine my nanoclusters’ role in the formation of other nanomaterials, such as Silica and Magnetite. https://t.co/8gGdTHcRDC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I am part of many other projects that utilise the aforementioned techniques. I like collaborations and expanding my knowledge! https://t.co/ySiukv44SX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So that’s it from me. I hope you enjoyed checking out my research this week. I had a great time disseminating it! You can find me @zimbitas for questions/queries! Brian here, over and out! https://t.co/ldTzQullBZ

Nanotechnology lowers costs, produces stronger and lighter wind turbines, improves fuel efficiency and, thanks to the thermal insulation of some nanocomponents, can save energy.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The natural(no pun intended) thing to explain first is what fouling is & why you should care. Fouling is essentially the accumulation of unwanted material on a surface (i.e. Plaque build-up on your teeth is a type of fouling & we all know how important it is to brush your teeth!) https://t.co/k2f8Hhu4Vt

tweets.text: Fouling is a huge problem in many industries ranging from medical implants to ships. Marine growth on ship hulls costs the US Navy $180-260M per year alone (Schultz, 2011). Fouling can be caused by organic(proteins, oils, bacteria etc) and inorganic substances. https://t.co/dYSfWBLojP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As I mentioned earlier in the week, my research is inspired by nature, more specifically by the kidney. Why the kidney? Because it's capable of producing 180L of primary urine everyday whilst still remaining intact and fouling free. Warning: there's a lot of bio in this thread!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
A quick refresher on kidney filtration:
Filtration is carried out by nephrons, each kidney has roughly 1million of these units. Within the nephron there are two stages of filtration
1) Glomerular filtration
2) Tubular reabsorption
(Labelled below, img: Wellcome trust) https://t.co/jytZs8Blvx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The first stage removes urea, ions (salts etc) and water from the blood stream to produce primary urine. The second stage selectively reabsorbs water and other small molecules that you need back into your blood stream

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My work is inspired by the 1st stage which is a bundle of specialised blood vessels. The wall is made up of multiple layers (see left). The really cool thing about this structure is that albumin (protein ~4nm) can be rejected by the 1st layer even though the gaps are 100nm https://t.co/jxTCzCPkDP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Why is this so cool? With a pore size of 100nm separation should be based on size (see quoted tweet). This layer shouldn't be able to reject such a small protein but somehow it does? Amazing!
https://t.co/DnGY6vTfcv https://t.co/Vwz0rxWlHJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: While there is no agreed filtration mechanism, my work looks mostly at how this system avoids the accumulation of plasma proteins and how I can adapt this for the application of water filtration. The most striking part is the hairy structure on top (see right) https://t.co/EsrtS00qc6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This structure is known as the endothelial surface layer. This layer is negatively charged and hydrophilic. This means that it can repel the plasma proteins (usually also negatively charged) and prevent adsorption by binding water within its structure.

tweets.text: Leading on from my nature inspiration in this previous thread, most of my current work revolves around the synthesis of polymer brushes. Polymer brushes are very aptly named, they're basically polymer chains that are tethered to a surface by one end like this 👇🏾 https://t.co/iXttYtYiPD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The two most popular methods of attaching these chains to a surface are:
1) Grafting to: premade polymer chains which bind to an anchoring site
2) Grating from: polymerisation of the chain from an initiating species on the surface https://t.co/gkFLkutvTT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Grafting from a surface is the most commonly used method. Different surface initiated controlled radical polymerisation (SI-CRP) techniques are used to graft these polymer brushes to create different (and all beautiful) polymer architectures https://t.co/YdW6jxsZIz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In a later thread I'll get into the different applications that polymer brushes are used in! Hopefully I'm starting to win you over about how cool polymer brushes are?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Polymer brushes have a very versatile portfolio. Flexibility over which polymer you graft can give you control over a material to make it: stimuli responsive (pH, temperature etc), compatible with different solvents, or further functionalised with desired compounds. https://t.co/h62W4Z4Xw7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Catalysis:
Polymer brushes can be used as a way to immobilise catalysts. One example is the grafting of PHEMA-PEG brushes on the interior of microreactor channels to immobilise gold and palladium nanoparticles. Paper doi: 10.1002/chem.201000948 https://t.co/tM59cm6POJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Energy storage:
Polymer brushes can provide an elegant solution to incompatibilities between ceramic and polymer matrixes in energy storage devices (e.g. batteries, capacitors). When used as a bridge between components, the energy density can increase. https://t.co/moeFOvTuKU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Fuel cells:
Polymer brushes can provide a platform to improve humidifying additives in proton conducting membranes. Silica nanoparticles modified with a polymer brush integrated into Nafion increased proton conductivity by 4x https://t.co/EoZbvPZPdK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Biosensors:
Polymer brushes can be end functionalised with groups to aid specific adsorption of the biomolecule in question while preventing non-specific adsorption by others (aka fouling 😉) https://t.co/DMs6tDeIXS

tweets.text:
So I'd like to talk about the most common anti-fouling techniques
1) Fouling resistance
2) Fouling release
3) Biofouling control
The first two are passive methods to reduce the interactions between the surface and foulants whereas the third is an active method to prevent biofilms https://t.co/UoqPeUN2sG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
1) Fouling resistance
This scheme is the most common anti-fouling technique which aims to prevent attachment through the hydrophilic nature of the surface. The bound hydration layer makes adsorption thermodynamically unfavourable for adsorption https://t.co/iMwvIwH5eN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
2) Fouling release
In this method, adsorption is not being prevented, instead the surface is modified so that the strength of the interaction between the foulant and the surface is low. That way they can be easily removed. Low surface energy is usually the aim of the modification https://t.co/zvwwtzEJs6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3) Biofouling control
The overarching aim here is control/prevent biofilm growth. This can be done in many ways i.e. using bacterial behaviour against them (quorum quenching), integrating biocidal elements into a matrix (antibiotic reagents, heavy metals) etc. https://t.co/QPY5d2mSyc

Polymer brushes as an antifouling technique! 🔊
So from my previous tweet you'll know the common antifouling strategies. Polymer brushes can be used to integrate one or more of these techniques to withstand adsorption of unwanted material. More examples below 👇🏾

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
1) Bactericidal brushes
Quaternary ammonium salts (QAS) show antibacterial activity. By grafting with QAS the brush is capable of killing the bacteria that settle onto its surface. https://t.co/YR88j39miu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
2) Biomedical devices
The formation of biofilms on biomedical devices(i.e. catheters) can lead to bacterial infection. By grafting polymer brushes, initial adhesion of bacteria (up to 90%) can be avoided. https://t.co/Q856DDv88e

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3) Contact lenses
If, like me, you wear contact lenses you'll know that protein buildup makes them very uncomfortable. By grafting polymer brushes to improve the hydrophilicity of the lens (fouling resistance), protein adsorption can be reduced https://t.co/B6IMlrF5UU

But what is diamond really and is a nanodiamond the same as a the gemstone we like to adorn ourselves with? 

At the very basis of it, yes gems and nanodiaomnds are made of the same stuff...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That is to be called a diamond (whether regular or nanosized) it must be Carbon (C) atoms arranged in a crystal lattice structure. This structure is a face-centred cubic, each C bonds to 4-neighbour C's forming a regular tetrahedral structure. https://t.co/YHFTy3E2q7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Naturally formed diamond is the result of C atoms being pressed together under High-pressures and high-temperature (HPHT) within the earth. This process can be replicated in the lab to make the synthetic material I study, which is sometimes called HPHT Diamond. https://t.co/OFj8o04ZnI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Note: there are several different ways to synthesis diamond in the lab, including the HPHT method, CVD (chemical vapour deposition) & Detonation methods

there are tone of great reviews on the diamond synthesis, I like this one focusing on nanodiamonds, https://t.co/p2Xheef5Qj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But any way you make it, the structure of the natural (mined) & synthetic (lab-grown) diamond are identical. But how do we make them nano?

Stay tuned for the next part where I'll discuss the top-down and bottom-up approaches to creating nanodiamonds https://t.co/D9nQf1BoqG

tweets.text: @IreneSuaMar No pressure then 🤣😊, oh wait, 💎 needs pressure 🤔

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Top-down synthesis refers to the process where we start with larger pieces of nanodiamond (ND) & make them smaller. E.g. we start with a micron-sized HPHT diamond &, crush it & then mill it to nanoparticles of diamond (NDs), similar to making flour from grains of wheat. https://t.co/BflF7mjQQo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Bottom-up methods include the so-called detonation nanodiamonds (DNDs) (yep what it sounds like). Carbon precursor is loaded into a chamber w/ an explosive (TNT). When the TNT is exploded creating conditions compatible with forming diamond crystal structure (see previous tweets) https://t.co/knR5S05Tge

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: First Let take a look at a couple of my samples under room light…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My FNDs can be dispersed in water (handy for bio-applications). They aren't very pretty to look at under room light. The 140 nm particles look very milky. This is due to the highly scattering nature of the particles. As we go smaller the solution becomes translucent & darker. https://t.co/p29sw8WbB6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So what about this fluorescence I keep promising… https://t.co/bS8egnss7u

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Well, Diamond, its self isn’t fluorescent, so I’ve not been exactly accurate when I say fluorescent diamonds. To get them to glow we need to create defects in the diamond lattice. https://t.co/8O9N3q83Ty

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These defects occur in natural diamonds which gives then colour, e.g. if a carbon atom is replaced by nitrogen then the diamond will look orange, the most expensive nitrogen coloured gem is “The Orange” diamonds (a whopping $35 M). https://t.co/ApVO4eEOj4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Nitrogen-substitution is the most common colour defect in diamonds & in my nanodiamonds also. So we have the N which helps to give the diamond the orange colour, but to get the funky fluorescence we need one more thing… https://t.co/UFiHhlW7y4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Or instead, we need to remove something. We remove a carbon atom from the diamond, creating a vacancy in the lattice structure! The removal of an atom is done by firing high energy electrons & the material, (there are other methods, but my NDs use electrons)… https://t.co/FP2CWN84v3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The Carbon atom is “knocked out” leaving the vacancy. Then we need the nitrogen & the vacancy to be next to each other. Luckily heating atoms makes them want to dance & its energetically favourable for the vacancy & the nitrogen to want to be together. This is called annealing! https://t.co/i1Zyd8duX8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So by replacing a carbon with nitrogen then removing some carbons and heating the sample we finally get the fluorescent centre called the nitrogen-vacancy centre or NV centre for short.

(Image from https://t.co/tuchTj1YJc) https://t.co/ryATZsjqQY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now we need to excite the NV centre, this means we need to give the electrons of the atoms some extra pep to make them jump out of their ground state to the excited state & as they relax back down they give off some excess energy as a Photons https://t.co/Sd0HcR1e4d

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
That is a very rough quick explanation of Fluorescence…
There are tons of great videos and books on fluorescence but here is an intro video that I like (they do lots of cool sci stuff)

https://t.co/FDPweKhiM3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
To excite the NV centre we use “green light”, we shine the green light (commonly 532 nm wavelength) and the NV centre will glow (Fluoresce) in the red & if we measure the emission spectra it will look like this 
(image https://t.co/u9qem55Kxc) https://t.co/ZfEUkzg2Pj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Notice in the spectrum, the two peaks labelled ZPL? This stands for Zero phono line. The NV centre has 2 ZPL because it can have 2-charge states, it can either have an extra Electron (NV minus [NV–] ) & No extra electron (NV neutral [NV0]).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So the NV spectrum is actually made up of two separate spectra, These charge states are part of what makes these types of fluorescent nanodiamonds (FNDS) so cool with a huge array of potential applications.
(image https://t.co/u9qem55Kxc) https://t.co/AIr2FWAomL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The NV centre is sensitive to its environment so it can be used to sense things, like magnetic fields, temperature changes, & chemical changes. https://t.co/tFmW2RGEsE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Due to COVID-19 the public is being exposed to more scientific terminology and concepts than ever before. This language can often be very jargony & difficult to penetrate. Even for those of us that work and study medical science, it can be a lot to get ones head around. https://t.co/MEfutpCZfn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: things I see in the media a lot are the terms PCR test, antigen v antibody test, diagnostic V screening, Rapid versus gold standard test. But what does all this mean in practice & what are the key distinctions?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Firstly, Diagnostic V screening: a diagnostic test is one that confirms someone's disease status, either that they are positive (have the disease) or are negative (do not currently have the disease. https://t.co/vzmIEfFFYb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A screening test is less certain, it indicates that someone may have the disease. typically screening is used when the risk is low or if their status is already confirmed positive & we want to know how they are responding to treatment.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Whether the test is classed as diagnostic or screening will typically depend on its sensitivity and specificity.
Sensitivity = how much of the test target (e.g. infection) needs to be present to show up in the test
Specificity = do the tests only detect the test target https://t.co/wT8NHSoU0Y

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: how sensitive or specific the test must be will depend on the disease it is testing. One disease may need the diagnostic to 100% sensitive & 99.5 % specific, while another could be 95% sensitive and 98% specific.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
PCR – Polymerase Chain reaction detects nucleic acids (think DNA) here is a great vid explainer 👇 

https://t.co/1NG0VPZ3iU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: An antigen (Ag) is a foreign or toxic substance that triggers an immune response they can be specific to a single species or common amongst a class of organisms.  So an Ag test detects the presence of the infecting organism or its antigenic proteins.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: An antibody is a blood protein that your cells produce in response to an antigen. They bind the antigen to help the immune system to clear the antigen from the body.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This video from https://t.co/KAClIKJQZm is a quick explainer of the difference between these tests. Note: there are now available Antigen tests of COVID-19. this vivid is 4 mths old, but it shows how quickly the technology is moving to help combat the current global pandemic

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The "gold standard" test typically refers to the legally approved method for diagnosing a disease. e.g. In Australia, there are 3 approved methods 
PCR - nucleic acid detection 
Rapid Antigen test
Serological test

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Note: although the newly approved Antigen Rapid test is classed as diagnostic all positive tests must be confirmed by the PCR test before being added to our COVID numbers. This practice is pretty standard in Australia for infectious disease rapid diagnostics.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All these terms, concepts and practices are strictly defined in documents called “Standards”, in Australia we used both Australia Standards (AS) & International standards (IOS). A Standard is a legal document that defines & outlines “best practice”.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: By using Standards, we help to ensure practices, like diagnostic tests are comparable from lab to lab. this is all highly regulated in countries like Australia and is partly why we have good reliable health care. https://t.co/rXOPdnOnW1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Approval of medical devices (e.g. test) is governed by an official agency, in Australia, it's the TGA (Therapeutic Goods Administration), in the USA the FDA (Food and drugs Administration) & in Europe the EMA (European Medicines Agency).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
For Australians, the TGA website is a great source of COVID testing information so if you want a deeper understanding please go there https://t.co/cVsWRdrHLF

for other countries & regions see your own governing bodies for relevant information

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A rapid diagnostic test (RDT), simply is a test that is faster than the existing gold standard. E.g. for bacterial infection PCR is classed as an RDT, the gold standard for diagnosing bacterial infections are biochemical tests that can take up to 10 days for the diagnosis.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In cases were PCR is now the “gold standard” an RDT could include an antigen test such as the one recently approved in Australia. Also in Australia Diagnosis of a disease can only be done by an approved lab using one of the approved methods.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Next, I’ll give a general walkthrough of what we do in a medical device evaluation @NRLScience 
without going into specifics because we deal with IP and confidential material.  I just want to give you an overview of this challenging but rewarding line of scientific work

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Evaluation of a proposed Rapid diagnostic test (RDT):
This evaluation can only be done by an approved lab with trained & qualified staff. For example, I recently joined a project to validate some RDTs, I have undergone intensive training, down to my competency to use a pipette. https://t.co/xNopR5fvfv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The process of making sure an RDT works as the manufacture says is heavily regulated. Each step & protocol is controlled, in fact, @NRLScince has 700+ controlled documents that we used to ensure we are compliant with the different entities we work with. https://t.co/F1TleNLD7s

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: They tell us how we are to conduct each task, although we don't need to know all of them. Some will be for tasks that I don't do. And I can look up the documents I need any time I need to refer to them.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let look a one way we might run an evaluation for an RDT. Say a company wants to get their new RDT out to market – they have tested it and are confident in the test, but they need to have it validated by an authorised & independent lab, such as @NRLScience.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Once the contract is agreed and the goals and parameters outlined we get to the practical task of testing the test. 

the example I'm giving here is for subjective tests, think pregnancy strip. Do I see a line or no line, Do I give it a 1 or a 3 etc.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We receive the RDT & assemble the test samples, these include controls & reference samples – a ref sample is a sample that has been tested using the gold standard & its status is known. All samples are randomised & the work is done blind (testers don’t know the sample status)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In my current role 3 of us work together so we can triple check our work. We then run the test according to the manufacture's protocol. The aim is for us to follow the test as it would be done by someone in the real world. We check the quality of the kit... https://t.co/U62nXrFmcn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We may also make notes on the ease of use, e.g. if the manufacture says the test could be done by someone with no scientific or medical training do we agree, are the instructions clear & easy to follow. These points are subjective that's why we have multiple people. https://t.co/A1BdwiKxhF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We run the test, this involves 100’s of samples over multiple manufactures Lots (different batches) of the RDT, this way we can see if the manufacturing quality is consistent from lot to lot... https://t.co/vmtHWV21fA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It’s no good if one Lot is 100% sensitive & 99.9% specific if the next lot is only 90 % sensitive. The RDT must perform the same (within a very narrow range) test-to-test and lot-to-lot. https://t.co/Sb2Lel9CEg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We then interpret the result, and check if all 3 of us are in agreement (again this is for a subjective test). 2 out of 3 of us must agree in our interpretation of the result, i.e. is the sample positive or negative?. If we don’t reach consensus the test is redone. https://t.co/ymmjbNnsqy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: you need to be confident in your evaluation, it's really important once we start that my grading scale is consistent from our first run to our last. And that I don't let my colleagues change my opinion on what looks like a positive V a negative to me. https://t.co/AkvGyPHFSG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We take detailed notes on each run and even take photos, we need to be scientific as possible and evidence must be given at the end of the evaluation. There are even regulation on how we write our notes 😳 https://t.co/Ztw1obh1ZP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This work is highly repetitive and we must do it methodically so breaks are important so we don’t get fatigued & make errors. We follow a work instruction, it's a little like doing a pre-flight checklist & excellent verbal communication is vital. https://t.co/jolrhRU9cc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This work is not for everyone, it requires focus & an eye for detail and an ability to follow a check-list and do a repetitive task the same again and again. It costs the manufacture a lot of money & lives might depend on us doing our job right. This is a lot of pressure. https://t.co/YEuPFBdprd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But, it is very rewarding knowing that you are contributing to work that can help improve health outcomes. https://t.co/cO9iZIRBCZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If this sounds like something you might find interesting & you are coming to the end of your science degree wondering what to do next. Jobs in evaluation come up often. Even if they don't have jobs listed it can be worth reaching out. Some labs will have studentships too.

tweets.text: Today we had a quick overview of my journey into the ‘nano’ area. Tomorrow we dive into the fascinating world of #nanozymes https://t.co/uL0k7akGW2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Time for some information about #nanozymes. The word NanoZyme comes from two words - NANOparticles and enZYME. A nanoparticle is called a nanozyme when it can mimic the catalytic activity of a natural enzyme. https://t.co/QyHGYJJ2VG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is quite fascinating! To think of it - an inorganic particle which does not show structural similarity or the complex folding patterns of a natural enzyme can still drive the same catalytic reaction to completion as seen in a natural enzyme.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As a biologist, the first curious question that comes to mind - if the complex folding plays an important role in the activity of natural enzymes what is the driving force in nanozymes?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It is the surface atoms in nanoparticles that play an important role in the catalytic activity

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Next obvious question is why do I need nanozymes? Natural enzymes are temperamental and difficult to work with. Let's be honest no one likes that :) NanoZymes are easier to work with, we can fine-tune the activity, and are robust.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It's not all positive for nanozymes - believe me. As amazing nanozymes are - we have not been able to achieve the high level of specificity and complexity we see in natural enzymatic systems. I talk about this in my biochemistry lectures https://t.co/ngeSx8oB0E

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For anyone who knows the concepts of Km and Vmax - you can ignore this post

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Compared to natural enzymes, nanozymes are sometimes better for their catalytic activity. How can we compare this?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are two factors we consider to compare enzyme and nanozyme - how much the enzyme loves its substrate (Km) and how fast can the enzyme convert the substrate to product (Vmax). https://t.co/xBOSVX8AfK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A simple analogy for this concept is your car (body), engine (enzyme) and fuel (substrate). Km is like your measure of fuel efficiency. The less fuel you need the more efficient your car is. Vmax is the fastest speed that you can drive at. So you need low Km and high Vmax.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Many of us have heard of an enzyme horseradish peroxidase (HRP). If I was to compare the peroxidase activity of this enzyme with nanozymes with respect to Km and Vmax, let us see what we get

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Woah! We can see some of the nanozymes are a lot better than HRP. Isn't this amazing. Although it took a lot of time to get to this point, it is great to see the performance of nanozymes keeps getting better. https://t.co/K8wun8Uj6v

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @avpoltral Lol. I still remember reading about enzyme kinetics as an undergrad student. Never thought I will ever use this in my career and here I am sitting and analysing kinetics data.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: An interesting fact about nanozymes # 1 - I heard that the first report on nanoparticles showing enzyme-mimic activity was a serendipitous discovery. This is something that we see a lot in research. Opens up exciting possibilities.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: An interesting fact about nanozymes # 2 - We have been able to mimic the catalytic activity of peroxidase, oxidase, catalase, haloperoxidase, glutathione peroxidase, uricase, methane monooxygenase, hydrolase, superoxide dismutase and pan-enzymatic activity. That is a lot.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: An interesting fact about nanozymes # 3 - We have a new field today called Nanozymology

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: An interesting fact about nanozymes # 4 - The word nanozyme was only coined in 2004.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let's play a game. Can you guess how many papers have been published this year in the area of nanozymes (don't worry about researching this - just take a guess). I will give you the answer tomorrow.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you have a question about any of the posts, do feel free to leave a comment or send me a message directly -@DrRajeshRMIT. I will get back to you as soon as possible.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Yesterday we got to see how fascinating #nanozymes are. We even saw that we can apply biochemical principles we use to understand natural enzymes can be applied to understand nanozymes as well. Today we look at how we can use nanozymes for sensing.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Yesterday we ran a poll trying to guess how many papers have been published in the area of nanozymes. The answer is...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: wait for it

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: wait for it

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Over 400 papers have been published just this year. So congrats to everyone who selected that option. https://t.co/U2vCbS4GQR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Before we dive into how we can use nanozymes in sensor development, there is something we need to know. For a sensor to be able to do its job, we need something that will recognise our analyte of interest in a complex sample matrix

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Sample matrix - this will contain a mixture of substances. For e.g., if I want to detect a pesticide, it may be present in the soil or on the surface of a fruit, which will contain a lot of unwanted molecules including other pesticides.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You need something that will specifically identify your analyte of interest. It is like finding a needle in a haystack.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can use antibodies, enzymes, proteins, lectins, carbohydrates or aptamers. Traditionally, we have focussed a lot of work on antibodies. In our work, we use aptamers to specifically bind to our target.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Lets first look at what is an aptamer. Aptamers are oligonucleotides or peptides and bind to their target analyte with high affinity. For instance, a DNA aptamer contains single-stranded DNA containing anywhere between 20-60 nucleotides.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This single-stranded DNA will fold and create a unique 3D structure that will then recognise its target. A very effective molecule to recognise its target. https://t.co/BiatWSWjyu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But why not just use an antibody? Aptamers offer better target discrimination, have lower batch-to-batch variability and in many instances have higher specificity towards its target. They are also easier to store. I say if it's better why not use this instead of an antibody

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Yesterday we saw that a nanozyme can catalyze a reaction similar to natural enzymes. Now we will see how we can combine aptamers and nanozymes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When we expose aptamers to a nanozyme, the aptamers bind to the surface of the nanozyme. In this process, they block the surface atoms. This results in the nanozyme to lose its catalytic activity.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Remember how we said that aptamers have a very high affinity to their target?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we now expose the aptamer-nanozyme complex to a solution containing a target that the aptamer recognises, they will dissociate from the surface of the nanozyme and bind to their target.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When aptamers dissociate, they expose the surface atoms of the nanozyme. This means, the nanozyme now regains its catalytic activity.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If I expose the aptamer-nanozyme to a solution containing a target that the aptamer does not recognise, they will not dissociate from the surface of the nanozyme. This means the nanozyme will still be inactive.  The figure here is quite useful to understand the concept https://t.co/E9w92k6Xjd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This simple yet effective strategy has helped us develop sensors to detect pesticides, an antibiotic, and even a whole virus.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here is the links for virus detection (https://t.co/KImIVxjIXw)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here is the link for pesticide detection (https://t.co/9KYDFWDcwL)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Time for another quiz today. Yesterday we said nanozyme was a serendipitous discovery. Can you guess which nanoparticle was the first to be reported for its ability to mimic the natural enzyme?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of my mentors told this to me once - A concept should be simple to understand. This means more people will appreciate it. Simple does not mean your science is less effective. I admire my mentor for telling me this. #Mentorship

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Wishing @RealSci_Nano a happy first birthday :)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ooooo looks like a lot of people voted for gold nanoparticles in yesterday’s poll. But the first report of nanoparticles showing enzyme like behaviour was - iron oxide nanoparticles. :)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So yesterday we saw how we can combine the strength of nanozymes and aptamers to create aptasensor platform. A simple yet effective tool to create a sensor.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today we look at how we look at combining natural enzymes and a nanozyme as well as a protein and nanozyme. Let's look at combining natural enzyme and a nanozyme

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In this example, we will look at the detection of urine glucose. We all have heard of diabetes. It is a disease that causes high blood sugar. If you have suffered from diabetes for a long time, it can lead to renal complications.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Interestingly, we have blood glucose monitors that are portable and easy to use. However, they do not give you any information about renal complications. We decided to address this.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We had a particularly challenging problem. The concentration of glucose in the urine is quite high - generally in the millimolar range. You see - we always had sensors to look at low concentrations. So the challenge was now to develop a sensor to look at high concentrations

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Instead of using nanoparticles directly, we embedded them in a piece of cotton fabric. WHY? Two reasons - (i) we can load a lot of nanoparticles and (ii) cotton being an absorbent material, it will bring the glucose in close proximity.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What was the recognition element in this case - easy - we used the enzyme glucose oxidase. This will specifically convert glucose to form hydrogen peroxide. This is the key. The hydrogen peroxide is one of the substrates for the nanozyme.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Before we go away, one last concept about how we can combine proteins and nanozymes. Yesterday if you recall, aptamers and nanozymes interact in a dynamic manner. That means, the aptamers can move from the nanozyme to bind to its target.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We found that this approach did not work in some cases. Don't you hate it when that happens! But we came up with an alternative approach. This is an example where the nanozyme activity is always ON.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let's see - we now have a protein called transferrin. This protein will specifically go bind to cells that have a transferrin receptor. The probe in this case is the nanozyme-protein conjugate. However, unlike yesterday, the nanozyme activity here is still on. https://t.co/SICHk0WmXL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If I mix some cells with this probe - say some specific type of cancer cells that have transferrin receptors. The transferrin protein-bound nanozyme will now go bind to these cells. If the probe does not find transferrin receptors they will be free.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we isolate the cells and wash them now - the free probe is gone. What we are left with is just the transferrin protein-bound nanozyme tightly stuck to the transferrin receptors. If we now do the assay, we get colour. Isn't this cool :)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We actually didn't just stop there. We also showed that this strategy can be used for receptor profiling - Oh sciency words. What I mean is I can look at how much transferrin receptors are produced by different cells using this :) https://t.co/gnjqC8p4a9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
For anyone who is interested in this - have a look at https://t.co/TqauIIfVyJ

For anyone who is interested in the glucose-sensing - have a look at https://t.co/cFmuz7GyIy (and a new one to be published very very very soon!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Tomorrow we look at how to kill some bugs using nanozyme!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @NotHF So true! Fenton reaction at its best :)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today we look at how we can kill bugs using nanozymes. We also look at how we can use light to enhance this process. https://t.co/8Tg1vSgKTb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The first one we will look at it just using a nanozyme without light. We already know how we can use a nanozyme to convert a colorless substrate to a colored product. One of these substrates is H2O2. Nanozymes  convert H2O2 to form a very reactive species called OH radicals https://t.co/ScYR5hvPXL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This radical targets the integrity of the bacterial cell - if the bacterial cell membrane is destroyed then the poor bacteria does not survive. Well the process is something like the one in the gif https://t.co/oiPwuroTFF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What does light have to do with the concept of nanozymes? Well, we know that nanoparticles interact with light. This leads to some interesting properties. Look at the GIF of the Lycurgus cup made in the 4th-century made by the Romans. https://t.co/YqTyMpE96Q

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It changes color as it has gold and silver nanoparticles embedded in the glass. This results in the change of color depending on where the light source is. We use the ability of nanoparticles to interact with light.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We saw that nanozymes can convert H2O2 to OH radicals (post in the morning). In that case, if the nanozyme is given 4 H2O2, it only converts one to OH radical. If we shine light on the same nanozyme, it will convert all 4 to OH radicals. https://t.co/ugGB6Q05O6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This means more killing of bacteria. :) It is important to remember that the light source to be used will be determined by the nanozyme composition and nanozyme morphology.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here is the work from the group where we have used visible light to improve the killing of bacteria. https://t.co/Sligcvxf4h

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What we show here is that light not only improves the affinity of the nanozyme to H2O2, it also improves the catalysis by 20 times. This is just an example of how we can use nanozymes to kill bacteria.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Has been quite a week with a lot of information about nanozymes. But isn't the concept fascinating? :) Tomorrow, I want to introduce you all to all the group members who do such an amazing job. Catch you tomorrow. Happy Friyay :) https://t.co/n74PYDfEU3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What a week it has been - we looked at how nanoparticles mimic the catalytic activity of natural enzymes - we call them nanozymes; how we can use nanozymes to develop sensors to detect small molecules to cells and also how we can use them to kill bacteria.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Yesterday we had the opportunity to meet the amazing young researchers who are part of the @RMIT_NBRL group

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today I want to deal with something we are all going through - COVID. I was just having a chat with my wife about how things are different now - we don't go to conferences anymore, we don't get to see each other, networking is down to people we know.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This led me to think - When I was a PhD student and an early career researcher - what was the thing that helped me the most? I could only think of one thing - networking, networking and networking.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Networking helped me to know researchers working in the area, made some amazing friends, ideas were exchanged, developed new projects, even submitted grants with some of them, got to understand how research works in different countries - I can keep going with this.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: With COVID how can we help students and ECRs to get the same level of exposure? In my mind, I think organising conferences within the department across the university or even have conferences with just two universities. It helps them with confidence and introduces new people.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Encourage students to attend virtual conferences - I know it is not the same but none-the-less useful.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Have departmental seminars where someone external to the university presents. This way students are exposed to work outside their university.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Encourage students to join Chemical / Engineering professional organisations - attend their events - generally, they are cheap or free for students - helps with networking (you never know - you may find your potential employer)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Introduce your collaborators to the group or have their students present their work once a fortnight. Helps them with interacting with researchers not directly associated with their work and will improve their perspective

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I would like to know what has helped everyone else during their PhD and post-doctoral career that they think the younger generation is missing out on due to COVID and how we can address this. Comment on the post and share your ideas. Would love to learn!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Graphene is a single layer of graphite, material commonly found in pencils. Main reason why pencils are so good for writing is that all of these graphene layers inside of #graphite are very weakly bound and separate easily, while leaving trail on the paper ✏️

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Graphene is 1 atomic layer thick, and is basically only a surface, so 2D. Really crazy thing, since our world is 3D!
All atoms in graphene are carbon atoms, and they are arranged in a honeycomb structure. Something like on this picture https://t.co/uajJIpC78i

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #Graphene was first isolated using a sticky tape, a really cool method. You first use sticky tape to peel off a bit of #graphite, and then you use another piece of sticky tape to thin it down. You keep doing this until you get only a single layer of graphite, #graphene https://t.co/5CdLXJ0Vt1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Once you are happy with the #graphene you got, you can either place it on a substrate you want to use, or on another 2D material. Sort of like arranging atomic Legos!!
If you are interested in how to make atomic Legos, check out the talk by @semontis #LEGO
https://t.co/iRlaiYVN33

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #Graphene has many really interesting properties. Despite being just a single layer of atoms thick, it is one of the strongest and most elastic materials we know! It also has a very special electronic properties, such as really fast electrons that have no (effective) mass.

#Electronic band structure describes the range of energy levels that electrons can occupy or not. States that electrons can occupy are called bands, and ones that they cannot occupy are called gaps.
 2 most important bands are called the valence and #conduction band https://t.co/uS2LOVn7l4

tweets.label: Takeover

These 2 bands are closest to the Fermi level. Fermi level is the highest energy #electron in the material can have.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Molecular assembly is a type of #chemistry driven bottom-up approach to grow #graphene. Bottom up meaning that we go from small nano-blocks to build a larger thing, graphene. This approach allows for an amazing control over how, for example, graphene edges are defined.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
A small molecular blocks, monomers, are combined on the surface and bound into larger units, polymers. 
Molecular assembly is most often used to grow a very specific kind of graphene, #graphene nanoribbons!
Different molecular precursors can be used to grow different nanoribbons. https://t.co/ozFGP3Z0Lx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
As molecules are used to grow #graphene (nanoribbons), the edges of the structure are always well defined on the #atomic level, which is really cool! 
Usual molecular precursors are various molecules that already have carbon atoms arranged in hexagonal rings.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is a good starting point to grow a larger sheet that is supposed to consist of infinitely repeating carbon hexagons! #graphene 💍 https://t.co/OFTziOqmG5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, or as I will call it ARPES, is a technique used to measure electronic band structure of materials. It is based on the photoelectric effect, a discovery for which #Einstein won the Noble prize in 1921! https://t.co/lXIsU5mJZH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Beam of light (blue) falls on the sample and photoexcites electrons (red). Electrons are captured by electrostatic an #Lens and pass through the analyser. Everything is designed in a way to preserve the information about the kinetic energy and angles that electrons have https://t.co/10hWYaHyBq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Electrons that pass through the analyser hit the array of electron multipliers (MCP) that boosts the signal which is then mapped on the phosphorous screen. Finally the photoemission intensity is captured by a CCD camera and you get an image like this (bilayer #graphene). https://t.co/DZ6ItDsNB5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ARPES only measures up to the Fermi level (highest energy state electron can occupy), which is seen as a sharp decrease in the intensity. Also, ARPES has to be done in vacuum. https://t.co/GrGAZUiueK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
ARPES can be done with different setups and different sources of light.
As a light source you can use a helium lamp, a #laser or a synchrotron! all of these systems have different advantages and disadvantages.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Synchrotrons are circular particle accelerators that accelerate electrons to speeds close to the speed of light and produce synchrotron light that is very intense. Synchrotron light is much more intense than if you produced X-rays with a lab source @lightsources https://t.co/oG9y9DSx4b

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Synchrotrons are also able to provide light of different energies (wavelengths), which can affect your energy resolution, but also whether you probe deep into your sample or just  the surface. It can produce light in VUV, sorf and hard X-ray range.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Different beamlines, places where light comes out of synchrotron and experiments are performed, will receive light in different energy range. 🌈 Beamline you use (and energy range) will depend on type of experiments and science you are doing.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Hard X-rays are more often used for #biology experiments, while material science and #physics is more often done on the soft X-ray end of the spectrum. Of course, that is not always the case.
ARPES experiments, though, are mostly done in the UV and sometimes soft X-ray range

And now briefly about how to become a synchrotron user!
Most synchrotrons have calls for proposals a few times a year, where you send them a short proposal on experiment that you would like to do. Good start is to check website of the synchrotron and see the format & check dates

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Most of beamlines have both technical data, that will make it easier for you to figure out whether your experiment can be done there or not, and also most recent publications. Is there anything from your field there, does it look like suitable for your project? https://t.co/HMpjowpAPv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You can also contact a beamline scientist working on the beamline you would like to apply for. They are very knowledgeable and experienced and can help you decide whether to apply or not.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: More practically, when applying, it is always good to have some initial data, to show that the project can actually be done. Also, you should have a plan B and come with several samples (of the same kind). Time is short, and maybe your 1st sample won't work, but 2nd will 🙂🙃
