#CarbonNanotubes (CNTs) are super cool materials – they’re basically a sheet of graphite (graphene) ✏️rolled up tightly into a tube. 

In the same way as rolling a sheet of paper makes it harder to bend, rolling up graphite makes it much stronger too 💪💪. https://t.co/CRELWloCsa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Unlike rolling a piece of paper, which is still a piece of paper that isn’t conductive🤦

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This happens because the electron orbitals on each atom are deformed by the CNT being rolled up – so they overlap a bit more.

So lets get starting making nanomaterials!

First – there are two main approaches:

1.Bottom up – starting from building blocks and making nanosized materials 📈
https://t.co/ECPZO1jb1a down – starting from a larger material and etching/milling it to make nanosized features 📉

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Nanomaterials are tricky to make – you need to give them energy to grow 📈– but stop the process before they get too big!

This means most processes use heat and/or pressure 🥵to provide energy to start the reaction – and cooling/quenching 🥶to stop it

Lets get into it!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We can do nanomaterials synthesis from gases, liquids or even solid starting material.

Gases ⛽️ (not that gas!) are my favourite – so I’ll start talking about my long acquaintance, Chemical Vapour deposition or CVD 🔥🔥. https://t.co/Wz0MdG0dU6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: CVD is a quite simple process to talk about – everything is in the name – you take some ‘chemical vapours’ (gases) and ‘deposit’ them on a substrate to form a new material. https://t.co/pgyZ02nNeH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In practice CVD is most commonly done with a tube furnace – effectively a long tube of quartz or alumina that runs through one or multiple furnaces. 

We hook this up to a vacuum pump so we can lower the pressure as needed. 👇

Thanks @stephen_beirne for the schematic! https://t.co/ZVvnFPW93R

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
High temperatures ♨️ means we can vapourise our precursors and provide energy for them to react

Low pressures 🌩️ makes it easier for our starting material to get into the gas phase or stay in the gas phase.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Choosing the substrate for the gases to ‘deposit’ on is crucial as the crystal structure 💎💠♦️(or lack thereof) 🪟 of the substrate affects how the nanomaterial assembles!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Lets talk about simple systems – carbons. Specifically carbon nanotubes. 

To grow carbon nanotubes we only need a single furnace, some hydrocarbon gas – typically methane, ethane, ethylene, or acetylene – and a metallic catalyst for the gases to deposit on. https://t.co/8P8wu2BBjl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We heat the gas up to around 1000C 🔥 which causes it to break down into its atomic carbon and hydrogen components 💥🌬️. 

At the same time, the metallic 🪙 catalyst is changed by the high temperature as well.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
When carbon radicals at this high temperature interact with certain metals (Iron, Cobalt, or Nickel most notably) they dissolve in it (like in iron to make steel). 

You can picture this as a sponge absorbing water - although the carbon is chemically bound to the metal!🧽🌊

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
These metal particles can only take so much carbon at once though, what happens when they’re full of carbon but we keep supplying hot gas?

⁉️🔎👇

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Well what happens is carbon keeps going into the metal particle, but because it’s full it pushes new solid carbon out of the other side, potentially forming carbon nanotubes!

This is called the Vapour-Liquid-Solid mechanism (VLS) 👇 https://t.co/J1OgjjrqtL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Depending on how fast you push carbon in (temperature/pressure/concentration), and what type of metal used, we can tune the length, diameter, and wall number of CNTs. 

This method is great for making large areas of nanotubes in defined geometries!

You can even line them up! https://t.co/f4dKDAQWHN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
One of the things I like about science is your ability to take something simple, and change it and make something new.

Carbon nanotubes are just hexagons all next to each other. 6⃣

What happens if you put a pentagon 5⃣ or heptagon 7⃣ in a CNT ⁉️

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Answer: They twist! https://t.co/teA2N8ldXY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The advantage of making twisted carbon nanotube is they open-up a lot of space between adjacent carbon nanotubes – meaning we can fill this space with interesting things like electrolytes for batteries 🔋or chemical functionality of sensors📤! 

All that space 👇 https://t.co/zfcDMpLGBc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We did this in our research by adding Sulfur to our CVD system, giving us exceptionally conductive, porous structures!

We also cheated a bit by using acetylene to bind individual CNTs into a single film – because it reacts with itself! https://t.co/7S8Fa6Ufqy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
If you’re interested in this type of thing:

We could use these devices for:

Capacitors: https://t.co/dlFW6WDX2U
Batteries: https://t.co/teVM1b8VyW
Fuel Cells: https://t.co/2LQMaqV9d1 

📰📰📰

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'll move onto graphene, and transition metal dichalcogenides synthesis via CVD in a new thread a little later today! https://t.co/99WxmYU0sg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Lets move away from Nanotubes 🗞️🗞️ now - into the wonderful world of 2D materials, Graphene and Transition Metal Dichalcogenides! 📜📃📄 https://t.co/dwhOhSoCDa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Lets start with graphene – it’s the same chemistry as CNTs – but a different growth process 💥🌬️⁉️

First of all, rather than use metallic catalysts and metal particles – we use metal sheets (normally Nickel or Copper).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Why the difference? – and I’ll focus on copper here because the nickel mechanism is a bit harder to explain.

Well, graphene grows by templating on the crystal lattice of the metal and the copper surface – normally (111) – is ideal for this. https://t.co/r6KxhQrxcD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Secondly, because the ‘solubility’ of carbon in copper is so low the reactive carbon species from our gas phase doesn’t dissolve in and then precipitate out of copper during cooling breaking the up the newly formed carbon layer! 

(from: https://t.co/EXozD0exzJ) https://t.co/ThQpvUMjev

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Since this method is effectively chemical self-assembly 🧪you can start to do 3D structures 👇📰– provided your starting architecture is smooth and pure enough! 

Getting graphene off 3D foams in one piece is a whole other problem - but that's not for today! 🤦‍♀️🤦‍♂️🤦 https://t.co/Z1x81Pohfz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Transition metal dichalcogenide CVD growth is a bit more complicated! ⁉️

They template on a substrate just like graphene ✅ – but now you need to have a chemical reaction between two different elements as well🧞🧙‍♀️! Don't worry - it's not magic - still chemistry!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Due to this difference you start to use a lot more gases! 

Rather than just a hydrocarbon and hydrogen as active gases, for TMDs you either use solid precursors, or inorganic vapours containing each element itself! https://t.co/o4pd8sPA7W

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
My work has focused on using solid precursors for synthesis – so I’ll focus on that here.

Because we are using different starting materials we now need different temperature at different points in the furnace 🔥 to get each one in the gas phase 💨 at the right time ⏲️!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
To give you an idea of the spread of temperatures – for one of the most common TMDS – tungsten sulphide (WS2) – we used 150C for sulfur and 850C for tungsten! 

This is a huge temperature gradient 🏔️.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Also because the ‘weight’ of the element being carried in the gas phase is a lot heavier – these will deposit on a substrate at different positions along the tube furnace.

Finding the right place where the right amount of S and W deposit is crucial! See below 👇 https://t.co/iuRRZkcTC2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you do it right though, you can get beautiful triangles. https://t.co/JvCkSXWtWl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Or beautiful films (the blue is MoS2, the purple is the silicon substrate!) https://t.co/NCsDrza2Oj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And if you change how the TMDs bind to the surface, you can even make the 3D structures I’m so fond of! https://t.co/fmzIikVZHF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
TMDs are great for catalysis!

Have a look how we used these systems to break down salt water here:
https://t.co/TUeOjJh1pC 

And how we describe the fundamental growth processes here:
https://t.co/jfcVYaT40E

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Moving on from gas 💨 phase synthesis - lets have a talk about how to make some selected nanomaterials in solution 🥤!

I'll talk about:
1. Transition metal dichalcogenides 📜📜; and
2. Metal nanoparticles 🪙 https://t.co/PzfqMQHLwk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Lets start with TMDs!

Growing TMDs in solution is quite tricky - you need to:

A) find two starting materials of the metal, and the chalcogen that can dissolve in the same solvent; ✅and 
B) Make them come together in the right way to grow a 2D material ✖️

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Luckily there are a lot of different precursors out there.

But making them come together in the right way is not so simple! https://t.co/YxAvwcsxlK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There are a lot of different variables that you can try in solution phase synthesis:

1. Temperature ♨️
2. Pressure 🌩️
3. Solvent 🥤
4. Precursor ⁉️
5. Concentration 📈
6. Rate of precursor addition 💉
7. Time ⏲️
8. Additives 💊

and many more https://t.co/kvtM9a9yxh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
For 2D materials - (like TMDs) - the key things to control that give you an advantage are the solvent and the additives.

It is crucial to select an additive (or ligand) that binds strongly to one 'face' of your material - this can stop your crystal growing in that direction!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The problem then becomes controlling nucleation - growing pure 2D sheets is hard - all start from the same point and grow outwards into beautiful flowers! 🌻🌹💮

Below is some of our work growing WSe2 and Bi2Te3 (ok tha'ts not a TMD but still 2D!)

Scale bar = 5 nm @MySci_PK https://t.co/aK8GkcB7pH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
If you're interested in reading on these type of things in more detail - including a great review on how to make TMDs in any way - check out these 👀👀: 

WSe2: 
https://t.co/ynt1AK8H9L 
Bi2Te3: https://t.co/N744tZXPJy
Review: https://t.co/wgsueaIwyX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now we've got the complexity of growing 2D materials in solution out of the way - lets talk about how to do metal nanoparticles. 

These are a lot simpler to control because you don't have worry about restricting their growth in any direction! 😅

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Instead, the key challenge in growing metal nanoparticles 🔹is to stop them growing into being - well - just particles 🔷!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Similar to the selective ligands we used for 2D materials, for metal nanoparticles a 'capping agent' to stop them continually growing or 'agglomerating' is normally used. 

The most common of these is sodium citrate - something that comes from citric acid!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There are a multitude of chemistries that you can use to make metal nanoparticles. 

I'm going to talk about my favourite way because it's:

1. Quick ⏲️
2. Easy ✅
3. Cheap 🪙

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you take a metal salt, something like Gold Chloride, and put it in Ethylene Glycol - heat it up and stir it overnight you'll notice you get a beautiful colour change 👇👇 - it's basic - but if you add NaOH it'll go even faster. https://t.co/f80UbWt5A8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This still takes a few hours - and if you're particularly impatient (like me) you'll want to harvest your gold dust even quicker. 

We're already heating ♨️, we're already adjusting pH 🧪 - so how do we speed it up even further?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Well, you really just need to find a way to provide more energy ⚡️ to your reaction!

The easiest way in this case was to place it in an old microwave! (yes the type you reheat food in) 🧑‍🍳

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you put the same solution in a microwave and turn it on for just 120s you get beautiful reduction (to give you an idea below here is the 'absorption spectra' of both normal, and microwave reduction) https://t.co/dvd7t4MjWd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm talking about gold here, but the same thing holds true for platinum, palladium, nickel, silver, copper, and cobalt nanoparticles - just with different starting precursors.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
120s is great, 2 minutes. But can we make this even faster??

The answer is yes✅! If you add a tiny amount of carbon nanotubes - you take this time from 120s to 10s for reduction⌛️.

Why? - what's going on here? https://t.co/BjuJukYdyG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Well, the structure of CNTs has lots of C=C double bonds - and one thing C=C double bonds are good at is absorbing microwave energy. 

This means at the wall of the CNTs two things are happening:
1. Localised heating; and
2. They become highly reactive (forming a carbon radical) https://t.co/xWwuzGiNIF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This carbon radical is highly highly reactive - and will donate it's electron to 'reduce' the metal salt in solution to a metal nanoparticle. 

The CNTs become a little less conductive - but we can live with that!

Proposed mechanism below 👇 (from: https://t.co/dlFW6WDX2U) https://t.co/ZbJHLyPZaW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So what does this look like? 

Beautiful assemblies of CNTs and metal nanoparticles - just the start of our assembling of the nano(avenger) materials!

All in just 10s! https://t.co/j0LUjttQPS

tweets.text:
We're getting towards the end of the week and ticking off topics ☑️✅✔️

Today I'll be talking about my favourite - assembling or 'structuring' nanomaterials 🗼

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Before we start - let's talk about why nanomaterials are so impactful for research 👩‍🔬and society👨‍👨‍👧‍👧

Then we can start talk about how and why we put them back together!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
When you take a large material and shrink it down to have nanoscale dimensions - quite a few things change - even if it maintains it's same shape. 

One of the biggest things is a dramatic increase in surface area 👇 https://t.co/N902sybB0V

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This increase is hugely important because surfaces are:

How the material interacts with its surrounding environment 🏝️
Where chemical reactions can occur ⚗️
High energy ⚡️- they want to merge together to form a lower energy system ❌!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This means as we make a material smaller, we can use less of the material but still have the same amount of chemical/electrical or device performance! https://t.co/Ps3JlUeFM3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
As you enter the nanosize domain, your nanomaterials typically have a dimension that is close to the wavelength of light (~400-700 nm). 

This means you also start to get some really cool optical effects! https://t.co/nPqKpI3HnC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Stopping to think about it - having all this surface area, and ability to interact with light is super cool. ❄️

I already mentioned the high surface area means things want to combine together to form a larger material again.

So how do we keep our amazing properties?

Assembly! https://t.co/hiElxbJNCU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Starting with my old favourite!

Carbon Nanotubes. 

I've already spoken about growing aligned carbon nanotubes via chemical vapour deposition 👇 https://t.co/SJUWTbWcwH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The aligned carbon nanotubes are amazing materials - but you'll notice that if you look at the top surface - there is zero space between adjacent CNTs. ❌

This is because of the strong 'van der Waals' interactions between adjacent CNTs leading to a tightly packed structure! 💪💪

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This means all that beautiful advantageous surface area I introduced above - we simply can't access! Nothing can get between the CNTs to interact with them. ☹️

(these find great applications in membranes). ✔️

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
However, by changing the growth process just slightly (adding in some Sulphur) - we can stop these materials stacking together - and suddenly we have a lot of free space and can access all the surface area of the carbon nanotubes! 

I've added a photo to give size context as well https://t.co/94Tc0rXFjV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This free space induced by our growth method is really important if you're looking at electrochemical energy storage devices. 

For those not familiar, supercapacitors, fuel cells, and batteries all rely on the interface between an electrolyte (containing ions) and an electrode.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The ions in the electrolyte need to be able to move freely in the device in response to either a load (discharging) or energy input (charging). 

Diffusion is a physical process - so having this open pore structure lets ions move much more quickly! So we can charge much faster! https://t.co/aNfLGVH8AF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
CNTs are great by themselves, they're electrically conductive, strong, and chemically stable. ☑️✅

However, if you're looking at something catalytic - like a fuel cell or water splitting - you typically need an active material.

You can probably guess - metal nanoparticles! https://t.co/hR1h2MVjF3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This year has been like no other. (Obviously).

It has disrupted every industry to some degree

Academic research is no different, my perspective is tinged from 🇦🇺Australia but there are common threads globally that tie it all together. 🌏

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Lets talk about immediate impacts ⏲️

1. Researchers unable to access lab facilities
This is the most obvious problem - the pipeline of experiments that flows is disrupted. People can keep generating outputs from previous data, but in 2021 and 2022 scientific reporting will drop.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
2. Significant delays in shipping ordering chemicals
Even when we get into the lab - getting anything is super slow, this makes planning - already ridiculously difficult at the moment - even harder

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3. Increased teaching load giving remote lectures. 
Each hour of lecturing takes 2 to 3 times longer to do remotely than to do face to face, this increase further takes away from researchers time doing, well, you know, research! 🧪

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Those are immediate, not including the huge mental health and anxiety challenges that are exasperated by the pandemic. 

Academia already has a disproportionally high rate of mental health issues. This needs to be addressed separately from the pandemic.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Slightly longer term:
1. Decreased enrollment numbers - means less student fees and less institutional funding for research AND less for research support - administration that is just as important.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2. Decreased access to undergraduate students - means it's challenging to recruit new Masters and PhD students into a lab. Couple this to:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3. Closed Borders - means getting international students in is nearly impossible right now. 

Again there will be a flow on effect in a couple of years from this. Students are finishing, there are very few to replace them.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4. University job losses - in the Australian sector these have been massive. We can't quantify them because of the casualisation of the workforce (another problem that needs a separate thread) - but even the fixed term/continuing staff that have been let go is a huge number.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This has all been negative so far, well unfortunately the pandemic has been pretty damn disruptive to scientific research, and government funding cuts/exclusion of universities from government pandemic support has made this worse.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There are positives through.
(Australian) Universities have been brilliantly positive in allowing people to work from home, we are able to keep getting paid, and work remotely - this is likely to continue into the new year.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There has been a boom in virtual conferences, allowing those who would otherwise be unable to travel able to access a much bigger pool of events.

Anything that helps inclusivity in science is important to preserve.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The constant 'Zooming' means there is very little difference if a collaborator is next door or halfway around the world - so it's easier to work with people globally.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are lower expectations. Science glorifies overworking, sacrificing everything for your 'passion', and a false belief that 'if there is a will there is a way' (there just isn't in the competitive nature of research funding sometimes - rejection isn't a reflection on you).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The pandemic has helped shift this (in Australia), people understand the challenges (like in my case daycare being closed so having a 2 year old climb over me constantly). 

Whether Institutions recognize this career interruption long term is a different story. https://t.co/ArZspoUR5c

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The pandemic has brought massive challenges to academic research, those changes will be felt for the next 10 years at least. 

You quite simply can't turn it on and off like a tap. It's a pipeline of skilled people who leak out of the system when the tap is off.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Right - away from that gloom! 

Advice for up-and-coming researchers 👇 https://t.co/Sf62szT47n

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
My biggest advice is always two things:
1. Find research you really enjoy, a topic you're interested in, or tasks you like doing - pursue that. There are benefits to academic life - but the pitfalls are so much worse if you're doing something you dont enjoy.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2. Find out what the group leader is like to work for, a good group leader makes your work enjoyable. A negative group leader will crush you - if you're applying for a Ph.D. this is particularly important, have a chat to previous Ph.D. students.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Apart from that it's about being proactive from the first day you step into research, apply for grants you're eligible for, be selective about (but definitely get involved in) relevant societies.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: and finally, put your face out there - talk to everyone. Network, network, network. Academia has a lot of nepotism (it's getting better but...) - getting to know people will give you an advantage in the job/PhD hunt.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Don't make assumptions about who someone is, take the time to meet and talk to everyone you can at conferences/events/meetings - you never know when that person next to you might be your best collaborator, or a future employer/industry rep interested in investing.

https://t.co/VhfiL03IlZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of the key questions which is still being investigated in detail is then, what the electron wavefunction looks like at the end of this tunnelling process. Does it have some momentum? How wide is its spread? https://t.co/UINPh87MuJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
These characteristics are important because they determine where the electron (probability distribution) will go subsequently, and this is precisely what is measured at the end on a detector. (video not mine)
https://t.co/BjnG6vdTkg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: By comparing simulations with different momentum distributions along the tunnel-ionisation direction against a set of experimental measurements, we found that the (previously common) assumption of (almost) 0 momentum along that direction is not a good approximation.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
publisher version:

open access (OA):
https://t.co/5YrHVTZ84l

tweets.text: I feel like my apartment has turned into a bit of a "sauna for beginners": higher room temperature than I would usually keep in wintertime, and more humid than usual in general (despite having open windows)...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm going to switch my plan around a bit. The exciting opportunities for future scientific and technological developments derived from #attoscience (and if I find the time, a project using nano-objects to modify the spatial dependence of my laser fields) will come later.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I already mentioned that I started my current position in February of this year. I moved from Dresden, Germany to London, UK at the end of January (yeah, I made it in right before the Brexit date). You can probably already guess where this is going...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I barely managed to find myself an apartment and scramble together a livable household by the time the first lockdown hit. On the afternoon of the first day when our group went into full-time home office, I finally got an internet connection installed.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (okay okay, you might argue about just how livable an apartment is that just got flooded 🤔🤭🤷‍♀️)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The plan of how the start of my new position would go did definitely not pan out that way. And having to settle down in a new country while in a lockdown created some unexpected additional challenges.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For example, my new GP practice sent me a form to be filled out and signed when I wanted to register with them. Only, I did not have a printer at home and I was not allowed on campus any more. Thankfully they accepted my digital scrawl 😆

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another effect was, that I barely got to know my new group (PI @CarlaFMFaria, my sort-of predecessor @DrAndyMaxwell, and colleagues @AbbieBrayPhys and @heloise_cho), let alone other colleagues in the institute before we were only able to see each other through screens.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So that definitely didn't help to mitigate the impact of the pandemic on my work productivity and how I was able to deal with all of it. Thankfully, we managed to strike up not only work meetings but also social meetings,

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: be that a regular socialising coffee/tea break with the entire group, or late-night online game sessions to just have a laugh from time to time (thank you @AbbieBrayPhys !).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As much as we're all trying our best to develop personal strategies to better cope with the increased pressure/mental health impact/loss of structure/health challenges/... and additional grievances of this year, it remains to be seen how this impact on our work

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ... will be taken into account down the road. I am mentioning this particularly from the point of view of a postdoc on a short fellowship (2 years), needing to be able to find a next position soon again in this nomad-academic stage.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I am very grateful that already in March @snsf_ch  reached out to us fellowship holders and informed us that they are introducing an option to apply for an extension of the fellowship term, on account of reduced productivity due to covid19 impact.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Still, how will future hiring/grant decisions weigh such aspects? At this point, I don't have any good answers. But I expect that a standard phrasing on CV's explaining a certain publication/citation/output break or slump will probably develop for many of us.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This was quite a different kind of thread from what I have done here before. Unlike my brother, I'm not a health expert. So I am in no place to judge the recent news about a possible effective vaccine. But even while telling myself to remain patient, cautious, and careful,

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: having that metaphorical carrot dangling in front of me did feel like a happy relief as we are moving towards the end of this year (and currently working through renewed lockdowns in many places).

tweets.text: I have this itch to swing back to talking about physics after yesterdays more meta thread, much like a pendulum always striving towards the middle position, but constantly overshooting. BTW, pendulums are an excellent representation of how short laser pulses are created! https://t.co/oDO2eRyvYq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
You have probably heard (or learned) that laser light has a very defined colour (one specific wavelength/frequency), and all photons are in phase with each other, all their waves are perfectly synchronised (coherent).
(Image source: https://t.co/ad2csUMm1u) https://t.co/hg0vR934iE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, if we only allow one single wavelength, then the laser light is continuous. Only when we add up several slightly different wavelengths (or frequencies) do we get a short and intense pulse, right at the moment when all those different waves happen to align with each other https://t.co/9iDFGM7JGG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Before and after, when all the different contributions are not perfectly aligned, their individual troths and peaks partially (or completely) compensate each other. https://t.co/X4Nn0k1TWS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Obeying the laws of the Fourier Transforms, shorter pulses require a broader spectrum. And ultrashort pulses consequently require a very broad spectrum, which means only very few lasing materials can be used to create these.
[https://t.co/7lC7vUJ2uH]

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
With Ti:sapphire lasers, the pulse duration can be around 5 - 30 femtoseconds (fs). For the attoclock method, this is fine because one rotation of the field is around 2.7 fs, giving attosecond resolution in the angle. 
https://t.co/ioQWdW4Gdu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But for most other methods, we need pulses which are themselves shorter than one femtosecond. We are exploiting an effect which is part of strong-field physics: High Harmonic Generation (HHG), which converts infrared photons of a fs pulse into extreme ultraviolet (XUV) photons. https://t.co/16JwRTPZmo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The key components of HHG are beautifully demonstrated in this video by the Photonics and Laser Applications Group of University of Salamanca, and JILA, University of Colorado
https://t.co/dJmHms6MGr

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In my own research, I have 1⃣ looked into phase-matching: How coherent are the different XUV photons which are being emitted by all the recombining electrons distributed in the gas cloud?

https://t.co/ugryUi8XzC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
and 2⃣ also played around with: what happens if the laser field is a mix of two very different frequencies creating a fancy pattern? And if additionally, you have nano-particles nearby, creating a spatial dependence in the laser field?
(second image: https://t.co/WYcVpxYaHc) https://t.co/D4AwqyBHwY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (yes, this is me actually talking about something nano finally 😉)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The three-fold symmetry is imprinted onto the typical paths that electrons are taking (first image). But with the spatial dependence on top, that symmetry is completely broken (second image), and the energies with which these electrons are recombining are vastly different. https://t.co/HZd5JlHs8m

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Preliminary results of this investigation are on arXiV: https://t.co/WwFYp4SKQ5

Hi everyone :-D
We have reached the weekend already. Over the last few days, I hope I managed to give you a small glimpse into my research field. But one promise I have not yet delivered on: Where will all of this lead? What's the point? https://t.co/42NTKJZwa7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
First of all, I don't think I have to convince you that the quantum tunnelling phenomenon is found in all kinds of fields. Recently I came across a paper discussing tunnelling times during a photosynthesis cycle in an organic molecule.
https://t.co/3TYV78sUPV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Many might be familiar with Scanning Tunnelling Microscope (STM) technique to investigate surface structures with (sub-)atomic spatial resolution (or make an atomic stop-motion movie 😄) https://t.co/kMEaFwxdFm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And an example of future innovation development is in transistors for electronics, where quantum tunnel leaking is currently presenting a limit on the miniaturization, and dedicated quantum transistors could present a new breakthrough. https://t.co/LwVO0AIF1p

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are of course many more fields and technologies. For any of them, new insights gained from #attoscience about the quantum tunnelling process itself can deliver new puzzle pieces.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another aspect: we study electron motion. And understanding charge transport (usually electrons moving from one place to another) at the microscopic level for example in heterojunctions of photovoltaic cells allow a possible new pathway of trying to improve their efficiency. https://t.co/ULzYm6M3yy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: More and more aims move from "observing" to "controlling" electron dynamics with tailored fields. This invites dreams and hopes of controlling electron dynamics for example during chemical reactions, taking femtochemistry (dynamics of nuclei) to the next level. https://t.co/qIEHb83LBS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Obviously, there are also more applications within #attoscience itself, where we're using the photoelectrons or emitted radiation as a secondary tool to investigate for example dynamics in molecular orbitals, and more. Some of the applications I have listed above are ongoing

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
already, others are still hopes, dreams and ideas. A lot of work still remains to be done, both by the attoscience community and also all related fields. After all, we're still a very young, exciting and growing field 😉
https://t.co/4cBH7CX5zr

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hi everyone, Chris Spicer (@spicerlab) from the University of York in the UK here, taking over the account for the week. Really excited to talk to you all about chemistry, nano science, and my life as a researcher over the next 7 days!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We've got lots of things planned for the week, but we'll be starting off with the story of how I've ended up where I am today

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Right, where it all began - as I started typing out this chain I realised I was giving hackers a ready made guide to those annoying password questions you have to answer about your first pet's favourite colour, so I'll keep the first 18 years of my life brief!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Born in the North of England, moved to the South when young - retained a love of gravy and football, and a hatred of ballet (poor satirical joke for the UK followers, #jakeberry). Enjoyed chemistry, biology, and maths at school, but had no idea what I wanted to study at uni. https://t.co/XSlxxTrkzt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So I ended up studying Natural Sciences, a real mish-mash of anything and everything science-related for the undecided! I loved the freedom I had to study evolution one day, thermodynamics the next (that's a lie, I hated thermodynamics and still do, but I did enjoy evolution).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There aren't that many universities in the UK that offer Natural Sciences courses still, but for young people who aren't sure what they want to do and don't want to be pinned to a decision yet, they're a great option. In the end, I specialised in chemistry and never looked back https://t.co/FLMZc77IAz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After a Masters project with @OScherman I moved to @OxfordChemistry  for my PhD (weirdly called a DPhil there). Looking back I was so naive about the project I chose, I was basically woo'ed by a 5 minute conversation about how powerful chemistry was as a tool to control biology.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But I got lucky and ended up on a great project, using transition metals (mainly palladium) to do some really cool chemistry on proteins. There are loads of reasons to want to do this, like attaching drugs to proteins that can deliver them around the body to treat disease or...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: making certain parts of a cell light up so we can study how these amazing building blocks of our bodies really work, or to allow us to make tests that can diagnose diseases really fast like a pregnancy test.... the list is endless

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: While there I was lucky enough to work in a lab with lots of amazing scientists: @ChalkerChem @Keribackus @charlogauthier @goodfellow_jj They probably don't realise it, but these people really influenced the way I approach science and I'm incredibly grateful to them!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Give these people a follow if you want to learn about some really exciting science (less so for @goodfellow_jj but he does have the world's cutest dog). I'm sure there are many more I've either forgotten or aren't on twitter, so sorry to them!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After my PhD I realised that while I loved the research I'd been doing, I wanted my career to be a bit more applied, developing the actual technologies that were going to make a difference to people's lives, rather than the key fundamental studies that would one day get there

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So I moved to @imperialcollege for a postdoc in bioengineering. This is where my love affair with nano- and materials science really began. https://t.co/kUVtzd7NT0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This was a big change in field for me and I was massively out of my depth - it was challenging at times, but I realised quickly that looking at a topic from the perspective of a complete newbie with a different set of skills could be a really useful way to do innovative research

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Having a different viewpoint is invaluable, and you should never be afraid to try and learn something new, ask a lot (I mean a LOT) of questions, talk to people in completely different fields to you - push yourself outside your comfort zone and you'll be amazed what can happen. https://t.co/IbzHUUCynp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After 3 fantastic years, I embarked on a new adventure @karolinskainst in Stockholm. My postdoc group had recently started a new satellite lab out there, and I had a fantastic 2 years in this unbelievably beautiful city with @GormleyLab @ChristineHorejs @derrick_a_rob @woodc1881 https://t.co/Vr6FYAy4MV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Learning a new culture (albeit one very similar to the UK with added coffee and fermented fish), a new way of working/researching, and making many new friends was an unforgettable experience, and I miss Sweden a lot, especially the snow and the days that the sun doesn't set!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All of this led me back to the UK 2 years ago @ChemistryatYork to start my new position as a Lecturer (Asst. prof. for the Americans). Having the opportunity to start my own research group has been amazing, and you'll hear all about what we're up to over the next few days https://t.co/qUtdHwJX1L

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But to finish a very long thread, here's a quick summary: Started as a chemist, learnt a bit of biology, got drawn into material and nano-science, learnt a bit more biology, and now run a group doing a mish-mash of all of it, back in a chemistry department where it all began!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hopefully that gives you a flavour of what you can expect to see over the next 7 days - it will be very varied, but I'm looking forward to it and hope you all enjoy the ride!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A new thread and some fun facts on where I am now, the beautiful city of York. Hit the motorway, follow the signs for The North (these actually exist in the UK), and keep going. 2 hrs from London or Edinburgh on the train, about 1 hr to Manchester, but that's the boring stuff https://t.co/djFSsot04b

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But why would you need to travel when York has so much to offer? 1. York Minster - one of Europe's biggest cathedrals and also one of its most beautiful. The Minster dominates the centre of York, you can't miss it and a tourist must see https://t.co/zQW8lAPO0M

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2. The Shambles - York city centre is packed full of small little Medieval streets, but the most famous is The Shambles - the setting of Diagon Alley, everyone's favourite place to buy their wands, broomsticks, and potions. Busy by day, stunning by night https://t.co/Vt7JootYdT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3. York City Walls - The walls have been around since Roman times in one shape or another, and are mostly intact. You can take a ~2 mile walk around them, giving stunning views of that pesky cathedral again https://t.co/wjC2QHP9Ec

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The gates in the walls are all called bars - Mickelgate Bar, Walmgate Bar, Monk Bar.... They sound unique but a nightmare when you're new to the city and trying to find your way round. Far too many bars

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4. Quite literally - York supposedly has a bar or pub for every day of the year, ranging from upmarket and trendy winebars, through to old traditional cosy pubs. Coming here from Sweden, where a beer cost ~£7, I was amazed to be able to buy a pint at my local for £1.50!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And nearly as many breweries - with the pubs shut at the moment a lot of local businesses are really struggling, so big shout out to @AinstyAles @brewyorkbeer @TreboomBrewery and many others who you can order deliveries from. Highly recommended for anyone in the UK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4. Speaking of which, how about the UKs number 1 independent high street @bishyroadnet? Full of amazing cafes and restaurants, hardware shops, greengrocers, butchers. York has an amazing independent shop scene that makes the city feel so friendly and welcoming https://t.co/icAg6nbUGR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5. York racecourse - home to some of the world's biggest races, and a great day out over the summer.... https://t.co/GWSVJg3NbI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And the beautiful Knavesmire when the races aren't on. There are loads of green spaces in York, as well as a beautiful river running through the middle. Ever so slightly prone to flooding, but we'll keep that bit quiet, the city's residents have learnt to deal with it. https://t.co/6UdF2Rn0Vi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 6. Rowntree Park is another crowd favourite - when I first moved here we lived just off the park, and had a quick google to see if it was safe. Apparently not. You run the risk of being attacked by the 100s of overly friendly geese, as bad as it gets in York https://t.co/KHtkNjkCP0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 7. Rowntree Park is named after the Rowntrees factory as a memorial to its employees who died in WW1 - chocolate and sweet making has always been big in York, not only Rowntrees but also everyone's favourite Christmas gift, the Terry's chocolate orange https://t.co/x1LukOeNXI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are loads more great things about York - it's not just residents who think it's great, York is often voted the UKs best place to live! So next time your in the North of England, come and give us a visit. I'll buy you a pint. https://t.co/GmqpYoN5fN

tweets.text: Morning everyone, I realised that two days in to curating this account and I still haven't really told you all about what we actually do! So today I'll be tweeting mainly about our research - why we do it, how we do it, and also some shameless plugs of some of our papers

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
[admin]

"A Chemist's guide to the Nanoscale"

Extended podcast with @spicerlab is here 🥳

https://t.co/ZztOxHcPDe

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let's start with a very broad overview - our goal is to design materials that we can use to treat disease, specifically those where one of the tissues in the body has been damaged in some way. This encompasses things like heart disease, arthritis, nerve damage, and loads others

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To do this the material should help us repair the damage, or replace the original function of the tissue somehow. This field is called 'tissue engineering', and the technologies it encompasses are really broad, from 3D printed organs, through to new tissues grown in petri dishes https://t.co/yWUJkJhteL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is a super interdisciplinary field, populated by engineers, materials scientists, tissue and cell biologists, surgeons, polymer chemists, imaging physicists....... I discovered yesterday that it's even been used in Grey's Anatomy (though have to admit I've never watched it) https://t.co/4mAtglKblt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One technology is to use material 'scaffolds' that can be used by cells as a framework to grow new tissue. Just like the scaffolding on a new house. Except ideally this scaffold should not only be structural, it should also tell cells what to do so that they form a new tissue

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Giving cells the right signals at the right times is REALLY hard. Nature is complex. We need to get way better at designing materials that recreate this complexity, but it's like having an IKEA manual for a Boeing 747. https://t.co/mtr4kcebPb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A lot of the 'tissues' we engineer therefore just can't function well enough to treat diseases in real patients. Tissue engineering has huge potential, but not that many technologies have actually benefited people suffering from these awful diseases yet

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's where we come in - we look at tissue engineering from a slightly different perspective, and look to use our skills as organic chemists and chemical biologists to see how manipulations at the molecular level can affect how cells behave at the scale of a tissue

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we can really control what's going on at the level of single molecules and how these interact at the nano scale, then we have far more chance of controlling what's happening at the level of something you can see and hold.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The grand vision is that we can then come up with better design principles, that then allow us to make better materials, that grow better tissues, that allow us to better overcome the symptoms of disease, and ultimately improve the lives of millions of peoples across the world. https://t.co/j9mXrYBxQQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For the rest of the day I'll be tweeting some examples of how we do this, as well as highlighting some of the challenges we face both as a group and a community moving forwards.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @ahugumrah I couldn't agree more! Experiments fail all the time, rather than hide failure we should own it, and learn from it! There's nothing worse than the phrase 'my experiment didn't work' - what about it didn't work? What happened instead? What could we do differently?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @ahugumrah In this instance, we ran some tests yesterday afternoon and turns out the gels we made were just too weak. Not as 'gel-like' as we hoped, and therefore they just fell apart overnight in the fridge and dried out. Lesson learnt, now we now what we have to do to improve the system

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This is the most recent example of this chemistry-led approach to biomaterial design, from my postdoc. We showed that we could design electroactive materials that could be used to stimulate neuronal cells and change their behaviour

https://t.co/IGLxYrVjzL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This was work that was mainly led by an amazing PhD student called Kaja who did a fantastic job bringing together a really interdisciplinary study. We're joint first authors on the paper but she needs to take most of the credit

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Key to this was some synthetic chemistry that I developed way back in 2017 for making a series of molecules known as oligoEDOTs. PEDOTS (the polymer equivalent of the molecules I made) are a bit like molecular wires, acting to conduct electricity
https://t.co/ZXCI6YaMfn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You could do similar things with metals, that conduct electricity better, but metals are stiff and inflexible - the complete opposite of what we want a material to look like to grow nerve tissue. Conductive polymers partly get around this problem.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Our oligoEDOTs are basically very short polymers, and are even better at overcoming the rubbish mechanical properties of metals. This is with a trade-off of much worse conductivity, but our recent work shows that they are electrically-active ENOUGH to be able to influence cells

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The benefit of our system was that we could create really cool architectures at the nanoscale using a technique called melt electrospinning, that basically draws lines of polymers like a printer would. This was a big advance in this work and something we were really proud of

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It's not a big jump to imagine using these materials to control the growth of nerve cells in particular orientations, allowing us to start to mimic the bundles of cells that form in your nerves.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Here's another from earlier this year. We got involved in this collaboration when I was in Stockholm with a group who were interested in making cements that could be used to glue biomaterials to tissues, particularly bone
https://t.co/mNyFzozUmM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is a really big problem - we are actually quite good at making materials that help to repair bone, but they can't be used in any part of the body that is subject to mechanical force because the interface between the bone and the material is really weak.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A couple of years back @alinavkirillova reported that adding a modified amino acid, phosphoserine, to a class of materials known as cements helped overcome this problem. Our collaborators (who aren't on twitter) had found the same thing but they didn't really understand why

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We realised that we'd need to understand what was happening at the nanoscale interface between the material and tissue, and also at the molecular level. If we could build a load of phosphoserine mimics with subtly different structures we might get some important insight

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What started off sounding easy led us down a rabbit hole that resulted in a new synthetic method to make phospho-amino acids, that we then used to make a library  of mimics. Using this we could really pinpoint what chemical features were essential for adhesion and which weren't

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Turns out having a phosphate group and a carboxylic acid is essential, but the amine is pretty much dispensable. This opens up lots of possibilities to make new additives for bone cements that might improve their mechanical and biological applications

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Huge potential for these kinds of materials in treating bone breaks and defects. At the moment one of the most popular treatments is to cut out a chunk of bone from somewhere else in the body and implant it at the site of damage, the use of cements would be a big step up on this!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: During my PhD my research focussed on developing new chemistries that could be used to modify proteins with high precision, at just a single amino acid. This is really difficult to do, proteins can be huge molecules composed of hundreds or even thousands of amino acids (1/12)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Modified proteins are hugely important for loads of applications, such as therapeutics (biologics were worth $240 billion last year), for visualising and understanding what is happening inside a cell, or for creating diagnostic devices for detecting disease (2/12)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Single amino acid precision is really important - if you don't have control, when you try and attach something to a protein you will often completely kill its activity and it becomes useless. Specificity and selectivity are key! But they're hard to achieve (3/12)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Making it even more complicated is the fact that these proteins are made up of just 20 amino acids, with an even smaller number of chemical functionalities. How can we selectively modify just one? One common approach is to use unnatural amino acids that are unique (4/12)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
These can be installed via a process called codon reassignment - very complicated, but very powerful. We wrote a review on it way back in 2015 that shows some of the diverse structures you can insert into a specific position in a protein (5/12)
https://t.co/ytNOGlduYd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Building on work by @ChalkerChem when he was in the group, I got working on trying to target one such unnatural amino acid using palladium catalysed reactions. These reactions have revolutionised chemistry over the last 50 years, but applying them to proteins was new (6/12)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
My very first paper back in 2011 showed that we could do one specific palladium-catalysed reaction, a Suzuki reaction, on a protein with high efficiency. This was a big breakthrough for us, as well as a special moment for me personally (7/12)
https://t.co/Rox5hyJseJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Apparently, Suzuki means sea bass in Japanese! Or so I've been told, happy to be corrected by any Japanese speakers out there. Had to talk my boss down from making a sea bass-based journal cover on more than one occasion (8/12) https://t.co/9q5Galh9Cf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Anyway, we then went one step further and showed we could even do Suzuki reactions on the surfaces of living bacteria. This work really set the groundwork for lots of advances in recent years doing metal catalysis inside cells. (9/12) 
https://t.co/0qN1IMVMDD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: An emerging strategy is even using these reactions in animals as a way to 'uncage' drugs, potentially minimising side effects and giving far more potent treatments for diseases like cancer. (10/12)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Another PhD student, Matt, went on to show why these Suzuki reactions were so powerful - he did an amazing job showing that they could be used to really probe the mechanism of a human protein called glycogenin went about storing glucose in the body (11/12)
https://t.co/o7SOJqptUa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This enzyme is key to energy storage in humans, and importantly no other chemical strategy was able to probe this mechanism in the same way. A really powerful example of how chemical biology can give us new understanding (12/12)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
A final one for today is a review article we published last month and are really pleased with. In it we provide an overview of how we can use light to make cyclic peptides. This important class of molecules have emerged as really promising drug candidates

https://t.co/i5dbh4njTa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Cyclic peptides can disrupt the interactions between two proteins in the body - interactions that are implicated in loads of diseases such as cancer, yet were previously thought to be 'undruggable'. By cyclising the peptides they become more more potent and more stable

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Making cyclic peptides can be tricky though. Using light to trigger reactions (photochemistry) has emerged over the last decade as a really useful way to achieve cyclisation. With ever increasing numbers of photochemical reactions out there, their use is only going to increase

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm particularly proud of this paper because it was the first written by members of my group since I started at York. PhD students Laetitia and Nick did a fantastic job writing it, all brilliantly overseen by our then-postdoc James. My input really was minimal

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Reviewing a paper today I was really impressed by the results it presented, until I got to the SI which was really poor - it didn't necessarily affect the results or conclusions of the paper, but it really affected the way I judged the paper and made me overly critical

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Made me think about how important this part of a paper is. In some ways the most important, in many journals it's the whole experimental - what the authors actually did and the data that supports their discussion. Yet so often it's left till last and done in a mad rush

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm always shocked by papers that have 2-3 page SI for a 10 page paper - how can the details that support that work be so scant? And so often it's just a couple of hastily thrown together graphs and no explanations, its pretty much meaningless.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My other major pet peeve is experimentals that just say 'we did it like these other people did'. I don't want to have to follow a literature trail (that can often go back 6 or 7 papers) just to find out how you did a simple experimental.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It would take the authors 5 minutes to just write it down, or me an hour to go searching for it. Why would you not want to make a reader of your papers experience as pleasant and easy as possible, so that people could reproduce your work and cite you?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Maybe I'm missing something and would be interested to hear people's thoughts. For me a robust, long, and detailed SI is always a good thing. If it's well organised and easier to follow, all the better. It will certainly make me feel a lot more positive when I review your paper!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: While I always try hard to not let my instincts affect my opinion/review, no matter how much you try to be objective we're all human and it is inevitable that it will cloud judgement. I don't get why you wouldn't put in that extra days effort to stop that affecting your paper!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
As a student from a state school, but a selective one (at the time, in the 1990s), what was it like at Cambridge?

DIFFICULT. Mostly because Natural Sciences is a very demanding course and it's meant to be difficult. But particularly maths-wise...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I had an AS level in maths. Everybody else had at least an A level, mostly one in Further Maths (exactly what it says on the tin) and some, mostly private school students, also had STEP qualifications (Yet More Maths I guess). So I had a lot of catching up to do.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I spent the first year feeling like an impostor & failure, and realise now, we were doing maths that the other students had seen before at school. In second year, everything was new to everybody, and suddenly they were just as stuck.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So I guess, for any teenager considering Cambridge Natural Sciences, I would advise: learn as much maths as you can get your hands on. Doesn't matter if you don't get it perfectly first time, but get to know its face so it doesn't jump out at you.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And remember that you can learn stuff as you go along. I still look up things whenever I do maths now. You don't have to be an "innate maths genius"; you have to be persistent and approach it in different ways & ask people for help when stuck. You can do it.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What else was it like at Cambridge? I met a lot of mean posh people, it's true. Some students, some older. But also some lovely people. (Shout out to my best mates Liz & Laura) And some LIBRARIES oh my gosh. It was nerd heaven, for nerds with a big jumper and 2 pairs of socks.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The best thing was the sheer passion of some of the lecturers for their subject and their research. It was like being shown around a magic forest. When it was good, it was very very good.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But when it was bad, it was... scornful. Muttering into the blackboard. Reading out pages of equations like they were a shopping list and not the very stuff of the universe. Talking at the other end of a loud bright room too fast for me to make notes or understand.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Am I glad I went? Yes. Would I have been glad to be at a non-Oxbridge university? Also yes. I had to do science or I would lose my mind. I gather things have improved since 2002 (would be amazed if nothing did!) but there were things to fix back then.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The best thing about Natural Sciences at Cambridge: it introduced me to MATERIALS SCIENCE which rapidly became my chosen field. I can hold things in my hand and know what they're like right down to the atoms. Can't beat that.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When I was 12 I learned about atoms and I have been looking at things ever since going "WOWWWWW". In Materials Science I can do that every day. It's like an adventure that always has more to give.

After undergrad, I did a PhD. Why? Lots of reasons, many probably "the wrong reason" but here goes.
1) I did my masters project and showed you could do tomography of dislocations in the transmission electron microscope (what?!! More later) and wanted to do more

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2) I found out from all the degree bits that I really REALLY like research. So I wanted to do more research and here was an opportunity to do more research so I pressed the "yes please" button.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3) There was A MYSTERY TO SOLVE (how come the tomography worked? What else would work? etc.) "Clues were left behind that suggested a mystery. And to many humans, a mystery is irresistible. It must be solved" - Jean-Luc Picard

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4) (and this is not fair and I'm sorry) I had a supervisor and a project lined up already and as long as I got the grades I would be able to afford to live for the next 3 years so...I did. Because I had been extremely broke and I was scared of being broker.

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.text: What was my PhD like? Lonely, because I was the only person in the group, in the WORLD at the time, doing my subject. There weren't other dislocation tomography people. So also, kind of uncertain and scary.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At the start, very scary, because I thought everybody in my group thought I was stupid and I just hid and read things. But I realised just because they knew stuff didn't mean they thought I suck, I was like a science beginner. So I got less scared.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I learned a LOT. How to do TEM. How to do the wrong thing on a TEM and get told off. How to code in different languages. Image simulation. All about tomography algorithms. Linux!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I learned that when you write something, there will always be somebody who would write it another way, and you have to figure out which bits of feedback are "you actually need to change this" and which are "this is not my writing style and it scares me".

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My supervisor (Paul Midgley, spin bowler of terror) prefers a formal style and thought mine was too chatty; my PhD examiners seemed to like it. So, it turns out, do undergraduates, because it's relatable and clear. There are merits to both, it's like personality.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I learned all the writing tips that are on the pinned post on my own Twitter account and are still the only way I can ever write anything! Which is here. https://t.co/GRaxSInSlk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I learned when you go to a conference, even though you/your funder already paid for the food, STOP BEFORE YOU'RE FULL. I mean eat enough, but don't then keep going until you are sleepy and a bit nauseous. You need to be able to listen.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But the most important thing I learned is that the most important quality in a PhD student is persistence. Stubbornly putting one foot in front of the other even when it's metaphorically raining, snowing, windy, etc. - never. Ever. Quit.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Unless you realise that actually you don't want a PhD, or you are being bullied to the point of illness by your supervisor and they will never change. In that case, run like hell. To another supervisor, or another topic, or another career. It's not worth your actual life.

tweets.text:
Next up: how did I get a postdoc? Because it's hard.
I kept applying and applying. Every unsuccessful application is a practice run at writing statements and doing interviews if you get that far.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To write an application statement for a postdoc: go through the job specification/person specification thingo they link to in the ad. Copy & paste the points into a Word or whatever document. Then write underneath each point, how you meet it - or, how you would learn it.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I found it easiest to write completely overhyped hubris in the very first draft, then go through and edit it to sound reasonable. "Electron microscopy skills" "I am the best microscopist in the world EVARRRR" - once you set the bar "too high" it's easier to edit down than edit up

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Sort of like haggling a price with your own embarrassment - start by stating a ridiculous amount and then you will end up somewhere reasonable in the middle. (Incidentally I suck at actual market haggling.)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You don't have to then turn it into prose - bullet points is quite possibly how the recruiting prof wants to think about it in their head anyway, so you may as well leave it like that as long as it's coherent.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Interview tips: if you don't know something, don't lie or bullshit (pardon my language). Say you don't know. Say how you would find out. It's easy to spot a bullshitter. And a prof usually wants somebody who will be honest about progress, not lie and then mess up the plan.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Have a lot of tea/coffee/cake/whatever makes you awake and happy in the morning. DO NOT go to an interview without breakfast. I did this once and looked like a total plonker until 10am when I woke up.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Most importantly: show your enthusiasm, about their project, about your previous projects, about your PhD, about science in general. Interviewing is boring. Running a project is often depressing. Be somebody who wakes them up and makes them feel happy and optimistic again.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This advice isn't a foolproof guide for how to get a job, it's just little bits I picked up.
