Good morning HU-MANS. Time for more science. Today I'm going to nerd about electron microscopes.

Many introductions to electron microscopy say that an electron microscope is like a light microscope but with a shorter wavelength to get better resolution. Well, sorta.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Electrons can act as waves and their wavelength is very short. Look up wavelength limit if interested. BUT. This is like using a Red Arrow performance jet to carry passengers to Germany faster. Like, you CAN. But it can do so much more.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A crystal is like a ceilidh for electrons, all dancing around in arrays that match where the atoms are. When another electron from the microscope comes in REALLY fast, Usain Bolt there has to get through a room of dancers, and join in the dance to get to the other side. https://t.co/phty9Mcokv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It's the outcome of all that dancing that makes it really interesting. The electron comes out of that a changed person. It's a different shaped wave. And some of the electrons hit things in the material and lose energy and you can measure all sorts of things from that.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Walking into the electron microscope room is like putting on 5 different sets of night vision goggles. You can see so many more things. This is why Geordie LaForge is my favourite Star Trek character (narrow margins). He walks around and sees all this with his actual face. https://t.co/l5NQxzXnam

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So. Some of the electrons get poinged back out the top of the sample. Some hit the electron clouds of the atoms near the top, and knock out some of those electrons which go flying out the top. Byeeee

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: How they fly out depends on where there are hills and valleys in the surface so if you count how many come out at each bit of surface, you can map the hills and valleys. That's a secondary electron image.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Some of the electrons get unlucky and manage to almost crash into an actual atomic nucleus. They get sort of slingshotted backout, and from a lot deeper in the sample. Those are called backscattered electrons.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A nucleus with more protons in it has a lot more flinging power. So if there's a blob of something heavy like tungsten hiding in your sample it will glow like a little fairy light. This is VERY useful for a first figure out of what's going on.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These kinds of images are all formed by scanning the electron beam over the top of the sample and recording the intensity of what comes back out the top and sorting it by beam position. So we do these in a machine called a scanning electron microscope.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I just had a look and all my SEM images are of super secret Rolls Royce things 😭if anybody has any awesome non-secret SEM images they would like to share, drop them here! (If nobody wants to, that's ok too)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Wait that's not quite true...here is a (I think) secondary electron image of a cube on a stick that's being sliced and diced by kickass Jack Donoghue in Manchester (more on slicing and dicing later). https://t.co/RCOGmjhEYX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @DrStuartR Beautiful!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can get even more cool stuff to happen if we - and bear with me here - chop off the bottom of the sample, leaving only 100 nm or even thinner, and make the electrons go a leeetle bit faster, so they can dance all the way through the sample and out the other side.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Then you can stick some more microscope on the bottom to deal with the electrons that have gone all the way through - it's called a transmission electron microscope.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At this point I need to introduce my glamourous assistant Colm O'Regan, experimental officer and champion eater of biscuits, who has been taking photos of microscopes for me, because I'm not allowed in the lab unless I have an actual experiment to do. https://t.co/LANdUczrXe

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: THIS is a transmission electron microscope. That door in the background is a normal sized door for people to walk through. The sample goes in behind that round blob on the front left. https://t.co/FckSoxAFU5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Front right. Not front left. I have always had problems between left and right.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The sample needs to be riiiight in the middle of that column, so it sits in the right place in the middle of the lenses to make the beam do the right thing. So we make this tiny thin disc 3mm across (more on that later and then we attach it to the end of a stick. https://t.co/jvbLKWmLp2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One such stick is in that clear box near the back of the table. The little cradle at the front is to hold another stick (sample holder) that is in the microscope with a sample attached. Also in the pic: tiny screwdriver for attaching. Loads of tweezers for sample handling!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So what cool stuff comes out the other side of the sample? First up: DIFFRACTION. The electron wave comes out arranged according to the crystal structure in a pattern of spots. The pattern tells us things about the crystal. See also: lots of maths. Here is a diffraction pattern. https://t.co/BvzIAXcB2G

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Things like crystal defects, that I was talking about yesterday, also put their imprint in the diffraction pattern. You see those streaks in between the dots? Yeah I have no idea what that is yet. Still got to analyse that data. But it'll be something like that.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When you have a glass lens for light, if you stand sort of halfway between the lens and where the image is in focus and put a screen up, you get a pattern equivalent for this one. (Lasers best. Don't go blind though.)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But for a TEM, you don't put a screen in halfway up the column. Electron lenses are special - you can change their strength. So you can tell the microscope to do some wacky projectory stuff and make the diffraction pattern end up on the screen at the bottom where you look.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Or - this is quite cool - if you blank off all the spots except one of those side spots and then tell the microscope to show you an image from JUST THAT SPOT, you can see crystal defects as little bright lines. Look, here they are! https://t.co/qXi6KEYn5A

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is what it looks like when you sit at the bottom of the microscope and look at the screen. The screen is inside that round hole but in this picture there is a detector for another instrument looking inside so we can't see into the microscope. https://t.co/raMgZwBLy6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The buttons and screens at the side are where you control all the lenses and widgets to make the beam move about and everything. It's like flying a plane except if you mess it up, nobody dies (unless you screw up so badly the centre manager loses it and kills you).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This microscope is my new best buddy the JEOL F200 at Sheffield by the way. https://t.co/YWaaymGwpn not pictured: room full of computers, cupboards, sample holders, boxes and chairs. And it being dark so you can see the screen when you're getting all the widgets set up right.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm going to have a little break now, but I will be back at 2ish to talk about how you make something 100 nm thin anyhow, and then some of the other things you can find out in a magic electron microscope.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @beamsontoast Aw man, I never even thought of that. And if you try and stand round the other side to use your left hand you'd be standing in the table. How annoying!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: SO as promised, this is how you make a thing less than 100 nm thick. There are two ways, really, and they all involve ending up with a thing 100nm thick stuck to another thing that is 100 microns thick so you can see it and handle it with tweezers.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The first way is by making a little disc and grinding it to 100 microns thick all the way across, then you erode the middle of it somehow until you get a hole, and the bit around the hole is thin enough to let the electrons through.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If it's a nice helpful metal you can squirt it with acid in cold gloopy solvents with an electric potential across it and if you get it right, your sample comes out lovely and smooth with a nice wide thin part. Here is the machine in a fume cupboard. (Thanks Colm) https://t.co/2sOooPmBjE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If it's not a nice helpful metal you can carefully polish the middle down with a tiny little grinding wheel, then you fire a broad beam of ions at it in this machine which works kind of the same. This is good for ceramics and semiconductors and stuff. https://t.co/mXfYoHy3Zb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The other way (and this is my favourite way because it's SO COOL) you can put it in an SEM with an extra bit attached to fire fast ions at things, and you can carve out a little bit, pick it up with a tiny stick, and glue it to a support with a tiny glue nozzle.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This way is also quite cool because you can look for a specific thing on the surface or just below the surface and dig just that bit out and look at that in the TEM. Let me see if I have some pictures of that somewhere...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Aha here is a picture of a little slice of material that's been dug around ready to lift out. The slug thing on top is platinum that you deposit on top to protect the top surface of the actual specimen when you're slicing and dicing round it. https://t.co/1LKeUYa5Xr

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The slicey dicey machine is called a FIB - focused ion beam. You can go even faster if you use Xe ions and let them make a bit of plasma (like the sun but less hot) around the surface while you're digging - then you can pull out a massive cube like this (Jack's!) https://t.co/VSDbOCTEbq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That picture is Jack picking up a 100 micron cube with the little pick-up stick, ready to stick it on the support in the picture I showed you yesterday to get cross-sectioned. The big tube is where the Pt comes out to deposit as that protective layer and as glue.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The last bit of electron microscopy that I haven't talked about yet is spectroscopy. That means you hit things with electrons and electrons or X-rays come out again whose energy depends on what element the electrons hit. It's very helpful for finding stuff...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The electrons in the beam can push an electron from a lower shell into a higher one, like from 1s into 2p or something. That means if you catch the original electron coming out the other side, it's missing that amount of energy.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Well you know how much energy it had to start with because you gave it the energy. So you can do a graph: electrons that came through vs how much energy they lost. And you get a spectrum that's like an autograph book for all the elements in that bit of the specimen.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's called electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS). You can also see clever stuff to do with chemical bonds. When atoms form bonds their electron levels move about, and the gaps between them change. And this information is in the EELS spectrum too, if you speak eel.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But there's another half to this story. Your beam electron pushed another electron from a 1s to a 2p orbital or whatever they were. But that electron doesn't want to stay where it fetched up now the bully has gone. So it hops down.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But one cannot simply HOP into another energy level. It has to shed some energy to do that. And that comes out as an X-ray. And just like the EELS electron, that has an energy that is a signature of the element. But this time not the bonding, just the atom. https://t.co/K2gtnnTIrp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's called Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy, EDS or EDX depending on how it feels (EDX is what its mum calls it when it's in trouble, EDS is for its mates). EDS and EELS are kind of like those friends that are a bit different but always get each other.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: EDS isn't that good with light elements, because their transitions are only little amounts of energy, and the EDS detector can't see them very well. EELS isn't that good with heavy elements, because the EELS signal gets weaker toward the big energies.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So if you use them both, you can find out loads of stuff. EELS on the left, EDS on the right. https://t.co/txUW9PIsX0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Back to the TEM picture: the bit at the top liberates electrons from a little bit of tungsten and flings them down the column through all the lenses and stuff. (This is the R005, an older TEM than the F200, which has extra glasses but is also harder to use.) https://t.co/8BZVyUEIm4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The EDS detector is that big thing on the right (yes the actual right this time) which is a tiny detector and a big tank of liquid nitrogen to keep it cold. That's an old design, new ones don't need the tank, and they are hidden away inside on the F200.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Electrons are not actually green - but when they fall on the screen at the bottom (behind the round hatch there) they hit a screen of phosphor which emits green light to show you where the electrons are, so you can line things up before you record your images and data.

Good morning Twitter people! Today I'm going to talk about alloys and why some of them are super. 

An alloy is a metal, with a mixture of elements in it. A normal alloy is mostly one metallic element with bits of other elements in.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A recent development is a thing called a "high entropy alloy" - which it turns out was not that high entropy, and has many other names now too - where you have about the same amount of multiple elements.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: High entropy alloys haven't proved awesome for anything yet, but people said that about electricity and the telephone, so...it's good to have them around and known about to see what happens. Anyway. That's not my area, I'm rambling.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'll cover a couple of alloy families that are put in the burny whooshy bit of aeroplane engines - nickel superalloys (they are rather super) and titanium alloys.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm going to unashamedly link to Wikipedia here, so that I know I'm not accidentally putting up something confidential from my own pile of diagrams. So. This is a jet engine. https://t.co/w57maRIuov

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm going to talk first about the spinning blades just after the bit where the burning happens - the last purple ones in that diagram. Those have one very important role that they have to not screw up. They have to spin round really fast in very hot gas and NOT GET LONGER.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If they get longer they scrape the outside of the combustion/hot gas chamber too hard and engine go kablooey. There is a very special class of materials made specially for this, called nickel superalloys. They are very super indeed. https://t.co/auiaMbLqw1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When an alloy is sort of more than halfway to its melting temperature, it wants to get longer if you hang a weight on it, or spin it around very fast. Atoms diffuse along defects in the structure where it's quite loose - grain boundaries and dislocations, mostly.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is called creep. (It creeps up on you and then crunch.) To make it not creep, we want to not have pathways of dislocations and grain boundaries going from the inside to the outside of the turbine blade, so the atoms can't sneak along them.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We do this with dislocations by tying them up in knots. If you make a certain composition range of Ni alloy, with a lot of Ti and Al, it forms these squarey precipitates called gamma prime γ'. Loads of them. Rafts and rafts of them. More than half the alloy can be precipitate.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A prof called Dierk Raabe made an AMAZING video showing this - it's at the top of this page. The thing at the start is a turbine blade. The blocky things when it's most of the way zoomed in are some of those precipitates. https://t.co/1BlrQ7vb8H

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This γ' precipitate is very clever because its structure is ALMOST the same as the Ni around it except some of the atom sites in the crystal structure are systematically occupied by Ti or Al not Ni.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If a dislocation goes through, it unzips the ordering and leaves a bit of really very unhappy material behind where the wrong atoms are next to each other. You can re-zip it by having a second dislocation follow the first one close behind.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So dislocations have to wait for a friend to join them to go through. But the dislocations in the Ni are in those narrow channels between the γ' blocks. It's like trying to find your mum again in the supermarket. So by and large, they are stuck and tangled up in the forest of γ'.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, there isn't a nice easy dislocation path for atoms to diffuse towards the outside of the turbine blade and make it grow. WIN. But there are still grain boundaries. We can deal with this in two ways: block them up with rubbish, or take them away altogether.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: By rubbish I mean carbides of heavy things like maybe Hf, Ta, W, what else...all sorts. There can be like 10 elements in one of these superduperalloys. These make the grain boundaries also not want to move about and line up along the blade, so they're not useful roads for atoms.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: They're kind of like if you wanted to run raindrops along string to the ground, but the string is stuck to a board with drawing pins.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's good enough for the really-quite-hot bits of the engine. For the very-hot-indeed bits, you take the grain boundaries out altogether and grow a turbine blade that is just one big crystal, by growing it with a squiggly bit at the bottom. What?!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Like in this video from the Prof Hongbiao Dong via Prof Sir Harry Bhadeshia https://t.co/aUtLfmkWWa The squiggle goes at the bottom of the blade; you can just see the bottom of the blade on the left. The bit on the right is sort of a supply vat.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ooh this video is awesome too, look! https://t.co/xzWNQifmhu I've been in that brick building to visit my colleagues in materials research. They have cabinets of old turbine blades and pictures and the way to the toilet was "left by the blades, right after the helicopter".

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I have to host a seminar soon, so I will be back this afternoon to ramble on about titanium.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm back! So, titanium. (I like it.) Titanium is light and strong at the same time. This is used for the slightly less hot bits of engine, because nickel is heavy. If you made all the turbine blades out of Ni you would use loads of fuel and put unnecessary stress on bits.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A lot of other bits are made of Ti alloys too - landing gear, engine casing, etc. plus all sorts of bits in other industries. So it is a very important and very cool metal.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Titanium on its own, not alloyed, likes to be hexagonal close packed at ordinary sort of temperatures (including in that bit of engine). Once you get to sort of 1200C it changes its mind and wants to be body centred cubic instead. https://t.co/1fgPyhdziD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hexagonal (hcp, α) is comparatively squishy, it can absorb some stress and move dislocations about and cope - it is tough. BCC (β) is comparatively stiff and strong. If you get both of them together, you get the toughness from α and the strength of β. TEAMWORK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You get this by putting other stuff in the Ti to make an alloy. For example something like Mo will make β happily stick around down to room temperature, and other elements will also make α be there too, so you get this nice strong tough both-together structure.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you get the heat treatments right you can also grow some big lumps of α to absorb energy & make it tough, then some middle sized ones, then some little ones with a good network of β between them for strength. Here is the sort of thing I mean https://t.co/wIQwDa3Hh6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's a backscattered image from an SEM - the β shows up bright because it has nice heavy Mo in it like I said before. That image is where I accidentally analysed the handle of a different thing (oops).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Because the microstructure is so so clever and particular and depends on heat treatments, it can be quite challenging to additive manufacture things out of Ti - I will talk more about this tomorrow!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So as a last bit for Wednesday - what do I do with these alloys? I get given bits that have been additive manufactured or processed by some other cool new method, and I find out what's inside.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I might be looking for particular features, or I might be finding out what the microstructure is like (and how it changes across the sample, sometimes). I will usually do some optical microscopy and make a plan first, because electron microscopes are expensive to use.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Then I will decide what length scale I need to look on and what analysis techniques I need to use, and make a Cunning Plan, usually involving FIB slicing and dicing somehow, to get the information we need. Then...I do it!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (There's usually an intermediate step of figuring out how much ££ it will cost, in microscope time and Jo time, and squeezing that through the Finance machine so I'm allowed to do the work...)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Once I have data, I have to sit and process it to find out what it says, and most importantly put it in a way that the sample's owner will undertand - especially important when it's a company and you might be talking to people who are not materials scientists by background.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Soooo that's me done for Wednesday. Tomorrow I will be writing about additive manufacturing, in between madly writing a thingo to try and get some ££ for a project about additive manufacturing, in some kind of supreme irony. Have a nice evening everybody!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Wowww I overslept. Today my plan is to tweet about additive manufacturing. Morning everybody.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ok so what's additive manufacturing? Making things bit by bit instead of all in one blob. Kind of like lego or knitting. You can do this with loads of different materials but in very different ways. It's called "3D printing" but that's only one bit of it.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3D printers that you can buy, use polymer in strings that is heated up to sort of melty temperature so it will stick together and you can build little plastic thingos from a hot print head that moves about in layers. That's nice and easy except when it gets lost and prints a mess

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's a very specific set of polymers - you can also do things with UV curing and all sorts. Polymers aren't really my field - @CandiceMajewski knows looooads about this.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You can also print ceramics in an organic sort of gloop, then burn away the gloop and you are left with a nice ceramic structure. There are all sorts of possibilities along the way. Look for...Iuliia Elizarovna and friends at Imperial College London, for example.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Metals are the bit of additive manufacturing that I'm involved with. They usually involve metal powder, a great big laser and a lot of pew pew pew, and I will talk more about that after lunch.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Most of my additive manufacturing work is with the MAPP consortium (Manufacturing by Advanced Powder Processing) @mapphub which involves Sheffield, Leeds, Manchester, Oxford, Diamond X-ray source, Imperial, UCL and...have I missed anybody? I hope not.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We work together on all sorts of additive manufacturing and general powder-related stuff, and do some exciting stuff. I will link to some stuff on MAPP's youtube account later when I talk about metals and pew pew lasers!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Ok metals! When you additive manufacture metals you need two things:
1) Metal
2) Energy
3) In many cases an inert gas atmosphere
4) A LOT of PPE for dealing with all that crazy ass metal powder.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The energy can be in the form of a laser (pew pew pew) or an electron beam (in which case everything happens in a vacuum). The metal can be in the form of powder or a wire like welding.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The powder can be introduced to the pew pew pew in two ways: you lay down a bed of powder and trace the laser/e- across it in the outline of the thing you're building, or you attach hoses to the laser and fire powder into the focus of the laser beam and hope it sticks.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When you've done one layer, you go back to the other end of the thing you're building, move up a bit and add another layer on the top. It sounds like a ridiculous idea but it happens like magic, suddenly there's this thing emerging.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The first one is called Selective Laser Melting or Powder Bed, the second one is Directed Energy Deposition or Blown Powder. Here is an animation from the MAPP Youtube channel about DED! https://t.co/QAdvmt1ICN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And here is a video from a company that make the machines for DED, called BeAM. PEW PEW PEW https://t.co/TKf3cequgK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You see there's a glowy bit at the top? That's mostly metal that's just solidified and is still glowing hot, but right under the beam is a bead of molten metal that's catching the melty bits of powder that have been through the laser, which we call the melt pool.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All sorts of cool stuff goes on in the melt pool. Because most liquid metals have a surface tension that depends strongly on temperature, and there's a massive laser at the top and a big lump of metal underneath, there is crazy fast stirring going on in that melt pool.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Which way the stirring goes and how fast it goes, and the shape and size of the melt pool, and how hot the layer underneath gets when you build the layer on top, and loads more things decide the microstructure of the metal you get.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The size and shape of the grains and which way round the crystal structure is compared to the shape of the part (orientation), and the shape & size of precipitates and little bits of phases in the metal (like α and β in Ti) are all affected by all those things.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The end result is that additive manufacturing of metal (and everything else) is really, REALLY complicated. But it's also really awesome. You can make stuff that you'd never be able to make any other way.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For example (and this isn't secret) many jet engine companies are starting to make bits of engine that have the discs and blades all forged into one lump, not separate blades that come off, so they can extract more power more efficiently from the engine.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When one of the turbine blades gets damaged, for example a bit of grit goes through the engine or a fatigue crack is found in regular inspection, it's silly to replace the entire massive part. It's better to cut off the broken bit and just...regrow a new bit on top.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So GE, Rolls Royce and a few more companies are doing a lot of work into being able to grow back a bit of engine with a little bit of powder, some PEW PEW PEW and some very clever machines.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So how do we untangle all this mess? A lot of approaches. Peter Lee & his group at UCL have a magic setup at the Diamond X-ray source where they can do the PEW PEW PEW in the middle of an X-ray imaging machine and make videos of what happens in the middle of hte melt pool!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You can also systematically vary different parameters and see what the outcome looks like in the final builds, which we do a LOT of at Sheffield. This goes in parallel with a lot of computer modelling, including machine learning, from other partners in MAPP.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Pores turn out to be a pain in the neck for additive manufacturing. Because of all this stirring, bits of gas can get stuck in the melt pool, both from the chamber and from any powder particles that were hollow. And some of them get stuck.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That leaves a pore in the finished build which is not helpful; it concentrates stress and makes it vulnerable for fatigue failure. I, Jack who I mentioned on Tuesday, and a team of other awesome people did a study on pores recently.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You can squish pores away under high-ish temperature, but if you then heat treat the material (like Ti alloys need to be the right microstructure) the pores grow back. We found that they grow back a really funny shape. (My little potatoes!) Paper out soon...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Oh! Talking of fatigue failure - a woman called Constance Tipper founded a lot of that entire field in the 1920s. Just look how awesome she was! https://t.co/z3CiVpcCDQ It is my absolute mission to put this woman in lecture notes one day. She was just great.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:

Tomorrow I will be tweeting about dyspraxia because I've got it like a slightly painful free gift. Right now though I have to calculate things with money. Wah. Byeeeee

tweets.text: @mapphub Awww thanks! 😊

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ok good morning! And quite a late morning because I had a lot of things to clear out of my brain before it had space to think. Today I am tweeting about dyspraxia!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What is dyspraxia? It's a thing where your brain deals with information strangely. This is most obvious in the way it deals with information about where your body is in relation to everything else - inaccurately. It is sometimes called "clumsy child syndrome".

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My brother has it worse than me and he literally walks into every new door frame he meets. I got a new bigger fridge what...2 months ago? Yeah, still crashing into that thing.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It's also most obvious in handwriting - fine motor control is difficult so our handwriting is terrible. My brother's is very large and angular and child-like. Mine is more...it's a line with lumps in. Nobody else can read it. Problem is nor can I most of the time.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As an undergrad this was PROBLEMATIC in lectures - doubly so because I didn't know that I had dyspraxia. I came on a fix where I would concentrate ONLY on writing the gist of what I heard, legibly, and go to the library in the afternoon to actually *understand* and rewrite.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This also means that we have to concentrate super hard on tasks like writing and walking. I do canoe slalom. I'm rubbish, I rarely come in the top half of my division. But my brain is working so hard. That's why I had to pick a sport that was great fun, to compensate.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And yes - I was terrible at PE at school - both because of this and because of the other features that I will talk about later today.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Finding small movements difficult makes TEM an...interesting career choice. I can only use one kind of tweezers, the kind that hold themselves closed, so I only need to think about moving and not gripping too. If I lose them, I can do nothing.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I lost my tweezers last year for a few days and I had to ask somebody else to mount my samples for me because I couldn't use tweezers anymore. I actually cried in the lab with frustration.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The physical part makes other things hard. Walking on an uneven surface - this is where I work https://t.co/K1Nel1711N you see the surface in front is all bibbly-bobbly and then goes down a hill? That is SO HARD to co-ordinate my feet on. Luckily there's a side door.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Building sites drive me crazy - suddenly a bit of pavement I at least knew is different and needs ALL my concentration to walk on - usually with cars going past so I need 2 brains, one for the cars, one for the ground.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And buses oh my GOD - walking to a seat, sitting on the seat, getting up from the seat, walking to the front. There are potholes right before my bus stop. Those b****ds have made me hit the bus floor several times. And I look drunk, and people frown. But I'm just different.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Maintaining posture is also tricky - my back bends a bit too much unless I concentrate really hard on it. And the ground. And the cars. And the person talking to me. And and and. It is all hard.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is why during lockdown I had an *easier* time than normal, and why only now do I have the brain space to career plan and apply for funding and things. Because I'm not always exhausted to the point of collapse from just getting to work and back every day anymore.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I have to go get a flu jab today (woohoo) but after that I will talk about how dyspraxia is different in different people, and the bits people miss until it causes a disaster - verbal processing and sensory processing.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I have been flu jabbed. My arm hurts. Ok back to dyspraxia.

Dyspraxia in my case strongly affects verbal processing. When I had the ability tests at Occ'l Health & got diagnosed I did pretty good on everything then when we did the verbal processing test she just...stared.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Apparently I am in the bottom 10th percentile of the population for verbal processing ability and the rest of my brain has been carrying that bit for my whole life. What does this mean in practice?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When I'm talking, it's hard to put the words in the sentence properly. Like, the right words in the right places to say the thing I want to say. The native language in my head is mostly pictures. This makes me quite good at languages, ironically, because I don't go via English.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So when I try to say something, sometimes the other person/people don't understand the sentence, it doesn't make sense. It's easier in text because I can read it back before I press enter. But in person I sometimes have to have a few goes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It made me very VERY bad at essays at school. Talking on the phone is hard too - I have to write a script to get it right. It's not just output that is affected - verbal input has problems too.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When I read scientific papers, I usually have to use 90% of concentration to understand the syntax of the sentence, and not enough is left to understand the actual meaning. So I have reading journals where I translate the paper into diagrams/brain language and then understand.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here is some journal - there are words but they're more like...names of things and ideas with symbols for how they relate to each other, than sentences. https://t.co/fozmmYFKCk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
(Also this is my bestest writing so that I can read it)

Writing is also a problem but...not as much, because I tend to write in very simple constructions, so I more get told it's too informal. Writing papers is like filling in a form where you know what to put where.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Because of the co-ordination thing, I also find food time at conferences difficult. I can stand and eat as long as nobody's watching. I can stand and talk but I tend to get nonsensical fast. Stand + eat + talk is usually a recipe for disaster, if I've been listening all day.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This does mean I get to meet some interesting people though because I started carrying a blanket to sit on the floor when there aren't enough chairs for everybody and it turns out I'm not the only one and often gain some lunch buddies.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Verbal processing's evil twin is: auditory processing disorder. This means I hear EVERYTHING equally. Listening to a seminar and a lorry drives past outside? Bye bye speaker's sentence. And when there are lot of people talking, I hear all of them and understand none.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (People who bring rustly food into seminars and eat it there have a special place in hell and that place is LOUD and ANNOYING)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In person, lip reading helps enormously. It's like a verification dataset for the stream of noise and its 50% accurate brain interpretation. On recorded media, captions are excellent. I rely on subtitles for Midsomer Murders exactly as much as for Wallander.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Remote meetings have been...interesting, for this. Ideally you can listen to the person talk and watch their lips and it's almost the same.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But in a big meeting people turn their cameras off to save bandwidth so they can hear. That means my brain is suddenly using all its effort to interpret the audio input because the lipreading has gone.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If I do that for an hour, I'm knackered until the next day. If I do that for four hours, the rest of the week is gone. And by knackered I mean, can't operate a bottle top or a teaspoon without 3 goes. It's ALL connected.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Not every conferencing platform is created equal. U. of Sheffield use Blackboard, which is adequate for a small number of people but for a big number something weird happens to the sound. Like some of the Fourier components get fluffy somehow. And parsing is even harder.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm told Zoom captions are usually adequate. But Blackboard captions are jellyfish cushion procrastination knife fork spoon brushing. I mean, so inaccurate as to be basically useless.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I found out last time I did a long Blackboard meeting that it's easier if I lie on the floor in a ball on a yoga mat with my eyes closed. Something to do with not needing to concentrate on posture or vision, I guess. Mmm, professional.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So the Year of the Plague has been...interesting.

Also a thing, coupling with auditory processing: sensory overload. I am usually operating at 90% brain load just to not get run down by a car or talk semi-coherently. So it doesn't take much to make by brain struggle.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Loud room full of jostling people? Loud noises? Fireworks? A really strong smell? Bright fluorescent lights? Bye bye ability to do things. (People who wear loads of cologne to microscope sessions can Just Stop It.) I turn out the lights in the FIB room to do a hard lift-out.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now a thread about late diagnosis. I didn't find out I have dyspraxia until a few years ago...34 maybe? 35? I had just gone through school accepting that PE teachers and English teachers thought I was lazy, stupid and/or and a bad person.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It didn't occur to me that there was some problem in the disparity of their opinion compared to science and maths. As a child you just...assimilate it into your idea of how the world goes. Some teachers hate me. Ok then. Maybe I suck.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the 80s and 90s, my brother was diagnosed with dyspraxia because he really, really had problems writing. Mine is less severe and I think it was easier then to write off a little girl as messy, a bit dozy, not really with it.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As a teenager I think I got sorted into "the technical type" so I was expected to be bad at English, History, home ec, art, etc. and it was seen as evidence that the model of the world as having two types of people is correct, rather than symptoms of a possible problem.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As an undergrad, I struggled enormously, with getting to practicals, doing practicals, HEARING in practicals, understanding lectures, almost everything. I thought, ok, finally the world is seeing that I do in fact suck, this is what I expected really.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But in the second and third years I started noticing what was easier and having the...confidence? No. Cheek? Maybe. To decide to do things a different way to how I was told to. Like scribbling the lecture notes in the morning then going to the library in the afternoon.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I found out, when there was practical work that involved figuring out how a material worked rather than following instructions from a long way away in a bright room, I was getting really good marks. So I worked my ass off on those, knowing my exams would suck.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My PhD was... honestly I liked it. I still didn't twig that things weren't this mismatched for other people. And my supervisor saying that reading wasn't work, didn't help at all. But I figured out ways through and somehow did it.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I only thought about a SpLD a few years ago when I went to a session on how to support students with SpLDs and they got to dyspraxia and I thought...waaaait...that's me. Then they said it runs in families and I went awwww shit, will you look at that.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So I got in touch with the Disability & Dyslexia Support Service and had some tests done of various dimensions of cognitive ability and it came out, yes, I have dyspraxia. And suddenly a lot of things made sense - and most things in my life were not in face because I suck.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So for anybody else out there who is really good at some things but every now and again you wonder why you are so stupid in very specific ways the "spiky profile" description - if you can, investigate. You never know.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So - last proper thread of the week. There may be some snaps of the weekend if I do anything fun.

What has dyspraxia taught me as a scientist?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It has made me be resourceful and courageous. If one way to do something isn't working, I know now to stop doing it that way and find another way that does work. Energy is precious. Other people's whining about appropriateness is infinite. Find a way that works.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It has made me need to be patient - especially talking to people, when they don't understand and I don't understand and I need to have a few tries.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It has made me STUBBORN. To be fair I think some of that might be genetic. I will. Not. Quit. Nope. If I have to crawl in a blizzard I will get that thing done. Because usually, I do end up doing the equivalent.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And it has made me understand deep down how things work. I couldn't get how to drive a car until I understood how the engine and the gears worked. I couldn't get how to use a sewing machine until I took the side off and watched it. And doing science, is ALL that.

tweets.text: @ZoeSchnepp The second is to be open with regards to choice of model. For example, DFT doesn't work, try molecular dynamics. Still no, try classical models, etc.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, what's DFT anyway? It's a smart idea to reduce the complexity of quantum mechanics. Quantum mechanics can be super complex, even for a single atom. DFT can let you do quantum mechanics for hundreds, or even thousands of atoms. DFT is so smart it got a Nobel prize. 1/n

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
What's meant by "do quantum mechanics"? I mean learn the properties of something. Formally speaking, it means solving the Schrodinger equation, one of the toughest equations in physics
2/n

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: and when you solve the Schrodinger equation, you learn the properties of your atom via the properties of its electrons. When there are so many electrons in the atom, it becomes pretty hard to solve its Schrodinger equation 3/n

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And that's where the coolness of DFT emerges: just don't bother about the electrons individually. Instead, deal with electrons as a "sea of charges". This reduced the complexity of quantum mechanics tremendously but at the expense of accuracy 4/n

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And here's why different papers would get different results for the same material using DFT: DFT is an approximation, and there are many flavors of DFT, each claiming to be a better approximation. So either the two papers used  different flavors, or one/both papers suck(s). 5/n

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: New DFT student wonders: which flavor to start with? Crystal systems? PBE is a good starting point, and then u can add sub-flavors to it.  Molecules? There's a war going on now on this - if I suggest #B3LYP (traditional choice) I'll hear shots being fired 😱 but its not bad. 6/n

tweets.text: Bacteria cells, in this case MRSA, contain efflux pumps that are able to resist treatment due to their ability to efflux multiple drugs outside of the cell

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Because of this, this allows cytotoxic escape in both bacterial infections and cancers. Studying the kinetics of these efflux pumps allows us to provide more efficient treatment

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We studied the kinetics of these efflux pumps by using Silver (Ag) Nanoparticles as optical probes in MRSA cells and observed them in real-time under Dark-Field Optical Microscopy, or DFOM https://t.co/cBqVYBSYVd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I called AgNPs “biological glitter” because there are 3 colors that are exhibited under the DFOM. 

Red, Blue, and Green! The same as primary colors 🥺

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, these 3 colors are indicative of different sizes of the AgNPs and the smallest of the 3 are blue, while red seemed to be the largest https://t.co/rilkJKiHD7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This is how the AgNPs loaded into the MRSA cells appear under the DFOM. See if you can spot all 3 colors!! 👀

*Side note: Dust is also really pretty under a DFOM 😂 https://t.co/1OtRnfNlrH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When the AgNPs are on the outside of the MRSA cells, they appear bright (pictured above), but when they are inside the cell, the intensity is very dim. This is how we are able to know if the AgNPs are inside of the cells

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We used the DFOM to record real-time of this constant in and out of the cells in 20 minute intervals. From the recordings, we are able to obtain snapshots at different time points as well so we can count the cells

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After counting, we were able to create this graph to visualize the AgNPs that were most prominent. In Trials 1 & 2, Blue was the most successful spending about an hour in the MRSA cells. Green and red AgNPs did not last as long. https://t.co/LZUcFEynyQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: From these results, we can conclude that smaller, blue AgNPs were the most effective at staying inside of the MRSA cells. Thus, these results are promising to the future of drug delivery. Here’s why!!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we are one day, able to combine these AgNPs with a drug to treat these bacterial infections, we are on our way to more efficient treatment! Also, we decrease the risk of these efflux pumps eliminating drugs before they get a chance to work.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So it turns out ✨biological glitter✨ is actually pretty useful! Let me know if you all have any questions!! https://t.co/yaujP1YXKr

tweets.text: So my Master’s thesis was based upon improving drug delivery to the posterior segment of the eye to better treat Age-Related Macular Degeneration https://t.co/Yh2aoc8qsH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In order to achieve this, I decided to use a MPEG-PCL micelles to encapsulate my drug. These polymeric nanoparticles are favorable due to their minuscule size and their proven biocompatibility

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The preparation of these nanoparticles include the sonification of MPEG-PCL polymer (A) and the anti-VEGF drug Sunitinib malate (B) into one mixture seen in the figure below https://t.co/ChLN86joP7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After prep, we confirmed the efficacy of our SM-MPEG-PCL formulation by using DSC Analysis. Chaotic, I know, but I can explain! https://t.co/azm3gKcI01

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Peaks represent a melting point for each of the 4 samples (Formulation, Drug, Polymer, and Physical mixture of drug & polymer)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: DSC Analysis confirmed that the nanoparticle formulation is stable and the drug was properly loaded into the polymer

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Further analysis included particle size, zeta potential, entrapment efficiency (~64.3%) for this particular formulation. The first picture is an TEM image of the size range of the nanoparticles seen here https://t.co/MSsS4owAN8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: MTT Assay of our formulation reported a cell viability of >88% for all concentrations at both 24 and 48h. 100% viability at 10 & 20 μM. Meaning that our formulation is nontoxic to ARPE-19 cells

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We also performed an anti-VEGF ELISA with the formulation and the analysis showed that the drug solution and formulation reduced VEGF expression up to 72h

First up: STRUCTURE. I often teach researchers about the Hero's Journey story structure. It's how many of us will intuitively tell stories anyway, but it's a helpful double-check of whether all the compelling details are in there...

https://t.co/nfElEVAocx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For example, in the Results sections of many papers,  experiments are often presented in a seemingly random order. The HJ says that all actions should be causal, and occur because of what came before. That's how we do science! But that's not often well-communicated in papers...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Second is CHARACTERISATION. We're trained as scientists to write/speak in the passive voice; "the experiment was done". Science is done by flawed humans, and I believe it's important to give scientists agency by including them in the stories we tell as we communicate the science.

So, How does someone end up working on microscopes with a physics degree? Well, physics includes the study of electromagnetism, one of the fundamental forces of nature. 

(Image courtesy of Wikipedia) https://t.co/g9I71calIB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Optics, the bit of physics that studies the interaction of light and matter, is kinda a subset of electromagnetism, and it is an important part of how we build everything from glasses to the lenses on your cellphone cameras to how we build microscopes

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So among the *many* strange corners of physics, there are labs that basically spend all their time applying these principles to trying to build fancier and fancier microscopes

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: this is not the only weird corner of physics involving optics btw, there are people out there levitating tiny bits of matter with lasers or using them to observe physical phenomena that happen on the pico-femtosecond time scale (under a trillionth of a second)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That said, the study of optics actually predates the existence of physics as a formal field of study. My favorite ancient optical physicist was Ibn al-Haytham, a Muslim scientist born what is now Iraq in the late 900s

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
He was a mathematician, an astronomer, a translator of ancient works and an actually foundational thinker in the  field which I now work over a thousand years later

tweets.text: Now we can move on to talking about microscopes proper. For people who don't work with them for a living, you probably haven't seen once since school and you remember them looking like this https://t.co/Y3DF2OIXw5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The strange thing is, that's not hugely different from what microscopes looked like for a long time.

Original microscope design in the 1600s looked like this. A single ball of glass in a metal holder https://t.co/ZnDOb6qvR4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Within a century though, they looked like this. And that fundamental design did't change hugely for a long time. Lens building got better, people figured out how to use bright lamps for light sources and focus them in samples, but the basic design didn't change too much https://t.co/xP08yKbOUZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So... What do they look like now?
Here are some examples of systems I have worked on/with https://t.co/FzBvzXBecv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If those don't look like you expect, it is because the last 3 decades or so have massively changed what microscopes look like and the ways they are used, and that change is accelerating

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The cause of those changes? Also Physics
(I may be a tad biased)

Basically optics got a little better, but what has really driven innovation has been three kinda connected things. Computing power, lasers and image sensors

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I say connected, because all three things exist because we discovered quantum physics in the mid 20th century and then applied it to understanding how materials behave. Hence solid state physics, hence lasers and transistors, hence the field that makes me a living

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Why lasers? Because most modern microscopy methods use a principle called fluorescence. Basically, you shine light of a specific wavelength/colour on a material, it absorbs that light and it emits light back at a different colour

(purple laser, blue fluorescence on the right) https://t.co/rfVbDhTaj7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Lasers allow us to deliver very bright light to a specific point in space, which is great for lighting up samples to be imaged. We use some fancy biochemistry to stick fluorescent molecules to the things we want to, we hit them with bright light, and we take a picture

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: RT @ShroukELA: My company is hiring! Lots of roles, including for bold and creative engineers looking for Electronic Engineering roles in M…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
To go one level down, why fluorescence? 
Because a cell is basically a sack made of fatty acids in which a whole bunch of chemistry happens. Most of the stuff biologists care about is transparent, so we have to label it to look at it

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Next, Image sensors, also known as the piece of silicon in your digital camera that actually collects the light and converts it to a digital signal.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Quick bit of history: Early microscopists looked through the glass and drew what they saw by hand. Then film cameras came along and people started mounting film cameras on microscopes, taking pictures of they samples, and developing them

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Then we got point detectors, which were sort of like reverse CRT screens. they could convert a spot of light focused on them into an electrical signal, so you could scan a point of light across a sample and record the light coming back one point at a time

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These existed in parallel with film for a while, because for some kinds of microscopy, point detectors didn't make much practical sense

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Then came image sensors, and all of a sudden biological images could be pushed directly from a microscope to a PC without a few hours of messing around with chemicals

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Also image sensor technology kept advancing and got so sensitive that they could detect single photons of light, so microscopes could "see" things that had previously been invisible

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Nowadays the kind of image sensors that end up in scientific cameras are almost as sensitive as the most sensitive point detectors, and almost as fast, but they can take a singe image at once instead of one point at a time, so they are more useful for most kinds of microscopy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And the thing that ties them all together, faster computers. To get why computers matter so much here it helps to realize that a digital image is a picture represented as a series of numbers, and you can therefore use maths to 'see' things in the image...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Since computers are good at maths, and since cameras can pump out images as fast as computers can see them, you can now create computerized tools for looking at pictures and extracting interesting data out of them

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So basically the kind of maths that can be used to recognise faces in photos can also be used to do things like count cells, measure their sizes and shapes, track their movements etc. etc.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You tie all of this together and all of a sudden microscopes become big data tools that can take incredibly large numbers of pictures of impossibly small amounts of light inside cells and turn that into numbers that tell us what is going on

tweets.label: Takeover

So... who wants to talk about diversity issues in science!

Or rather, who wants to listen to me rant and occasionally interject?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So where are we starting today? With a story about the microscope I already showed in this tweet

https://t.co/TmA8cxgfSE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: that microscope is based on the one that would have been used by Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch businessman and scientist who lived in the mid 1600-early 1700s and is widely regarded as one of the foundational figures in the history of microscopy and microbiology

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Sidenote: The businessman part is important because it is worth noting that a lot of the structures of modern science was created by wealthy European men working in their spare time. I'll talk a bit more later about why this matters

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For now, the important thing is that van Leeuwenhoek made what were at the time incredibly sensitive microscopes, then applied them to looking discovering microscopic life. Including his own semen

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (and yes, I have made all the jokes that I could think of about how he acquired his samples)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When van Leeuwenhoek and his assistants described what they saw while looking at semen, they all claimed to be able to see little people inside of the sperm cells they saw wriggling around

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now:
(a) those microscopes probably weren't powerful enough to allow them to see tiny people inside of cells
but more importantly
(b) We know now that there are no tiny people inside sperm cells

So why make the claim?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: RT @Hayley_Barlow: TONIGHT: shocking Channel 4 News report reveals how hundreds of overseas students have become destitute in the UK during…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To understand that, you have to understand that there was a long history in western philosophy of the idea that men provided the "seeds" of what makes a person and women purely provided the "soil" for the new person to grow

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ... and those ideas had grown into a legitimate scientific theory by the time van Leeuwenhoek looked through his microscope at those sperm cells. He was aware of these ideas, probably took them seriously.....

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ...and so when he saw his own "seeds" it wasn't a huge step to conclude that there were actually people in them

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: the lesson here isn't that he set out to mislead people or that he was a bad scientist, it is that he was a man who grew up in a world that fed him certain ideas about how the world worked, and those ideas leaked into his observations of the world

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (It is also worth noticing that science and philosophy in his era were both the domains of rich European men, and that had to have an effect on which ideas were considered legitimate and which weren't)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The lessons of this story:
Science as a discipline is meant to be a completely objective context-free search for the truth, and sometimes scientists assume this means *we* are also magically objective creatures who exist only to search for the truth

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In reality though, scientists are people, and like all people, we absorb the biases and prejudices of the societies we are surrounded are. And if we go on to build institutions, we embed those biases in them

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
we are surrounded *by*

I desperately need a proof reader

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Anyway, this observation becomes really important when you consider that, like I said earlier, the foundation of modern science were mostly erected over the last 500 years ago by a group almost exclusively made up of well-off European men

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: and baked into the institutions they created are a series of prejudices they inherited and formalised around race, gender, class, sexuality, disability etc.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And that process is as much a part of the history of science as the invention of the microscope or the discovery of DNA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Also, the consequences of that process live with us now, in terms of who is allowed to take part in the creation of new science and what kinds of questions are considered worthy of study

tweets.text:
Things I would recommend that I did:
(a) Try really hard to work for decent people and avoid terrible ones
(b) Follow what you find interesting/exciting

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (c) Try to be a decent person yourself. Be the person who people in your circles know they can come to if they have a problem

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Things I recommend that I am terrible at:
(a) Invest *heavily* in time management skills. Make the best use you can of your work hours, be as productive as possible
(b) Have long term plans. Have a feel for what you want your future to look like and plan for it

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
(c) Prioritize academic output. Don't put your name on terrible papers, but if you do anything actually interesting, get it published
(d) Be tactical. Chase collaborations, chase speaking engagements, make sure important people know who you are

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Also, be realistic about job prospects. Academic science in the 2020s is not a viable career path for the majority of the people who are skilled enough and motivated enough to do the work

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ...So keep an eye out on all of the possible career paths that exist outside of academia. And recognise that you aren't planning this because you are incapable of doing the work, but because you may not get a chance regardless

tweets.text: Hi everyone! My name is Otto Mustonen and it's my pleasure to curate Real Scientists Nano this week. I'm going to tweet about quantum materials and doing experiments at neutron and muon facilities. @OHJMustonen @isisneutronmuon @ILLGrenoble @msesheffield

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Quantum materials is a research area in the intersection of physics, chemistry and materials science. The peculiarities of quantum mechanics give rise to exotic properties and states in these materials. This often involves the collective behavior of electrons. It's like magic. https://t.co/wBtMiAA4XN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Quantum materials include superconductors, multiferroics, quantum magnetism, topological insulators and Weyl semimetals etc. The unusual properties can be the total loss of electrical resistivity, massive quantum entangled states and even magnetic monopoles.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The applications of quantum materials are often related to quantum technologies in general such as quantum computing, but we all use these materials when we get an MRI or when we read data off a HDD.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The 2021 quantum materials roadmap gives an excellent overview of the different types of quantum materials and the main challenges in the field. It is also open access! https://t.co/y2TrhTnULn @IOPscience @IOPmaterials #quantummaterials #openaccess

tweets.text: In 1911, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes was investigating the properties of metals at very low temperatures. When he cooled mercury to below 4.2 K, its resistivity suddenly dropped to zero. He had discovered superconductivity. #superconductors #NobelPrize https://t.co/TFiPsYXo4P

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This experiment was possible due to Kamerlingh Onnes' other great gift to science: liquid helium. Helium has the lowest boiling point of any gas at 4.2 K. It is used for cooling in almost all low-temperature physics. A good helium cryostat will get you down to 1.5 K. @OxInst https://t.co/V2mexWscGS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The superconducting state has two important properties: the absence of any resistivity and the expulsion of magnetic fields. The latter is called the Meissner effect (perfect diamagnetism), and is the reason why a magnet will levitate on top of a superconductor. #levitation https://t.co/qF5DKDGuR8

tweets.text: Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer developed a microscopic theory of superconductivity. An electron moving in a crystal will feel resistance, but two electrons can pair up to move without resistance. At low temperatures these Cooper pairs condensate to form the superconducting state.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The pairs are bound by a weak interaction with the lattice, and can be easily broken up as temperature increases. Here's the weird part: the electrons in the Cooper pair are hundreds of nanometers apart and moving in opposite directions! https://t.co/ul2jqMKGGX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: John Bardeen won the Nobel Prize in physics for both the BCS theory of superconductivity and for inventing the transistor. That is quite the legacy!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @JoFeanelwa Hi Jo! New Cooper pairs are formed spontaneously, because they have a lower energy than individual free electrons in a superconductor. The interaction between the pair is something that is just not strong. In the BCS theory it occurs via a lattice vibration (phonon).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @JoFeanelwa A negatively charged electron moving in the lattice of positively charged ions causes a small movement of the ions toward the electron. This displacement of the ions then attracts an electron moving in the opposite direction. This interaction binds the electrons into a pair. https://t.co/LmvuR1meh6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @JoFeanelwa The interaction via this displacement is surprisingly long range, so the electrons can get pretty far away form each other before separating (>100 nm). But yes!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @JoFeanelwa To be honest I don't know, but I don't think it can be done on the level of measuring the individual displacements of ions. The lattice vibrations (phonons) can be measured with techniques such as inelastic neutron scattering and it is possible to measure electron-phonon coupling

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Conventional superconductors are metals or intermetallic compounds. In 1986, Bednorz and Müller discovered superconductivity in a ceramic copper oxide at 30 K, a temperature on the edge of what was thought possible by BCS theory. https://t.co/UkIFbU8SLn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The next year Chu and coworkers discovered YBCO (YBa2Cu3O7-d), a superconductor with a previously unthinkable critical temperature of over 90 K. This allowed the use of liquid nitrogen (77 K) instead of liquid helium (4.2 K) for cooling the material to the superconducting state. https://t.co/BFqKTSbdkq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Anderson proposed this high-Tc superconductivity might be related to a novel quantum state known as the resonating valence bond state (a type of quantum spin liquid). I'll talk more about this in relation to my own research later.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The high-Tc superconductors are very different from the materials before. They are ceramic instead of metallic, their parent phases are magnetic whereas magnetism usually destroys superconductivity, and they have layered structures with a superconducting CuO2 layer.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The high-Tc cuprate superconductors are part of quantum materials known as strongly correlated electron systems. These materials cannot be described using conventional band theory, which assumes individual electrons do not interact with each other.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This often involves materials with partially filled d or f shells, which are more localized on the ion compared to s and p orbitals and therefore interact more strongly. In the cuprates, the superconductivity arises from the interactions of the strongly correlated Cu2+ 3d9 states

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Magnetism in solids is a bit tricky to explain. We all learn in school that an electric current going round and round in a loop will induce a magnetic moment. This is how electromagnets work. We can use this analogy for electrons and cations in solids. #magnetism #miracles https://t.co/ZioUxIEFPM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Electrons have a negative charge, and so they also have a magnetic moment when they go round and round. Electrons have an inherent magnetic moment called spin, which is due them spinning around their axis (kind of). They also have a moment related to their orbital in an ion. https://t.co/sDjTq19gES

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Magnetism of filled orbitals and electron shells cancels out. Magnetism in solids requires unpaired electrons! These are found in transition metals such as iron and lanthanides such as neodymium. Magnetic moment of a cation is related to the number of unpaired electrons it has.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can treat magnetic cations as tiny magnets inside a solid. Magnetic properties of a material are defined by what the cation is, how they are arranged and how they interact with each other. The interactions cannot be described without quantum mechanics, but that's ok.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Quantum magnetism occurs, when this "oh they're just tiny magnets" analogy breaks down. This occurs when the cation only has one unpaired electron, which can then start to misbehave due to quantum mechanics and do all sorts of weird things. https://t.co/bB9tk7YPrY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @goldclusters Excellent question! The idea here is that if you have a localized electron on a d orbital and you put another electron on the same orbital, the presence of the first electron will strongly affect the second one and you have to take this electron correlation into account.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @goldclusters This correlation is a really complex many-body problem. When the electrons are delocalized, they are far away from each other and can be modeled like a non-interacting free electron gas. The electrons don't spend much time close to each other, and this approximation is alright.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Magnetic interactions try to align spins (moments) in a material either parallel (ferro-) or antiparallel (antiferromagnetic) to each other. When all the interactions between spins cannot be satisfied at the same time, the material is frustrated. https://t.co/MHhVoNJemz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Frustration occurs when the spins are arranged in certain shapes such as triangles, tetrahedrons or squares. It can stop materials from magnetically ordering (all spins have a fixed direction). Instead, the spins can form collective quantum entangled states with weird properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Anderson proposed a quantum spin liquid state on a triangular lattice of spins (moments). In this state, the spins do not freeze even at absolute zero. Instead, they pair up to form valence bonds. The QSL is a superposition of all the different ways to cover the lattice in bonds. https://t.co/d0psDda6UU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: QSLs are quantum states with a massive number of entangled spins. They're very weird. If given some energy, the QSL state can have excitations that carry only spin instead of both spin and charge like electrons. QSLs could have applications in a new type of quantum computer.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A number of excellent QSL candidate materials are known. Herbertsmithite ZnCu3(OH)6Cl2 is a QSL candidate with a Kagome lattice of Cu2+ spins (see the Kagome basket below). There is no single "smoking gun" experiment for identifying a QSL, which makes it all quite difficult. https://t.co/k1UvR8BUbS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This review by Leon Balents is an excellent introduction to the field of quantum spin liquids. https://t.co/6Mq3rVEQtf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Anderson proposed a quantum spin liquid state also on the square lattice, which is found in high-Tc superconductors. For over 30 years there were no QSL candidates on the square, until me and coworkers discovered one. https://t.co/dDA1GMCrmu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This was a collaboration between my PhD supervisor Maarit Karppinen's group at @AaltoUniversity, physicists in Brazil, Germany and Japan and muon and neutron scientists at @psich_en and @isisneutronmuon. Thank you so much everyone!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Two different antiferromagnetic arrangements of spins are possible on the square. The one observed depends on the interactions in a material. However, if the interactions are just right between these states, a QSL might be found. https://t.co/zWLltQG1ex

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We found that two almost identical copper compounds have these different magnetic states, with the only difference being a Te6+ (d10) instead of a W6+ (d0) cation. I had the simple idea of let's just mix the two and see what happens. And it worked!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This mixed compound Sr2CuTe0.5W0.5O6 has many of the properties expected of a QSL. Most importantly it does not magnetically order down to 19 mK despite antiferromagnetic interactions. This material could be a QSL or a QSL-like random singlet state.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Measuring this compound at @psich_en was probably the coolest moment in my (brief) scientific career. We had no idea what would happen going in, and I was just so excited to find out it might be a QSL. And then we walked to a nearby village for a lovely dinner. https://t.co/T3vhEvlZes
