tweets.text: Neutrons are subatomic particles that help keep the cores of atoms together. But they are also waves! This means we can do science with neutron beams like we would with beams of light. Neutron scattering is a powerful technique for investigating materials. #waveparticleduality https://t.co/utFxkYWgdg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Neutrons can be used to measure the structure of solids at the atomic level and dynamics like lattice vibrations. Neutrons penetrate deep into materials. This means we can use neutrons to study the strains and stresses in large objects like turbine blades.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Most importantly for me: neutrons have a magnetic moment. This makes them very useful for studying magnetic materials, since they are scattered by the spins (magnetic moments) in materials unlike X-rays. #magnetism #neutrons

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are two ways to make neutrons. In nuclear fission, the nucleus of a heavy element splits into lighter ones while releasing energy and neutrons. The other is spallation: a proton travelling almost at the speed of light hits a nucleus shooting neutrons all over. #neutrons https://t.co/NfaO2GH7t8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The need for a nuclear reactor or a particle accelerator means neutron science can only be done at large central facilities. Reactor sources include @ILLGrenoble and @ANSTO while spallation sources include @isisneutronmuon, @ORNLNeutrons, @psich_en and @essneutron. #neutrons

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I went on a trip to a nuclear power plant when I was a kid. I was so disappointed we only got to see the visitor center! I finally got to go inside the actual reactor building at @ILLGrenoble , which was really cool. #neutrons https://t.co/rEcZseQVNo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Understanding how the atomic level structure of materials affects their properties is one of the cornerstones of materials science. Neutron diffraction is an excellent method to determine that atomic and crystal structure. #neutrons #diffraction https://t.co/4d1grBNqdo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Most solids are made of tiny crystals with all the atoms arranged in a repeating pattern. Neutrons (or X-rays, or electrons) only scatter from crystals at certain allowed angles depending on their crystal structure. This is called diffraction. #braggslaw https://t.co/FzFpYkX9Hh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Neutron diffraction makes it possible to accurately determine the positions of light atoms like lithium and oxygen, which is difficult with X-rays. Hydrogen is still problematic as it increases the background, and it is often replaced with deuterium for neutron experiments.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In magnetic materials, the directions of the spins (magnetic moments) of all the magnetic ions can be determined with neutrons. This is possible, because neutrons have their own spin and are scattered by the magnetic ions. #neutrons #magnetism https://t.co/gGNmpNl42z

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Inelastic neutron scattering is a technique, where the neutrons lose energy as they scatter from the material. This makes it possible to study excitations such as lattice vibrations (phonons) and spin waves, which are tiny distortions of the ordered magnetic structure. #neutrons https://t.co/vCC3Re5rfD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Lattice vibrations play an important role in heat conduction, electric transport and superconductivity. Investigating the spin waves of a magnetic material make it possible to determine its magnetic interactions.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Our recent paper on magnetic double perovskites highlights some neutron scattering techniques. We used neutron diffraction to solve the magnetic structure and inelastic neutron scattering to investigate magnetic interactions. @isisneutronmuon @msesheffield https://t.co/SteTJ0TcCJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Inelastic neutron scattering data just looks cool. Each yellow or light blue point corresponds to a neutron exciting a spin wave. Measured data on the left, simulation on the right. https://t.co/NUZedpcrUS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These experiments allowed us to formulate simple rules for magnetism in double perovskites that have a nonmagnetic d10 or d0 cation on one of the B-sites. d10 cations will lead to Type 1 magnetic order and d0 cations will lead to Type 2 order. #perovskites https://t.co/mBtGqmcVoF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This week I'm running an experiment at the D7 polarized neutron diffractometer at @ILLGrenoble . Polarization analysis allows the separation of the structural and magnetic scattering from each other. This can be used to study dynamic magnetic states like spin liquids. #neutrons https://t.co/eBtUxS1fRT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm very sad this is a remote experiment as I love Grenoble. Beamtime is my favorite part of the job, and it's just not the same when you're sitting at home. That said, many thanks to all the dedicated instrument scientists who make these experiments possible at all! #beamtime

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The real cost of beamtime at a neutron facility is of the order of £20 000 a day. This means we always need to apply for beamtime even though we don't directly pay for it. The proposals are ranked by a scientific panel, and the best ones get beamtime. #neutrons #beamtime https://t.co/Bh6zKw5EXp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A beamtime proposal will include the scientific background including what you already know about your sample, an overview of the proposed experiment and what it will tell you, and the reason why neutrons are the only/best way to find out.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you're interested in doing an experiment at a neutron facility, instrument scientists are the best people to contact. They will be able to tell you if your proposed experiment is sensible and the best instrument for it. Instrument scientists are awesome! https://t.co/OYytsnMfes

tweets.text: Muons are short-lived elementary particles that are a bit like heavy electrons. They are produced when cosmic rays hit the atmosphere and in particle accelerators. Muons are a highly sensitive local probe of magnetism. Muon sources: @isisneutronmuon @psich_en @TRIUMFLab @J_PARC https://t.co/78OF7dY6Ia

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Muons have a fun property: their magnetic moment points in the opposite direction of where they're going. We can use this spin polarization in muon spectroscopy to study magnetic materials, superconductors and ionic conductivity in batteries. #muons #musr https://t.co/dRsu5VkW2j

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In muon spectroscopy, positive muons are implanted in the sample. The muon spin will start to rotate in the internal magnetic field. The muon quickly decays into a positron, which flys mainly in the direction of the muon spin at time of decay. The positrons then are measured. https://t.co/IXIGOGsBDQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Where the positrons are going tells us what the muon spin is doing as function of time, which in turn gives us information on the properties of the material. Muon spectroscopy is related to NMR, but it works even in zero magnetic field.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Muon spectroscopy can be used to study both both static and dynamic magnetism. It's great for quantum spin liquids, which have no "smoking gun" experimental signature. But muons allow us to rule out more common states such as magnetic order or a spin! #muons #spinliquids https://t.co/dQFKIZ6Qx8

My scientific career pt I: 
How did I decide to become a scientist?
Until I was 19 I lived near Oristano, a small city in Sardinia (Italy). 1/5 https://t.co/Q7kHLVG2C2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: During my first years of elementary and middle school I wanted to become an archeologist and I did not care a lot about science, but I enjoyed math. 2/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When I was 12 years old we started talking about chemistry at school and I really didn't like it. I struggled a lot to understand the beauty and utility of it. 3/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At that point my mother, librarian, decided that a book could be a good solution for my chemical problems and she got me "Uncle Tungsten - Memories of a chemical boyhood" by Oliver Sacks. That book helped me see chemistry as the beautiful and amazing science it is. 4/5 https://t.co/pyRwBgQfS1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After that it become quite clear that I would have been a chemist and I continued reading about it during all my high school years. I had a periodic table all the time with me. The future was decided! 5/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @JoFeanelwa I envied the protagonist so much! He was free of making experiments, visit all London's museums..

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
My scientific career pt II: 
I obtained my bachelor degree in Chemistry and Materials Chemistry at @UniboMagazine. My bachelor thesis was a spectroscopic + computational study of the structure of an amino-alcohol (https://t.co/uWwHyQkL3A). 1/3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I stayed in Bologna for my master. For my thesis I started working on computational graphene chemistry, studying the carbo-catalytic reduction of a sugar. 2/3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I enjoyed that project so much that I decided to do a PhD in that field and I was very happy when I found my current position, as a PhD in Computational Carbon Chemistry. 3/3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What is computational chemistry? We can say that is the use of computer simulations (in silico experiments) to solve chemical problems. But this actually covers a lot of different fields and applications, from drug design to astrochemistry. 1/5 https://t.co/LsGEIijr6N

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Nowadays it is mainly used to give guidelines to scientists performing experiments, speeding up the research process. And, with the development of software and hardware, computational sciences are becoming more important. 2/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The efficiency and low cost of computer simulations makes them the perfect tool to predict properties and behaviour of different substances and then proceed to test non-virtually just the ones with a specific profile. 3/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I apply these concepts to understand how different 2D-materials can be exploited for analysis, electronics or catalysis. I still rely on good experimental data  to check the accuracy of my simulations and to reproduce, as much as possible, the real-world conditions. 4/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Of course still a lot of progress is needed in computational chemistry. We work with approximations and it is impossible to reproduce everything that happens. We can just try to find better models and methods, and improve the efficiency of the algorithms used. 5/5

tweets.text:
Graphene: what is it and how was it discovered?
#graphene is a 2D material composed only by carbon atoms. These atoms are disposed in a hexagonal lattice, like a honeycomb. It is an extremely robust, conductive material, with a lot of possible applications (see next tweets). 1/3 https://t.co/76yyHICc4J

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Graphene is obtained by graphite (the main ingredient of pencils leads). Graphite is composed by a lot of super-thin (one atom thin) layers of carbon sheets. Each one of these is a graphene sheet. 2/3 https://t.co/kXmJLRDu9m

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The first report of graphene was just in 2004, by professors Geim and Novoselov. They discovered the secret amazing material hidden in the underestimated  graphite. If you want to know more about the discovery and the discoverers:  https://t.co/ohhr06nsZS 3/3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Pristine graphene, as the perfect infinite hexagonal lattice we are used to see, is an ideal material. What it is obtained in a reality is a material containing defect, holes and impurities. The ideal graphene does not exist but there are bright sides. 1/4 https://t.co/GhxYv0ZbA0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The possibility of changing the structure and the composition of graphene during the synthesis allows us to obtain a whole family of compounds: graphene-based materials (GBMs). 2/4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We have then a big pool of 2D materials to exploit and study! While some defects or functionalities are randomly introduced during the production of graphene, some of them can be introduced voluntarily, using different synthetic conditions. 3/4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Some of these "defects" are quite useful. For example, it was discovered that, while pristine graphene is almost useless in catalysis (not very reactive), a simple oxidation of it allows to unlock good catalytic performances. 4/4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @goldclusters Partially yes but also the ways to obtain graphene are responsible for it. The conditions used introduce new defects.. like if you form it on a metal surface some metal atoms "enter" in the lattice or if you exfoliate graphite holes or deformations can be produced

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Using computational chemistry is it possible to study the properties of molecules, understanding the mechanism of reactions and design drugs or catalysts. But it also possible to design a material. How can we do it? 1/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 1)think about which kind of material we want, both composition (graphene derivative? inorganic material?..) and function (adsorbant? sensor? ..). At that point it is necessary to check the literature to see how different material perform for the desired task. 2/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At that point it starts the difficult part: we need to find some property we can calculate or simulate and try to see if there is a relationship between the performance shown by the material and the computed property. 3/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you find that the relationship exist then we can "design" a material, compute the property and from that predict how well it will perform. If we don't find a relationship probably the chosen property has no effect on the performance and we should try others. 4/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are some challenges: use accurate methods to simulate the material and compute the property, the need to consider the different experimental conditions in which our data were measured, the performance probably depends on more than a single property.. 5/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Graphene and its derivatives are the most famous between 2D materials. These materials are very interesting because:
- high surface/volume ratio
- usually high mechanical robustness
- particular optical and electrical properties
- tunability of structure and properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2D materials can be used, exploiting their particular properties for a lot of different applications, from nanoelectronics to water depuration. 1/4 https://t.co/aBCLEK6ydu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My interest in mainly in environmental applications. As I said 2D materials have an high surface/volume ratio, so if they interact with contaminants they can be used as filters for water or air. 2/4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Many 2D materials (like graphene derivatives) are semiconductors and they can be used as sensors, to determine the quantity of contaminants in a sample. The molecules will get adsorbed and this will cause a measurable change in the properties of the sensing material. 3/4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are a lot of other amazing applications for 2D materials. They have been used to obtain highly efficient solar cells, they have been used in photothermal therapy and to enhance the mechanical properties of hydrogels. 4/4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Today is my last day of take-over and I want to talk about the future of my field. The future for computational chemistry looks exciting and full of challenges and possibilities. New developments in computer science are giving scientists amazing tools! 1/4
#compchem https://t.co/ocsepZS0sz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Machine learning is one of the most hyped and promising tools. The possibility for a machine to find trend and properties in large datasets of molecules, with the aim to predict and design new systems is incredible and almost scary. (https://t.co/P2NWFom1Ix) 2/4 
#machinelearning

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The development of super efficient computational algorithms has also offered the possibility of analysis large numbers of systems, causing the building of large databases, so the choice of the studied set is becoming less difficult, because it is possible to not be selective. 3/4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The role of the computational chemist is clearly changing and developing. It is still important for chemist to invest time and research into developing computational methods, to couple the performance of machines with the experience and instinct of chemists. 4/4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is the end of my take-over. I'm really glad for this opportunity to share my research and my ideas! If you are interested in computational chemistry and 2D materials follow me at @AnnaPiras19

Computational research goes better with experimental results.

As a purely computational group, we rely on experimentalists to provide their data for comparison. https://t.co/hj8QzsC6Bm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
A common way is comparing vibrational spectra. 

But my clusters are metallic and the metal-metal interaction falls in the Far infrared spectrum, which is not easy to observe experimentally.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
You need a laser that has:

✅tunable wavelength
✅wavelenght at the Far IR 
✅powerful enough

A Free-electron laser ticks all the boxes

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Like the one in Nijmegen (The Netherlands) at Radboud University. Its name is FELIX. https://t.co/8um9uXg5qO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Obtaining the IR spectrum computationally is relatively easy, all you need is a Frequency calculation. https://t.co/5VSNxlAkLS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another way to compare experimental data with theoretical results is using mass spectrometry.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
After photofragmentation experiments, we can obtain a mass spectrum informing us about the relative stability of our clusters. 

A high intensity in the spectra indicates a high relative stability of these clusters.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Then we calculate dissociation energies using Density Functional Theory. A higher dissociation energy will indicate that the cluster is more stable.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This way we can find which clusters are more stable, what we call: magic numbers and magic clusters. https://t.co/DyV6AWdZ6H

1/ So what IS a semiconductor?

There exists a loose definition saying that semiconductors are materials with an electrical conductivity somewhere between that of metals (very conductive) and insulators (not conductive at all). Of course that is very difficult to quantify.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
2/ What threshold value of the conductivity does the material have to exceed to qualify? This is not a good definition. We'll come back to one later.

In terms of conductivity, solid state physics only knows two types of solids: conductors (metals) and non-conductors (insulators)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3/ The distinction is made by looking at where electrons in the solid "live". More specifically, which energies can electrons in the solid have? Atoms have fixed energies for each electron orbital. In solid matter, which is built up from atoms, this scheme is partially preserved. https://t.co/LKB9W6teJc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4/ Singe-energy levels from atoms will combine to broad regions with "allowed energies", called bands. Sometimes, these bands are being pushed into each other, and they merge into one broader band. In other cases, there will be a gap between some states -- the so called band gap.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5/ When we now "fill" these states (figuratively) with electrons, they will occupy the available states. When all electrons a material ahs have been "poured" into the solid, we get to an energy that separates occupied from unoccupied states. https://t.co/YTdMip8iOu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 6/ In the example above, one band has been completely filled, and one is completely empty. There is no possibility for carrier movement in any of the two bands -- one has no room to move, the other one has no electrons. This material is an insulator.

1/ Good morning!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2/ Microprocessors consist of incredibly large numbers of nano-sized electrical switches called transistors. The same type of devices is behind the electronics controlling the screens on our mobile devices. Solar cells are nothing else but a "block" of semiconductor absorbing...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3/ light and converting its energy to usable electrical power. LEDs are in a way a "reversed solar cell", converting charge carriers into photons. High-power electronics are part of our power grid systems, converting the electricity coming from power plants to "usable" values.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
4/ For all these devices, it is extremely important that charge carriers can move as freely as possible. Defects can mess with that by capturing charge carriers.

In some cases, already one defect per 10 billion atoms (!) can make the difference between a good and a bad device.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5/ This means that we need VERY sensitive equipment to find out if defects are present in this concentration range, and to study how they interact with charge carriers.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:

https://t.co/DfJSSb8NQY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2/ to illuminate a sample, the electrons go into a short period of being "excited" (i.e. having a bit larger energy than in their ground state) and then fall back to where they were before, re-emitting light of a specific wavelength that we can detect.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3/ Each defect has characteristic emission lines, similar to what atoms do when you "excite" them. By identifying these lines, we can learn which defects are present in the sample.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:

tweets.text: Today I had planned to talk about a little about the things defects can actually be good for. So far, I only mentioned the downsides of having them in semiconductors, but there is actually many ways of turning their presence into something useful: the functionalization of defects

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The live experiment took longer than I had expected, so I'll make a shorter thread now about one of the ideas people have for defect functionalization, and maybe another one tomorrow, if you're interested!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
1/ How defects can be useful for neuromorphic computing: a 🧵!

A defect of any species is tied to a certain site in the crystal lattice. For example, a Ni vacancy in nickel oxide can, by definition, only "live" where Ni atoms belong. But this doesn't mean defects don't move!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2/ Quite the contrary. High temperatures, electric fields or other driving forces can lead to atoms redistributing in the lattice. By moving a Ni atom into the Ni vacancy, the defect and the atom "swap sites", which can happen again with the next Ni neighbor and so on.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3/ This diffusive movement of Ni vacancies at higher temperatures is something we have directly observed recently, by doing electrical measurements with an extremely high-precision method, called broadband dielectric spectroscopy (BDS). Here's the paper:

https://t.co/sAiP9jQq9H

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4/ Because the Ni vacancy is also responsible for the electrical conductivity in these samples, that means that by targetedly moving Ni atoms (or vacancies) around, we can in principle create and destroy conductive paths through a NiO layer.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5/ This is related to a phenomenon that occurs in a lot of metal oxides: resistive switching. Simply by applying a voltage across a piece of them, they change between a conductive and a resistive state. The transition between these can be incredibly fast -- below 1 nanosecond!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 6/ There are two general mechanisms that cause this switching: the filament and the interface mechanism. Here is a schematics of what happens in these two. In the filament process, defects migrate to form a conductive chain that connects the two electrodes. In the interface... https://t.co/VmWtOsdqWJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
7/ process, the cell's resistance is increased because defects accumulate below one of the electrodes. Both of these processes are reversible, i.e. they can be repeated many times. 

This is similar to what conventional transistors in modern microelectronics do, just A LOT faster

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
8/ They are also much simpler from a device design perspective: they only have two electrodes. Transistors typically have three, separating current conduction and control over conductivity. 

The simpler principle of resistive switching cells and their high speed makes them...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
9/ good candidates for artificial neurons! 

Here is a relatively recent paper with a tutorial on how one could use resistive switching cells to emulate biological brains:

https://t.co/BSTP6gvNre

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 10/ So far, nothing of that magnitude has been achieved yet. There are many problems around these resistive switching cells, many of which relate to the fact that we don't really understand the physics behind the switching. Since it is ultimately because of defect movement...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 11/ this means we need to understand better how (and which!) defects move in these materials, how they form larger structures in electric fields and temperature gradients, how they break down again, and what can be done to make the process more robust and predictable.

1/ What is transparent photovoltaics?

The sunlight that reaches Earth's surface contains up to ~1 kilowatts per square meter of optical power. That's quite a lot: every m² receives enough power to supply a vacuum cleaner! This immense potential is the reason why photovoltaics...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
2/ have become so important in the past two decades.

To harvest all that energy, we use solar cells that we put up in areas that we don't use otherwise, like on our roofs or as huge solar power plants in the uninhabited countryside. 

But there are many surfaces around us that..

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3/ are also illuminated by the sun, but that cannot actually be equipped with conventional solar cells. Large glazed facades of buildings, or their roofs. Or cars, or even the displays of our mobile devices. 

You don't want to have normal cells on them, because they change...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
4/ the way these surfaces look, or even function (a window would become completely opaque). And here is where transparent photovoltaics comes in!

Half of the power contained in the sunlight is in wavelength regions we cannot see. Most of that (93%) is in the infrared (IR)...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
5/ and about 7% in the ultraviolet (UV) spectral ranges. Solar cells that use this light, but let the visible parts pass through, would be almost invisible to the human eye, while providing us with electrical energy.

And because they're invisible, we could put them wherever!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
6/ There is an incredibly large amount of research around this. See this review: 

https://t.co/6U8u1m4a2Y

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
7/ The tricky part is to get the visible light (medium photon energy) through while at the same time absorbing the lower-energy photons from the IR. 

From the perspective of a semiconductor physicist, making a UV solar cell, however, is the obvious first step. All we need is...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 8/ a semiconductor that starts absorbing light in the UV. It is then naturally transparent for all the lower-energy light. It won't convert IR light though, so it is going to be less efficient. But this may be compensated by the simplicity of the device, of its fabrication, and..

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
9/ the low cost of the materials we use.

In my PhD thesis, I studied (among other devices) transparent solar cells made from the inexpensive 
and easy-to-process materials zinc oxide and nickel oxide.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 1/ The transparent solar cell project became quite a success very soon after we started. We found that a simple device, that basically only consisted of a layer of ZnO in contact with a layer of NiO, plus a front and back electrode, did the trick. The cells we made immediately...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
2/ beat the previous world record of the conversion efficiency for UV solar cells by a factor of 20!

3/ After that, I started looking more into what still went wrong. And it turned out defects were behind most of it!

tweets.text: I've seen that some people think that academics have a very secure job. But whilst this might be the case for a few (not all) tenured positions, the rest of us are in the constant look for available positions, and even when you get one, we need to find a way to finance our work.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Therefore, something that becomes more and more evident that one of, if not the key, skill one needs as a scientist is that of writing. #academicwriting

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Even when considering writing, a lot of focus (at least in my experience) is given to paper writing. Which, don't get me wrong, is indispensable, as this is how we are often evaluated. But if one wants to keep writing papers, then you need, blu tly put: money!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, I was never offered a workshop on grant proposal writing. I have now managed to write one by looking at other people's proposals, and by getting feedback from. But I was lucky, many people do not have good mentors, for example.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Also, grant proposal writing is very different from paper writing. Yes, the science must be there, but it is more of a sales pitch, think of a Dragon's den or a Shark's tank. You need to sell your idea, that you're the right person, and have a coherent plan for the research.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is just my first grant proposal, so I am sure it has many 'areas of opportunity', but it has deeply made me ponder on why I do what I do, which path I might want to take, and how being a researcher is never what you though it would be.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Which is why, I think that people coming from certain areas of industry or working at the interface might have a better chance at getting grants. As they have had to hone their communication skills. But this is just a thought.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What becomes to me ever more  clear is that scientists, at their core, are communicators. We pass our lives writing about what we have done, presenting our work to our peers, or if one is into #scicomm to non-academics, or to scientists outside our area. #communication

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We need to be versatile as we need to communicate these ideas to a variety of audiences, with different purposes, we need to be able to find the thread connecting it all to bring a coherent story.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I was once said that the science should speak by itself, in the context of getting prestige perhaps or grants. But I think it is up to us which voice we want to give to it. If it is secretive, mysterious, or if it is open. #scicomm #academicWriting

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So the first thing that is different between the XFEL and a synchrotron is their shape. In a synchtrotron, you first accelerate electrons (in a linear accelerator) and then you put them in the storange ring. Ring being the key thing. Whilst an XFEL is "just" a linear accelerator.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The XFELs can be from a bit more one km one, like the one in Korea, or over 3 km long, like that in Germany (@EuropeanXFEL ) or the one in Standford (@SLAClab).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In XFELs you accelerate the electrons to high energies, then they go and wiggle around through magnets (called undulators), where they emit X-ray radiation. Importantly, the radiation keeps getting amplified here, and the electrons organise themselves into thin disks, leading to

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: X-ray flashes!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So here you do not really get a continuous stream of radiation, but rather pulses. These pulses are then controlled in spacing and duration, allowing us to access molecular processes and structures never seen before. I will actually tell you later how we have used them.

tweets.text: Thing is, cocoa butter, fats, when solid, they form crystals! Yes, crystals are not only minerals, like the ones you see for healing, meditating and stuff...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And since it is not straightforward for molecules to arrange themselves into a nice periodic structure that has local and long-range order, we have different types of crystalline forms of cocoa butter. We call this property "polymorphism" so multiple forms.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Some people call them with roman numerals from I up to VI, and then, we have the greek letters sub-alpha or gamma, alpha, beta prime (III and IV) and beta (V and VI) in order of increasing stability (melting temperature!).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So yeah, even scientists can't agree on how to name things...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But anyways, of all of these crystals we want, not crystal VI, but crystal V! Why? Crystal VI is too hard, has a higher melting point, but Crystal V is the best for a good sensory experience, it is the one that melts at body temperature.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So how do we get the right crystal? By using a process called tempering, which people in metallurgy might be familiar with! Although also, foodies, chocolate aficionados and the like.

tweets.text: I left off saying that to get the right crystal we need to temper the chocolate. But how does this process look? Well basically it is a temperature game.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You first melt your chocolate (depending on the type, the temperature, being the highest for dark and the lowest for white), and you keep it there for enough time that all, or most of the crystals disappear and become liquid.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Then, you cool it down carefully to roughly 27 °C (again, lower for milk and white), so that the beta prime and beta crystals form. If you go lower, lots of alpha, unstable crystals will form.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And finally, you want to get rid of the beta prime crystals, and only leave the beautiful beta V. For this, you can take advantage of their different thermal stability. So you heat your chocolate to 30/32 °C, thus melting the beta prime, and leaving only the beta V.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You can then pour your chocolate into moulds and let it set! If it has been well tempered, the chocolate will contract, making extraction of the moulds very simple. Otherwise, you will have a hard time taking out, unless you heat your mold and melt it all again. #chocolate https://t.co/wzfcgYV3AN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now, if you have done tempering at home or in a cooking class, this might not be the method you have followed, but rather, you might have added some shavings of chocolate, to your molten mass. This method is called seeding.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Basically those chocolate shavings serve as "seeds" from which beta V crystals can grow. https://t.co/ejP7VJHCnf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It is really convenient for very small batches, but not so much in industry because cocoa butter really likes being in the most stable forms (The betas! For once beta means better than the alpha...), so crystallisation tends to happen so fast, and grows like a monster...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You can imagine it gets then really hard to pump the chocolate into the moulds for bon bons and bars...

tweets.text: So one of the things that I was interested in was if the most frequently used temperature (60 °C) was ideal or if you need to heat it more (above 80 °C). Note, that a higher temperature in chocolate itself is not advisable due to the interactions with other ingredients.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What I observed and reported in my thesis was that the temperature at which you melted cocoa butter, before you cooled it down, did affect the order in which the different crystal forms would appear. So by heating it to a higher temperature, it would take longer to crystallise...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But the transformations were not affected, actually there was a hint that transformation to the beta-V might be accelerated. But this was pure cocoa butter. And you always have something else in chocolate...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As to why it would crystallise faster if I first melted at 60 rather than 100 °C? It is hard to tell, I did check for oxidation, but my cocoa butter was stable for a few solid hours before degrading...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The trouble with working with natural fats is that they are not only made of one component, but rather by a multitude of them!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Cocoa butter, as well as most other fasts and oils, is composed by molecules called triglycerides, which are three (hence the tri) fatty acids (heard of omega 3, or palmitic acid?) that are joined together by a molecule called glycerol (you guessed it, glyceride comes from it)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now these triglycerides, or more correctly triacylglycerols can have different fatty acids, attached in different order. And these fatty acids can be all straight, or have kinks because of two atoms sharing a double bond.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Cocoa butter has many different triglycerides (let's call them TAGs). OK, not as many as milk fat... but amongst these, it's main ones are the ones I, and others, like calling SOS, POP, and POS. So easy to remember...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The S (Stearic) and the P (palmitic) fatty acids are the straight chains, and the only difference between them is that one is shorter than the other, so they get along together pretty well when they are closely packed in the crystals.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Whereas, the O (oleic acid) has an insaturation, a kink. So that kink, unless it is next to another kink that gives it space (kinda like two spoons), it is unhappy, because then it is sitting too close to another atom...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @mkolsek Perhaps you are tempted now to have some chocolate? Would be a nice pick-me-up for a Wednesday...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So yeah, those oleic acids like spooning. https://t.co/NtHix5YnuU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is what drives the different stabilities in the different crystal forms. In the less stable phases, they arrange in what we call a 2 L phase, so the length of the layer of the crystal is that of two fatty acid chains. This means that some kinks will be unhappy.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You could in very broad terms say this is because they are in a hurry to get into a packed solid structure, so they do not get into the most perfect packing.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After some time though, or if you crystallise at a higher temperature and have the patience to wait a bit more, like in tempering, the packing changes into a 3L structure. And yes, this means that the length of the crystal layer is of 3 fatty acid chains.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To achieve this, all, or most, of the oleic acid chains get on a single line, separating themselves from the rest.

tweets.text: But why should we care about supercooled water? Besides the obvious (supercool remember? * sorry not sorry *).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It turns out that water is a pretty unusual liquid, yes, it is ubiquitous on our planet, but it does not behave as normal liquids should! #strangewater #water #anomalous.  For example, your usual water cubes float in liquid water, whereas a normal liquid sinks, such as methanol! https://t.co/MCOUJ2WQFI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If one fits a power law to the thermodynamic properties (density, compressibility, heat capacity...) of water, they all seem to diverge at a temperature of 228 K. (https://t.co/ZwdvFhCWVI)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But what is happening here? There has been several hypothesis, supported by theory and molecular simulations, but one of these is that water is in fact two liquids, a high-density one, and a low-density one. At very low temperatures you would be able to see the transition.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: *hypotheses

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Not only this but as one approaches the temperature mentioned before, at positive pressures, one reaches a critical point (LLCP) where the two liquids coexist but are fluctuating constantly. These density fluctuations are thought to then be the origin of the anomalous properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So far, it had not been possible to study this region experimentally, as crystallisation (ice formation) happens incredibly fast, which is why this region has been called "no man's land", it has been unchartered territory for a long time.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But I have been lucky enough to have been part of the team that has managed to go past the icy wall, to tread where no one had (am I being too proud of the achievement of the team?). And all thanks to the amazing XFELs!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the cropped image you can see above, you will see that it says "amorphous ices" and you might wonder why, as I have been talking about supercooled water so far.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To get to the supercooled regime, you can come from the top (higher temp) or the bottom (lower temp). If you come from the top, at least in our group, we tend to use droplets under vacuum, which will then cool down by evaporative cooling, kinda like how sweat cools you down.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But we have "only" managed to go down to 227 K... https://t.co/ZuWmENK3sO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That is relatively straightforward to understand, you come from liquid water and you cool it, but what lurks in the depths of the phase diagram of water, at really low temperatures and higher pressures? Yup, amorphous ices.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: They were first discovered in the 80s by Mishima, and they can be formed in the lab by crushing crystalline ice, and then by annealing (like maturing) at specific temperatures and pressure you can get different types.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We primarily have two: low-density amorphous ice (LDA) and high-density amorphous ice (HDA), I know, not super original, but very descriptive, which is what we need.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It is easy then to suspect that they might relate to the high- and low-density liquids (HDL and LDL). This is indeed then how we approach things from the bottom up, and is what we did in the Science paper.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We basically had our grid with HDA and then fired a lase to increase its temperature really fast, and then we shot the ice with X-rays to probe it and take a "picture" of it. We took X-rays at different times after we "pumped" the ice with the laser. This is known as "pump-probe"

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Between our previous knowledge (both from within the group and literature), and through simulations, we could ascertain that the HDA had transformed into HDL, and then to LDL, and finally crystalline ice.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now you might wonder why all this is ultrafast! As I said before, crystallisation happens crazy fast, with this experiment we saw it begins at around 1 to 3 microseconds at 205 K, so we if take our sweet time to heat and measure, we miss this transition.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You might think that this is really nice and pretty, but it is all "in the lab" and that you might only care about "real" ice (so ice I). The thing is,  the most common ice in our Universe is not ice I, but it seems that it would be something more like our LDA.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You heard that right, amorphous ice is prevalent in our Universe, it is present in interstellar dust. If you want to get closer to our planet, it seems that before ice I forms in clouds, we first have amorphous ice.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That is all from me for today, but I will leave you once more with a poll. Now that you learned about amorphous ices: HDA and LDA, what do you think you are seeing in the small video I posted this morning?

tweets.text: I thought I would talk to you a little bit about how COVID 19 has affected my research. At least in terms of the practicalities of it. I do not want to focus on the "doom and gloom", not take seriousness out of it, but because there is a lot of bad stuff to read in the news.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Of course, it has affected me mentally, yes even if I have been in "lockdown-free" Sweden. I am not one to be able to carry on when the whole planet is in pain, and especially when far away from my family and friends.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But focusing only on this, only makes things harder, plus, I am sure that lots of you know how hard it has been, and still is.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The main way in which COVID 19 has affected my research are beamtimes! Yes, they have been limited now because of the type of work I do. I know people have not been able to access their labs in many places, but here, sometimes I wish I would do more lab-based stuff...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Some of the X-ray facilities have closed for different periods of time. And when reopening, they have several restrictions, on top of the traveling restrictions from that country. This makes it hard for us....

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are some groups and teams that have been able to pursue their experiments, sometimes because they are within the same country so things like quarantine are not needed, or their experiments can and have been adapted for "online" or "distance" beamtimes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Some experiments might be more routine-like and are already customarily done remotely, by sending the samples in, but others have required a vast effort from both the facilities and the user's to perform the experiment!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But some of us have setups and samples that cannot be adapted to this kind of beamtimes. Our setups are custom-made, our samples need to be AT ALL TIMES under liquid nitrogen, and are awfully fragile! So, unfortunately, we are only able to have beamtimes if travelling is possible

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Of course, flying to Germany is indeed feasible, but how affordable is it to stay in isolation for two full weeks, plus the week of the experiment? Not that much, especially if we are talking of a team of at least 4 people.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We still managed to have a beamtime last year @desynews !!! :D This was end of August, when cases had dropped across Europe. Part of the team drove up there, and we were limited to four people total, max two at a time, and mask-wearing was, of course, a must.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All of these facilities, just like everything else, has had to adapt. First delaying beamtimes, in the hopes of a soon resolution, but now a complete rescheduling of beamtimes as we do not know for how long COVID-19 is here to stay.

tweets.text: Between the long computer hours because of grant proposal writing, and this week's quarantine, I've developed a lovely back/sciatica pain. I'm no stranger to back pain, as I've had lower back problems since I was 15... #backpain

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And this pain makes sense, bad posture, non-ergonomic chairs, at my place I've no desk, and then there's the lack of movement. Of course having made a short exercise program would've made sense, but my mind was elsewhere engaged. Which means that better planning is due next time!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This (and ofc the covid scare) has actually made me reflect on, of course, health, how precious it is... Last year, as COVID started, COVID was not my only health concern, the previous November I had tripped on the stairs and hit my knee. Not broken, just damaged the nerves.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I was given anti-inflammatories, asked to not walk (yay for a month in bed...) things got better, but then I flew from Mexico to Sweden and all my efforts went down the drain... In the end, after some physiotherapy, I can walk more than 10 min now without pain or my knee swelling

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But it's still incredibly weak. I'm trying to strengthen it, but it's not easy. Also, there's stuff that still isn't right, if I sit or stand for long periods of time, it still gets funny. So yeah, seems the damage is here to stay. #kneeproblems

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But as aware as I was always tried to be for other people's predicaments, it's never the same as actually living through them. The fact that I could not dance, run, or even walk for long periods of time as I used, to took a big tall on my mental health. I lost motivation.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Then, why not, came COVID and everything it has brought to us. I can honestly say I was struggling a lot, I was especially worried about my family. Also, after only a year in Stockholm, I didn't quite have a strong support network, my close friends are scattered across the globe.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But somehow, I ploughed through it, and it's brought me closer to the few friends that I had managed to make in that year. Also, one eventually learns how to live in this madness, although it's not smooth sailing all the time ofc.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I must say there was one cool thing amongst all the bad stuff with my knee! For the airport, as I had a very short connection in Amsterdam, I requested help. This was seriously awesome....

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To get me off the plane, they have this amazing lift-cars, so basically it looks like a regular van but it has this supports to lift it up to the airplane door. So they basically put me on the wheelchair, pushed me inside the van thing, and down we went. It was great fun!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Once at the airport, I also met a lovely man who pushed me in my chair around the airport. He told me he used to have a shop, but he felt he was fooling people by selling for a higher price than to what he bought the goods for.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So he closed it down and got the job he now had @Schiphol Airport. And he said he loved it, because he was helping others, and he also got to meet people from around the world. And that for him was more important. Sadly, I did not get his name. But he was inspiring.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I guess what I learned from him, from what we've all been through is that there's no time like the present. Make a priority of that or who is most important to you, and if you're sacrificing something to achieve a goal, make sure that it's worth it.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But most importantly, be kind to others. We're all going through hard times, and there's no need to make it harder. #kindness

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Here in Zurich with @NorrisOMEL I work on semiconductor nanocrystals. 

Because they're so small, these nanometer-sized crystals have properties that are dependent on their size and shape.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The most well known manifestation of this is that larger particles absorb/emit longer wavelength light.

In this picture by Stefan Meyer, all these vials are filled with the same material, CdSe nanocrystals, but with different shapes sizes giving them different colors. https://t.co/qljtx7HNx5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Working with my PI David is a great because he's knows so much about nanocrystals. In fact, he's literally been studying them since before I was born!

For example this project he worked on in the 90s really made controlled nanocrystal synthesis possible:

https://t.co/V2ghUTIHgc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Specifically I work on magic-sized nanocrystals. These grow via discrete jumps in size, rather than the continuous growth seen in conventional nanocrystals https://t.co/juKKrqqDZn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I actually first heard about these magic-sized nanocrystals when I was a grad student in Columbia. @brandicossairt and @theowenlab did a lot of great work in this field some years back.

https://t.co/DZSoP3R74m

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of the big issues with nanocrystal synthesis is a distribution of particle sizes. The stepwise growth of magic-sized nanocrystals could help us get around this, giving us batches of nanocrystals with more uniform sizes and properties

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Sergio and @AniketMule93 recently showed that magic-sized nanocrystals are tetrahedra that grow layer-by-layer. Only perfect tetrahedra exist since they're local energy minima. And this is the reason for the stepwise growth we see.

https://t.co/PhXuUl3ehL

tweets.text:
Hello again :)
I am gonna start now with what I currently do ;)
As I said I am an instrument scientist @RESEDA_MLZ, but what does that actually mean?

@RESEDA_MLZ is one of many neutron scattering instruments at the @mlz_garching near Munich in Germany. https://t.co/qGAoY0gGeW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We are all getting our #neutrons from the FRM2, a research reactor that produces more than 1E14 neutrons per cm² per second through the nuclear fission of uranium. 

Here’s a picture of the FRM2 next to its predecessor the “Atom Egg”, now a landmark (Foto: W. Schürmann) https://t.co/UFZSx21LC2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These #neutrons are used by around 30 different instruments doing groundbreaking research in many, MANY different fields of science. This week I will focus on magnetic phenomena, but if you are interested in what else neutrons can be used for you should follow @mlz_garching...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
...and check out our webpage. From battery research to biological systems, neutrons are a unique tool to explore different materials! 
(Three Instruments even have their own twitter account: @RESEDA_MLZ, @PandaMlz, @ErwiN_at_MLZ)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As an instrument scientist, I am responsible for one of the instruments @mlz_garching. In my case @RESEDA_MLZ. Firstly this means I need to make sure everything works ;) and since we are a user facility (scientists can write proposals and apply for beam time ...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ... at any of our instruments) I am also responsible to help the visiting scientists with their experiments. And of course I get to do my own experiments as well (as you can see in this picture) https://t.co/RHfcbl3JDt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, I hope you all had a good day, and are still up for some tweet sized bits of information about #neutron scattering and why neutrons are such a unique probe: https://t.co/zjRJYT7G6L

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Neutrons are NOT charged, but they possess a magnetic spin. This allows them to penetrate deep into matter, and they are sensitive to magnetic phenomena within a sample. https://t.co/qzG4QoMnsN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: On the downside the lack of electric charge makes them very hard to transport, since they can’t be accelerated with an electric field like charged particles...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For a long time neutrons were just flying through the air to pass from the source to instrument. Many neutrons were lost this way. Since the 70ies neutron guides have been in use...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
They consist of nanostructured multilayers and transport neutrons of a certain wavelength range. Mostly they are made of Fe/Si or Ni/Ti.
And this is what it looks like if you look through one: (Foto: @MCQST_cluster, Jan Greune) https://t.co/f7rMNgtrPX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One big advantage of neutrons is that in contrast to X-rays, the scattering cross-section of neutrons with the different elements does NOT scale with atomic number: https://t.co/c8NTN3iKam

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Therefore, neutrons are much better at distinguishing elements that are next to each other in the periodic table. It is even possible to distinguish different isotopes (Image: https://t.co/8nOAqdyTMq)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
@gns6w3 Indeed! It is crazy how well you can distinguish those with #neutrons and what possibilities this offers for soft matter research. 
Although for me personally as a hard condensed matter gal (and having had a pretty bad experience with a wrongly labelled target box)....

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @gns6w3 ... the most amazing part is that you can distinguish Fe and Co so well :D

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Before starting with more #neutron scattering today, I wanna promote this nice Heraeus Seminar my colleagues are organizing! 
You will learn all there is to know about #magnetic SANS, plus there will be a lecture on MIEZE-SANS by yours truly @jkj_2309. 
Application is still open! https://t.co/HRzhnN5Tv4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Let’s dive a bit further into #neutron scattering. 
First a disclaimer: I am by far not an expert in all neutron scattering techniques, but I for sure can point you towards at least one for each of them if you want more information 😉

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So, I will give you a brief overview of the different techniques, before diving into my field of expertise, the MIEZE technique, pretty fascinating a #neutron spin-echo technique
(fun fact: MIEZE is basically German for kitty, which is why I got these nice ears in our hutch) https://t.co/jU4th4KahE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Let’s start with #neutron diffraction:
Many of the (#nano) scientists here will be familiar with X-ray diffraction. Neutron diffraction is based on the same principles. A particle hits our sample, and we can observe a diffraction pattern. https://t.co/6d39vQ9MgA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For this we need to remember that the neutron can not just be described as a particle, but also as a wave. https://t.co/WhFLGWOWEr

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
From the diffraction pattern we can discern the crystal structure of our sample.
#neutron vs. #Xray scattering?
Due to their magnetic spin, neutrons can see underlying magnetic structures, so the diffraction pattern shows structural AND magnetic peaks. HOWEVER…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (since my background is nano science I am always a bit sad about the fact that the possibilities for #neutron scattering on nano structures is limited. There are of course neutron techniques for thin films, but we will get to that later)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I went to the FRM2 today, because a colleague told me he could show me a very special view of the triple axes spectrometer @PandaMlz. I am gonna share this with you:
You can see here one of the monochromators of PANDA where #neutrons of a very specific energy are selected. https://t.co/DrmCUh8cO6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
From this point, the neutrons fly towards the sample, which is where I am looking from.
The 3 axes spectrometer gets its name from its 3 axes that can be moved completely independent from each other.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
(In comparison, a #neutron diffraction instrument could also be called a 2 axes instrument). 
With a 3 axes spectrometer it is possible to measure excitations in a material with extreme accuracy .For example the energy dispersion of phonons, spin waves or any other excitation

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The order in which I wanted to go through the different #neutron scattering instruments got a bit jumbled up yesterday when I got to see all the way inside @PandaMlz. But, I still think that was pretty cool, and I had to share it :)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And I just remembered that I did a crazy detailed sketch of @PandaMlz for the colleague who showed me this awesomeness, so, I am gonna share that now: https://t.co/0x3y0jtkf2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Next up is a spectroscopic method that is nicely complementary to 3 axis spectroscopy, #neutron Time-of-Flight (mostly referred to as ToF) spectroscopy. While for 3 axis spectroscopy the incoming neutron energy gets selected and scanned carefully to map out an excitation…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: in ToF #neutrons of many different energies hit the sample. To gain information about the energy of the incoming and detected #neutron, their flight times are measured. ToF instruments usually have HUGE detector tanks to catch #neutrons in as large a solid angle as possible.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, simplifying a lot, one could say that with a ToF instrument, you can cover excitations in a very large range of phase space, so it is amazing to get an overview of what is happening in your material…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: With a 3 axes instrument on the other hand you can map out specific excitations in amazing detail. (Yes this is simplifying it a lot, but to really do these techniques justice would require a lecture of several hours for each of them, as you might guess from the sketch 😉)

tweets.label: Takeover

Before diving into detail about @RESEDA_MLZ, which uses another #neutron spectroscopic method, I want to still mention some other cool #neutron scattering techniques. 
Going back to #neutron diffraction…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There is a #neutron diffraction setup specialized for structures that are between a few and a few thousand Angstroms “large” → the Small Angle Neutron Scattering Setup or SANS for short.
SANS instruments are great at measuring the long range order of magnetic phenomena…

tweets.label: Takeover

… as well as biological systems, polymers etc. 
Fun Fact: SANS machines are really long, and look a bit like Submarines, like for example the one @BNCHungary, which is even called “Yellow Submarine” (Image: https://t.co/cWDYzNAiM8) https://t.co/2JSb6FDvpD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Next up: #neutrons for #nanostructures ;)
(Polarized) #neutron reflectometry, is the technique to study your thin film/superlattice/multilayer system. It provides information on structure and magnetism as a function of depth.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We actually measured a Co/CoO layer that was merely 3.5nm thick, as you can see in the sketch and beautiful #AFM image ;) 
(https://t.co/SSnnydH5Pm) https://t.co/nG4Nr4jdCg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I am gonna finish the round of #neutron scattering techniques with neutron imaging, which is a great way to look inside a thing, without destroying it.
I attached a tweet with a super cool image comparing neutron and x-ray imaging on a camera...

tweets.label: Takeover

and how awesomely they complement each other:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So, are you ready to learn more about spin-echo (SE) techniques and eventually @RESEDA_MLZ?
Firstly, SE techniques use the fact that a spin in a magnetic field starts to precess like a spinning top… https://t.co/iyl3768J62

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now, if we have a very well defined magnetic field region (we know the length and field strength very well), and we know the speed/wavelength of our neutron (which we can ;) ) we can calculate how often the spin precesses. https://t.co/5hS18YtqNh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In a magnetic field that has the same length, and field strength but opposite sign, the spin would precess all the way back, like winding and then unwinding a watch.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So if we take two such magnetic fields, put a sample in between and a detector at the end, we can actually measure the dynamic properties of materials (yes I am simplifying here a bit as well 😉) https://t.co/TAq6DsZuGc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This technique is excellent to measure the dynamics of soft matter samples. However, it gets tricky if you want to measure anything magnetic. Because a magnetic field at the sample position would depolarize our neutron beam (mess with the “precession pattern”)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There is a SE technique that is optimized for anything magnetic, which is called MIEZE, and is the technique we used the most @RESEDA_MLZ. As you can see in the figure, RESEDA has two “arms”, so we can do spin-echo AND MIEZE. (Foto: Jan Greune @MCQST_cluster) https://t.co/NgosbiBCDw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: More about MIEZE and RESEDA after lunch 😉 Stay tuned!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
@gns6w3 Thank you! 🙂
For me the trickiest thing is always to know which explanation to go with, since there are so many ways of explaining SE... Classical, Semi-classical, Quantum Mechanical... Their suitability completely depends on the audience 😅

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
@gns6w3 Unfortunately, for MIEZE the classical explanation doesn't quite work anymore, and I am still trying to find the most intuitive way to explain it...
I guess my audience here will serve as somewhat of a test audience 😅

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
@RESEDA_MLZ isn’t a classical SE setup. It is actually a #neutron RESONANT SEsetup. But what’s the difference?

SE measures the (normalized intermediate) Scattering Function as a function of TIME rather than energy, which is what most other spectroscopic neutron instruments do…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The maximum time that can be reached depends on the length and strength of the magnetic field in the main coils. The larger they are the larger the time. Achieving a homogeneous magnetic field with larger and larger coils becomes exceedingly difficult...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So, Golub and Gähler came up with the idea to replace the big coils with resonant spin flippers, which are placed at the position where the edges of the big coil would be, the neutron resonant spin echo (NRSE)
And you know what? The neutron doesn’t really notice the difference… https://t.co/jvf66aGhwD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The downside of this approach is, that the beam size usually has to be a bit smaller and some intensity is lost, which is why there are still more classical #neutron SE instruments, some of which are now using #superconducting coils! (e.g.: J-NSE @mlz_garching, Foto: O. Holderer) https://t.co/QWTmMykXOp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Let’s go to another advantage of NRSE:
Imagine the neutron precessing in the magnetic field. To actually have it precess nicely (so the beam doesn’t depolarize) you need a minimum field, otherwise all sorts of magnetic field, even the earth magnetic field will disturb the neutron

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: NRSE offers a solution for this: Since there is now more space, since spin flippers are more compact than big solenoids, you can add another coil in between the flippers which can help you access shorter spin-echo times.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now, it will become a bit tricky, since to explain MIEZE I will need a dash of quantum mechanics, but I hope you will bear with me…
Let’s quickly remember, that while we can describe a neutron as a particle, we can also describe it as a wave! https://t.co/FztpdxUK0z

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So instead of imagining a beam of neutrons flying through @RESEDA_MLZ, we can imagine neutron wave packets (yes we are going a bit #quantum here now).
Much like #Schrödinger’s cat can quantum mechanically alive and dead… https://t.co/uFv0L6VmZH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (I know simplifying and trying to make quantum mechanics more intuitive is dangerous I hope all hard core quantum physicists forgive me for this)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The neutron wave packet we are looking at now has up and down spin. The spin flipper however treats up and down differently. The up-spin “part” gets faster while the down-spin “part” gets slower with respect to each other.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is compensated at the second spin flipper. The trick is now however, to OVERCOMPENSATE. So the two parts of the wave package still need some time to catch up to each other, and at the point in space where they do, we put our detector.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Between the 2nd flipper and the detector we have an analyzer and our sample. The 2 wave packet parts will not arrive at the sample at the same time. So if in the time between their arrival something changes in the sample, we will notice this by a loss of contrast at the detector.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Since this is all a bit difficult to understand (believe me it took me months and many, MANY discussions with my colleagues before I finally understood this), I tried to nicely sum this all up in a #sketchnote https://t.co/cMOX93dudw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Since this was a bit intense, I will stop for now 😉
But later (or tomorrow, let’s see 😄) I will show you what cool science we can do using the MIEZE technique @RESEDA_MLZ

I guess you have all heard about iron, and that it is a ferromagnet. But have you ever wonder what actually happens at the ferromagnetic - to paramagnetic phase transition?

Hi everyone, here's some of our PROTEIN CAGE research.

Here, we show how to re-program #encapsulin protein nanocages into photosensitizing nanoreactors for photodynamic therapy! 

I'll share the highlights below...

https://t.co/se1aoDwyC6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Encapsulins are unique protein cages that self-assemble around #proteins tagged with an encapsulation signal peptide (ESig). We adapted this system to load the photosensitizing protein mini-SOG into the nanocages. Mini-SOG produces reactive oxygen species (ROS) under a blue-light

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Excitingly, we found that these mini-SOG loaded encapsulins were capable of generating significant amounts of ROS when we fired a blue laser beam at them.

...We had made a light-activatable encapsulin nanoreactor that generates ROS "on-demand" https://t.co/XTI5nPAoH5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As a proof-of-concept, we explored the application of this nanoreactor in photodynamic therapy (PDT). In PDT, photosensitizing agents are activated by light to convert the oxygen inside tumor cells into lethal ROS, killing the cell.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We visualised the delivery of the encapsulin nanoreactor into tumour cells. Once inside, the nanoreactor was excited by blue-light and generated ROS, which induced intracellular oxidative stress and lowered tumor cell viability! This suggests our nanoreactor has potential in PDT! https://t.co/JdwXpjhr9X

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Overall, our study showed that encapsulin protein cages can be readily bioengineered and are heaps of fun to play around with! 

We hope our work will encourage everyone to exploit the unique properties of these protein nanocages to create cool innovative #nanotechnologies https://t.co/P5sJuofJFf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Good morning everybody! ☀️ Today it's time to discuss a bit about perovskites and how they behave under pressure 🗜️🤯

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What is #perovskite? It's a class of compounds which have the same type of crystal structure as CaTiO3, known as the perovskite structure. Although the mineral was discovered in the Ural Mountains in 1839, its use in the field of PV, LEDs, scintillators (...) is quite recent

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In particular, the type of perovskite used in these fields is the metal-halide perovskite with formula ABX3 where B is a divalent cation (mainly Pb2+ or Sn2+), X is the halide (I-, Br- or Cl-), and A+ is a monovalent cation that can be either organic or inorganic https://t.co/g69taq5ZHy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The structure I showed before is related to the 3D perovskite but there are also 2D ones used for the same applications. This class is even younger! In simple words, the idea here is that an A+ cation with a long chain (or an aromatic ring) is used as spacer inducing confinement https://t.co/RWqIAcVcs4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now perovskites are very popular and you can also find lead-free perovskite and double perovskites where the Pb2+ is replaced by two cations of different oxidation state (a B+ and a B3+ for example) https://t.co/xBJFJ9oUz6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @ElAbdleb https://t.co/BP5GiqbeLb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As this material is so popular, it is easy to get confused about what is a perovskite from a crystallographic point of view. We tend to call everything derived from the ABX3 structure "perovskite" but it is not always correct: https://t.co/9ZWwJXAzZg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But why are these #perovskites so popular? Their easy fabrication in solution is one of the reason. You just need to mix the precursors in the solvents with no special expensive treatment to obtain your precursor solution. The most common solvents are DMF, DMSO, NMP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What is really amazing of this fabrication is that by changing the ratio of the precursor materials you can also tune the bandgap of your perovskite! For example, if you start to replace part of iodide with a bromide precursors you will obtain higher energy bandgap! https://t.co/pCOUMvzGKa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For the people not in the field, you should know that we like to use A LOT abbreviations. MA is the methylammonium cation and MAPI stands for MAPbI3, the most common perovskite we use

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Speaking of the easy fabrication and easy bandgap tunability, these are very interesting for application where you want to be able to tune the bandgap of the material for example LEDs or tandem solar cells. But not all that glitters is gold...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you have a mixed-halide perovskite in thin films and you apply an external bias or you illuminate the material,  you loose the bandgap due to a process called "phase segregation". Ions in the perovskite are very mobile, and when illuminated they form I- and Br-rich domains https://t.co/hhRq0Qyfci

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is the paper: Hoke et al., Chem. Sci., 2015, 6, 613-617

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Two questions raise now (or maybe more, so please ask in the comments!) : how do we investigate this process? What is the origin of this process? https://t.co/Ovus5x1WQG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
[admin]

Extended conversation with @la_muscarella is out now, give it a listen 👇🎙️🎧
