tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One technique for probing the phase segregation could be a photoluminescence-based technique, very common in many labs but... all the charges funnel into the low-energy iodide-rich domain so we cannot really probe the PL of all the domains https://t.co/h01tA9HwN0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We decided to use a pump-probe technique based on absorption, transient absorption spectroscopy setup. Clearly you can probe the mixed-phase but also the bromide and iodide-rich phase if you repeat the experiment after illuminating the film. https://t.co/zKE0Vwpny5 https://t.co/Xxtv9RkcRz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now that we know what technique to use, let's do a step back to understand what possibly is the origin and how we can validate some theory...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One hypothesis for explaining why after illumination the series of mixed-halide shows a PL at 1.7 eV (= composition of 20% Br- incorporation) was a phase transition from tetragonal to cubic when the %Br is > than 20%. #Inotherwords the cubic structure is unstable...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I worked together with @emhutter1 on this project, it was a great time and fun together! There were also some very frustrating days but we know... it is how science works! We combined a transient absorption setup with a pressure cell to induce external compression in our films https://t.co/hg7hKJnAF1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Challenging? We had to perfectly align 3 beams inside this pressure cell. It looks big but the windows are very small... 3 beams for excitation, probing and inducing the phase segregation via light-soaking. It took a while but I am proud to share the results of all these efforts! https://t.co/GPxPxqxkGT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But okay, you might wonder, why pressure? In the range of pressure we use (0 to 0.3 GPa) there is no phase transition from cubic to tetragonal. So, if phase segregation stops cannot be due to the phase transition to the tetragonal phase

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In addition, bromide and iodide-based perovskites have different compressibility (different bulk modulus) and the Gibbs free energy contains a PDV term we could use to see if pressure has a significant impact on the thermodynamic stability of our material...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is what you get with a 50%Br sample when you illuminate at 0 and 0.3 GPa. At 0 GPa, immediately there is the formation of iodide- and bromide-rich phase (high and low energy), but very different behavior under pressure! More here: https://t.co/uv06kTk44i https://t.co/RmjxOXZxBj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is true also when 70% of bromide is incorporated in the composition. Seems to be a very general effect. Btw, this is what each datapoint in the 2D plot I showed look like. These are the ground state bleach of the mixed, iodide- and bromide-rich domain https://t.co/dyHxPvooIG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we fit all these peaks, this is what we get: the peak energy as a function of real time and pressure. https://t.co/QXereFEVcp https://t.co/HTyLR9db9S

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
First result: the final composition after light-soaking is different as a function of pressure (unit cell volume). The higher the pressure, the closer to the original mixed composition. Terminal x-value determined by volume instead of phase transition!
  https://t.co/0hmoG2tJpd https://t.co/V253au4irA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Under pressure, phase segregation becomes slower. If we derive the relation between the migration rate and the activation energy for the halides using the diffusion coefficient formula, we see that pressure seems to increase the activation energy for these halides to migrate https://t.co/PzBHUzktmf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Before to leave you for today, I have to tell you what we think is going on with pressure and these mixed-halide perovskites 🤔

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When we compress the mixed-halide perovskite we are changing the PDV term in the Gibbs free energy of mixing. This term is usually overlooked for other semiconductors as much more stiff than perovskites. We also change the enthalpic term (due to strain in the material)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The enthalpic term is positive at ambient pressure and quite high because there is a lattice mismatch between the iodide- and the bromide- lattice. Under P, the iodide lattice compresses more (smaller bulk moduli than the bromide one) and the lattice mismatch reduces

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #inotherwords: enthalpy dominates at ambient pressure, entropy dominates at high pressure where the enthalpic term reduces. Read more here: https://t.co/uv06kTk44i https://t.co/ICE2hvLWNb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You might say "Yeah, nice but we cannot put solar cells/LEDs under pressure". True, but we can induce strain to simulate the effect of the external pressure! We reduced the unit cell volume by using Cs+ instead of MA+. Similar results! https://t.co/QXereFEVcp https://t.co/VhVlZAwOIo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These works are just two examples on how fundamental studies can be useful for further optimization of devices. If you are doing fundamental science, it doesn't mean that is not important for applications! Actually, I think the opposite 🔥

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Perovskite solar cells or LEDs cannot be put under pressure in real life, but they behave extremely good when a stress is applied. Next step? Let's transform this external pressure into internal pressure to obtain the same result 🧐

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It's time to sleep here, but tomorrow I will talk a bit about another interesting effect of pressure on perovskites and my experience during the #ErasmusPlus  project. Good night 🌙

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Goodmorning world! ☀️ Yesterday I promised a bit more of perovskites under pressure and here it is..

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another interesting property of these halide perovskites is the extremely slow hot-carrier cooling in comparison with other semiconductors

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When you excite a semiconductor with energy higher than the bandgap of the material you have excess of energy. When carriers move to the band edge to be collected (e.g. in solar cells), this excess of energy is lost... and also almost 35% of the efficiency...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This schematic from T. Gong et al., J. of Photonics for Energy, 6(4), 042510 (2016) can be very useful to visualize the process https://t.co/jzncewbj98

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The timescale of this hot-carrier cooling (HCC) is still quite fast: picoseconds. Carriers cool down through scattering and being able to manipulate the scattering of electrons with phonons can have an impact on the HCC especially for polar semiconductors as perovskites

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We need a technique fast enough to capture the evolution of these hot-carriers. It is high-speed photography. We need to make a ton of picture of our electrons/holes to look at this fast process in detail https://t.co/txirZYR3xC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And once again, I combined this with hydrostatic pressure. Why? Perovskites are polar semiconductors and electronic properties are expected to be strongly coupled with the lattice vibrations. Pressure can have an effect on phonons and therefore on the cooling https://t.co/acO9fd2LeG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The perovskite I studied here is the MAPI - the simplest perovskite with the A+ cation organic

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We follow the tail of the ground state bleach as a function of time and pressure. The broad tail represents the presence of hot-electrons (with high energy). As a function of pressure the decay of the tail becomes faster and so the cooling. More here: https://t.co/He6X1kj1kx https://t.co/IDtvfz75bj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You see here that this effect is present only at a certain excitation density. We chose these two because these represent excitation density below and above the Mott transition (where polarons overlap). Below this threshold, pressure has no effect

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Our collaborator @JarvistFrost calculated the electron-phonon coupling for each phonon mode as a function of pressure. The mode mostly affected by pressure is the one around 1 Thz, the octahedral twist. https://t.co/si1DyjbNhm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We think that when above the Mott transition, polarons overlap and form hotspot where heat is difficult to dissipate. Pressure increases the electron-phonon coupling and therefore offers new pathways to dissipate the excess of energy https://t.co/k5yOtEYHIQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is a fundamental study, how can this be used in real life? HCC is important for many applications. For example, thermoelectric devices require slow HCC, lasers and single-photon sources a fast one. Tuning the HCC allows to optimize the material depending on the application!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At @_amolf we also have a very special system for Electron Backscatter Diffraction (#EBSD). Maybe some of you working in material science know already this technique. It is combined with the SEM and we can construct spatially-resolved maps with structural data. Credits: Ivar Pel https://t.co/g6WCihg5Dl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Why is this special? It is a direct-electron detector meaning that there is no phosphor screen to enhance the signal. By using this, we can work with very low current and exposure time. Perovskites are also very sensitive (really to everything!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is my first work as PhD. I looked at MAPI perovskite and EBSD maps show that "grains" we see in the SEM most of the time are not a real grain but made of many crystallographic grains. Watch out for misleading SEM! More here: https://t.co/6gq2FDDgCn https://t.co/jDv0wR2nhb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I promised to talk about my experience as student in the context of the #Erasmus project. I definitely recommend all the students to apply for this opportunity. It’s not all rainbows and unicorns but it's a great experience everyone should do once in a lifetime

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I found out about this Erasmus opportunity thanks to my Bachelor's thesis advisor (Prof. Ilaria Fratoddi, La Sapienza). She was coordinator of the Erasmus office. Every year she was trying to convince students to apply to do an experience abroad, either for exams or thesis

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I was skeptical, i didn't want to do exams abroad (the ones at my uni were quite tough but the level was very high) but i wanted to see how people were working in Europe. On the other hand, i was just a student and my finances were not that great to live abroad for too long

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My parents were ready to help me (as they were already doing since I decided to live in Rome for my studies) but let's be honest... Some countries in Europe are definitely much more expensive than living in Italy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Positive sides of the Erasmus scholarship is 1) you have a lot of choices. That depends a bit on your university but usually you have quite a lot of options. There are two version of this scholarship, in Europe or in the World

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2) Part of your expenses are covered by the scholarship. Usually, depending on how "rich" is the destination country, you will receive more or less money. For example, Amsterdam is quite expensive and therefore I received more money than who went for example in Spain

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3) you have to prove that you are actually doing what you were supposed to do. #inotherwords you cannot be paid by Erasmus to watch Netflix all day long but you have to show you attended classes, did exams or the internship

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4) you meet a lot of people from different countries, with a different language, cousine culture and so on. You have no idea how much will enrich your soul! Diversity is what makes us better!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5) You go out from your "comfort zone". We are all good in doing what we always do, but there is no better way of learning new things by travelling, meeting people and experiencing a new environment

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 6) Professionally, you create a NETWORK. As scientists, we cannot work alone. We need collaboration to develop new concepts. Interdisciplinarity is the key of the future. Having a network of different scientists will bring a great benefit to your science and career!

tweets.text: Amsterdam is very cool if you come here with the Erasmus scholarship but it also has one major drawback to be aware of... housing! 🏠 Here, it is quite challenging to find an accomodation as there are many students and prices are not low. I had to change 2 times house in 6 months

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hi everyone! This week I'll be tweeting about my experience as a scientist. But since my trajectory is not the standard, I'll start by talking about how I got to where I am today. https://t.co/fUdrfSqM1Z

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the spring of 2003 I was about to graduate in Condensed Matter Physics at the Complutense University of Madrid @Fisicas_UCM. https://t.co/JWn6KE8Pvb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I was not sure what I wanted to do in the future. I saw then an advert of Nanotec Electronica (#Nanotec), looking for a recent graduate to join its staff. I applied and after a couple of interviews I got the position 🥳🥳

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #Nanotec was a company devoted to the design, development and commercialization of scanning probe microscopes #SPM, mainly atomic force microscopes #AFM, so working for #Nanotec as an application scientist allowed me to have direct interaction with both industry and research https://t.co/r8A2krIggP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #Nanotec was a small company, spin off from the Autonomous University of Madrid @UAM_Madrid. It combined very talented people with different backgrounds (physicists, software and electronic engineers, chemists, technicians...) https://t.co/aVAqcfrcGG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At this time, I learnt a lot about #AFM, developing the technique and collaborating with researchers worldwide on different projects, which was great as it allowed me to see many of the things that can be done with an #AFM. https://t.co/yggsJa3Kz2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Basically, an #AFM uses a very tiny tip to "see" surfaces with nanometric resolution (later this week I'll talk more about how an #AFM works). For example, it can be used to study 0D materials such as nanoparticles or viruses https://t.co/wtAUsIu21O

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And one of the best things is that the tip can be used also to modify and manipulate the samples, as for example indenting a virus to study its mechanical properties https://t.co/pF5JjvC9DM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can also study 1D materials, such as carbon nanotubes, DNA or viral fibers, to name a few https://t.co/drTWuH75H5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2D materials, like the nowadays ubiquitous wonder material #graphene https://t.co/u59zDasi1d

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Or 3D nanostructures such as cells, lithography features or different patterns on thin films https://t.co/M9A3D64Jvd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But as I told you, one of the best (and funniest) things of an #AFM is its ability to modify/manipulate things. Here is another example, making nanometric drawings, in this case by local oxidation of a silicon substrate https://t.co/d1TGPbcSIS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As #Nanotec was a small company, I had to do many different things, such as designing new parts for the microscopes, testing new developments, writing manuals, technical support, trainings and installations, attending conferences, demos for potential customers... https://t.co/7hSqPOjiCB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of the things we did was to check that all our microscopes were able to "see" atoms, making sure the stability and noise levels were optimum https://t.co/24ZHsTBbpF

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today I will try to show some of the basics of Scanning Probe Microscopy #SPM, and in particular, Atomic Force Microscopy #AFM. An easy way to understand how it works is to think on how the blind use their canes to follow the height changes in the floor. https://t.co/mBV25M3HJ0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Scanning Probe Microscopy #SPM is the general name of the family of microscopes that use a very sharp tip to detect an interaction with the surface. If this interaction decays very fast with tip-sample distance, then it will allow very small height changes to be detected.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The first #SPM was the Scanning Tunneling Microscope #STM. It takes advantage of the quantum tunneling effect. If a metal tip is at atomic distances(!!) of a metallic or semiconducting surface, a tunneling current that depends exponentially with the tip-sample distance can appear https://t.co/lXv0bEQHoo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The first #STM out of the IBM labs in Zurich @IBM was brought to the Autonoums University of Madrid @UAM_Madrid, being the origin of the #SPM tradition at UAM in particular, and in Spain in general. https://t.co/xIZNW44jQg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After the #STM, the #AFM (or SFM, from Scanning Force Microscopy) was developed. In this case, forces between tip and sample are detected. This allows to study any kind of sample, not only conductors or semiconductors, giving it a lot of versatility. https://t.co/ngQWGOByny

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are other #SPMs that can also detect light, and thanks to having the tip so close to the sample, they can overcome the diffraction limit. https://t.co/yEWZpRQQVd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Some of main components of an #AFM are the tip, the scanner, the control unit and the software. https://t.co/FL9ZrEya0R

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Most of the #AFM tips come at the end of a cantilever beam integrated into a carrier chip. They are consumables and depending of the shape, size and material of the cantilever, we will have access to different ranges of forces and properties. https://t.co/Lp69dfpPD6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To detect the force between tip and sample, the deflection of the cantilever is detected. The most usual method for this is known as beam deflection: a laser is focused at the end of the cantilever and its reflection is monitored in a photodiode (gif from the University of Basel) https://t.co/P49VKl0WJR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Using a 4-cuadrant photodiode allows obtaining both the vertical deflection: Normal force, and the torsion of the cantilever: Lateral force, which is related to the friction. https://t.co/bv3uqXZEx3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Typical scanners in #AFMs are made of piezoelectric materials. These expand/contract when a voltage is applied to them, allowing atomic displacements in a very controlled way. They are used to scan the tip or sample and to move it up/down following the surface topography. https://t.co/HTiiDbKcYK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The control unit and the software drive the signals from/to the #AFM head, allowing the implementation of different measuring modes and custom experiments.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #AFMs spatial range typically is 0.1 nm-100 microns, and can detect forces between 10 pN and 10 microN, making #AFMs ideal tools for the nanoscale. https://t.co/0tyKe7vLFp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In #AFM, there are different interactions between the tip and the sample. This allows getting a lot of extra information apart from just topography. https://t.co/dI8upDS67J

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This also enables multiple #AFM modes depending on the information you get. Sometimes the nomenclature can be overwhelming 🥴, but in the end all are #AFM 😅. But almost all of them are based on 3 basic modes: Contact, Dynamic (sometimes known as Tapping) and Force-distance based https://t.co/aKBoypTlOZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In Contact mode the tip is touching the surface. This allows for example to obtain friction information. https://t.co/eEM7Z2TxuS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In Dynamic modes, the cantilever oscillates at or near its resonant frequency, either without touching the sample (non-contact) or with intermittent contact (depending on the oscillation settings). The Phase shift of the oscillation can map variations in surface properties. https://t.co/myviZ2jP2p

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In Force-distance based modes, at each pixel of the image the tip is approaching/withdrawing from the surface (literally "jumping" from one point to another). This allows very precise control of the applied load and allows for adhesion and stiffness mapping. https://t.co/isNy1uHhye

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #AFM also allows spectroscopic modes. The most basic spectroscopy is Force vs. distance plots, recording the force change with the tip-sample distance. From these plots a lot of information of the tip-sample interaction and properties of the surface can be gained. https://t.co/a6iy18VH2j

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A clear utility of these curves is, for example, the study of protein folding, by pulling the bound proteins between an #AFM tip and a surface to understand their mechanical properties and interactions. https://t.co/07g8mRkVv5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Other #AFM modes allow for different characterization of samples. For example, in Conductive AFM #CAFM a conductive tip is used as a second mobile electrode to study transport properties on the nanoscale. https://t.co/eMgIOCuZWl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Or in Magnetic Force Microscopy #MFM, where a magnetic tip is used to probe nanoscale magnetic domains. As the magnetic interaction has a relative long range, by lifting the tip a few nm over the surface it can detect the magnetic interactions. https://t.co/R5AuyTAC6a

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
As I told you, there are plenty of different modes, so I will not go through all of them. 

Then, we also have the lithographic modes, where the tip is used to draw/modifiy/manipulate the samples. There are plenty of modes as well, I will mention now some of the most popular:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Among the most widespread we can find local oxidation, where the tip is used to carry out a local chemical reaction on the surface. https://t.co/jGcTh3wHMQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Dip-pen nanolithography, where the tip is used as a "pen" to draw with a controlled release of molecules as "ink". https://t.co/6JPE6aATVR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Thermal scanning probe lithography t-SPL, where a special tip that can be heated is used for nano-patterning. https://t.co/Rgkvn0Ev6p

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Nanomanipulation, to move nanoparticles, nanotubes, nanowires... In this case we can see the tip as a "finger" that can manipulate nano-objects at will. https://t.co/tOePviIuHq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All the capablities already mentioned together with the possibility of working under different environments make #AFM an extremely versatile tool. https://t.co/2cGMxwBVtw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Being able to work in liquids, its application for biological research is gaining more and more importance. Even more so with the latest generation of AFMs, which can work at high speed, allowing the visualisation of biological processes. See for example https://t.co/QvP0bF8XiK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It can also operate in ultra-high vacuum #UHV conditions at cryogenic temperatures. Under these conditions, a CO molecule can be attached to the tip end, allowing experiments with unprecedented resolution. https://t.co/FMACqYnA0S

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Despite celebrating its 35th anniversary this year, #AFM is still an evolving technique in which a new breakthrough is made every few years. What will be the next...? https://t.co/kaonLH6fnK

tweets.text: Today I will continue to talk about some of my work, focusing on 0D and 1D materials studied with #AFM. https://t.co/qEj9bq3R7M

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'll start with the development of Magnetic Force Microscopy #MFM in liquids, together with @JrcMiriam and @aasenjobar, allowing #MFM to study nano-bio-magnetic samples in their natural environment, hampered by how an #AFM works in liquid. Details here 👉🏼 https://t.co/giUz3oPlW1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: First of all, just an idea on how the magnetic contrast appears in #MFM images. Depending on the orientation of the magnetic domains (out of plane, in plane or combinations), we will detect bright and dark contrast regions, as depicted here 👇🏼 https://t.co/k2NEu3FYsJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The #MFM contrast is typically obtained in a Dynamic mode, in the Phase shift (or the Frequency shift) signal at a given lift distance. But a cantilever oscillating in liquid is subjected to much more drag than in air (or vacuum), worsening the signal. https://t.co/4FvVhM8fBX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We optimized the measuring mode and acquisition conditions to be able to detect similar #MFM constrasts in air and in liquid. We first used a calibration sample, such as a piece of a hard disk drive, visualizing its magnetic bits. https://t.co/dieffYyVlg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We observed that in liquids we could get the #MFM contrast oscillating the tip closer to the sample, allowing similar contrasts but noisier data, due to intrinsic limitations on the characteristics of the commercial #MFM probes, which are designed for measurements in air. https://t.co/Qqhj8HFDIz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Then we studied the magnetic contrast of 0D magnetic nanoparticles, such as those studied for hyperthermia cancer treatments, in buffer conditions somehow similar as to when injected into a human body. https://t.co/Y7M7eYJnNn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: With such a demanding sample we were able to again obtain similar #MFM contrasts as in air, although not so good due to these intrinsic limitations on the probes. https://t.co/QODVuHY867

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That is why, in collaboration with @deteresa5 group, we developed a method to fabricate magnetic tips on cantilevers designed for liquid measurements. Here all the details 👉🏼 https://t.co/pKYyrhU93i https://t.co/aagUUFbQ4m

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We again tested these tips with a calibration hard disk drive, obtaining now results in liquid as good as in air. And moreover these tips are less invasive for the samples. In conclusion, the #MFM in liquids is now ready for the most demanding samples. https://t.co/UIGDJx00LV

tweets.text: I will go on with another development, a setup for simultaneous high resolution #AFM and Total Internal Reflection Fluorescence #TIRF microscopy, really useful for studies at the single molecule level of viruses. This work was carried out in collaboration with Dr. P.J. de Pablo. https://t.co/tkkszncGiJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In a #TIRF microscope the light is driven at the total internal reflection angle, and therefore only an evanescent wave reaches the sample, observing fluorescence mostly just from the nano-objects attached to the coverslip. https://t.co/8bRe1Sq0TU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The development of a simultaneous #AFM - #TIRF suitable for high resolution studies presents some challenges. Luckily, @alvrooe, who got his PhD with P.J. de Pablo and also worked with Dr. I. Schaap, had experience on it. https://t.co/93IQrIarp6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We designed a setup minimizing the mechanical loop of the system to reduce as much as possible instabilities, and used @WSXM_official to control our microscope, taking advantage of all its capabilities. We first tested it in ambient conditions, ensuring its high stability. https://t.co/RoJ9g7V2sx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We then tested it in buffer conditions, studying P22 viral particles, being able to visualize them and resolve different adsorption geometries and the capsomers forming the capsid. https://t.co/uXZvwfp8ZO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To test the combination of #AFM and #TIRF, we used commercial fluorescent polymer beads. We first simultaneously visualized them both with #AFM and #TIRF https://t.co/jVdvRVJpFW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And then we carried out a nanomanipulation experiment, removing on of the beads with the #AFM tip while we monitored it with the #TIRF https://t.co/ePeeehnDsA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This system is now operative at the @fmcatuam and @ifimacuam for a hot topic such as the study of viruses. A setup based on this one is also under construction at @UoMPhysics, as a multiplatform for simultaneous #AFM and optical studies.

I'll move forward now to some examples of 1D nanostructures studied with #AFM. 
The first case is the high resolution visualization of double standed RNA #dsRNA in buffer conditions using different #AFM acquisition modes. Work in collaboration with @FMorenoHerrero. https://t.co/agtZdm7FHy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The details can be found in these two publications: https://t.co/lvZKIf4LfY
 https://t.co/8wO6vKx5Vf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #dsRNA plays an increasing list of roles: genetic material of a number of viruses, a key activator of the immune response against viral infections, and mediates the suppression of specific gene expression. All this raised interest to study its mechanical properties and structure.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #dsDNA had been extensively observed at high resolution with #AFM, but similar studies were lacking in #dsRNA. This was very likely because of the higher complexity of imaging the #dsRNA structure. https://t.co/D8CD2ew1RE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We first used #dsDNA as a molecular standard to adjust the conditions for high resolution imaging of nucleic acids in liquid. Then we imaged for the first time #dsRNA with a lateral resolution sufficient to resolve its helical periodicity with different #AFM acquisition modes. https://t.co/bbHf8aGZ8e

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Finally, we simulated how the molecules would look like from their crystal structures with different tip radii R, finding that R<~2.5 nm allowed for both major and minor grooves visualization, while ~2.5 nm<R<~5.5 nm led to images where only a single periodicity was detected. https://t.co/LKeJF0oFeG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This work pointed out two critical aspects for high resolution of nucleic acids in liquid: 1- The interacting force, minimized fine-tuning each imaging mode parameter. 2- The sharpness of the tip, likely arising from a protrusion or a small feature at the apex of the tip.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I will now leave liquids aside and move on to another 1D system. In this case I will show you our results on the conductive properties of metal-organic fibres at the single-molecule level. This was the first of multiple fruitful collaborations with @fzamora0 https://t.co/cKWEoCcdl7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The details of the work can be found here 👉🏼 https://t.co/5PFvaksVpa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: MMX metal-organic polymers are quasi-1D sequences of single halide atoms X bridging subunits with two metal ions MM connected by organic ligands. They are excellent conductors in bulk and as nanoribbons, but theoretical calculations predict even higher conductances than reported. https://t.co/CMtITMUoZ5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In this work we were able to produce individual chains of the above MMX polymer by a simple drop-casting procedure. By optical inspection we located the thicker fibres, and then with #AFM we could locate chains down to 1-2 nm height, compatible with just 1-2 MMX molecules. https://t.co/wBcioqwrzW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Next, we evaporated a sharp-edged electrode and observed it for molecules protruding. On these, with a metal-coated tip, we performed conductive #AFM, with the tip as a second mobile electrode. We were able to obtain resistance vs. lentgh plots down to the single-molecule level. https://t.co/DS8cs9bBV5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We found significative currents for a single-molecule experiment, even at distances beyond 250 nm, surpassing that of all other molecular wires reported so far!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, the resistance was still much higher than predicted by calculations. Its exponential dependence with the distance pointed to Anderson localization caused by the interaction of electrons with structural defects.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To verify this, we did theoretical simulations at different levels, mimicking possible defects. We observed that iodine vacancies are the ones that reduce electron transmission the most, and that only 6-8% of vacancies would be responsible for the observed exponential behaviour. https://t.co/R9aEZog7Ht

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This work puts into perspective the role of defects in electrical transport at the single-molecule level. And that, despite the influence of defects on electrical conductance, coordination polymers are one of the best choices for long-distance molecular wires.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @inaquantumdot These were done by our colleagues J.J Palacios and J. Soler. They basically first simulate the defects with Density Functional Theory (DFT), obtaining the electron transmission for each type.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @inaquantumdot Then, for the vacancy, they carried out quantum transport calculations using a single-orbital tight-binding model, with parameters fitted to reproduce the single-defect transmission.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To finish with 1D systems, I will show our work on the fabrication of nanoelectrodes by #AFM nanomanipulation and cold welding of gold nanowires, one of the funniest works I have done, also in collaboration with @fzamora. You can find the details here 👉🏼  https://t.co/bKv7XzNOXu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In our experiments studying electrical transport on the nanoscale, we found that conventional micro- and nanoelectrode fabrication presents some limitations: high temperatures while metal depositions, use of resins, chemical agents or static electrodes (non-reconfigurable)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We needed to overcome those limitations. We got to know about the work by Lu et al., Nat. Nanotechnol. 5, 218-224, 2010, where they used Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) to visualize the cold welding of gold nanowires #AuNWs, just by mechanical contact! https://t.co/89ol8m4Mtm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is due to their high surface-to-volume ratio, similar to two water droplets merging into one when they touch. https://t.co/IWUNTowdPA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So we deposited #AuNWs on a substrate and using an #AFM tip successfully manipulated and cold welded them. https://t.co/weUuxG2PrG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We then fabricated devices following this procedure 👇🏼 https://t.co/oLD5s0dSlG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This way we obtained clean and reconfigurable nanoelectrodes, without the need of high temperatures, resins or chemical agents, that we could assembly into different configurations. https://t.co/fWbBlr0wP6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We first tested few-layer graphene, as it is a very well-studied material, with a single #AuNWs electrode + a metal #AFM tip as a second mobile electrode. We found electrical characteristics similar as using standard fabrication, but overcoming their abovementioned limitations. https://t.co/2VslGRGoqt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We wanted to check the quality of our #AuNWs electrodes, so we fabricated one close to 150 microns long, with almost 100 NWs. We found that its conductivity was almost that of bulk gold, with just a single grain boundary in each NW junction (BTW we contacted several 2D flakes 😅) https://t.co/hsxURwlDri

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To test our nanoelectrodes we carried out multiple experiments in different configurations. Here my colleague M. Moreno-Moreno did an awesome job. For example, we fabricated another device on a few-laer graphene flake, but in this case in a more standard 4-terminal configuration. https://t.co/2DvJFjRuzO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We also wanted to push the limits of the technique, so we proceeded to make a device connecting a ~10 nm gold nanoparticle, something quite difficult without very expensive dedicated nanofabrication setups. https://t.co/tQ2mxyMLn8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Finally, we also explored its potential for molecular electronics. To this end, we approached two #AuNWs avoiding contact, and then coated them with 1,4-benzenedithiol molecules, measuring stable currents through the molecules for hours at room temperature, with great stability. https://t.co/7yfpWGrkHY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I think this is only the tip of the iceberg. #AFM is a very common tool, present in many labs and easily available, so this technique has the potential to provide a new and accessible platform for nanocircuitry fabrication, opening the door to a plethora of new experiments. https://t.co/800X3on7LZ

tweets.text: Today and tomorrow I will continue to tweet about some of my work, focusing now on AFM studies of 2D materials. https://t.co/xVM8ZujUez

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I will start with a work on #graphene, where we tune its properties by applying ultrahigh pressures with a diamond 💎 #AFM tip. Details on this work can be found here 👉🏼 https://t.co/LXizWFTdBg https://t.co/UGZH2Wpdx6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: An #AFM with a diamond tip can be seen as a nanotechnology version of a diamond anvil cell, the standard instrument for ultrahigh pressure experiments. https://t.co/ncDlIRMWcy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Since the Pressure is Force/Area, and the #AFM tips have nm-sized radii, with moderate forces we can apply ultrahigh pressures in a simple way. https://t.co/5mQSa6fB3K

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When we were thinking about which material to try to squeeze hard with the tip of the #AFM, immediatly #graphene came to our minds. https://t.co/SO0SOYPppC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We used mechanically exfoliated high quality monolayer #graphene crystals. https://t.co/hECHKnv75w

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We first imaged the flake in a Dynamic mode. Then we brought the tip into contact with a Pressure setpoint value and scanned under these conditions in a given area. After this, we brought the tip back to Dyanmic mode to visualize the modifications. https://t.co/M07dFyIRrJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: By controlling the Pressure setpoint we observed that we could control #graphene coupling with the underlying SiO2 substrate. https://t.co/UPO0uQcRXA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As the doping level is known to depend on this degree of coupling, we were expecting to control the doping level locally on these areas, which we confirmed by Raman spectrosocopy https://t.co/G9l9Hnzigm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And also by Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy, #KPFM, an advanced electrical #AFM mode that allows to measure surface potential differences. https://t.co/iqlIeusEPu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Therefore, with this ultrahigh pressure modifications, we were able to tune locally the electronic properties of #graphene. https://t.co/MHsAQJODQw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To understand the origin of this doping, we carried out some theoretical simulations, that pointed out that some of the carbon atoms of #graphene could be bonding to the substrate, even if very few, being responsible for the observed charge transfer. https://t.co/hl0Tp88LEV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We took some samples to the Elettra Synchrotron in Trieste, to a beamline allowing imaging spectromicroscopy and microspot spectroscopic modes. The spectra showed an extra component in the carbon peak, compatible with some carbon atoms of #graphene bonding to the substrate. https://t.co/UQrZxJMJL8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We studied the electrical resistance of ultrahigh pressure modifed areas using conductive #AFM. These doped areas presented lower resistance, therefore this appraoch could be used to improve metal contacts in #graphene devices, leading for example to less power comsuption. https://t.co/sgxbONUbfX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I will continue with ultrahigh pressure experiments on #graphene. Since we could improve the coupling to the substrate, we decided to apply it to better seal blisters consisting on #graphene over microcavities, a standard setup for nanomechanical devices and membrane applications https://t.co/mIl5kjRUGm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Some of the people involved in this work include @yolicomoelrio, @JrcMiriam, and the details are here: https://t.co/kxLwg6IBoN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the group there was a lot of experience studying #graphene mechanical properties upon #AFM nanoindentations with these blisters, also at different pressures, having an #AFM in a variable pressure chamber from high vacuum to several bar. So we could inflate/deflate the blisters https://t.co/M94LhXk2Sm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Studying the height evolution with time, we saw the gas inside our blisters typically leaked in a few hours. https://t.co/400J9yshfZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The leakage was faster in a given flake for blisters closer to the flake's edge. With a simple toy model (tha gas leaking through a cilindrical pipe), we could estimate an effective leakage radius, and this was independent of the distance to the edge for a given flake. https://t.co/RAT3iB5XcL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Since the leaks of the blisters can be a drawback for technological applications, we tried to improve them by sealing the blisters applying ultrahigh pressures with the shape of a nanometric wide square rim. https://t.co/kzoTJychqj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In this way, we effectively sealed the blisters, significantly increasing leakage times. Importantly, this demonstrated that most of the gas leakage takes place at the interface between #graphene and the substrate and not by diffusion through the microcavity walls. https://t.co/rOTWhdxn5u

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We observed an improvement of the leakage times and a reduction of the effective leakage radius in all the cases, proving this methodology as a simple way for easy  improvement of devices and membrane applications based on #graphene on SiO2 substrates. https://t.co/LuZEpcXFLw

tweets.text: Many people involved, including @Fernandastico, @alonsoxK93, @SDiazTendero, @fzamora0, @carlosgp92, @__mariavarela, @Gonzalo_Abellan, together with other #notinTweeter authors. Here the links for the two main publications: https://t.co/aU53SRdBGy   https://t.co/h3r1tR4SmE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Back in 2015, there was a great interest (and there is still) in finding 2D materials with electronic gaps between 0.5 and 1.5 eV, suitable for some optoelectronic applications. Thin layers of Black Phosphorus (BP) were isolated, presenting gaps on this range. https://t.co/4CuanfW1c9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But BP is highly hygroscopic, this is, it absorbs water from ambient humidity, degrading and changing completely its properties, needing to work under control environments or to encapsulate it to take advantage of all its potential. https://t.co/ZPGKOt8grD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the same column of the periodic table as phosphorus is antimony, which is also a layered material, although with stronger interactions between the layers. https://t.co/6G25p38Wcj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At that time, there were a lot of theoretical papers predicting very interesting properties for #antimonene and few-layer antimonene, but nobody had isolated it yet. https://t.co/AHVyfZBscg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We were able to isolate it, first using a micromechanical exfoliation approach and later using a liquid phase exfoliation procedure. https://t.co/nWIt6vHlzi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After exfoliation and deposition on a substrate, we inspect it with optical microscopy, finding large thick flakes. But when scanning with the #AFM around these flakes, we usually found smaller thinner ones, with terraces down to ~2 nm, compatible with 2-3 layers. https://t.co/YaYP9FRvjy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We used a battery of techniques to confirm the antimony nature of these flakes, including high resolution #AFM visualizing their atomic lattice. https://t.co/KyEfSn1ZET

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We sometimes found terraces below 1 nm, compatible with single layers (the presence of trapped molecules between flakes and the substrate can induce to observe these heights when scanning single layers of 2D materials). How to check if these terraces where indeed single layers?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We used again #AFM, in this case to manipulate a terrace, folding it over the rest of the flake. By measuring the height of a sinlge fold we found ~0.4 nm, in good agreement with a single layer of #antimonene. https://t.co/bixEblMl2U

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Finally, we tested their stability, imaging some flakes with #AFM. After 2 months in a box at ambient conditions, we imaged them again and they looked exactly the same. We immersed them in water, and they still looked the same (even seeing the atomic lattice in these conditions) https://t.co/7PwQe316jP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These experiments demonstrated the possibility of isolating #antimonene and proved its stability, opening the door to its use for different purposes. https://t.co/VK0oNXTpba

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'll finish today by delving a little deeper into #antimonene. We also did some studies on its optical properties and noncovalent functionalization. The details for these two works in these links: https://t.co/zlmhMS8j7T   https://t.co/N9DsT8a7Br

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We combined optical microscopy characterization at different wavelengths with #AFM heights to obtain few-layer #antimonene refraction index, following a similar prodecure used with #graphene and other 2D materials, based on a Fresnel law model. https://t.co/xIEAkqporY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In this way, we were able to obtain the refraction index in the visible region and also to study the optical contrast as a function of the thickness of the SiO2 substrate, finding the optimal ones to work with #antimonene. https://t.co/2GvlzZcDzK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We also explored chemical properties of #antimonene, carrying out the noncovalent functionalization of few-layer flakes.  We functionalized the flakes by drop-casting a THF solution of a tailormade EDTA-PDI (EDTA=ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) derivative on the flakes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We characterized them using different techniques, including #AFM, which for example allowed us to quantify the increment in thickness from the molecules attached to the flakes. https://t.co/ZhiNpy7JCl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We carried out synchrotron measurements, showing that the functionalizing molecule acts as an electron acceptor, in good agreement with our theoterical calculations. https://t.co/uBRwYbCYwf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These experiments indicate that the noncovalent functionalization of #antimonene gives rise to a charge-transfer band gap of ~ 1 eV, being a promising route for tailoring its electronic properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today I will continue to tweet about some of my AFM studies on 2D materials. Let's try to debunk the myth that sequels are never any good! 😅 https://t.co/XxbH3QV0Y0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I will start with our work using 2D materials to fabricate nanochannels to confine water with atomic-thickness precision and then study its dielectric properties once confined. https://t.co/RjxjYhQ7aP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here I want to shout-out to @lfumagalli28: she led the project and is one of the world's experts in scanning dielectric microscopy. The details of the work here 👉🏼 https://t.co/1bCrAqrj0F

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Taking advantage of the experience and facilities at @UoMPhysics @UoMGraphene, we fabricated nanochannel devices where the height of the channels is given by the thickness of layers of 2D materials, enabling to control it at the atomic level. https://t.co/zkbY6E2ve0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here are some optical images from our devices, where the thicker channels are clearly visible, and even where we could see when water filled them. https://t.co/pw9AkzYrIm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But for the thinner channels it was not possible to detect optically if the water was in. To this end, we used #AFM to image the devices before and after water filling. https://t.co/N76hc3UGeD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When the channels are empty, the top cover sags into them, but when water is present, the water pushes it upwards and the sagging disappears. https://t.co/cbwR4dE2HC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Then, by using scanning dielectric microscopy, we were able to probe the out-of-plane dielectric properties of the water confined in the nanochannels. https://t.co/xUfS3lMLJZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We found a strong contrast that reversed with decreasing thickness, indicating that the polarizability of confined water strongly depended on its thickness and reaches values less than that of hBN, with an already low dielectric constant of ~3.5 https://t.co/6YxqF83emV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: By carefully determining the tip geometry and its radius, using finite-element analysis we could quantify the value of the out-of-plane dielectric constant of water for the different thicknesses. Recognition here to @reneif07 as well. https://t.co/KFJxaRhmFv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: By doing so, we could plot the out-of-plane dielectric constant of water as a function of thickness down to less than 1 nm, finding an anomalously low value of ~2 when extremely confined!! https://t.co/KC7WiBcu8l

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Our results revealed the presence of an interfacial "dead" layer two to three molecules thick, and are important for better understanding interactions in biological systems, in areas such as electrochemistry and energy storage, or to fine-tune future simulations of confined water

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The gif above was incomplete 😅, here is the right one https://t.co/qrLA31g9KI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I will go on with our work on studying the piezoelectric properties of single layer #hBN using #AFM electrostatic measurements #EFM. People in this work also include @lfumagalli28, and the details can be found here: https://t.co/TPaPrA5z2J https://t.co/iFdqyH5zXs

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The piezoelectric effect is an important property consisting in the internal generation of electrical charge resulting from an applied mechanical force. https://t.co/t4FcLhFNcH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For piezoelectricity to appear, it is needed a broken symmetry in the material structure. Centrosymetric crystals, such as graphene for instance, where all are carbon atoms, are not piezoelectric. https://t.co/0ro2lBXspi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When symmetry is broken, as in non-centrosymmetric crystals, piezoelectricity arises. This is the case of single layers of 2D materials such as #MoS2 or #hBN, for example. But when symmetry is recovered, as in bilayers (in general, even number of layers), piezoelectricity is lost https://t.co/XNS6ubYoNK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We used a variant of electrostatic force microscopy #EFM in such a way that we got an electric image, coming from the electric fields from the sample, and a simultaneous dielectric map, that we used as a control image to rule out artefacts and crosstalks. https://t.co/MZcvK5FNEa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We deposited single layers of #hBN on other 2D (starting with bottom #hBN), favouring bubbles and creases. We then obtained #EFM images of these areas, as bubbles and creases are features inducing high strain, observing high contrast within and especially around the bubbles. https://t.co/SPL0KDKo2C

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The contrast inside the bubbles was also visible in the dielectric maps, and could also come from the substances trapped inside or be a topographical crosstalk. But around the bubbles the areas are perfectly clean and flat, so the contrast could be due to piezoelectricity.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We took images of bubbles with well-defined shapes and made theoretical simulations mimicking those shapes, finding a fairly good agreement, confirming the piezoelectric origin of the observed contrast. https://t.co/ikdwh6u96q

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the case of depositing single layer #hBN on bottom #graphene, we also observed contrast around bubbles. https://t.co/j8PTxIUdU1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A closer look at this areas indicated the presence of ultrathin creases, which we also mimicked theoretically, showing a good agreeement with the measurements. https://t.co/kM4tT998uR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We confirmed the piezoelectric origin carrying out a battery of control experiments where no piezoelectricity was expected, such as areas without strain, bilayer #hBN or graphene bubbles and ultrathin creases. None of them showed the contrast observed in single layer #hBN. https://t.co/ftGQ2VrTvN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Our work gave evidence of the generation of piezoelectric fields in highly strained single layer #hBN, important if monolayer #hBN is used to encapsulate other 2Ds, and we also showed how electrostatic #AFM (#EFM, #KPFM) can be used to detect piezoelectricity on the nanoscale.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I will continue with more experiments related to bubbles in 2D materials. In particular, the effects of van der Waals (vdW) interactions in the formation of wrinkles around bubbles. Again with @lfumagalli28 among other #notinTwitter authors. Details here 👉🏼https://t.co/z2Cb0WK5G8 https://t.co/eakCj6LjnQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: While studying the piezoelectricity in single layer #hBN, we noticed the occasional appearance of wrinkles around bubbles. For example, their formation was favoured by exposure of the samples to high humidity. https://t.co/pMTCXNRiqL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We prepared high-quality vdW heterostructures with atomically flat monocrystals of #hBN and #MoS2 presenting different thicknesses, promoting the formation of wrinkles around bubbles. We imaged them using #AFM and measured the wavelentgh of the undulations. https://t.co/IdjRmgNFmI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We started with incommensurate samples (atomic lattices between the botom and the top 2D materials were not aligned) and we observed radial wrinkles whose wavelength ℓ depended on the thickness of the membranes. https://t.co/akrq5d6Qfl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We developed a theoretical framework based on the "local wavelength law". The bending rigidity favors undulations with large ℓ, and the restoring forces small ℓ. At long ℓ, the mutual slippage between the layers is suppressed while at short ℓ, intralayer slippage is prominent https://t.co/qzJjMPitEB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We also produced commensurate samples (atomic lattices aligned between bottom and top 2Ds) of monolayer #hBN. A moiré pattern appeared and the behavior was different: the wrinkles exhibited a substantial deviation from radial orientation and became constrained to the moiré. https://t.co/eDqCch4kNB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Our #AFM measurements of the various features of the deformed membranes can be harnessed to provide a very convenient, indirect metrological probe for the dependence of the bending rigidity on the number of atomic layers and for the magnitude and steepness of the vdW potential. https://t.co/RXB5ZyFrsl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The last work I'll tweet about is our study of #hBN crystals stacked at small twist angle. We used #AFM to see ferroelectric-like domains arranged in triangular superlattices. People in this work include again @lfumagalli28 and @reneif07, details here 👉🏼 https://t.co/bWqnKv7nRF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of the most promising avenues for controlling the properties of vdW heterostructures is to adjust the angle between the stacked 2D crystals. https://t.co/pMj44bO8bP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In this work, we produced #hBN crystals placed at an intentionally small twist angle, so they create a superlattice of charge-polarized macroscopic domains confined to the interface. https://t.co/UqXnKUVuEa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The #hBN unit cell has two non-identical sublattices, resulting in two cases of perfect alignment, parallel and antiparallel, giving rise to six highly symmetric stacking configurations for an hBN-hBN interface that differ in the position of the interfacial N and B atoms. https://t.co/EWJbPVX9YI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We used #AFM electrostatic modes #EFM and #KPFM to visualize the ferroelectric-like electrostatic supperlattices caused by the different stacking domains in vdW structures of several thicknesses. https://t.co/4xAtF4L6do

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We detected no superlattice patterns in the topography images, but we detected clear  triangular domains periodically arranged in many regions in the electrostatic images. https://t.co/V2noDOnqqG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Twisted heterostructures with monolayer steps on the surface of the bottom #hBN crystal showed clear triangular pattern only on one side of the terrace, suggesting that periodic domains are possible only for one orientation type, either parallel or antiparallel. https://t.co/eticI4TIZc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We calculated superlattice reconstructions at the twisted hBN interface, that when compared with the #EFM and #KPFM results strongly suggest that the observed superlattices represent the parallel alignment with alternating AB and BA domains. https://t.co/QSc6mgdgzd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This worked showed a simple and non-destructive #AFM technique able to visualize moiré-superlattice electrostatic potentials. The demonstrated charge-polarized superlattices provide a fascinating platform to study superlattice phenomena and engineer vdW heterostructures.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Good morning everyone, great to be here this week! My name is Dr William Brant and I am an Assisstant Professor in the @StructuralChem1 group which is part of the @chem_angstrom department at @UU_University.  See below for a preview of what I will talk about this week. https://t.co/x6zP4G8iTv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I will kick this week off by talking about how I got to where I am today almost 16 000 km away from home. What really attracted me to the science that made me relocate this far and naturally some details about the science.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Of course, science is a big part of my life but it is not all there is to it. So later today I will give a sneak peek into a very nerdy hobby that I have :).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For now, it is Monday morning and that means group meetings! It is good to start the week with a refresher on what is to come when you have a fresh head. I will return in 2 hours! https://t.co/RnLuEyT3Es

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Ok morning meetings done! I will kick off today by talking a little bit about how I ended up all the way in Sweden.

I originally did my undergraduate studies within at @Sydney_Uni. I was actually originally studying a combined science, commerce degree at the time!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, in my third year I rediscovered my love for crystals and discovered the joys of #crystallography in the solid state chemistry course. This led to a research project in @SydneyChemistry in 2009 on lithium conduction in defect perovskites that grew into my PhD project. https://t.co/kvxdQYj7hG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I will talk more on the science of my project later. For now how did I find my way to Sweden? Well, I was fortunate enough in my PhD to have to opportunity to travel abroad to conferences. Such as AsCA in Busan Korea (where I looked very different compared to today...) https://t.co/0dU1K9q8QD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Attending conferences is a great way to meet and network with others in the field. It was one conference in particular that really taught me that its not what you know but who you know. This was the International Meeting of Lithium-Ion Batteries on Jeju Island, Korea in 2012.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There I met a researcher from the @angstromABC who was working on building devices for studying battery materials using #neutrons. As I was working on this too I started a dialogue with him which turned into discussions of a collaboration.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Next thing you know, a year later I found myself in Sweden and then the @isisneutronmuon source to perform experiments connected to this collaboration. It was also my first experience of building batteries in a glovebox...it isn't easy. https://t.co/uLu5RTfzQG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, the week I was in Sweden preparing I had the great fortune to meet @KristinaEdstrm2 and Dr Torbjörn Gustafsson, both of whom had a long history of studying battery materials with diffraction. Including the first in situ neutron experiment on a custom built battery.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: While brief, this meeting led to Prof. Edström offering me a postdoc position in 2015 working in the @StructuralChem1 group and continuing my work on methods of studying batteries during operation using diffraction. I have been here ever since :).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So, what have I learned from this journey? 

- You never know where or when you might run into that career changing collaboration
- Networking is key for finding opportunities in the first place
- Sometimes relocating to a new country is needed to utilise these opportunities

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I think one final thing I need to add is that, looking back I never would have predicted this path. Or that I would end up potentially permantly in Sweden. So keep an open mind about career paths and opportunities :) https://t.co/8QRD7iK8Uc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @M_LaddParada I wanted to mention also all the friends I have made on the way :)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So I talked about the how...but why did I choose to go into science in the first place? Relocating to a new country isn't a small decision and not an easy one.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Since I was a kid, I was always captivated by crystals. Their shape, the colour and multiple varieties. I had a small collection going at one period of time. But it was only a passing fancy, one that I didn't think about again until the final year of university. https://t.co/VEiXECsu0t

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As I mentioned, I took a solid state chemistry course which introduced me not just the beautiful macroscopic properties of crystals, but the hidden atomic patterns which lay within and how #structure determines materials #properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I began studying a class of materials known as A-site deficient perovskites and used X-ray and neutron #diffraction to understand how the structure impacted the #lithium storage ability. Materials which can reversibly store lithium could be used in rechargeable Li-ion batteries!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A real highlight from these early days was seeing that yes, lithium does rapidly insert into this material creating a dramatic colour change. A simple thing but it really blew me away back then. I then had to understand how ions are transported through solid materials. https://t.co/V7whjPnm0l

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I began to construct "batteries" (they were a bit...rough 😅) which enabled simultaneous diffraction experiments to study how the material changed during lithium insertion. (I am happy to say I am much better at designing these batteries now 😁) https://t.co/FcQyK1qcz3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The ability to watch how the atomic structure changed during the electrochemical process was fascinating to me. It was a kind of X-ray vision🙃. This was what set the stage for my persistent research theme of studying crystalline materials under change.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The deeper I went into studying how structure influences properties the more fascinating it became. It became clearer how one could modify and engineer new materials for actual applications. https://t.co/7S6hEWvVEQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Finally, the raw problem solving that one encounters in research is addictive. I lived for working through a challenging problem, deconstructing the components and putting everything back together again into a coherent story.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After four years of independent research and personally experiencing the joy of discovery, I couldn't just leave it behind. So I took the dive to come to Sweden to continue in research and actually learn a thing or two about batteries.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ok so I have now talked about the how and why of my research path, but now I think it is time to introduce the "what". What exactly am I doing?? This will be a brief overview as I will dig into the details during the week. https://t.co/pDjVdXieXT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As mentioned, I like to study crystalline materials as they are changing. This change could be during synthesis, when the materials are being utilised in a battery or when the materials have been accidentally left out on a bench and slowly degrading

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To study these changes I use diffraction. In this experiment, X-rays (or neutrons) are directed at a crystalline sample. The X-rays scatter from the array of atoms in the sample forming an interference pattern. From the pattern we can determine atom identities and their locations

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For example, below I have a series of diffraction patterns collected during lithium insertion and extraction from a material. You can see the peak shift corresponding to a volume expansion and contraction. Copper is present as an inert current collector so it doesn't change https://t.co/7onRjawAOV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That is my main methodology, the materials which I investigate are known as rock-salt derived oxides and Prussian blue analogues. Rock-salt derived oxides are a class of structure that most commercialised cathode materials for Li-ion batteries adopt. https://t.co/k4hIlGo6yG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Finally, Prussian blue analogues are a class of porous framework materials based around transition metals bridged by cyanide ligands. They have an open structure making them ideal for the larger cations utilised in sodium and potassium ion batteries https://t.co/J9YYmOzj6B

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Over the next few days I will describe how we study the material changes during synthesis, storage and battery operation using advanced in-situ and operando diffraction techniques. The end goal being to design greener materials which lead to better performing batteries!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Last post for today, what I do occasionally in my free time, when I have free time. Is play table top role playing games like Dungeons and Dragons! https://t.co/ATETutZtlg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To get into character I have a hat that I wear during the sessions😋. It is "role play lite", but its a good excuse to wear my Akubra and put on a ridiculous Australian accent. https://t.co/212ePIqckd

tweets.text: Good morning everyone! Today is fairly quiet in the morning so I will take the time to introduce you to the lab and to some of the work that @ashok_menon12 has done. Then I will have a 5 hour workshop for @Altris_ab so will need to drop out early for today

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But first, I think it is good to generally introduce what a Li or Na-ion #battery is built up from. While I am not an electrochemist by any stretch, I do work a lot with batteries and will mention them often.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A battery is comprised of four key components. Two electrodes connected to an external circuit: a positive (high potential) and a negative (lower potential) electrode. These are electrically isolated from each other by a separator soaked in electrolyte allowing ions to pass. https://t.co/suyzENp5Mq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The electrons pass via an external circuit where they perform work during battery use. Both the positive and negative electrode materials need to accept both electrons and ions (such as Li+) reversibly. Designing materials which can do this is quite challenging.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In modern lithium-ion batteries the negative electrode (often called the anode) is graphite and the positive electrode (cathode) is either a metal oxide with a rock salt type structure or a polyanionic structure, namely LiFePO4 (LFP)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It is interesting to reflect on the fact that the first commercially successful positive electrode material was developed in 1980 (LiCoO2), and most commercial materials today are based on this same structure. https://t.co/eLJuN4hWFY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Aside from LiFePO4 which is quite different, are there no other viable positive electrode material classes for lithium-ion batteries? There are many being investigated but not so many that make the cut for commercialisation.

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.text: Ok lets take a look through the @StructuralChem1  lab! Development of new technologies begins with synthesis of new materials. This synthesis is carried out in many of the fumehoods that we have available https://t.co/PWXXdU5rTq

tweets.text: We just got back from a group lunch/farewell to @ashok_menon12. I will use this opportunity to talk a little bit about what Ashok has done during his PhD. Ashok has worked with what is known as Li and Mn-rich layered oxides.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The Li and Mn rich oxide materials are interesting as they have the potential to store a lot more energy compared to regular battery cathodes. https://t.co/QlHZIRrgz5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The reason is due to the excess lithium which sits in the transition metal layer. The presence of Li in this layer creates local Li-O-Li bonding environments allowing of anionic redox due to unhybridised O orbitals. Below I show the regular LiCoO2 (yellow) and Li2MnO3 (purple). https://t.co/BsbGu4Fh6U

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, this excess lithium has other structural consequences. Namely, the formation of a hexagonal arrangement of cations in the transition metal layer. https://t.co/kD8tTwxknR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, how these layers in the structure arrange  can shift. Leading to a kind of disorder known as stacking faults. In the clip I represent Li and Mn environments as hexagons. The shifts show how two adjacent layers can be placed relative to each other. https://t.co/zcNvFrysnf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The question that Ashok aimed to answer was how the synthesis route impacted the degree of faulting and properties in the relatively simple compound Li2MnO3. https://t.co/wNeSyuxIa6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It turns out that the synthesis route did have a significant impact with a solid state "shake and bake" route producing a mix of faulted and unfaulted structures and the solgel route forming a more homogeneous structure.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We didn't know it at the time...but this would be significant foreshadowing for what would become the theme of his whole PhD thesis. More on that soon https://t.co/h88y0BNDoe
