tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After our initial work on Li2MnO3, we discovered that there was a debate in the literature for a related compound. The more promising Li1.2Mn0.54Ni0.13Co0.13O2. It is the Li and Mn rich analogue to the Li[NiMnCo]O2 oxides used in commercial batteries.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What was this debate? It was whether the material existed as a solid solution or if it was an intergrowth or mix of Li2MnO3 and Li[NiMnCo]O2. Ie, if the composition crystallised as one or two phases. Here is an excerpt highlighting the debate https://t.co/rNJ2ihG8uY https://t.co/aTr4I7Sr8J

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And here is what the two proposed models are. In the multi-phase model the hexagonal ordering occurs exclusively for Li and Mn whereas in the single phase Li in the transition metal layer can also have Ni and Co as nearest neighbours. https://t.co/X1ch7X4gcN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Why does this matter? It has been argued that the additional capacity, specifically the anionic redox capacity, originated from the Li2MnO3 phase. Thus, its presence is necessary for that additional capacity.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So why is this so difficult? Surely a diffraction experiment can tell you whether multiple phases are present. Lets play a game of spot the difference🙂. Below are diffraction patterns (X-rays and neutrons) from a confirmed "single" and "multi" phase samples https://t.co/wDCj3VYNSu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Aside from intensity differences in the neutron diffraction pattern, they look pretty similar. Figuring out this puzzle is further complicated since the compound has disorder over several length scales. Short to long: Atomic site mixing, stacking faults and phase segregation https://t.co/3mKL1M8idR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Disorder over multiple length scales means to answer this question multiple characterisation tools are needed. This is what we did, looking at both local and long range information. The methods were diffraction, raman spectroscopy, magnetic susceptibility, and STEM measurements https://t.co/Ly1atHr4tA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What did we learn? Is the material one or two phases?? The answer is: both and it depends on how you synthesise the material. Similar to the first paper, solid state gives an inhomogeneous distribution of elements whereas the sol gel method is more homogeneous https://t.co/tSuRtdUUEI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It is not too surprising that this has led to conflicting results over the years. It does raise some interesting ideas about tailoring phase intergrowth via different synthetic pathways however.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The full story can be found here: https://t.co/GSJts7b2AJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @realscientists This is actually a great idea, I might have to borrow that one🙂

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now to talk about Prussian blue analogues! To begin I have to tell the story behind them because it is one of my favourite pieces of chemical history. It is a tale of alchemists, theologians, famous paintings and about 200 years of wondering what Prussian blue was. https://t.co/rbeaQIJeEd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It all began in Berlin in 1704 with an enterprising dye maker by the name of Heinrich Diesbach. He was most interested in producing a red dye by the name of Cochineal red lake. The ingredients were iron sulphate, potash and crushed up beetles #alchemy https://t.co/0GxjR9T9AY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But Diesbach was running low on potash. Enter the scene one Johann Conrad Dippel. Master theologian, physician, alchemist. Dippel was captured by the allure of alchemy and like any good alchemist began his attempts at transmuting gold. https://t.co/flKvNWZRGk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This failed, but it did not deter him from making a miraculous "animal oil" and releasing it upon an unsuspecting public. The concoction, distilled from the ground up remains of animals, was so foul it was believed it must be good for you (like any good medicine right?)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What does this have to do with a dye maker? Diesbach is said to have been preparing his dyes in Dippels laboratories. His potash shortage was solved by buying from Dippel. Now, Dippel was not a great alchemist and a terrible chemist so of course the potash was contaminated

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And so, unsuspectingly using the potash contaminated with animal remains Diesbach tried to produce his red dye. He did not get a red dye. He produced a very blue powder instead. https://t.co/4Tva0GXC1k

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Keep in mind that obtaining vibrant blue colours for paint or clothing in these times was not easy, and not cheap. Diesbach knew this and quickly attempted to recreate the recipe and sell his new blue pigment to the world leading to several famous paintings. https://t.co/Iads1W6V3i

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The original recipe called for dried ox blood as a key ingredient. Of course, they can't have known what was really going on at the time because the discovery of several key elements had not yet happened (like nitrogen in 1772). So what did they really make?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The key ingredients are iron and cyanide. The cyanide, which originated from various alkyl cyanides in the animal remains, dramatically changed the reaction leading to what is now known as Prussian blue. But it took a few hundred years to figure this out https://t.co/5zkyzWKRSY https://t.co/rOnZ9EqqKJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Finally, using X-ray diffraction, it was determined that Prussian blue was a coordination framework compound consisting of iron centers bridged together by cyanide ligands. Each iron can be coordinated by six cyanides giving the porous cubic structure. https://t.co/kL6P23luoa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This was just the beginning. Prussian blue is one member of a family of compounds known as Prussian blue analogues. They share the same coordination environment of CN bridges, but the transition metal can change and the pores in the structure can host many different species.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Many different compositions leads to a variety of properties and applications. Prussian blue analogues are more than just pretty colours. They can be used for treating Cesium and thallium poisoning, CO2 capture, in electrochromic windows and of course, in batteries! (and more) https://t.co/AtYlncEnq8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For more detail on the history of Prussian blue, I recommend the work by Alexander Kraft, who has written a few times on the history of the pigment (https://t.co/is3OMqFpuQ) and also a nice perspective by Andreas Ludi: https://t.co/ogjXNcAWFp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So how about Prussian blue analogues (PBAs) in batteries? In addition to @Altris_ab there are a number of other companies developing this class of compounds for energy storage applications. What makes them so attractive?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: PBAs are commonly used as the positive electrode in beyond Li-ion batteries (sodium, potassium). They have an open structure leading to fast cation insertion. Additionally, due to the strong bonding of the cyanide ligand transition metals like iron have a decent voltage output. https://t.co/vjzNrlIjVD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Indeed, the performance metrics of PBAs, in particular the iron-based Na2Fe[Fe(CN)6], are quite similar to those of LiFePO4 (LFP). However, PBAs have the additional advantage of a simple and low cost synthesis making them very interesting to develop cheap sustainable batteries https://t.co/4KDjKd01L3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Also the electrodes cast using PBAs look really nice :) https://t.co/kbwR71naE7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It was the simplicity of synthesis and performance reliability which first attracted @RezaYounesi and his PhD student Ronnie Mogensen to Prussian blue analogues. The full story on this is coming up next🙂

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The story of how @Altris_ab came to be and my involvement in PBA research is also a nice one. It was really a combination of the right people meeting at the right time and at the right place.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It began with Ronnie Mogensen, who was working on polymer electrolytes at the time and just needed a reliable positive electrode that was easy to make. He tried NaFePO4 which didn't always function. Then he turned to NaxFe[Fe(CN)6]. This always worked to a reasonable degree

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: He then stumbled upon a paper where the group of John Goodenough (Nobel laureate in chemistry for Li-ion #batteries) made rhombohedral Prussian white. https://t.co/xdiIwbj6Mj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What is Prussian white? Specifically, when the sodium content in NaxFe[Fe(CN)6] reaches a maximum with few structural defects, the material adopts a white colour rather than its famous blue. https://t.co/n5S7Xv9P02

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It also has very impressive electrochemical performance with a capacity around 160 mAhg-1 and an average voltage of 3.4 V. Needless to say, @RezaYounesi was intrigued and wanted to produce the material for his #sodium #battery research.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The problem was the synthesis, which required the use of a hydrothermal reactor with a built in stirrer. We did not have such an autoclave available so he needed an alternative approach.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It should be mentioned that until this stage, most synthesis routes to prepare PBAs for electrodes resulted in low capacities and low reversibility due to the presence of [Fe(CN)6]3- vacancies and water in the structure. So this needed to be addressed

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This was around the time that I got involved in the project, purely because I happened to be in the department and eager to collaborate. However, I had some light experience working with PBAs and methods of chemically intercalating materials. So together we devised a new approach

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The original idea of the synthesis was to optimise for low vacancies, high sodium content and low water in separate steps with sodium and water contents reliant on a low vacancy content. We split up the process and recreated the result from Goodenough but with simple equipment. https://t.co/Y1jB41yZR5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And here is a picture of the compound before (right) and after (left) the sodium enrichment step. https://t.co/TqIhOWUmn2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Given our success Reza suggested we should patent this, why not? Afterall, in Sweden the researchers own the idea, not the university. Of course we needed to pay for this ourselves but thanks to the generousity of @KristinaEdstrm2 we had available funding to do just that.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So we were pretty happy with managing to patent our idea. However, it was not the end as another chance encounter with Adam Dahlquist from @InnoEnergyEU pushed us in a new direction: Creating @Altris_ab

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Adam introduced us to Paul Larsson to take care of the business side of things and we set to work on first creating the company and then taking on the hard work to get into the EIT InnoEnergy Highway® program, which in 2017 we succeeded in doing

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This was quite unusual because when we started the application, Altris didn't even exist. But the four of us really believed in the idea. Plus, the willingness to bring in Paul and share the company was positively recieved. Afterall 1% of 1 million is better than 100% of nothing https://t.co/qrPy2cHnkU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now the real work began. Scaling up production. Here we hired Dr Tim Nordh as our first ever employee and began to scale up the synthesis within the @StructuralChem1 labs. https://t.co/KLGd9tcVV3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We also started collaborating with a local company LiFeSiZE to produce prototype #batteries. https://t.co/WlnLghzmcn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These were extremely challenging years as we were finding our feet as a company, looking for financing, trying to get things right with scaling up the synthesis AND building prototype cells for the first time. Many road blocks were encountered. https://t.co/c7zTutF68i

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But we persevered! And very soon out grew the university as we were ready for the next step. Adam Dahlquist joined the company in 2019 and began pushing expansion. We obtained a site for a small pilot factory and then built the place ourselves (or Tim and Ronnie did).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here is a photo of the team as it was at this stage. It is one of my favourites :) https://t.co/lRomVqPHVC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Back onto the science before I head out for vaccination. How have I contributed to the PBA work? One of the earliest questions we were asked by funding agencies was about the thermal stability of Prussian white. So we dug into this question: https://t.co/7iLq5UUBFU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of the main concerns was that Prussian white would exhibit thermal stability similar to that other PBAs which have been shown to release CN compounds at around 200C https://t.co/KlwAMyxqVH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What we determined was that if you already have a low vacancy structure like Prussian white, the thermal stability is determined by the sodium content. The more sodium the more thermally stable it is. A bonus result was that the water uptake is also increased for increased sodium https://t.co/MBPRf02PCF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The latter result is important to consider since Prussian white should be used in non aqueous batteries. So removing all the water prior to implementation in a battery is essential. Understanding the material drying parameters has improved our sample processing @Altris_ab

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Of course, the thermal stability is highly dependent on the environment and the conditions tested here aren't the same as in a battery. Regardless, relative to other PBAs it seems that Prussian white is more thermally stable under the same conditions. https://t.co/tSDYLlLKB5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here I made a nice table of contents figure summarising the key take home messages. https://t.co/CoQYz7MS70

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Lunch time question to you all! How important do you think understanding visual #design is for scientists? I spend a lot of time making TOC images but am not the best designer :p. Feel free to write your opinion too!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @ChirpDontTweet Yeah, I would tend to agree. You don't have to do much for good data visualisation to raise the quality over what is generally out there. Less is more as they say.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Nice to see that many think its important. Of course when I say visual design I mean data visualisation #dataviz. Presenting data in a way which is clear and conveys the correct message without ambiguity I think is really important

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The other aspect related to PBAs in #batteries are their moisture sensitivity. PBAs, like many porous compounds, are hygroscopic and adsorb moisture from the air. For Prussian white this comes with a colour change. Left is sample exposed to oxygen, right is to air. https://t.co/5sYkcA4IQp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is a little bit of a problem since you don't want water in a battery, this leads to all kinds of nasty side reactions. So how do we solve this? Well, my mantra is if you want to solve a problem you must first understand it. https://t.co/0gnG5FcTTx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The question I wanted to answer, jokingly, was what happens if I accidentally leave my Prussian white on the bench for a month? The actual question was, how does moisture exposure during storage impact capacity fade? https://t.co/m951WWdsIi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It is useful to point out at this stage that Prussian white exists in two forms. The hydrated, monoclinic phase with water inside the pores and a dehydrated rhombohedral phase, which is a slightly collapsed structure. What comes out of a reactor is the monoclinic phase. https://t.co/9XPyzfmqge

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When you dry the material you transform to the rhombohedral phase. We exposed both forms of Prussian white to different humidity levels for 7 days. The monoclinic was unchanged up to 75% relative humidity. The rhombohedral degraded heavily. Left: pristine. Right: exposed https://t.co/ElJ5QPnuIv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Not only were the particles visibly damaged, when held at 55% relative humidity for up to 90 days the capacity was found to rapidly decay before stabilising. It also seemed to occur from one plateau only. So we began to dig into the mechanism for this fade. https://t.co/9KazJwMLkj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To cut a long story and complex puzzle short. Using X-ray diffraction, XPS, mössbauer spectroscopy, IR and Raman we determined that the material degraded in two steps. First the reversible extraction of sodium to form NaOH, then the irreversible basic degradation of the framework https://t.co/4SYWRZM5jA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Such degradation is not unknown for PBAs, however, the impact on electrochemical performance had not been quantified before. Follow on studies from this have significantly impacted how we handle and treat PBA material at Altris.

tweets.text: The other side of my research which I have not talked so much about is development of tools to study structure change in operando. tweets.text: Since coming to Uppsala I have focused more on battery cells for X-ray #diffraction, and mostly using our in house diffractometer. This has been work I have done for others in the group. Its amazing how much you can achieve without going to a #synchrotron (though I do miss going)

tweets.label: Takeover

Good morning/afternoon, folks!

I'm Sebastian from the THz Structural Dynamics group at FHI of the MPG in Berlin, Germany.

This week, I'll be tweeting about our advantures in the world of #ultrafast phenomena. Thus no n̶a̶n̶o̶ scale, but #pico- and #femto-seconds this time! ⏱️ https://t.co/8jKRyJcCxx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Before we start diving into science, allow me to introduce the team first: 
I started my research group 1 year ago with this amazing bunch of talented students (Marie, Leona, Max). Since then we are working towards #THz & #MIR control of structural dynamics. Why that? Stay tuned! https://t.co/28Ka3nfFNt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So why *structural dynamics*?
Material properties are fundamentally determined by the spatial arrangement of atoms, ions or molecules. If we can modulate this spatial structure on ultrafast time scales, we might control properties on demand or even discover new material features. https://t.co/5jIruHWDsv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @_AFox_ Thanks, very solid question: In the field of laser spectroscopy people loosely refer every faster than a couple of hundred picoseconds (ps) as "ultrafast". What is important here are the natural oscillation periods of elementary vibrations, usually a couple of ps.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
And why *THz* or *MIR*? 
Intense and phase stable laser pulses in the THz to MIR spectral range enable us to directly drive specific resonances on their fundamental time and energy scales. With these, we can control IR-active modes resonantly and Raman-active ones nonlinearly. https://t.co/HaaYTptiQ6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Where to get these high-field THz / MIR pulses from?

Unfortunately there's no out-of-the-box laser pointer for that. So one of the main tasks in our group is to keep our big baby happy and running. #Laserlife

More lab impressions to come on #LaserLabThursday. @sfmaehrlein Labs https://t.co/QVEPNTm8jl

tweets.text:
Can we access novel spin states via specific lattice vibrations?

Yes! In the ferrimagnetic insulator Yttrium Iron Garnet, we showed that resonant lattice excitation leads to a transient spin-state of elevated temperature, but yet unchanged magnetization

https://t.co/iz61Z7SNmd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let's kick off day 3⃣ digit three with a few fundamental scientific questions.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
How fast is the angular momentum transfer between spins and the lattice?

In magnetic insulators, when angular momentum transfer has to rely on spin-orbit coupling, it is slow ~ns compared to the lattice excitation. Thus the intermediate state is determined by constraint heating. https://t.co/CLJTWPm4hg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Thermodynamic picture:
A) Lattice heating under the constraint of conserved total spin angular momentum (pot+lid) ➡️built up of "spin pressure"  ➡️ B) new state: internal spin redistribution ➡️C) demagnetization via angular momentum release to lattice 🧲

https://t.co/YJjB91BgYb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Okay, #phonon #control seems useful, but what if there's a desired target mode without electric dipole moment for coupling to the #THz field?

We found the sum-frequency counterpart of stimulated #RamanScattering to access these previously IR-silent modes.
https://t.co/0x6FrEWAIB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The same sum-frequency excitation can be driven by phoNons instead of phoTons via #NonlinearPhonincs: Anharmonic coupling can lead to sum-frequency ionic Raman scattering.
Great theory collaboration with D.M. Jurascheck (@NarangLab, prev. @NicolaSpaldin)
https://t.co/dk5fqx6JYq https://t.co/OJrsLfzFRS

tweets.text: Hi everyone! I´m Ferry Prins (@FerryPrins), group leader at the Condensed Matter Physics Center (@ifimacuam) in Madrid. My group focusses on visualizing the interaction of #light with #nanomaterials. This week I´ll give a behind-the-scenes of the lab! https://t.co/fMdLSk8u5h

so what´s in store? 

Day1⃣- As tradition @RealSci_Nano, today I´ll give a brief story of how I got to my current position🧑‍🔬🔬
Day2⃣- Lab tour! and all the ins and outs of how we make little energy transport movies 🎬
Day3⃣- Nanofabrication with nanomaterials...

Day5⃣- An older topic for me: the fun 🥳 and frustrations 🤯 of single-molecule electronics! 

Looking forward to sharing some of these things with you and I hope you will enjoy it!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
1/ My academic journey started at Leiden University, in the footsteps of Rembrandt, Huygens, Snellius, Lorentz, vd Waals, Zeeman, and Kamerlingh Onnes… 

I was just an undergrad in synthetic chemistry, and not a very talented one 😅… https://t.co/cgKNx2TLcL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2/ So, when looking for a PhD, I decided to gamble a bit and apply to physics programs. I got lucky at the group of Herre vd Zant at TUDelft, who was looking to diversify his physics team with more chemistry backgrounds.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3/ The change was tough at first, but you catch on quickly. 

Years later I told Herre that when he hired me he took quite a risk taking on a synthetic chemist… he just laughed and asked: and YOU didn’t? 😅

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
4/ My project was on single-molecule transistors stable enough to work at room temperature. 

So you take a single molecule, place it between a pair of electrodes that are separated by about a nanometer, and then you measure the current through it… at room temperature. https://t.co/GcxIWgOHqM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
5/ turned out it was not impossible… just incredibly frustrating to get there. 

(I´ll tell you all about these adventures on Friday in an extended thread on single-molecule electronics!) https://t.co/ZB3y6X2n5p

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 6/ The PhD programme at Delft was great. I learned a ton of new skills in low-noise electronics, nano fabrication, programming. On top, different soft-skills courses were organised on presenting and project management. I even got to spend 2 months in Japan at NTT.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
7/ I finished my thesis in 2011 and defended during one of those typical costume parties that Dutch universities organise for you. 

I decided that I wanted to continue in academia but I was also quite sure that I had had enough of single-molecule electronics. https://t.co/0yKiqsaxQg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 8/ So, next challenge: finding the right postdoc position while switching fields! Stay tuned for a little thread on my postdoc search...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
1/ As promised, thread on the postdoc search and how i ended up in an empty lab in Boston.

1st, the problem we all face: PIs never reply to our emails! Cant blame them, applications come by the dozens and there´s simply no time to reply to all, let alone interview. 

What to do? https://t.co/eJMMRXa3UC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
2/ I´d say just insist, firmly but politely… 

Seriously, ask any PI and they will most likely tell you that they are always happy to receive reminders! It even shows that you are really interested and not just sending blanket applications.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3/ After a long search I got a job offer from @TisdaleWA, who was just starting his own group at MIT on nanomaterial spectroscopy… 

Now of course everyone told me, NEVER do a postdoc in a new lab!!! Cause you loose the first year building up… https://t.co/I6SE4hico1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
4/ I admit it was a big gamble to join an empty lab, but it all worked out for me and the experience has really helped me later on when I had to build my own lab. 

(stay tuned for more on this on Thursday, when I´ll post on my experience starting a lab from scratch!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5/ I had already decided I wanted to try more nanomaterials-related work toward the end of my PhD, with a side project on nanoscale photodetectors using colloidal quantum dots - my 1st project in which things were reproducible (not a single molecule that refuses to sit still)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 6/  Colloidal quantum dots (semiconductor nanocrystals) were already the big promise for next-gen solar cells and LEDs at the time… the great benefit is that they change their bandgap with the size of the nanocrystal. (bonus: they look awesome!) https://t.co/2h9KCByQjd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 7/ I got to work with a lot of talented people at the Tisdale lab, looking at spatial dynamics of carriers in semiconductors (lots of colorful quantum-dot thin films!). Together with the Bulovic lab we laid the foundation for what is now the field of #transientmicroscopy.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
8/ Transient microscopy allows to visualize carrier transport. You create a tiny population of carriers with an excitation laser, and follow how this population broadens using time & spatially resolved detection. 

Tomorrow I´ll tell all about the early days and state-of-the-art! https://t.co/pUfwmUn83q

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 9/ after two really great years in Boston, I decided it was time to try and get my own lab started back in Europe. All about that in a next thread!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 1/ now on the final hurdles before ending up with my own lab in Spain 🇪🇸… and how it needed a little bit of Swiss🇨🇭encouragement… https://t.co/RihwKrirvq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
2/ To start, looking for faculty positions in Europe has its challenges. Unlike in the US, there is no application cycle… jobs can be advertised any time, and anywhere (and sometimes nowhere, you just have to know). 

That means it can take time… https://t.co/pDPrk3AFfB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3/ and even though I managed to get to some interviews, it just didn’t happen at the time. 

I almost dropped out of academia but decided to give myself one more chance and took on an offer from @NorrisOMEL at ETH Zurich for a 1 year postdoc.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
4/ That 1 year got extended thanks to the @snsf_ch that awarded me an Ambizione grant – a 3 year fellowship for senior postdocs to work toward independence under the wing of a senior PI. 

(more on my time @NorrisOMEL on Wednesday!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
5/ while not originally in the planning, the intermediate step of an Ambizione suddenly bought me more time to look for that faculty position and gave me already quite some independence. 

(More countries need such bridging programs!) https://t.co/BjuFaOClfw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
6/ picking up the faculty search again, I finally got a tenure-track offer from @ifimacuam - a chance to build up my own lab from scratch! 

I negotiated to start a year later to wrap things up in Zurich, making the move to Madrid in 2017. (more on that in the coming days!)

tweets.label: Takeover

7/ I guess what I learned on the job search, is that the standard route of one successful postdoc and then landing your tenure track position is really not the only way to get there. 

So if you really want that faculty job: don´t get discouraged if things take time! https://t.co/O7IieeqSTV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 1/ as promised, today a lab tour @PhoND_UAM! In bits and pieces, I´ll give you the ins and outs of our work on visualising energy transport in nanomaterials... First a general tour of our laser lab! 🔬 https://t.co/kgPCNgANaC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2/ Our labs are located at the @UAM_Madrid  Cantoblanco campus on the north side of Madrid. We are in the basement, which is really quite convenient when trying to keep sunlight out of the lab (cause sun we have in Madrid 😄🌞) https://t.co/AZH5wvdJqW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3/ The most important piece of optics we have is the 18 m2 L-shaped floating table. This is where we perform all our most sensitive microscopy and spectroscopy measurements. https://t.co/yE5f1LCZOd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4/ we love inverted optical microscopes, cause the exit ports at the bottom allow you to easily couple the light out of your microscope and send it free-space to your favourite detector. https://t.co/m47C25jdUU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
5/ many of our ports are equipped with @Thorlabs  adapters to directly mount cages, making for easy alignment in and out of the microscope. 

Here for example, you see the in-coupling of our single-mode excitation laser for diffraction limited illumination. https://t.co/9OIfuih0ZF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
6/ we use diffraction limited excitation of our samples to generate the fluorescent signals that give us a ton of info about the material. 

we analyse these signals using different space, time, and energy resolved techniques. https://t.co/HpbmrKE8HJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 7/ our favorite layout uses relay lenses to project the image onto the slit of an imaging spectrograph. The slit is motorized such that we can either propagate the spectrum to the camera (slit closed, grating in place) or the full image (slit open, mirror instead of grating) https://t.co/KgmNYG12MS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 8/ The best part of this layout is that you have plenty of space to introduce for example polarisers, additional filters, or a so-called Bertrand lens that allows you to do angle resolved spectroscopy(more about that tomorrow!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 9/ for spectroscopy, we really like our imaging spectrographs with double exit ports. The standard layout gives you the spectral dispersion directly on your camera (EMCCD in our case). But alternatively, you can send the light out to the side to an avalanche photodiode. https://t.co/NWSxJZVgeV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 10/ this gives you the option to do spectrally resolved lifetime measurements... basically it´s very a simple streak camera with a timing of some 100 ps and spectral resolution depending on your grating.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
11/ Finally, on the other side of the microscope, we have our scanning avalanche photodiode, which has a ridiculously simple layout, but is the key to all our energy transport measurements. 

I will tell you all about transient microscopy in a dedicated thread! https://t.co/VWi0CvFUwY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
1/ A thread on transient microscopy techniques! This simple technique allows you to visualise carrier transport in a variety of materials, giving direct information about how fast and how far carriers move. 

(this is going to be a long thread, bear with me!) https://t.co/EZ8vIl8vFi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2/ Understanding carrier transport is crucial for optoelectronics. In a solar cell, for example, carriers need to travel as far as possible to reach charge collecting interfaces. https://t.co/3jnWU1z2Vp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3/ traditional techniques are time-averaged methods that only measure the average speed of the carriers during its lifetime. This works well for perfect lattices of a single crystalline semiconductor where speeds are constant... but not for more complex nanomaterials!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4/ we started working on this problem around 2013 at MIT, with a team of people from the Bulovic and Tisdale labs. The idea was to create exciations in one spot, and detect how long it would take for that excitation to reach a different position. https://t.co/BxShPvKr2s

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5/ Gleb Akselrod, a senior grad student at the Bulovic lab, built the first version of the transient microscope, and it was remarkably simple: a fixed diffraction limited excitation, and a motorized APD in the image plane for raster scanning. https://t.co/BMOTPoTeUQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 6/ the excitation spot is kept tiny using a high NA objective (>250 nm), and by scanning the APD across the fixed exciation spot, you obtain a beautiful visualization of the broadening of the carrier population! https://t.co/vspwzIpb5q

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
7/ if your material is isotropic, a single line scan gives you all the info you need. But as Gleb showed beautifully in the first publication on transport in tetracene organic crystals, different axis can give anisotropic transport.
 https://t.co/O7liprXJl3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 8/ In the tetracene paper, things were relatively easy cause carriers are triplet excitons that live very long and travel far (100s of nm)... but what about single excitons with short lifetimes?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 9/ we tested this with thin films of colloidal quantum dots, where singlet excitons hop from one particle to the next through energy transfer. This process is slow, and excitons only live about 20 ns in these materials. The transport was therefore not expected to go very far.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 10/ but transient microscopy can measure tiny displacements far below the diffraction limit! This is because you only need to determine the difference between the population width at different times and to determine the width, it´s all signal-to-noise! https://t.co/euf1S93g3q

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 11/ the precise determination of the width at different times is what allows us to determine the mean-square-displacement (MSD) of the population, and the slope of the MSD tells us how fast the carriers move.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
12/ back to the QD thin films: because they are so bright, signal to noise is awesome! So we showed that even the tiniest displacements could be resolved using transient microscopy... travelling just 10s of nm during their lifetimes!

https://t.co/paVtwvs0eh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 13/ this is a bit short of course for a solar cell, but turns out well for an LED for example. More important was all the info we got from these measurements... cause it turned out the transport was really not your conventional random walk.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 14/ As I mentioned, the slope of the MSD tells us how fast the carriers move. If the slope is constant, the speed is constant and we have a normal random walk. But for QDs the slope is never constant and transport is always slowing down (subdiffusion)! https://t.co/zSO0B95eii

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 15/ Carriers slowing down is a clear indication of a bumpy energy landscape. Carriers start at the top of the hills, move down relatively fast, but slow down as they reach the valleys.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 16/ We could relate this directly back to the tiny variations in size of the different QDs, which give tiny variations in the optical bandgap of the particles.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 17/ The study on QDs really showed the strength of transient microscopy, cause it turns out that in nanostructured semiconductors, transport almost never undergoes a standard random walk. This technique is what allows you to visualize that.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 18/ okay, going to try to wrap up this thread by showing some of the newer developments in transient microscopy. The early days used fluorescence as the probe of the carriers, but that only works for bright materials. What if your cariers dont like to emit light?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 19/ the @HuangLabPurdue for example haev pioneered transient absorption microscopy. Rather than looking at emission as the probe, they look at the change in absorption when a carrier is present. An extremely versatile technique! https://t.co/gGOrjJn4BK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
20/ and more recently, an interferometric scattering based technique has been developed by the Ginsberg group at Berkeley - an extremely powerful demonstration that really boosts the signal from any carrier! 
https://t.co/RPVNSfDA7n

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 21/ sorry for rambling on 😉... I´ll try to find some time later to tell you about more recent work from my own lab, where we use transient microscopy to visualize transport in perovskite materials! https://t.co/CY3RvrAirM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
ps: really nice review on the topic is this one by Ginsberg and Tisdale:
https://t.co/EiXmyFf1Ll

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
1/ ok, final thread of the day... let´s see if I can keep it shorter than the previous one 😉... we continue with transient microscopy, but now on the family of 2D perovskites! 

Specifically, how tiny changes in the perovskite composition have a huge impact on energy transport! https://t.co/v43h5DyQoN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2/ so perovskites are all the hype right now of course, showing really promising efficiencies for solar cells. Main issues that remain are related to the stability and this is where lower dimensional perovskites (such as 2Ds) can help.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3/ using long organic cations, you can cut up the conventional 3D perovskite lattice into layers, forming the 2D perovskite lattice. The long cations protect the soft inorganic lattice from exposure to air and humidity, improving the stability of the material. https://t.co/nTTocmLGGq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4/ but, cutting up your lattice changes everything in terms of carrier transport! Not only do you place these organic barriers there, the confinement of the carriers to a thin plane changes their interaction: free charges become bound electron-hole pairs (or excitons). https://t.co/oydM2yTzfI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
5/ so how do excitons move through these layers? Can they move between layers? And how do changes in the composition change the transport characteristics?

Due to their tunability, layered perovskites are a perfect platform to study structure-property relations 👌

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 6/ so first, if we want to study structure-property relations... we need to make different perovskite variations. Luckily, 2D perovskites are extremely forgiving and crystallise very easily from concentrated solutions... you literally see them grow! https://t.co/HDZnyhYvf3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 7/ we grow the crystals on glass slides and use good old scotch tape exfoliation to isolate single crystalline flakes large enough for transient microscopy measurements. https://t.co/SrYjJKrNXo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
8/ then we run our favorite experiment again, first on one of the typical 2D perovskites, with a phenethylammonium (PEA) organic spacer between the layers.

The population of excitons broadens fast, so transport in the 2D plane is efficient! https://t.co/AevUVWdd0G

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
9/ but what if we change the spacer to another commonly used example: butylammonium (BA)... 

to our surprise it behaved completely different! https://t.co/MLcgNj8vGl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
10/ if we translate it to a diffusion length L_D, it´s a massive difference! 

Why? Especially considering that the carrier live in the inorganic lattice, and the spacers should have little influence on the electronic properties. https://t.co/KNUK5mvYmu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 11/ by exploring more spacer cations, we found that exciton transport scales beautifully with the stiffness of the lattice, showing that exciton-phonon interactions are the dominant parameter determining transport. https://t.co/YYwAT2vwmw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 12/ knowing this relation between transport and lattice stiffness, we can now start thinking of designing even better 2D perovskites for energy transport. These results were summarized in the first big publication coming out of our madrid lab. https://t.co/k1laNQIDWs

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
13/ beyond the clear differences, transient microscopy can also give very subtle info on the details of transport, for example about the types of traps you have in your material. 
https://t.co/rvscrtX7fm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
14/ and how about interlayer transport? Turns out it is really quite efficient in 2D perovskites! 

https://t.co/FIumX55Jkn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 15/ more stories are coming up soon, as we are still exploring the large parameter space of these materials... and other systems are lying on the shelve... measurements take time though, and careful data analysis is crucial in this field!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 16/ last week we celebrated the PhD defence of @M1chaelSeitz, who has been the driving force of setting up this work. While it is sad to see talented people go, we can be very proud of the result! Luckily we have a very talented @Alvaro_Mgd who has taken over 🙂 https://t.co/bbGSndN3Et

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 17/ with that I close for the day! tomorrow I´ll be back her @RealSci_Nano  with some nanofabrication of nanomaterials!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:

"Nanoscale Energy Transport: The Motion Picture"

Longer conversation with @FerryPrins is out now 👇🎧

https://t.co/EseHse1jwg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
1/ Today I want to talk a bit about nanofabrication with nanomaterials! We are used to do nanofabrication on metals and crystalline semiconductors, but how to create structures out of softer nanostructured materials? 

for example, a pyramid from (roughly) 250.000 nanoparticles? https://t.co/JZkHMbsn4D

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2/ during my time @NorrisOMEL, we were always looking for new tricks to structure optical materials and improve their photonic properties. The specialty of the group was (and still is) a technique called template-stripping, but till then was mostly used on plasmonic metal films.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3/ template-stripping of metallic films was developed by David Norris together with Sang-Hyun Oh (@OhLabUMN) during their time together at Minnesota. 

It´s an amazingly powerful and simple technique to create extremely high quality structures! 

https://t.co/b39WZLdmkL https://t.co/pFt5S6CPij

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4/ You start with a simple Si wafer, and do your favorite patterning (litho&etch) to create what we call the template. You then evaporate your material onto the template and glue a glass slide (UV epoxy). Final step: you separate the glass slide with the metal from the template. https://t.co/e0ZL9NfrSc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5/ the beauty is that now you have exposed an ultrasmooth, patterned surface! While the evaporated metal film has nm-scale roughness, your stripped surface is as smooth as your silicon template. For plasmonics this is essential: any roughness can scatter your propagating plasmon.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
6/ ok, back to the patterning of nanoparticle films... can we use template stripping to structure thin films of colloidal quantum dots for example? 

The problem is that when your materials sticks too much to the silicon, the stripping gets ugly.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
7/ then we remembered this really nice paper by Lee et al., in which they make a silicon wafer super non-sticky (extremely hydrophobic) to QDs using a dense self assembled monolayer (SAM).

https://t.co/Bif2XsbOXC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
8/ so, template stripping of QD thin films using a template with a SAM? Works beautifully! 

drop cast your solution onto the template and just clip it of... https://t.co/ABkhznOg5k

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 9/ here are thin films of different colors of QDs, stripped from their templates shown on the left. https://t.co/ofnZxwJzlN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 10/ First structures we tried were simple gratings out of QDs, which would allow you to couple light out of the film more easily. This SEM image shows nicely the arrangement of particles for a 400 nm periodicity of a grating. https://t.co/3DURqt4tql

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
11/ so why the grating? Cause it can help the outcoupling of emission from the film. 

For a flat film of QDs, a lot of light get´s trapped into waveguide modes due to total internal reflection (a problem of momentum mismatch). This can be as much as 80% loss! https://t.co/Nzu3aQzw3C

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
12/ the grating creates Bragg scattering at the interface, giving the waveguided light a bit of extra momentum that helps it to couple to free space. 

by changing the periodicity of the grating, we can control which wavelength couples out under which angle. https://t.co/qDI5CLi1gR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
13/ here you can see circular gratings of different periodicities (pitches), where the red emission couples out under a straight 90 degrees angle for a periodicity of 400 nm.

So, patterning is a great way of improving the brightness of your QD film! https://t.co/gt1VQeALm3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
14/ we did a bunch of other demonstrations, mixing different colors, and making the patterned films on flexible substrates. 

https://t.co/BhDkolaDqf https://t.co/KSrIgN06LD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
15/ beyond gratings, you can also make waveguides out of QDs, and this turns out to be a great way to make a ring laser!

here you can see the transition from just waveguiding to the lasing action at higher pump fluence.

https://t.co/F4z24qtBaF https://t.co/WGmY627O1L

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
16/ the nice thing is that the template stripping can also be applied to other solution processable materials. 

Here an example of patterning of a perovskite thin film with feature sizes below a micron! 👇

https://t.co/060vf8pLEd https://t.co/8QqQPioxHq

tweets.text:
1/ so as I mentioned earlier, when we pattern the surface of a thin film of quantum dots with a periodic grating, we can control the angle of outcoupling of the emission. 

So how do we measure angles? A small thread on angle-resolved microscopy! https://t.co/HhXVfPgkz9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
2/ let´s think for a second about how an objective works: it collimates a cone of angles. This means that the so-called back-focal-plane (BFP) of the objective is a map of all the angles of the light! 

This is the basis for BFP imaging (aka fourier or k-space imaging) https://t.co/JXsz6n33IB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3/ the size of the BFP is given by the NA of the objective, and translates directly to the k-vectors (or angles) of the collected light. The larger the NA, the wider your angular map you can obtain.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4/ but how do you get this map? For this you need to introduce a Bertrand lens into your optical path. This sounds like a magical piece, but is just an ordinary lens placed at the focal length from the fourier plane of your collimating lens. https://t.co/FXikaEBJrf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
5/ flipping the Bertrand lens in and out in this configuration allows you to switch immediately from a real-space image to the fourier image.

there are many guides online, particularly good is this one by the group of Rashid Zia: https://t.co/EoR8DhoLhT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 6/ you get beautiful images of the angular emission patterns of your samples. In our case with the patterned circular gratings of quantum dot thin films, the right pitch gives a beam of light at perpendicular angle, while other pitches couple at higher angles giving donuts. https://t.co/no84Y0dHDl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
7/ it gets even better if you project your fourier image on the entrance slit of your imaging spectrograph... by dispersing the angular pattern you get direct access to the photonic band diagram of your structure! 

(shown here for a linear grating)
https://t.co/hIHpWqPeUF https://t.co/k5Nip6beFT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 8/ so check it out, cause angle-resolved microscopy and spectroscopy are really not as difficult as it sometimes sounds (I was surprised how easy it was when I first set it up). You can get a ton of extra info about your samples!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
9/ further reading: another really nice reference on this is from the group of Femius Koenderink @_amolf, where they set up angle-resolved microscopy with polarimetry. This paper contains a ton of nice technical details to help you. 

https://t.co/uqXFtBEIkp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
10/ another favorite of mine is this paper by Schuller et al on the measurement of the dipole orientations in 2D materials using angle-resolved microscopy: 

https://t.co/PoAXH25Gae

1/ Today: things I learned building up a new lab! 

Things I was told by helpful seniors beforehand 🙏 and things I wish I´d known 😬

parts of a long thread along the day:
1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝
2⃣-all things purchasing 💸
3⃣-staying sane ❤️

Part1⃣coming up! https://t.co/v9yrelQGMa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
2/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝

When you finally get that precious offer the temptation is high to just accept and jump right in... but no need to rush🙂 In many cases there is a ton of things to negotiate. Some examples of things I´ve come across👇

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝

👉 Most importantly, you can often negotiate your starting date. If you still have a year left on your PD, just wait! It´s precious time to wrap up things and start preparing construction of your lab and team. https://t.co/gPTjhi0qr3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
4/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝

👉 now, salaries and startup packages can often not be negotiated, but some places do give a relocation package if you (and your family) are coming in from abroad. Worth checking.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
5/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝

👉 absolutely critical is to get as much lab space as you can at the beginning. It´s the only time you can get space without going having to fight a massive department battle! Be generous on your estimates!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
6/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝

👉 if they are constructing a new lab for you, dont rush it! Of course you want the key as soon as possible, but an incomplete lab costs you time later on. Ask for all the connections and gas lines you may need!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
7/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝

👉 similarly, check what can be included in the construction budget. Getting fumehoods, exhausts, safety measures included saves money on your startup package (I´ve heard some people getting even laser tables included 😉)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
8/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝

👉 important: if you already owned some equipment at your old institution, negotiate that your new employer pays for the shipping and possible amortised cost.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
9/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝

👉 If you are planning to use a specific facility at your new institution a lot, you can sometimes negotiate a discount or even waiver of the user costs for your group. This can save you a lot of money in the long run!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
9/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝

👉 Negotiate your teaching load! Especially in the first year. You´re going to be overwhelmed just with building up everything and getting settles. Less teaching hours or even a complete exempt year can help a lot. https://t.co/19VsjIYc7k

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
10/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝

👉 If you are on a tenure track, get as clear as possible what are the conditions for your tenure evaluation! It may seem far away, but surprises halfway can cause huge amounts of stress toward the end.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
11/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝

👉 Finally, if you are moving to a new location with a family, try to get support for the job/school search through your new employer. In some cases, the university can even find direct employment for your spouse!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
12/ Part1⃣-before getting started (negotiate!) 🤝

OK, these where the things I could think of. if anyone has more tips (or questions), please share them in the comments! 

I´ll be back later with the next thread... navigating the madness of purchasing an entire lab from scratch!

tweets.text:
13/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸

This 2nd part is all on purchasing, which can be one of the most overwhelming things in the beginning. So now you have this start-up package - how to spend it without going crazy (and how to save some money along the way) https://t.co/R8rrsimO7q

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
14/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸

👉 vendors are your friends! Explain them your plans and let them think along. They can come up with surprising or innovative solutions! A state-of-the-art solution can give you advantage over the competition.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
15/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸

👉 Vendors are your friends, but please negotiate prices for everything, big or small! You´d be surprised how much margin there is... I´ve seen discounts up to 50% on big items. Play hard-to-get! https://t.co/ImkxjAFm9P

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
16/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸

👉 know what equipment more of less should cost before negotiating. Prices are never listed, so  talk to colleagues to get ballpark figures. "What´s your budget?" is the first thing a vendor will ask, and you better give a smallish number😉 https://t.co/uK4go6JpAx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
17/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸

👉 as with all bargaining, discounts get bigger when you buy in big quantities, so if you can combine different pieces of equipment into one big order from the same vendor, you may save money.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
18/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸

👉 I personally dont like to micromanage, but for big purchases it´s critical! I´ve lost months on some purchases because the paperwork of the public tender got messed up. Admin can be complicated, ask for help to seniors with experience! https://t.co/ar1ERnAxnK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
19/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸

👉 for capital equipment, local service beats the lowest price. For example, dont buy a glove-box if the vendor cannot guarantee a local service engineer. Flying in the engineer for repairs can cost a lot in the long run!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
19/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸

👉 same thing with the delivery... ask for details before buying! You´ll regret the moment they drop a massive crate on your doorstep and run off... (though it gives you awesome stories to tell when you´re older 😉) https://t.co/oUkQQS8ViW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
20/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸

👉 same thing with the installation... I had one vendor deliver me complex optical equipment and tell me I probably knew better than him how to align it... he was not my friend anymore after that 🤨. Make sure things are clear before buying.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
20/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸

👉 new lab discounts!!! yes, this is a thing. If you´re planning to spend a lot of small items with one vendor, they sometimes offer a new lab discount (usually 5-10% for a year). This is awesome!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
21/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸

👉 academic discounts!!! yes, this is also a thing. Some places offer you academic discounts, cause compared to industry, we are relatively poor. Just ask!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
22/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸

👉 check out the local workshop and make friends there! here @UAM_Madrid we have a great glass blower that only charges the raw materials... your Schlenck line is suddenly a 10th of the cost! Same for electronics and vacuum pieces. https://t.co/kuv8ou0lR2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
22/ Part2⃣-all things purchasing💸

👉 finally, talk to your admins to set up a good work flow of invoices and payments... it´s the only way to stay sane through the purchasing storm at the beginning... 

more on staying sane in the 3rd and final part of this loooong thread 🙂

23/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️

Perhaps the most important part of this thread: how to manage stress and not underestimate the risk of a burn-out when starting your faculty job... https://t.co/8xKoMHnhxp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
24/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️

👉put priorities, perhaps first get settled yourself. Many of us move to a new place/country for the faculty job... first arrange your housing, school, immigration, make sure you and your family are comfortable... juggling all at once can be too much.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
25/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️

👉think on how fast you want to grow your team... getting many people started right away costs a ton of time. It may be good to start small in the first year.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
26/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️

👉once you start having a team, dont be afraid to delegate some of the tasks. Dont overwhelm your students of course, but establishing group responsibilities is a great way to involve everyone in the lab.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
27/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️

👉a very pratical tool to protect your time a bit: Slack workspaces. You can automatically turn off notifications out of office hours and it clearly separates work messaging from your personal life. https://t.co/qA2ew1xnCD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
28/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️

👉similarly, dont be afraid to put out-of-office replies when you take some days off. You´d be surprised how many things already got resolved while you were away 😉 https://t.co/nepJHO86p1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
29/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️

👉think of the projects you want to tackle... maybe mix big ambitious ones with some lower hanging fruit. Biggest stress comes often from a lack of output in the beginning. A small methods paper after two years can help a lot 🙂

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
30/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️

👉finally, and most importantly, surround yourself with people that can support you... faculty colleagues that can mentor you and people outside of academia that you can blow off some steam with. Dont try to do it all by yourself!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
31/ Part3⃣- staying sane ❤️

ok, so much for all the unsolicited advice from my side. Starting your own group is a lot of fun, but there can be a lot of stress coming along with the new responsibilities. 

tldr: Pace yourself 🙂

1/ a change of scenery today, with a thread on single-molecule electronics! My favorite topic during my younger years as a grad student... 

👉 take an individual molecule and hook it up to an electronic circuit using two electrodes with about a nm separation👌 https://t.co/LXRiXO7pLy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
2/ it´s kind of your ultimate pleny-of-room-at-the-bottom experiment... 

it´s also pretty much a nightmare of failed device after failed device... 😉 https://t.co/Ex2A3gH840

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3/ now, of course you could just use an STM to measure the current through a molecule on a substrate, but for some people that´s not complicated enough: what if you want to make a transistor out of it? - meaning you need a gate electrode as well...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
4/ in 2000, in a paper that is one of the true classics of nanoscience, this impressive list of nanoscience pioneers reported on a the measurement of a single C60 molecule in a three-terminal device.
https://t.co/gcscd39hGB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5/ the key in this paper was the use of so-called electromigration to break a gold wire into nm-separated electrodes. Like this, you have a planar device that can be gated using a back electrode.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 6/ electromigration can be a pretty dramatic though: at very high current density in a metallic wire, the electrons start hitting the atoms so hard that atoms get displaced. It´s well known in integrated circuits as a source of breakdown.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
7/ to make nm-separated electrodes more reproducible, feedback control of electromigration was introduced by Strachan et al. This gave gaps that were way cleaner. https://t.co/f5XK0XsDvB

a number of such advances allowed us to do the final breaking way more gradual. https://t.co/0T0fHMY4F1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 8/ biggest issue was though that gold is not very stable at room temperature - it behaves almost like a liquid at the nanoscale! So unless you did all your measurements at cryogenic measurements, your gap would continue to grow and your molecule would not be able to bridge!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
9/ in comes my PhD project @tudelft: can we make a single molecule transistor that is stable a room temperature? 

So this meant stepping away from Au electrodes... it was not until my final year in 2011 that a completely failed experiment brought the solution.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 10/ I was helping a colleague cleaning graphene transistors using the feedback control I mentioned earlier. The surface of graphene can be cleaned at high current densities due to Joule heating. The feedback was to prevent it from blowing up, but this failed at some point.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 11/ Just for fun we checked the result under the AFM and to our surprise we saw that a beautiful nanogap had formed, exactly like an electromigrated gold nanogap! But of course, the covalent bond structure of graphene is fully stable at room temperature. https://t.co/QdNIWDGkge

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
12/ we optimized the feedback, and realized that this was more like "electroburning", making graphene react with oxygen at high temperatures. 

Still at the height of the graphene hype, the joke quickly became that even burned graphene serves a purpose.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
13/ so, long story short, we placed some molecules on our graphene nanogaps and managed to measure some gate modulation at room temperature! 

All well that ends well, but the four years of blowing up devices that led up to this were not easy 🙂

https://t.co/8bm6Vmp3uj https://t.co/NgCF3lilPH

For her was a huge surprise to discover that an atomic force microscope not only could be used to make images and characterize properties of a material, but also as a lithographic tool
Image: slide of PhD defense presentation in 2015 (the surprise lasted until then, still lasts) https://t.co/ADEISOQ3W6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: During my PhD, I developed my work using the oxidation SPL modality to fabricate nanostructures and electronic devices. In oxidation SPL, the AFM tip approaches to the surface. A voltage is applied between them, within a water meniscus.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The water meniscus acts like an electrochemical cell at the nanoscale. The high electric field formed inside the cell induces the hydrolysis of water. The oxygen species are directed to the sample oxidizing it.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The main parameters to control the width and height of the oxides are the relative humidity, the oxidation voltage and the oxidation time.
Source: https://t.co/97MqafyfNp https://t.co/6OV0onUN1A

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2013. "Single Nanometer Manufacturing for beyond CMOS devices" European project started. I worked in this project and I could learn a lot of lithographic techniques and be in contact with state-of-the art centres such as IMEC, IBM Zurich and beyond https://t.co/RvfvEEB0mF https://t.co/uNmMcAEwXw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I used o-SPL to fabricate silicon oxide masks on an ultrathin silicon on insulator substrates to achieve silicon nanowires by dry etching transfer (Reactive Ion Etching).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The control of the mask size by o-SPL parameters and the control of the RIE conditions were key to achieve the SiNWs with the highest resolution possible and fully transferred onto the 12 nm thick silicon top layer 
Source: https://t.co/6OaDR4agsp https://t.co/Ko7wO1VXV2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Different lithographic techniques: photolithography, electron beam lithography, focused ion beam, SPL...can be used to fabricate the same nanostructures o devices. Therefore, they must be compared and position each other in terms of resolution, cost-effectiveness and throughput

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I fabricated SiNW-based field-effect transistors by SPL and EBL using the same starting substrate (silicon on insulator) and the most similar geometry possible in order to check if the performance of the SiNW FETs fabricated by o-SPL were comparable to the ones fabricated by EBL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
And indeed! After rapid thermal annealing to improve the metal/SiNW contact, the devices fabricated by the two methods behave similarly!
Source: https://t.co/Fg6w7bSomx https://t.co/9x5Jj7rTKY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I started to discover also the 2D materials! We performed o-SPL on WSe2 thin layers. We controlled the size of the structures by controlling the relative humidity, the oxidation voltage and the oxidation time https://t.co/07g5WAmXlt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We also discovered that the oxides generated by o-SPL were soluble in water, so after wet etching in deionized H2O the oxides left a groove, since the oxides by o-SPL grow above and below the surface.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We could controlled the thickness of the oxides below the substrate surface as a function of the thikness of the oxides grown above the surface. We exploited this to define isolated high-resolution constrictions in WSe2 thin layers
Source: https://t.co/37sdZeoeCe https://t.co/TIISgugyc8

tweets.text:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In the story of my academic life, today: 
"CHAPTER II. POSTDOC AT IBM ZURICH AND THERMAL SCANNING PROBE LITHOGRAPHY (t-SPL)"
If you want to read the chapter, follow the #thread! https://t.co/N6AxqN1cRh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After I finished my PhD, I wanted to continue learning and working on SPL. I had the opportunity to do a postdoctoral stay in the group of Dr. Armin Knoll, the group where the thermal SPL was developed, at IBM Zurich where...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ...the Scanning Tunneling Microscope (Nobel Prize in Physics 1986) and the Atomic Force Microscope (Kavli Prize in Nanoscience 2016) were invented!!! https://t.co/Fra3K8Q6Fq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In thermal SPL, a devoted cantilever with three silicon legs that have different doping levels to heat the tip was developed. The technique has a close-loop system that allows the in-situ inspection of the written line and

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
the correction of the writing parameters for the next line. By this way, the user can monitor the writing process while happening and interrupt it if the patterning will not be successful.
Sources: https://t.co/3KjQdkcwd4
https://t.co/D8icGlgb5s https://t.co/cyhB6NGGVA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
t-SPL can be performed at ambient conditions, no cleanroom requirements are needed. The main parameters that control the size of the nanostructures are the tip temperature and the tip-sample contact force.
Also, t-SPL can be used to do 3D lithography with nanometric precision.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The hot tip can be used to indent resist layers or modify a material directly with the contact. The tip, when is "cold" can be used to image the topography of the written patterns like an AFM. If you want to read more: https://t.co/v0rz7MOfMO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Moreover, in t-SPL there is no need to fabricate localization markers because the topography of the buried nanostructures can be taken with the tool and then, design the patterns on the topo image and then, write the patterns:
Source: https://t.co/D3lQCePYWE https://t.co/fVOrT5l8CC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
During my stay at IBM Zurich, I studied the writing conditions, the thickness of the imaging resist layer (PPA) and the RIE conditions, achieving the record of resolution in t-SPL up to now: 7 nm wide SiNWs array at 14 nm half-pitch!!!
Source: https://t.co/NKifC0TwvY https://t.co/fBqULYZay2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I also participated in the fabrication of the first devices using a mix-and-match or hybrid lithography prototype that the lab at IBM Zurich had developed. Sequential lithographic techniques such as Electron Beam Lithography or Scanning Probe Lithography have a main drawback:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: a low-throughput. One of the strategies to overcome this issue is called: mix-and-match lithography. It consists in the combination of two or more lithographies in a cost-effective way, where the smallest nanostructures are defined by the high-resolution lithography and

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: the microstructures in large areas are defined by the high-throughput lithography.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In my group, a laser writing setup had been developed coupling it with the t-SPL writing setup. By this way, the high-resolution parts were fabricated by t-SPL and the large areas by optical lithography, within a single step, using a single tool. https://t.co/3oapg6sRUn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We demonstrated the fabrication of a set of two silicon single electron transistors in an area of 30x30 microns square in less than 5 minutes.
Source: https://t.co/u92t1c4cjA https://t.co/Afmy9or9ZG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Finally, I participated in a nice collaboration with the group of Prof. @MuranoPerez (@imb_cnm). We applied t-SPL in order to create guiding patterns to order blockcopolymer(BCP) domains at high-resolution.
Sources: https://t.co/CLAD5FgNvj
https://t.co/LfAbmwBAA5 https://t.co/ZX7GohBpaw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Finally...You must know! t-SPL has reached a high technological maturity (it keeps under continuous development), so much that the awesome tool is at the commercial level by @HeidelbergInstr @SwissLitho 
https://t.co/SyElLYuPSl https://t.co/MdK6TXPQdO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In the story of my academic life, today: 
"CHAPTER III. POSTDOCs AT ICMM (CSIC): OXIDATION SCANNING PROBE LITHOGRAPHY AND STRAINTRONICS
If you want to read the chapter, follow the #thread! https://t.co/37eaiSz70o

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After IBM Zurich I came back to Spain and I did first a postdoc stay in the group of my PhD supervisor, Ricardo Garcia, at ICMM (CSIC), to continue working in the systematization of o-SPL on 2D materials, concretely transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We discovered that o-SPL on pristine MoS2, MoSe2 and WSe2 thin layers did not produce nanopatterns with controllable sizes and geometry (height, depth, width, array of periodic nanowires...) because of the influence of the 2D materials crystal lattice symmetry...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Therefore, we had to grow a thin oxide layer on top of the MoS2, MoSe2 and WSe2 surface by a short oxygen plasma. This thin, uniform oxide layer screens the crystal lattice and allows to control the size of the structures by the oxidation parameters, as expected. https://t.co/7j3VG8Ybex

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Since we could now control the patterning of these 2D materials by o-SPL, for example, in the case of MoS2 thin layers, we were able to achieve a sub-10 nm constriction and we developed a process to fabricate nanoribbons based FETs (applicable for all the studied materials). https://t.co/8fiGz796aB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Sources: https://t.co/6RKLYhnw1U
https://t.co/ncn98fiWkM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Then, I had the opportunity to do a postdoc in the group of Dr. Andres Castellanos-Gomez, also in the same institute (ICMM, CSIC)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I participated in a review with @Andres_2DMat and @RiccardoFrisen2 about how to fabricate van der Waals superlattices using 2D materials. There are so many ways to modulate the properties of 2D materials😮 Look at this table!
Source: https://t.co/7d39tBi9kF https://t.co/69XMvUuI6t

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The review also earned a front cover, made by the fantastic scientist-artist @Scixel https://t.co/AH66ki0QC3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I also participated in a work inside the field of straintronics. We modulated the bandgap of MoS2 few layers by biaxial strain. This biaxial strain was induced transferring the MoS2 flakes by dry deterministic transfer (https://t.co/jhvHJT5fqN)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: into the middle of a metallic microheater fabricated by photolithography on polypropylene, a polymeric substrate. Under different applied voltages, the current through the microheaters heated the polymer causing the biaxial strain on the 2D material.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The different applicable temperatures induced different levels of strain, which were monitorized as shifts of the excitonic peaks by differential reflectance spectroscopy (https://t.co/4mOLVO6ank).
Source: https://t.co/j7J8jYcJm8 https://t.co/lN2KaobxVd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Finally today I am going to explain the current chapter in my academic life. https://t.co/b6oWqen4Y0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I work as a postdoc at Instituto de Sistemas Optoelectrónicos y Microtecnología (Universidad Politécnica de Madrid) @IsomUpm, in the group of ISOM Graphene. The institute is a member of the cleanroom network #Micronanofabs, together with @imb_cnm and @upvntc https://t.co/iqRVhz1iu5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @IsomUpm has a lot of cool instruments to perform photolithography, electron beam lithography, to grow thin magnetic and semiconductor films, to do dry etching,  to characterize the materials and devices electrically and structurally... (Just to name a few from the list!!!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For a person who loves lithography and optoelectronic devices...It is like working in Disneyland!😆

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In our group, ISOM Graphene, we work with graphene fabricated by different methods for three main applications: health, ICT and energy.
https://t.co/gjx1GSYm2q

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I am inside the research line of the group corresponding to graphene in energy applications.
(a) We are exploring graphene monolayers as transparent electrodes and active components in solar cells.
(b) porous graphene foams/networks for supercapacitors.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We love graphene for energy applications because we believe that this exceptional material can contribute to reach some of the Sustainable Development Goals defined by UN
https://t.co/MsIV1W7Yv8 https://t.co/dBPbnpKBJe

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I started to work in the group in 2020 just before the pandemic scenario and the lockdown!!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But during this time, I had the chance to read a lot of bibliography about graphene based solar cells and supercapacitors and our group published a cool review on graphene-based supercapacitors.
https://t.co/tdHWg1OYCp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It earned a cover, which Andrés Velasco @And95es designed gorgeously! It represents a graphene-foam nanocity 🤣 https://t.co/ylD9HMWRpT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And now, during 2021, we could come back to the labs and do a lot of cool experiments again😎...So stay tuned to see our future works!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: With this, I have finished to tell you the story of my academic life. It seems that started with scanning probe lithography to lately, more directed to 2D materials...However, don't think I have forgotten SPL at all! When the love is real...😉
