tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Hello everybody!

My name is Servet Ozdemir (@ServetOzdemiro) and I will be in charge of the @RealSci_Nano Twitter account this week. 

I hope to keep you stimulated with interesting tweets. Today I will let you know about who I am, what I do and how I got here.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Due to my passion for #physics back in school days, as an undergraduate I have enrolled to a BSci + MPhys degree at University of Warwick (@warwickuni). Here, as I progressed through my degree, I fell in love with solid state physics which has huge overlaps with #nanoscience

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: During my Master's year at Warwick I was working on fascinating two dimensional electron transport properties of traditionally grown #Germanium #Quantumwells and it was during this project I came across #graphene and the wonderful physics displayed by it.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Following my deep interest in #graphene and #2Dmaterials I have enrolled at Univerisity of Manchester(@OfficialUoM) Graphene NOWNANO Centre of Doctoral Training(@NOWNANO_CDT) where after receiving an initial 6months training in graphene and nanomaterials I started my #PhD project

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For my #PhD project I was fortunate enough to work as a student of Sir Kostya Novoselov, the co-discoverer of #graphene. Following on from my masters project, my PhD topic became electron transport properties of van der Waals heterostructures of graphene and #2Dcrystals.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: During my PhD I was fortunate enough to be part of the team that carried out first ever systematic investigation of electron transport properties of nanostructures of #rhombohedral #graphite crystals encapsulated by #hBN substrates which made it to @Nature https://t.co/8KSlI4GTLt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Aside from that, I was also involved in demonstration of a novel, CVD grown, hBN embedded graphene quantum dots as vertical tunnelling #single #electron #transistors.

https://t.co/QLAgkZ58NK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Another work I carried out during my PhD was demonstration of hBN encapsulated Graphene as a #hot electron #lightbulb in #air. You can check this work out open access using the link below

https://t.co/cElxBzhDDg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As well as rhombohedral structural phase of graphite, I also had a chance to be involved in experiments demonstrating a dimensional reduction accompanied #quantum #hall #effect and layer parity in over a 100nm's of hexagonal graphite. This work was on the cover of @NaturePhysics https://t.co/MlfNyA1HqX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
You can check this paper out using this link
https://t.co/BHqbVWR4YB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Having finished and submitted my PhD thesis, titled 'Electronic Properties of Rhombohedral Graphite' in September 2020, I am currently working as a research associate at the Quantum Photonics Laboratory of Prof. Brian Gerardot @HeriotWattUni

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hi again, its my Day 2 on the @RealSci_Nano account today as @ServetOzdemiro. Today I will give a brief history of the field of 2D materials from a physicists perspective, how it all began in 2004 and where it is now! 🙂

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The story begins with the paper 'Electric field effect in atomically thin carbon films' published in the journal @ScienceMagazine. The incredible Sir Kostya Novoselov was able to find extremely thin pieces of graphite crystals down to 1 atom thickness. https://t.co/F7CrZla1Hr

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Remarkably, the 1 atom thick graphite pieces, which was dubbed as graphene long before 2004 was isolated using a very simplistic method namely by using the adhesive properties of a scotch tape to detach graphene layers attached to each other by van der Waals forces. https://t.co/TFZzxppuzT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Only a year after the publication of the first paper in 2004, two papers have appeared back to back in @Nature in 2005. The papers reported relativistic nature of the electrons in graphene, with Berry phase manifesting itself in the observed quantum Hall effect.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Here are the links to two papers, first one by Novoselov and Geim from Manchester group:
https://t.co/810B1INxjX

And the second one by the group of Philip Kim which was at the time at Columbia
https://t.co/FQsMfRym27

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Geim and Novoselov also in 2005 showed that scotch tape method was applicable to other crystals, reporting isolation of atomically thin layers of Boron Nitride, and Transition Metal Dichalcogenides in a paper titled 'Two dimensional atomic crystals'
https://t.co/xX3TRCzkTh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In the coming years, en explosion of research occurred in the field of nanoscience on graphene, which is touched upon on this early review article
https://t.co/5KDVS1BpCL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In 2010, just as some were believing that things were saturing in the field,   Hone and Dean et al. from Columbia have shown superior electronic properties of graphene when it is on top of an atomically smooth hBN substrate. https://t.co/LFZbPeY8hR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
At this point, the field has moved from studying isolated 2D crystals to studies of van der Waals heterostructures of them, showing that by combining crystals with different properties in a specific way, unique physics can be unleashed. 
https://t.co/yadvmzTajl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In 2013, three groups have demonstrated a fractal phenomenon in the altered electronic structure of graphene (when it's aligned with hBN substrate crystal) known as Hofstadher Butterfly, for which the observation previously required gigantic magnetic fields which wasn't possible. https://t.co/xbMXclr33G

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Links to the 3 papers are:

https://t.co/X7gtjfKSy4

https://t.co/h7wLFAzl1y

https://t.co/71jahZYQiL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Things have also become very stimulating in the field from an #optical perspective when 4 groups in 2015 have demonstrated single photon emission from localized sites in 2D semiconductor WSe2 flakes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Below are the links to 4 papers:

https://t.co/JMyEY4jeHY

https://t.co/eEid0miRfb

https://t.co/ANAGmay62Z

https://t.co/Jc2rzkbA4Q

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Despite the observation of many exotic phenomena including Ising superconductivity in MoS2 and NbSe2, no intrinsic magnetism was observed in any 2D crystal ubtil 2017, when a layer dependent ferromagnetism was shown on air sensitive CrI3 crystals.
https://t.co/pPeRDiAOGM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The moire superlattice work initially kickstarted on hBN/graphene heterostructures took a completely different spin in 2018 when Herero group from MIT showed superconductivity on the predicted moire flat bands of two 1.1° aligned graphene crystals.
https://t.co/r60vhOfFiF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Twistronics, 2D Magnetism and Excitonics remain to be current hottest topics in the field of 2D Materials 🙂.

tweets.text: @igordownunder My apologies 🙏

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
@igordownunder Below is the link to 5th paper 🙂
https://t.co/kNd9yUJbAJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hello, today my Day 3 as the @RealSci_Nano content curator as @ServetOzdemiro. Today I will talk about the fascinating physics I discovered during my PhD on rhombohedral graphite crystals 🙂

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Natural #graphite occurs in two forms, which are namely, the Bernal hexagonal stacking and the #rhombohedral stacking which are both illustrated on the picture below. https://t.co/VqlssA2LH2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Due to the Bernal graphite being more energetically abundant, experimental investigations into Rhombohedral graphite were limited to a few layers, until Henni et al. showed rhombohedral stacking on exfoliated graphite crystals up to 16 layers in 2016
https://t.co/942Xz4Dqpt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This was very exciting from an electronics point of view, as rhombohedral graphite thin films are a 3D generalisation of simplest 1D topological insulator system Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain https://t.co/rkyvC2UHH9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Therefore, being a nodal line semimetal in bulk limit, rhombohedral graphite in thin film limit had flat bands with simplest tight binding calculations suggesting a p^N dispersion, where N is the number of layers, being susceptible to magnetic and superconducting interactions.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
https://t.co/ZmcA7f3he8

https://t.co/ArszJbLGT1

https://t.co/jTV7lZSV5r

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Plenty of electronic interactions being predicted at the low energy limit, the challenge was to study scotch tape exfoliated rhombohedral domains in high quality electronic devices after encapsulating them with hBN crystals
https://t.co/Pv1WB67ZtS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Following finding of rhombohedral domains in hBN encapsulated graphite flakes, electronic devices in form of Hall bars were formed, enabling Landau level spectroscopy in presence of magnetic fields https://t.co/RchEwwaB7C

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Following magnetic field characterisation of the samples, aftwr reaching to temperatures down to 10mK, we have found that the electronic structure of rhombohedral graphite films is an N-layer generilisation of graphene, with flat bands being quadratically dispersing https://t.co/9ZOG8FaZPo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Being accompanied by a Berry phase of NPi, the flat bands display a spontenous metal-insulator transition for the case of 9-12 layers of graphene thick samples with magnetic field characterisation suggesting a magnetic nature of the gap responsible for the transition https://t.co/eFlUYV2jX0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Being an alternative to twisted graphene systems, the predicted superconductivity in rhombohedral graphite is yet to be seen. For more details on rhombohedral graphite please look at our paper published last year @Nature 
https://t.co/8KSlI4GTLt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hello everyone, for a 4th day content on the @RealSci_Nano account, today I will be tweeting about the work of my current research group, Quantum Photonics Laboratory of the Heriot Watt University, on 2D materials and van der Waals heterostructures.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
One of the early works of the group on 2D crystals was demonstration of strain induced single photon emission sites, on mono- and bi-layer WSe2 flakes, on nano-pillars fabricated by e-beam lithography. Here is the link for the paper
https://t.co/syOdsQvxQ3 https://t.co/J7Zu9WiT7P

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Another work of the group was demonstration of out-of plane luminescent excitons in air sensitive monolayer InSe crystals in contrast to in-plane ones in WSe2 and MoSe2
https://t.co/cnUl4yHK6Z

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Utilizing a monolayer hBN tunnel barrier to separate a quantum dot in monolayer WSe2 from a Fermi reservoir in few layer graphene in 2019 the group reported Columb blockade accompanied by spin conserving tunnelling of charges through the hBN
https://t.co/uW1mjXhTaJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In 2020, spin-layer locking on interlayer excitons trapped in moire potentials formed in a heterostructure of bilayer 2H-MoSe2 and a monolayer WSe2 was reported. This lead to two types of excitons with distinct spin-layer-valley configurations.

https://t.co/Y9vDDbbnnD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There are currently two preprint on Arxiv about moire trapped interlayer trions in WSe2/MoSe2 heterobilayer and Coulomb staircases in moire superlattice
https://t.co/YkqunkQlzz
https://t.co/oexCBBiY9T

Broadly, the goal of my PhD was to find new ways in which nanophotonics could improve the performance of solid-state light-emitting devices. 

We focused on arrays of resonant metallic nanostructures (nano-antennas), which enhance the light emission from a top layer👇 https://t.co/fUfDiJHF8H

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I'll highlight some results, but first an overview of PhD papers:
I published 20 articles, including 4 PRLs, 1 PRX, 2 LS&A, 1 Nano Lett, 1 ACS Nano / Phot. etc. In 14 papers, I am 1st or co-1st author. 
I worked hard, but most important I had an AMAZING team and tech support. https://t.co/vYnJBIdEUa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
My first PhD paper was in PRX 👇

We studied metallic nanoparticle arrays supporting collective optical resonances. These emerge from  coupling localized surface plasmons to diffraction. 

We coined the term SURFACE LATTICE RESONANCE, now used by many

https://t.co/uUgsDQX4gm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
These resonances were actually first studied inthe 80s, by KT Carron et al:
https://t.co/gu2SR9F73f

~20 years later, GC Schatz et al. revived interest in them when they found extremely sharp (for plasmonic standards),  <1 meV, resonances.

J. Chem. Phys. 121, 12606 (2004); https://t.co/7vj4nyCVKi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Few years later came this 👇 important/beautiful paper from the group of Prof. Bill Barnes at Exeter.

They reported collective resonances in Au (no data supporting collectiveness)

BTW: I highly admire Bill Barnes: Brilliant, playful, & humble scientist

https://t.co/BEs6bJ7JnX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So we followed up on that, and published another nice result in my PhD. 👇

We showed (exp+theory) that surface lattice resonances are indeed collective, i.e. their quality factor depends on the number of particles (see legend below) in the array. 

https://t.co/DAUrQELJHT https://t.co/GWK0ACIkBZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
You may now wonder: Who cares about these collective resonances in metallic nanoparticle arrays?

Why was it so important that these resonances )in contrast to localized surface plasmon resonances) are sharp?

What are the implications? https://t.co/kgIklvHuAj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Around that time we put a thin luminescent layer on top of metallic nanoparticle arrays supporting SURFACE LATTICE RESONANCES. 

Lo and behold, the light emission from the layer got A LOT brigher!

White spot below is blue laser + yellow luminescence. Diffraction -> small spots. https://t.co/aY0CfsjJo2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
When I showed the above effect to my advisor, he got extremely excited. 

He called the BIG BOSS at Philips, so he could, with the naked eye, see the light emission enhancement from metallic nano-antennas.

When the big boss saw this, a LOT (!) of money came in from our research https://t.co/EKKZh9QLAB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
With that money, the group massively expanded and deepened on "Plasmonics for Solid State Lighting".

The idea was simple: Replace lossy and bulky secondary optics in modern LEDS (see 👇) with metallic nanoatennas!

The antennas  enhance & redirect light emitted from the layer. https://t.co/6TTLKEGBvj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We published LOTs of nice papers on how metallic nanoatennas can enhance light emission from thin layers. We probed configurations similar to those in modern white LEDs, where a blue LED pumps a yellow phosphor to create white light (blue+ yellow=white).  Brief highlights below.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Here we showed how to get direction emission from  surface lattice resonances (SLRs) in nanoatenna arrays:

https://t.co/7vU1bftP66

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Then we published this nice paper (my most cited one) where we showed, in greater detail, the various ways in which metallic nano-antennas could revolutionize solid-state lighting.

https://t.co/b4t5skAimn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We also used plasmon resonances to couple into guided modes in luminescent layers.

We found👇  how nanoantennas can enhance the light emission (local field at emitter position) despite being nearly transparent in the far field!

https://t.co/KzvJXKPU81

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:

We showed that by breaking the symmetry of the metallic nano-antennas out of the periodicity plane, we could fulfill a long-standing goal in solid-state lighting: Emit light in one direction only!

https://t.co/UwwNEINmX8

In this 4th and final 🧵 for today, I will share with you my postdoc experience. 

During the PhD, I became very interested in polaritons: hybrid light-matter quasi-particles formed by strong exciton-photon coupling in a cavity.

tweets.text:
So I went to one of the best experimental groups in the world of polariton physics: The group led by Jacqueline Bloch and Alberto Amo, at the Center for Nanoscience and Nanotechnologies @C2N_com  (back then called LPN) in France.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Shortly after I arrived, I received the news that I was granted a Marie Curie individual fellowship. My proposal received a grade of 97% (!) thereby ranking among the highest of all physics in Europe. 
The proposal was about taking polaritons a step closer to the quantum regime. https://t.co/ZebNCe5o38

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
First paper from my postdoc:

We showed how to control the phase that photons pick, when hopping from one cavity to another, via the incident optical power (effective photon-photon interactions).

Check out the phase measurements in there 😉

https://t.co/IqSdXN1LrN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Then came the most extensive & important work from my postdoc: 

We probed a Dissipative Phase Transition (DPT) of light by measuring the dynamic optical hysteresis of a micro cavity.  👇

https://t.co/AvBuWovAvB https://t.co/70BhmxmONL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
A DPT is to dissipative systems what a 'normal' phase transition is to Hamiltonian systems.  Instead of the  Hamiltonian gap closing at the transition, the Liouvillian gap closes. 
Its really fascinating physics! A new way to understand phase transitions of open quantum systems.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The physics of DPT and dynamic optical hysteresis has strong connections to the beautiful & universal physics of the famous Kibble-Zurek Mechanism, relevant to many areas of condensed matter physics 👇

Check out our PRL mentioned above for details. https://t.co/IduGaUhkeX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:

That powerful realization would re-orient my career, again. https://t.co/MsXoLUTNMo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The name of my group is 'Interacting Photons'.  

Hopefully that tickles some of you. It's "common wisdom" that photons do NOT interact. 

IF free-space photons would interact, we would see them scatter off each other, like 👇

But we dont see that!

Image: Christine Daniloff/MIT https://t.co/2175qOciKn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The trick is  that IN NONLINEAR MATERIALS photons effectively interact.  To make interactions stronger, we confine the photons to a small volume where the nonlinear material is.
We achieve that with a pair of mirrors facing each other, which make a cavity. 

Our typical system 👇 https://t.co/WTh02CueYT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Yoy may now wonder: Why go through all that trouble *just* to make photons interact? https://t.co/fIwoF2ZEq0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Well, there's really a LOT you can do IFF photons interact.  To give you a flavor: Some of the things we look at are novel optical sensors, computing systems, signal transmission schemes , funky nonlinear dynamics, memories, energy harvesters, and more.  Ill share that later   😉

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But if the above doesnt resonate with you, then this is the killer argument to make photons interact:  You can make lightsabers, a la Star Wars!  

Two of my group members (Falco & Giel) showed how to control one light beam with another in the @amolf open day 2 of years ago 👇 https://t.co/wACM4bjX8k

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There are several nonlinear optical materials where photons can effective interact. In my group we use two materials.
1. A drop of oil (like olive, castor, or macadamia oil)

2. Semiconductors (like perovskite, the beloved one of our solar cells friends)

Pros & cons below figs👇 https://t.co/Zi1jwJsQMg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I still recall the first time I told my colleagues (and student): Let's put olive oil in the cavity!

Everyone laughed 👇

Honestly, I felt uncofortable.🙄

But then it worked !!!!! https://t.co/sd3GGY9Nms

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Let me first tell you how I got into this topic.

As a postdoc, I was studying a new type of dissipative phase transition of open quantum systems. 👇

Noise played a prominent role in those experiments, so I started to dig more into 'stochastic systems'

https://t.co/AvBuWovAvB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
During my literature search, and also hearing 1 colleague  (who is now retired) in the field of polaritons, I came across the term "STOCHASTIC RESONANCE".

This is a phenomenon wherein a certain amount of noise (in a nonlinear system) AMPLIFIES a periodic signal. I was 👇 https://t.co/06dVOdt5Qu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
STOCHASTIC RESONANCE was introduced as a plausible explanation for the recurrence of ice ages in our planet. 
https://t.co/45H3RADhEm

Did you know our planet goes into an ice age every 10^5 years or so?  

It was really difficult to explain this time scale. But SR *could* do it. https://t.co/KfSKFYXAgQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There are actually much 'faster' variations in our planet's temperature too. See e.g. the figure👇, taken from https://t.co/u1TZToDCYX
Every time I see this plot, I realize:
a)We're so lucky to live in a warm (unstable) RARE EVENT
b)Our planet's T is so fragile to perturbations! https://t.co/hzsjMQ8EDE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We literally owe life in this planet, as we know it, to noise.  

So how does that work? 

I'll try to explain the mechanism of Stochastic Resonance in the next few  tweets👇 https://t.co/08daYYuSCv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
First: Huge Thanks to @KJH_Peters for the GIFs!

Imagine you have a Brownian particle in a double well potential (DWP), like this 👇

The particle's position fluctuates, due to (thermal) noise. Meanwhile, the DWP is modulated at period T. For weak noise, the part stays in 1 well. https://t.co/xJWV1eIqQl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If the noise strength increases a little, the particle can now make *random* jumps between the potential wells, like this👇 https://t.co/SkRW0ZSjEl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If the noise is VERY strong, the particle now makes LOTS of random jumps between the potential wells. Notice there are many (>>2) jumps per modulation period. https://t.co/rlXN8u58C9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But if the noise strength is right --- not too weak, not too strong ---, the random jumps of the Brownian particle can synchronize with the modulation. 👇

This occurs when the mod. period T is ~twice the avg escape time of the particle from a well.

THIS IS STOCHASTIC RESONANCE. https://t.co/AgFvJCapNN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This simple model - Brownian particle in a double well potential - allows us to understand SO much.
You'd be surprise to discover how many different systems, dead & alive, can be understood in this way. 

And so many display STOCHASTIC RESONANCE!

Some examples below👇

Seeing all this made me curious.

How can stochastic resonance  manifest in so many systems, when the phenomenon itself is so fragile?

Remember we have to match the escape time to the modulation period, and the escape time depends EXPONENTIALLY on barrier heigth / noise strength

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So we took a step back, and went to the beginning. Really, the beginning👇

Remember Newton's laws?

Well, fundamentally, they're wrong.  He argued that there are instantaneous forces. 

But NOTHING responds instantaneously! https://t.co/8ABnuWIHrH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Examples: When you pull a rope, someone at the other side doesnt feel your force instantaneously. The 'pull'  has to travel via rope, and that takes time.

Or if you dial up the heating (or cooling), that also takes time. https://t.co/wbMocTSs03

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So we took at look at what happens to stochastic resonance when you let the NONLINEAR part of the force be non-instantaneous.
We start from a so-called overdamped Langevin equation (x=position, F=force, \Xi =noise), and then we introduce a memory kernel for the nonlinearity. https://t.co/dDDJwm9kQk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The oil-filled optical cavity I mentioned yesterday is nicely explained by such a model. 
However, instead of position, we describe the light field in the cavity.  The non-instataneous nonlinearity arises because the oil takes some time to warm up after the laser hits it 😉 https://t.co/UfXJsB0NCB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We then imprint a signal on the incident (continuous wave) laser by modulating the cavity length. 

Further, we add noise to the laser's amplitude and phase using modulators. 

So our experiment looked liked this 👇 https://t.co/ZH2JnMoJdR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We then measured the transmitted signal to noise ratio (SNR) as a function of the *input* noise.

And found the peak characteristic of stochastic resonance. 

So our optical signal is amplified by a finite amoutn of noise. https://t.co/hCswN47Zcn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The cool part of the experiment 
(details here: https://t.co/uzVKP3VQHJ  )

is that the frequency range over which we could observe stochastic resonance is enhanced, BY ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE, thanks to the non-instantaneous nonlinear response 😁

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In that paper we also consider, theoretically, applications to energy harvesting. We find that the non-instantaneous nonlinearity can enhance the efficiency of those devices by a factor of 10 or more! 😮

Hello friends! Today I share about the fascinating physics of fluids of light! 🧵

Did you know that light in a cavity behaves like a fluid?

Top image is a boat cruising through a lake.

Bottom image is our laser cruising through the cavity mirrors and scattering off a defect.😮 https://t.co/1iuEmNmVEH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Normally, when light encounters an obstacle it scatters. Then, incident & scatttered light interfere, resulting in fringes. See image above 👆

However, in 1999 Chiao et al. predicted that  light may transition to a SUPERFLUID and flow without scattering!

https://t.co/IfCKUNY4V5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
However, to realize superfluid light,  photons need to interact. And they normally dont. 

So, Iacopo Carusotto & @CristianoCiuti  proposed leveraging the strong interactions of polaritons (1/2 light, 1/2 exciton quasiparticles) to realize superfluidity!
https://t.co/5dAswzs3Xd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This is a figure copied from their article, cited 👆

On the left you see a polariton fluid scattering off a defect in the center. 

On the right you see a polariton superfluid, which doesnt scatter. To get there, they increased the laser power (fluid density).

Amazing effect!😉 https://t.co/2VMig92Si8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Then, in 2009 came these beautiful experiments by Alberto Amo (one of my postdoc advisors) et al verifying the predictions of Ciuti & Carusotto. 
https://t.co/wveXhNNlU8

Left: 'Normal' polariton fluid, scattering off a defect.
Right: Polariton SUPERfluid, flowing past the defect https://t.co/YvT6Q6BGLa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The results above gave birth to a new research field called "Quantum fluids of light". 

Results up to 2013 were reviewed in this nice & didactic Review of Modern Physics by Carusotto & Ciuti.  Check it out if you're curious about the physics 😉

https://t.co/ro1Fi8nWan

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The experiments of Amo et al used a sample at ~5K. It needed to be so cold for polaritons to exist and strongly interact. 

So several researchers began working on new platforms where superfluids of light can exist at room temperature.

Major result 👇

https://t.co/vtWuCbMFJU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The above result (group of Daniele Sanvitto) is VERY nice. They showed, for the first time, a polariton superfluid at room temperature.

However, since interactions in organics are so weak, they pumped the sample with a powerful amplified laser. And the fluid died within 0.1 ps😖

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Inspired by all results above (+others), my group started an experiment aimed at observing superfluidity of light (photons, not polaritons) at room temperature AND in steady state. Imagine: A photon superfluid that lives forever😮

Our sample👇:  A cavity filled with olive oil 😋 https://t.co/2q0el5692c

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Together with Giel Keijsers (formerly MSc, now PhD student ) we got some nice results: https://t.co/ppmnaWyVeB

Check out our preprint if you're curious about how a drop of olive oil between 2 mirror can suppress scattering of a light 😉

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Here an movie of our data. 

Left: Real space, laser flows left-to-right to defect.  
Right: Momentum space. 

As time progresses, the photon fluid velocity increases. We start in the superfluid state, which later breaks down at high velocities -- fringes & backscattering appear. https://t.co/V2qpRRRXC8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Our manuscript shows many nice measurements. But, I admit, results are not as strong & conclusive as we would like. The referees, while most supporting publication, picked on that. 

So we've been doing new experiments for past months. We have amazing result in store for them😁

Hello friends!  Before leaving this account, I'd like to share valuable insights  & experiences I gained as PhD #student, #postdoc, and #newPI.  These are on various aspects of science.

My insights are obviously not universal. Please take them with a 'big grain of salt'.
Open 🧵

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #1.  NEVER EVER write an email when overwhelmed by emotion. This is especially relevant when the emotion is anger, regardless of whether it is justified or not.  When receiving  bad / unpleasant news, it's best to let it rest AT LEAST 1-2 days before responding.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
#2. In myself and in my scientific team members,  I welcome every feeling/state (expressed with respect)  EXCEPT BOREDOM.

A person that is bored has lost curiousity, and awareness of how little she/he knows of this AMAZING universe.  There is always something great to learn!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
#3 A. When searching for PhD/PD position, many these days recommend setting "emotional support" as no. 1  in search criteria.  

I never did that. For em. supp. I have my wife, my parents, close friends, and coach. Of course, em. support from PI is very important, but not enough.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In a #PI, I searched for someone with:
1. Inspiration & Creativity
2. Scientific & Personal Qualities which I lack, and ability to teach them
3. Resources
4. Ability to guide with enthusiasm
5. Local environment where I can thrive 
6. Strong Internatl Network
7 Easy to talk with

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
#4. You can learn what you need along the way. 

Ex: As young student, I thought I should the be able to solve all (or nearly all) problems in Jackson (hard book!) before doing any research in E&M / Optics.  I was wrong. Solid foundation is good, but adaptability also. 

.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
#5. A highly DANGEROUS time (physically) for an academic is during PhD thesis writing. 

I foolishly thought "I will not stand until I finish writing this section". So I spent too many hours sitting.  I injured my back badly (sciattica) and suffered for years after. Health FIRST!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #6. Between my PhD and PD, I published my 1st single-author paper. I highly recommend that.  It's a good way to demonstrate independence, as well as ability to conceive, implement, and finalize a scientific project. It can also prove good writing skills --- essential in academia.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #7. Every paper that I wrote eventually got published. Sometimes many things had to change, and once the revision process took 3 years. But eventually it was published. So I've learned not to sweat paper rejections. I know the outcome 😉 (Grants are different 😖).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #8. As #newPI in experimental group, I've learned to ask my students if they would like me to  join them in their experiment. Some students feel pressured by my presence. Others feel supported. So I just ask , and I'm happy to join when my presence helps. And not sad otherwise.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
#9. When responding to referees, remember: their (our) only reward is the satisfaction of helping a good paper become better (rejected papers appear elsewhere later). 
So I listen to referees & follow their advice as much as possible. It's better than to fight them all the time😉

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
#10. When a Referee is unreasonable/absurd (rare, but can happen), remember:  we do NOT have to convince Referees. The Editor decides. 
That's why I rather publish in journals where Editorial decisions can be assessed by members of the science community via appeals, if necessary.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
#11. Time is our most valuable resource.
Many people ask: Is this an idea worth researching, or a paper worth writing?  That's a bad question - can lead to time waste.

I rather ask: Is this the *best* idea worth researching, or best paper worth writing, given our possibilities?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
#12. More experiments/data alone rarely lead to deeper understanding.  Actually, they often strengthen  the confusion.

Understanding emerges from our ability to reproduce and predict partial observations using a "simple" model/abstraction of reality.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
#13. For me, the best experiments (worth doing) are those for which I don't know the result in advance, can surprise me, or are beyond theoretical reach.   

Otherwise, if the theory has been tested to death, and we know it faithfully models our system, why do the experiment?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
#14. I've seen many students choose to work on a topic because of its *potential* relevance to an issue they care about, e.g. health, sustainability.   But many soon realize that they do not enjoy their daily activities so much.

Daily inspiration is AS IMPORTANT as purpose.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
#15. A great challenge as a PI: 
When someone systematically doesn't honor IMPORTANT agreements (they may think it's not important), how to express that behavior is unacceptable WITHOUT diminishing their motivation?
Nobody likes to be reminded of agreements they didnt fulfill.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Todayyy a short thread about our favorite issue in the lab! Exfoliation!!! 😍

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As you probably know, exfoliation is a technique to obtain very thin samples of layered materials. And it's very extended! So, if you are familiar with the technique, do not hesitate and tell us your experience :) (luckily I'll complete the thread with some pics tomorrow)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: First of all, you need a small (but macroscopic) piece of the material that you want to use. And put some of it in a scotch tape. Then, you peel it with the tape, and if you are lucky, there will be some very thin and large layers of whatever you are exfoliating...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Directly pressing the substrate where you want to build the sample against the tape. Then, look in the optical microscope and search if there is any layer adhered to your substrate.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There may be many, but if you are interested in a specific thickness and area, finding a good one usually takes many tries and a lot of time...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I think that the second most common technique is, first, pressing a layer of a viscoelastic material (such as PDMS) and then transferring it to the exact place where you want your flake to be.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you put everything in contact, and then tear the viscoelastic very slow and gently, the flake will remain where you put it in the substrate. Some groups use commercial PDMS, others make their own... what do you think is better?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Also this transferring technique allows making heterostructures of many layers, as you know exactly where the new flake will be in the substrate. You can even create rotated samples!!!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But I forgot to talk about the most important thing when preparing samples 😱 which material do you want? 😱

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The only thing you need to know before starting to exfoliate, is if your material can be layered. The difficulty will vary depending on the interaction between the layers, so you need a lot of patience. Also optical contrast will change depending on the material and thickness.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is something that a lot of people do, specially at the beginning of our journey in 2D materials, and can be a bit boring and/or stressful, so I'd recommend that you exercise your eyes and let them rest while listening some good song! Can you recommend any?

Good morning!
Today's and tomorrow's thead(s) will be about AFM and its possibilities.
Today: I'll tell you the two basic modes to take topography images, and some other techniques I've used so far.
Tomorrow: techniques I haven't used but are super interesting and useful.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In simple words, an AFM consists of a very thin tip at the end of a cantilever that you can move around a sample with very high precision. 
Depending on your system, is the tip or the sample what moves!
You measure the deflection of the cantilever by reflecting a laser on it.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: By doing this, you can measure the force between the sample and the tip, as the cantilever will bend depending on it. If you put the tip in contact with a surface and sweep it keeping the force constant, you can actually have an image of its shape!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: https://t.co/rf8K8zQdVV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: https://t.co/3ZpZekeM6H

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: https://t.co/ddCfNRepyO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: https://t.co/836AYW2aMx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: https://t.co/IqDhDy8AkK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Something you can do when mapping the topography of the sample is applying a constant voltage. If the tip is conductive, it allows mapping electrical properties of your sample 😏 (current maps)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If the applied voltage oscillates, then you can even map the piezorresponse of the material 😱 (piezorresponse force microscopy)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It is also possible to follow the topography in dynamic mode. In this case, the tip is in constant oscillation, and what remains constant is the amplitude and phase of the oscillation when it interacts with the sample at short distances (5-20 nm)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This other method is less invasive as you are never applying force in the sample, so it is useful for soft materials, for example.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Going one step further, you can also apply an oscillating voltage to the tip 😱 two oscillations at the same time 😱 that's Kelvin Probe Microscopy (KPM). Following the phase of this second oscillation it is possible to map the electrostatic potential of metallic samples ❤

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Other uses of AFM are possible when combining dynamic and contact modes 😀

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Indentations: with the dynamic mode you can locate the tip in a specific point of the surface. Then, in this point, you can apply a force and/or a voltage leaving the rest of the sample untouched.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: SPANC! Scanning probe assisted nano-circuitry. Several nanowires and particles on a surface can become a circuit with some help of an AFM tip. If they are not very attached to the surface, the tip can move them with a touch, and map the resulting circuit without touching :)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To explain thin films, we first need to define what a surface is. This might seem obvious to some, but when we talk about a surface in science, we mean the outside layer of an object, usually the 'top' as a lot of the objects we work with are 2D, like silicon wafers! https://t.co/rtcybo5j49

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A 'thin film' is a coating that we typically deposit onto a surface, usually nanometers (0.000000001 m) to micrometers (0.000001 m) thick! Typically we refer to these materials that we coat as substrates. https://t.co/uVS37ioIVK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @ChrisMillsRD @realscientists I'm #FirsGen too. I don't know what it's like in other countries, but my lecturers regularly told us all about summer job/project opportunities. I got my cement QC job through my own initiative, but I'm pretty sure the research project would have been widely advertised.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now that we know what a thin film is? What type of thin films are there out there? And how do we deposit them?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Thin films can be organic (only containing O, C, N, H, S, P) or inorganic (Like Al2O3, ZnO, SiO2 etc.)

Whether you need an organic or inorganic film depends on what you want your film to do! And type of film you want dictates what deposition methods you need!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Thin film deposition can range from quite crude, such as using a doctors blade, where you're simply spreading a paste onto your surface that then dries and forms the thin film! https://t.co/kg6YOM11qc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Or you can have very precise deposition, like atomic layer deposition (ALD) where you're actually growing ultra thin layers atomically on a surface! https://t.co/Wrdlm5edI4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm going to be focus on the more precise lab scale thin film deposition technqiues, which we typically separate into physical vapour deposition (PVD) or chemical vapour deposition (CVD).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So what's the difference between PVD and CVD?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Physical vapour deposition (PVD) typically has the substrate mounted opposite the source material which then physically deposit the source material on the substrate by heating/ablating/sputter of the source material https://t.co/8cZuDfmQRB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Some example of PVD are sputter coating, thermal evaporation, electron beam evaporation etc. https://t.co/VEoxrnFVHS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now that I've covered PVD, it's time for CVD! 

In Chemical vapour deposition (CVD) the wafer surface is exposed to one or more  precursors, which react and/or decompose onto the substrate surface to produce the desired thin film https://t.co/S38RmxASrH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Examples of CVD techniques aerosol assisted CVD, plasma enhanced CVD, hot/cold wall CVD, metal organic CVD etc. Plasma polymerisation is a type of CVD, that I'll be discussing in more detail later today! https://t.co/0ACpFgdf7Y

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is a special type of CVD, where the film grows atomically. By keeping the deposition in the ALD rather than CVD regime, specific film properties, such retarding moisture/oxygen permeation, can be produced! https://t.co/lxsRiJFDzb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So what's the advantages and disadvantages of PVD and CVD? 

PVD: Typically deposits single single/simple materials but harder coatings, wide variety of film types available across a variety of techniques, but also require 'line of sight', so difficult to coat complex geometries

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: CVD: Typically produces more uniform coatings and onto more complex geometires, can be used to deposit coatings that do not have suitable PVD sources but often requires higher temperatures for the reactions to occur

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here's some useful figures that compare PVD, CVD and ALD! https://t.co/dOcRD5hn5v

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now that we've covered PVD and CVD broadly, now its time to introduce my thin film deposition technique of choice.....PLASMA POLYMERISATION!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But before we explain plasma polymerisation, lets familiarize everyone with plasma itself! 

Plasma is the 4th state of matter, and results from the excitation of a gas, which fragments the vapour molecules. This fragmentation is what produces the characteristic plasma glow! https://t.co/wqE72FaGGi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
99.9 % of the universe is plasma, because most of space is comprised of plasma!

Some examples of plasma here on Earth you might have seen are neon signs, lightning or the Aurora Borealis/Australis! https://t.co/5vIz9MkWeZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now that we're familiar with plasma, how do we use it to deposit thin films?

Plasma polymerisation is actually the same as plasma enhanced CVD (PE-CVD), but is typically used to refer to the deposition of specifically organic thin films.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Our plasma polymerisation takes place in a vacuum reactor, where we suck out the air to reduce the pressure. A medium vacuum (10-3 to 10-2 mbar) is required for plasma polymerisation. We won't be able to ignite the plasma if the pressure is too high or too low! https://t.co/MMUW1mNX9z

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We place our sample onto the sample stage.... https://t.co/fgiwTDSAex

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And once the pressure is suitable, we can introduce our liquid monomer. This monomer either has the chemistry we want to add to our surface, or makes a film that has the properties that we're after! Introducing the monomer to the vacuum evaporates it into a vapour. https://t.co/VnuTqEDRTi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Once we have our vacuum chamber filled with the vapour, we can ignite our plasma! The monomer is fragmented, and produces the plasma glow! These fragments deposits on everything inside our chamber, including our sample! https://t.co/97Y5M1nvMZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We call the films we deposit 'plasma polymers', although that's not true in a traditional sense, as they don't have the repeating sub-units of conventional polymers such as PET or PVC! https://t.co/GVIrmzoqmd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @SvenAskes No, but typically unsaturated molecules fragment to form more stable films due to their double bonds. Saturated monomers tend to fragment too much and deposit deposit as stable films, especially if you want to put them in solution!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Last tweets for today.....so what type of films can we deposit with plasma polymerisation?

The films that we most commonly do are:
-Allylamine: forms +ve amine terminated films
-Acrylic acid: forms -ve carboxyl terminated films
-Octadiene: forms carbon rich hydrophobic films

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But, there's a whole lot of other monomers out there

-Cineole: deposits films with antibacterial properties
-NIPAM: deposits temperature responsive films
-Allyl alcohol: deposits hydroxyl terminated films
-Glyme (glycol ethers): deposit low fouling/protein adsorbing films

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Signing off here for today! If you're interested in what sort of applications we use plasma polymers for, come back on Friday when I'll be exploring how we encounter thin films in our everyday lives!

tweets.text: Good morning everyone! Today I'm going to be tweeting about the organisation that I work for (@ANFFHQ - The Australian National Fabrication Facility) and discuss the benefits of open access user facilities!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The Australian National Fabrication Facility (ANFF) provides open access to micro and nanofabrication facilites for Australian researchers.

The ANFF network is made up of over 500 instruments spread across 20 sites.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ANFF also has over 100 staff that can train users to independently use the ANFF instruments after training or have their work performed by ANFF staff under a fee-for-service agreement.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Since forming in 2007, ANFF has grown from 360 users
and 38,000 user hours to 3000 users and 245,000 user hours in 2019/2020.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The instruments at ANFF are separated into the broad categories below, with some examples:
- Deposition (ALD, CVD) 
- Etching (RIE/DRIE)
- Lithography (EBL)
- Packaging (Bonding and wafer dicing)
- Testing and validation (XPS, profilometry, ellipsometry)

The ANFF @ANFFHQ network is composed of eight nodes, with their locations and specialties below!

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover

To name but a few!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now lets talk about open access user facilities in general. I've listed some of the ones available in Australia, what about in your country? Have you used any of them?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Open access user facilities, for research typically mean you can use the facilities of another institution, usually for a fee. You can either get them to 'do' the work for you, or they can train you to do the work using their equipment.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So what are the advantages? I'm going to focus on those relevant for physical sciences, but there will be some overlap with other areas of research!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
1. Expertise - You can utilize the knowledge and skill of staff to help you with an idea/process that you don't possess and may not have the time (i.e. during a PhD or an industry project) to develop

2. Access - You can access a tool quickly without purchasing or setting it up

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3. Cost- Being able to access multi-million dollar equipment and processes that your organisation can't afford

4. Maintenance - Someone else's job to pay for and maintain costly equipment

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5. Niche - Being able to access equipment that you might only need short term access to, so isn't worthwhile your group/university buying. Also may only be required by a small user base, so no point multiple institutions having one if its only used occasionally.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
6. Optimisation - Accessing equipment to see if it works for a particular process before purchasing. Especially useful for industry! 

So, can you think of any other advantages of open access user facilities for research?

My next favourite.....it's full name is a variable angle spectroscopic ellipsometer (VASE), but we just call it an ellipsometer! I've recently written an online learning module about ellipsometry, so I'll be stealing some of that info!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ellipsometry is a quick, highly sensitive and non-destructive technique that is used to determine the thickness and optical properties of thin films from a few microns down to sub-nanometre. Here's our ellipsometer! https://t.co/rMZiIEULV8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ellipsometry theory is complex, but put simply, a light at variable wavelength (200 - 1600 nm typically) is shone our sample, some is absorbed, some is reflected. The changes in the light that are reflected back to the detector, can be used to determine properties of the film. https://t.co/LhdNBy6l3o

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In ellipsometry, the thickness and other properties of the film aren't measured directly. You need to create a model that generates a data set, and that data set is compared to the experimental data and is then used to calculate the various film properties

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here's an example of the data collected during ellipsometry. The red and the green lines are the parameters collected by ellipsometery (Psi and Delta) at the different wavelengths. https://t.co/4yHTRFZ8I3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here's the process you go through to measure and fit ellipsometry data! https://t.co/UqGrOHADmc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To start the ellipsometry fitting process, you'll have your data (red and green lines) and model (black dotted line), and you'll need to change the parameters of your model for it to fit the data! Compare these unfit and fit data sets! https://t.co/RcY2HBaI3q

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We typically use ellipsometry to measure film thickness, but it can also be used to investigate film:
▪Thickness
▪Surface roughness
▪Interfacial mixing
▪Composition
▪Crystallinity
▪Anisotropy
▪Uniformity

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Apart from taking simple measurements, we can do a whole lot of cool things with ellipsometry!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: By compiling single measurements across a silicon wafer, we can building mapping scans to tell us how uniform our coating is https://t.co/muXm2pJceg

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.text: It's Friday! I think I'm most excited about the content I have for you today, because you'll be able to see how the stuff I've talked about all week is actually all around us!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Today, I'm going to be tweet about what surface properties we can modify withthin film coatings and then what applications thin films are used for.

I'm going to be talking in general about thin films, so hard/soft, organic/inorganic, so not all films will do all of these things!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
What surface properties can we modify with thin films? This list is not exhaustive. I'll discuss each one in more detail later.

-Charge
-Wettability
-Reflectivity
-Biocompatibility/Cell growth
-Conductivity
-Bacterial growth
-Biofouling
-Hardness
-Colour

Any others?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Lets start with colour, because its a fun one. No real scientific use here, but there's a lot of thin films that are used just for decorative purposes.

You may have seen these cool rainbow coloured objects! https://t.co/scLcsj8KCN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the lab, these rainbow coatings mean we have a non-uniform film, because colour gives us information about film thickness. But what is the relationship between colour and film thickness? https://t.co/c9bvQ47eSU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To start with, we need to actually explain what 'colour' is. If you have a red shirt, it appears red because it's reflecting the 'red' wavelength, back to you. All light has a wavelength, which determines if we can see it or not and if we can, what colour is it? https://t.co/Hnah7GvUlA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, the colour of a thin film is determined by what colour/wavelength light it is reflecting. This changes depending on how thick the film is, as shown in these images! https://t.co/I5XaYiAnEA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Next up is wettability. If a surface is hydrophilic (water loving) then a water droplet will spread. If a surface is hydrophobic (water hating) then a water droplet will bead! Below are some examples of how wettability influences surfaces! https://t.co/uBWvpW6lP7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Generally, you can make a surface more wettable by adding oxygen groups to the surface or make it less wettable by adding F or C groups. https://t.co/AwwTG9FUsG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Both hydrophilic and hydrophobic coatings are required for different applications! 'Self cleaning' windows can be made using a hydrophilic coating, where the water runs off the surface. Hydrophobic particles can be used to remove oil contaminants from water! https://t.co/dGeQ8jI0cY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Surfaces can also be made 'super hydrophobic' by making the surface rough, but this usually needs another technique to roughen up the surface in addition to just thin films! https://t.co/Uzf5sSkgL4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Next up is reflectivity. Anyone who's got glasses might have been sold 'anti-reflective coatings' when they bought their glasses. Often this appears as a green tinge on the surface. That's the thin film!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Anti-reflective coatings work by increasing the transmission of light and decreasing the reflection of light through the glass, so that they appear clearer! https://t.co/if6zPR7sYk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: https://t.co/LMdVifu1ws

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We might want a certain surface charge so we can build up a film, layer by layer! https://t.co/Gg3DPHLC4q

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Or we might want to attract something out of solution, to remove it! In this photo below, I removed humic acid (-ve charged water contaminant) using a positively charge plasma polymer to produce clear water! https://t.co/YAHI6bCdmn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Making surface conductive is super important these days, given all the devices we have in our bags/pockets/houses! We also need conductive films for solar cells! There are a number of thin films that can be used to create conductive surfaces! https://t.co/nemKgJ1c2w

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Creating hard surfaces is also really important, especially for a number of engineering applications. These are typically metal/metal oxide films. No body wants a drill bit that keeps breaking! https://t.co/5RNMOF0k5h

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now we've just got biological surfaces to talk about. When we're talking about surfaces for biofouling, biocompatiblity, cell or bacteria growth, it's really the sample principle. What is it that we want to attract and/or repel!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In marine biofouling, you want to put a thin film down that repels the ocean critter than gum up the bottom of a boat! https://t.co/3hp7JQvD8M

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we've got an implant we want to put in the body, like for a tooth or a hip, we want it integrate into the bone, so it doesn't become loose. In this case, we'd put a thin film on that promotes bone integration! https://t.co/ds9WpUsdNy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We might also want to put an implant into the body that repels bacteria growth, or something like a door handle that can also prevent bacterial growth! There's thin films that can do that too! https://t.co/vc3PiumdW8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, it's Sunday afternoon of my last day of tweeting. I'm going to follow the lead from last week, and finish off with my words of wisdom!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #1 - I mentioned this during the week. Take advantage of summer projects, internships, work experience etc. Science is so broad, so you it's really important to find out where your interests lie!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #2 - Work life balance. It's really hard to maintain work life balance when you see those around you working really long hours in the lab and writing papers and grants. Especially when it looks like they're getting ahead. Find out what work life balance looks like for you!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #3 - Success. There are so many ways to be a 'successful scientist' and being an academic is only one tiny fragment of that. Those working in industry, government, comms, are all still 'scientists'. Just because you're not at the bench, doesn't mean you're not still a scientist!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #4 - Personality. This kind of links in with #1, but find what type of job suits your personality. If you want to work in a basement lab and not talk to anyone all day, that's cool! I like working with people, so I love that my job involves working with others!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Honestly....I can't think of any others! Hope you've enjoyed my content this week! I've really enjoyed tweeting my work out and wishing you all good luck and happiness if your scientific journeys!

tweets.text: Let’s talk about SYNCHROTRONS! These are giant circular machines – sometimes a mile or more in circumference – with the purpose of accelerating charged particles using giant magnets. As the charged particles dash through, they emit a broad continuous radiation (X-rays!) (1/n)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These precious X-rays are used to study matter. The materials and nanoscience community owes a lot to these user-facilities. These studies reveal fundamental understanding of atoms in materials we see around us. (2/n)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Using this understanding, materials can be manipulated to tune their properties, bringing them closer to the industry. (3/n)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Synchrotrons have played a big role in my research career. I have used the ALS, BNL, CLS and CHESS facilities to explore semiconductor thin-films. Primarily, I have looked at the role of microstructure using a technique called ‘X-ray scattering’.  (4/n)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When the X-rays strike atoms in the semiconductor films, they get reflected. Capturing these reflected rays and decoding them reveals insights about how films are formed. In particular, I have studied large-scale fabrication of semiconductor films. (5/n)

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.text: Perovskites form the bleeding edge of research on next-generation solar cells. These are low-cost semiconductor inks that can be converted into optoelectronic devices by simply casting them onto a surface using coating techniques. (1/n) https://t.co/FuoltrK8zi

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Any defects in the conventional semiconductors can ruin their properties – but perovskites don’t really seem to care! They are defect-tolerant. (3/n)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Power-conversion-efficiencies as high as 25% have been reported for perovskite solar cells, and several start-ups around the globe are trying to commercialize them for terrestrial applications. (4/n)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A low-hanging fruit is a tandem solar cell that can combine the benefits of the age-old Silicon cells with perovskites. The extra power tandems will deliver will drive the solar costs down, helping us combat climate change faster. (5/n)

INTERFACE will be the highlight of my tweet thread later today. The basic tool to explore interfaces & surfaces is: Photoelectron Spectroscopy (PES). This can be done in-house or at synchrotrons. Here is how an PES system looks like (my 2021 front cover). Stay tuned!
#SciArt. https://t.co/OUrXMwHorb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hope you all are having a great weekend! Here are some facts on Photoemission Spectroscopy (PES) - a great tool to have in the toolkit of a materials scientist. /1 https://t.co/WAeNKIofRC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: PES is based on the photoelectron effect. The sample to be studied (film, powder, crystal) is excited with photons of a certain energy. The electrons emitted from the sample upon absorption of these incident photons are collected and parsed for crucial info about the sample. /2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are 2 modes of PES. One uses high-energy X-ray photons (>1000 eV) and studies the chemical composition. Chemical environment, oxidation states, etc can be clearly explained. This is called XPS (X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When low-energy photons (usually UV) with energies in the range of 10s-100s eV are used, electrons that form the valence band structure of the sample are detected. This is UPS (Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: UPS reveals information about energy levels, work function and defect states. Great tool to study optoelectronic devices!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Great thing about PES is that it's highly surface sensitive, and a usual in-house system gives information about the top 1-5 nm of the sample surface! Thin crusts and interfaces can be studied in detail - Interfaces that define optoelectronic devices!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I have used PES extensively – both in-house and @CanLightSource – to characterize interfaces in solar cells. https://t.co/WAeNKI6Et2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These studies revealed a wealth of insights into nanocrystal and perovskite surfaces, specially on how the environment interacts with these materials, and what strategies need to be in place to make more stable optoelectronics.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Good morning! I am Niklas Friedrich, a PhD-student working in the group of @NatxoPas in @nanogune! I’m looking forward to discussing #surfacescience, #magnetic #graphene and #work-life balance here in the coming week. Please ask lots of questions!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To start: This is “my” machine. A homebuild #ultrahighvacuum chamber, and a #cryostat and a look inside the chamber, where we prepare the samples (banana for scale) https://t.co/hyzMxIxtT3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The heart of it all: a #ScanningTunnelingMicroscope or #STM, what a beauty! 

Inside the chamber it is hidden by thermal shields, but outside it is showing its whole beauty. Fotos from before and after mounting lenses to collect light and a low temperature #AFM amplifier. https://t.co/IsMo8dkizu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @AndrewR_Physics The head is a commercial slider-head from createc. The chamber around it is designed by us

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @ulrich_hofmann @NatxoPas @nanoGUNE There are a bunch of ways to get spin-polarization into graphene. Two examples are: #topological #bandengineering in #graphene #nano|ribbon. Or in small nanoflakes an imbalance between the two different sublattices. Check the publications of @Springfetopen for details and refs

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
What can we do with it? We can look at single #atoms or #molecules like these:

Thanks to Stefano for the image of the atoms https://t.co/l2EXgvckii

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: How does it work? Imagine being an #electron in a metal, you are free to surf around your wavefunction anywhere in the metal, actually, even outside the metal! Physically speaking you can “penetrate into the energy barrier” #Donttrythisathome https://t.co/fgiKIcLqm1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you find another piece of metal in that tiny distance you can jump there. This is called #tunneling. If there is a bias voltage applied between the first and the second metal piece, we can measure the current flowing, even if the two metal pieces don’t touch

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the experiment we move a sharp needle, the tip, very close to the surface that we want to look at. Changing the distance between tip and surface by about one atom changes the current by a factor of ten!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ever used an electric lighter? You press it, this creates a bias voltage and a current flows. We use it the other way round. We apply a bias voltage and the piezocrystal squeezes together some fraction of a #nano|meter. That’s how we move the tip so precise.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now we only need a tip that ends in one single #atom and we can get beautiful images… okay, and a sample to look at… https://t.co/kzswMURldU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Our project partners in @springfetopen at @IBMResearch in the group of Leo Gross are experts in #AtomicForceMicroscopy. It works almost the same as an STM, but with forces instead of current, that way they can work on insulating samples

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Can we go smaller? Of course! Placing a single CO-molecule on the tip apex of your microscope will give you #atomicresolution inside a single #molecule  (sadly though, it is hidden from the public by a big paywall since 12 years) doi:10.1126/science.1176210 https://t.co/liLb0g42YQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
During my master I worked on another exciting #research project: #ScanningQuantumDotMicroscopy or #SQDM in the group of Stefan Tautz at @fz_juelich 
This is a very underrated technique, a powerful tool to image #electronic #surface properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I worked with #PTCDA, but it works also with other #molecules. It is an incredible technique where you use a single #molecule hanging from the tip of an #AFM to measure electric #dipoles on the surface with atomic precision.
https://t.co/85ETaNMAfF

tweets.label: Takeover

Reading my tweets about #science and #work|ing in science? Would you like to work in science or #academia? 
Tell me why!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You are essentially a #selfemployed #scientist, although you work for a university or institute. It will always be your name on the #publications that counts. If you want to keep doing what you do, better invest a 👉lot👈 of time

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you want to #stayinresearch, you are competing over #money (salary or to spend) against everyone in #science, many times even against people from very different fields. The metric you compete on: #paper|s and #citations

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As #science is a #creative process it is difficult to judge what is good science and what isn’t. To come up with “objective” criteria, #scientists are judged mostly by their written, hopefully #peerreview|ed publications, mostly in expensive journals

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You are forced to focus on publishing as many #paper|s as possible, because #citations, number of #publications and #hindex are very important factors when you apply for a scholarship, a grant or a position at an institute or university.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I guess you get an idea, why there are #scientists publishing #junkscience in #predatorjournals, a practice that is obviously bad and hurts #science. Still, I understand the structural dynamics leading to these decisions.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The #publishorperish mentality is clearly not in the interest of the individual, as it incentives to push yourself beyond the limit. #Depression and #Anxiety are very high under #PhDs. #mentalhealth is only slowly leaving the tabu-status @Nature https://t.co/C8YwAh9DFo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Bad for #scientists, good for #science? No. #Science is a creative process that connects ideas, you need time to play around, to try, most importantly to #fail! Focusing on publishing many #papers forces you to take tiny steps forward. #IncrementalScience

Hello! I’m Giulia Pacchioni, @Giulia_Pacc, tweeting for the week from London!

I’m a Senior Editor at @NatRevMater, where I handle content on a broad range of topics in materials science. This week I'll share some tips on writing, publishing & on life as an editor. https://t.co/IcErSb0ryN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today I will put the spotlight on editorial jobs, telling you about how my own path led me to this fun career and what an editor actually does.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I'm a physicist by training: I did my master and bachelor degrees at @LaStatale in Milan, then moved to @EPFL_en in Lausanne for my PhD. I worked with scanning tunnelling microscopy, something you have learned about last week from
@cienciaparaelf2! Here's me with my STM in 2014 https://t.co/azlAnsfwGc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My PhD project, in Harald Brune's group, involved studying how (and why) small molecules self-organize on surfaces & how the patterns they form can be used to template the organization of atoms & clusters with cool catalytic/magnetic properties. STM pictures in silly colours ⬇️ https://t.co/xV7aewaV2D

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As I was nearing the end of my PhD, a friend pointed out that an editorial job would bring together all the things I was passionate about: physics, writing, and science communication. He was right!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I started collaborating with blogs discussing science and co-organized a summer school to tailor my CV to this type of job, and landed a position on the launch team of @NatRevMater, which was, and still is, my dream journal 🙃 https://t.co/CYukVsMMM1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Over the years I have also worked with @NatRevPhys to prepare their launch in 2019, and for a few months with Nature Materials. I will tell you more about how to find editorial jobs and what an editor does in my next threads! https://t.co/lwd9Spi5yd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let me tell you more about my job as an editor at @NatRevMater. We are a team of 3 (with @ChristineHorejs & @arianevartanian) and publish Reviews and Perspectives on all topics materials science, + Comments on topics such as mentoring & inclusivity in academia. Lots of variety! https://t.co/TmtcxQJev6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Editors also write content such as Research Highlights & Editorials -- the latter require a lot of reading and thinking and are a stimulating team effort, such as this recent one led by our brilliant team member Ariane: https://t.co/gUVSol0jcS https://t.co/taZin0y0zp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As editors we need to know what’s new in the fields we cover; we keep up to date reading the literature and going to conferences & talks (now virtually!) to identify both timely topics and interesting authors. We also encourage unsolicited submissions. https://t.co/LLvSEGGddW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We ask authors to prepare an outline of their Review planning how much content to cover, how to structure it, and ideas for figures & tables; we give feedback on the outline trying to ensure the angle of the article is clear and the amount of content appropriate https://t.co/JJfCGOksNm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We then keep in mind the submission timelines of each manuscript and check on authors regularly. We publish a fixed number of articles per month, so it’s important to ensure we have a steady number of submissions through the year, but we also need to plan for unexpected delays

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Once submitted, if a manuscript is not in top shape we suggest ways to improve the structure, clarity & accessibility of the text and to make the figures easier to understand and more useful for readers. https://t.co/Cct4ieWNF1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As you have guessed, the next step is to find expert reviewers to comment on the manuscript and, when the reports are back, guide the authors through the revision process https://t.co/6WsKGtW7GS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The most involved step of the process is the in-depth editing of the text to ensure every paragraph is clear & precise and the writing concise. Our art editor applies our colour palette and fonts to all figures & redraws schematic so they are all consistent across the manuscript https://t.co/47Q3TSIDMk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The final step is checking the proof to ensure everything is in good order before publication, and enjoying the article in its final, highly polished form. Publication is always a proud moment, sometimes the culmination of a process of over 2 years since inviting the author! https://t.co/2rULyvZI1e
