The craziness is now down because we've just moved all desks around so lots of personal stuff was taken home, but last week I found the cutest fluffy antibody bound to its little antigen. Also lots of interesting books are scattered around. https://t.co/uxwbwkmtdL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The best feature of the office though is the Nature archive, where physical copies of every issue of Nature ever published are kept. Here are some pictures of random articles from 1874, 1989, 2000 & 2013. Fun to see how the look of articles has changed! https://t.co/cr6qiEY9YK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Finally, here is me enjoying the best window desk! https://t.co/YAvTC43CiX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let’s now look at some simple writing tips. The main thing to keep in mind when writing scientific articles is that the point is not to write beautiful prose, but to be understood clearly. We are not Shakespeare! In our case, clarity is better than beauty. https://t.co/48FAZYsbtZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You want your paper to tell a story. Start with your scientific question & how it fits in the context of previous results. Then state what you did & how (in logical, not chronological order) and what you found. Finish with *reasonable* implications and next steps. https://t.co/OQFhxDHma9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Use a clear structure to guide the reader. One paragraph, one idea. Use short sentences linked by appropriate connectors (therefore, however) Use simple but precise words, always using the same word to describe the same thing. Avoid empty words (very, quite) Define all acronyms!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Metaphors can be confusing, and we often don’t realize how strongly related to our own culture they are. We don’t all grow up with the same myths and stories, hence, if you don’t want your metaphors to become your Achilles’ heel, avoid them. https://t.co/DA9KnMRQMW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
As a reviews editor I get often asked ⭐What makes a good Review?⭐ Here is a summary of my answer in 8 points:

1- Timely: cover an emerging topic or address a need for clarity in a specific area. Make sure you can answer the question ‘why now?’ before you start writing. https://t.co/2tc41jk3PP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2- Original: ensure you have a new angle/message such that the new review is a useful contribution to the literature. Writing a good review is a lot of work, so make sure the final product will be valuable for readers. Make it count! https://t.co/rxHxrztMXw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3- Insightful: you don’t want your review to be a laundry list of results in the field. Use your experience to select the most important results, assess them critically and show readers how they fit together in a bigger story https://t.co/qKe0kZnMQD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4- Balanced: cover fairly the contribution of the various groups active in the field. If there are different points of view, acknowledge them. It’s not always possible to be fully comprehensive, but make sure you clarify what is your focus and how you selected the works to cover https://t.co/ViDxGHqY8Y

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5- Accessible: explain non-obvious concepts, use clear definitions and briefly introduce the important ideas in the field so newbies can delve into the topic. Reference tutorial reviews where the can learn the basics. https://t.co/qzeFnSrSLY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 6- Well illustrated: mix published figures that exemplify important results in the field and new figures such as schematics of processes & graphs comparing results or showing trends to illustrate your main points clearly and effectively https://t.co/x8r4YOe0xS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 7- Forward looking: think carefully about your conclusions and perspectives: What are the open problems in the field? What are the promising directions? Here is the place where you can be a bit more opinionated and discuss your own insights on the future of the field https://t.co/Q6HXTf3li0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 8- Well-planned: once you choose a journal for your review, discuss with editors to see if they have suggestions on the focus or specific guidelines for length and format. Do this before writing the whole thing! This step can save you a lot of work revising.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The topics I want to cover today are ⚡️cover letters⚡️ & ✨appeals✨. What's the point of a COVER LETTER? It is your opportunity to briefly highlight the main point & significance of your work. Don’t copy and paste the abstract! Editors read both. Keep it brief & to the point. https://t.co/9Nkk3ziErY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A common question is how to address the letter. With ‘Dear Editor’ you never go wrong. Avoid ‘Dear Sir/Madam’: it’s outdated, and the editor is likely a Dr anyway! Check out this blog post by @stuartcantrill  for detailed cover letter tips: https://t.co/mQnBLxAQyT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: APPEALS: Not happy with the editor’s decision? You can always appeal. Make sure you clarify any misunderstandings & explain why you think your paper should be reconsidered. Don’t just ask the editor to rethink their decision: add new data/information to help change their minds.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Avoid just stating how much your previous articles are cited, or insulting the editor & reviewers. Be polite and use constructive arguments to make your point. Appeals take time, so avoid just ‘trying’. Read more in this @NaturePhysics editorial: https://t.co/pSIfABhAn6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I was forgetting to share a useful resource: a great @NatRevChem editorial discussing how to pitch review ideas to journals: https://t.co/QZYPZrjNe6 https://t.co/5uNXlquDYu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let me tell you what I love about being an editor, and why it’s a great career option for those who don’t wish to go down the academic career path, but want to keep having fun with science

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As an editor, you work on a variety of tasks, including reading, making decisions, editing & writing, and you're exposed to a broad variety of topics. You get to interact with a lot of passionate scientists at all career levels.  It’s rarely boring!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Editors travel quite a lot: in non-pandemic times I used to attend a couple of big conferences a year (such as APS & MRS meetings), plus several more focused conferences. We also organize lab visits &  give publishing talks. I have visited a lot of amazing places through my job!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A big advantage of editorial jobs is that they're secure and flexible. Meeting publication deadlines can be stressful, but generally the pressure is much lower than in academia. Note that things can be different at different journals, this thread just reflects my own experience🙂

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, how to find editorial jobs? A good place to start is the Nature Careers website, https://t.co/RT9n5PMbPO, where you can find listings for editorial jobs both at Springer Nature and other publishers. Don’t be shy to reach out to editors on Twitter if you have questions!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A good way to add to your CV something valuable when applying for editorial positions is to co-organize a conference: it showcases organizational skills, enthusiasm & the ability to select good topics. For example MRS Spring 2023 is looking for organizers: https://t.co/dtKaU467lN

"Creating New Quantum Materials Atom by Atom"

Please welcome @UltracoldTiff of @Cambridge_Uni and listen to the podcast to know what is coming your way this week 👇🎧🎙️

#UnderTheMicroscope #SciencePodcast

https://t.co/WqpmdBz6Oe

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hello! I’m Dr Tiffany Harte (aka @UltracoldTiff), a postdoc in the many-body quantum dynamics group @CaMBQD in @DeptOfPhysics @Cambridge_Uni. Join me this week to read about Ultracold Atoms and their applications, and get a glimpse into my week as a scientist! #ColdAtoms

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: How cold is Ultracold? https://t.co/T3Q24FmTOI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Absolute zero is at 0 Kelvin, or -273°C - this is the lower limit on absolute temperature and it becomes increasingly difficult to reach the colder you get (negative absolute temperatures are an interesting but separate discussion!).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Water freezes at 273 K, and the Antarctic can get as low as 190 K. Cryogenic systems can use e.g. liquid nitrogen (77 K) or liquid helium (4 K), but are limited to a few mK. Even outer space is around 2.7 K from the cosmic microwave background. We need to go much colder!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A cloud of atoms can be cooled down to temperatures approaching absolute zero - commonly a few hundred nano Kelvin (nK - a billionth of a °C) but sometimes as low as tens of pico Kelvin (pK - a trillionth of a °C) - more on how to do this later!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I’m referring to a ‘cloud’ of atoms because we work with a dilute gas of atoms held inside a vacuum chamber. Each cold atom (or molecule) experiment will be carefully designed around a small number of atomic species depending on the application.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The temperature of the atom cloud is related to the velocity distribution of the atoms. To cool the cloud, we want to narrow this distribution and reduce the atom velocity. Tune in at lunchtime to find out how!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: How do we cool atoms down? (Part 1 of 3) https://t.co/9mjaTNtioG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are lots of ways to cool an atom cloud, and the methods used will vary between experiments and different atomic species - but there are a few methods that many experiments have in common.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here’s a photo of a potassium source: we buy the source in a sealed ampoule and place it inside our vacuum. We break the ampoule and the source gradually vaporises (sometimes helped by heating). These ampoules should produce enough atoms for several years of operation! https://t.co/O8g4qspD2B

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Once we have enough atomic vapour we use lasers to slow the atoms down and reduce their temperature - lasers don’t just heat things up!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If the laser beam is at a wavelength that matches an atomic transition, an atom can absorb photons, transferring the photon momentum to the atom. When the atom returns to its ground state and releases a photon, this gives another kick, but in a random direction.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So if we want to slow down an atom then we need to make sure that it can be cooled from all directions, but preferentially absorbs photons from a direction that opposes its motion. We use the Doppler shift to achieve this!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we set the laser to a slightly longer wavelength than the transition, an atom moving towards that laser beam will see the light Doppler shifted to a shorter wavelength - back into resonance with the transition and more likely to be absorbed.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To make sure that we can slow an atom moving in any direction we overlap three orthogonal pairs of beams propagating in opposite directions. This is called optical molasses because it makes a ‘sticky’ region that slows down (but doesn’t trap) the atoms. https://t.co/GfVJQMrPJm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To turn this into a trap we add a weak magnetic field that creates a force imbalance and a restoring force to the centre of the beams - a ‘magneto-optical trap’.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here’s a photo of some of the lasers we use to cool potassium and rubidium - the optics on the table are used to distribute the light, precisely shift the frequencies of different beams, and shutter the light at different times in the experiment sequence. https://t.co/Qv0v7zvoPD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: How do we cool atoms down? (Part 2 of 3)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are a few laser cooling temperature limits. The Doppler limit is proportional to the linewidth of the atomic transition, and is related to to the random direction of photon emission when the atom de-excites (after absorbing the initial photon from the laser beam).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Fluctuations cause a random walk in the atom velocity and so limit the temperature. This limit varies a lot with atomic species - e.g. 146 μK for rubidium, but just 180 nK for strontium which has a very narrow linewidth transition.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The Doppler limit is an exciting chapter in cold atom history! In 1988 experiments showed temperatures much lower than those predicted by theory: https://t.co/GagJyLyoyQ. This turned out to be due to a more complex atomic energy level structure than was originally accounted for.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Work on laser cooling won the 1997 Nobel Physics prize: https://t.co/qsgexg1TeL.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another temperature limit is the recoil limit, from the energy associated with the momentum kick of a single photon. This is determined by the mass of the atom and wavelength of the transition - e.g. 360 nK for rubidium-87.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This still isn’t the final limit though - various sub-recoil methods have also been developed, for example by preventing atoms from absorbing photons if their velocity falls below the recoil velocity.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: How far the atoms are cooled with laser cooling methods depends on the atomic species, the goals of an experiment, and the choices and interests of the research group. Generally speaking, these methods get harder to implement the colder you want to go!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: How do we cool atoms down? (Part 3 of 3)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Laser cooling is often followed by evaporative cooling. Evaporative cooling is pretty much the same process as the evaporation of your afternoon coffee! The highest-energy atoms leave the trap, and the remaining atoms rethermalise at a lower temperature.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The atoms are trapped using laser beams or magnetic fields (sometimes both!), and the higher-energy atoms are pushed out of the trap by lowering the trap walls or applying a field that drives them into an untrapped state. A lot of atoms are lost during this stage of cooling!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There are of course a lot of other methods, tricks, and details I haven’t mentioned! But this outlines the basic atom-cooling toolkit.

If this all seems like a lot of effort, join me this evening to find out why we care about making our atoms ultracold!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The next few hours will be quiet from me because I’m teaching tutorials this afternoon (called ‘supervisions’ in Cambridge). Today we’re looking at magnetostatics! After atomic physics, I think electromagnetism is my favourite part of an undergrad physics course - what’s yours?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A lot of interesting things happen when you cool atoms to ultracold temperatures https://t.co/BacR3fSqcJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle tells us the position of an atom is spread out in space - the position uncertainty increases as you decrease kinetic energy. This is described by the de Broglie wavelength, which is inversely proportional to the square root of temperature.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At room temperature, the de Broglie wavelength is much smaller than the spacing between atoms, but as you cool the cloud this approaches the atom spacing. Atoms might now try to occupy the same quantum states - this is where atoms will behave in a way that depends on their spin.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Bosons (particles with integer spin) are able to occupy the same state - at some phase-space density (the number density multiplied by de Broglie wavelength cubed) the particles will fall into the ground state, acting like a single wavefunction - a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The BEC transition can be seen by looking at the atom momentum. We release the cloud from the trap and allow atoms to move freely for several ms, which maps their initial momentum into position.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A thermal cloud has a Gaussian distribution, but a BEC looks like an inverted parabola - you can see the BEC peak emerge as you go further in the evaporation process! Here's a gif of the BEC signal appearing as we evaporate (decreasing the power of an optical trap). https://t.co/4dhDCBLJkm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In contrast, fermions (particles with half-integer spin) are forbidden from occupying the same state by the Pauli exclusion principle. The atoms will instead fill the available energy levels sequentially, and become a degenerate Fermi gas.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Starting tomorrow we’re going to look at some applications of cold atom systems, starting with the example of building experimental simulations of complex quantum materials!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Unfortunately the gif I pasted into my last thread didn't work - here it is in the original post! https://t.co/v2feEx98k4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Every Tuesday morning the @CaMBQD group gets together for #JournalClub where we read a paper in advance and then discuss it. This week we’re looking at a paper by our PI @UlrichCamPhy so we’ll have the expert on hand! Why not read along with us?
https://t.co/C9z75kOf1D

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can use #ColdAtoms to create experimental simulations of complicated systems. Today I’ll show you the first experiment that I worked on in Cambridge, building a quantum simulator for the physics of flat energy bands and frustrated magnetism!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The first step in building a cold atom quantum simulator is encoding the problem so that the behaviour of the cold atoms captures all the important characteristics.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For example, a lot of interesting materials have a periodic structure with a lattice of positively charged ions surrounded by a sea of negatively charged electrons. These lattices and the associated electron behaviour can produce some incredibly complex material properties!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This complex quantum behaviour can be difficult to directly measure or numerically simulate, so we construct an experimental simulation on a larger scale, using patterns of laser light to represent the lattice of the real material and ultracold atoms to represent the electrons.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This creates a very clean system that has the same or similar geometry to the real material, so that it captures the same physics. We can tune details like how tightly the atoms are held to a lattice site, the interactions between atoms, and can introduce noise or other features.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Because the cold atom system is on a larger scale than the real material (atoms representing electrons, and lattice sites separated by hundreds of nm instead of hundreds of pm) we can measure dynamics of the system at a single-site level using atom fluorescence and a good camera.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
These experimental models are therefore tuneable, easy* to measure, and capture the quantum properties of the real material. This means we can use them to get additional insight into the properties and behaviour of the systems we're modelling

*relatively easy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Tune back in over lunchtime to see just how we use laser light to create the structure of the quantum simulator! https://t.co/W4gUqh2nB5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Yesterday we saw that laser light can be used to cool atoms. Because a light field affects the atom's energy levels, lasers can also be used to trap them!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If the wavelength of the light is longer than the atomic energy transition (“red detuned”) the atom is attracted to high intensities. If it is shorter (“blue detuned”) the atom is repelled.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So if we can make patterns of light with a geometry that captures the physics we’re interested in simulating, we can use this to trap the atoms and create our simulator!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A popular method of creating patterned light is to use the interference between overlapping waves. You’ve seen this effect before - think of the patterns that form when two ripples overlap on a lake or pond!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The same thing happens with light - when the waves overlap they add together, creating variations in intensity with a length scale smaller than the laser wavelength (hundreds of nm). By shining laser beams with a certain geometry we can create a huge range of  patterns!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here’s an illustration from my research group @CaMBQD - laser beams (blue) are reflected from mirrors (circles). Where each beam overlaps with its reflection, interference creates a pancake-like structure. Where beam pairs overlap we get a 3D cube of high/low intensity. https://t.co/alcGiNOJ66

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Here’s another example from my research group (I don’t work on this experiment) - four laser beams (blue arrows) are reflected from mirrors (grey circles). This particular symmetry creates a quasicrystal instead of a periodic structure.
￼
Image credit: Dr Ed Carter (PhD thesis) https://t.co/7ACSAAzeUI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Learn more about quasicrystals here: https://t.co/Nzet1hUCA1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We also have an experiment studying the kagome lattice (this is the experiment I started building when I first moved to Cambridge). The kagome lattice is the pattern of triangles pictured below. https://t.co/aeaU7YiQya

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We need two laser wavelengths to create the kagome lattice! A blue detuned interference pattern (short wavelength, atoms repelled from high intensity) is overlapped with a red detuned pattern (long wavelength, atoms attracted to high intensity).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is shown here - arrows represent the laser beams (no reflection this time!) and where these arrows overlap I’ve shown the spatial variation in atomic energy levels - atoms are trapped by purple and pushed away from yellow. Adding the lattices creates the kagome structure. https://t.co/AoglB1N4eP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: More about the interesting physics of the kagome lattice later today!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One interesting property of the kagome lattice is geometric frustration where particles that want to align with their spins (arrows) opposite the spin of their neighbours find that they can’t - quantum simulation is one approach to working out how these systems behave. https://t.co/ARM3sB69zK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The (calculated) energy structure of the kagome lattice is pictured here (energy on the y axis) - one feature here is a flat energy band, where particles should behave as though strongly correlated and infinitely heavy. We want to study this flat band physics! https://t.co/F9EdT0bxI3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The kagome lattice exists in solid state systems too - see e.g. https://t.co/CtENOj8rqH and https://t.co/HbSewzXVRM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A quantum simulator can give tremendous insight into the physics of a complicated system - however I think it's important that we acknowledge both the power and limitations of the technique, and keep talking to scientists tackling similar problems using different methods!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Join me later for a virtual lab tour to see how these different ideas come together to create a real quantum simulator!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Time for a lab tour!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The kagome lab uses rubidium (bosons) and potassium (bosons and fermions). We prepare all the light for laser cooling, optical trapping and optical lattices on two big optical tables, and our vacuum system sits on a third. Here are our laser tables: https://t.co/OnolDfz0zX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is a CAD model of our vacuum system - atoms are cooled from left to right in the system following the methods described yesterday (see posts below) https://t.co/7M0WSVPsMz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The ampoules of potassium and rubidium sit in the bellows labelled ’source’ and atoms diffuse into the rectangular chambers above. These are our 2D magneto-optical traps (MOTs) - the first stage of laser cooling.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A beam of laser cooled atoms is pushed into the 3D MOT, where we continue laser cooling. The atoms fluoresce - here’s a photograph of a brightly-glowing cloud of laser-cooled rubidium (a few tens of million atoms, at around 200 μK). In reality this is a beautiful red colour! https://t.co/nMQEaTICIV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We turn up a strong magnetic field and a laser beam (together making a ‘hybrid’ trap) to trap our atoms for evaporative cooling. We load atoms at a few μK into a focussed laser beam and use lenses with a tuneable focal length to transport the atoms 50 cm into our science chamber.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the science chamber we can evaporate the atoms further, by lowering the depth of an optical trap made of crossed laser beams, and then load into our optical lattice. Our lattice lasers only arrived a few weeks ago so this is still a work in progress!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We also have the label for ‘DMD’ potential - this is a plan for the future, where we will project additional laser patterns onto the lattice using a programmable micromirror array.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The ‘quantum gas microscope’ is for single lattice site imaging. We will make the lattice very deep (to hold the atoms in place) and then simultaneously laser cool the atoms and gather their fluorescence using an objective lens inside the vacuum chamber.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Putting the objective in the vacuum system was daunting - the objective had to be perfectly aligned to the lower viewport. Fortunately we measured this carefully before pumping out our vacuum - the first time we put it in there was a slight tilt! Second time worked perfectly😅

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here’s a photo of PhD student Dan carefully placing the objective lens inside our vacuum system - and the same chamber once sealed and surrounded by coils and optics! https://t.co/T94E3mSxW4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can get complementary information about the cold atom system by dropping the atoms as I described yesterday - releasing them from the trap and letting them fall freely will give us useful information about their momentum.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A cold atom quantum simulator takes a long time to build! Over the last four years we've turned an empty lab into a working cold atom apparatus and are currently making the last refinements to turn this into a fully operational quantum simulator.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We have plenty of experiments planned out, so the next few years will be filled with data analysis and exciting results!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of my favourite things about being an experimentalist is that you get to think and learn about both the practical aspects of building an apparatus and the exciting physics that the experiment is used to study!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All experiments are a team effort! The current kagome team is PI Ulrich Schneider @UlrichCamPhy, postdocs Tiffany Harte (me!) and Mehedi Hasan @mhasan137, and students Dan Reed @danreedphysics, Max Melchner, Luca Donini @lucad_96, Sompob Shanokprasith and Dan Braun.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Today I've been getting things ready for us to start assembling the vacuum chambers for our new experiment where we'll use #ColdAtoms to detect #DarkMatter and #GravitationalWaves! 

More details about that coming tomorrow!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Yesterday I talked about using #ColdAtoms trapped in laser light patterns to build experimental simulations of quantum materials.

Today let’s look at a different application of similar techniques: atom interferometry to detect #DarkMatter and #GravitationalWaves.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Interferometry is commonly seen using light. Here is a sketch of a Mach-Zehnder interferometer, where a laser beam is split in two then recombined, and the signal detected by photodiodes (grey semicircles) reveals any difference in phase between the two branches. https://t.co/jUmPOpmsaO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Atom interferometry is exactly the same idea, but using clouds of cold atoms instead of light! Lasers (yes, lasers again!) can drive transitions between atomic states. This can either create a superposition of states (a ‘beamsplitter’) or completely switch states (a ‘mirror’).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here’s a Mach-Zehnder interferometer for atoms (straight lines): blue is the ground state, and dashed purple the excited state. Grey wavy lines are the laser pulses that act as mirror and beamsplitters. https://t.co/Rss13zu89d

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The ground and excited states have different momenta, so travel along different trajectories. Any difference in phase that these clouds accumulate can be inferred from the interference pattern obtained after the final ‘beamsplitter’ laser pulse recombines the clouds.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The atom interferometer is therefore sensitive to anything that might change the phase evolution between the two branches - tune back in at lunchtime to see how this relates to dark matter and gravitational waves!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I’m currently working in a new consortium called AION (Atom Interferometry Observatory and Network) which plans to build cold atom detectors to test ideas about fundamental physics and complement traditional technologies such as LIGO.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We will operate two interferometers in parallel, separated by a very long distance - 1 km separation is planned for the final terrestrial detector, and then we plan to put the interferometers into space! The detector will look like this:

(Image https://t.co/KAFNOhmgzI  ) https://t.co/lsLAWpRky3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Each 'atom source' is a cold atom cloud that we launch in an interferometry sequence. The red shading represents the laser beams used to create the beamsplitter and mirror interactions.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We will make a differential measurement between the two separate cold atom interferometers, and will be sensitive to any differences between them.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For example, a gravitational wave will stretch and compress space-time. This will change the amount of time that it takes laser light to travel between the two interferometers - we will detect this as a time-varying difference in the interferometer phase.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We will be sensitive to mid-frequency gravitational waves (tens of mHz to a few Hz) which will complement the sensitivity of LIGO (tens of Hz to kHz) and the planned LISA detector (below Hz) - this means we can get information about different stages in e.g. black hole mergers.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Dark matter is a very different detection problem because it’s still such a mystery! An atom interferometer will be sensitive to the predicted couplings of dark matter models to standard model fields, and so can be used to either detect or exclude certain interactions.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: e.g. ultra-light scalar dark matter is predicted to be an oscillating field that will change the electron mass and fine structure constant. This will change the atomic transition frequency and so the phase evolution that we can detect in the differential measurement.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
A longer separation between interferometers will give a greater sensitivity but will also have technical challenges - space missions and even a 1 km terrestrial detector are still decades in the future! 

This afternoon I’ll describe the work we’re doing now towards this goal.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I got caught up in work this afternoon so forgot to post! A very long thread is incoming…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Over the next 2-3 years, we'll develop technologies that will make the large-scale AION detectors possible. There are 5 cold atom research groups, each with our own apparatus so that we can research in parallel and then combine all the techniques in a single prototype.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This project is a new way of working for me! In cold atoms we typically work in small groups to build and operate an experiment. Here we’re working extremely closely with the other experimental teams - it’s more like being in one big research group spread across multiple sites!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This level of collaboration means a lot of meetings, and disagreements about the best way to build an experiment! But it’s also a great way to spread the workload and have access to expertise in different areas. It’s also a great chance to work with and learn from more people!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Right now we’re working on preparing a suitably cold cloud to use in the interferometer - our final target is less than 1 nK! There are also teams looking at improving sensitivity, such as by increasing the separation between the interferometer arms with repeated laser pulses.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The colder the cloud, the less it will spread out and so the longer the possible duration of the interferometry sequence - this increases the detector sensitivity.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A compact cloud also means the atoms should all see a more uniform laser intensity, improving the fidelity of the interactions between atoms and light.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We’re going to start assembling our vacuum system in the next few weeks, and this is what it will look like: (description below) https://t.co/3fdhCPbklI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Like the apparatus I showed you yesterday we start with laser cooling in a 2D magneto-optical trap (MOT) (see Monday’s thread on laser cooling) to create a pre-cooled beam for laser cooling in a 3D MOT.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We will then trap in a laser beam to evaporatively cool the atoms and transport them by moving the laser beam focus into a test chamber for interferometry.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This final chamber isn’t the long tower that we’ll be working with in future years! We’ll develop the technologies on an apparatus that fits nicely on an optical table, then transfer the upgraded cold atom source (everything up to and including transport) onto the final detector.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We’re using ultracold strontium atoms - I’ve previously only worked with rubidium and potassium (group 1) so it’s exciting to be working with a group 2 element!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Strontium has an energy transition with an extremely narrow linewidth (mHz) and a correspondingly long-lived state - this is called a clock transition because it's very useful for keeping time! https://t.co/oNJAyJfUoz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This narrow clock transition allows us to use a single-photon instead of two-photon process for our mirrors and beamsplitters, eliminating laser noise in the differential measurement and allowing us to use a large separation between the interferometers (increasing sensitivity).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The Cambridge team is working on the techniques to cool and transport the atom cloud, to provide the best possible starting point for interferometry. Our goal is to provide atom clouds with as many atoms as possible, as cold as possible, and produced as fast as possible!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This includes the methods I’ve discussed previously, as well as tricks like using carefully controlled laser pulses to act like lenses to collimate or focus the cloud as it travels (https://t.co/OGM3SZxfu0).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The project started in May, and we've spent the last few months designing the apparatus, working on calculations, and setting up the lab. We’ve also been testing some optical transport techniques so that we can transport the atoms with as little heating or atom loss as possible.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We’re at an exciting time for the experiment, getting the vacuum chambers assembled and filling our tables with laser cooling optics! 

We’ll be spending some time tomorrow tidying the lab and making space for deliveries - an experimentalist’s job isn’t always glamorous!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Once again this is of course a team effort! The current (Cambridge) AION team is PI Ulrich Schneider, postdocs Tiffany Harte (me!) and Kimberly Tkalčec, and students Xintong Su, Michael Hsu, Brian Bostwick and Zach Eyler. The full AION collaboration list is very long!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Tomorrow I’m going to change direction and talk more about myself, and how and why I became a physicist.

Since we're approaching the end of my week here, let me know if there are any other aspects of my experiments you'd like to hear about!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I became interested in #Physics as a teenager because I loved reading fantasy books 📚

The one that influenced me the most was Philip Pullman's #HisDarkMaterials which has lots of science ideas woven through it, including atoms and dark matter, parallel universes and more!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I started reading about the science behind all this and knew I had to keep learning more! 

Chemistry was my favourite subject at school but I knew  early on that I wanted to study physics at university, and that I wanted to be a scientist working on 'magic' in real life!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Are there any books or authors that changed the way you see the world, or that you think influenced your life choices?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @Felgraf_Physics Yes! His books are incredible, I wish I'd started reading them earlier. Although at least that means that there are still plenty that I can still enjoy for the first time now!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I studied undergraduate physics at the University of St Andrews in Scotland and loved the physics department @PhysAstroStAnd. 

The department clearly cared about teaching, and the academics were always so supportive and welcoming of questions.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Students were encouraged to do (paid!) research projects over the summer, and this was a fantastic way of integrating undergraduates with the research activities in the department. As a student it was great to get experience of research before committing to a PhD.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I had two amazing summer projects - one in cold atoms @UltracoldStAnd and one on scanning tunnelling microscopy in the predecessor of @Kinggroup_ARPES.

The research groups were incredibly welcoming and supportive of students making mistakes and finding their feet in the lab!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It was then that I fell in love with cold atoms 😍 The experimental techniques are fun and varied, and the underlying physics and experiment goals seemed incredible.

When I first stepped into the cold atom lab it felt like I'd finally found the magic I'd been looking for!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I was lucky enough to be working on a really fun project - designing holograms to use as traps for ultracold atoms, supervised by then-PhD student @grahamdbruce.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This used a spatial light modulator, a programmable liquid crystal array that imprints a phase pattern on a laser beam (by slowing down different parts of the beam). After some simple optics this phase pattern creates intensity variations, making an interesting optical trap!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I continued working on this for my MPhys research (the final year project for an integrated undergraduate masters), and developed a flexible approach to calculating the phase patterns based on cost function minimisation (https://t.co/aU5azvl1LJ)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The research (and team) was so much fun that I continued some work with them after I'd left - extending the holographic trapping work and applying the methods to a completely different (theory) problem with @PhysicsSteve (https://t.co/fnMqyPLstd, https://t.co/sgE9gfo4XY)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I feel so lucky to have had such an amazing undergraduate experience! 

I'm incredibly grateful to all my lecturers and tutors, especially those who patiently answered my long lists of questions - I now have a better appreciation for how busy they must have been!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
During one of my summer projects I read a paper about creating vortices by rotating a cold atom cloud, a branch of quantum simulation that uses parallels between the forces on rotating neutral atoms and charged particles in a magnetic field.
https://t.co/IHPYdYQIrF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I knew at that stage that I wanted to do a PhD, and was pretty certain I wanted to continue with cold atoms, so I applied to (and was accepted by) the cold atom group at the University of Oxford who had written that paper.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (This is a compressed version of that story! I applied to several research groups, who all do incredibly exciting work. I definitely recommend students explore their options and apply to (and visit) several groups to work out what research and group dynamic works for them.)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My PhD research was on radiofrequency-dressed magnetic traps for ultracold atoms. These are magnetic traps with a radiofrequency field applied to create a trapping surface where the atomic energy level splitting due to the magnetic field is resonant with this frequency.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
For us this created tuneable ellipsoidal trapping surfaces, and my main PhD result was the first experimental demonstration of using several radiofrequency fields to create concentric trapping surfaces for quantum simulation or atom interferometry.
https://t.co/Hmrz9fKemQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I also continued working on shaped optical traps - this time using the deflection of a laser beam by acousto-optic devices (where an acoustic wave in a crystal creates a diffraction grating) to rapidly ‘paint’ and also create precisely-controllable arrays of individual beams.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I quickly felt overwhelmed when I started my PhD. I had expected a steep learning curve, but I wasn’t prepared for such a ‘sink or swim’ environment.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I’m sure this works well for some people, and there can be a lot of value in being given the independence to try things out for yourself and make mistakes - but I think this should be balanced with enough guidance and support for each student to thrive.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, this PhD experience gave me the confidence of knowing that I could learn to understand, build and fix a complicated system. I also learnt a lot of interesting physics, and good science practice along the way!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I was also fortunate to share most of my PhD years with the best possible lab-mate, @drbentine, and other fantastic students. I learnt the value of teamwork in facing challenges that would be much more difficult alone!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I finished my PhD knowing that I wanted new challenges, but also that I wanted to continue working in cold atoms. That's why I was so excited to start a postdoc building a new experiment and working on optical lattices!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I started my postdoc at @Cambridge_Uni @DeptofPhysics four years ago, and have grown a lot as a researcher both inside and outside the lab. 

I’ve talked a lot about my research over the last couple of days, so this will be a short thread about some of the other things I do.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I’ve been lucky enough to belong to a college while here - first @JesusCollegeCam and now @Kings_College.

College membership is a nice way to stay connected with the broader life of the university. There’s a great community and opportunities to learn about interesting research!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Through college I was able to start running some of my own public outreach and engagement events. 

I love running workshops for primary school children and seeing their enthusiasm for science! I’m also really excited about an upcoming game exploring quasicrystals and 4d space!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I’m co-chair (with the amazing @beth_tennyson) of the department Research Staff Committee, where we represent postdocs in the wider department, and build a community for research staff.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We’ve been organising discussions and social events exploring ethics in physics research. I think that researchers should be aware of the impact of their work, and some study of ethics could be a useful part of researcher training.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It’s very easy to become single-minded about your research but I think I’m a much better scientist (and a happier human) when I make time to pursue other projects and interests!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I’m not sure what my career holds next. I'm enjoying my current research and am trying to learn more about funding processes. I have a few applications currently in progress so hopefully the next few months will bring good news!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This will be my last day on this account - I’m following my own advice and taking the weekend off from anything remotely adjacent to work!

Today I will talk about some of the practical side of working with cold atoms, and offer some advice for people interested in the field.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of the things I love about our experiments is that we tend to work in small teams building our own apparatus, so you have to be familiar with every part of the experiment.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (This is less true of my new interferometry research, where a huge team will be involved in building the full-size detector. Being less directly involved in various aspects of the experiment and apparatus is something I’ll have to get used to!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This means understanding an experiment timing system that will control laser powers and frequencies, shutter light, and control magnetic field sweeps - all at μs precision or better. This includes both hardware and the software that controls it.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
You will spend a lot of your time working with optics and lasers - optics alignment can get competitive!

You will work on ultra-high vacuum systems if you’re building or extending an apparatus. There are always small (or large) electronics tasks so you’ll be good at soldering!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You will also do a lot of computational simulation and modelling to explore ideas for new experiments and help inform design choices. Once an experiment is running you'll need to be able to analyse and understand the results.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Disclaimer - this is a list based on my own experiences! Different research groups operate differently, and there will be an emphasis on certain tasks more than others at various stages of an experiment’s lifetime.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This means there are always opportunities to develop new skills! Absolutely no-one enters the field with all those skills already, and joining a new research group is a learning curve even if you’ve already worked on similar experiments before.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You’re unlikely to enjoy every part of the work - e.g. I really don’t enjoy machining parts so am glad now that I can delegate those jobs! Everyone has natural strengths and interests that they will gravitate towards in finding their niche in the team.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
And let’s not forget the other important research skills - teamwork, communication, problem-solving, planning, and time-management. As you progress in your career, leadership and management.

These are so often overlooked but research would fall apart without them!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I think that the most important skills I’ve developed during my career have been general problem solving: being able to take a complicated problem or system and work out how to methodically break it down into solvable parts.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Thread on my advice if you’re a student interested in a cold atom PhD, or a PhD or postdoc looking for a change in direction - bear in mind that this is based just on my own experiences and opinions!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It’s worth thinking about what skills you want to develop and where your interests are. e.g. are you more interested in thinking about physics goals and analysing data from an experiment that’s already running, or would you like to be part of the design and engineering process?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Try to align this with your long-term goals (with the understanding that these might change!) - e.g. if you want to run your own group one day it’s a good idea to get some experience of building an experiment.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But also consider that this will affect your publications - unfortunately these matter! A brand new apparatus might take 3 or more years before you start seeing high-impact papers, so weigh this against the skills you’ll develop during the building stage.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That is something I should have considered more seriously! If you are at the start of the building process make sure that your funding covers long enough to have a reasonable chance of publications, and discuss the option of publishable side-projects with the PI.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Think about how your previous experience and existing skills fit in with the type of work you’d be doing. A lack of direct experience shouldn’t prevent you from joining an experiment (in my opinion) but think about how your existing skills and interests can be expanded.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Personally I’m always happy to be contacted by prospective students by email, but we can have a much more constructive conversation if you show that you’ve looked into our research and have a general idea about the kinds of work this would involve.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Try to visit a research group and speak with the current students and postdocs. Don’t be afraid to ask awkward questions to check it would be a good fit for your specific needs and goals. If you want to spend time on e.g. outreach or teaching, make sure the PI would be on board.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I mentioned this yesterday, but invest time in developing other skills and interests - this makes you a happier person, increases your skills, exposes you to different career options, and can end up increasing your motivation for your research!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Finally: the experiment will always be there. Don’t be afraid to go on holiday, spend time with friends or family, or take weekends off - sometimes an emergency or set of measurement will require long hours but this shouldn’t become your standard way of working!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
That’s all from me - I hope you’ve enjoyed hearing about my work and the world of the ultracold this week.

Thanks so much to the RealSci_Nano team for having me, and follow me @UltracoldTiff for more updates! https://t.co/54mKV3xNsA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hello Materials/NanoScience Enthusiasts! My name is Burak Guzelturk. I’m excited to share my journey in science this week. Before kicking in with exciting ultrafast X-ray science - big applause to organizers of this account for bringing wider voice to scientists around the world!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A little intro about me: I am a beamline scientist at Advanced Photon Source, a synchrotron part of Argonne National Laboratory. In our beamline, we are doing time-resolved X-ray scattering and spectroscopy experiments on a wide range of material systems.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We are shooting lasers and X-rays onto the samples at the same time and watching how atoms jiggle and wiggle due to excitation, how they interact and relax over time. https://t.co/bQ6sw8po0W

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You will hear some of the recent exciting stuff using such ultrafast structural measurement techniques throughout this week, how useful they are... Also tips and tricks on how to get beamtimes at large user facilities, prepare for beamtimes and hopefully get successful results! https://t.co/5t5p1TBoPi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Alright, let's get into business of ultrafast X-rays!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Synchrotrons (and XFELs) are basically giant machines acting as X-ray lasers! https://t.co/4TbCYgS5fg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These places provide pulsed X-rays with well defined repetition rate, which enables time-resolved X-ray experiments. APS has 24 bunch mode, giving 24 X-ray bunches separated by 153 ns within a period of the storage ring, so simply an X-ray laser with 6.5 MHz repetition rate.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We synchronize our ultrafast lasers that can produce visible/IR light with the repetition rate of the X-rays. Therefore, we can adjust the arrival time of a laser pulse with respect to that of the X-ray pulse quite precisely, the technique known as pump-probe in optical domain

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This has similarities to a stop-motion photography or slow-mo which helps to to resolve fast motion happening 
Image ref:https://t.co/YVERqBkpso https://t.co/FLdx2VqIWj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But, different than macro-scale, we are interested in visualizing dynamics happening at the atomic scale following a laser excitation. Non-equilibrium induced by the excited state and its relaxation.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As compared to complimentary techniques such as optical transient absorption, time-resolved photoluminescence, TR-ARPES etc etc. probes like X-rays and electrons provide the point of view of the atomic structure different than electronic structure and provides new aspects https://t.co/oqxyKEqk1Z

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let’s talk about how optical pump / X-ray diffraction/absorption probe experiments. Why are they useful? And how? https://t.co/0EJpsGzpCP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Two directions: (1) Visualization of energy conversion processes in photoactive materials (Ex/ photocatalysts and photovoltaic materials) by probing how light energy and hot-carriers are turned into into lattice heating or carrier trapping causing local lattice deformations... https://t.co/ROEmte0K13

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (2) Manipulating matter with laser pulses and creating dynamic new states. Optical pump/X-ray probe allows probing these states: Ex/ transient phase transformations, light-induced bond-breaking-forming etc.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Before we dive into some cool examples, let’s check out what are key observables in these experiments

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In optical pump/X-ray diffraction probe, we basically do XRD transiently. Therefore, observables are Bragg peaks, their positions, intensities and widths.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Bragg peaks may shift to low Q for example. It means the material expands. It typically happens when hot-carrier relax via electron - phonon coupling. There could be other ways that cause shift of Bragg peaks due to induced and relaxed strain in the material. https://t.co/WpNGaES1tK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Specific phonon modes may be launched due to photoexcitation. This can lead to periodic modulation of the structure factor, hence up and down periodic changes of the Bragg peak intensities https://t.co/yx86vVRbZI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Or, some of the Bragg peaks may disappear while other may appear. The number of peaks may go down if the material converts from a lower symmetry structure to a higher symmetry structure. All these changes indicate the unit cell representing the material is now different. https://t.co/SciSMGRp82

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Last example of observables in optical pump/XRD probe experiments is the changes in the Bragg peak intensity and width. Peak intensities can go down if the material is becoming more disoredered. This happens, for example, when you heat up a material https://t.co/3kOwe9t8cX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can also talk about different set of observables associated with  optical pump/X-ray absorption experiments. I am showing here a Co K-edge X-ray absorption spectrum. The spectral region around the absorption edge is called XANES - X-ray absorption near edge structure. https://t.co/xZHkz29VuS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: XANES  region is sensitive to electronic perturbations. Localization of an electron or hole around the element gives rise to shifts to either low or higher energy. As well as pre-edge structures can change due to this.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: EXAFS is the absorption that extends many 100 eV away from the absorption edge itself which is mainly sensitive to the local structure, i.e., bonding, around the element withing the material. Changes in this region indicates changes in the bond lengths.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These regions are overall summarized here https://t.co/PlecozD8VY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
These hopefully give more concerete sense on what these measurements show and why we do them... 
Next up: some of the literature examples! https://t.co/WiKbm2W4Uz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let’s check out some classical work that utilized ultrafast structural measurements and also more recent ones. This is definitely not an exhaustive list of papers but some that I personally find useful (and also a little bit of shameless self-promotion of our work)! https://t.co/2wAbt7KHq6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Early work was focused on using optical pump / X-ray (or electron) diffraction probe experiments to investigate how fast bonds break and how fast materials transform. Questions like how fast can you melt a material or how fast can you break a bond? https://t.co/GmbVIVxrGq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Tribute to late Ahmed Zewail who pioneered a lot in ultrafast comunity. His group’s paper back in 1997 is one of the first to resolve chemical bond breaking in a molecule after photoexcitation. https://t.co/YVXipbSQkw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Another early paper is from Bradley Siwick and Dwayne Miller in 2003. They visualized transient melting of aluminum after laser excitation. Aluminum film can melt as fast as 3.5 ps after laser excitation.  
https://t.co/AUaZjjeCEl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: More recent work attempted to use such measurements to characterize how atomic structure deforms due to an electronic excited state, the so-called polarons which play important roles in optoelectronic properties of materials using for photocatalysis and photovoltaics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: An example is using transient X-ray absorption experiments resolving carrier localization and small polaron formation in iron oxide nanoparticles commonly used as catalysts in various applications. They utilized iron edge transient XANES measurements. https://t.co/6WSLRUqqob

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
More recent example is from our work, where we used transient diffuse X-ray scattering to visualize dynamic growth of point-defect like structural deformations after photoexcitation in lead halide perovskites indicating the presence of large polarons  
https://t.co/j3iCT4QnGF https://t.co/gVaMLaoXQ1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Also, it turns out ultrafast structural measurements are excellent ways to make transient thermometry of materials at picosecond timescales which is otherwise quite challenging task via optical methods. This allows one to characterize how fast hot carrier cool and lattice heat up https://t.co/zSZzAgEc1R

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Therefore, one may call “hot carrier cooling” == “cold lattice heating” https://t.co/AwK5sK9Meo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: An example of this is from our work where we looked into hot carrier cooling and electron phonon coupling  in gold nanocrystals and showed strong size and surface chemistry dependence. Larger particles have weaker electron – phonon coupling, hence longer lived hot carriers.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
However, ligands such as thiols that strongly bound to the gold surface can slow down hot-carrier cooling via transient surface energy transfer across metal – ligand interaface.  
https://t.co/e2IEpunPM5 https://t.co/uA1ZnkaBvM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Other recent work have attempted to resolving transient strain in materials and especially in nano-objects under non-equilibrium conditions

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This paper by Ian Robinson has beautifully resolved transient strain evolution in large gold nanoparticles (>300 nm) by applying a coherent Bragg diffraction imaging technique combined with a pump/probe scheme. https://t.co/IyxohHCHZN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another example is a recent work of ours where we looked at smaller CdSe/CdS nanocrystals that are used in QLED TVs. Under UV light, highly localized lattice deformations arise due to trapping of carriers on surfaces that dynamically distorts the surface https://t.co/KYzVVgCC9U

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Other examples include novl ways to utilize lasers or external excitation means to create useful states of matter for potential applications such as computing, information storage etc...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One such example is electrical pump / X-ray diffraction probe experiment on ferroelectric samples. They looking into speed limits of ferroelectric polarization switching and showed sub-nanosecond regime is possible https://t.co/svChDHJroP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another cool example using laser pulses to make a transient superconductor. https://t.co/DrgWV5zW9D

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Creation of supercrytals upon photoexcitation is also another quite interesting finding in complex oxides. This state of matter could not be created by just heating up or cooling down the material but just through intense laser excitation. https://t.co/XHtqIm1ZNB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Final example is a switch, "crystal symmetry switch". Light excitation generates a shear mode in a two dimensional material and modulates the crystal structure from a high symmetry one to a non-centrosymmetric, a new way to store info with >500 GHz. https://t.co/dF2Sntkrj0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Huh, a long chain of tweets! If you reached this point, congrats!!! Tomorrow I will talk more on the fun aspects of being a beamline scientist and will start talking more on how to get beamtimes, how to prepare and tips!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Synchrotrons are very dynamic places to work at. At APS there are 60+ beamlines, meaning 60+ different experiments going on simultaneously on the experimental floor on a typical day.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are always new experiments and new challenges. That I find quite exciting. Also, working with people from all around the world is quite fun and a continuous learning experience.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Technique development and improvements at the beamlines is significant part of the job of a beamline scientist in addition to supporting experiments and attracting researchers and forming flourishing user base at the beamline.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you are new to synchrotron based experiments, but do not know where to start. Check out the technique you are interested in, locate the relevant beamtime and then email beamline scientists working.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Beamline staff will be happy to chat, provide information about the capabilities, if needed set up a meeting and discuss about needs of your potential experiments.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The next step is to get a beamtime is to submitting a proposal. The next step is to get a beamtime is to submitting a proposal which is generally 3-5 pages of document answering questions like scientific purpose, why need for synchrotron, what is the need for specific beamline...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Key aspect is to convince the external reviewers about the feasibility of the experiment in addition to the novelty/importance of the scientific question. Getting feedback from beamline scientists is quite useful before the submission and it definitely does not hurt!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Let’s say that you got a beamtime awarded. Now what? https://t.co/hlhkUXbCqD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Preparation is everything! All the way from sample preparation to logistics, team work and data analysis. Beamtimes are generally for few days to whole week that continue for 24 hr. Therefore, it is not a one person’s job but requires multiple people, an experiment team.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Sample prep and making contingency plans is needed as some samples can turn out to be low quality or degraded. Or, they might degrade under X-rays... Therefore, having a set of samples and various backups is critical.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another important aspect is the on-line data analysis. Most beamlines have some sort of analysis environments for typical experiments. However, for specific experiments, new data analysis scripts may be needed and users should take initiative to prepare this before the beamtime.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Having data but not knowing what it tells you can be really bad especially when you need to make decisions  during the beamtime like what parameters to choose next or scan. Asking beamline staff for exemplary data beforehand to familiarize your self ahead of time is a great idea.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The week is about to end and I have a a short story about a recent paper of mine before my curation ends here @RealSci_Nano

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This week one of my paper got accepted in ACS Photonics that will be online soon. This paper has an interesting story with it that I thought I would share it with you all.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: During my postdoc, I was studying terahertz emission spectroscopy on various solar energy materials. One of the samples that I studied was PbTe. THz emission showed quite interesting dynamics and spectral responses from PbTe.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We thought THz emission from PbTe may help to explain some of the mistery on  optical phonon modes in this material. It has a simple cubic crystal structure but neutron measurements showed multiple transverse-like phonons at zone center that are not expected

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Some of these paper reporting phonon anomalies in PbTe: https://t.co/uDKAqq5CbC and potential Pb off-centering https://t.co/nmJzFoi4yc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I did a time-frequency domain analysis (moving window FFT) analysis on my data, and we were seeing delayed responses associated with a transverse optical mode with respect to others and we thought we might be seeing the anharmonic phonon-phonon renormalization in real-time.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If this was true, then it would mean that we could solve some of the mistery in this material...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We got some theory support doing some MD simulations and overall things were looking consistent. I wrote the paper and got it polished it. We were about to submit it. All this was back in summer of 2018.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There was a little point about the moving window FFT analysis that was bugging me. I was worried whether the result can be uniquely explained by different onset times of two modes, so whether there was a real time delay between spectral features.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Before we submitted the paper, I decided to play around more and simulated some signals mimicking the experiment and THz emission. I realized that this type of analysis cannot differentiate phase difference or time (on-set) delay. Therefore, our results were not conclusive!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This was frustrating at first. I had spent many months on the data, experiments and paper... Anyway, I decided to hold off the manuscript.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After three years, last summer I decided to go back and look at the data now with a fresh eye. I realized there was already quite interesting response in the Thz emission that I did not pay attention much as got so focused on phonon anharmonicity aspect.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: THz emission from PbTe could be significantly tuned spectrally under varying photoexcitation density. Tunability was quite significant from 3.2 to 2.4 THz and such large tunability was not observed in other THz emitter before. I thought this is something to tell to the community

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Therefore, I decided to re-write the paper and still disseminate these results. The reviewers really appreciated the results and the paper got quickly accepted.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I think if we have kept forward back in 2018, that paper could got published... but potentially would create more conflict in the community than solution. I think one of the take-home message behind this story is that scientific rigor is essential no matter what!
