tweets.text: Time for fun facts! Today's topic is anisotropy. Anisotropy is the property of a material showing the difference of the physical or mechanical properties when measured under different directions, as opposed to isotropy. This is a concept across many fields https://t.co/9Nz3S5O3K4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
For example, wood is stronger along the grain than perpendicular to the grain. Strength is a property of the wood and this property depends on the direction, which is wood's anisotropy. For more details, check out the wiki page above☝️
Picture courtesy of AhsanAronno https://t.co/TwM6bVljHo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here I want to focus on the optical anisotropy of crystals. The crystals are anisotropic to light. Many of you may hear of birefringence or double reflection, which is commonly seen in polarization optics. It is interesting to learn about how optical anisotropy develops.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The discovery of birefringence in a crystalline material can be traced back to 1669. Erasmus Bartholinus, a Danish physicist and mathematician, discovered the phenomenon of double refraction of calc-spar (a type of calcite). 
Pictures from Science Photo Library and Wikipedia https://t.co/C6fBS0O4Zm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In 1690, Christian Huygens, a Dutch physicist (yep who proposed Huygens principle), interpreted the
double refraction by assuming that in the crystal there is a secondary ellipsoidal wave in addition to a primary spherical wave, which is the fundamental discovery of polarization.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Isaac Newton explained this phenomenon by assuming that light particles have "sides", and used it as an argument against Hooke's wave optics. At that time, only longitudinal (acoustic) waves were known, and they could not explain transverse polarization.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In 1808 Étienne Malus observed the reflection of direct sunlight from a window through calcite and found the two images obtained by double refraction varied in relative intensities as rotating the crystal.He formulated Malus law and applied first the term "polarization" to light

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In 1809 Arago discovered the polarization of light from the clear blue sky.
In 1811 Arago observed the optical activity of quartz, and Biot discovered the high polarization of the rainbow.
In 1812 Arago constructed a filter from a pile of glass sheets.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In 1815 Biot established the optical activity of certain liquids and discovered the strong dichroism of tourmaline crystals. 
In the same year, Brewster discovered the law of Brewster's angle, also known as the polarization angle.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In 1828 Nicol invented a prism, which was the first easily usable polarizing filter.
After that, the theory and experiment of optical anisotropy and polarization optics were being improved and developed. The story never ends.
Next I will introduce what we discovered on this topic

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Source and reference:
1. Historical notes on anisotropy
https://t.co/Ed4xVmUzaw
2. Gabor Horvath’s thesis 
https://t.co/UdanJMIt2G
3. Conifold's answer from @StackExchange 
https://t.co/iUBV1VPcPx
4. https://t.co/WCZZnzJDBJ
5. https://t.co/jCqsslR4YF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Why do we care about optical anisotropy?
In the sense of polarization optics, there are devices that we commonly use, such as wire grid polarizers, polarizing beam splitters, waveplates... All of them rely on some kind of optical anisotropy to manipulate the polarization of light https://t.co/qd4g1l52tB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For wire grid polarizers, structural anisotropy in terms of patterned wires can absorb/reflect light at a certain polarization. But for PBS and waveplates, the anisotropy comes from the crystal structure itself of the material. For these systems, large anisotropy is the key. https://t.co/VLGUJEjt6P

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For uniaxial materials, birefringence is to quantify the anisotropy of a material, which is the difference between extraordinary (along the optical axis) and ordinary (perpendicular to the optical axis) refractive index (delta_n). https://t.co/fLLe7lskOx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The most commonly-used birefringent materials are calcite, rutile, and cadmium selenide. Calcite has a large birefringence span UV through near-infrared. And rutile extending more towards mid-infrared. Cadmium selenide is another birefringent material working in mid-infrared.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But you can see their delta_n are actually very small. So this leads to a question, can we find, or create a material that is highly birefringent across the infrared ranges? And this leads us to this concept of engineering the polarizability of a crystal structure.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Given the idea of polarizability engineering, we looked at a perovskite-type crystal structure. Its crystal structure is anisotropic and intrinsically has in-plane anisotropy. https://t.co/BGvvLLTIe3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Besides the fact that the crystal is anisotropic, we also need to think about what kind of chemicals can we use to maximize the polarizability difference between the planes. So we want to pick chemicals that give us lower polarizability in one direction versus the other. https://t.co/Zb6Iw9m8pM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In this case, barium, titanium, and sulfur provide good candidates. And this is our first attempt at engineering polarizability. In 2018, our group, together with Prof. Ravichandran's group and Prof. Han Wang's group from @USCViterbi reported giant birefringence of BaTiS3 (BTS)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
https://t.co/TzzTYX3vZQ
In this paper, we reported a difference between the ordinary and extraordinary refractive index up to 0.76 in a mid-infrared region of transparency, which is the largest of any bulk material with the in-plane optical axis that we know at that time. https://t.co/v02McOop6j

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But after that, during an experiment we found that the refractive indices of extraordinary and ordinary of BTS were mixed up. Actually it has positive birefringence instead of negative in the infrared range, and its giant anisotropy still works. This mistake was surprising to us.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After that, we submitted the author correction and right now it's up online. https://t.co/jCWg2WLV05

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So I'd love to walk you through how we characterize this anisotropic material and how these mistakes occurred. As a super early-stage researcher, it's worth learning and thinking about "science is always self-correcting"

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For this work, we came up with a comprehensive optical characterization method by combining polarized infrared spectroscopy with generalized spectroscopic ellipsometry. This allows us to extract optical properties spanning UV to mid/far infrared range. https://t.co/8022uWr5G0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We used VASE from @JAWoollamCo to collect ellipsometry data across UV to near IR range. The idea of ellipsometry is to build up an optical model that can fit the values. here we created a generalized oscillator model that is a summation of Kramers-Kronig- consistent oscillators. https://t.co/wFUi1MdoXx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To further expand to mid/far infrared range, we can include the polarized reflection spectroscopy data in our fitting data set. By manipulating the oscillators, reflection data can also be fitted. https://t.co/5uzQGSriLz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: From that, we're now able to extract the optical properties of BTS from UV to mid/far IR. As I mentioned above, we ended up mixing the ordinary and extraordinary refractive index. This is due to two mistakes we made during the fitting.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The first error, we found that wrong Euler angles were defined in the model. The ellipsometer we used defines the c-axis into the substrate (out-of-plane), but we set the c-axis along the substrate (in-plane), which rendered a 90° offset. https://t.co/5KLD6z0lkq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Second, the direction of our IR polarizer was mixed up. Wire grid polarizer is vertically polarized when the value is set to be 0° but we did it wrong previously. So the sets of the polarized reflection data are flipped for perpendicular and parallel directions during fitting. https://t.co/N1NstHXCNv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The lucky thing is they both got 90° offsets and the two errors actually cancelled out, so the fitting is still valid, but the definition of the axes was wrong. To make it more clear, I put the original figure in the paper and our corrected figure here. https://t.co/SeqLuVSl2e

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: By now, it seems we are done with BTS but this group of perovskite material really has a lot of interesting things to explore. So besides BaTiS3, we also looked at other combinations of elements to get a better understanding. Further interesting works are in progress.😉

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Focused ion beam (FIB) is a technique frequently used in semiconductor industry, materials science, and biological field. A FIB instrument is almost identical to an SEM, but uses a beam of ions rather than electrons.
Pictures from:
https://t.co/l96Un7Vpyy
https://t.co/X2dhK5Hp6v https://t.co/Axhr3xeBcL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: FIB is a well-established technique for high-resolution area-selective milling and deposition. We can use a FIB to directly mill the specimen surface, which can be controlled with nanometer precision. FIB-assisted deposition has also been broadly used in micro-/nano-modification. https://t.co/DR6xbxeqOF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Our new effort is to use a FIB to realize direct writing, mask-free, any number of doping levels in a single step. We demonstrate the spatial modification of the optical properties of metal oxides (zinc oxide ZnO and vanadium dioxide VO2) using a commercial FIB system.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: First, we demonstrate ion implantation using FIB, where we used zin oxide (ZnO) as a host material. Using a 30keV Ga+ FIB and thermal annealing, we demonstrated variable doping of ZnO, achieving plasma wavelengths from the mid-infrared to the near-infrared range. https://t.co/ABj1e4yTiQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Then we demonstrate defect engineering of VO2 using FIB. FIB implantation (without annealing) can also be used to introduce structural defects into a material, and the induced defect density can be continuously controlled by varying the ion fluence. https://t.co/AXafqfGciO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Such defect-engineering techniques can be useful for locally modulating the insulator-to-metal transition (IMT) temperature of thin-film VO2. We achieved a reduction of the IMT temperature by ~15 °C in VO2. https://t.co/fSsJLd3RXe

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The FIB process doesn't require lithography or masking process. Due to the versatility of commercial FIBs, this technique can be used to modify and engineer materials with high resolution even for irregularly shaped materials where conventional lithography is challenging.

tweets.text: First off: "emergent phases and where to find them". https://t.co/XPjuADZEX1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So we can find examples of emergence all around us, nature is full of it! The basic idea is how collections of objects behave differently from individual objects in isolation. https://t.co/ZtZoG92FhN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
@sfmaehrlein Don't worry, there will be plenty of emerging buzz 😉
https://t.co/rNYfpV4jDG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So in the example pictured here, a large number of fish form into tightly formed shoal, as a way to deter predators. This collective response is an example of emergence.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Sand dunes formations are another example: one grain of sand is, well, just that. But many grains together form into beautiful and dynamic shapes. https://t.co/jPkbts2OAt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And one for the winter season: those gorgeous geometric patterns that appear from frozen water drops, each one subtely different to the last. Snow! https://t.co/GjALHPzHWJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Not much snow in Berlin so far this winter, one thing I'm going to miss from Switzerland.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In my research I'm interested in the collective behaviour that appears in materials, specifically in solids.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Solids are made up of lots of atoms, and have a huge number of electrons jostling around inside them. 

With all those charges running around and interacting with each other, something interesting is bound to happen, right? https://t.co/RKNleojokv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
One quite famous example of that is superconductivity: electrons passing through a material without any resistance at all! 

Maybe you've seen these "floating" crystals before? Those are superconductors! Wow! https://t.co/rG7rAjKggm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are lots of amazing emergent behaviours that pop up in solids: feel free to share your favourite in the comments! https://t.co/oRPVR2dyJv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Personally I've been thinking a lot recently about materials that switch between a metal and an insulator because of the strong repulsive interactions between electrons: the "Mott transition".

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: RT @Prokaryota: Applying for a postdoc fellowship in the UK? Here's a list of 100 Q&A questions to help you prepare for the interview 🙌💬 St…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @DanGRMead Right. Whether we're talking about nanometers or kilometers, femtoseconds or years, we'll find different behaviour appearing at each level.

Hi again everyone: today I'll talk a bit about how electrons are organised in materials, and venture into the lab!
While I prepare some material, let's see how everyone's doing:

How do you like Tuesdays?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So as we saw yesterday, there are LOADS of electrons in your average material. How can we organize them? 

We do this with the "band structure", for which a quick image search gives us lots of funky stuff! https://t.co/iS1vRZu7Tz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These busy figures are sometimes affectionately called "spaghetti" plots 😅. https://t.co/Jn70Ets4XJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @bkpipr I'm not an expert on calculations myself, but there are lots of good online resources. I'll try to look something out.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So where do these "bands" come from?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ok let's start from the top with a very simple "material": two hydrogen atoms "A" and "B". https://t.co/bFMRWCEI6U

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Each atom has a single electron that is found somewhere near the nucleus. Exactly where, we don't know, but the possible locations are shown by the little peak above each atom, representing the wavefunction.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Both electrons will have the same energy level (shown on the right) when the atoms are far enough apart that they don't see each other.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And if we bring them close together so they can see each other? What happens then to the energies of the two electrons? https://t.co/kWZXncg9Hd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The region in red is key. That's where the atoms can interact: where their wavefunctions overlap.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now instead of two separate atoms we have one combined system, and it's the combinations of the wavefunctions that give us our new energies.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Turns out we have two ways to combine these two electrons, as sketched here. Remember, it's that interaction region in red that's key! https://t.co/fnWKp1wArm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can either have a combination that adds togther in the interaction region (which we call "bonding") or subtracts and gives a zero crossing ("anti-bonding").

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These two possibilities have different energies, with the bonding state lower in energy than the anti-bonding one.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
As we add more atoms to our little system, there are more and more ways to combine all the electrons, so there are more energy levels!

Here's a nice way of seeing that that I've taken from Hoffmann's paper:
https://t.co/Q8uwVfTZK5 https://t.co/Z9q1I5xXLJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The dark and light balls represent the bonding and anti-bonding type pictures I drew before.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So now we have a whole lot of energy levels. But it would still be useful to organise them a bit better.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
To do that we use not the real-space positions of the electrons but their MOMENTUM (k) in the crystal as an index along the x-axis.

In this case we still have the bonding states at lowest energy, and the anti-bonding states at higher.
Hoffmann: https://t.co/mhkoi8kpvd https://t.co/HcRVUhtBjQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And that is our "band" in energy and momentum space. All the complex spaghetti from before comes from this, just with more and different atoms! https://t.co/1g84DhYDBN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Phew, we made it! And as a reward, this afternoon we can go and take a peak in the lab 😉. https://t.co/DYvnD0Zjjh

tweets.text: Tuesday does not seem to be popular 😅.

tweets.text: As I mentioned in the podcast chat, I'm interested in the DYNAMICS of electronic strucures (see also yesterday: spaghetti 😉)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
What that means for me is looking at how electrons behave on really short timescales: 10^-15 s or "femtoseconds".
https://t.co/4hDJH2s1Gm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We need to look at those very short times since that's where electrons do stuff like transfer energy. They are ultra fast! https://t.co/9KvGSbzkT9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So our experiments use pulsed lasers to measure at such short times. Basically it goes like this:
Excitation pulse (red)
Wait...
Probing pulse (blue)
Electrons are detected
https://t.co/Le4M3ODlHn https://t.co/vYYuYvfiX5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So the excitation pulse gives energy to the system, and then the probe pulse takes a snapshot of what the electrons are doing depending on how long we wait between them.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we change the delay we can see how the electrons behave at all time points after the excitation pulse, and putting all those snapshots together we get a moving view on the electrons!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It's kind of like making a slow motion movie:
we take quick snapshots at lots of times and then put it all together.
https://t.co/fT5PR39UYU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And just like the video of the bursting water balloon helps us see how that process occurs, our electronic movies help us see the details of what exactly is going on inside materials! https://t.co/WgjNXnv5os

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Stay tuned for some real life examples!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Like I said before, in our lab we use pulsed lasers to follow electronic behaviour down at the femtosecond timescale.
The kinds of materials we're interested in can often dramatically change their physical properties. https://t.co/kiwfhDaqnh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:

https://t.co/FftlR8qGhW
You can see really clear differences before and after we excite the material (check out the timer on the right). https://t.co/BdEu5S3d2R

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: From this data we can extract a lot of information about about the way this material behaves, both from the electronic and crystal point of view. Pretty neat, huh?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Using different types of analysers gives us the opportunity to measure different aspects of the dynamics too, for example with a "momentum micrscope" we can look at scattering all throughout the Brillouin zone at once! https://t.co/I6wVbsWRyQ

1/ Onwards and upwards! Or perhaps backwards (in time). 
I'd like to share parts of my journey from an BSc in EE to multifunctional nanomaterials and to pin-point the moment I was hooked on doing science - I hope you'll share yours (Refs. welcomed)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2/ I joined a nanoelectronics lab for MSc (Yaish lab) when the nanoworld was gaining much attention. My project which was about single Si nanowire FETs. Naturally, it evolved to something completely different within a few months - mechanical properties of suspended SiNWs>> https://t.co/6nR3c4dCl6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3/ It was pretty cool: the bottom-up NWs on the growth substrate looked like a spaghetti bowl, but you could still disperse individual ones, make them out in an optical mic. (despite ~ 30-60 nm in diameter) and use e-beam lithography and make suspended devices (Fig from paper) https://t.co/fJcUj7ndMW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
4/ at that time, using an AFM to bend/deform such NWs was quite common and the scientific community was in turmoil: what happens to the elastic properties of nanomaterials? 
Experimental reports were showing different trends...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5/ It's a good time to remember a fundamental truth about nanomaterials: surface is much more important in nanomaterials. Think about the ratio between the surface area and volume of a sphere, it follows ~ 1/r. https://t.co/iYqJ5eJElc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 6/ So people said that the SiO2 surrounding the NW plays an important role in the mechanical properties as it is actually a core/shell composite. That's true - but not the whole story and does not account for the results

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 7/ There is another interesting property of nanomaterials: they are much more flexible. As you recall, the NWs look like spaghetti, although they're made of brittle Si. That's because of their aspect ratio, which is very different than that of the Si wafer you use in the lab https://t.co/XF6kzGJoAh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 8/ So these tiny beams, although made of a relatively rigid material, exhibited quite the deformation under an AFM tip - in fact, the elastic regime went from bending to tension - as evident from the recorded force curves that displayed stiffening (Fig from paper) https://t.co/BHEDqs7CD3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
9/ So now we had basic beam theory (Euler–Bernoulli)
and the addition of tension (great paper by Heidelberg et al) however, fitting the tension model to our measurements did not yield reasonable results (huge Youngs modulus for Si). 
that's when I got hooked on science https://t.co/4tJ6ikTbq9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 10/ We realized that people disregard the residual stress in the beams, and that it can be detrimental, especially if you use the linear model. So we added a residual stress term to the model, and kaboom - model yields very reasonable results

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
11/ we found our wires belonged to two populations of Young's moduli - which was in agreement with their known crystalline orientations.
and I know I have to keep on doing this thing :)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hello everyone! My name is Rebecca and I'll be taking over RealSci Nano this week. I'm a PhD student at @UofG_MCMP in the University of Glasgow and I can't wait to tell you about my research this week!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm going to start off by introducing myself a bit more, and talk about how I ended up doing my PhD! I always loved physics, and knew from pretty young that I wanted to study it at uni and ended up doing an integrated masters in physics at the University of Kent

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It was there that I got into materials physics... kind of by accident. I was doing study abroad and missed the deadline for picking my masters project! I got assigned a materials project and very luckily, I loved it!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My project was looking for a new phase in bismuth ferrite using x-ray absorption spectroscopy, specifically extended x-ray absorption fine structure, or EXAFS. As part of my project I got to go to Diamond Light Source, which felt like finally taking part in “proper” science!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After that I decided to apply for PhDs because I knew I wanted to carry on studying, and because I’d really enjoyed my masters I decided to apply for materials projects. I accepted an offer from Glasgow, and that’s how I ended up where I am now!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Finishing up the day by talking a little bit about my PhD! My project uses electron energy loss spectroscopy (or EELS - remember this term! We'll be coming back to it later in the week) to look at the mirror coatings of gravitational wave detectors

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'll be going more into the specifics of my PhD later in the week, but suffice to say, knowing the structure of the mirror coatings can be really important to gravitational wave detectors, even though they're such a small component!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So although I'm a materials scientist, my samples are used for gravitational wave astronomy. That's probably my favourite part of materials, and spectroscopy in particular; how cross discipline its applications are!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'll be talking about my research in more depth tomorrow but that's it for today, I'll leave you with a picture of the sun catching the buildings opposite my newly-returned-to office: https://t.co/EHBKbJEb6L

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today I’m going to be talking about my PhD project (and definitely not procrastinating writing my thesis…). So like I said yesterday, my project uses electron energy loss spectroscopy to investigate the mirror coatings of gravitational wave detectors

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Starting with some context: why are the mirror coatings of GW detectors important? GWD are huge interferometers and they have have a bunch of mirrors inside them, not just at the end of the arms. The mirrors are made of silica...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: and it’s crucial they absorb as few of the laser photons as possible, as this would lead to heating of the mirrors, and cause warping, and affect the sensitivity of the detector.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of the things done to mitigate this is to coat the mirrors in multi-layer coatings, of high-refractive index and low-refractive index layers, but the coatings also contribute to the noise in the detector, particularly through thermal noise.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Fully understanding the structure of the coatings is the first step in characterising that noise so it can be subtracted from the GW signal, or eliminating it entirely!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So that’s the background for why coatings characterisation is important, I’ll be back after lunch to talk about HOW we do it!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: While coatings characterisation can take many forms, I use EELS. Very simple, for any unfamiliar with it, use an ARM, shoot electrons through sample, how much energy they’ve lost will tell you what elements are in your sample.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The intensity of edge at the characteristic energy-loss is proportional to the amount of the element in the sample. We can also use high-angle annular dark field imaging to spatially resolve microscope images the heavy atoms will deflect the electron beam more strongly...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: providing images with Z-contrast. Combining these two (with some clever maths) gives you spatially resolved images with absolute quantification, i.e. you can count the number of atoms of a specific element in any given pixel.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Going back to the coatings, it was known that there was argon in the coatings that wasn’t supposed to be there, and that there were little holes in the coatings. Using our technique we found they weren’t holes at all, but rather bubbles of argon.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Because we could count the number of argon atoms in the pixels we could work out the pressures and densities of the argon bubbles! And this research has applications outside GW detectors -- bubbles of noble gas form in the cladding of nuclear reactors in a similar process!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Took an unexpected break yesterday because it ended up being busier than expected! Thought I'd talk a bit about what my days have looked like this week as a final year PhD student!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Monday morning was very typical, admin and planning out my week! In the afternoon I was marking second year literature reports and then had another look at some code that suddenly broke on Friday

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Tuesday was similar, replied to some questions about the marks from the students and made a little progress on my thesis. My code was still being recalcitrant so I decided to go work at a coffee shop in the hope that a change of scenery might help

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And it did! Except I just copied the code into a new notebook and it suddenly worked... I didn't change any of the actual text so I'm still completely baffled by that one but I'm not complaining!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Like I said, Wednesday was a little busier, lost my morning to an unexpected appointment and then had demonstrating in the afternoon. I spent some time investigating potential postdocs and got stressed out thinking about the future 🙈

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today I have demonstrating again in the afternoon! Apart from that I'm adjusting a figure for a paper I'm working on after feedback from my supervisor and then I'm planning to make some thesis figures as I'll be in the figure making zone!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Fridays are always my least PhD-productive day. Our group does cake on Friday mornings, with us all taking turns to bring it in and early afternoons I have Italian class, as I wanted to do something apart from my PhD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Pre-pandemic I was part of a wind band but that obviously fell by the wayside, and I haven't managed to go back yet. I'll do some Italian prep in the morning around cake and then after see what odds and ends need doing before wrapping up for the weekend!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Thought I'd round up the week by talking a bit about  spectroscopy itself! While the GW part of my research is very cool, it's the spectroscopy that I really love, so lets do a quick rundown!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: EELS, my speciality and therefore obviosuly the best kind, is done in a microscope. Advantages: if you have a microscope it can be done in house, high spatial resolution, other characterisation can be done with the microscope's other capabilities

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But it also has disadvantages, most notably that microscope samples are easily damaged by the beam and signal to noise is often a problem

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: X-ray absorption spectroscopy is the other spectroscopy type that I have some hands-on experience with. Work very similarly to EELS, except you're using an x-ray beam at a synchtrotron.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy is a type I don't have any experience with but works by exposing a sample to light and seeing what characteristic frequencies are absorbed

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: X-ray fluorescence is the last type I'm going to talk about, and it works a little differently, rather than looking at what is absorbed, you expose your sample to X-rays and then see what is fluoresced by your sample

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All these spectroscopy types rely on the fact that the energy levels of different elements are different and unique, so you can figure out what elements are in your sample by looking for information at characteristic energies (543eV is the oxygen k-edge for example)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you have a spike at 543eV, there's oxygen in your sample!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But why did I pick those two types of spectroscopy, when there's dozens to go around? Quite simple really, they're used a lot for one of my favourite applications of spectroscopy: conservation

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: No, not the ecological kind but rather conservation of artworks and cultural artificacts! For these types of samples, understanding their structure and how they've changed since they were created can give important information on how to preserve them

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For really old samples, they can even tell us what they used to look like! For example, we know that old frescoes and the like used to be painted in vibrant colours thanks to trace amounts of these elements left behind

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is part of why I really love spectroscopy; although there are lots of varieties the principles are the same throughout, and they can be used for such a variety of things from helping observe the universe to preserving our history!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Part of this was due to the (continuing!) poor data correction standards, more on this later. Another problem is the inherent complexities in accurate TEM size distribution determinations, which an electron microscopist can explain far better than I. 3/7 https://t.co/f6Hl0d1wBU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But a main problem is that X-ray scattering gives a signal that closely matches a volume-weighted representation of the size distribution. (typically monodisperse) standards don’t have this, and voila, the size match between TEM and X-ray scattering is near perfect. 4/7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But add a bit of polydispersity, and all intercomparisons must be corrected either one way or the other before comparing. tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Happy Monday everyone! I'm Jarrett (@jdillenburger) and I will be this week's curator! I am an inorganic materials chemist working on my graduate studies @Penn @PennChemistry in the @MalloukLab

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This week's podcast is titled "Lasagna á la Nano" 

I think Lasagna is a tasty way to highlight the unique structure of layered materials!

Just like lasagna, layered materials are made up of stacks of repeating layers! https://t.co/366toz3Wwh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @SvenAskes Haha! It always makes me hungry when I'm working in the lab!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For a quick personal bio, I am currently a grad student in the @MalloukLab. I study layered materials --> transition metal dichalcogenides (TMD) and layered double hydroxides (LDH).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Before grad school, I attended @DenisonU in central Ohio where I received a B.S. in chemistry. Attending a PUI, I got great 1:1 mentorship from my professors who inspired me to go to grad school!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I started researching layered materials at @PSU with Tom Mallouk. I investigated layered sulfide perovskites with ferroelectric properties. We transitioned to @PennChemistry in 2019 and I started work on functionalizing TMD basal planes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Recently I've been exploring layered double hydroxides to understand their water retention properties in bulk and as nanomaterials. I'm hoping to apply this work to making new types of alkaline fuel cells!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @goldclusters @MalloukLab I am so glad to hear that! What do you focus on?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @Andre_marinho91 Awesome! What kind of layered materials do you work with? TMDs?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I hope you’ve all decided to have lasagna tonight! 🍴

Inorganic layered materials encompass many different compositions and structural motifs 

Let me tell you about a few of the awesome variations out there: 💪

Threading🧵

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Graphite and hexagonal boronitride (h-BN):

These materials are made of one-atom-thick nanosheets. The individual 2D nanosheets are formed by covalent bonds forming repeating hexagonal structures. Meanwhile, the stack of sheets are held together only by weak Van der Waals forces https://t.co/jDiPFhwBNr

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Transition Metal Dichalcogenides (TMDs):

TMDs have nanosheets that are typically three atoms thick. The transition metal, (i.e.Molybdenum), is sandwiched between layers of dichalcogenides (i.e sulfur). Here again, only Van der Waals forces hold stacks of nanosheets together. https://t.co/2EJxhYk2ZG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Layered Double Hydroxides (LDH):  😍

LDHs are a class of anionic clays (i.e. hydrotalcite). The nanosheets have a positive charge and often anions like carbonate or chloride are found in between the layers along with water molecules. H-bonding makes them difficult to exfoliate. https://t.co/SLBF4zgTju

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Intergrowth Structures:
A broad class of materials that often includes layered metal oxides and perovskites structures. (also layered oxysulfides, sulfides, and oxyfluorides) Some of these materials can be exfoliated into nanosheets while others refuse to. https://t.co/BkGqNCz3Jc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Lasagna á la Nano:

The most delicious type of layered material. Flexible sheets of pasta are separated by interlayer spaces filled with ricotta or béchamel, and bolognese sauces. Easy to mechanically exfoliate with a fork. 😂 https://t.co/j4aqf3u5aQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today I'm going to be talking about how I synthesize different inorganic layered materials. Not all methods need high temperatures, but this one does! #chemtwitter https://t.co/m0wXhJ3vND

tweets.text: When making bulk transition metal dichalcogenides (i.e. NbS2 or MoS2), I seal the elemental powders in an evacuated quartz ampule and heat them. It results in beautiful phase-pure crystals! https://t.co/0E5Vmi4K4O

"Electrifying Science"

Please welcome @MicrotoPico of @fzj_iek and @SchoolBaccara, @WWU_Muenster alumni for an electrifying week of science 😄 

On #177 episode of #UnderTheMicroscope Kerstin tells us about what is in store for this week🎧

https://t.co/AueMQSdxxW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Good morning everybody. My name is Kerstin Neuhaus (@MicrotoPico) and I am super excited to curate the Twitter channel @RealSci_Nano this week. I'm looking forward to the interaction and many questions. Also, I am always open for collaborations – just get in contact.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I already have a lot planned for the next seven days. First of all, today I would like to introduce myself and tell you how I came to research with atomic force microscopy. https://t.co/N6R82HLd0L

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I am already at the institute, but I will start with a little journey on how to become a #battery reseatcher, when you start out studying Earth Sciences...As a teenager, I participated in science competitions several times (@jugend_forscht) and couldn't decide

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: what excited me the most: chemistry or biology or geography? Therefore, I got the idea early on that geosciences could be the ideal study as it combines the complete field of STEM. I was particularly fascinated then, and still am, by space exploration and volcano research.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is me on Tenerife in 2010, enjoying a hike at Teide volcano. https://t.co/rteSrCNvLS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If geology is something that excites you, too, please follow @Geology_History for a daily dose of Geology, and attend the annual Mineral Cup @MineralCup on Twitter for some fun information on various minerals.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So almost twenty years ago I enrolled in earth sciences at @WWU_Muenster and actually wrote my bachelor thesis in #planetology on the weathering of the meteorite El Hammami on different substrates (a chondrule of El Hammami still is my Twitter avatar). https://t.co/Lslj4ZLsE2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you are interested in El Hammami, please also have a look at one of my old tweets. https://t.co/dRSFRcJdMO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In parallel, I worked in mineralogy and planetology as a student assistant and got a lot of experience working with SEM/EDX and preparing samples for TEM. I fell in love with microscopy ♥️🔬

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: While the work on #meteorites was incredibly exciting, I found it lacking in application. In addition, jobs in the field of #planetology are not that common. That's why, in addition to planetology, I focused on #mineralogy and #materialsscience in my master's degree and 1/8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: also attended lectures on solid-state chemistry in the chemistry department. This turned out to be a great stroke of luck later on. But first of all, I wrote my master's thesis on microstructure development in piezoelectric PZT fibers 2/8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: under different manufacturing conditions at @Fraunhofer_ISC in Würzburg/Germany for one year, which also included a lot of SEM research.3/8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I had been thinking for a long time that I wanted to continue working in research and applied to several PhD positions. In 2008 the master's degree was still relatively new in Germany; we previously had a 5-year diploma, which is a bit like integrated BS-MS. In addition, 4/8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: many PIs apparently didn’t know anything about the subject of geosciences and were looking for a chemist for microscopy-based research, although analytics and, in particular, light microscopy and SEM are extremely important components of our studies. 5/8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After getting several rejections, I contacted the Prof. Wiemhöfer from the Chemistry Department of WWU with whom I had heard several lectures at the beginning of the master's and asked him 6/8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: if he could maybe give me some advice on where I could possibly still apply for a PhD position.Only a short time later the answer came: "You don't need to apply elsewhere, I would like to have you as a PhD student" ...7/8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: and thus my scientific career in the field of #AFM + #energy materials began. 8/8 https://t.co/xxnn3wHyG6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My dissertation topic was "Electrochemical Characterization of mixed ionic-electronic conductive ceramic membranes and the influence of carbon dioxide treatment" and revolved around oxygen permeation membranes, but I will go into more detail on this later. 1/7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So this is me right after getting my doctorate: we traditionally get a hat made by our colleagues and in addition, new doctors are pulled through the town on a decorated cart. 2/7 https://t.co/bt2ssIFdN5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: During my PhD phase, in addition to my actual PhD topic, I was in charge of setting up a microscopy lab in our working group and assisting my colleagues with measurements on their materials (mainly ion-conducting polymers such as polysiloxanes and polyphosphazenes). 3/7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I ended up being scientifically responsible for three AFMs (two instruments from Keysight and a Cypher S from Asylum Research), a JEOL SEM, and a mineralogical light microscope, so I really had all the facilities to study my materials microscopically. 4/7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The good equipment is also the reason why I stayed in the same research group for seven more years after my PhD, first as a post-doc, then as an independent junior scientist with my own projects. Unlike many other colleagues, I only had very short research stays abroad. 5/7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A particular highlight was a trip to the Danish Technical University @DTUtweet, where I had the opportunity to work on the CAHT-SPM (Controlled Atmosphere High Temperature Scanning Probe Microscope, https://t.co/giN8ZSKJkE) at the research facility in #risø for some weeks. 6/7 https://t.co/O5Sljdzwwd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This instrument allows AFM-based measurements to be performed in various gas environments with variable pO2 and at temperatures up to 850 °C: Ideal conditions for the CeO2-based materials I was working on. 7/7 https://t.co/cLel0zrwZY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In April 2020, in the middle of the early days of the Corona pandemic, I moved from the university to the Helmholtz Institute Münster (HI MS) @fzj_iek, because I got the opportunity for a tenured position there,1/3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: which on the one hand requires me to work in the administration of the institute, but on the other hand allows me to build up my own small research group. #NewPI  2/3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Since my husband is also a scientist and also holds a tenured position in the same city, we thus hit the academic couples jackpot. This also helps extremely with being parents in academia 3/3 https://t.co/D7uG3LKQeU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I've moved from the office to the home office and am currently rewarding myself with homemade rhubarb pie from yesterday and a big coffee. In a moment, I'll tell you a bit about #Münster as a Germany-wide hotspot for #battery research. https://t.co/ektexpsKdv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But before that, in preparation for my day tomorrow, I would like to know from you which microscopes you mainly work with.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In case you have nothing planned for this afternoon and would like to hear a talk on #batteries, the International School for Battery Chemistry @SchoolBaccara has a public lecture series, which takes place on Monday afternoons at 3:30 CEST. Please join at  https://t.co/s1DcFnE24R https://t.co/qWdY3g2VfL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now, I would like to say some words about the #Battery research in #Münster. Batteries are a very special topic here as Münster has rapidly become a hot spot for battery research in Germany in the last 15 years. In addition to the Department of Chemistry 1/3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: and Pharmacy @WWU_Muenster and the #MEET Battery Research Center at the university, there are several scientific institutions and companies involved in research in this field. 2/3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is the #MEET Battery Research Center in the background. In front is the site, where our new Helmholtz Institute will be. Hopefully, the institute building will be finalized 2023/2024, because currently we mainly share university premises and do not have our own labs. 3/3 https://t.co/sXcWlAjvf5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @svenja_lohmann Ok, that is special😃

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In 2014, the Helmholtz Institute Münster (Institute for Energy and Climate Research 12 or HI MS) @fzj_iek (https://t.co/y4Y70jwHJS) where I have been working since 2020 was founded here as a branch of the Forschungszentrum Jülich @fz_juelich.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The institute is a collaboration of FZ Jülich, RWTH Aachen and WWU Münster. We deal with Ionics in Energy Storage, i.e. #electrolytes of all kinds. Research here ranges from solid electrolytes to polymer electrolytes, liquid electrolytes, and hybrid electrolytes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This includes #material #synthesis as well as development or adaption of #measurement methods. All this is done in very close cooperation with the #MEET Battery Research Center (https://t.co/30RkkSMaRi), but of course we also have project partners from all over the world.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In addition to the university and the HI MS, the @Fraunhofer Research Institution for Battery Cell Production (https://t.co/sioyGyls6v) as part of the project FoFeBat (“Forschungsfertigung Batteriezelle”) was launched in Münster in 2019 as a cooperation of

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 14 Fraunhofer Institutes, RWTH Aachen University, WWU Münster with the MEET Battery Research Center, HI MS and the Center for Solar Energy and Hydrogen Research (Baden-Württemberg) as well as TU Braunschweig. The project is funded by the federal government and the state

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: of North Rhine-Westphalia with a total of about 680 million euros. The factory, which will be built at the outskirts of #Münster, will provide the infrastructure with which companies and research institutions can optimize the near-series production of new #batteries.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In addition, a facility for research on #battery #recycling will be founded in Ibbenbüren, which is a small town not far away from Münster.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ok,now I am off to listen to the talk of Prof. Andreas Heuer at the public lecture series. See you later 😃

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, listened to another very nice talk 😃If you are generally interested in battery research, there are also several other great projects on this topic. For Germany/EU you can follow @2030Battery, @ClusterPolis, and @BIGMAP_EU and among others.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For battery research in general, there are e.g. accounts like @BatterySolid and @IntercalationSt who post news from this rapidly developing field. Also, if you speak German, I can really recommend the podcast of the research Cluster PoLis https://t.co/BxEazfM7ux.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Tomorrow I will be focusing a little bit more on lab work and have a look at different AFM-based measurement techniques.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hey #AFM community. This could be something for you: next round of the @SchoolBaccara and @ECS_Muenster public lecture series will be by Prof. Florian Hausen on in-situ AFM measurements ⬇️⬇️ https://t.co/KQMs0n2aye

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Good morning to all. Today I am staying in home office to finish analysis on some recent measurements on electrode materials we performed for a colleague from #MEET. So, from the poll yesterday (https://t.co/I893pyYwdq),

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: there are a lot of people reading this texts who are quite familiar with #AFM. Nevertheless, we will start with some basics 😃First, I'll take you on a tour through our lab. https://t.co/TOd4eTpewl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Admittedly, I'm very bad at filming, but you get an overview of our lab we are using at the Department of Inorganic and Analytical Chemistry. There are 3 AFMs (the big black box on the left also is an AFM), an SEM and a light microscope. We mainly work with the two AFMs I opened.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So, today is dedicated to writing a bit about atomic force microscopy (#AFM) and related techniques for electrochemical analysis and the possibilities in our lab.
We were finally able to get our own AFM last October, and I am super happy that we now have all possibilities

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
to perform measurements at different temperatures between 0-120 °C and also in different gas environments and also in liquids. 
This is me in front of the new instrument, looking very relieved that the installation (finished on the previous day) went so well. https://t.co/4Qf5xVAamq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @Loberd3 I was really lucky to acquire so much money over the years to get my hands on 3 of them. The Keysights (black big box -> 5600 LS, small grey box -> 5500) were purchased during my doctoral studies at the Chemistry department and the Cypher ES  is for my new group at @fzj_iek

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @Loberd3 @fzj_iek But you are right: AFM experiments are extremely time consuming...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Most of you will already have an idea how an atomic force microscope works. Basically, a very small tip with a reflective backside is dragged along a sample surface. 
An AFM tip is really small. In the image, what you can see is the chip, on which the cantilever https://t.co/EqLtvsryEq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (the small antenna protruding from the pointy part of the chip) is mounted. At the end of the cantilever, pointing in the direction of the viewer, sits the AFM tip. It is only visible under the microscope.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is how it look when we fix the cantilever into the tip holder of our Cypher ES. If you are tired, drank too much coffee, are excited, are clumsy, drank too few coffee… there are 1000 reasons, why mounting the #AFM tip can go wrong. https://t.co/yYgN25P18V

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.text: Good morning everyone. Today I would to zoom in a little bit more on materials we discussed previously and talk again about boundaires, in this case about grain boundaries. So, what is a grain boundary (GB) and why are they so important? 1/6 https://t.co/Ihb7Ou8hSZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Crystallographically speaking, a grain boundary in a single phase material is a very small area (1-2 nm width) in a crystalline material, where two areas - the grains - with different crystallographic orientation touch each other. There is a certain amount of lattice 2/6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: mismatch and overall confusion in this zone, so it’s the preferred place for single phase materials to dump all the ions which do not perfectly match the lattice. Also, point defects such as voids or “vacancies” in the lattice normally occur in a higher concentration at GB. 3/6 https://t.co/zNMcSXHLvU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This increased concentration of so-called defects (e.g. vacancies, dopant ions, contaminations) severely change the characteristics of the charge transport at grain boundaries compared to the bulk of the material. In acceptor doped ceria, GB are mainly slowing down the oxygen 4/6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ion transport in perpendicular direction, while the electron conductivity along the GB is often enhanced, especially when transition metal oxides are added e.g. as sintering aids. 5/6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This also leads to a difference of the surface potential of the GB compared to the bulk, which can be measured with KPFM and related techniques. 6/6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the past, I have worked with other research groups to investigate grain boundaries in a very exciting and versatile material: ZnO. This material normally is not so well known for its ionic conductivity (although there is some proton conductivity possible) but for

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: electronic applications. Historically, it has been used as a pigment, but nowadays you can also meet it in sunscreen or ointments for baby butts because it has an anti-inflammatory effect. https://t.co/AvYpVyzjKs

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Regarding the electrochemical aspects of the GB: it has been shown that negative charges represented by missing zinc cations agglomerate directly at the grain boundary, while a positively charged space charge layer (SCL) surrounds the grain boundary. This SCL is produced

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: mainly by increased concentrations of oxygen vacancies and zinc on interstitial lattice sites but also impurity donor cations (D) at the place of zinc. D can either be donor dopants (H+ can also be a donor dopant in ZnO) or impurities like Bi or Sb. https://t.co/FiBbazBfqJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In a collaboration with @JGonzalez_83, we were able to show by #KPFM measurements, that the potential barrier height at the grain boundaries of ZnO is strongly depending on the synthesis process. https://t.co/4CFXVl1V3g 
The work was focused on a new sintering method (spark 1/4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: plasma sintering with addition of a small amount of water) that achieved dense, nanocrystalline ZnO pellets at only 250 °C. tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: show what was going on at the GB. By using #KPFM and supported by impedance spectroscopy measurements focusing on the bulk and grain boundary conductivity, we were able to show that the treatment led to very high potential differences between grains and grain boundaries, 3/4

tweets.text: which means that there are a lot of defects around. For sintering, this is beneficial, as a high concentration of defects lowers the activation energy of the atomic diffusion. This is of course a simplified version, so for more details, please have a look at the paper😃🔬📚4/4

lattice allow for oxygen ions to move through the material by a hopping mechanism.

tweets.text: standard material for oxygen permeation (Gd-doped ceria) and added Al2O3 to get a model system. Al2O3 is an insulator and it has already been shown that increased concentrations of Al2O3 in combination with ceria (which is used for catalysis reactions where ceria is

the catalyst and Al2O3 is the substrate) increase the potential barrier at GB ➡️limited oxygen transport.

Hello All, 
I am Reza and I am a PhD student in THz Physics group in Free University of Berlin. I am so excited to curate the Science Talk channel this week. 

First I’ll introduce myself and talk about my carrier path.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I studied my B. Sc. In electrical Engineering in Shiraz. 
Shiraz is located in the south of Iran and has a population of approx. 1.5 million people. 
Shiraz is a really beautiful city which has so many famous gardens. I’ll share below few photos which I took few months ago https://t.co/2LKCVFuW76

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Shiraz is famous for few things in Iran: 
1) Shiraz wine
2) Poetry 
3) Relaxed and chilled people 
As you can see all three are highly related :)) 
Famous poets are Hafez and Saadi.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Shiraz University is one of the top 5 university in Iran. It has more than 20K students and so many campuses around the city. I studied Electrical Engineering from 2010 to 2014 there. 
The photo shown below is the main campus of Shiraz University. https://t.co/FnGN1iJEqT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
After finishing my bachelor, I moved to Milano, Italy. I studied Telecommunication Engineering in Politecnico di Milano.
You can see the main campus of Politecnico do Milano in picture below https://t.co/LWH9imQB20

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
After Milano, I moved to Berlin and started my PhD in Physics. It was a quite big change and it was challenging at the beginning. 
I am now living in Berlin for 5 years and I’m at the end of my PhD and Hopefully will finish this year. Below You can see a picture from FU Berlin. https://t.co/tcwthjaRzm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I am also a member of International Max-Planck Research School (IMPRS) in Berlin. 
I am doing my PhD in THz Physics group with supervision of Prof. Tobias Kampfrath. Our lab is located at Fritz-Haber-Institut (FHI) and Free university of Berlin. Below you can see a FHI picture https://t.co/m0iDuhiShg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Today I’ll talk about metasurfaces. Below you can see an example of a metasurface I designed few years ago.
Metasurfaces are artificial surfaces which are designed to achieve functionalities beyond the natural surfaces. Let me explain simply what is the metasurface below (1/6) https://t.co/Tl9mdIxzJL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Metallic surfaces reflect the electromagnetic wave in GHz frequencies fully but they apply a 180 degree phase shift (the reflection coefficient is r=-1). We can design an artificial surface which reflects the EM wave with 0 degree phase shift ( r=+1). (2/6)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
These surfaces are called artificial magnetic conductors (AMC). Why do we need a surface which has r=+1 ?
There are so many applications for such a surfaces, but one important one is to design high gain and more compact antennas, for example in your mobile phones. (3/6)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The prototype shown above is an artificial magnetic conductor working on f=11 GHz with 21% bandwidth. I worked on this project during my bachelor and my master studies ( 4/6) https://t.co/hSARMjgpSQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
You can check the paper below which is published in IEEE

R. Rouzegar, A. Alighanbari and O. M. Ramahi, "Wideband Uniplanar Artificial Magnetic Conductors Based on Curved Coupled Microstrip Line Resonators," in IEEE Microwave and Wireless Components Letters, vol. 27, no. 4, 2017.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you have questions about metasurfaces I would be happy to answer. (6/6)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Good afternoon everyone! I am Lea Nienhaus, an assistant professor @floridastate and I'm super excited to take over @RealSci_Nano this week!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We will be taking you through scanning tunneling microscopy, #glowythings, #upconversion, #kitchenspectroscopy and more this week!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Starting off with some introductions: My beginnings in science were early, playing with a chemistry kit when I was about 6 years old... and dry ice to play with at birthday parties (clearly, the daughter of scientists!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I received by https://t.co/1h1cI4KKle. from @uni_ulm. Ulm is famous for having the highest church steeple in the world (for now...) and being the birth city of Albert Einstein. https://t.co/yDWan0W2fg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I then moved on to the cornfields of central Illinois and obtained by PhD in Physical Chemistry working on Optical Scanning Tunneling Microscopy @ChemistryUIUC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Following my PhD, I moved to @ChemistryMIT to learn all about #glowythings and #upconversion in the Bawendi lab

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Then in 2018 - the Nienhaus lab at @floridastate was established. 🎉🎊

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hi there! My name is Rachel Weiss and I have been working in the Nienhaus lab at FSU for almost a year now. I study semiconductor nanocrystals (NCs) and my research focuses on optimizing them for use as triplet sensitizers (more on that later this week).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My incredible high school chem teacher, Ms. Massi, encouraged me to consider a career in chemistry, after previously never considered myself good at math or science. I later got my B.S. in chemistry @JacksonvilleU with a math minor (who would’ve guessed!?) https://t.co/1JkPmD72m0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: During an REU @SUChemistry in Dr. Zheng’s lab, I discovered my love of glowy things and research. I studied ligand exchanges in perovskite NCs and I even got to present my research at the NCUR REU conference! https://t.co/OCqIOiHEg5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: since then - we've been having fun with #glowythings in lab and at home! https://t.co/LCZRIBABV1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These days I am happily working in the Nienhaus lab, where I get to make glowy things all the time! You can see what I am up to @Rachel591 😋 https://t.co/szbTWlyC2F

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Today we will be tweeting about scanning tunneling microscopy! 

An 'atomically' sharp tip raster scans the surface and can map electron density on a sub-nanoscale size, enabling the visualization of single atoms 🤯 https://t.co/joGCHEWOKV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For this technique to work, a bias is applied between the tip and the sample - enabling quantum tunneling of electrons between the tip and the sample!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: STM is so sensitive that even music playing nearby is picked up in the tunneling current/topography, enjoy our "acoustic STM" rendition of Queen's "Another Perovskite Bites the Dust" https://t.co/mtwf6N2zTb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Did you know that you can combine STM and optical absorption spectroscopy? 

Single Molecule Absorption STM: SMA-STM

Adding laser illumination changes the populated electron levels in the sample - resulting in a change in the tunneling current. https://t.co/270zrZGYUQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Using this technique, I've looked at 'atomic orbitals of PbS quantum dots during my PhD, and more recently we've applied this technique to #perovskites, stay tuned for more updates soon at @NienhausFSU...

https://t.co/ywWhNADj9k

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So... as if adding optical spectroscopy to STM isn't hard enough, why don't we throw some X-rays in the mix? Using XTIP at the 4-ID-E beamline at @argonne National Lab, we do X-ray absorption spectroscopy on the nanoscale, using the STM tip as a local probe. https://t.co/sYcPUAdcVV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
with this, we've been able to track the palladium M2,3 edges when doped into perovskites:

https://t.co/J8hwFRXy6E

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In a different study, we've investigated the effect of bias polarity on the local environment of iodide in perovskites:

https://t.co/jDkkuu7tc5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Spoiler alert: More coming soon....

"Glowy Things & Why They Glow"

Deeper dive into @NienhausFSU is out now! 🥳🎧👇

#MaterialsScience #UnderTheMicroscope #ScienceTwitter #WomenInSTEM #Nanoscience #womeninscience @academicvoices 

https://t.co/o0zNIEqJqI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Today - what you've all been waiting for! We will talk about #glowythings. 

Today's topic is nanocrystals!!! https://t.co/AP2hq7HMHS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now that we've seen atoms, let's talk about "artificial atoms", also known as quantum dots!

Quantum dots bridge the gap between atoms and bulk materials, they have unique properties due to so-called quantum confinement effects. https://t.co/QtNChyzfcJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Quantum confinement occurs when you force an electron-hole pair to be in a box that is smaller in size than its natural size, much like this reddit cat squishing into a box that's too small for it. https://t.co/FrKuWPzBkz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Therefore, different sized nanocrystals (quantum dots) absorb and emit different colors, as shown here for CdSe https://t.co/7xoyOipapv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: How are these magical #glowythings made? We use the hot injection method where quantum dots nucleate and grow at high temperatures. Injection of precursors looks something like this for CdSe... https://t.co/o4V666DtUs

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Sometimes you can even track the nanocrystal growth directly during synthesis. This is a hot injection process under UV light to see the beautiful glow. https://t.co/3R2goRuWRM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Sometimes we even invite theorists into the lab for some hands-on experience with #glowythings. This is our "interdepartmental outreach program" 😆 https://t.co/dqbGdwLAiV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It made our resident theorist @DePrinceFSU so happy! https://t.co/4ClPS55OfF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Perovskite nanoplatelets can also be made through a ligand assisted reprecipitation method at room temperature, watch them glow! https://t.co/0QyUuw4F8M

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What is a nanoplatelet, you may ask? A nanocrystal that is quantum confined in only one direction, and results in a rectangular shape when we look at them under a transmission electron microscope. Image from @ZacharyVanOrman paper https://t.co/YsrjZUl6P5 https://t.co/SoU87zHQc4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @sciencenotscary I think you might mean sulfur.... ??? that stinks. Never smelled anything bad using Se...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @ZacharyVanOrman We can also make nanorods, where the excitons are quantum confined in two directions - sort of like a cat stuck in a tube. Scanning transmission electron microscopy image from @ZacharyVanOrman paper on CdTe nanorods, which we like to call "nanobananas" 😁 https://t.co/e2cCqi3k87 https://t.co/sy2KyAVaG8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today we will be talking about bulk perovskites!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: “Perovskite” is a general term for a crystal with an ABX3 structure. A is a monovalent cation, B is a divalent cation, and X is a monovalent anion. The composition can be customized, and you can even make mixed compositions, like the mixed halides we make in our lab. https://t.co/dLwDe84ePj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We make bulk perovskite thin films by spin coating precursor solutions onto glass and drop casting an antisolvent. The perovskite crystal structure is formed upon annealing, leading to a visible color change as the perovskite forms. https://t.co/j2NvU2JAyB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is a mixed halide perovskite thin film in 405nm light. Perovskites are great at absorbing light, which is why they are used in photovoltaics. The blue emission is from the epoxy used to encapsulate the film, since perovskites are sensitive to oxygen and water. https://t.co/UkYoZCfPuY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Perovskites can be investigated by many different methods...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For example, atomic force microscopy can be used to determine surface morphology, as shown in our recent collaboration with @toniobuonassisi, @SunShijing and @SarahWi8 https://t.co/DMK7yegngT https://t.co/BOIdmzUm0d

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: PL mapping can show heterogeneities in the emission intensity and lifetime across the surface. https://t.co/sELuBfipEp https://t.co/L7zIPetBGc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You can also make single crystal perovskites, like this MAPbBr3 made by our undergraduate student, @Gregers00. How beautiful! https://t.co/LzlXUYsM8x

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: XRF mapping can also be used to determine the location of dopants in the perovskite. https://t.co/sELuBf0OfP https://t.co/ImrqrTsXkm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Of course, we also investigate perovskites with our old friend STM. STM can give insight into e.g., the effect of an electric field on the soft perovskite lattice. https://t.co/DSciVpV0sQ https://t.co/ztg7k2qlrQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Why do we care about perovskites? They're fascinating materials, they glow, they make great solar cells, and they sensitize upconversion - stay tuned!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today we will be talking about photon upconversion @Rachel591 https://t.co/G7ygKWr1Cl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Why do glowy things glow? If a photon (AKA a shiny crumb) is absorbed, an electron is promoted from its ground state to a higher excited state. When this excited electron relaxes back to the ground state, the energy can be released as light. This is called photoluminescence.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The excited states of our molecules come in two different flavors: singlets and triplets. In a singlet state (vanilla), the electron spins are opposite, while in the triplet state (rocky road) the electron spins are the same. This causes problems when you want things to glow…. https://t.co/D3cAYDSPoi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: “Fluorescence” is photoluminescence from an excited singlet state. “Phosphorescence” is photoluminescence from an excited triplet state. But the optical transition into a triplet state is forbidden by selection rules ☹️.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Why do we care? We study photon upconversion, a process where low energy light is absorbed and high energy light is emitted. Do you believe in magic??? https://t.co/beWLBVDahe

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Photoluminescence in general involves a loss of energy – higher energy light is input, lower energy light is output. In upconversion, higher energy is output. How does this not violate the fundamental laws of thermodynamics? When two become one…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Triplet-triplet annihilation (TTA) is our favorite mechanism of upconversion. Basically, two triplet states are smushed together into one higher energy singlet state, just like Kelvin and Fred smooshed into this cuddle puddle. No spin flips are required... https://t.co/RFvLSM2DYx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Since TTA requires excited triplet states, and triplet states aren’t readily formed by optical absorption, we use triplet sensitizers. The molecules that undergo TTA are often called “annihilators” or “emitters”.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: More info on TTA in a recent perspective with @schmidtim, @drjessalves and @JialeF  https://t.co/2aAxRXBo29

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We use bulk perovskites and semiconductor nanocrystals as triplet sensitizers. These materials have two different triplet sensitization mechanisms.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Nanocrystals generally populate the triplet state of the annihilator by exciton transfer, while perovskites inject free charges to the triplet state. https://t.co/BzK81ge2gv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In this photo by @ZacharyVanOrman, inputting green (lower energy) light onto the sample leads to blue (higher energy) emission, AKA, upconversion! #FluorescenceFriday  https://t.co/ahoJBrx9tM https://t.co/7Gp76Ea8dz https://t.co/aSLC63Ouik

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In these photos by @NienhausFSU, infrared light is upconverted to visible light. #FluorescenceFriday 
For more on bulk perovskite sensitized upconversion, see https://t.co/opNQes1Dl0 https://t.co/YPXl1O725m

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In addition to looking cool 😎, upconversion has many applications and allows us to learn about energy transfer processes, charge transfer processes, energy levels, fluorescence, etc…
https://t.co/GudgAHSiG9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After a long day of research, members of the Nienhaus lab go home to their pets. Today we will have a tribute to the furry friends of our lab, @NienhausFSU.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In addition to being great models of singlet and triplet states, Fred and Kelvin have been known to help @NienhausFSU write grant proposals. #Caturday https://t.co/i8CNheOH94

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Occasionally, they’re joined by visiting scholar, Knödel, the beloved cat of @SarahWi8. https://t.co/NcHFwzsRdS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Junebug enjoys relaxing with @CleverChemPun after long days working in the lab. Junebug also loves to play, but she has been known to prefer trash instead of cat toys. https://t.co/Qds6H14RWy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Waiting back home for her is the cat of visiting student @ElenaCambiotti, who famously joined her in studying for an inorganic chemistry exam. https://t.co/LrrN48t9sO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Onto the dogs of the lab! Starting with Frankie, who serves as an audience member for @Rachel591 during presentation practice. In her free time, Frankie works as an “analytical chemist” - detecting molecular amounts of food particles on the ground. https://t.co/QQlcdoW3Ve

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: While his dogs live a few hours away, @AlexanderBiebe6  credits Akira and Koda with helping him stay sane throughout the ups and downs of graduate school. https://t.co/rtTVl93xGq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here we have Cooper, whose pictures serve as interim figures when @ZacharyVanOrman writes papers. Cooper's favorite glowy things include tennis balls and a glow in the dark collar. https://t.co/4cnXbXk0sf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Last but certainly not least is Ava, who @colettems_5 says is so cute that she makes you forget about any difficulties of day-to-day research.
That's all for today, folks! Happy #Caturday (and dog day!) https://t.co/AdAD3TAAgi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Today, we will wrap up the week with some #kitchenspectroscopy! 

When the pandemic first hit, we couldn’t play with #glowythings anymore… at least that’s what we first thought.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But then, with a simple blacklight, we managed to have a bunch of fun in the kitchen! https://t.co/VZWfRKhtXq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
With the help of @ZacharyVanOrman, I wrote one of my favorite papers on #glowythings at home! 

https://t.co/hN7HKW8lvd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are so many #glowythings you can find around the house, can you recognize them all? https://t.co/jif8qTdbEA

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Staying with the gin theme…More #kitchenspectroscopy can be done with purple gin, which is an awesome pH indicator (and tastes better than cabbage juice 🤢) https://t.co/D228po9OOD

Finally, in honor of my last day of curating this page, I baked a glowy bread 😁😁
