Hi all! I’m taking over @RealSci_Nano this week, so I'll quickly introduce myself before getting into the science talk!  

My name is Dr. Stephanie Gallant, and I am a materials chemist currently working as a postdoc with the Masson Group at the University of Montreal ⚜️ (1/3)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm originally from Newfoundland, Canada 🐟🍁 and recently finished my PhD at Memorial University. I defended my dissertation at the end of January, and moved to Montreal for my new role just two weeks later 🤯 (2/2)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
My current and previous work has involved using plasmonic nanomaterials to develop new light-based sensors  ⚡️🔎

I can’t wait to tell you all about my career path, the cool research I’ve gotten to work on, and my hopes for the future of nanomaterial sensors! Stay tuned! (3/3)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Today, I'll start things off by telling you a bit about my early days!

As a kid, I always had a grand curiosity about everything. I gained a reputation for asking a truly unbelievable number of questions 😅🤷🏻‍♀️ I simply needed to know the how and why for... everything! (1/6)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I have always loved learning new things and finding out whatever I could. Nothing was too mundane to observe, as exhibited by this qualitative study of human versus rabbit hair, from my beloved first furry pet 🐇 (2/6) https://t.co/cQZLJxAIki

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: By jr. high school, I was involved in science fairs, competing both regionally and nationally over several years. These were a wonderful experience into performing “real” science in a methodical way, as well as great practice in public speaking! (3/6)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here is me around 14, taken at the national competition for Sanofi-Aventis Biotech Challenge (now Biogenius Canada), before giving a nerve-wracking presentation at the NRC in Ottawa! This also unknowingly prepared me so well for many elements of grad school! (4/6) https://t.co/OeELB1bhpA

tweets.text:

Now that you know a bit more about me, 
@ChemGallant, let's talk some science!

I've been active in research since 2014, mid-BSc at Memorial University 🇨🇦 When meeting w/ the prof for my inorganic course (@merschrod), she offered me a research position for the term! 

(1/10)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Her group works in materials and surface science, studying both biological materials and novel sensing methods/materials. I ended up on the sensing side of things! 

This work involved developing + testing new sensors for Raman spectroscopy. 

(2/10)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We were working on enviro. sensors for monitoring  polyaromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in water - highly-stable major by-products of oil & gas processes. 

Since detection at low concs (≤ μg/L) was of interest, we worked w/ surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS)! 

(3/10) https://t.co/WEHJvXL120

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Raman scattering is an inherently weak effect — only 1 in 1,000,000 photons will be inelastically scattered!

SERS uses materials which boost the local electromagnetic field via oscillating surface electron clouds, allowing more photons-of-interest to be collected 😎 

(4/10) https://t.co/LqzcLPKTzJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
These signal-boosters are known as plasmonic materials, where those oscillating e- clouds are referred to as a "plasmon" (a quasiparticle, depending on who you ask 😉)

The classic examples of plasmonic materials are roughened silver or gold!  🪙🥈 

(5/10) https://t.co/vDC6Fx9Wup

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Whether presented as roughened surfaces or as individual particles, these plasmonic materials all have something in common: nanoscale features! 

The unique physical and optical properties of nanomaterials in general make them fantastic tools for spectroscopy. 

(6/10) https://t.co/AkS4z7DbjM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
A quick example fr. my own work of how small nanoscale changes lead to differing properties: 

The pale pink slides here have an uneven gold film roughly 5 nm in thickness, while the dark purple-pink slide is after annealing the same slide at 300°C for a few hours. 

(7/10) https://t.co/hq0cT3tR4p

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This image shows height mapping via atomic force microscopy (AFM) of these two gold surfaces, where we can see that the annealed sample is much more consistent (in height variation and pattern across its surface) compared to the freshly sputtered one. Wow!

(8/10) https://t.co/YJxOjS8OxV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Nanoscale and plasmonic materials are clearly fascinating subjects, having so much potential for use in many fields. 

Most people have observed the beauty of the nanoscale without realizing it — a great example is stained glass, often made with metal NP colloids 😍✨ 

(9/10) https://t.co/QZsrSXCshy

I began grad school in 2016, and was lucky to have the opportunity to design my own project from the ground-up. I chose to study use of nanoscale magnetic metal oxides as the main sensing component of a SERS sensor. 

Was this an out-there idea? Maybe! Probably! 
(1/?)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Plenty of research exists looking at properties and uses of magnetic NPs; some work is specific to SERS/plasmonics, though most of the studies at the time only used the magnetism for easy handling/movement of NPs. 

(2/?) https://t.co/XNXK0jMq00

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Such “core-shell” NPs are used for SERS where the outer layer of the NPs = classic plasmonic metal (Au, Ag), while the interior NP is made of another material, often magnetic iron oxides for quick manipulation through fluid/tissues/etc. 

(DOI: 10.1016/j.jmmm.2015.06.012) 

(3/?) https://t.co/cHLFqOBHQs

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I noted that many of these studies around the time tended to ignore any contributions of the iron oxide nanoparticle (IONP) cores to the SERS activity, despite them often being in local range of the sensing surface! 

The IONPs:

(4/?) https://t.co/GheLOLWVbA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Many researchers were then beginning to, and still are, looking into new classes/combos of plasmonic materials beyond Au or Ag, studying various metal oxide NPs, semiconductors, graphene/GO, carbon nanotubes, and more! 

(img DOI: 10.1063/5.0020752)

(5/?) https://t.co/XNB43Qaq5U

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It was this exploration of new, "unconventional" materials done by others for SERS which gave me some confidence to explore use of magnetic NPs as a major contributor to the SERS enhancement, and create a new design. 

A scary but exciting scientific chance!

(6/?) https://t.co/iuaL5ZLjVD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There was a lot of learning and troubleshooting in this new project — I had never even made nanoparticles before this, nor worked in an inert environment — though some of that could just be said about grad school in general 🤔😂

(7/?)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But eventually, I made reliable magnetic IONPs! Here are some scanning electron microscope images of them 💪🏼🧲 

(left: plain as-made NPs; right: organosilane-capped w/ APTES)

(8/?) https://t.co/A0kKeQMWgz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Then the task was to design a "deconstructed" version of the Fe3O4@Au core-shell sensors, using the gold layer in a more background role, and the IONPs at the surface of the design... 

(9/)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It turns out the usual film-formation methods are challenging when your particles are magnetic, and you haven't forced colloidal stability and/or discouraged aggregation. 

Films were too thin at best, uneven and not reproducible at worst!

(10/?) https://t.co/2h1hs8Tj0U

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We tried switching our capping silane to a thiol-terminal one for better Au adhesion, but this caused some strange activity of the surface upon irradiation at 830 nm. 

We’re talking… fully saturated detector @ only 1% laser power🥴 along with changing peaks over time!

(11/?)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
New bonds/complexes forming seemed likely; w/ some digging, it turns out research existed showing the catalytic activity of MPTMS, particularly on NP surfaces, including reducing capabilities. 

In any case, we had to scrap that mystery + head back to the drawing board.

(12/?)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
When drying IONP films onto our Au coated substrates, space was limited in the glovebox, so I ended up placing some atop the hot plate inside. When I took the dried samples out, they amazingly looked uniform, which I realized was fr. the magnet of the plate! 

(13/?)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Though these films were also too thin, as glass fluorescence still dominated the Raman spectrum (a constant issue!).

But the idea was sparked: could I just... use external mag fields to direct the NPs into ordered layers...?!

(14/?) https://t.co/sZeXkyHJQa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Running with this, I tried several iterations, and long story short — it worked! 

What we ended up designing was a patterned multilayer of IONPs, forming a wheel-and-spoke type shape across the 2D surface, following the radial mag. field lines (atop a cylindrical stack)

(15/?) https://t.co/dBxmU5xIVH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The many layers result in a rippling texture, with “hills” + “valleys” of NPs, where the base Au film can show through. 

Here is a depth profile of a region on one of the sensors! The sensing spot size for SERS at 20x would take up about a 20 x 20 μm area in the centre.

(16/?) https://t.co/VhViqpiDKu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Testing our new nano/micro-featured surface, we determined a few important things for optimal function of the sensor:

1. Both the Au thin film + mag NPs needed to be present
2. The NPs had to be patterned 
3. The laser had to be focused -within- the NP multilayer  

(17/?)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Here is our report including all the details for the research I've laid out so far! This covers our inital sensor design, testing/optimising this version, and trials for sensing PAHs in complex real-world samples (validated by GC-MS). 

https://t.co/zQ8lnqGw20

(18/?)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I had been continually interested in analogous forms of these magnetic iron oxides (Fe3O4/γ-Fe2O3) where the Fe2+ is swapped out for another transition metal — commonly Co2+ or Ni2+ — and the inverse spinel crystal structure is maintained. 

(DOI: 10.1002/sia.6568)

(19/?) https://t.co/Q7BLPQxVKb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The type of magnetism does come down to e- counts and geometry, so that is a consideration when planning for a particular product! "Magnetic" = ferro- or ferrimagnetic = must have a net moment across the material.  

All considered, I chose to explore CoFe2O4!
 
(20/?) https://t.co/ivDikMHijA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Our big manuscript is still in-progress on a lot of this cobalt ferrite sensor work, but I can share a few snippets! 

Largely, the tl;dr of it all is that scaling of nanoparticle syntheses are RARELY straightforward, but "bad" products aren't necessarily useless 😉🤔

(21/?)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Following a very similar synthesis to that of our IONPs, the products were -supposed- to be spherical little darlings... spoiler alert: not at ALL!

We got mixed geometries as we scaled the reaction volume, but I decided to try making sensors with these products anyhow.

(22/?) https://t.co/kFyNMcWSXM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
All of the CFNPs had fairly different magnetic parameters than the IONPs — significantly larger coercivity and remanance values! This means these behave as permenant mini-magnets themselves, and ALSO respond to an external field. This vid shows how strong they are!

(23/?) https://t.co/kZsfyr9fGz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Excitingly, the sensors patterned with these various CFNPs performed better than the previous version, boasting things like more sensitive signal detection at low concs and better reproducibility across replicate sensors. 

(24/?)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
These sensors being better in function largely comes down to two factors: 

(1) The varied geometries + size scales of NPs
(2) The large magnetic remanance + coercivity. 

(25/?)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
(1) Geometry is super important for plasmonics, as we want lots of so-called "hot-spots" where we find the greatest density of electron clouds! Angular shapes can be better (cubes, octahedra), and lots of NPs touching help in coupling their individual e- clouds together.

(26/?) https://t.co/6EM61UZBw2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
(1, con't) We have angular morphologies [big octahedra], along w/ round shapes [very small spheres, medium disks], all patterned together on the surface. 

Lots of opportunities for coupling, especially w/ varied scales — eg. many spheres touching one big Oh crystal

(27/?) https://t.co/riFh6g3sTG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @Orad Fumbling upwards on my own basically -does- describe the trajectory, and I stand by that 😤

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @lukeweston Yes! People are doing similar things currently re: theranostics, and this has been on my mind especially since switching over to biosensing in my postdoc. Lots of potential there!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
On point (2), as their properties allow the NPs to work as mini magnets individually, this means a magnetic field is being exerted (at least)  locally on the surface w/o any additional influence. This backs up our original hypothesis that magnetism is impactful for SERS!

(28/)

tweets.text:
Optimal analyte sensing happens within the NP layers, so our laser is interacting w/ the particles/their fields + vice versa. 

While there may be some directional element of the fields to further explore, we are dealing with scattering of light in many directions anyhow! 
(29/?)

There are many hopes I have for continuation of this work, but as I've moved on to a new role, it's uncertain if or how things will continue. There is so much potential for new variations, futher fleshing out the surface and enhancement model, etc.!

But! Luckily familiarity is setting in, and I've enjoyed getting to work in tandem with this "new" by working on things I'm more familiar with: Raman sensing, NP synthesis, and other various bits of chemistry.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: First off, I wanted to share how I got started in science, because that's really where my journey begins! I did my undergraduate degree at @TuftsUniversity, where I majored in chemistry and math and got involved in undergraduate research almost right away. 🐘👩‍🔬

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My research in Prof. Mary Jane Shultz's lab looked at the surface structure of ice, trying to understand which crystal face dominates when you grow solid ice from liquid water. This is actually a really hard question to answer, because all of the different crystalline faces...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
...are really similar in surface energy! This is why snowflakes are all so unique ❄️ In the lab, I would grow single-crystal ice samples and then etch their surfaces to reveal the crystal structure below. 

Here, you can see the interface between two crystalline domains! https://t.co/WxGrVcSUNH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Next up: graduate school! I chose @NUChemistry because I loved how interdisciplinary the department was. You can really tell an NU alum by their work-- it's like everyone is doing materials/nano work! 🤩

Lake Michigan also might have sweetened the deal... https://t.co/kWtnvCyO8T

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At NU, I joined the group of Prof. Richard Schaller, who works jointly between @NUChemistry and the Center for Nanoscale Materials @argonne. I was SO lucky to be able to call these two places my home-- the user staff at the CNM was so kind and was always willing to help me out.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The focus of my graduate research was the photophysics of CdSe nanoplatelets, which are nanoparticles shaped like playing cards: they are really thin in one dimension, but their lateral dimensions are (relatively) quite large. My thesis aimed to understand... https://t.co/aX3YojsjWJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ...how this dimensionality mismatch affected the dynamics and optoelectronic properties of these colloidal 2D nanoparticles, which are even more promising than conventional quantum dots for applications like LEDs and lasing.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: On my way to group meeting this morning! All our meetings are at 9am, which is not my cup of tea... https://t.co/RvQ74lSFXH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today, I've been in the lab! For my postdoc, I made a pretty big switch from my PhD, moving from ultrafast spectroscopy of semiconductor nanoparticles to self-assembly of polymer nanocomposites 😅 Right now, I am trying to understand how we can use external fields...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ...like magnetic fields to control the hierarchical structure of nanocomposites. For example, by drying iron oxide/supramolecular nanocomposites in a 0.1 T magnetic field, we can produce composites that have the same nanostructure (positioning of nanoparticles, polymers, etc) https://t.co/nqNr4wequ5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
...but that have completely different microstructures (larger scale order when you zoom out). This raises the question, can you make a whole suite of structures where the nanostructure is the same but the microstructure is varied? 

https://t.co/KDUNdUdfbM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Making such a big switch for my postdoc has been a massive challenge. But it has also really helped me refine my ideas and expand my knowledge. 

I definitely wish the community were more tolerant of exploration this "late" in a career!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
For the most part, postdocs are valued for their expertise. Yet the whole point of pursuing a postdoc (from my perspective) is to gain additional training. This dichotomy is something I have really struggled with.

On top of that, add in the pressure to publish in a short time.

tweets.text: @buerviper You could isolate the effect of microstructure on material properties. In a hierarchical material, each layer contributes to the overall properties. To understand how the microstructure plays a role, we need to be able to change the microstructure without changing anything else.

What is @ANSTO’s @ausynchrotron? 

It is a light source facility - in comparison to colliders (like CERN). 

We produce electrons with an electron gun and accelerate them to almost the speed of light (99.999987%) before forcing them with magnets on a circular motion. https://t.co/vXfNa6Pvzd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Those fast electrons don’t really like being forced on a ring by magnets🧲, so every time they are bent, they give of synchrotron light of all wavelength. 💫🌈

This light is extremely bright😎 and can be used by different instrument endstations, so called beamlines for research. https://t.co/ONCp7hBiCS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We currently have 10 operational beamlines - with another 8 being currently built as part of the BRIGHT program. 👩‍🔧👨‍🔧

But the synchrotron is more than just the science 🧬🦠🔬🩻

We celebrate the connection to Aboriginal knowledge and diversity of international staff and users. https://t.co/JhNoE214f7

1️⃣ First up: Imaging and Medical Beamline 

Abbreviation: IMBL

Fun fact: size matters - these guys have the world’s widest Xray beam 😉

Coolest gimmick: a monitor showing some examples of their 3D scans 🤩

1/5 🧵 https://t.co/S65005CuWt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This beamline is one of only a few of its type in the world! 🌏

Researchers use it for dynamic, high resolution, phase contrast 3D Xray imaging for tissues and bones for biomedical investigations 🤓

That’s quite a mouth full. But what does that mean? 

2/5 https://t.co/37Zh4NHovo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The images you get from this beamline are similar to a medical Xray 🩻 BUT IMBL does that much faster and with higher precision. 

They can also scan in layers through an object and therefore create these lovely 3D images. And all of that in a non-destructive manner 👍🏼

3/5 https://t.co/HmKlwuc9o5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The team looks at all sorts of samples: shark heads 🦈, rhino skulls 🦏, full grown trees 🌳 and even living animals 🐑🐁.
We have a vet and animal pen on site for that, to keep everyone safe and happy! 

The next step is to treat cancer in humans! 🤯

4/5 https://t.co/9b0itP1eiM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
To get the world’s widest beam, they have a huge distance from the Xray source (🍩) to the detector - measuring in a satellite building 135m away, connected through a tunnel. 
The result is a beam width of about 45cm! 

This is also the reason we can’t run laps around the ring!🏃 https://t.co/tlF5550Ur9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
2️⃣ next up: Xray Fluorescence Microscopy 

Abbreviation: XFM

Fun fact: discovering hidden paintings is their speciality 🎨

Coolest gimmick: the most beautiful, coloured images of worms and plants 🌱 

1/4 https://t.co/qR96XcCiqa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This beamline can map a range of elements at low concentrations but with very high resolution in a range of samples. 

Researchers use it for biological 🪴🪱, geological 🪨, cultural heritage ⛰ and industrial 🏭 samples. 

2/4 https://t.co/NJyulW79Fq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
They use the Xray beam from the source (🍩) to raster over a sample - which can be quite large - in micrometer precision to get quantitative elemental concentration maps. 🗺 

This leads to these lovely colour 🎨 overlayed images showing where certain elements can be found.

3/4 https://t.co/qxL1DCO6rp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
XFM can therefore reveal features from more than just the surface, demonstrated brilliantly in their collaborative project with the @NGVMelbourne  where they revealed a hidden painting under Edgar Degas’ “Portrait of a Woman”. This made the news 🗞 📰 

https://t.co/wJBla6UXny

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3️⃣&4️⃣ Macromolecular & Micro-Crystallography Beamline(s) 

Abbreviation: MX1 & MX2

Fun fact: these are 2 different beamlines but I shall present them as a double up here. 

Coolest gimmick: @Elamanor’s artwork on their user cabin windows 🎨😍

1/5 https://t.co/maiFw1EIDC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Both these beamlines use Xray diffraction to determine the atomic structure of crystalline samples. 💎

The difference is that on one of them, samples are usually protein crystals, while on the other researchers are looking at chemical crystals. 🧬🧪

2/5 https://t.co/Bx08ks9Nqo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
These beamlines are the workhorses 🐎 of the @ausynchrotron! Their super-fast and high throughput data collection means they can measure many 100s of samples per day - collecting a full data set of a crystal in as little as 18s!!! 

3/5 https://t.co/aDuzfdRQUE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
On top of that they have a sample mounting robot 🤖 for remote access, so researchers from all over Australia 🇦🇺 and the world 🌍 can send samples and run the beamlines from the comfort of their home. 🏡

4/5 https://t.co/lGdw2RguSJ

Abbreviation: IRM 

Fun fact: they can run even without the source (🍩) with a separate light source

Coolest gimmick: they don’t need lead shielding so they don’t need to search hutches to operate 🙌🏼

1/4 https://t.co/kfdQZOlSlf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This beamline combines the brilliance of the source (🍩) with a FTIR spectrometer and a microscope 🔬. This way researchers can analyse microscopic samples, like particles, thin layers or coatings. 

It accesses a wider range than lab IRs in combination with a microscope. 

2/4 https://t.co/ttvsauDu5G

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The molecular vibrations detectable with IRM are like signatures or fingerprints of molecules. 👍

Through a spatial mapping feature of the microscope, chemical maps of biological🕷, biomedical🦴 or food science🧀 as well as materials and forensics samples can be analysed. 

3/4 https://t.co/iDC9taJmT8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The team works with researchers to look into the secrets of Australian basket-web spider’s silk 🕷🕸 to develop new biomimetic fibres for textiles, tissue engineering and medical applications. 

Spiders are definitely friends around here 😉 https://t.co/pRN8UzkUtc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Btw their neighbour beamline is our number 

6️⃣ Terahertz / Far-Infrared Beamline 

Abbreviation: THz/Far-IR 

Due to a range of components and accessories available, researchers can do a variety of gas and condensed phase experiments here. https://t.co/oc2epTsRr9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
7️⃣ inching closer to my workplace: Soft Xray Spectroscopy 

Abbreviation: SXR

Fun fact: I call it the “airship” - like spaceship but reverse

Coolest gimmick: their Toroidal Analyser on wheels that are controlled by a console controller 🎮 

1/5 https://t.co/eS5RmsXEpQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The SXR beamline is set up for Xray absorption spectroscopy of surfaces with low atomic number elements. 🆒

And with surface, they mean it as their Xrays only penetrate 10nm to a few Angstrom of the sample surface. 🤩

2/5 https://t.co/dXarUK0ruI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The wavelength of Xrays SXR uses is so high, that we call them “soft” and they are get completely absorbed by the first ~200nm of material.

That’s why their endstation doesn’t need any shielding (no hutch).

3/5 https://t.co/vCiVGNttY5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
That’s also why their endstations need to be under Ultra High Vacuum to be able to measure anything. 

The vacuum conditions are similar to that in outer space! 🚀 it’s basically an airship - an inverted spaceship 🛸

4/5 https://t.co/qkg3S0Wpqr

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Their Toroidal Analyser for Angle Resolved Photoelectron Spectroscopy (ARPES) is the only instrument of its kind, as it was designed and built in Australia in collaboration with @latrobe. 

This enables excellent research into 2D materials like Graphene etc. 

5/5 https://t.co/MWwEdDf7HA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
8️⃣ welcome home: Small and Wide Angle Xray Scattering

Abbreviation: SAXS / WAXS

Fun fact: I work here 😂 - no “seriously”: we are known to constantly upgrade our beamline. When you come back, something has changed.

Coolest gimmick: our wall of post-it thank you notes 🥰

1/6 https://t.co/d7tjsTVYF6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This beamline is probably one of the most versatile beamlines at the @ausynchrotron. 🙏

Due to our open sample mounting table, we can accomodate for all types of sample environments and experiments. 🧪🔬💉

And we can look at objects between 0.5 and 500nm.

2/6 https://t.co/M9OOanCf6i

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The motto “everything goes” is sometimes taken quite literally: we can measure basically everything you can get Xrays through. Samples can be solids, liquids, powders, fibres, films, biological or synthetic, wet or dry, stationary or moving, hot or cold etc. 

3/6 https://t.co/h03YrrHS2B

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
SAXS generally measures elastic scattering from Xrays, similar to diffraction. We talk in scattering angle, which follows a reciprocal rule to the dimension of the sample feature.

Small or Wide Angle refers to the angular region of scattered beam to primary beam. 📐 

4/6 https://t.co/AlK7PBLJMb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
You might already know quite a bit about #SAXSland if you followed @drheaddamage in his week here.

I do want to talk about some things specific to our beamline a little bit later 😉 

5/6 https://t.co/e1aMnhJZ6t

tweets.text:
One of the prime examples from our beamline in recent years is the “Malaria Milkshake” 🥛🦠 project we’re working on together with @group_boyd at @MonashUni. 

They / we recently won a @eurekaprizes for this research. You can read all about it here: 

https://t.co/qCFmenWFgi

6/6

9️⃣ onto the finish line: Xray Absorption Spectroscopy 

Abbreviation: XAS

Fun fact: XAS is a synchrotron-only technique! Can’t do that in the lab 🥼 

Coolest gimmick: they currently have a High Energy Resolution Fluorescence Detection setup in one of the hutches

1/4 https://t.co/DpnzGgcK2e

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
XAS uses hard Xrays (so the opposite of SXR) to look at different oxidation states and chemical environments of specific elements in samples. 

They can also get information about the distance to and identify the neighbouring atoms of that element. 💁

2/4 https://t.co/KgJacmQdin

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Samples can be liquid, solid or gas, but most often researchers opt for powders! 

Our XAS beamline can look at all elements between Titanium (Ti) and Plutonium (Pu), and at very low concentrations of them (100 ppm) 👌

3/4 https://t.co/2vLg1USxO9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
During the pandemic, they worked with researchers from @excitonscience @UniMelb to analyse different batches of magnetic nanoparticles 🧲 for COVID test kits. 🦠

You can read about it here:

https://t.co/NFHJULGs5b

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
🔟 last but not least: Powder Diffraction 

Abbreviation: PD

Fun fact: they have one of the smallest datasets per measurement- only ~400KB

Coolest gimmick: they can heat up and measure samples up to 1600 degrees 🔥 and cool them down to 10K 🥶 

1/4 https://t.co/s3x6XSkzVm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This beamline can be used to look at crystal atomic structure both qualitatively (as a fingerprint) to see what phases are present and quantitatively, to see how much of each phase is present. 👍

2/4 https://t.co/GTaODjfqi5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
PD is invaluable as a vast extension to lab XRD, as it can use different sample environments and has a large angle high resolution Mythen II detector, collecting data simultaneously over 80 degree. 📐 

3/4 https://t.co/ktH79pgjqR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Busy day at work at the beamline 🤗 

But what does this SAXS beamline actually do 🤨 and how does it work? 🧐

A thread 🧵👇 https://t.co/FUFJMtZmyo

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: SAXS is another form of light scattering - similar to blue skies 🏞 or red sunsets 🌅. While they are visible light from the sun ☀️ scattered by gas molecules or dust in the air and atmosphere, SAXS is scattering of Xrays, with a wavelength 1000times smaller than visible light. https://t.co/uC4AiLOyo9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We use it to analyse the internal structure of solids, liquids or surfaces. 🧊

And with structure I mean how the matter inside a sample is arranged over a wide range of sizes 📏 https://t.co/vS4mbJKtdt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So what happens when we put a sample at the beamline? 🤷🏼‍♀️
The incoming Xrays are scattered off the electrons from atoms of the sample ⚛️
How they are scattered depends on how the electrons are arranged spatially. They can have different density variations, distances or direction. https://t.co/5LOUYWkuoP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
All of this influences the scattering pattern that comes out the other end. 💠

We use a sensitive 2D detector to collect these patterns. From that we can calculate the internal structure. ✳️

Unlike other instruments, for us samples don’t need to be optically transparent! 🔍 https://t.co/TBXRPqvhZ9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Let’s talk samples! 🧬🧫🧪 

What can we actually measure - and how - at #SAXSland ?! 

Here is the thread 🧵 for all of you who are thinking of measuring SAXS 🧵👇 https://t.co/NXWFKV7sPy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The most common experiments and also the majority (so far 😉) are TRANSMISSION measurements. The principle is pretty straight forward: we measure through the sample 

➡️➡️➡️🧪➡️➡️➡️ https://t.co/iPHbz0DttB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A small, highly parallel Xray beam hits the sample, some Xrays get absorbed but most travel straight through. These will be absorbed by a beamstop to protect our detector from being damaged. https://t.co/JZoKJCxIpa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Some Xrays that hit the sample are scattered in different angles as they pass through, forming a 2D, angle-dependent scattering pattern.            ↗️
                     ↗️
➡️➡️➡️🧪

These hold all the info about the structure and orientation of the measured sample. https://t.co/dKuv5FJnvV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Which angles are captured depends on the position of the detector relative to the sample. 

We can go as close as 600mm and as far as 7m - and everything in between. https://t.co/LnE6Ea2M49

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The other measurement style is called GRAZING INCIDENCE. Here, we look at the surface of a sample by detecting the refracted beam. 

This is typically used to look at crystalline structures dependent on the incident angle of the beam. 📐 https://t.co/eFBgd7vZDX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For this method, we usually use a 6-axis motorised hexapod. This piece of equipment enables us to not only move in x-, y-, and z-direction but also precisely control pitch, yaw and roll angle of the samples. https://t.co/1XZdH0OmnB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Both of these types of measurement can be performed either in AIR or in VACUUM, depending on your sample! 

We have a super versatile sample table, several standard setups and a vacuum sample vessel, minimising background scattering to basically not existing! https://t.co/fpS2XGroJy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Oh and before I log off for tonight, I can’t forget to mention that we also do super fancy equipments. 

As I said, we’re a super versatile beamline and we give almost everything a go… https://t.co/sz3fO7NcL6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The latest addition is our shiny new @AntonPaar Rheometer. We got it through a collaboration with @SoftMatterHackr and are finalising the installation at our beamline. Soon we can do rheology and SAXS simultaneously 😵‍💫 https://t.co/VkvSpOVZ2X

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
My favourite, however, are microfluidic setups. Pushing the boundaries of fluid dynamics. 😍 

I have been part of some pretty funky experiments in this field. But I will tell you a bit more about that tomorrow. https://t.co/XhkRNs6yk4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
What has Microfluidics to do with Mario Bros? 

People working with microfludics are basically tiny plumbers. 🪠
Microfluidics is a multidisciplinary field dealing with the behaviour of liquids 💦 in dimensions below 1mm. 📏 https://t.co/rhyqdLrtAx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So why warp pipe? 

Microfluidic systems typically transport, mix, separate or otherwise process and control fluids in small channels on devices. These can also include micropumps or microvalves. https://t.co/xpPOnPKv0Z

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
And why do we need this? 

Microfluidics is an extremely powerful tool to perform quantitative and qualitative analysis of a small amount of sample with high sensitivity and resolution. 🧪

They are also usually quite low cost devices, making testing and adjusting very easy! 🤑 https://t.co/GeH5CeYtcG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
What can they be used for? 

Applications range across various fields, like analytics 💻, biology 🧬, chemistry 🧪, medicine 🩺 and technology 📱.

“Standard” designs are trying to scale down chemistry labs to so-called lab-on-a-chip devices https://t.co/7UHlkJUoyd

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But there is also a lot of development happening to produce efficient microarrays - so-called DNA chips 🧬- and even reproduce complete organs in microfluidics, called “organ-on-a-chip”🫀🫁🧠, which is a significant step away from animal testing! 🐭🐰 https://t.co/9C7oxT1VtA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
RT @_SuSiSe_: Today I take you on a deep dive down the Mario Bros warp pipe of microfluidics!! 

Head over to @RealSci_Nano and read the in…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now what did I use microfluidics for? 

I user 3D hydrodynamic focussing devices to look at super fast reaction kinetics during continuous flow. https://t.co/L7vPWkmOKE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Transferring reactions from batch to microfluidics is particularly useful to transfer a time axis (= fast reaction occuring) onto a distance axis (= measure along the channel of the microfluidic device) https://t.co/ELQJDPdwGw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When combining this now with a powerful technique like SAXS, we can follow the reaction at very fast timescales, like milliseconds, a measurement at a time = a step along the device at a time. https://t.co/UjltZ5t2FH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I used this to follow the nucleation and growth of nanoparticles, the shape evolution of nanorods from seeded growth and the assembly of anisotropic, pH sensitive particles. 

You can also couple this with different optical methods like fluorescence or absorption measurements. https://t.co/BkHgqh7dF1

tweets.text: Mutations in over 50 genes are causative in ALS. 8 are direct regulators of the cytoskeleton including: Peripherin, Neurofilament, spastin, a tubulin isotype, dynactin subunit-1, kinesin5a, alsin, and profilin.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We are using biochemistry and cell biology to study mutations in profilin, which regulates both actin and microtubule assembly!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Surprisingly, we have have a bit of a handle on what happens to  the microtubule cytosksleton in ALS. Long story short, if you mess up the tracks or detach the motors that shuttle protein cargos around the cell... its not so great for your neurons and they die.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
some of the profilin mutations disrupt microtubule dynamics by no longer binding to the sides of MTs (M114T, E117G, and G118V).

While almost all mutations (8 total) disrupt direct interactions between profilin and actin monomers

tweets.label: Takeover

NO CELLS HERE!

its time for "intriguing open questions"

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hi there! I’m @JulienBarrier, a researcher in condensed matter physics at @UoMPhysics. Sounds vague? Follow the threads and hopefully by the end of the week you will know everything about this field of research!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: RT @JulienBarrier: This week, I'll be talking over the @RealSci_Nano account to talk, day-to-day about my research. Check it out!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm studying condensed matter physics (CMP), and within this field, I'm working on electron transport in graphene and graphene heterostructures. I'll talk a bit more about the science in the coming days

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm currently in Manchester (UK), the birthplace of graphene, but I haven't been there my whole life

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Before Manchester, I studied chemical physics at @ESPCI_Paris in France. This is a small institution, enrolling cohorts of 100, with a curriculum at the crossroads of physics and chemistry

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The curriculum @ESPCI_Paris is simple:
a) it teaches experimental science, 50% of the time spent on hands-on practice at the bench
b) it gives a mixed culture: physicists able to carry out basic chemical synthesis, chemists who understand the physical properties of their material

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At the end of my MSc degree, I flew to California to study the phase behaviour of halide perovskite alloys in the lab of @MMfToney at @SLAClab

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Halide perovskites are exciting materials, showing promising photovoltaic performances but are prone to phase instabilities leading to degradation and thus performance loss

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There, I used X-ray diffraction to understand the degradation and phase-separation mechanism. It resulted in 2 papers:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the first, we characterise the light-induced demixing. Under illumination, the material segregates into two phases, altering the performance of solar devices. It was published in @Matter_CP, and I contributed to the X-ray analysis https://t.co/a69hN0lQSq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the second, we used X-ray diffraction (XRD) to understand the heterogeneity better. Before that paper, it was very hard to monitor structural heterogeneity at length scales between 1nm and 100nm. Drawback overcome with XRD. Published in @EES_journal https://t.co/Y2scygKCWW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm talking about the papers, but they can be quite intimidating to read because it's how we - scientists - communicate our latest scientific advances to the rest of the scientific community. Don't hesitate to ask questions here!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After this experience in characterising the physical properties of nanomaterials with XRD, I started my PhD in Manchester @UoMPhysics

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Despite the notorious English rain, Manchester is a cool city: small enough that it's easy to walk/cycle everywhere, but big enough so that there are lots to do on the weekend

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In terms of Science, Manchester is the birthplace of graphene (@UoMGraphene), so we have nice facilities covering the full chain:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here, the National Graphene Institute is dedicated to basic research and fabrication of devices. Note the physics formula on the facade. https://t.co/3HElxXU7ON

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: .@JulienBarrier back here! Let's talk about some of the particularities of the British research system

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So I said I am currently an @EPSRC Fellow. What does it mean?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In most academic systems, a typical career path would be PhD > postdocs > assistant prof. > associate prof. > full prof. with naming differences depending on the country.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the UK, it is similar, the typical career path follows PhD > postdocs > lecturer > reader > professor. But there's another way: fellowships.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The idea is that a career move from the lecturer stage would be decided by how much grant money a researcher brings to their institution. Postdocs are not used to apply for grants, so hiring directly at the lecturer stage can be risky for an institution

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Fellowships in the UK are a way for early career researchers (postdoc level) to prove that they can bring grant money and therefore are worth hiring on a permanent contract (tenure)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are multiple fellowships awarded after a competitive application process by both public and private bodies: EPSRC, Leverhulme Trust, Wellcome Trust, Royal Academy of Engineering, Royal Society, etc.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Right after my PhD, I was awarded the EPSRC Doctoral Prize Fellowship. It is a relatively small one but gives me my own research budget (consumables + travel) to manage and pays my salary. I am currently hosted in an existing group, therefore can't get large equipment.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The next career move would be to apply to other fellowships (longer, more budget). In some of them, the researcher can apply for grants. If granted, this is a very strong case for a lectureship.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
One issue: they are very competitive. Much more than a usual postdoc:
a) one needs to find a group to host them
b) institutions can usually present only a limited number of applicants: it's competitive at institution level
c) there's limited funding: competitive at national level

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The main advantage is that it shows independence. I wrote my own proposal, follow my own ideas, carry out my own independent research, and manage my own research budget

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: On the + side, I'm considered a postdoc, therefore don't have teaching or administrative duties, and can focus on my research 100% (and writing proposals for the next step 😰)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What do you think about such a system? Would you like to have such opportunities? Or would you find it overwhelming?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Heya! @JulienBarrier here. Today, I want to tell you about the transition from chemical physics in my Master's project to condensed matter physics in my PhD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As I said yesterday, I worked on X-ray characterisation of halide perovskites at the end of my master's degree

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It would have been a natural way to transition to a PhD in that field. And originally, that was what I did

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In fact, I submitted a research proposal to my PhD supervisor at the interface between his expertise and my experience. This is how I got the PhD position

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So I proposed to exfoliate halide perovskites and make van der Waals heterostructures with graphene and perovskites. For those interested about the proposal: https://t.co/o674j9Ln71

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So I arrived in this lab in September 2018 and tried to do this. The goal was to make halide perovskite monolayers and then contact them with graphene to explore their electronic properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The issue is that these perovskites are already unstable as bulk crystals, I let you imagine how unstable it is when you manage to have a few atomic layers…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I tried several methods, but the halide perovskite would systematically degrade before it could be encapsulated with any other crystal. After 6 months, we decided I could not achieve the impossible, and we dropped this original project.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In hindsight, I'm glad I had the chance to try that direction! I think we lacked good chemistry methodology: some other groups focused on chemistry ventured into this direction and obtained pretty good results: https://t.co/LW0D0aQU59

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The exfoliation method, which my group specialised in, yields good quality stable crystals (like graphene) but was not efficient for these perovskites.
On that path, I learned a lot in microfabrication techniques!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After we decided to drop the perovskites, my supervisor suggested I took charge of a dilution refrigerator. The goal: measure electronic devices at temperatures 0.01 degrees above absolute zero.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I accepted since that was the natural direction I intended to pursue: a) fabricate perovskite, b) measure them in the facilities. Since I couldn't fabricate, I would measure other sorts of devices

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Tomorrow I'll talk a bit more about dilution refrigeration, that's a fascinating technique!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Since I started measuring electronic devices, I found a few interesting phenomena involving the behaviour of electrons at low temperatures and high magnetic fields. More of this later!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So... this is how I moved from chemical physics training to being a condensed matter physicist, studying the behaviour of electrons at ultra-low temperatures!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Good morning everyone! @JulienBarrier here. Let's talk about cryogenics! https://t.co/a0GLa8pGbl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We use dilution refrigerators to cool down to millikelvin temperatures.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Why so? At low temperatures, atoms and molecules move around less: they are basically frozen. The only thing that moves are electrons, and we want to study their transport properties

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There is another reason: at low temperatures, you get rid of perturbations from the outside world, and quantum effects can emerge. We expect new physics!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: How low is a millikelvin? That's one thousand of a degree (C) above absolute zero, -273.15°C or about -450°F. Very, very cold! https://t.co/9EAQIbjkoH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To cool down a device, there are different methods. The easiest: liquefy a gas and place your device inside. Here Liquid nitrogen, at 77K (-195.8°C, -320°F) https://t.co/UrsD4PEVnt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To cool down further, one can use liquid helium, that boils at 4.2K (-269°C, -452.11°F)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The method to cool down even further is to pump on a liquid bath of helium. When atoms are pumped away from the vapour phase, the most energetic atoms (the warmest) leave the liquid and replenish the vapour. This effectively cools down the liquid helium

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This method can achieve 1.3K with helium. That's already very cold!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we want to cool down even further, we can use 3He, an isotope with 2 protons and 1 neutron (the usual 4He has 2 protons and 2 neutrons). Pumping on a 3He liquid can cool down to 0.3K

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: How do we cool down further? We mix 3He and 4He! This is done in a dilution refrigerator, an instrument that was imagined almost 60years ago!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The working principle is based on the dilution of 3-He in 4-He. To understand it, here is the phase diagram of 3He in 4He https://t.co/CGX0UX1Ibz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The most important parameter: below 0.87K, there is a forbidden region, and the two isotopes are only miscible for some concentrations

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Close to absolute zero, one can get almost pure 3He (right side) and a dilute phase with 6.5% of 3He in 4-He.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The magic here is that helium is a quantum liquid, and we use all the properties of quantum physics to cool down! https://t.co/YGszXn2Mq8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: On this left side of the diagram, 4He is superfluid (so has no excitation like phonons), and basically acts as an inert background for 3He. On that side, 3He is a fermion and the interatomic distance is controlled by its concentration in 4He

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Important, below 0.8K, the mixture is phase-separated, like oil in water: the 3He-rich phase (concentrated phase) sits above the dilute phase

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If we take atoms from the concentrated phase to place them into the dilute phase, they will split up but this needs energy. Guess where the energy comes from?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: From temperature! The mixing of 3He in 4He is endothermic. That's how we cool. This technique was first proposed in 1962 and achieved experimentally at @UoMPhysics in 1965

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here are the first prototypes of dilution refrigerators, created by Prof Henry Hall https://t.co/GlULEejzjs

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here is a schematic of the inner circuit. The dilution occurs in the mixing chamber (MC). 3He/4He from the dilute phase are distilled in the Still. This pumps atoms from the dilute phase, forcing 3He to move from the concentrated phase back to the dilute phase. https://t.co/Ow7b1yaSml

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is a closed circuit: 3He atoms pumped away on the top come back to the concentrated phase through the thin line.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To cool down a device then, we bolt it to the MC and circulate the helium mixture, taking heat from the device to work!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here is a picture of the mixing chamber in my setup. It is bolted to a plate, to which we attach all devices to cool down. The blue items are thermometers. The rings are heat exchangers that allow the mixture to flow to the still and the incoming, pure 3He to be cooled down https://t.co/kWhe1VE5Xf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In practice, the system is a tad more complicated, there are multiple plates that are cooled down to different temperatures, to maintain the whole system cold https://t.co/IwLloRNvkJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Of course, we cannot leave the system in the air, it would never cool down. We place it in a vacuum can to isolate each element from one another and prevent heat leaks https://t.co/3E2ACzcpV1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For those interested in the history of dilution refrigerators at Manchester, there was a conference in 2015 on the 50 years of the first DR. Presentations here: https://t.co/fhKZjwW0GJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hi there! @JulienBarrier again. Let's talk about graphene electronic devices and how I measure them

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I am studying van der Waals heterostructures made of graphene and other 2D materials. The principle: take several atomically-thin materials, stack them together and voilà! https://t.co/2k1l5ucSiT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For example, we like to work with graphene and hexagonal boron nitride, an insulator that protects a material to study (here graphene). The picture shows the fabrication process of such heterostructure https://t.co/8o5NWxdGnY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Once a stack is made, it is etched into a shape of interest, and metallic electrodes are added. The structure can be very complicated depending on the project's aim. Here the width of the purple strip is 1.5µm https://t.co/XpFM8qPxIb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All of this is done in a cleanroom, a highly controlled environment, where dust is minimal, humidity and temperature well calibrated

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Outside of the cleanroom, we "bond" the device to a chip carrier holder. Here the silicon wafer is 5mm wide.  This is a very precise activity https://t.co/7hxxiLsBjW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Under a magnifying lens, we deposit droplets of silver-charged conducting epoxy on the contacts created by lithography. We do this with a sharpened toothpick. Then, we connect these pads with gold wire to the chip carrier. Everything by hand!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The last step: placing the chip carrier in a sample holder, ready for measurement in the dilution fridge! https://t.co/osd6ozl1cc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Once the sample is loaded in the fridge, we can measure its electrical properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The principle of our measurement is simple: flow a current throughout the device, and measure a voltage drop at different contacts, using a variety of equipments to tune the properties https://t.co/K8vnF2DG6v

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That way, we can measure a device's resistance and deduce some properties : the mobility (how much electrons are accelerated by an electric field), the mean free path (how far can an electron go before bumping into another electron or a phonon), etc.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The typical device has a transistor architecture: we connect it to a "gate", which is a metal plate below or above the device, that we can charge with electrons or holes

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Because our devices are atomically thin, applying a gate voltage changes the energy level (the Fermi level) within the device, allowing to study the electronic response for different chemical potentials https://t.co/iH3pP89458

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This technique of gating a device via field-effect is not possible in all materials: 3D bulk crystals will feel the field effect only in the surface, for example

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: but for 2D materials and van der Waals heterostructures, this is one of the most powerful tool!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For example in cuprate high-temperature superconductors (3D), different phases appear with different dopings. To change the doping, one needs to synthesise a new crystal, with a different chemical composition each time! https://t.co/EYhgTmaIuk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In van der Waals heterostructures, it became possible to change the doping via tuning the gate voltage: the same phase can be described in a continuous measurement! https://t.co/5Hweu55dMa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The doping level is not the only parameter to vary:
we can change the temperature, apply a magnetic field to the device, apply different sorts of electric fields, etc. Some people use lasers as an additional tuning knob

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Later today, I'll talk about our recent results in graphene superlattices, combining variation of the Fermi level (via gate voltage tuning), magnetic field, and ultra low temperatures. Stay tuned!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hey folks! @JulienBarrier here! Let's talk about one of my recent projects: Brown-Zak fermions in graphene superlattices

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you sandwich graphene between two layers of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), you'll get high-quality graphene. If now, one of the two layers of hBN is exactly aligned with the graphene layer, the magic starts

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In fact, hBN has a similar lattice structure as graphene, but 1.8% larger. When aligning them, we get a long-range superlattice pattern, called moiré (like moiré fabrics) https://t.co/zAudK5uD1x

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When measuring the resistance as a function of the gate voltage (therefore doping) of a superlattice device, we observe peaks. They correspond to features associated with the main graphene (0V) and the long-range moiré (other satellite peaks) https://t.co/Uq51TTkXV6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And in practice, the band structure is changed: the resistance features correspond to new mini-cones at high doping (in blue) https://t.co/RAYkA2DTO0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The physics is relatively easy to understand with a physics background; it is based on the Bloch theorem.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you take free electrons, their band dispersion will be parabolic. If now you add an atomic lattice, gaps emerge, and the band can be folded in a Brillouin zone https://t.co/LhN9XVAMX9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is the same when you add an hBN moiré to the graphene layer, the band folds (again) in a mini-Brillouin zone, smaller than the graphene Brillouin zone. Gaps appear, and resistive features are observed

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now let's add a magnetic field perpendicular to the graphene. If you study 2D electrons in a magnetic field, they will form orbits (quantised!), with a characteristic length scale that is the magnetic length lb: https://t.co/M5r5yZVcEM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The question we tried to answer is: what happens when lb becomes comparable to the lattice constant a?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Well, in a usual material, that would be hard to achieve: a magnetic length comparable to a few Å lattice constant would mean a magnetic field of 10 000T. The best magnets on earth achieve around 50T, so it wouldn't be possible

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Not if you use graphene superlattices! With a superlattice constant of a few 10nm, you only need 30T to have a comparable magnetic length!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We did the experiment: placed a graphene superlattice device at ultra low temperature, in a magnetic field, and measured the resistance

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Usually, the resistance of any metal exposed to an increasing magnetic field, increases as well

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This was not the case in the devices we measured. The resistance increased roughly, but whenever the magnetic length became a fraction of the lattice constant, the resistance dropped

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In terms of physics, that is something unexpected, the resistance should not drop, since the electrons follow circular trajectories, and should not contribute to electronic transport anymore

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So we understood that whenever one orbit had a size of a few superlattice unit cells, the band structure changes. In fact, the combination of the magnetic field and the superlattice results in the emergence of new quasiparticles

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Quasiparticles are a framework we use to describe the electronic behaviour in simple mathematical terms: instead of adding a loads of parameters in the equation, we use a simple equation, where the mass is changed to reflect interactions

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We named these new quasiparticles the Brown-Zak fermions, in honour of two theoretical physicists, Brown and Zak, who studied the "magnetic translation group", a mathematical framework for superlattices in high magnetic fields

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The physics is actually much richer than resistance drops. This is for example a map of the conductance as a function of the gate voltage and magnetic field. The conductance peaks for fractions of the superlattice unit cell, and decreases above https://t.co/PwVMYS03IZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you're interested, more details are available in our paper https://t.co/9OlBeasZ4y, + it's #OpenAccess

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is 100% fundamental science; it's really hard to think about any application for this

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, in condensed matter physics, it can take 50 years before blue sky research can be transformed into an application

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Think about, for example, superconductivity. Discovered in 1911, it's only in the 1960s that people started fabricating superconducting magnets, used today in MRI!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hi everyone, it's my last day on this account! I'll be happy to take questions on the science I presented or about the life as an early career researcher!

tweets.text: Hi from Hamburg. I am so excited to do this weeks takeover.🥳 My name is Rebecca (@RPittkowski)👩‍🔬 and I am a PostDoc at @UCPH_Research in Copenhagen🇩🇰. But today I am starting with a little impression from our current experiment at DESY @desynews in Hamburg/Germany🇩🇪 https://t.co/mH8Z2JKVLV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So, what is DESY @desynews? Or more general, what is a synchrotron facility? And what makes our #research so exciting that we happily work #nightshifts and on #weekends?  #ScienceNeverSleeps

A thread 🧵 1/5 @RPittkowski https://t.co/YU5EOyBbgi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: DESY @desynews stands for "Deutsches Elektronen Synchrotron" and is a large scale research facility located in Hamburg. The PETRAIII ring at DESY, a 2.3 km ring underneath the city, was once the largest particle collider worldwide, but has since been rebuild to supply X-rays. 2/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: PETRA III is a storage ring generating extremely high energy X-rays. The electrons in the ring are accelerated to 6 billion electronvolts (6GeV) particle energy and race around the ring close to the speed of light. They can provide X-rays with energies up to 200 keV. 3/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Scientist can use these high energetic and intense X-rays at ca. 40 end-stations, where different experiments and techniques run e.g. to study tiny objects: proteins, small nano-particles,interactions of matter, or look into thick samples, to study processes in e.g. a battery 4/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We are currently sitting with a team from @jensengroup_cph at one of these end-stations (@p021_desy), and are shooting X-rays at small capillaries full of newly synthesized materials, to understand how the atoms are arranged in our nano-particles. 5/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We finished this morning! After 48 h of experiments, with two sets of 12 h shifts - running on Chocolate, Cola and Coffee☕️ Nerves always run high at beam time, so the tiredness comes when everything is done. Now we are happy to get home to Copenhagen, just a 5h train ride away🚅 https://t.co/uKULfaSK9y

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I will try to give you a little #glimpse of the experiments we were running the past days at the P02.1 beamline at DESY @p021_desy 
The experiments did involve a #robot 🤓🤖 and many, many tiny glass capillaries....

A #thread 🧵 with a robot #video  1/6 @RPittkowski https://t.co/ephy7qZXNH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: First, we place capillaries filled with #nanoparticles (small glass tubes) on a holder, which the robot can later grab. This involves a lot of wax and steady hands, to place the capillaries in a straight way. In the picture you can see a sample rack full of capillaries. 2/6 https://t.co/jITlI7KkDx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here you can see a sample spinning in the lab, to  check if the capillaries are straight, or if we need to move them a little to even out any wobbling👩‍🔬- we can melt the wax again and angle them new 3/6 https://t.co/KSfcgLFQLy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The sample racks with capillaries go into the experimental hutch, the place where all the #Xray #action happens. It is closed off with heavy lead and once the X-ray beam is on, you cannot enter. So the #robot grabs a sample & puts it in the Xrays. see ultra cool robot video-4/6 https://t.co/i2RzoeWheI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Because we cannot enter with the beam on, there are a lot of cameras 🎥 installed through which we can double check that everything is running smoothly.
Here a photo of a camera image, where we watch the #robot arm picking up a sample. 5/6 https://t.co/KkREYdE1L9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When the X-ray beam hits our capillary, the particles inside the capillary #scatter the X-rays. The scattering is detected by a 2D detector, and we can see such a pretty scattering image. We integrate the images, to get a diffraction pattern to analyze. More on that later 6/6 https://t.co/ufzKxTsX1T

After yesterday's Nobel celebration we are back on track . I believe I promised something on #data #analysis 
A  thread 🧵on how we extract the data from our #robot beamtime @desynews @p021_desy and how we figure out the #arrangement of #atoms in our samples /@RPittkowski 1/6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We get these beautiful 2D images from where the #scattered #X-ray beam hits the detector plate. What you see below is the scattering recorded for LaB6 - not surprising that we use it as a standard for calibration when you look at the beautiful #rings 2/6 https://t.co/9TybK0Ljem

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: By radial integration we get a 1D diffraction pattern, which shows distinct Bragg peaks for each ring on the 2D image. I made a very boring #GIF where you can see how the #rings relate to #peaks in the pattern 3/6 https://t.co/zybBlmw2S8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Such a a beautiful #diffraction pattern we get for powder #crystalline samples. The #periodic lattice planes reflect the X-rays periodically which leads to interference. Maybe you remember #BraggsLaw 🤓 4/6 (image credit @kirsten_mj) https://t.co/ZLJgxMsBOz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can identify many  #crystalline compounds based on their #diffraction #pattern which serves as a kind of #fingerprint and can be compared to #database structures. There exist many databases with hundreds of thousand structures - a good start to identify your structure 5/6 https://t.co/I0rEXPwLuQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But what happens when we #go #nano ? By downsizing the crystal we lose most of the periodic lattice planes  - so no more beautiful rings💍or Bragg peaks 🤔Not to worry, we can still get structural information - from #PDF (not the #fileformat 📰) - but that deserves its own🧵6/6 https://t.co/088BSj3XGA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @drheaddamage Dioptas

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Finally, the thread (you didn't know) you have been waiting for 🥳 "How can we use X-ray scattering to learn about the way the atoms sit in a #small #nanoparticle?" - lets use the Pair Distribution Function #PDF ! It's all about the neighbors  1/6 /@RPittkowski https://t.co/LzQLBXBwad

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To get information from small #nanoparticles, where periodic lattice planes are rare, we measure the X-ray scattering to very large scattering angles. This is called #Xray #totalscattering. So we need to come veeeery close with the detector to our sample.😱😬 2/6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Again, we integrate our scattering image (check up older tweets), but we are not done yet. More data treatment is necessary. We use a #Fouriertransform and transform from reciprocal (Q) space to #real #space - and there we have it, our PDF 😍3/6 https://t.co/6Ayj3Q6Oze

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We see that we have distinct peaks at certain distances. These correspond to specific #distances between #atom #pairs . And we can use the distances  to characterize the atomic structure in our sample 4/6 https://t.co/Tm5lPix5RZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The distances prominent in the example, agree with the atomic pairs in a metal phase, where the atoms are densely packed (face centered cubic). We can also #fit our structural #model to the PDF data to confirm - our particles are #metallic and have an fcc #lattice 5/6 https://t.co/ZqlEl5t5tj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But we can get more #information from the PDF. As the PDF shows the interatomic distances in the particle, it tells us when there are no longer characteristic #distances, so the particle probably ends. This can give an idea of #size - we have around 1nm metal fcc particles 🥳6/6 https://t.co/Jo9JhRCeZO

tweets.text:

What is a metamaterial?

My humble attempt to explain it in this thread!

👇👇👇

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
"Typical" materials derive their properties from their chemistry, from the elements in them.

For example, glass is transparent and brittle cos it is silicon and oxygen atoms.

In metamaterials, the properties are instead derived from their "designed/engineered structure".

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Look at these images. 

This is what we mean by "structure".

Do you see the periodicity? That a certain pattern repeats? This is the engineered geometry, this is what gives the metamaterials their properties. https://t.co/MUfOVW40V0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
To circumvent copyright issues, I asked @craiyonAI to draw me a "metamaterial".

From what I know about artificial intelligence, the fact that it comes up with this kind of structure indicates the kind of images typically published with the marker "metamaterial". https://t.co/Td3RLDGJgP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
However, there are many objects around us that have a "designed structure" and aren't metamaterials. Think about a wheel!

On top of that, the structure of a bone looks fairly similar to the images of metamaterials...

The "structural" definition is a bit more complex! https://t.co/d16nwE7Gat

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This designed structure needs to be way smaller than the property it is designed for.

In the case of optical metamaterials, this is straightforward: the designed geometry needs to be described by distances several times smaller than the wavelength of interest. https://t.co/VWjUacEaeJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
That is why, although the idea of negative-index metamaterials was developed in the 60s, it wasn't until 40 years later that it was achieved and ONLY with microwaves, which have rather long wavelengths.

We need to fabricate fairly small structures! https://t.co/RfyfiFtJc3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There is still another component to the definition:

Metamaterials show properties that are not found (some downgrade it to "not very common") in nature.

Let's see some examples:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Negative refraction.

Light changes direction when it goes from one material to the other, aka refraction. In nature, refraction is "always positive".

We all know what a straw in a glass of water looks like. With negative refraction, it looks quite different... https://t.co/zJNTiaq3Cq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
To the best of my knowledge, negative refraction metamaterials are what started the field.

My personal fav example of how this looks is the example with a swimming pool that I found in @drskyskull, check this blog post for a more detailed explanation:

https://t.co/FRVzK7c4JO https://t.co/hsStwYatuG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Negative Poisson Ratio

When you compress a material in one direction, it typically expands in the other one. This is measured by the Poisson ratio.

If you compress a negative poison ratio material in one direction, it also compresses in the other!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The great @TEDxTalks from Bas Overbelde shows this (1:40-2:20 approx) and more about mechanical metamaterials.

Some recognition to him, he was the supervisor of @GiorgioOliveri4, who gifted me the metamaterial that I showed at @the_ScienceTalk!

https://t.co/tVWkKgGldw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Following the "negative" properties of metamaterials, there are even metamaterials that behave like they had negative density!  

This is found in acoustic metamaterials and pretty far away from my expertise, but still fascinating!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
To sum up:

Metamaterials are engineered metamaterials that derive their exotic and non-common properties from a designed structure much smaller than the scale of these properties!

tweets.text:
For now: stress is the force that we apply to a material, and strain is the deformation that it causes. 

The stress-strain curve shows that and this is how a typical one looks.

Initially, the relationship is proportional. Then, it is not, and eventually, the material breaks. https://t.co/QQdfBNgxaM

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover

There are basically two kinds of optical materials: metals, which reflect light, and dielectrics, which transmit it.

Hyperbolic metamaterials close the gap between these two kinds of materials: they are metallic in one direction and dielectric in the other!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This extreme change in the optical properties depending on the direction can be exploited to get, for example, a specific kind of negative refraction.

https://t.co/v2XEwxvbxP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Hyperbolic metamaterials have lots of proposed applications. 

They are superabsorbent, blacker than black!

They allow us to see and detect very small things with regular light, with no need for electrons!

https://t.co/IKo0kqlpA5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
More examples!

Hyperbolic metamaterials have been proposed for energy solutions (thermophotovoltaics, radiative cooling) and for disease treatments (hyperthermia).

These applications require materials to deal with high temperatures, though. That is a problem for multilayers.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The components of a multilayer can react with each other at high temperatures if the elements like each other (see reactive multilayers!).

If they don't, they can try to get away from each other, which doesn't happen if they don't have enough energy (temperature!)

Until the 19th century, a metal was simply "a dense element". The first known metals were #HeavyMetal after all!

After 1809, light metals like sodium and later aluminium were discovered.

So don't use density as a definition, you are wrong by 2 centuries!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Actually even nowadays different disciplines use different definitions.
Astronomers consider that everything that isn't Hydrogen or Helium is a metal...

So, why does the cake start breaking at the bottom? Understanding that could help us identify why the degradation is happening and what is driving it.

There are basically three reasons for degradation :
1 dissolve in each other (not here)
2 move to try to minimize the area of one element that is in contact with the other 
3 move to minimize how stressed they are.
Most literature focusses on 2, but we find that 3 is dominating!
