tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Today has been full of talks about graph-based machine learning (ML)

What is graph-based ML and why is it important for chemistry? 🤔 https://t.co/P3FjIANoP0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Graph-based ML uses the concept of nodes and edges to represent your data in a different way than traditional ML.

For example, a chemical compound can be represented with a graph by assigning the atoms as nodes and the atomic bonds as edges, connecting the nodes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Nodes and edges can contain multiple attributes! 😲 For the example of chemical compounds, nodes and edges could contain such attributes as atomic numbers, valence electrons, and atomic distances.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here we describe a metallic nanoparticle using graphs. The nodes are assigned atomic positions and numbers, and the edges are assigned distances between neighboring atoms. Edges exist exclusively between nearest neighbouring atoms. https://t.co/ygXmTOaSWx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Why do we need machine learning to analyse x-ray scattering patterns? 🤔

An x-ray scattering pattern is like a fingerprint of the chemical species. So, let’s zoom into a crime scene and follow the work of a detective….

A 🧵

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
What does a detective do when he/she finds a fingerprint?

He/she gathers suspects! 
He/she gathers fingerprints!

He/she compares the fingerprints with the fingerprint he/she found on the crime scene :O https://t.co/J4xEQWAKQz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We can do the same with x-ray scattering patterns!

We simulate our suspects' x-ray scattering patterns and compare them to our measured data! 👊

However, if the database is large and we have to go through every entry, this is a very time-consuming process. 😑 https://t.co/K1h6SgU3VK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Instead, we can use supervised machine learning! 

From the chemical species and their x-ray scattering patterns, we train an ML model. 

This ML model can predict the chemical species from a dataset within a second!😲 https://t.co/YjVofoOpYm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But what do we do if the chemical species is not in our database? 🙃

We have tried to address this issue with our ML model, DeepStruc, which I further explain here: 
https://t.co/WCxA30cZKs https://t.co/uYDDDZAuMB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Synchrotrons allow us to measure x-ray scattering data fast! 🥳

In-house instruments are beginning to achieve quality x-ray scattering patterns within hours, but for synchrotrons, we can achieve quality data with second-resolution. 

🧵

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
A previous Twitter takeover @RPittkowski has explained the use of synchrotrons here:
https://t.co/IvWWAVHrSO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
When we measure more data, we need more efficient tools for data analysis! 🤔

This is where machine learning (ML) comes in helpful! 
ML is super fast analysing data and often orders of magnitudes faster than traditional minimization techniques like least-squares refinements.😲

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Can we understand how the machine thinks? 🤔

While the Machine is finding trends in large datasets that we, humans, cannot find, they are often still a black box. By opening the black box, we can begin to discover new science. This is referred to as explainable ML. 😏

🧵

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In this thread, I explain how we have explored the use of explainable ML to analyse x-ray scattering data. 
https://t.co/SBXuvocujB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Whereas we with conventional approaches can refine a structural model to x-ray scattering data, now we can, with explainable ML, get an estimate of how much each atom contributes to the goodness-of-fit. 😲

Please give a warm welcome to this week’s real nano scientist @DrClaireDancer 

https://t.co/fwDnYLF02u

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hello everyone! I'm very excited to be taking over the @RealSci_Nano account this week. This one is promising to be quite a whirlwind with a little bit of everything in my academic life - not typical, but at least you'll get to see the breadth of activities I'm involved in!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: First up, let me introduce myself and tell you a bit about me. I'm @drclairedancer and I'm a Reader (the level between Associate Prof and Professor) at the Warwick Manufacturing Group @wmgwarwick at the University of Warwick @warwickuni in Coventry in the United Kingdom.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My research group work on ceramic materials for a whole range of applications and I'm involved in a wide range of other activities including being the Co-I of the UK Metamaterials Network @MetamaterialsUK.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: During the week I'm going to tell you about me, and how I got here, about my fascination for ceramics, and about how metamaterials can be made. Along the way I have a lecture and a tutorial to give, a whole load of end-of-term meetings, and a bunch of other activities.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At the end of this week you'll be tagging along owith me to the @MetamaterialsUK  "Metamaterials in the Real World" event @NPL! This is a showcase of a whole range of Outreach activities network members have developed, followed by our advisory board meeting.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: First though my inbox is calling, and I have a quiet hour to get through some of the messages at least. Coffee at the ready! Back later when I'll tell you about how I ended up as a materials scientist at @warwickuni

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Well, some emails got sent, others got deleted, and in what I feel may be typical for this untypical week I did an interview for a film @wmgwarwick are making about what it's like to work here! Can't wait to see the final version! https://t.co/FEnsY5TrYw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, let's tell a bit of my story. I grew up in South Wales, near Cardiff, and knew from quite an early age that I wanted to be either a physicist or an engineer - ending up as a materials scientist seems quite natural now, but I didn't know anything about the subject from school.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After school I went to the University of Cambridge to study Natural Sciences. This proved to be an amazing thing for me as the course structure there is really why I ended up in materials rather than physics as I'd planned.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At Cambridge you don't choose your science specialism straight away, in first year you do maths and 3 other broad sciences. I chose physics and chemistry, and then for the 3rd opted for "materials and mineral sciences" - sounds interesting enough for my third choice, I thought.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It took less than half the first term for me to realise that materials was my subject. We learned about symmetry in crystals, and how they can be studied and understood from the placement of atoms, to the microstructure of grains and defects, up to their macroscopic properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We learned about metals, ceramics, polymers, and composites, and how materials are characterised. And I've never really stopped learning - I find materials science fascinating, and I love how understanding materials helps me understand the world. I have @cumat to thank for that!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I made some amazing friends at Cambridge, and had the most incredible four years including a summer on an ERASMUS project at ETH-Zurich @ETH_Materials  where I decided I wanted to do a PhD, but I wanted a change from the Cambridge bubble.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So I took the not particularly radical path for of moving to the University of Oxford @OxfordMaterials. Mostly  due to the project there which was exactly what I wanted to study, as it had been the subject of my 3rd year project. So what could hold such fascination? More later…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Back from giving my lecture - one of my favourites! We teach a degree apprenticeship here @wmgwarwick - the students work for their sponsoring companies and come to campus for block teaching a week at a time. Intense but very popular way to study. https://t.co/tiuJq8xoS8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We have a lovely shiny bright red building to teach them in too. Today I was teaching a 3rd year lecture on ceramics. It focuses on properties of ceramics through the window of their applications - I think it's surprising quite how many variations there are!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
My favourite is probably the ceramic knife. Always quite a surprise to those who haven't encountered these - but they are really excellent knives! And I have this Kyocera video https://t.co/HRtbNg99UC
which is excellent for learning about how they are made and how to use them!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @JoFeanelwa @wmgwarwick It is an easy one to direct people to that's for sure!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, returning to my doctoral studies. The material which fascinated me is what I still believe is a genuinely incredible material called magnesium diboride.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: MgB2  sounds like nothing special, but in 2001 a prediction that it was a superconductor was verified experimentally, and the superconductor research community exploded into a frenzy. They're an excitable bunch anyway but this material was quite extraordinary😁

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The reason? That simple formula. Magnesium and two borons. No non-stoichiometric complex oxides. No arsenic or thallium or rare materials. Simple, available to buy from chemical suppliers - and with a superconducting transition temperature of 39K.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So this seemed like an absolute dream compared to the alternatives! And there was a huge drive to make MgB2 into wires, to use in MRI scanners. So lots of people were doing MgB2 research, and finding good, if not exceptional, performance.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To me as a materials scientist the microstructures didn't look great, and it felt like this was a material which wasn't living up to its potential. There was a big gap between what was easily achievable, and what would actually be technologically useful enough for industry.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So with all that activity going on around me I embarked on a project to look at how to process MgB2 to get the best properties. It became apparent in my first year that really the processes being used to make the MgB2 wires and pellets from powders weren't very effective.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Under the microscope they still just looked like powders, because really they were. The process of solid-state consolidation of ceramics which we call "sintering" wasn't happening at the temperatures being used. But going too high in temperature made it decompose. https://t.co/TesnOLQFgZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So the ultimate question of my project became "Does Magnesium Diboride Sinter?" And after a lot of work I came up with an answer - yes! But not easily. And not under ambient pressure.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To get MgB2 to sinter you need a reducing atmosphere (or at least not an oxidising one), uniaxial pressure, and a moderate temperature. And if you get it right you can get fantastic properties. One of the pellets I made achieved a record magnetic performance at 20K. https://t.co/SmXNz6lJm1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And so that was where I ended up at the end of my doctoral studies, with a very good understanding of how to process a rather awkward, water and air reacting ceramic which was great for a particular purpose.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But I was a bit fed up of awkward, and understand ceramics more generally, and to do that I wanted to study some "conventional" ceramics. So while MgB2 was the start, it was by no means the end.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm going to sign off there - but tomorrow I'll tell you more about ceramics and why I've ended up devoting my research career to how to make them more effectively and efficiently. See you tomorrow!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Good morning everyone! It is rather chilly here in the West Midlands today. And there are rumours of snow coming later this week, which is always a dramatic experience in the UK - we grind to a halt when it snows!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One final note on MgB2 and Superconductors left from yesterday - if you want to read more I hugely recommend this book by my incredible friend @SusieSpeller - it's written in a really accessible way, but without compromising on scientific accuracy. https://t.co/Sea32MhAYt https://t.co/wLUKtsQxgR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I managed to snag a copy last week when I was in Oxford and get @susiespeller to sign it - and read it on the train home! I suspect it's one I'm going to be lending out though, as it's a good book for people beginning work on any functional ceramics, not just superconductors.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today is rather less busy than yesterday; mostly I have meetings with various types of students, so I think I can stay warm in my office and talk to you all about ceramics.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So perhaps to get started, let's have a little quiz. Which of these is a ceramic? https://t.co/GAVvG0oYyO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Which of these is a ceramic?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @philjemmett https://t.co/993XU93YRV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Well, I have good news for all of you - you are all correct! https://t.co/8PCf4uOxEN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Yes, these are all ceramic materials - but most people don't think of them all as the same type of material. That's because the ceramic class of materials covers a huge range of materials types, which have really quite varied properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So what makes them a class of materials which we can group together if the properties are varied? Well one behaviour is common to them all: the mechanical properties.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ceramics, unlike metals and polymers, are very brittle. This means that they deform only very slightly (and reversibly at that) before they break (fracture). Under normal conditions we do not see the irreversible deformation (plasticity) which we see in metals and polymers.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ceramics can also be rather hard to work with because of a statistical scatter in their strength from one sample to another. This is because fracture in a ceramic material is caused by tiny flaws inside it which can't be accurately detected by non-destructive methods.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The flaw which causes failure will nominally be the largest one, but must also be orientated correctly in the sample to be able to cause a crack to go through the material in the right direction to cause it to crack.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It is not possible to specify the strength of a ceramic part - I can't say a ceramic will definitely withstand a certain level of force on them, for instance. We can only specify that they will have a 95, 98, 99% chance of failing under that level of load.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All of which makes ceramics a bit tricky to design with mechanically. And often we need to avoid placing them in situations where cracks are likely to open - i.e. where there are tensile (opening) forces on the cracks.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But if we can do that we reap the benefits. Ceramics are incredibly durable, and very chemically inert. They can be used in extreme environments where no other material can be. Often the "material of last resort" - but without them we wouldn't be able to do all sorts of things.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Silicon solar cell - most definitely ceramic, but not much confidence! Teapot - most likely made of porcelain ceramic, as the majority knew. Helmet made of boron carbide, which can be shaped and is very effective. And brick: probably one of the most familiar ceramics around.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @jose__op No no no!! Definitely wrong!! 😁

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Wow, today has been busy! Part of the problem with travelling away from campus during the week is balancing the time for meetings on all the other days. And with a module to teach all of next week it's been quite tough to squeeze everything in.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today has been a bit of an out and about day - and it's freezing so big coat required! First I headed up past the still frosty pond to the main building to teach a maths tutorial on differentiation to my first year engineers. Already the last tutorial of term! https://t.co/jGDUQlYGgV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Then I headed over to the building where I'll be teaching next week as I wasn't sure how to find the room. This is the Lord Bhattacharyya building, named after @wmgwarwick's founder - it's an enormous building! And has a pretty Christmas tree up! https://t.co/UJfhFCSoIc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After lunch came an exciting project supervision meeting - in person, in the workshop, with the real 3D version of @wmgwarwick Outreach supremo @philjemmett! This is our main workshop, it's a huge space but the scale of some of the manufacturing processes we study require it! https://t.co/7YFs2qtuVP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Our student is working on making some of our "bendy wood" samples in a more systematic way - we have a theory about how the pattern relates to bendiness. Samples are cut, how to test them is an interesting question - more work to do next term! https://t.co/hHbvumnHZP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Obviously had to grab the chance to get a video of the laser cutter in action! And some of the samples. And I also grabbed the things I need at the @MetamaterialsUK Network Exhibition on Friday - looking forward to showing off the fancy new setup! https://t.co/AS4xyYMZ6a

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here's the video. It's incredibly quick! https://t.co/PD3DQGx1hP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'll talk more about my work on metamaterials on Friday but if you're curious to learn more in the meantime previous @RealSci_Nano curator @jose__op told us all about them just a few weeks ago! Start from this post to learn more: https://t.co/6EI36BPSo2

1/8 Hello again to all!! 🙋
Quantum physics has deep historical roots in Ireland 🍀. Let’s explore this and why Ireland still has a large Quantum contingent 🧵⤵️ https://t.co/FH5Pag2FnM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2/8 Sir William Hamiltonian, born 1805 in Dublin, Ireland, laid down an important formalism for quantum mechanics through his formulation of Hamiltonian mechanics. This was a powerful new technique used for working with equations of motion.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3/8 He also discovered the non-commutative algebraic system known as quaternions: where he famously carved an equation on the Broom Bridge in Dublin.  More can be found here : https://t.co/Aw9ijGPoAZ https://t.co/8pit93ItNx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4/8 Erwin Schrödinger of the famous “Schrödinger cat” 🐈‍⬛ born 1887 in Austria-Hungarian Vienna carried out his work in Ireland for 17 years, a controversial figure who explored a unified field theory whilst in the Emerald Isle. https://t.co/JswbQCcQVX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5/8 John Steward Bell born 1928 in Belfast, Northern Ireland wrote a famous paper “On the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen paradox” where he derived the famous “Bell’s Theorem”. Original paper: https://t.co/FdZap6B9tp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 6/8 This paved the way for the 2022 Nobel prize in physics award to Alain Aspect, John Clauser, and Anton Zeilinger propelling the area of quantum information and showed quantum mechanics cannot be replaced using a hidden variable theory. Learn more here: https://t.co/pf2WOLId4T

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 7/8 Now we have the next generation of world leading quantum physicists with groups in Belfast, Cork, and Dublin to name a few — alongside a strong industrial contingent & government investment 🥳

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.text: 1/24 Tonight we will be talking to Dr. Steve Campbell (@quantumwizard) who provides us with his journey to becoming a professor, alongside advice to undergraduates, PhD researchers, and Postdocs  🧵⤵️ https://t.co/ftQIY5vgER

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2/24 Q: Why did you choose to do a PhD in the domain of quantum science? 🤔 https://t.co/LFnRGN9i3k

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3/24 A: As an undergraduate student, any quantum related modules resonated the most with me. Competition for PhD positions was no where near as high in 2008 so I had some options, but I was most drawn to the quantum related ones.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4/24 cont’d: At that stage I didn’t know about quantum computers or quantum information, but there were two projects in particular that I found interesting. Unbeknownst to me however, they both offered the chance to work with Prof. Paternostro.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5/24 Q: What was your favourite part of doing a PhD? https://t.co/t6lGWYbpS9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 6/24 A: I was very fortunate in that I collaborated with many people in my works — I really enjoyed that element. It offered the chance to not only learn from new perspectives but also to travel.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 7/24 cont’d: My favourite thing however, was the feeling I had when I first published a paper. It was really exciting that something I worked on was now out there and ‘good enough’ for others to build on.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 8/24 Q: What was your favourite part of doing a Postdoc? https://t.co/N1tw9ABYhB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 9/24 A: Here I had the chance to really travel a lot and participate in many new cultures, living in Ireland, Japan, and Italy. This was also the time that I managed to develop myself the most as a researcher.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 10/24 cont’d: By joining different groups I learned many new techniques and heard interesting schools of thought. I also had the chance to be more independent, working on two single author projects.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 11/24 cont’d: That was particularly useful in improving my self confidence as an independent researcher. It was also the time I cultivated my most significant collaborators, with whom I still work with closely to date.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 12/24 Q: What was the transition from PhD to Postdoc like? https://t.co/qGE97xbUIe

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 13/24 A:  The first year was very tough! I was in a completely different research group, with a different work culture and working in an area I wasn’t too familiar with.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 14/24 cont’d: The level of responsibility was also orders of magnitude different. As a Postdoc you have to be an autonomous researcher, contributing to the development of students, while also developing yourself and career.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 15/24 Q: Tell us about your journey of Postdoc to Professor for those looking to make that next step! https://t.co/9uJqDIPg2u

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 16/24 See this thread: https://t.co/0oiXzDIrm6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 17/24 Q: Can you give some advice to undergrad students looking to do research? https://t.co/o3lHBfGhWj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 18/24 A: Make sure you find an area you are *passionate about*. Doing a PhD is a massive commitment, and is not immediately financially rewarding, so make sure you choose a topic you love.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 19/24 cont’d: Also, to get accepted to a PhD program nowadays is significantly more challenging than it was in my day. Take every opportunity as an undergraduate student to be as competitive as possible.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 20/24 Q: Could you give some advice to PhD students? https://t.co/3EvSuxHlJA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 21/24 A: DO NOT WORRY ABOUT METRICS‼️ Do not place value on quantity (of papers) and metrics over quality and understanding.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 22/24 Q: What are the biggest challenges as a Prof? https://t.co/aHksBtqHmk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 23/24 A: The time constraints — you have a wider diversity of responsibilities, and therefore less time to dig into the weeds. This is compensated by working more closely with students and teaching undergrads.

tweets.text: 1/33 Today we speak to Jonas Rigo, a final year PhD researcher in the nanoelectronics group, with expertise in machine learning methods and many body quantum physics :)

tweets.text: 2/33 Q: why did you decide to do a PhD? https://t.co/0BZr0rwdVp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3/33 A: At the end of my undergraduate degree, although I both enjoyed myself and learned a lot of physics, I still felt there was so much within physics I wanted to learn about.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4/33 cont’d: So I felt that doing a Masters degree would help satisfy my curiosity and quench my thirst for physics knowledge. Again, at the end of my masters, I still felt there was so much to be explored and to be learned.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 5/33 cont’d: So, this then naturally lead me to pursue a PhD, where research would grant me the opportunity to dig even deeper into the weeds. Coming to the end of my PhD now, I still feel that there is so much physics that I want to explore..

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 6/33 Q: Is doing a PhD what you expected?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 7/33 A: In many ways it is how I imagined it would be. I was very fortunate, in the university of Innsbruck (where I did my undergraduate) there is a strong focus on research.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 8/33 cont’d: Here undergraduate students were encouraged to attend seminars, colloquiums, and journal clubs. This was further amplified as a masters student.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #9/33 cont’d: These  experiences helped inform me on how research was conducted, so I had fair idea of what doing a PhD would be like.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 10/33 cont’d: One thing about research that I was very excited about was how collaborative it is, and how it allows one to interact with new people and ways of doing physics.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 11/33 cont’d: Unfortunately , due to the pandemic, I didn’t have the opportunity to collaborate as much as I would’ve liked too with other researchers outside of my group.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 12/33 Q: Coming from abroad, what’s one item that you liked about doing your PhD in Ireland?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 13/33 A: One thing I noticed is that, both in Italy (where Jonas is from) and in Austria, the research groups are larger, with many postdoctoral and PhD researchers.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 14/33 cont’d: In practice, because of group size, this means that the PhD researchers are often guided and trained by the postdoctoral researchers, rather than directly by the supervisor with whom one applied to research with in the first place.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 15/33 cont’d: In this situation, your supervisor is more like your boss. To contrast this, in Ireland I’ve noticed that your supervisor is more like your peer, and directly a collaborator. This is very nice.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 16/33 Q: How was it like settling here, and were there any challenges in doing a PhD here?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 17/33 A: Having moved from Italy to Austria to pursue my undergraduate and masters, I’ve had some prior experience living abroad.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 18/33 cont’d: Logistically speaking, I found moving to Ireland (as an EU citizen) was quite easy compared to Austria. This is because as a PhD researcher in Ireland, you’re technically not employed.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 19/33 cont’d; This means that you don’t have to worry about sorting taxes out etc. However, this is also a huge downside..

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 20/33 cont’d: You basically don’t exist in the eyes of the state; for 4 years you don’t have any contribution toward a pension; you have to pay for really expensive health insurance; and you’re paid less than the EU min. wage.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 21/33 cont’d: This is all technically allowed as you’re not an employee! This then ties in with other issues; in Ireland, it’s impossible to find a place to live.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 22/33 cont’d: In reality, to find somewhere to live often requires you “know a guy”. Then when you finally find a place, the rent is untenable given how small the stipends are.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 23/33 cont’d: This is a massive challenge.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 24/33 Q: You’re a final year PhD researcher, how’s that like and do you have any general advice to other PhDs in training?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 25/33 A: Final year is stressful — it’s putting together the largest block of study (in my case 10 years) you’ve done to date into context. It makes you revise all the choices you’ve made along the way.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 26/33 cont’d: But, now is the time to assess if you want to change career or continue down the academic path.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 27/33 cont’d: I’ve done many interviews, both in the industrial sector and the academic one to help inform my future career path. I have many friends working in R&D for companies.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 28/33 cont’d: It’s made me realise that intellectual property has a lot of value nowadays & that, as researchers, we are perfectly positioned to enter this domain. Research is a mindset and skill.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 29/33 cont’d: My biggest advice to people in their latter years of a PhD is to do many interviews. The more the better, as you not only improve in taking them, but it also teaches you to more critically contextualise everything you’ve done.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 30/33 Q: To wrap up, what’s been your favourite work to date?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 31/33 lA: I really enjoyed working on making the NRG differentiable. This is a process inspired from machine learning which we apply to the numerical renormalization group.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 32/33 cont’d: This is a powerful many body computational technique. I’m most proud of this work because it randomly occurred to me that maybe it could be done, and we actually did it! https://t.co/PD8pIHgMf7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 33/33 That’s a wrap! Thank you to Jonas for his time and insights, if you want to learn more about machine learning methods in many body quantum physics or quantum transport, check out his Google Scholar: https://t.co/azq96GuOXY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Well, that’s me signing off! It was a really fun week. I hope we were able to give you guys a flavour of a researchers perspective & some insights into the booming area of quantum science and technology! May the force be with you all ✌🏼 https://t.co/Fgo80k6dG8 https://t.co/qqF8xgkWUd

Hi everyone! I’m Júlio and I’m taking over the @RealNano_Sci account this week =D

To get started, I invite you to think about The Little Price and its relationship with his little planet (asteroid B-612). The planet is so tiny that he walks around it and feels its curvature. 1/5 https://t.co/vLftPizl9m

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: He is always in contact with everything in his planet and he sees all of it at all times. When he goes to the Earth, the story changes: he doesn’t feel the curvature or interact with every being on Earth. That’s just because the Earth is so much bigger than he is. 2/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We spend our wholes lives in the Earth (at least most of us) and we never get to see all of it or interact with everybody who lives on it. 3/5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The Little Prince’s height in the same order of magnitude of the diameter of his planet, which is def no true for the Earth (see picture). This scale similarity (or difference) changes the way he perceives the world around him, and we can extrapolate this logic to molecules. 4/5 https://t.co/nMyK6DmdHC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When molecules are confined in tiny (nano) spaces, they can behave differently. They may be affected by the curves on the walls of the confining media, have enhanced interactions with the atoms on the walls and with other molecules in the same space. 4/5

tweets.text: Today a thread about my fav science thing  - beamtimes! https://t.co/8znOw0jQMa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But lets first take a step back first. So I am a 'condensed matter physicist'. We make up the LARGEST group of physicists (about 1/3 of us work in this area). It's a big field b/c it underpins many of the technologies we use every day. https://t.co/WFs12FJ4rC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Never heard of it? Yep - definitely not one of the commonly known sub disciplines of physics (no-one on a TV show like the big bang theory would be a condensed matter physicist!) but its super cool and really overlooked by students IMHO..

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Many students coming into physics want to study astrophysics or quantum.. but often they tell me they don't want to just do theory or analyze data... they want to work in the lab and do experiments.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Condensed matter physics can be theory or experimental-based (or both). I am experimental and honestly its a LOT of cool experiments, techniques, equipment and tackles lots of real-world problems.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In my work I use so many very cool bits of equipment from electron microscopes.. 

Scanning electron image of an indent in a 'brittle' semiconductor (Ge)! https://t.co/7CdEFa5npD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
To atomic force microscopes.. 

A series of phase transformation areas on Si after etching.. https://t.co/mzZHLrLQzo

tweets.label: Takeover

To Raman spectroscopy.. 

Me and our Raman system.. https://t.co/kzTebnuJUO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: BUT most of all I love it when we go on a beamtime and use synchrotron x-rays to measure our crystals. https://t.co/NFP5Un7Ues

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I usually go to the Advanced Photon Source near Chicago and use the high pressure beamline. (Unfortunately we cant do these experiments in Australia... yet!) 

https://t.co/cAJQQrrrVw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We need to write applications for time and its quite competitive. The experiments are run 24/7 and we usually only get 48 hrs of precious beamtime per trip. https://t.co/6e7wmHLAL1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Those 48 hrs need to be planned very well and we usually have a small team of 2-4 who travel over there. We have a Plan A, Plan B, Plan C etc.. 

My aim is to never waste a photon! https://t.co/JklKAaefrj

tweets.label: Takeover

(beamtime also runs on coffee.. and chocolate.. can you see why I love it!). https://t.co/v5r0aaPgHY

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hey everyone! So great to be able to spend the week talking to you about all things #nanomedicine and #precisionmaterials. My name is Steve @Street_Research, and I am currently a postdoc in the @MannersResearch group at @UVic on Vancouver Island in Canada 🇨🇦 1/7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This week I’ll give you an insight into what life is like as a nanoscientist in Canada, and introduce you to my research on polymeric nanomaterials for therapeutic delivery. Today I just wanted to introduce myself and explain my career choices to date! 2/7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But first, where do I live? Victoria is a smallish city on  Vancouver Island off the West Coast of Canada in British Columbia. We are a 4h ferry ride from Vancouver and Seattle. The first thing most people who live here will tell you is that it is beautiful! 😍 3/7 https://t.co/pyxY2qeW0y

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you like nature and the outdoors, this place is heaven! Victoria is 3h from a ski resort, and it has some of the most beautiful mountains, lakes, beaches and ancient forests. The island has everything from bears, wolves, cougars, and elk, to sea lions, orcas and whales! 4/7 https://t.co/KZEMLcXPLS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Victoria is a nice enough place to live. It has everything you need including some amazing breweries, vineyards and restaurants. There are loads of cool hikes to do, and lots of sports like open-water swimming, kayaking, cycling, climbing, surfing and fishing! 5/7 https://t.co/rK7bVncWa4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It does have its problems too though. Because of high demand, housing here is expensive – the average property price in Victoria is over $1,000,000! This means rent is also expensive here, reaching an average of $2000 for a 1-bed apartment. 6/7 https://t.co/4k0R1mNRht

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Victoria really is a lovely place to live though. It is a popular tourist destination, and I highly recommend a visit if you get a chance! Later on I'll speak about my career choices and what I am getting up to today - stay tuned! 7/7 https://t.co/eI6DesFsgD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hey again! It’s an interesting week to be doing a takeover... Today I attended a demonstration at UVic that was organized by @SupportOurSci. They organised a nationwide walk-out to advocate for living wages for grad students and postdocs in Canada. 1/4 https://t.co/Sn6fwfe6ji

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Funding for science in Canada has not changed since 2003, so Canadian researchers have effectively received 20 years of real-term pay cuts (inflation over this time is ~50%!). 2/4 https://t.co/UzHC60yA6d

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Pay ranges from $17,500 to $35,000 per year for masters students and PhD students. But remember rent is ~$2,000 per month in Victoria! Grad students are also expected to pay $8,000 in tuition fees per year, which further adds to their financial pressures. 3/4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The ‘Support our Science’ campaign aims to increase funding for science so that researchers are more fairly paid and no longer living below the poverty line! We had a pretty good turnout at UVic today. Let's hope things change! 4/4 https://t.co/aubVBYNLy8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Morning everyone! Today I wanted to tell you a bit more about myself and my career choices. Buckle up! I grew up in London, in the UK. I went to a comprehensive school, and was the first in my family to go to university. I was never sure what I wanted to do when I was older. 1/25 https://t.co/pjqaw3gcFb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Growing up, whenever I was faced with a decision about my future, I just chose what I enjoyed doing the most. This led me to study Maths, Chemistry, IT and history for my A-levels. 2/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When it came to choosing what degree to study, I thought I wanted to study computer science. Maths was too abstract at that level, and history was more of an interest than a career choice. After some open days, I was put off of comp. sci, and enthused by chemistry instead. 3/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, all did not go to plan. I did poorly in my AS levels (the exams you take at 17 in the UK), getting C,C,D,E, with an E in AS chemistry! Shortly after I was also hit by a car and missed several months of school. 🚗🤕🩼 4/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Faced with an uphill battle, my parents got me a tutor in maths and chemistry to help me catch up. I worked hard and managed to improve by a grade in every subject, getting B,B,D for my A-levels (I dropped history after AS). 5/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Curiously, the chemistry tutor taught me for a couple of lessons before telling my parents that “I wasn’t learning anything and that I would never be any good at chemistry”. This probably marks the lowest point in my chemistry career. 6/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My parents got me a new tutor, and I like to think I’ve proved the old one wrong on that front now 😅. Don’t let anyone tell you what you can and can’t do, because you can achieve ANYTHING if you set your mind on it. 7/25 https://t.co/CBmzXbMwTr

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: With a D in chemistry I didn’t get into my first choice university, but my backup choice was @UniofReading, who had space on their MChem Chemistry course and took a chance on me. I am very grateful to them as my life would be very different otherwise! 8/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: All of us who got a D had to go to special Saturday classes in our first year to catch up with everyone else. Ironically, those who went to these classes usually ended up getting better grades in their 1st year than those who didn’t! 9/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I had a great time at Reading, and I made many friends for life. I managed to improve on my grades every year, whilst also working 12+h a week in a bar so that I could afford to live. I definitely struck the work/life balance perfectly, and had my fair share of nights out! 10/25 https://t.co/b6KGRYPiyv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At the end of my degree, 5 years after getting an E, I graduated with a first – the highest grade you can get in the UK. I was one of the top students on my course, and won an award for “the most improved chemistry student”! 🏆 11/25 https://t.co/j6YPXrOfzr

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Explosives like TNT go boom because they have a lot of high-energy nitrogen and oxygen atoms forced into a small space. When they detonate, they release N2 and O2 which is a strongly exothermic reaction. 3/30 https://t.co/SCV6xrncVZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The molecular tweezers I was working with contained electron rich ‘prongs’ that bound to the electron-poor TNT. This changed the fluorescence of the tweezer, allowing us to ‘sense’ the amount of TNT present by how much they glowed! 4/30

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But what is cancer? Well, in short it’s a collection of diseases that lead to uncontrolled growth of the bodies own cells. These mutant cells spread throughout your body, taking over vital functions and ultimately leading to death. 11/30 https://t.co/OND66ZdF3P

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It’s hard to treat because you need to find a way of selectively killing the mutant cells, without also killing the healthy cells! BUT, the mutant cells used to be healthy, so there are few differences between them! 12/30

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Cancer research is therefore all about finding these differences and making medications that selectively kill the cancer cells without also killing healthy cells. Common treatments include surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy. Chemotherapy is treating cancer with drugs! 13/30

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But, many of the older chemotherapy agents like cisplatin are not selective for cancer cells – they kill all cells, so the aim is to kill the rapidly dividing cancer cells before you harm the patient. This is why chemotherapy often has bad side effects like hair loss. 14/30

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The story of how the first chemotherapy drugs came about is really cool, and involves mustard gas, and a WW2 bombing! 15/30 https://t.co/qNqHpGWpii

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Nitrogen mustard (aka mustard gas) was the first chemotherapeutic. It was developed into Cyclophosphamide, which remains a frontline chemotherapeutic today! 16/30

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Luckily for us, we are entering a new age of ‘precision medicine’, with more specific treatments for cancer appearing all the time. Side note: The first targeted cancer treatment (and my fav drug) is called imatinib. It’s a really cool story! 17/30 https://t.co/330uv46rc7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The target of my research was a unique 4-stranded DNA structure called a ‘G-quadruplex’ (G4). G4s are very interesting structures, and we are still learning about them. They are involved in key genome functions, and have many links to cancer biology. 18/30 https://t.co/kSfQok0WUB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Many proteins involved in cancer have G4s in their genes. By stabilizing the G4, you can stop protein production and kill the cell. G4s also affect a key cancer enzyme called telomerase, which is responsible for immortality! 19/30 https://t.co/r6Ait7YBjv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To stabilize a G4, chemists have been designing and testing small molecules that can bind to G4s and prevent them from unfolding. As G4s are enriched in cancer-associated locations, they should be more specific for treating cancer than the older chemotherapy treatments. 20/30

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We hoped that the sugars could be used to bind to G4s in a specific way. I developed some odd molecules with sugars, and showed that they had anti-cancer activity! I tested the anti-cancer activity myself, so I learnt cell culture at this time. 21/30 https://t.co/gk2TNTwmP8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This project took most of my PhD, and was the only published paper from my main PhD project when I graduated. Since then, with lots of help from collaborators and coworkers, we have published a further two papers on G4s! 23/30 https://t.co/E9Pz1cn4HE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We also showed that they can have antiparasitic activity, for e.g. Leishmaniasis. We performed lots of ‘Structure-Activity Relationship’ (SAR) studies, which is varying the structure to see if it works better – a common task in med chem! 24/30 https://t.co/ssdoHsMEFY

tweets.text: However, the road to getting a drug into the clinic is expensive and fraught with failure – it takes years, and millions of $ to get a new drug through clinical trials, and for every 10,000 drug candidates evaluated, only 1 will make it. So the chance of success is slim! 25/30

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It’s time to learn about nanomedicine and nano-sticks! Let’s start with the 3 different classes of medicines. First, you have small molecule drugs, such as cisplatin or doxorubicin (both anti cancer drugs). This is the oldest class, which still pulls its weight to this day! 1/25 https://t.co/kCJinIWk5i

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Small molecules typically have a biological ‘target’, which they bind to, to have their intended effect. Designing the ideal drug that works on its intended target without having off-target effects or issues with delivery around the body is a big challenge. 2/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Next, you have what are called ‘biologics’, which is a fancy name for things which are derived from biology, such as proteins, hormones, and antibodies. These are usually much more complex mixtures, and typically larger in size than small molecules too. 3/25 https://t.co/U5siaTPBxI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Biologics might also have a biological target that they inhibit (like antibodies), or they might be therapeutics themselves (like insulin). 4/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The third class is ‘nucleic acids’ (NAs). This includes both DNA and RNA therapeutics. Advances in science mean that this new kid on the block is rapidly growing and becoming a powerful method for treating disease. Examples include mRNA vaccines, and siRNA cancer therapies. 5/25 https://t.co/fQuWKxxyAN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A separate, but related area is gene therapy, which aims to cure genetic conditions like sickle cell anemia. One popular gene editing method is called CRISPR (it won the nobel prize in 2020). Both NAs and biologics can be gene therapies. 6/25 https://t.co/98nlQGh1I2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, all of these classes of medicine suffer from the same problem: It is bloody hard to get them to their desired location inside specific cells in your body. A number of issues have to be overcome, at multiple different stages of the process. 7/25 https://t.co/HpaYjl1gqb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It’s kind of like trying to pull off the ultimate heist (Oceans 11?). You have many barriers to overcome, and you need to overcome them all otherwise you’ll fail. Evade casino security? Get down into the vault? Open the vault door? All challenges to be overcome! 8/25 https://t.co/fqal7Lno5W

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Sometimes, small molecules and biologics can be designed in a smart way so that they don;t need any help – they have to have the perfect balance between activity and delivery effectiveness. But this is hard, and many small molecule drugs, biologics and NAs  do need help. 9/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The body is especially good at breaking down and recycling materials ♻️. This means we often need to protect the valuable therapeutic cargo from degradation. NAs are especially prone to degradation, which is an issue as they are so useful! 10/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One solution to this problem is to use a delivery system for your therapeutic. Delivery systems play multiple roles – they are expected to protect the valuable cargo, whilst ensuring that it reaches its intended destination at the right time. 11/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is exactly like real life delivery companies! We hope our delivery systems are more like @Amazon, and less like Hermes/Evri! 🚚📦 There are many different delivery technologies, each with their own quirks. 12/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The most popular are viruses like adeno-associated viruses (AAVs), and lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Viruses are the most common delivery system used, as they evolved to do exactly this job! LNPs were used in the COVID RNA vaccines, and are the major rival system to viruses. 13/25 https://t.co/KWL2XkDbjE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Polymers are a third important type of delivery system, which is where my research comes in! Polymers and LNPs can both be used to deliver small molecules, NAs, and even biologics! One example of a LNP therapy is Myocet, which contains the anticancer drug Doxorubicin. 14/25 https://t.co/w3LWDQ37g8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are MANY factors that affect how good a drug delivery system is. Some of the main ones are: particle size, shape, hardness, surface charge, surface chemistry, and architecture. Most delivery systems are nanoscopic, so they are very small! 15/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: How small you ask? Well, typically they are ~100nm, which is 1000x smaller than the width of a human hair. To put that another way, they are ~100x bigger than the speed your hair grows every second! At this scale, controlling the size and shape of objects is hard. 16/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This size is too small to physically manipulate, though ‘top-down’ methods such as lithography are used to try and ‘cut’ nanoparticles out! (e.g. look up DeSimone’s PRINT). This size is also much bigger than the molecular world. For example, a glucose molecule is ~1nm wide! 17/25 https://t.co/RDigADTjKZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, we have to try ‘bottom-up’ processes, which aim to make larger structures from molecular building blocks. This is challenging as you have to rely on fundamental physics to get the building blocks to ‘self-assemble’ into the shape you want. 18/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A sphere has the lowest volume out of any shape, so when these building blocks ‘self-assemble’, they usually form spheres to minimize their energy and avoid unwanted interactions. Making non-spherical nanomaterials is therefore a big challenge! 19/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Both the AAV viruses and LNPs that are mentioned above are spherical or quasi-spherical. One of the aims of my research is to make non-spherical delivery systems to see if other shapes are better at delivering medicines! 20/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But, there are limited methods for making non-spherical nanomaterials, and making them all the same size and shape is hard. This is important for medicine though! The study of using nanoparticles in medicine is called ‘nanomedicine’ 21/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In 2007, the @MannersResearch and Winnick labs pioneered a method for making non-spherical nanoparticles, called ‘Crystallization-Driven Self-Assembly’ (CDSA). CDSA is (literally) driven by the crystallization of polymers. Crystals are rigid and prefer non-spherical shapes. 22/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can make sticks, called ‘nanofibers’, as well as ‘platelets’ which are flat, 2D structures. A whole bunch of other different particles have been made through CDSA too, and we are discovering more all the time! 23/25 https://t.co/rlb83nulMR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One promising aspect of this technology was that you can control the size of these unique shapes too. For example, you can choose the length of nanofibers, or the area of platelets. The resulting particles are all very similar in size, which is good! 24/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What happens next? Find out later on in the epic conclusion to this tale! Happy Friday! 25/25

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What is my research all about? Well, I want to turn these tiny sticks from a research curiosity into a useful material for society. I am especially interested in using them to treat diseases, because I think they will be really useful in this area. 1/20

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At the start, these tiny sticks could only be made in organic solvents, and they were not degradable. This was a problem, as for nanomedicine applications we needed them to be biodegradable so they are non-toxic, as well as water soluble, as humans are mostly water! 2/20

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: By the time I started, the first examples of water-soluble and biodegradable nanofibers had just appeared in the literature. These works showed that it was possible to make nanofibers that could be useful for nanomedicine! 3/20

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The first thing I worked on was helping to develop a new system with a biodegradable core that was stable in water. We showed they were non-toxic, which was a promising start! But, the polymer wasn’t functional – it couldn’t really do anything useful. 4/20 https://t.co/f0SNLhE5sy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, I set about designing a new system that could do something. I thought things would be smoothest if I used ‘off the shelf’ components, so I combined several pre-existing technologies together to come up with nanofibers that I hoped would be able to bind and deliver DNA. 5/20

tweets.label: Takeover

First of all, what is chirality 🤔

Consider your left hand and your right hand. They look very similar, right? If you place your left hand on a mirror, and you compare the left hand reflection in the mirror to your right hand, you'll notice they look identical!

But are they..? https://t.co/mhPx5jc3LA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The short answer is - no🤯

If you try to place your left hand directly on top of your right hand, you'll find that they don't match up perfectly - they are perfect mirror images of each other.

This concept of mirror image symmetry is the key to understanding chirality 🔑 https://t.co/whptw6WcW7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In chemistry, chirality refers to the property of certain molecules that have mirror-image forms, just like your hands 👐

Just as your left and right hands cannot be superimposed on each other, chiral molecules cannot be superimposed on their mirror images ❌ https://t.co/kqVTE7Gnuy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Chiral molecules have two forms, usually called enantiomers, which are kind of like left-handed and right-handed versions of the same molecule.

They have the same chemical formula, and the atoms are connected in the same way, but their arrangement in space is different 🧬 https://t.co/FBNKZs2fbC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Our cells are mostly composed of chiral molecules, and they are very sensitive to chiral environments.

So for example, when designing a new drug, we have to consider it's chirality - one enantiomer can be beneficial, while the other can be toxic☠️

https://t.co/aS8dG7djkb

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover

First things first: what are ferroelectrics?

📔Textbook definition: Ferroelectrics are materials with spontaneous switchable electric polarization.

Too complicated? No, actually it's not! 👇

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Imagine the magnets (that we also have on our fridges). 🧲They have a magnetic field within them naturally, with two magnetic poles N(orth) and S(outh) indicating the direction of the magnetic field.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ferroelectrics are also similar, they have two poles. But this time the poles are not magnetic; instead, they consist of separated electric charges with opposite signs: positive and negative. https://t.co/MMkWFGjXJL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These separated opposite charges create an electric field inside the material, which is called electric polarization (P). For a polar material to be ferroelectric, the direction of the polarization needs to be switchable. ⚡️⚡️

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
🤨: Cool! But how do we switch/control ferroelectrics?? 

In many ways! That's what makes them amazing! The main ways can be listed as:
 
1⃣By applying an electric field ⚡️
2⃣Using mechanical force 🔨 / sound wawes 🔊
3⃣Heating up / cooling down 🌡️🔥❄️
4⃣Shining light on them 💡

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
What does this exactly mean? 🧐

It means that we can convert all of these different energy resources into electrical signals. Having an electrical signal means that we can put them in our electronics or we can make devices from them. 🤩

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Indeed! Actually, we already have ferroelectrics in many devices around us: 
- Acoustic sensors, electromechanical sensors/transducers, imaging sensors, microphones 
- Infrared/UV detectors
- Memory devices 
- Capacitors
- Energy harvesters 
📱💿🎙️📻🔌

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There are many types of microscope (as you'll see this week!) but the most widely known type is the light microscope (from https://t.co/2iXIi1ZrZE) https://t.co/RoQy6mgasK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Light from a lamp or laser is pointed at the specimen. This light is reflected, absorbed, transmitted, or scattered (RATS 🐀) by the sample. A set of lenses collect this light and direct it to a camera or eyepieces.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Light microscopes have been around for ≈400 years 😮. Here's a sketch of a louse and a Grey Drone Fly from Micrographia by Robert Hooke, 1665 (https://t.co/581VW1b0rH). Most microscope photographs ("micrographs") you've seen are probably from a light microscope. https://t.co/5uZSkY6cCh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Light microscopy is particularly impactful in the life sciences. Or so I'm told. I'm a physicist so I don't have any of my own biological microscopy images. So here are some entries into the @LightMicroAus 2022 micrograph competition (see https://t.co/ZLrp3iqG9C) https://t.co/ljIqb1Rp1a

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Light microscopes are also valuable in studying materials - this includes alloys, ceramics, polymers, and much more. My research is in materials science, so that will be the focus of my Tweets this week.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This micrograph (also my Twitter profile header) shows a polished copper-manganese alloy, with dark crosses of manganese oxide and light crosses of manganese-enriched alloy. These features are bad for the application of this alloy, but make for pretty pictures. https://t.co/eqSpfSpQRn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's a common theme in my work: using microscopes to see what has gone wrong. We'll revisit this theme throughout the week.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My main weapons are electron microscopes. Here's a scanning electron microscope (SEM) from our labs. An unassuming little white box, but a powerful machine 🧵 https://t.co/i5tJoEsSVr

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: SEMs scan a focused beam of electrons across a sample, and produce images of the surface. They're capable of amazing things. They can handle many different types of samples...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For example, here is the face of a moth (from https://t.co/qmg7CtHW8p). Microscale features are resolved in incredible detail. https://t.co/yvvJKmadRt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And here is a scale from a butterfly wing (also https://t.co/qmg7CtHW8p). https://t.co/mNdPcLIhIg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The SEM is also very useful in materials science (aka my domain). Here are some sodium tungsten bronze nanocubes aka jersey caramels (see https://t.co/UiJlLASbfh) https://t.co/tdUwkbvuSs

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here is a needle-shaped specimen of a highly-alloyed steel. Various types of carbides are visible. This specimen was prepared for atom probe tomography, which you'll see later in the week (see https://t.co/yJhZMEyWLs) https://t.co/Y62a4QXmTH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My research focus recently has been in nanoporous metals as a way to hold water ice for other microscopy. At the nanoscale they're very beautiful... https://t.co/k7Y8U26Js3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ... even these very undesirable cracks make for dramatic images. That's what my career has been all about: taking pretty micrographs of failed samples. https://t.co/vGjlQkT1qG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here's a transmission electron microscope (TEM) from our labs. Big and mighty in both stature and function! https://t.co/TI07MAX9qA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The SEM (see yesterday) usually looks at the surface of the sample. The TEM looks through the material. It's basically the same as a light microscope (Monday) but it uses electrons instead. (from https://t.co/5Ev7kPjG7K) https://t.co/m1g6XZglqF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We've had electron microscopes since the 1930s. Here's the first electron micrograph of a biological object from 1936. (from https://t.co/C7NQEWOdp7) https://t.co/W8fKjaH85z

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As you might expect, microscope technology has improved a lot in the last 90 years! Today the TEM is used to image all sorts of samples at all sorts of magnifications. The key requirement is the sample be very thin, ideally < 100 nm ...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ... if you can make a sample this thin, the TEM is a very powerful instrument. Here are some examples:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A very thin sheet of nanoporous gold - a different view of a nanoporous metal from what I showed yesterday (from https://t.co/aV3QblGANa) https://t.co/mbU7vXHjXj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Cryogenic TEM (cryo-TEM) of the very popular SARS-CoV-2 viron. Capturing lots of images of the spike protein from different angles allows for a 3D reconstruction of its structure! https://t.co/vXYiSxjNKY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Incredible magnetic structures in a Fe-Co-Ge thin sheet as the external magnetic field is increased (from https://t.co/PokizELWIH) https://t.co/douNp4Dly3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (more images to come later in the week, stay tuned!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When the electron beam in an electron microscope hits the sample, all sorts of signals are produced (see the legendary https://t.co/z3UngyGs9L) https://t.co/2whGM1l5AD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can form different images of the sample depending on which signals we collect. The images shown so far have collected secondary electrons (SEM) and direct beam (TEM). But there's so much more to see!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the SEM, back-scattered electrons (BSE) can diffract (EBSD) from the crystalline sample. Collecting the diffraction pattern allows determination of the crystal structure and orientation at the beam position ... (see https://t.co/L5UEuAAdBt) https://t.co/JG0bOmxGHM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here's (A) light microscope image and (B-D) SEM+EBSD of a martian meteroite. Although some features are visible in the light micrograph, the EBSD data more clearly shows areas that are (B,C) highly deformed and (D) mechanically twinned (from @Daly_Planet https://t.co/NKM6FPJ4FA https://t.co/UnvfKL23tp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: More EBSD, this time comparing grain structure of an (a-c) additively-manufactured and (d-e) wrought titanium alloy (see https://t.co/Oeond66BVh) https://t.co/7pv67aDpwc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The beam can also knock-out core electrons from atoms. An outer electron can take its place, releasing an X-ray, which we collect in energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). Here's EDS maps of a multiple principle-component alloy (see https://t.co/3olqFpNzh4). https://t.co/ERXwJW17MO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @the_ScienceTalk Caption says "coloured transmission electron micrograph of carbon nanocoils". Very beautiful!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can put a saw INSIDE THE SEM CHAMBER to image a surface, cut it off, image the new surface, and repeat. The images can be stacked up to give a 3D view of the sample. Here's the anchoring of spiders silk! https://t.co/zh5gfkxaJ5 (see https://t.co/RdiopvvBo2)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the TEM, the electron beam can be diffracted by the crystalline order in the sample. We can configure the lenses to project the image onto the screen. Behold: dots and a cube! (from https://t.co/Naj6jtUEBr) https://t.co/Y2uY3cVsSZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The atom probe is a whole other beast. A very high voltage is used to ionise and rip atoms from the surface of the specimen. We time their flight and catch them on a dartboard, and use their score to determine where they started. (see https://t.co/5ihCyKyiB9) https://t.co/jFUAseFVJl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The result is an "atom map" of the sample. Here is an aluminium alloy showing nanometre-scale rod-shaped precipitates (aka gummy worms) (from https://t.co/wrXOgdS6k4) https://t.co/ffMxv0luBh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here's a whole range of geological samples. Nanodiamonds!! (from https://t.co/dtiX8GLTO6) https://t.co/XOKrTajLX0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Another aluminium alloy, but this one is dripping with hydrogen. Atom probe is one of the few techniques which can detect hydrogen (so long as great care is taken) (see https://t.co/wqcUEXkOrX) https://t.co/Va3z6b5D8p

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This wild three-phase microstructure of a samarium-cobalt magnet (from @bkhm1234 https://t.co/3Yy6OBrns1) https://t.co/LsJYcTagaC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Some electrons lose energy when they pass through the sample, e.g. they ionise (producing X-rays: see EDS above), or they excite something "optical". We can collect the beam and disperse it to a spectrum: electron energy-loss spectroscopy. (from https://t.co/z3UngyGs9L) https://t.co/k65JbwfkNE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The low-loss part of the spectrum includes interband transitions and plasmons. Here's surface plasmon mapping of the cube from the other thread (see https://t.co/wDLcALpQMi) https://t.co/76jxwE6DIt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The high-loss (or "core loss") part includes all the ionisations, and allows for chemical "mapping" similar to EDS, above. Here's distribution of N, O, Ti and Co (cyan) in a semiconductor device (from https://t.co/4mbRRdLLBe) https://t.co/feS4NaDjKi

tweets.text:

Please welcome @ljtegg of @Sydney_Uni for a week of microscopes microscope and some more mi…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This week has been all about microscopy, but here's a short thread on my other baby: X-ray / neutron powder diffraction. Like electron diffraction, X-rays/neutrons can diffract from crystalline specimens ... https://t.co/GNRtVcgSz3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ... giving information about the crystalline phases (and their quantity) in a sample. Here are some examples of the power of powder diffraction.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Lead-halide perovskites have applications as photovoltaics and in other light-harvesting applications. Neutron and X-ray powder diffraction was used to accurately determine the crystal structure of FaPBI3 (see https://t.co/Gq8rLDtQXz) https://t.co/6YjGNUfe3F

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Powder diffraction can (usually) handle samples containing multiple phases. Here's XRD patterns of samples of W-Al-B showing many different phases, clearly distinguished (see https://t.co/DyFbj99nJZ) https://t.co/w2feBRag7F

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Powder diffraction also very good for in-situ or in-operando studies: we change something about the sample and watch how the phases/structures vary. Here we heat reagents and watch as they thermally expand then react to form the product ... (from https://t.co/YMcao1cQrM) https://t.co/3TCsKPTEcZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ... analysis of the pattern at each time step allows us to see how the balance of phases changes over the course of the reaction. https://t.co/wi9I2X73MC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hydrogen is quite mobile so work like this usually requires a cryogenic workflow: samples are prepared, milled, or transferred while at cryogenic (~-200 degC) temperatures ... (e.g. https://t.co/HWMktXazD7 or https://t.co/pJn5bFOnml) https://t.co/1jAT3Cfohk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm using these cryo workflows with atom probe to study (frozen) water. Water is hard to make into a sharp needle so the community has come up with some creative sample preparation techniques:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Water separates from its substrate easily. "Dealloy" an Au-Ag alloy to prepare nanoporous Au. Keep it wet, and use the focused ion beam (FIB) to mill-out a needle. (see https://t.co/uO7wBFn0z8) https://t.co/HUM1SOsbcp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Cool tungsten wire in liquid nitrogen + break it + pipette a drop of water on the fracture surface (which freezes) transfer to FIB + transfer to atom probe. (see https://t.co/zsIjL5M7xS) https://t.co/R6wGox3aXc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The protein ferritin is rispersedin a resin, then FIB + lift-out is used to make a specimen (see https://t.co/N90zaLjE27) https://t.co/LHj5Z2tTFR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Trap liquid between a pre-sharpened tip and individual layers of graphene. This one doesn't even need cryo - the water stays trapped under the graphene, even in air and under vacuum! (see https://t.co/LmPt3qqU9Z) https://t.co/AwOjzXc6q5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Two big conferences coming up for microscopy and atom probe: IMC in Busan Korea, followed up by APT&M in Leuven, Belgium. If you're there, find me (@ljtegg) and say hi!
