tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hello RealScientist Nano followers! This week I, @Ana_Mikheenkova , am happy to take over the account with energetic insights into battery science 🔋! First, a huge thanks to @svenja_lohmann for inviting me! Today I would like to start with me sharing my scientific journey.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I did my bachelor's at Samara Aerospace University, the city where I grew up, and since an early age, most of my interests were around physics, engineering, and space. I was lucky to be granted early lab access.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And I start doing little science projects in the Chromatography lab since my first year of University which I presented at many student conferences. Photo of me with our mini chromatograph https://t.co/dt8WludmHN

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At that time, I was over-glamorizing the scientific career path: I saw intelligent and interesting, multifaceted people, who were working to solve people's struggles and constantly travel to meet and exchange with other brightest minds of humanity. Isn’t it the coolest job ever?!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After my bachelor’s I had no doubt but to get more scientific experience and I saw @Erasmus_Mundus joint programmes as an excellent opportunity to study in several countries, meet people from different cultures and learn how to create a fruitful collaborations across countries.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @Erasmus_Mundus The program MaMaSELF (Material Science powEred by Large Scale Facilities has opened me new opportunities. I spent my first year in @UnivRennes1DSI where we delved into fundamental physics behind material science and my second year in @unito with a lot of applied studies. https://t.co/2fHeudsruI

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What I valued even more are the internships: after my first year I went to @psich_en in @cv_villevieille group where I discovered for myself an amazing world of batteries. I enjoyed my project on optimization of Na-ion battery and my time in the supporting and diverse community. https://t.co/4xBvqgGR73

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @cv_villevieille @psich_en Thank you Claire 😊

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Before graduating I felt that I was lacking experience in neutrons and I joined a project that connected my passion and my needs - I was investigating stress in satellite compounds using neutron diffraction at @ILLGrenoble for my master thesis. https://t.co/17HsNt7NN8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After moving between 3 countries in 2 years, I was happy to stay for a little longer as a PhD student at @UU_University where I can finally applied all studied skills of material characterization and apply them to something that can help to fight the global warming- batteries. https://t.co/U68xzVBLCf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And I will come back tomorrow with sharing most important battery concepts 😉 Meanwhile, feel free to ask me any questions about my journey, I am happy to share all I know on getting scholarships and applying for programmes and internships 😊

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Today we’ll refresh our knowledge of some of the battery terms. Let’s start from the beginning: we call a battery a device that converts chemical into electric energy using redox reactions. To narrow it down, let’s focus on batteries which use Li (Li-ion batteries).
image:iStock https://t.co/XqHqXg8qXF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It is a secondary (rechargeable) battery which uses reversible reactions with Li-ion to store energy.
fig:https://t.co/bMWuELalAX https://t.co/P4WUqJLAp4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Redox  (oxidation-reduction) reactions involve transfer of electrons between two substances. As a result of gaining or losing electron, oxidation state of the substances changes.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Common example from LIB: oxidation reaction on anode: LiC6 → C6 + Li+ + e- (which describes delithiation of graphite); reduction reaction on cathode: CoO2 + Li+ + e- → LiCoO2 (lithiation of LCO positive electrode).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So far we've mentioned cathode and anode, both of them contain active materials - a chemical which participates in redox reaction. However, they also have inactive materials which also play important role.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
A typical electrode coating consist of mixture of active material, binder (polymer which ensures mechanical stability) and carbon (conductive additive to enhance electric conductivity).
doi: https://t.co/wqzXqJXO7O https://t.co/HXrkTlTiIS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This mixture is coated onto current collector: aluminum for positive electrode and copper for negative (to avoid lithium loss due to allowing with Cu at low potentials).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Other elements of a typical cell are electrolyte, which lets ion pass form cathode to anode and typically consist of Li salts dissolved in organic electrolytes, and separator - a polymer membrane which isolates cathode and anode from contact (that would short circuit the cell).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now let's look at the most popular battery terms: 1. (Nominal) Voltage  - is the amount of voltage output a cell gives out when charged. It is defined by cell chemistry, which will depend on redox centers of both positive and negative electrodes. Image: https://t.co/PghKDJw7ku https://t.co/PDquGXYOMt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 2. Capacity: how much current it can provide to a load or how much charge is stored in a battery. A term related to that is State of Charge (SoC) and Depth of Discharge (DoD). Image: https://t.co/Vf2WrRUT2r https://t.co/V2SKesHqZC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 3. Internal Resistance: Resistance of the battery. The higher resistance, the lower efficiency the battery has, and the lower the actual capacity it can deliver as well as it will be problematic to use for high current.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 4. Energy density: how size or weight efficient the battery is. The higher energy density, the more energy can be stored while occupying less space or being more lightweight.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And that’s main terminology simplified. Tomorrow we will look at how these useful devices degrade.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
How do batteries degrade? Yesterday we checked some important concepts and today we can describe what can go wrong with the device we rely on a lot, especially when it comes to mitigating global warming.
image:https://t.co/Kq9YtDTsd4 https://t.co/ce0ISRRHPt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When we say that a battery reached the end of its life, usually we mean that it lost 20% of its initial capacity. Why 20%? Good question 😉 Generally, the degradation of the battery is not linear. After 20% of capacity loss, it fades much faster with rapidly degreasing safety.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As we saw yesterday, a battery has many components: metallic, polymer, solid, liquid, crystalline and amorphous, some contain heavy metals and light elements. It must be a headache to analyze, right? Well, some see problems, and others anticipate opportunities 😉 Joking! or…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To make our lives easier, all degradation mechanisms are split into three types depending on their effect: Loss of lithium inventory, loss of active material, and increase of resistance. Yes, it is simplified but still helpful.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
If you ever heard about the ageing of lithium-ion batteries, the first thing you probably saw is this figure. It quite nicely summarizes the main mechanisms and how they relate to the degradation modes.
doi: https://t.co/070uRG9nKa https://t.co/ZdafvoMfOx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In real systems, degradation depends on cell chemistry, cell optimization, cycling conditions and other factors. Our recent study focuses on testing batteries from an electric car and evaluating degradation based on cycling conditions
check it out: https://t.co/QLYJ6WXXF4 https://t.co/6VATBQ5fIW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As you can see here we highlight some of the mechanisms which are relevant for Ni-rich positive electrode: transition metal dissolution, void formation, formation of CEI (we tested 2 working temperatures and 3 state-of-change windows). Check it out to see more details!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It was also very interesting to study the negative electrode: blend of graphite and SiOx. These compounds degrade differently and it was fun to be able to decouple that!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So for now, we saw some degradation modes and a fancy figure with many mechanisms attributing to these modes. Now let’s see how we can analyze a couple of them.

Fig: https://t.co/rtEyOFalsK https://t.co/MonTj7moyM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
First al all, it is quite important to take into account testing conditions: ex situ, in situ and operando are the terms we see a lot. They refer to the state of the material we analyze. Let me just put a fun picture so you get the analogy.
doi: https://t.co/C54QByTdFA https://t.co/l3XxJ03Dvb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Then, I would say, the two approach to characterize the batteries are electrochemical and material analysis. My biggest passion is the second one, but with we can’t put apart electrochemistry. Not in battery science 😁

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So let’s start from electrochemistry. One can do many things: cycle batteries, apply pulse techniques or use impedance spectroscopy. All depend on what you actually want to know. Another thing to take into account is the configuration of your cell.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In some cases, i.e. in real battery systems, we have to look at full cells. Which means that we test both electrodes and their responses vs each other. If we would like to know more about one electrode or the other, the simplest thing is to assemble half cells or 3 ed cells.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In order to understand changes in capacity, increase in resistance or have an estimation of LAM and LLI, chronopotentiometry and follow-up data analysis can be applied (DVA and ICA).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In order to follow time-resolved processes, for example, Li diffusion, perturbation techniques can be used: PITT, GITT, EIS, ICI.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I think my favorite will always be EIS, it’s tricky, involves quite some assumptions, yet, you can learn a lot about your system.
I’d also take a change to promote a nice online resource with good educational materials about batteries and electrochemistry: https://t.co/DOd87b6rle

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As for the rest, let’s meet here tomorrow and talk about material analysis!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Yesterday we briefly checked on electrochemical methods for battery characterization. Today is the time for material analysis!
fig: https://t.co/hZT5GjMQwa https://t.co/udmX4vH15w

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
When choosing a method for analysis, many factors should be considered:
- Scale of studied phenomenon and probing depth
- Properties of studied species (light/heavy elements, crystalline/amorphous)
- Level of analysis (structure/chemical bonds/etc)
- In-house/LSF
- Operando/etc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: During the previous week, @ljtegg gave a very nice overview of how microscopy and XRD works. Let’s see how it can be applied to batteries.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: SEM and TEM are extensively used to study battery materials. Morphology observations to spot degradation, deposition of side products and particle cracking - it is fun to see it all!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One thing is that sample preparation is very important: battery materials from LIB are often air sensitive so proper handling is a must.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
As for X-rays, not only XRD can be used: XAS is widely applied to learn about chemical state of atoms, as well as bond and coordination environment.
Read more in this nice review: https://t.co/HjAJhaShYE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
My favorite example is the study where we looked at charge compensation mechanisms in actual commercial battery materials using EXAFS, TEM and RIXS (yes, oxygen matters 😉). Read more here:
https://t.co/nJY3pf4oYV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My PhD is a part of a project called ALINE which stands from swedish abbreviation for Aging of Ni rich Li-ion Batteries. It is a big project which involves @volvocars @VolvoGroup @UU_University @KTHuniversity and @chalmersuniv .

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The focus is on analysis of batteries for and from electric cars and trucks. Today we have a project meeting and I got to drive an electric truck, two hybrid ones and electric bus! https://t.co/0Cxp72IWrE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Also I take this opportunity to share some of our results which has been published:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Exposing Heterogeneous Degradation in Prismatic Lithium-Ion Cells:

https://t.co/GgG9SP4Rv9 https://t.co/OfMvJT8L7b

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Ageing of High Energy Density Automotive Li-Ion Batteries: The Effect of Temperature and State-of-Charge

https://t.co/QLYJ6WXXF4 https://t.co/5sqP2Tea61

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Resolving high potential structural deterioration in Ni-rich layered cathode materials for lithium-ion batteries operando
https://t.co/ph5I4bnkZc

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And many more!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A small break from 🔋 to talk about something important: #equality and #inclusion in #science. During my PhD I was a part of Chemistry Dep Equal Opportunity group and PhD ombudsman. Here is a couple of concepts to be aware of and tools to improve the environment in science:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: #Discrimination - “the unjust or prejudicial treatment of different categories of people, especially on the grounds of ethnicity, age, sex, or disability”. How to understand that you or someone at your workplace  are discriminated:

tweets.label: Takeover
Takeover
tweets.text: Microagressions - “brief, sometimes subtle, everyday exchanges that either consciously or unconsciously disparage others based on their personal characteristics or perceived group membership”.  How to identify them?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Sadly, usually just but knowing what has been actually been said. A couple of examples:
more examples https://t.co/c3QdXK3Q5K https://t.co/b0EcGI1dfb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Academic housekeeping - “type of work tasks within university departments that are low-status, time-consuming, largely invisible, and that nevertheless need to be done”. The study published in swedish became a topic of discussion around the world. Sadly, for a reason.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The article focuses on gender based aspects of how academic housekeeping tasks are distributed and shows “that women carry out a disproportionate share of academic housekeeping tasks”. https://t.co/i4PEVX1q6M

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Just one more concept to see how it is important to act even if you are not personally affected:
#Bystander effect “occurs when the presence of others discourages an individual from intervening in an emergency situation, against a bully, or during an assault or other crime”

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Sadly, presence of passive bystanders increase the detrimental effect of the situation. It is important to take an action and it’s also important to know how to do it depending on situation and people involved:

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Active bystanders “are aware of when someone’s behaviour is inappropriate or threatening and choosing to challenge it.” And there some strategies one can use:

tweets.label: Takeover
Takeover
tweets.text: If you decided to act, remember there are different ways of doing that. Remember 4Ds: direct, distract, delegate, and delay.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Direct action - is to call on the negative behavior directly, telling the aggressor to stop.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Distract - move attention of the aggressor or the whole group from the situation to something else. It lets the target to also move away towards safe environment while attention is somewhere else.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Delegate - there is no shame to feel to stressed to act right on point, but it is important to ask someone who is in power to change the situation to pay attention to the problem.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Delay - if the situation is too dangerous to be act upon directly, remember to come back to the problem later, when things feel safer: ask the affected person. If they are ok and whether they need help.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I believe that little steps lead to big changes. We are not always prepared to challenges we are facing. However, spreading information on what are the signs of discrimination and how to act if you encounter or witness one, can evolve the working culture of #academia for better.

tweets.text:
Today we're talking science!

Have you ever thought about how we got from these huge computers in the past to devices that are so small that you can fit in your pocket?

What if I say this was possible because of Quantum Mechanics?

https://t.co/emt7d5dGuL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I need to explain roughly how computers work. Can I do it in a single tweet?

They are machines that convert a signal (speaking, typing) into a string of 0's and 1's. These digits are called bits. Some math happens in the computer and it returns something else (image, sound).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
"So computers do math?"

Yes. But in a very different way. The input signal is converted into an electric signal:
- 0's: no electric current passing
- 1's: electric current is passing

The "math" is how the electric signal travels in the complex circuit inside the computer.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So we need an electronic device that allows current to pass or not. Something like a water valve, but for an electric signal.

These exist, and is how we used to do electronics in the past. https://t.co/3JbLvqBYjU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But the image in the previous tweet also shows something. These electronic valves are large! Is not very easy to shrink the size of a computer if inside it there are a bunch of empty glass bulbs.

That is definitely not how we make a cell phone!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So let's think again.

It would be great if we had a tiny piece of material that we control if it is a conductor or insulator of electricity. That'd make our valve much smaller!

So what are really conductors and insulators?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
To answer, we need to talk about atoms.

In school we learn that atoms are constituted by two parts: a heavy positively-charged nucleus; and a bunch of light negatively-charged particles, called electrons, orbiting the nucleus. https://t.co/RKRSy9ZOz5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But these electrons cannot orbit as they wish. Quantum Mechanics says that they can only occupy orbits with a well-defined energy.

Also, electrons don't occupy an orbit where there's already another electron.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So if you put atoms together, the orbits cannot be identical to how they were before. That would mean many electrons occupying identical orbits.

As a consequence, the energy of these orbits changes by a bit, forming what we call energy bands. https://t.co/geTgvp9PMr

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
That's what happens inside any material. And whether it is an insulator or a conductor depends on where the last electron is.

We start populating the bands with lower energy. And if the last electron we put is in the middle of the band, we call it a conductor. https://t.co/XSlOMnnl1r

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If the last electron is at the very top of the band, we need a very large energy to put it in another orbital. And because of this energy gap, we call the material an insulator. https://t.co/J97UeGWEsz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But there are materials with a gap that is not so large. And these materials we can actually control if they should behave as insulators or conductors. These materials are called semiconductors.

We found what we needed! https://t.co/2DyVADOArq

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
That's how the transistor was created -- the electronic valve that requires no empty bulb.

Since then, there were basically no limits on how small one could make a computer. And that's how you are reading this thread on a much smaller computer!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Have you heard all the fuzz about #LK99 some time ago?

If you didn't: some researchers claimed that they discovered a room temperature superconductor.

But what are superconductors anyway?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
More than 100 years ago now, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes was working in a laboratory in city nearby (Leiden) trying to obtain get lower and lower temperatures in his lab.

Eventually, he managed to liquify helium. A process that happens at 4.2K (-269 Celsius)!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And what do you think a scientist do when you get such low temperatures? They (responsibly) throw whatever you can in there.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: He was particularly curious about how metals conduct electricity at low temperatures. Especially if these metals are very pure, their resistance should SLOWLY drop more and more.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
To purify metals, you need to melt them and let all the impurities evaporate. So what are the easiest metals to melt? The ones that are already liquid in room temperature.

So Heike choose Mercury.

https://t.co/7d6nlWx9j9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But something unnexpected happened: the resistance dropped SUNDENLY to zero!

After many checks, he concluded that this was indeed happening and the phenomenon was coined superconductivity.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It took from 1911 to 1957 for physicists to find an explanation for this phenomenon. And even today, this explanation only holds for some materials.

And guess what: the reason why it happens is because electrons ATTRACT each other! 😱

https://t.co/6mXVw2QK6A

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It turns out that at very low temperatures, electrons don't have a lot of energy. And when atoms vibrate by a tiny bit, they can cause electrons to attract each other.

As a consequence electrons move in pairs (called Cooper pairs) inside a superconductor.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We don't have yet a room-temperature superconductor. But we already use superconductivity in many devices.

Stay tuned and you'll learn more about where we use them!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Today I’m doing something different: I’m in Leiden attending a PhD defense.

And the topic of the thesis inspired me to write about my favorite material today: graphene!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Let's start with graphite. Yes, the same material as the one in your pencil.

If you look into the atomic structure of graphite, you will notice that it consists of many layers of carbon. Each layer is organized in a honeycomb structure. https://t.co/CoLJlWUbQS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In fact, this structure is the very reason we use graphite to write. These many carbon layers detach easily from each other. As a consequence, if you slide it on paper, some layers just stay there.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
It's actually so easy to detach these layers that with scotch tape and some patience you can isolate a single layer. And that is how graphene was made in a lab for the first time.

https://t.co/vKDJcRNARg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But what is so nice about this material? Well, many things. I will list the ones that are quite important for my research.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
1 - It is easy to combine it with similar materials

Many materials out there have a similar layered structure. And in the same way that is easy to detach these layers, is also easy to combine them.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
For example, we can encapsulate graphene with an insulating material to protect it from the external environment.

This idea is actually what enabled graphene-based devices to work much better than other materials.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can also use this property to combine graphene with other materials. For example, we can use a layered magnetic material to make graphene magnetic. Or a superconducting material to make it a superconductor.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
2 - Electrons move as if they don't have mass

Electrons inside a material can behave in a very different way to their behavior in free space. In particular, electrons move in a graphene crystal as if they were massless particles.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
3 - It is an actual two-dimensional system

Before graphene devices were fabricated for the first time, the only way to confine electron motion in two dimensions was by growing complicated crystals. Graphene is already two-dimensional, so no engineering is needed.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
4 - You can twist!

Since these atomic layers are weakly bonded to each other, you can twist them. In fact, that changes a lot of the electronic properties of graphene. For example, with the appropriate twisting angle, you can make it a superconductor! https://t.co/YFPgQF979C

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There's way more, and I could keep writing. But I think you got why I like this material so much!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
To start, insulators and topological insulators have something in common: they both have a band gap.

But what happens when we put insulators in contact with each other?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Well, if all of them are trivial insulators, nothing really happens. For example, nothing really fun happens if my coffee mug is in contact with the table it's sitting on: both are gapped and when they are in contact their interface also has a gap.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now if my mug was made out of a topological insulator material something curious would happen.

The energy gap of a trivial and a topological insulator is inequivalent. Therefore, as you go from a point inside the mug to a point inside the table, the gap must close and reopen.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The energy gap closes at the interface between the trivial and the topological insulator. And, as you learned before, if there's no energy gap, the interface becomes an electric conductor.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Even if you mess up with the table and the mug, they will still have an interface. Since the interface doesn't care about the quality of any of the insulators, this conducting layer is a very good conductor!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Hi again!

I was out yesteday for an event from my department. But now I'm back!

I explained to you how an insulator works earlier this week. But what is a topological insulator?

https://t.co/KwUoZjQfp8

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
To start, insulators and topological insulators have something in common: they both have a band gap.

But what happens when we put insulators in contact with each other?

https://t.co/cmhK5Xg7UW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Well, if all of them are trivial insulators, nothing really happens. For example, nothing really fun happens if my coffee mug is in contact with the table it's sitting on: both are gapped and when they are in contact their interface also has a gap.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
If my mug was made out of a topological insulator material something curious would happen.

The energy gap of a trivial and a topological insulator are not equivalent. Therefore, as you go from a point inside the mug to a point inside the table, the gap must close and reopen.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The energy gap closes at the interface between the trivial and the topological insulator. And, as you learned before, if there's no energy gap, the interface becomes an electric conductor.

https://t.co/XNFtpxATDX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Even if you mess up with the table and the mug, they will still have an interface. Since the interface doesn't care about the quality of any of the insulators, this conducting layer is a very good conductor!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Now that I told you about topological insulators, time to explain what are topological superconductors and Majorana particles!

https://t.co/FG45OanGJ4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
So, I just told you that topological insulators have an energy gap different from a trivial insulator. The same applies to superconductors.

But how can a conductor have an energy gap and still conduct electricity?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Well, I also told you earlier this week that electrons inside a superconductor pair with other electrons. So we cannot really put one electron at a time in a superconductor...

https://t.co/zqBbnHzlHB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
...unless this electron has enough energy.

This energy is what we call a superconducting gap!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The rest works just like an insulator. At the interface between a topological superconductor and any material with a trivial gap, the gap closes.

But differently from a topological insulator, the particles moving at the interface are not electrons, but Majorana particles.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
These Majoranas are part of a family of particles called anyons. And because of that, they can be used to build fault-tolerant quantum computers.

https://t.co/qaLRAliov0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Obtaining Majoranas in the lab is a very complicated task. And is for example what many of my colleagues @qutechNews do!

And in fact, they just made a simpler version of these Majorana particles recently.

https://t.co/58ewfDQcjl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These devices are very similar to the ones I simulate at work. And I want to end the science section today by talking about a recent work that I co-authored that was inspired by these experiments. https://t.co/bNOarp1MlQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But I already wrote a thread about it when this work came out. So I'll be a little lazy and link it here for you. 😄

https://t.co/7Vofmvhuo3

At the moment I am actually in lovely Leiden, attending a workshop on #Quantum #Magnetic #Materials in @lorentzcenter that I co-organised with @dsoriano_david @mhdguimaraes and @ZeilaZanolli 
It's going to be an exciting week with a lot of discussions! https://t.co/wC9Mhy10Ef

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @lorentzcenter @dsoriano_david @mhdguimaraes @ZeilaZanolli @lorentzcenter workshops are unique in their focus on interactivity and discussions,  and our workshops is not an exemption. We have a lot of discussions sessions scheduled,  introductory seminars, and even a tutorial from @Qnami_ https://t.co/5a37ADzkRu

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Our first day of the workshop is over,  but what are some of the things one needs to do when organising a conference? 
The list is quite long, and I will mention just a couple of things starting with time and planning.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Why am I starting with this?  Because we started planning our @lorentzcenter workshops already in December 2022!
Of course,  you start slow - by deciding on the topic and finding people to co-organise with you.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @lorentzcenter We had to write an application to Lorentz Centre for our workshop - and this included description of the workshop, topics we want to cover,  tentative planning and list of activities we wanted to have- and list of key participants.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @lorentzcenter This all goes for the review, and then we got comments from the reviewers and adapted the final draft based on this - similar to the case of an article under review.  And once you are awarded a workshop week, that's when the real work begins!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @lorentzcenter You have to finalise the participant list to know how many people will attend (in our case we had a limitation to 55 participants), and you also need to ensure that all of your key participants can attend.  If not, you need to go for a backup plan!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @lorentzcenter Of course  organising a conference costs money, so dealing with funding is an important step. We are lucky that we got some funding from @lorentzcenter  and they also provide us with space, office and an amazing organisational support!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
@lorentzcenter We still had to obtain additional funding, in this case it came from our personal grants andour industrial participants. 
How to get in contact with companies?  It helps if you know someone working there. It is also very important that there is a good connection their work.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What did we use this extra funding for? We are covering costs of our podcast, use it to provide lunch for the participants, and to provide travel support for PhDs and postdocs who needed it!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What are other things you need to do when organising a conference?  Well, you select speakers/key participants. We took great care to cover our key topics well, and to have representation of all the fields, (including theory vs experiments), seniority,  gender and nationalities

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You actually need to secure your speakers quite early. Of course,  things might change closer to the date, but the sooner you contact your speakers,  the better!  Especially if they are travelling from far away,  or have a heavy teaching load and need to time conferences well.

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Most of the professors in the Netherlands need to obtain a University Teaching Qualification (UTQ, or BKO). How you get it depends on your University. In case of the University of Groningen,  we take classes given by education experts,  have homework and a final portfolio.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Today I was taking classes on modes of assessment, advantages and disadvantages different modes and some mistakes that are good to avoid when making exams. The classes are for all of the lectures, so you might end up in a group with people working at a very different places.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So far I've been in groups with lecturers from economics, law, history of architecture, medical school, computer science- and one fellow physicist. It is an good place meet your fellow colleagues, and see how different teaching can be. But sometimes it can be very difficult.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We use different language,  
departments have different lecture modes, and we might not even know anything about the field of the colleague.  I'm usually always happy when I end up in a group with colleagues from #science and #engineering faculty, as we can talk easily.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These course are not completely theoretical.  We actually have to time it well, as we need take certain moduels while we are teaching, as we have 2 experienced people to come and observe us while teaching. One is am expected colleagues,  another our teaching coach.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Yes, we got a coach 📢
It is typically an education expert that is supposed to track our progress,  and help us with pur portfolio.

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But as a curriculum committee member, it is kinda your job to read up on these hings - and it counts in your service hours, so it is a good deal. So what do we do in this committee?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We look at the curriculum as a whole, courses that are offered and input from the students, and can propose changes. We can suggest that courses are rearranged, changes, removed from the curriculum or propose new ones.

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: You might wonder how long this takes -and the answer is that it varies. We do need to finish before Christmas as that is when the plan for the next academic year (teaching wise) is made, so we do have a hard deadline!

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Well, we actually make plans for the courses close to a year ahead! I don't mean that we have a schedule or start working on the lectures, but we need to know which courses are taught and when, so that students are informed in time.

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover

Today's topic - my recent paper that I am super excited about and that I already mentioned in the podcast with @MySci_PK !
In Situ Exfoliation Method of Large‐Area 2D Materials - also known as KISS method (kinetic in situ single-layer synthesis) 💋
https://t.co/8yaj7A6wla

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is my first work that came out since I joined @ZernikeInst , and it was mainly done when I moved there. And yes, this is the work done with the international team of scientific besties 🥰💜

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
@ZernikeInst What is this method about?
Well, it is an #exfoliaiton #method that uses atomically clean surfaces as both a substrate for 2D #materials and a sort of a sticky tape for their exfolation

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Method is made to really work well for different #surface #science techniques, as that is my main branch of work, and all of the tools are simply tools you would find in your average surface science #lab!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: How does it work? Well, we take a substrate - in our case often a single #crystal metals, as we like conducting surfaces, such as Au(111)🥇 and Ag(111)🥈and we use sputtering & annealing methods to make them extremely clean. All done in ultra-high vacuum!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the meantime, we also prepare a layered crystal that we would like to exfoliate in a 2D form, let's say WSe2. How do we prepare ti? Well, we use a little pin- or a sticky tape (!)- to remove top layers in ultrahigh vacuum, so that crystal also has super clean surface

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
And then we simply bring these 2 atomically clean surfaces in contact and make them KISS 💋
We do have a little addition - layered crystal is on a sample holder with a spring- to make it easier to aling things, and to know for sure when things are brought in contact.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Once you separate them, you are left with your layered crystal AND substrate that has large area 2D film (in our example case of WSe2).
Large area is the key here. All methods that I use usually require samples of at least 200 um, preferably larger. and KISS method makes them!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Sounds quite neat, right?
We also tried it on semiconductors (Ge), and also on air sensitive materials such as WTe2, and it works like a charm! We've done these measurements at a couple of places  @ZernikeInst @KTHuniversity and @AarhusUni_int and it worked quite nicely!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @ZernikeInst @KTHuniversity @AarhusUni_int We managed to measure the electronic structure, which is one of the most interesting things to me, and it also seems that it is interesting to other people in the surface science community - which is what we hoped for!

tweets.text: As today is my last day here, I thought I will tell you a bit about how my career changed since I was here 2-3 years ago (also week 42!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Last time I was Tweeting from this profile, I was a #postdoc @KTHuniversity . That was also during COVID19 time, so I have to admit that I did not see too much of #Stockholm and #Sweden. Quite unfortunate as it is a country with beautiful nature.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I was there on a 2 year postdoctoral fellowship,with a possibility of extension. Not to bad of a deal (no one wants to move during a pandemic...).
During that time, I received an email via a mailing list advertising a tenure track position @ZernikeInst @univgroningen

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I've never been to Groningen at that point, but the position looked perfect to me, as it was really in the field that I was interested in - ultrafast #Science 
And I even had a background in it! I was considering whether to apply or not, as I wasn't sure I really stand a chance..

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
But I thought positions that sound perfect don't appear that often, and I can at least use it as a practice.
It definitely helped to have a supporting partner -and supportive work #friends who were telling me to definitely apply.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I took it as a bit of a research project - I checked what is all the information they need, and how it should be written: CV, publications, cover letter, research and #teaching statement...
I also asked friends for examples of their applications to have an idea how they did it.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: After being on a hiring committee myself - I can tell you that (at least at my university) all of the requested information is relevant. Yes, we are the most interested in your research (for research position), but we also really care about your teaching, and collegiality.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
When preparing for an application, I also read about the university, and the institute I was applying with. Who works there, can I collaborate with someone? And also, what are some classes I could teach.
It is also good to check possible funding you can apply with.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And then I did my best, sent an application, and got a glass of wine! 🍷

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Some time later, I was informed that I am shortlisted, and that they would like to do an online interview (remember, COVID19 time...).
This was both exciting, and a bit terrifying. Luckily for me, I have great friends and colleagues who helped me prepare.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I was scheduled to give a seminar to the department, and then a 5 min presentation on my research and teaching vision, respectively.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I made several different versions of each, until I was happy. And I asked people for help.
My PhD supervisor is amazing, and he checked my research plan and my seminar. Gave really helpful advice.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I had a meeting with my former colleague about teaching, and I even had a chat with two former collaborators who work(ed) in the Netherlands  to prepare better.
If you can, do ask people for advice. Most of the time people are happy to help you, and want to see you succeed!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I am really privileged to have an amazing #PhD supervisor, and great friends from my PhD time that I consider family at this point who helped and supported me in this journey. If you are not as lucky, you should still try to contact people you know.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Maybe you collaborated with someone who work at the place you are applying at, or you met someone at the conference some time ago, and you had a great discussion? Do contact them and see if they are willing to meet with you!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And don't underestimate importance of all the things they asked for in the application. In my interview, everything was covered - from research to teaching and management. One of the committee members was a senior master student and they had a lot of questions about teaching.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Of course, before doing online or in person interview, check who you will be talking to, so that you can prepare. It is your interview, sure, but you are also interviewing them! You might end up working with these people next 30-40 years so take the opportunity to ask questions.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I've discussed my research, teaching, even outreach with the committee members!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
If interview is online - plan to have an evening off afterwards. It is an exhausting process even if you have good conversations and never leave your room/office.
In person, well, it is even more exhausting, but you do avoid possible internet connections issues 🫣

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Something I will not go in details, but is also important, is the part when you are offered a position and need to negotiate your contract/starting package.
It varies A LOT from a place to a place, even in the same country. For this, you do want to talk to someone, if you can.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
And you want to talk to someone from at least the same country - again, as this vastly differs from a place to a place.

tweets.text: 👋 Hi everyone!  I'm @DrCBrew and I'm taking over this week to share a bit about what I am up to and have been up to.  I'm currently a postdoc in the Walker group at @UTDMaterialsSci and we'll also be talking about the current work going on in the group!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'll have more to share once its daytime in Dallas.  I'll answer the most important question though...  the chance of a Porkchop feature this week is non-zero.  😼

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Who am I?  Here's a brief run through this week's curator's academic history and the road to it!  🧵

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My interest in science was really sparked while working at the Museum of Science and Industry (MOSI, @mositampa ) in Tampa from 2006 - 2015!  Here's a few photos I could dig out from that many years back. https://t.co/o58aAGD0nV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At @mositampa I actually started my research career in education, working with a team of researchers on developing successful scaffolding strategies for informal education centers.  (If you look closely in the photo, you'll see 16 year old me) https://t.co/fSwTRwVdr5

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I received my BS in Chem and Biochem from Florida State University in 2014.  I began to get my gloves wet working with Prof Lei Zhu (@ChemistryFsu) synthesizing bisazides for molecular linkers and developing methodology for synthesizing bistriazoles.  https://t.co/7xkBJfWSIb

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: While at FSU, I also continued exploring my interest in education by doing demonstrations and outreach for @ChemistryFsu!  (At one show I even had a chance to get the church cat involved!) https://t.co/lrFQ44StsE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I moved to University of Florida (@UFChemistry), where I worked with @McElweeWhite designing precursors for a few different deposition techniques, while also studying the decomposition pathways for the precursors.  Here's photo-decomposition:  https://t.co/AOixSXh9AH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I also designed molecules for focused electron beam induced deposition as well:  https://t.co/82VAngLnnM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: While at UF, I worked with @UFHonors to develop a Harry Potter themed Potions Camp (Potterology) for incoming freshmen into the Honors Program!  It is interdisciplinary, so courses like Herbology are also included!  I have had the pleasure of teaching this course 7 times. https://t.co/MPsxFN59Jj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In 2021, I graduated from UF with my PhD in Chemistry.  In case you were curious, I did take graduation photos with my cat!  https://t.co/NYx2SEIqMA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: From 2021 - 2023, I was a Postdoc @NCStateChem, working with @CastellanoGroup designing organic chromophores for OLEDs!  I developed a strategy for designing emitters with tunable properties. https://t.co/7pRxq2q7Rn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you'd like to hear more about my chromophore design work, I'll be sharing the story at #AVS69 @AVS_Members

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In September 2023 I moved to @UTDMaterialsSci to join the Walker Group and am now working on developing methods for depositing transition metal chalcogenides by Chemical Bath Deposition.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Stay tuned this week to see more about the work I have been up to as well as the rest of the work being done in the Walker lab! https://t.co/eJi1xVU1CM

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of the projects that we have going on in the lab is Photoassisted Chemical Vapor Deposition (PACVD).  While I was a graduate student with @McElweeWhite, I also had the chance to travel to @UTDMaterialsSci to use the reactor with the precursors I synthesized!  🧵 https://t.co/P49Ieh8p22

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: While at @UFChemistry, my major contribution was to design the precursors and study their photo-decomposition pathways and quantum yields so that we can understand what makes a suitable precursor for PACVD.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Where I started on this process as a first year grad student was drawing designs for a setup and a phone call to Newport to place an order for an Hg(Xe) arc lamp.  We've since upgraded the setup to use LEDs and a solar cell detector!  (https://t.co/y5KYyFSh7i) https://t.co/hvz3TJPfZK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We setup a dark room to make it easier to run these experiments and characterize the samples.  We called it the Red Light District! https://t.co/gQcUNA2b4M

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you'd like to read about the first set of compounds I studied, we published the work in Organometallics:  https://t.co/OigCJ7ibzt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A fun fact though, the most effective way to synthesize some of my reference compounds ended up with me on the roof of the building using the sunlight as my light source! https://t.co/TxfYYZ7X34

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Running reactions on the roof of the building did lead to some unique photo-ops for my reactions. https://t.co/6KwIPlafzD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We have also published the PACVD results from the (allyl)Ru(CO)3X series, which does show a dependence on the halide atom.  https://t.co/eVZajLLb7F

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The next series of compounds that I studied was a series of Ru(0) diene complexes.  We have sorted out the photo-decomposition and PACVD experiments are underway!  https://t.co/jsYOB9GqGD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Synthesis of the Ru(0) diene complexes was simplified by a custom built photoreactor from the @UFChemistry Machine and Electronics shops, with the ability to perform high intensity irradiations at multiple wavelengths! https://t.co/8gxVZKH1ro

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Except for the cyclobutadiene complex, which insisted on liquid NH3 and Na. https://t.co/aVLoC3UnLh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Ru is not the only metal that we have looked at for PACVD.  My colleague Hanwen investigated Pt precursors for PACVD:  https://t.co/jbbWIZMfXX

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A long story short though, we actually discovered that the Pt precursors did not require light, and instead we were able to deposit Pt by low temperature CVD.  https://t.co/K1A9HECBWf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Which takes us back a little to the origins of the PACVD project, using trimethylaluminum for area selective, room temperature CVD.  https://t.co/RYR6lHwnIx

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: UV light does enhance the deposition of Al at room temperature though.  https://t.co/HErjLvVnSg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Which is where we got the idea to investigate photo-active Ru compounds for PACVD!  https://t.co/AcMWgnQm5U

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The substrates that we are using for these depositions are self-assembled monolayers on Au.  We are using this as a model system for metallizing organic substrates. https://t.co/WszTt5Bfu1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you've stuck with me this long, that is a brief history of the PACVD project I worked on as a grad student!  Work is continuing with Bishwa, Rashmi, and Xin at UF.  Kongkona is handling depositions at UTD, where sometimes I also have the chance to jump back in as well!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Data interpretation on this work was open to all paws!  Porkchop found the molecular orbitals very interesting.  Pictured is him sharing his thoughts on the orbitals during a Zoom call.  He also prefers to have a front row seat while surfing the web for info. https://t.co/Lqrtt1Nass https://t.co/qBPuoKtYLB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For something a little different today, another project that we have going on in the lab is investigating model systems to better understand degradation pathways and restoration methods for lead-glazed ceramics. https://t.co/DhPlfaXdwv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Some of our studies are done on real ceramic artifacts like the one from the photo!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We use tools like XPS and Raman Spectroscopy to understand more about the composition of the materials.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Based on what we observe spectroscopically in the ceramics, we can develop model systems to test decomposition pathways and probe potential restoration methods before we try on the real ceramics.  We've got a pretty bright outlook on the involvement of light in these processes! https://t.co/fBDzK3ePdP

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This work is led by Ally, who also shared her work today at the Graduate Student Poster Competition!  This work isn't published yet though, so Temoc wooshed in to hide everything except the title as I was taking the photo. https://t.co/jfa7yoJYm3

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: "Chemical Bathtubs", where did we get that title?  Well, it comes from the technique I (@DrCBrew) use in my work, Chemical Bath Deposition (CBD) of transition metal chalcogenides.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In simple terms, CBD is a method for depositing a material onto a substrate by placing the substrate into a solution containing a mixture of chemical components. https://t.co/UdyuBuOHco

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Like our other deposition project (PACVD), the substrates that I use here are self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) on Au, which are a model system for depositing onto other organic substrates.  https://t.co/40GYOuMCjs

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We use different functionalized SAMs to determine how a functional group influences the deposition of a material.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Functionalized SAMs also allow us to look at performing area selective deposition of our materials by using patterned SAMs.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The common components in a CBD bath are a metal source, a chalcogen source, and a complexing agent.  Other properties of the bath (like pH) can also be tuned!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We do all of our depositions at room temperature.  So we typically tune amounts/ concentrations of components, the components used, and pH.  With this we can modify, the reaction pathways occuring, their kinetics, and some of the surface chemistry.  (Likely over simplification!)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The deposits that we get from CBD are thick enough you can see them with your eye! https://t.co/dfw7ANtBjL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Our common initial characterization includes optical microscopy, Raman spectroscopy, and XPS. https://t.co/2ylTItKaMQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: My work is not published yet (I do talk a little bit about what I am doing in the podcast though!), but I can share a bit about some of the prior CBD work we have done in the lab.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Previous lab members done some work on CBD of MoS2 films in the past:  https://t.co/YpB2e9dymE

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For a look at area selective deposition of CuS by CBD, check out some of our previous lab member's work!  https://t.co/gRMNOT4OCK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Depending on how you tune your bath pH, you can control the deposit between Cu2S and CuS!  https://t.co/hKozU1UWiC

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hopefully you find chemical bathtubs as exciting as I do now!  I'm looking forward to being able to share my work once it is ready

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Once we have synthesized our dyes, we add them to a squeeze bottle and apply them to our mordanted shirts.  The dyes stick to the shirts quite well!  The shirt that I am wearing in this week's profile photo has been washed several times since applying the dyes. https://t.co/HoZfh0ktFv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: N-S you beauty: At the heart of fluid dynamics lies the Navier-Stokes equations, governing the motion of fluids. These equations are derivatives of basic laws of #physics viz. Mass conservation and Newton's Second law applied to Fluid Flow https://t.co/veHn4E3jk1

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The Clay Institute's problem revolves around proving the existence and smoothness of solutions to these equations. While solutions are available in limited cases, a universal understanding remains elusive. This challenge stands as one of the seven problems.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 💰 A $1 million reward awaits anyone who cracks the code! Mathematicians worldwide are drawn to the challenge, making it a pinnacle of mathematical exploration.

tweets.label: Takeover

Vortex-based #cavitation involves the controlled formation and implosion of tiny bubbles in a fluid, creating powerful shockwaves. This phenomenon is harnessed to enhance processes like #mixing, #reactions,  #emulsions, and #crystallization.
https://t.co/qOmjtm4gzt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Unlike traditional #cavitation, where the collapse of bubbles can be destructive, vortex-based devices leverage controlled cavitation. The result? Enhanced mixing efficiency, accelerated reactions, and improved performance in various applications.https://t.co/A0qI6yYuDS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: From chemical processing to wastewater treatment, vortex-based cavitation devices hold promise in diverse fields. These devices can optimize energy transfer, reduce resource consumption, and improve overall process efficiency.https://t.co/B5s8ccqNHR https://t.co/QiOohvikzG

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Crystallization is a process widely used for purification and synthesis of drugs and biomolecules in the pharmaceutical industry. The critical quality attributes (CQA) of the crystals help us decide whether the crystals produced are fit for our application or not. 💎✨

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Along with purity, polymorphic form, shape of the crystal, and particle size is an important CQA. The crystals formed are not all of the same size and hence we refer to the distribution of the sizes as the particle size distribution (PSD). https://t.co/dNo8o1K7FK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One of the major goals in the pharmaceutical industry is to achieve a uniform particle size. We need to incorporate tools that help us monitor the process while it is happening👩‍🔬These tools are referred to as PAT tools or process analytical tech tools.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The focused beam reflectance measurement (FBRM) is one such PAT tool that uses the measurement of the reflectance of a laser beam off the surface of the particles as an indicator of the size and number of particles. 🔦⚡https://t.co/kzVxgiOn7u

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The FBRM measures the length of a random chord (CLD) on the particles and not the actual size. The inversion of CLD to PSD for spherical particles has been discussed before. https://t.co/kT4O5C06kD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: While everything would seem easy-peasy with the instrument telling us the size of our particles as we are crystallizing them, it is unfortunately not so easy for irregular-shaped particles. https://t.co/U1zFcMBmej

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At MRing @VyshnvyH has developed a mathematical model that helps us convert the CLD of needle-like particles to its corresponding PSD. These models are applicable in the case of irregular particles as well as to systems described by bimodal PSDs. @SSPCentre  @ChemicalSciUL https://t.co/9oOBQVoPkK

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Hi everyone! I am @DrSofia_F_T and I am currently a postdoctoral researcher @nanoGUNE! I 
am thrilled to be taking over this week to show you all about what I do and have done over the 
years! It will be a healthy mix of science, hobbies and most likely cats. Stay tuned!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, who am I? My name is Sofia Ferreira Teixeira, and I am originally from Portugal. I am a #physicist, besides being a crazy cat lady and loving music a bit too much. So, how did I end up here? A🧵

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It all started in 2011, with the Summer School of Physics @UPorto @ciencias_fcup for high school students. It was a week full of lectures and in the Physics Department labs, where I felt at home.  We also had a project that we presented (see photo!) It was an amazing experience! https://t.co/CzXiBZPmzA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @UPorto @ciencias_fcup Having discovered my love for Physics that week, I decided to do a BSc in Physics @UPorto @ciencias_fcup. During the 3 years, I learnt I love experimental work! I also enjoyed my time as a uni student, with a bunch of traditions, like the "traje" we are wearing in the photo! https://t.co/siftKKjMUs

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @MySci_PK @UPorto @ciencias_fcup Yes! The project was called "Nanoparticles for medicine" and the idea was to use carbon nanotubes to carry certain drugs. We spent the whole week doing these nanotubes and it was awesome!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: A brief pause on showing how I got here, because today is a very special day at my group @CICNanodevices @nanoGUNE: we will have a new doctor! Isabel is defending today her PhD on topological insulators and Spintronics devices! 🥳🥳 https://t.co/ZkollabfHe

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Tune in later today to find out more about what these topological insulators are and why they are interesting for Spintronics ;)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: During my time as a student, I had several opportunities to know different fields of physics and how research is, which made me want to do science. One of them was my time as a @CERN Summer Student! It was a fantastic time, full of experiments and experiences! https://t.co/HNlLVFHZh6

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @CERN Another opportunity was the internships offered by @ciencias_fcup. I did 3 internships on the same topic: thermoelectric effect! I loved the topic and enjoyed working with my supervisor and his team at IFIMUP! It also gave me the chance to present at conferences for the 1st time! https://t.co/sR9SoxOFGf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Realising I wanted to do research and that I loved experimental work, I did a MSc in Physics @UPorto @ciencias_fcup and IFIMUP, focusing on material physics. My thesis was about electronic properties of topological insulator thin films! It envolved a lot of fun clean room days😆 https://t.co/WyikoQdeyn

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I started my PhD in 2018, studying the magnetic and electric properties of topological insulator/ferromagnetic nanostructures. During my 2nd year, I spent 6 months @imperialcollege, measuring samples, learning from my colleagues and having this view from the Physics common room! https://t.co/HGLH8I209L

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: At the end of March 2022, I defended my PhD in Physics. It took me just over 3 hours but eventually I was indeed called a Dr! The defense was still hybrid: some of the jury was online, but in the audience I had my family and friends, which made the moment that more special! https://t.co/kff6mtdnFf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And here I am now: a postdoc @nanoGUNE in the @CICNanodevices group! I now work on Van der Waals materials and heterostructures towards novel (spintronics) devices. It continues to envolve a lot of clean room time and experiments! And this week I will show you some of it!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Good morning! Tuesday mornings for me mean a subgroup meeting! 👩‍🏫 My colleagues and I share what we did the week before and discuss the latest measurements or any problem we found!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Now that you know how I got here, you may be asking what is or was my work. 🔬 👩‍🔬 Well, if you already listened to the podcast, you may already know, but here is an overview of it😉

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Nowadays, @nanoGUNE, I work with van der Waals (vdW) materials. Have you heard of graphene?✏️Well, it is a vdW material, but since its "exfoliation" (remember this word) a lot of other materials like it have appeared, from magnets, like the ones on the fridge, to superconductors!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @nanoGUNE But now you ask me, well but why do you care about them? What is so special about these materials? And what do you do with them?🤔

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And while I let you think about why we care about vdW materials 😉, it is time for a Basque (Euskera) class at @nanoGUNE! Euskera is spoken here in the Basque Country, and the classes are always a fun break to learn and discover more about the region! https://t.co/B3o6aS5kFh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The vdW materials have a wide range of applications due to some extraordinary properties! 💫 They are made up of layers connected by these vdW forces, which are very weak. Thus, one fantastic property is that we can separate the layers, aka exfoliate, and get very thin flakes!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In a magnetic vdW material, we can play with its magnetism: we can go from a ferromagnet, like the fridge ones, to different magnetic phases like antiferromagnet 🧲 We can also end up with different magnetic orientations, called anisotropies, which we look for in certain things!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @nanoGUNE I am exploring the magnetic and transport properties of these vdW magnets, also called layered magnetic materials.🔎 We study how they behave when we apply magnetic or electric fields and then we try to tune and control their behaviour! 🔧🎮

tweets.label: Takeover
Takeover
tweets.text: @nanoGUNE Due to the vdW forces magic 🪄 we create these devices like we play with Legos: we stack one vdW material on top of another! 🧱 So we can combine a vdW magnet with another vdW material that, by generating a spin current, controls its magnetism! The possibilities are endless!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @nanoGUNE So, some days this is me! (With tiny flakes and in a clean room suit but an accurate representation 😅) https://t.co/OmSeNrsOC0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I showed you how I play with legos, aka build nanostructures of van der Waals materials, and study the magnetic and electronic properties of these. But, how do we fabricate these materials to be able to explore their properties? Come with me and let's fabricate a device!🧵

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It all starts with a bulk crystal! 🪨 This is a piece of material that is macroscopic that we can hold in our hands. But it is made up of thousands and thousands of layers connected by vdW forces, so if we want just a few layers, what do we do? We exfoliate with scotch tape!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Yes, you read that right! We put the crystal between two pieces of a special scotch tape and we seperate them. This separates the layers of the material. And if we keep going and going we can reach very thin flakes, aka pieces of the material with very few layers!🤏

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Sometimes these materials don't like being in normal air conditions, too much oxygen and water for their liking🌬️💧 for these we exfoliate inside a Glovebox: a box where the air is controlled to minimise O2 and H2O that we access with gloves (the name is very apt isn't it?)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, now we have our thin flakes on the scotch tape, but how do we study it? We need to transfer the material onto a substrate where we can then do all we need. We mostly use silicon substrates with an oxidized layer, aka Si/SiO2. This is what it looks like! https://t.co/ebxnGHN4SS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We end up with many flakes on the substrate and now comes the best part for some, the worst for others: we need to search and choose the flake we want to study! For that, we use a simple optical microscope🔬and take a📸! What do you think, would you like to search for flakes?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We now have our flake!🥳But how do we measure its electronic properties? We need to contact the flake with electrical contacts! We use a metal, like Gold or Platinum . But before we use up our Gold, we have to do the part I like the most: design the contacts! ✍️

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For this we use a method called Lithography, which comes from Greek and means writing in stone✍️🪨But if you draw by hand, your design is too big! So we use something else to write: light🔦and if we really want to go small, we even use electrons⚡️!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is because the wavelength of light or of electrons is small enough that we can write micro or nanometric things〰️! And this is precisely the size we need for the contacts to our flake! But now you are thinking, if we are "writing" with light, what is our paper (or stone)?📜

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Light sensitive polymers and we call them photoresists! We put a resist layer on the substrate with our flake and then we shine with light to draw our design. If it is a➕resist, the area iluminated can be removed, but with➖resist, this area stays and everything else goes away!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Here @nanoGUNE we can do it with light in a machine we call the Laser Writer (because it uses an UV light laser) 🔦 or we can use an eBL, which stands for electron beam lithography ⚡️, and uses an electron gun to write our devices!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @nanoGUNE Here is an example! You see on the left our flakes on the substrate, and we want to study the thin blueish one, marked with the green line. And on the right, you see the result after we do the lithography and we develop (yes! like an old photographic film) the resist! https://t.co/YOGnhB2EwH

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @nanoGUNE On the right, the green area and the very big flake are still covered with the resist. In the purple area, the resist has gone away and we are left with holes, that we can fill with gold and thus contact and measure the sample!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @nanoGUNE We have our device almost fabricated, only two steps to go! We need to fill the opened resist holes with Gold. For that we deposit a thin film of gold or platinum, with a nanometric thickness, so also very small😉

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @nanoGUNE We can use an Evaporator: we heat the gold to make it evaporate and it forms a film. Or we use a sputtering: we have a target of platinum at which we throw Argon ions so fast that some platinum is removed and is deposited! Here is a GIF of some sputtering I did in my PhD! https://t.co/4hvlcq9vdy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @nanoGUNE Almost there! Now we have or metal on the holes contacting the flake but also on top of the rest of the substrate that had the resist. So, how are we just left with the contacts? Well, we do what we call a lift-off 🏋️and we remove the resist, and thus also the metal on top!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @nanoGUNE This is the most nerve wracking step for me. After so many steps and effort, everything can be destroyed by a simple bad lift-off! But have no fear! We place our device in acetone and it worked! We get all the resist away and we are left with a nice contacted flake, our device!🥳 https://t.co/UffqDbJ0LQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: RT @DrSofia_F_T: Halfway there with the fabrication! We already see some drawn contacts! 👀👀 @nanoGUNE @RealSci_Nano

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: RT @DrSofia_F_T: A GIF done by chance on a clean room "boring" day! And it is one of the things I have used most in my presentations, from…

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: RT @DrSofia_F_T: And the final device, isn't it cute? Or is it just me that finds it cute?  @nanoGUNE @RealSci_Nano

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Having our device all ready, we can meaure it⚡️but not yet! This week, I managed to get a booking only on the weekend, since our measurement system is loved by everyone🥲, aka heavily used! The life of a scientist: a Saturday can be a Monday and a Monday a Saturday 📅🔁📆

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So what am I doing today? Well, first catching up on some literature and reading some papers for my upcoming measurements! So this is me this morning! 📄👀 https://t.co/Ou3d61CbKF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Measuring days and I was mia for them. You plan your best but something happens and you need to adapt to what your sample wants to do, which can be just "I do not want to be measured" 🥲 But don't lose all hope, I am measuring and will take you through it! A thread 🧵😊

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you remember, we had our devices, contacted with metal and all ready to be measured. 🥳 Well, what do we actually want to measure here? 🤔

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This material is a magnetic semiconductor, so we can explore its magnetic properties through measurements of its electric resistance and its dependence on temperature 🌡️, magnetic fields 🧲 (Magnetoresistance) or electric fields ⚡️ (Gate dependence)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We know what we want to measure, so let's get our device ready! We have to connect the metal that is on our flake to all the cables, to apply electric currents and measure voltages. We use a wire bonder: we connect our device with small wires of Gold or Aluminium to a puck! 🪡

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is what it looks like! I have 2 substrates, the shiny squares each with one device. You can see the squares of gold (or pink in the bottom one, do you know why they have different colours?), the tiny wires connected to them and the gold rectangles on the green puck! https://t.co/vABvME7scO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And here is a zoom into the puck, with other devices I have measured bonded. You can see how the tiny wires go from the Gold rectangles in the puck to the Gold pads of our devices! 🟨🪡🟪 https://t.co/dkxUYhaUuJ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Depending on the size of nanometric Gold, its colour changes! In this case the thickness of the metallic thin film is different, the pinkish squares are around 15 nm whereas the other ones are almost 50 nm!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Devices are ready to be measured! And we do this in a PPMS: a Physical Properties Measurement System! And yes, you read that right, a lot of the physical properties of materials can be measured in these systems, from optical, to thermal, to electrical as in our case!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: They are super cool machines because we can measure things at temperatures all the way down to 2K and with magnetic fields up to 9T! And this is what one of our systems looks like at @nanoGUNE! To me it looks like a tiny space ship🚀, what do you think? https://t.co/R9zoi0O73b

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @nanoGUNE Our device goes inside and, if the gods of the labs shine upon us, we can measure it and acquire a lot of data that we analyse to understand our materials! So, that is also what I end up doing in days when there is no lab work: a lot of fun with spreadsheets! 📊 https://t.co/PVPbROaHiT

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @nanoGUNE Aka, this is what I will be doing next week with the data of this weekend😉 https://t.co/8A2g1wD55v

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So, this week (and weekend) was mostly focused on work... But a life of a scientist is not only work, and as I promised, and as you heard on the podcast (if not, go on and give a listen to it!), here are other things that keep me "busy" on my free time 😌
