tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Hello! I’m @xamberlim, and I will be your guest scientist this week! I’m a chemistry PhD student in the @Fredrickson_UW group at @UWMadisonChem by day, and also an art-loving, D&D-playing nerd 24/7! This week I’m going to cover 💎Crystals! 👩‍🎨 Comics! & 💻 Calculations!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: 💎 Crystals! I study intermetallic solid state chemistry. In molecular chemistry, the kinds of chemicals we study are often smaller, singular units. In solid state chemistry, our chemicals are linked together in one large unit that extends beyond the atomic scale.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is one aspect that makes it challenging to research the solid state. Not only do we need to consider local effects around individual atoms, but also consider long-range or bulk effects.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Crystals are one type of solid. In science, we describe crystals with a unit cell, which gives us information about how atoms are arranged. These unit cells repeat in 3-D space, very much like a 3-D wallpaper. (Comic excerpt from our group website: https://t.co/l6eUWuWDGK) https://t.co/5zr9h3Ja5n

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I study intermetallic crystals because metals are so diverse! Metal atoms can have varying sizes, electron counts, and electronegativities. As a result, when metal elements come together to form a new intermetallic compound, the bonds between them can have different characters!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This diversity of bonding in solids can be understood with the van Arkel-Ketalaar Triangle, which shows that bonding is a spectrum rather than a fixed types. https://t.co/THOLpjGL1d

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Intermetallic materials can have bonds that have a mixture of these characters. My job and my passion is to understand the complex bonding in these types of materials, and I do that mainly through computational chemistry. https://t.co/3yvrsyz8UO

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Of course, there's experimental aspects in this field of work too! I used to do experiments as an undergraduate researcher, but I have since turned my focus to pure computational work. I do miss getting pretty crystals though! (CuP2 below) https://t.co/14XmYiCNcG

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Stay tuned this week to learn how I tackle these problems!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
One perspective our group uses to study the formation of intermetallic materials is through the lens of FAST: Frustrated and Allowed Structural Transitions. 🚌💨

Before we talk about FAST, let's dive into some background...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There are three different factors we use to understand why solid state materials form:
(1) Atomic size effects
(2) Electronic structure
(3) Electronegativity
These are often called Hume-Rothery factors.

In my research, I will focus on the first two factors! https://t.co/0t9kOycXfk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Atomic size effects: One way to think of our materials is to think of them as hard spheres in a box. A lot of metallic elements pack in certain patterns (hcp, bcc, fcc). If you’ve seen produce in pyramids at the grocery store, you may be familiar with these ordered packings. https://t.co/Xw1dezaHUR

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When the atoms are different sizes, however, the problem of filling up space in an ordered way becomes more complex, as we can see in this holiday-themed example. 🎄 https://t.co/9jwUyUYJ1D

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Electronic structure: A core part of chemistry is understanding how electrons interact with each other and nuclei. We have so many electron-counting concepts in chemistry (such as the octet rule and formal charges for Lewis dot structures) to rationalize structure.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the field of solid state chemistry, we have many models and electron-counting principles as well, including but not limited to the Zintl concept, the Mott-Jones model, and Wade-Mingos rules. https://t.co/iofeU67s8G

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These fundamental principles help us to determine whether systems are "electronically favorable" based on whether they ✅ perfectly satisfy the rules, 🆗 are very close to meeting them, or ⛔ don't fit at all.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Lastly, Electronegativity! This is the tendency of an element to attract electrons. Electronegativity is intertwined with electronic structure because differences in electronegativity can lead to different kinds of bonding (see the van Arkel-Ketalaar triangle in the last thread).

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We tie these concepts together with the FAST principle. Overall structural stability can be viewed as a combination of these factors.

When atomic packing conditions and the electronic structure are both favorable, the crystal structure will easily form.
👍 + 👍 = 👍

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
When these factors disagree, the crystal structure will be harder to form. In fact, we may see some ✨interesting, more complex structures✨ (such as intergrowths and modulated structures) as the factors compete on a local and global level.

👍 + 👎 = ⁉😱⁉

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For an introduction to the FAST concept and a cool, modulated structure, check out this paper by my former colleague! It's a long one, but it's a good one! https://t.co/btYfkZzCnB

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Tomorrow, I'll talk more about my specific research project. 👋😉 Signing off for today.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Today, I’ll give an overview of my specific project:
✨ 18-n+m isomerism in T-E intermetallics✨

Whoa, what a mouthful! 💦 Isomerism? 18-n+m? What does that mean?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Yesterday, I talked about electron-counting rules in chemistry, each useful in specific contexts and bonding. https://t.co/m6wt5zDf3Z

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
One domain of bonding we’re interested in is when compounds have both metallic and covalent characteristics.
Transition metal (T) - main group metal (E) intermetallics are perfect candidates for this investigation, and furthermore, there's some interesting structural trends...! https://t.co/avXZIBXmKL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
T-T connectivity in the crystal structure can be related to its electron count. We call this concept the 18-n+m rule, though it's also known in one of its forms as the 18-n rule.

How does this rule work? We know that closed-shell compounds are electronically stable. https://t.co/zrVabk6hRp

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Transition metal atoms can achieve closed-shell stability with multi-center T-T bonds, which we call isolobal bonds. These bonds are enabled through the support of main group atoms.

The number of electrons shared in these bonds correspond to the "n" in the 18-n rule. https://t.co/qtT49WpGyV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
In the case of ScAl3, we have 12 valence electrons, so using the 18-n rule...
18-n = 12
Then n=6!
This is exactly what we see in ScAl3, which forms the AuCu3 type. Sc can form 6 Sc-Sc contacts, all supported by Al atoms. https://t.co/jvFocRsczg

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For detailed reading and examples of the 18-n rule, I recommend this excellent article, aptly titled, "Generality of the 18-n rule". https://t.co/p0BS3orTge

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
What about the 18-n+m rule?

m corresponds to the number of electrons that are NOT associated with the transition metal atoms. These atoms are based in main group-only states.

e.g. for Ir3Sn7, 1 electron goes in the isolobal bond, and 1.33 electrons populate the Sn-Sn σ bond. https://t.co/6abvBRX41D

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This electron-counting rule has been helpful for us to rationalize a number of structures!

However, you can see in the below example that I can have different (n,m) configurations at the same electron count... https://t.co/eU7bCCYydm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Herein lies the problem of 18-n+m isomerism. If we can have multiple (n,m) configurations and still be electronically stable, how do we know which structure type is the best candidate? https://t.co/nRj4eKQe6S

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
This is where the FAST concept I talked about yesterday comes in! We break down the candidate systems into two analyses.

(1) ⚛ Electronics: How does the 18-n+m rule apply?
(2) 💥Atomic packing: What kind of packing tensions are present in the systems?
https://t.co/8k1vDF2rp9

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's it for now! Later, I'll talk about the two analyses in detail, then bring them together to solve the conundrum of 18-n+m isomerism. 👋

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Happy Wednesday! ☕ Today I'll be talking about the theoretical methods we use to explore our crystal systems! While I prepare those tweets, have another one of my desk companions 🦆 and a 20 oz. coffee mug for scale. My roommate got me this mug to celebrate this paper! https://t.co/0TtMmwXasa

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: As the holiday traveling season approaches, PACKING may be on your mind. How are you going to pack all those gifts and clothes into one carry-on bag? https://t.co/AAnVgljZ2G

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Well, I don’t have an answer for that, but I do have a theoretical tool for understanding packing in solid state materials. Introducing the ✨DFT-Chemical Pressure analysis!✨
(TOC image from https://t.co/v5M8cTzizO) https://t.co/F9fsFWXFKW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
What’s Chemical Pressure?
Imagine a 2D lattice of atoms. These atoms are the same element and are placed at their equilibrium distances. If we replace one atom with a smaller one, its contacts must shorten but at the expense of other contacts!
We have packing tensions! https://t.co/JWGN6NPnLU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We encapsulate this concept in calculating "chemical pressures" for our system. To do this, we:
(1)  Use DFT packages to calculate energies of our system at its normal volume, a slightly bigger one, and a slightly smaller one.
(2) Calculate a pressure for every voxel (a 3D pixel) https://t.co/Ak7Qelv19z

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
(3) Project the 3D chemical pressure information onto spherical harmonics centered on atoms. This gives us a means to interpret contact-wise chemical pressures.

* This is a simplified version of the whole DFT-CP process.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
These spherical harmonics (called CP features) tell us which contacts are too long and which contacts are too short.

Black = -CP. Energy DECREASES as the atoms come closer. The contact is too long!
White = +CP, Energy INCREASES as the atoms come closer. The contact is too short! https://t.co/eNcTYOEyXU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: These CP schemes are useful, as they can tell us what the local packing tensions are. In general, we can compare two CP schemes of structures of the same composition to identify which structure type reduces packing tensions, and how it does so!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One way I used DFT-CP was to look at a series of intergrowth structures in the REAl3 series! We combed through literature and found a trend that compounds with larger RE atoms tend to have more of the hexagonal Ni3Sn type than the cubic AuCu3 type. https://t.co/FqxQPBRBPr

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This suggested to us that atomic size and packing effects played a large role in which structure type forms. But why? We could look at tables of covalent and metallic radii, but this wasn't enough for us. DFT-CP came to the rescue! 🦸‍♀️

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We calculated the DFT-CP schemes of a selection of these compounds and found that the Ni3Sn type relieves packing tensions in the AuCu3 type for compounds with larger RE atoms (illustrated below with YAl3). https://t.co/Troza2MLMU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can see some problems in the hypothetical AuCu3-type YAl3 packing scheme. The Y atoms have a white positive pressure all around it, meaning it's feeling rather constricted. Expansion of its coordination environment, however, is hindered by negative CPs along Al-Al contacts.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We can see how replacing the Y atom with something smaller, say a Sc atom, can be more favorable!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: (Side note: Calculations are great! You can get information about hypothetical systems that you can't realize IRL with experiments! But of course, you need to be careful about drawing conclusions because it's a hypothetical system.)

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
When we compare this to the CP scheme of the Ni3Sn-type YAl3, we note some key differences:
(1) Al-Al negative pressures are reduced within the newly formed columns
(2) Positive pressures on Y are reduced in the ab plane, forming an hourglass shape. https://t.co/6lR37QcgUz

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: DFT-CP shows us exactly which packing tensions are relieved by the Ni3Sn structure type, and why it's a better arrangement for REAl3 compounds with larger RE atoms!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: If you want to read more about this, plus some interesting electronic considerations, check out my paper in Inorganic Chemistry! https://t.co/CdSP9sMnTU

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I also designed a very cool cover for that issue related to the work, which I think you should look at. 👀https://t.co/GHuBlrSYPX https://t.co/zVdIyGNEw0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Thanks for tuning into this thread over the DFT-Chemical Pressure method! Stay tuned later today for MORE applications of DFT-CP, including phonons! 😲

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
For reading on the Chemical Pressure concept and some advances in the methodology, check out these papers or our publications list: https://t.co/rfmpWr6HqR

1st CP paper: https://t.co/Hlfo0s2aEr
1st DFT-CP paper: https://t.co/sCgkhUKyV0
Latest updates: https://t.co/vw4FnnmcKt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Earlier today, I talked about the DFT-CP method. Now, let’s talk about a special CP feature, which we call the CP quadrupole! This unique feature is linked to cool phenomena, including phonons, incommensurate modulations, and guest atoms. Let’s dive right in! https://t.co/yRTt3LNQyt

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: CP quadrupoles (QPs) are features where the distribution of positive and negative pressures on an atom are perpendicular to each other. As a result, these QPs look very much like d-orbitals! https://t.co/noUZemz8Sw

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: QPs are linked to anisotropic motion of atoms. If an atom moves along the negative CPs, that motion or vibration will be relatively unhindered, resulting in soft atomic motions or low energy vibrations. https://t.co/ogt2ZUMV81

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
On the other hand, movement along positive CPs, where the contact is already too short, is very unfavorable, and vibrations in those directions will be higher in energy.

These energies and atomic motions can be then linked to phonons... But what are phonons?

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Phonons are vibrations for crystal structures. Instead of just one pairwise vibration, now we have concerted motions!
(img src: https://t.co/cRFiczIjWw) https://t.co/YVObNRris4

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So if QPs show us the directions of low and high energy vibrations, we should be able to see that in phonon band structures, which we do! The lowest frequency optical mode has displacements along those negative CPs, and the highest frequency modes has them along the positive CPs! https://t.co/97s7BxrlWk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is exciting, because we can take this idea even further. One of my projects is the investigation of the polymorphs of IrIn3. The phase transition temperature is approx. 350C, which is pretty low for an intermetallic! Why is that? https://t.co/y3gITfcYBW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: When we compare the CP schemes of both polymorphs, we see CP quadrupoles are present in the CoGa3 type but not the IrIn3 type. These QPs are enabled due to the large void spaces in the CoGa3 type structure, which the IrIn3 type doesn't have. https://t.co/zEQcOxzt65

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: And as expected, the atomic motions are correlated to low and high frequency phonon modes. In fact, the separation in frequency of these states is so large we see a phonon band gap! https://t.co/Qa2AoHhSJY

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
If we compare the phonon DOS of the CoGa3 type to the IrIn3 type, we see that the IrIn3 type doesn't have comparable low energy modes.

This tracks, because any motions along negative CPs will be hindered by positive CPs. The IrIn3 type simply doesn't have as much QP character. https://t.co/L7mHmxA7DW

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
And this is a critical point: low energy vibrations are easier to access and thus contribute more to vibrational entropy than high energy vibrations, illustrated by the figure below.

The CoGa3 type then must have greater vibrational entropy than the IrIn3 type... https://t.co/X9M65iOyNQ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We can then use our gen chem knowledge to do a simple calculation to get the phase transition temperature, using
ΔG = ΔE -TΔSvib

The phase transition should occur when the free energies are the same.

Behold! Our calculated phase transition temperature is 410! Pretty close! 😲 https://t.co/FqHzIIMIP0

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To demonstrate how important those low energy phonons (motions into the void spaces of the CoGa3 type), we artificially shift the frequencies in the CoGa3 type up +0.53 THz, and our "new" phase transition temp is now 912C, much, MUCH larger than before! https://t.co/Ki6wBa1Cqy

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
From this, I've learned two things!
(1) CP quadrupoles are great for anticipating these high and low energy vibrational effects, which is awesome since they're cheaper than phonon calcs.
(2) Those void spaces in the CoGa3 type enable entropic stabilization.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's partly why the CoGa3 type is the higher temperature phase, and also why the phase transition temperature is so low for an intermetallic!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There's a lot more that CP quadrupoles can tell us. I won't spoil more for now, but I highly recommend reading this paper by Dr. Kendall Kamp, who did a lot of work in this area! https://t.co/nRX9vzP9ym

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm also leaving a lot of cool details out in the IrIn3 polymorphism paper, so go read that too! I'm quite proud of this work. https://t.co/i7W0XEeLlF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: That's all I got for now! See you tomorrow, where we'll be exploring ELECTRONICS and COMPUTATIONS!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: @goldclusters @InorgChem Love to see mugs from a fellow Inorganic Chemistry author!!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Good morning! Today I will be talking about the electronic structure analysis I do. A big part of it is running calculations and writing code! So I thought I'd give you all a sneak peak at what it's like to be a computational chemist.

What's on YOUR desk? https://t.co/1rs4dJffUk

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: An essential part of being a grad student is running down to the seminar hall when they announce free food up for grabs. 🏃‍♂️💨 https://t.co/Cfyj4IsROv

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Part of my work this week is writing a manuscript! Though writing is not my favorite aspect of research, it's an important process that helps me think deeply about my scientific findings and how it fits into what we currently know.
Here's my flowchart with how I approach writing! https://t.co/KhGDPrdxo2

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I start writing highly detailed work first (such as the experimental section), then slowly work towards more generalized or abstract sections. I like to leave the title for last! This allows me to brain dump, organize my thoughts, then form a larger story for my work.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: So what does a computational chemist do to understand solid state structures? How does one even approach computations? Let's have a tour!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Say you want to know about the electronic structure of a solid state system. You know you can do ab-initio computations somehow!  Where do you start? 🤔

You start with the crystal structure!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We typically use Crystallographic Information Files (CIFs) as a starting point for building crystal structures. I like to look in the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database (ICSD) for CIFs of my system, or if they're not available, CIFs of the same structure type as my system. https://t.co/hKcB8XPCJA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I typically open these CIFs in a visualization program like VESTA or Diamond to understand what's going on. For the compounds I study, drawing homoatomic bonds is very helpful! https://t.co/4KmdatVMLf

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Next, I put the crystallographic information into the input files for computational chemistry packages. Our group uses VASP and ABINIT, two common DFT packages. Since these calculations can be intense, we use our department's computing cluster to run this software.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: We have to run software from the command line. It's a bit of a hurdle when you initially learn it, but it is very powerful! 💪💻 (Plus it makes you feel like a hacker in the movies...) https://t.co/2UuSQZbphA

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Not only do we need to put in crystallographic information, we have to tell the program what kind of settings we want to use! My input files start to look like some kind of hidden code. 😵 That's why I like to put some comments in my template files. https://t.co/BVOrCUhQJD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Let's fast-forward!
The first calculations we do are for setting certain parameters, like the energy cutoff and k-point mesh. Though we don't get info from these calculations, we need to do this to find the right balance between precision and computational cost! https://t.co/AynZKG7ppD

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This is important, because we can get *super* precise, but if your basic calculation takes months to run, it's not very practical.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Once those are set, we need to optimize our crystal's geometry! For our purposes, need to have our system at the energetic minimum to extract meaningful, accurate data.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
We do this geometry optimization in two steps:
(1) atoms are allowed to shift
(2) atoms and unit cell shape are allowed to shift

This two-step procedure helps the software find the equilibrium geometry efficiently. https://t.co/3GRK6MLf1x

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Once we have our equilibrium geometry, we run static calculations, where the atoms are now locked in place and we can get the data we want!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For example, we can get info about the electronic density of states, which can tell us things such as whether our crystal is a conductor/insulator or what kind of orbital characteristics our bands have. https://t.co/AM4iFqqyEL

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: For my research, the region around the Fermi energy (EF) is of interest! Typically, compounds that follow the 18-n+m rule have a dip in their density of states at the EF in the form of a pseudo- or band gap. Sometimes, they don't, like in the IrIn3 type in the above image.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Why do some 18-n+m compounds not show that band or pseudogap at the Fermi energy? To investigate this, I use one of our group's tools called DFT-raMO! This is a tool that uses the occupied crystal orbitals (which we get from DFT calculations) to make molecular analogies.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: DFT calculations on crystal structures use planewave basis sets to describe the information about the electrons of a system. Think sin and cosine functions! https://t.co/iiiGz55kxV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Instead of analyzing waves that are spread out, we want to understand the electronics in a localized context. This allows us to understand the bonding in our system by making analogies to molecular orbitals. https://t.co/qV3IBi4kmF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: To do this analysis, we wrote software in MATLAB* that does some BIG matrix math to transform wavefunction information into approximate molecular orbitals! Each of these new functions contains 2 electrons, so we have a way of doing electron-counting for our system.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: * It's in MATLAB, for now, but I'm currently rewriting it in the Julia programming language.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: The plot here shows the output of some DFT-raMO analysis, with one dot representing one reconstructed molecular-like orbital. You can see that we're able to generate atomic- and molecular orbital-like isosurfaces! https://t.co/uyz1QsBRiF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But what's that on the y-axis? That's Psphere, which is a tool that helps us evaluate the localization of our reconstructed function. It's calculated as the ratio of electron density in a defined sphere over the electron density in the whole unit cell. https://t.co/WlVal4O82W

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: What's important to us is that Psphere is consistent, meaning our reconstructed molecular orbitals are well-localized. When it drops sharply, it's an indication of delocalization. Or in simple terms, electrons can't be fully occupying those orbitals!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This tool helped me with a lot of projects! Remember the REAl3 story? With DFT-raMO, I was able to show which orbitals were associated with electrons n=7 and m=1 in the 18-n+m rule! https://t.co/TbJI0elCDV

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: In the story of IrIn3 polymorphism, DFT-raMO helped showed that m electrons were localized in the void spaces of CoGa3! https://t.co/FUOX3470zS

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: There's still more we can plan to do with DFT-raMO, and part of my work is expanding its functionality by writing code! I've been working on the newest version of it for almost two years now, and I am pleased to say that it's more efficient and has quality-of-life improvements. https://t.co/XCxmx80BmZ

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: ... and this is where we get into one aspect of computational chemistry. Coding and software! https://t.co/YZtafUzay7

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Before I begin, a disclaimer: I haven't taken a single coding class since high school, so a lot is learned on-the-job or self taught! 😱

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
Not all computational chemists write code regularly, but sometimes they write scripts to automate their tasks or process data! These scripts are relatively simple.

When you need a collection of scripts to perform complex tasks, you might consider writing a software package.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I find myself coding in short bursts rather than on a daily basis! This is because I have other tasks to do, like analyzing data or writing manuscripts!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: But if you catch me on a coding day, my screen might look something like this! https://t.co/HEtXxnEOgl

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I also use Github for version-control, which is something I learned a couple years ago. It has changed my life immensely, and if you are a coder but haven't used any form of version-control, what are you doing!!!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The coding process is usually:

idea -> sketch it out -> attempt to code -> test -> debug -> debug -> debug -> debug -> debug ... -> commit change

It's almost similar to writing a manuscript in that aspect. 😅

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: It's a challenging (and sometimes painful) process, but I also find it deeply rewarding, and I learn new things all the time! The biggest challenge for me is trying to keep the BIG PICTURE in mind while still minding all the small details.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'm still working on my DFT-raMO.jl package, but I'm excited to get it published and shared with the scientific community so anyone can use it! 🤞 Coming soon 2024...

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I'd love to answer any questions you may have about computational solid state chemistry, writing scientific code/scripts, or DFT-raMO if you have any!

tweets.label: Takeover

In the meantime, I will close with relevant further reading!

Good morning, scientists! ☕ It's a cloudy day in Madison, and you can just see the Capitol from the chemistry building. Unfortunately, a crane is blocking the way.

For my last day, I want to talk about my journey as a scientist, as well as fun stuff outside of research! https://t.co/CDmr8FMfOj

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: Like many other people, I didn't have a linear path to research! I meandered and explored other careers (journalism, anyone?) before deciding that I was set on entering graduate school for chemistry.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: One key experience that led me to research was the opportunity to do summer research at the University of Texas at Austin with Prof. Lauren Webb and Dr. Annette Raigoza. This wouldn't have been possible without the funding of the Welch Foundation.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I had ZERO idea what research was like, and the experience was nothing like high school labs! I learned things like how to safely use a hydrogen torch, or how to use piranha solution to clean substrates. It was a whole new world to say the least.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I also learned about the less flashy side of science, which includes collecting data and writing reports. The poster I made still lives in my closet. I was even rewarded years later with seeing my name on a paper! https://t.co/8FGRatEbDF

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: This summer program was vital, because when I entered college, it prompted me to consider undergraduate research!

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I joined Prof. Jakoah Brgoch's lab, and here, I had my introduction to solid state chemistry in the lab! I⚡ arc melted metals, 💎 grew crystals from flux synthesis, and performed powder X-ray diffraction! https://t.co/woTUBNIThh

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: However, some of my samples kept exploding in the furnaces! 💥😱 While we figured out what was going on, I started doing more computational work. I still have pictures of the apology brownies I baked at that time... https://t.co/ji7l18qEYi

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text: I soon found out that I liked doing more computational work, and that lead me to pursuing further studies in computational solid state chemistry! And that's how I got to where I am.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
I do miss doing experimental work, but I'm happy to watch my coworkers do grow crystals with new and exciting structures!

Here, my colleague Jonathan Van Buskirk is showing what happens to the graphite powder insulating his sample immediately after microwave synthesis. https://t.co/TjQWpf0WOu

The last 10 years of our research (https://t.co/GebQNF01Vc) at TIFR Hyderabad, India mainly focused on the development and studies of materials for applications, in energy, including renewable energy harvesting, electrocatalysis, & energy storage, as well as, in electronics.

tweets.label: Takeover

Our materials engineering approaches reside in the modulation of different mesoscopic interfaces & probing their interfacial properties. For this we study light-matter interactions, electrode-electrolyte phenomena, interfacial electron/ion transport & quasiparticle dynamics.

We also focus on the controllable development and optimization of atomically thin layers and their heterostructures using different physical and chemical routes.

Light as a probing tool for materials’ topological properties is another active area of our research. We also have close associations with different industries and institutions around the globe in various aspects of our research.

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
The detectors are based on superconductivity. 
In a superconducter electrons form Cooper pairs below a critical Temperature. 
The Cooper pairs are able to flow through the material without giving off energy. 
Therefore the resistance is zero.

https://t.co/mAqVVQGKMm

tweets.label: Takeover
tweets.text:
There is a critical current above which the detector loses its superconducting state. 
If the detector is operated slightly below this current, a photon hitting the detector will break Cooper pairs and create a resistance region,
resulting in a measurable voltage spike.

tweets.text: If you are following QuanTour from its start, you have already met the quantum dot: a nanostructure made of tens of thousands of atoms. We are interested in how they emit entangled photons. https://t.co/6Q9KqFssxq

tweets.text: In our game, instead of a number the information is encoded in the polarization of light https://t.co/VXthaqMuW5

tweets.label: Takeover

tweets.label: Takeover
